Oracle and SelVS remain principal comparators, substantially changing the validation-free comparison set.

E3.justification: New protocols include m-sharpness evaluation using 2,048 training examples, batches of 128, 20 ascent steps, perturbation radius 0.05, and a 15% training-accuracy filter. The FashionMNIST experiment uses full-batch gradient descent and an initialization-scale sweep. Grid robustness changes from regular interval slicing to randomly removing 20–80% of configurations. Newly supplied settings for retained benchmarks are documentation additions, not evidence that those experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V1's Quickshift-parameter ablation disappears, while v2 adds separability-threshold sensitivity and replaces regular grid-density tests with random-sparsity analysis. It also adds scaling-law goodness-of-fit analyses, configuration-wise accuracy distributions, and transfer-learning loss/norm diagnostics. Early-stopping and optimizer analyses are retained with revisions; transfer learning is partly relocated rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: V2 explicitly repeats random grid removal across 50 seeds and displays the resulting MAE distributions in Figure 6, adding uncertainty reporting to the grid-robustness analysis. This is a localized addition; neither PDF supplies comparable repeated-training uncertainty estimates for the principal benchmark tables.

E6.justification: Under the retained reported small-data settings, Twin's EN-B0 average changes from 71.3% to 69.5%, RN50 from 75.5% to 76.2%, and RNX101 from 75.4% to 75.6%. Medical accuracy changes from 82.9% to 83.1%. V2 adds sharpness-comparison, FashionMNIST, threshold, sparsity, and scaling-fit results. The natural-image table omits two RN20 rows, preventing direct comparison of its aggregate means. V2 also changes RNX101's Oracle EuroSAT score from 88.6% to 90.0% while retaining an inconsistent 75.9% average.

M1.justification: V1 selects the minimum-norm model within a training-loss region identified using outlier filtering, normalization, and Quickshift segmentation. V2 replaces this central procedure with an accuracy-based rule: select the minimum-norm model among configurations exceeding 99% training accuracy, or select minimum training loss if none qualifies. Section 3.3 and Algorithm 1 therefore describe an actual algorithm change.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method narrative, experimental interpretations, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. V2 introduces a separate problem-definition section, moves related work after experiments, organizes evaluations by comparison type, and relocates most transfer-learning discussion to Appendix E. The title and terminology also change substantially.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the overview diagram, replaces the segmentation-pipeline presentation with Algorithm 1, and introduces numerous scaling, sensitivity, and distribution plots. Benchmark tables gain model-class, win-count, or difference fields and lose SelTS entries. The transfer-learning figure is relocated and updated. Wider pages and text wrapping around figures and tables substantially alter the layout.

R1.justification: The primary grounding shifts from Liu et al.'s learning-phase framework to Lyu and Li's margin-maximization results and research on optimization regimes and loss-to-loss scaling. V2 substantially expands positioning against generalization-gap prediction, sharpness-based selection, and validation-free early stopping in Sections 2 and 5, replacing much of v1's image-classification-centered related-work discussion.

T1.justification: V2 adds a formal HPO formulation, homogeneous-network margin definitions and bounds, an assumed train-test power-law relationship, and derivative and critical-point analyses in Sections 2–3. These substantially replace v1's qualitative learning-phase rationale. The validation-error variance argument is largely retained in Appendix A; the new scaling relationship is explicitly an empirical modeling assumption, not a universal theorem.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves reproducibility and scrutiny of the selection rule through Algorithm 1, the implementation details missing from the supplied v1, the sharpness comparison, and threshold, sparsity, and scaling-fit analyses. Appendices C and F make assumptions and applicability limits more explicit. Removing SelTS loses a useful control, performance changes are mixed, and Table 2 introduces an inconsistent Oracle average. Nevertheless, the gains in specification, empirical examination, and qualification provide a substantial net improvement, without relying on higher reported accuracy or treating the empirical scaling assumption as a proven guarantee.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Twin research and provide readable methods, experiments, equations, and figures. However, v1 repeatedly references an appendix that is absent from the supplied PDF, which ends after its references. V2 includes Appendices A–G; the unavailable earlier supplemental details limit that part of the comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark results, a FashionMNIST experiment, sharpness comparisons, sensitivity analyses, and scaling-law fits in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original image-classification experiments on small, medical, and natural-image datasets, including transfer learning and ablations in Section 4.

results.title: Twin: Tuning Learning Rate and Weight Decay of Deep Homogeneous Classifiers without Validation

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same central contributions: combining Scaffnew with compression, introducing three variants and reducing communication in heterogeneous federated learning. The revised conclusion preserves that central claim; the additional experiments expand its supporting evidence.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands interpretation and limitations. Section 5 explicitly acknowledges missing guarantees even for convex objectives, distinguishes GPU timing from edge-device latency and energy costs, and explains restricted baseline coverage. Broader Impact adds the specific risk that biased compression underrepresents minority or rare client data.

D1.justification: V2 adds FedJAX preprocessing references, new-model specifications, partial-sorting and vectorized-compression implementation descriptions, and A100 40GB timing details. Existing software versions and the promised future code release remain unchanged. Figure 1 loses the explanation that Table 1 accuracies are maxima after hyperparameter tuning.

E1.justification: V2 adds FEMNIST handwriting classification with writer-based clients and Shakespeare next-character prediction with role-based clients. These extend the original FedMNIST/FedCIFAR10 coverage to naturally partitioned populations and a language task.

E2.justification: The existing comparisons retain FedAvg, sparseFedAvg and Scaffold; the added benchmarks reuse existing comparators. FedProx, FedDyn, FedNova and sign-based methods receive discussion but no newly reported evaluated comparisons.

E3.justification: The added benchmarks introduce study-specific settings: 3,000 communication rounds, 10 sampled clients per round, a FEMNIST CNN and a two-layer, 256-unit Shakespeare LSTM. V2 also adds rounds-to-target-accuracy evaluation and controlled local-update timing. Settings for the retained MNIST/CIFAR10 experiments are unchanged; the new study's description of p as a participation rate is ambiguous.

E4.justification: Appendix C.5 adds a supplementary analysis of compression overhead, comparing uncompressed, TopK and quantized local-update times across four models. Existing sparsity, heterogeneity, local-iteration, variant and double-compression ablations are retained. Appendix C.4 mainly interprets existing convergence plots.

E5.justification: Appendix C.5 newly states that timing measurements are averaged over 10 runs. V1 contains no corresponding run-count disclosure. This does not establish increased repetitions or new uncertainty reporting for the retained accuracy experiments.

E6.justification: Original numerical tables and plotted results are retained. New Table 3 reports FedComLoc-Com accuracy of 82.31%/51.56% on FEMNIST/Shakespeare versus SparseFedAvg's 78.14%/43.55%, while dense FedAvg remains higher at 86.63%/56.29%. Table 4 adds 84.7%/77.1% reductions in rounds to specified targets, and Table 5 adds measured compression overhead below 2%.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the same updates, control variates and three compression placements. Section 3.2 expands their explanation without establishing a changed procedure. Combined sparsification and quantization already appeared in v1 Appendix B.3.

P1.justification: Editorial changes concentrate in the expanded variant explanations and rewritten closing material, now separated into Discussion, Conclusion and Broader Impact. V2 also adds a contents list and related-work appendix. Most existing introduction, related-work and experimental prose remains substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: The paper changes from a two-column main text to a single-column journal layout, with redesigned front matter and widespread resizing and relocation of displays. Tables 3–5 are added while original plots are retained. Figure 1 gains misleading '100% Top-K' and '30% Top-K' subplot labels although both columns show multiple ratios.

R1.justification: New Appendix A discusses SignSGD, momentum-based sign methods and variance-reduced sign methods, citing Bernstein, Sun and Jiang. FEMNIST and FedJAX references are also added, and Section 5.5 positions additional FL frameworks as complementary. The main positioning relative to Scaffnew remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The optimization objective, compressor definitions and mathematical updates are unchanged. Despite their headings, Section 5.1 and Appendix C.4 introduce neither convergence theorems nor proofs: they discuss missing guarantees and empirical convergence.

improvement.justification: The naturally partitioned handwriting and language benchmarks in Tables 3–4 substantially address v1's limited practical validation, while Table 5 adds measured computational overhead. Explicit theoretical, hardware and fairness limitations improve transparency. Ambiguous participation wording and misleading Figure 1 labels weaken reporting, but these localized problems do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical coverage and qualification.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FedComLoc work. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite substantial reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and adds original FEMNIST and Shakespeare results in Section 4.8 and compression timing measurements in Appendix C.5.

before.justification: V1 reports original FedMNIST and FedCIFAR10 experiments, including accuracy, convergence, communication comparisons and compression ablations in Section 4 and Appendix B.

results.title: FedComLoc: Communication-Efficient Distributed Training of Sparse and Quantized Models

C1.justification: v1 presents GUMP as achieving an optimal oversquashing Jacobian measure while preserving structural bias. v2 refocuses the contribution on stability of the aggregate graph-propagation factor under explicit assumptions and preservation of admissible edge-to-edge transitions. Its abstract also uses competitive-or-superior performance claims against stronger comparisons. These substantially narrow and redefine the central claims.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly states that row-energy conservation guarantees neither individual source-target influence nor a depth-invariant full Jacobian. It qualifies the Jacobian plots as directionally consistent with the theory rather than direct validation of its quantity. Limitations now analyze degree-sensitive expansion costs and the exact-theory/finite-iteration gap, supported by numerical diagnostics and runtime evidence, substantially extending v1's brief computational caveats.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-availability URL and specifies the previously abstract Scatter operation as an incoming-edge mean, with zero output for isolated nodes. It supplies synthetic-task hyperparameters, numerical-diagnostic initialization and tolerance, CPU information, and training-time/batching details. Shared benchmark hyperparameter rows largely persist. The iteration budget used for the main accuracy results remains unspecified.

E1.justification: v2 adds CrossedRing, Ring, and CliquePath synthetic tasks, ogbg-molhiv molecular classification, and Cora/Citeseer node classification. It removes IMDB-Binary and PCQM-contact throughout the paper and appendices, eliminating the previously evaluated link-prediction task. Five TU datasets and the two peptide tasks remain.

E2.justification: The retained TU comparison gains ELDANADD, ADGN, GRAND, GPS, Ortho-GConv, GRIT, and Kiani et al. The LRGB comparison adds numerous methods, including Exphormer, Graph ViT, G-MLPMixer, Drew-GCN, and k-GCN-SSM. Appendix Figure 6 also adds ADGN and Drew to the Jacobian comparison. These are reported comparisons, not merely new citations.

E3.justification: New protocols include synthetic distances 4–28 with depth tied to distance, official scaffold-split ROC-AUC evaluation on ogbg-molhiv, block diagnostics at tolerance 10^-7 with five versus ten projection iterations, and runtime comparisons with matched propagated-node budgets. The main Jacobian sweep extends to 200 layers. LRGB now references the Tönshoff evaluation protocol and flags Kiani et al.'s different setup; common TU split proportions and listed hyperparameters are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix D.1 adds substantial tests of block rank, conditioning, and finite-step projection accuracy using random continuous representations. v2 also adds synthetic distance stress tests, extends depth/Jacobian analyses, compares ADGN and Drew's Jacobian behavior, and measures computational overhead under two batching controls. The original component ablations and NCI1 accuracy-versus-depth analysis largely remain.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly reports averaging three random seeds for the new synthetic experiments. Both versions retain 100 random TU train/validation splits and 95% confidence intervals. The PDFs do not establish increased repetitions or a changed uncertainty-estimation procedure for the retained benchmark experiments.

E6.justification: v2 adds synthetic, molecular, node-classification, projection, and runtime results. Reported peptide AP changes from 0.6843 to 0.7088 and MAE from 0.2564 to 0.2438; these are revised reports with method/protocol differences, not established same-setting gains. TU results are internally unreconciled: v2 Table 1 gives GIN-GUMP ENZYMES accuracy 53.11±5.80, while v1 Table 2 and v2 Appendix Table 7 give 48.43±1.24.

M1.justification: Algorithm 2 changes from exact blockwise polar projection in v1 to normalized, finite-step Newton–Schulz projection in v2. This changes the computed propagation operator to an approximation with an iteration-dependent accuracy tradeoff. The underlying line-graph transformation, attention weights, and scatter/concatenation architecture remain recognizable.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten around training stability. Main-text related work moves to Appendix A, Section 2 becomes unitarity/stability preliminaries, and the conclusion becomes an expanded discussion of limitations. Method explanations and theoretical exposition are substantially reorganized; authorship and publication headers also change.

P2.justification: v2 switches the main paper from two-column to single-column layout, redesigns the overview, and adds an introductory results figure. The retained TU comparison moves into Appendix Table 7 while a broader main comparison is introduced. Synthetic plots and diagnostic, molecular, node-classification, and runtime tables are added; model-analysis axes, legends, and table highlighting are revised.

R1.justification: Related work expands from oversquashing and unitary networks to oversmoothing, line-graph and edge-centric methods, newer recurrent architectures, and unitary optimization. Appendix A adds substantial positioning against CensNet, LGLP, LGCL, and related approaches. v2 also explicitly distinguishes its construction from Kiani et al.'s 2024 unitary graph convolutions and discusses their different computational bottlenecks.

T1.justification: v1's expected-Jacobian O(1) versus O(c^L) theorems are replaced by a newly defined source-averaged row-energy quantity, exact unitary conservation at 1/N, and decay bounds for normalized propagation's non-stationary component. v2 explicitly separates gate and weight assumptions, adds admissible-transition support preservation, repairs the existence argument for disconnected graphs, and substantially revises the corresponding proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves the central reasoning by replacing v1's overly broad Jacobian conclusions with explicit row-energy conservation and a stationary/non-stationary spectral analysis. Stronger comparisons, numerical diagnostics, reproducibility details, and measured computational limitations make the evidence more informative. Unexplained TU table discrepancies, removal of two benchmarks, and the remaining exact-theory/approximate-implementation gap are material drawbacks, but the corrected theoretical scope and expanded validation provide a clear substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Graph Unitary Message Passing, with clearly corresponding algorithms, experiments, and mathematical foundations. The complete main texts and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revision.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark and synthetic-task results, plus appendix experiments on molecular and node classification, projection diagnostics, and runtime.

before.justification: v1 reports original GUMP results on TU and LRGB datasets, alongside Jacobian, network-depth, and component-ablation experiments.

results.title: Graph Unitary Message Passing

C1.justification: The central probabilistic-fragmentation contribution and state-of-the-art prediction/retrieval claims remain. The contribution list replaces scalability with prediction error as an explicitly advertised property, and the discussion extends its stated practical-utility claim to peak annotation.

C2.justification: v1 emphasizes using annotation disagreement to flag unreliable explanations; v2 emphasizes robust ensemble-mode agreement despite entropy differences, while retaining the distinction between consistency and chemical correctness. v2 also adds explanations for weak edge-ablation effects and qualifications concerning fragment-merging self-edges and implementation-dependent runtime comparisons.

D1.justification: v2 adds detailed preprocessing filters, fragment-merging implementation information, baseline training details, a code-access link, a 100-trial hyperparameter-search description, and timing hardware and batching settings. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation without establishing that every newly described setting changed. Conversely, most exact software-version pins from v1 Appendix L are removed.

E1.justification: NIST20 spectrum prediction and PubChem-based retrieval remain within the same Orbitrap [M+H]+ domain. v2 adds formula-annotation evaluation against NIST20 expert labels (Section 5.3), also using those labels to construct the GrAFF-MS formula library. This is a bounded expansion of tasks and supervision rather than a new dataset or domain.

E2.justification: v2 adds GrAFF-MS and Precursor-Only as evaluated spectrum-prediction comparators; GrAFF-MS was previously only cited. It also reports an ICEBERG batching-bug correction and removes FraGNNet-D3 from retrieval comparisons. ICEBERG-ADV persists as ICEBERG (+OptFrag) in Table 8, so its renaming and relocation are not a new baseline.

E3.justification: Hungarian matching changes from pair-dependent 10 ppm tolerance to true-mass-dependent tolerance with a 0.002 Da floor. Retrieval expands from Hungarian cosine ranking to multiple similarities, intensity transformations, and model-specific best-ranking selections. Ablations move from validation to test data, and annotation experiments change from two D3 ensemble configurations to four D4 configurations.

E4.justification: The annotation analysis changes from within-ensemble consensus and majority voting to individual-versus-ensemble predictions and agreement across four entropy configurations. v2 adds retrieval-ranking sensitivity analyses, DAG precision statistics, and runtime benchmarking. Collision-energy and edge ablations remain, but the D4 (+Edges) result in v1 Table 6 is absent from v2 Table 7.

E5.justification: Five-seed means and standard deviations already accompany prediction and ablation results in v1. v2 extends this reporting to retrieval, where v1 provided point estimates, and adds individual-model standard-deviation bars to ensemble plots. This establishes expanded uncertainty reporting, not an increase in runs for the retained experiments.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces D4 InChIKey cosine scores of 0.717/0.691 with 0.736/0.709, while main-table retrieval Top-1 changes from 23.8% to 36.0%. Changed matching and retrieval protocols prevent treating these uniformly as same-setting gains. New formula-annotation results report F1 scores of 0.89 for D4, 0.74 for GrAFF-MS, and 0.79 for ICEBERG; ensemble and runtime findings are also added.

M1.justification: The core fragmentation procedure, two-stage neural model, and losses remain. v2 additionally evaluates ensemble predictors that average latent distributions and spectra (Appendix A.16), whereas v1 uses ensembles to compare individual-model annotations and majority agreement.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the background and annotation narrative, clarifies formula versus fragment annotations, and replaces resolution terminology with mass accuracy throughout. It reorganizes baseline discussions and appendices, separates formula evaluation from fragment consistency, and adds author-contribution and acknowledgement sections.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, and major tables are redesigned to place dataset splits side by side. Out-of-support results move to a separate appendix table. Ensemble bar charts and agreement heatmaps replace the earlier annotation tables, additional evaluation tables appear, and existing illustrative figures are visually revised.

R1.justification: v2 updates the literature with works including MassSpecGym, DiffMS, FIORA, and MadGen, and adds annotation and entropy-metric references. It sharpens the distinction between FraGNNet's latent distributions and ICEBERG's binned outputs. The existing binned/structured taxonomy and much of the CFM/ICEBERG positioning already present in v1 Appendix C remain.

T1.justification: v2 tightens Definition 4.1 to single-edge-removal transitions and corrects the recall formula's normalization. It adds a short entropy-concavity proof for ensembling, a derivation relating Jensen-Shannon and spectral-entropy similarity, and revised annotation-agreement definitions. The central probabilistic formulation and loss mathematics remain.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the paper's interpretability and practical-utility claims through expert-label formula evaluation, broader baseline comparisons, retrieval uncertainty reporting, and runtime measurements. Expanded preprocessing and implementation documentation also makes the work more assessable and reproducible. Although exact dependency versions are lost and changed protocols prevent simple cross-version performance claims, these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FraGNNet and contain readable main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The substantial revision can be reliably compared after matching relocated and renamed material.

after.justification: v2 reports original prediction and retrieval experiments, formula-annotation evaluation, revised ensemble analyses, and inference-speed measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original NIST20 spectrum-prediction, compound-retrieval, ablation, and annotation-consistency results in Section 5 and the appendices.

results.title: FraGNNet: A Deep Probabilistic Model for Tandem Mass Spectrum Prediction

C1.justification: The entropy-guided depth-reduction claim remains, but v2 broadens the claimed applicability to NLP and pruning criteria beyond magnitude. Its conclusion additionally presents unstructured pruning as implicit depth regularization producing flatter loss landscapes. The earlier claim of being the first unstructured method to reduce network depth is dropped.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of baseline failures, flatness and generalization, and latency savings despite possible sparsity fill-in. It explicitly qualifies smooth-rectifier linearization and identifies average neuron entropy as a proxy rather than joint entropy. Conversely, v1's explicit discussion of failure on underfitting ImageNet models disappears, although the corresponding results remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds NLP optimizer settings, sequence length, prunable-layer details, GPU identification, hardware-specific measurements, and training-time columns in the detailed result tables. Its abstract supplies a code-repository URL where v1 promised future release, although Appendix C retains the older release wording.

E1.justification: v2 extends the vision-only evaluation to SST-2 sentiment classification, QNLI and RTE language-inference tasks, and the MMLU high-school US-history subset. The original vision datasets remain; ImageNet was already evaluated in v1's supplement.

E2.justification: v2 removes the evaluated Layer Folding comparisons from v1 Tables 2 and 21. It retains IMP and adds smallest-weight and smallest-gradient layer removal, HRank on CIFAR-10, group lasso, and EGP comparisons. Table 5 also adds a depth-matched model trained from initialization.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce ResNet-50/152 and MobileNetV2-0.75 configurations, three-epoch AdamW NLP training, FP16 Llama evaluation without fine-tuning, a depth-matched initialization control, and sharpness and hardware-efficiency measurements. The shared vision training schedules and augmentation policies remain unchanged between v1 Table 5 and v2 Appendix C.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component and activation studies, v2 adds pruning-rate sensitivity, a Swin-T/Tiny-ImageNet component ablation, the initialization control, loss-landscape sharpness analysis, SSL and Wanda variants, and comparative layer-removal diagnostics. Appendix D.5 adds weight and activation histograms to examine the Gaussian assumptions.

E5.justification: Neither version reports random seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or performance uncertainty bars. v2's new histograms describe weight and activation distributions rather than uncertainty in experimental outcomes.

E6.justification: The detailed original vision trajectories and ImageNet scores are retained, but v2 adds NLP/LLM, model-scaling, sharpness, pruning-variant, and efficiency results and removes Layer Folding results. For example, Table 10 newly reports 3.32 ms dense versus 2.96 ms pruned inference time for ResNet-18/CIFAR-10. Some IMP summary scores differ from retained appendix values without clarified iteration selection, preventing direct performance-change conclusions.

M1.justification: The core entropy-guided iterative pruning framework remains. However, Equation (13) changes from averaging neuron-level entropy–magnitude products to multiplying layer-average entropy by layer-average magnitude, which is generally non-equivalent. v2 also introduces variants incorporating SSL regularization and replacing magnitude pruning with Wanda. These are revisions and extensions within the existing framework.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related-work discussion, experimental narrative, and conclusion are substantially rewritten around layer collapse. The method subsections are consolidated, the experiments are reorganized, and the supplement is restructured into thematic Appendices A–D.

P2.justification: Table 2 is reorganized with model groups and dataset columns, and detailed tables gain training-time columns. The pseudocode is split into two algorithms, Figure 1 is revised, and Figure 3 is resized and relabeled. New comparison curves, interval diagrams, hardware tables, and distribution panels substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially through discussion of Wanda, HRank, SSL, EASIER, and transformer layer merging. The already cited Liao et al. (2023) work is now explicitly identified as EGP, evaluated, and positioned as the closest predecessor. This materially revises the novelty positioning rather than merely expanding references.

T1.justification: v2 adds smooth-rectifier approximation and propagated-error bounds in Appendix A and a formal ReLU6 interval analysis in Appendix B. It also corrects the state definition to use pre-activations and changes Equation (11)'s probability event from Z > 0 to Z > epsilon. These extend and revise the earlier mathematical treatment.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central generality and efficiency claims through NLP evaluations, a depth-matched control, sensitivity analyses, and measured deployment benefits that v1 did not provide. The approximation and entropy-proxy qualifications also improve interpretability. These gains outweigh the removed Layer Folding comparisons and explicit ImageNet failure discussion, although insufficiently reconciled summary and appendix scores remain a material reporting weakness.

A1.justification: Despite the changed title, both PDFs describe the same NEPENTHE research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original vision experiments and adds NLP evaluations, pruning variants, efficiency measurements, and supplementary analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-classification experiments, pruning trajectories, layer-removal results, and component and activation ablations in Section 4 and the supplement.

results.title: Layer Collapse Can be Induced by Unstructured Pruning

C1.justification: The abstract drops v1's claim of comparative computational efficiency. The central abstract and introduction claims remain: reward-model-free alignment, global regularization, and adjustable softmax convergence under the BT assumption. The technical extensions do not substantially rewrite this central framing.

C2.justification: V4 Section 9 explicitly identifies unexamined dependence on dataset size and preference-label noise, and learning from implicit preferences as future work. Computational overhead from online sampling and the token-wise KL bias–variance tradeoff were already discussed in v1 Section 5 and Appendix B.

D1.justification: V4 newly documents accelerator configurations, including four H100 GPUs for AlpacaFarm and A100 GPUs for TinyStories, gradient accumulation, method-specific hyperparameter ranges, ranking-weight decay settings, and four-story labeling and filtering instructions (Appendices D–E). The existing practice of generating 32 regularization samples every eight steps is retained for TinyStories.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates pairwise preference alignment on TinyStories-derived stories. V4 adds AlpacaFarm question answering evaluated through AlpacaEval 2, and replaces the pairwise story experiment with four-story ranking and best-of-n alignment tasks (Sections 7.1–7.2).

E2.justification: Beyond v1's DPO comparison, v4 evaluates IPO, KTO, CPO, R-DPO, and SimPO alongside DPO on AlpacaFarm (Table 1). The story comparisons add S-DPO and Best-response-SFT; Table 2 evaluates a ranking adaptation of DPO, while Table 3 does not include DPO.

E3.justification: The story experiments change from GPT3.5-Turbo labeling and evaluation to GPT4o-2024-08-06, approximately 100,000 retained pairs to 5,000 four-story groups, and batches of 128 pairs to 32 groups. The win-rate opponent changes from the pretrained model to Best-response-SFT. The new question-answering protocol uses Llama2-7B, four training epochs, GPT4-Turbo evaluation, and both conventional and length-controlled win rates.

E4.justification: V1 Figure 1 compares weighting choices and DPO regularization coefficients over training. V4 removes those trajectories and adds a controlled comparison of global KL against three dataset-restricted regularizers (Table 4). Weighting analyses extend to question answering, ranking, and best-of-n alignment, including a reported lack of benefit for ranking.

E5.justification: V1 averages story win rates over 1,000 pairs without quantifying their estimation uncertainty. V4 Appendix D.2 uses the same evaluation sample count and newly reports an estimation-error standard deviation below 0.015. This is not evidence of repeated training runs; neither version reports training-seed variability or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: V1's 72% SPO versus 68% DPO peak win rates and subsequent training trajectories are replaced by results under different settings. V4 Table 1 reports SPO at 61.63% conventional and 56.25% length-controlled win rate, versus DPO at 59.16% and 51.26%. Tables 2–3 add SPO ranking and best-of-n win rates of 68.5% and 70.5% against Best-response-SFT. These are new comparisons, not same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: V4 adds best-of-n and ranked-preference objectives beyond v1's pairwise method (Section 5, Eqs. 16–17). It also replaces the SoftImportance weighting formula in v1 Eq. 24 with a differently scaled, power-based formula in v4 Eq. 13. Intermittent online sampling and token-wise KL regularization already existed in v1.

P1.justification: V4 moves practical KL computation from the appendix into the main algorithm section, condenses the SPO–DPO comparison, reorganizes experiments into three subsections, and separates experimental settings and dataset generation into Appendices D–E. It also adds a Limitations section, renames method sections, and changes numbered citations to author-year citations.

P2.justification: V1's training-curve figure is removed. V4 adds four result and ablation tables, including side-by-side ranking and best-of-n tables, plus an algorithm display. The main-text story prompt and worked response are replaced by a different, full-page ranking-prompt display in Appendix E.

R1.justification: V4 substantially expands positioning through Nash/game-based alignment, token-level DPO, KTO, SimPO, and R-DPO discussions. Section 8 also explicitly positions CPO as concurrent work sharing SPO's basic contrastive loss, distinguishing SPO through global regularization, weighting, additional preference types, and theoretical guarantees.

T1.justification: V4 adds formal n-ary preference assumptions, Theorems 3–4 for best-of-n and ranked preferences, and their proofs in Appendices B–C, including a new supporting inequality lemma. The pairwise Theorems 1–2 and the central Appendix A proof argument are largely retained.

improvement.justification: V4 addresses v1's reliance on one small synthetic story task against DPO by adding 7B question answering, broader baselines, length-controlled evaluation, and direct regularizer ablations. These provide substantially more informative empirical support, alongside formalized preference extensions and expanded implementation details. Losing the training curves, limited uncertainty reporting, and the unresolved 'xx%' placeholder in Section 7.3 weaken reporting, but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SPO research. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, figures, and tables, are readable and support reliable matching of retained, revised, and added content.

after.justification: Section 7 and Tables 1–4 report original question-answering and story-alignment experiments, including regularizer ablations. Appendices D–E document their implementation and data generation.

before.justification: Section 6 and Figure 1 report original TinyStories alignment experiments comparing SPO and DPO, including measured win rates throughout training.

results.title:
Soft Preference Optimization: Aligning Language Models to Expert
  Distributions

C1.justification: The central claims of O(M+N) scaling, superposition-based generalisation and approximately 5% error remain. However, the introduction refocuses the physical contribution from Maxwell/Fourier motivation to explicitly enforcing conservative fields through potential gradients, while the abstract and conclusion more clearly distinguish field and potential outputs.

C2.justification: v2 replaces v1's deferred FMM comparison and single-shape limitation with substantive interpretations of near-source approximation errors, FMM's quadtree advantage, and FC+ILR failures for small sources and near-zero potentials. It also specifies restrictions imposed by training ranges and the need to retrain for different geometries. These materially sharpen applicability boundaries and explanations of performance.

D1.justification: v2 adds explicit Huber-loss definitions and weights, source-feature vectors and sampling distributions, exact Fourier frequencies, GELU activations and weight initialisation. It also documents prism-model resources, FMM precision and parallel hardware, and FNO architecture, preprocessing and optimisation. The code repository target is unchanged; displaying its URL explicitly does not constitute a new release.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained circular-source experiments and 1D illustration, v2 trains and evaluates variable-size prism sources and introduces overlapping-source and non-overlapping quadtree scenarios in Section 6. These substantially broaden the represented geometries and spatial configurations within magnetic-field and potential inference.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated comparisons against FMM, including corrected and uncorrected variants in Figure 5, and FNO at two input resolutions in Appendix E. MagTense also becomes an explicit runtime comparator. v1 discussed FMM but deferred comparison; its existing FC+INR and Linear comparisons remain.

E3.justification: New prism experiments introduce 200,000 training samples, a different training schedule and field-loss weighting, specified source-count sweeps, and normalised MAE alongside relative error. Runtime tests compare sequential and parallel execution with N=M. Appendix E adds grid preprocessing and FNO training/resolution protocols. These are added experimental designs, not demonstrated reruns of the retained disk results.

E4.justification: v2 adds error-versus-distance and source-size analyses, spatial failure cases for small sources, and FNO input-resolution sensitivity. Appendix C.3 reports exploratory dipole-correction training, oversampling and magnetisation-rescaling trials, including unsuccessful approaches. These substantially extend v1's retained direct/indirect prediction and architecture comparisons.

E5.justification: For Figure 3, the stated ensemble changes from ten random initialisations in v1 to five in v2; this does not establish that experiments were rerun. Table 2 retains its ± values but loses the explanation that they are 1σ estimates from ten runs. New Tables 3 and 5 explicitly report variability across ten test samples.

E6.justification: Table 2's original numerical results remain unchanged. Substantial new results include Table 3's 1,000-overlapping-source errors of 4.21% for FC+ILR and 5.32% for FMM, and Table 5's 50-source quadtree errors of 63.8% for FNO128, 5.70% for FC+ILR and 2.69% for FMM. Runtime and diagnostic findings are also added; these concern new settings rather than same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The additive hypernetwork, summed source embeddings, Fourier representation and FC+ILR final-layer construction are retained. Log-spaced Fourier modes and joint potential/field fitting already appear in v1's supplementary material. v2 explicitly documents losses and instantiates the same geometry-conditioned framework for prisms, without introducing a new proposed model component or inference procedure.

P1.justification: The background, method and related-work narratives are extensively rewritten and reorganised, including dedicated hypernetwork and direct/indirect formulation subsections. Existing analytical and superposition material moves into Appendix B, and the earlier hyperparameter and tuning material becomes Appendix C. These structural and explanatory revisions extend well beyond the insertion of new experiments.

P2.justification: The architecture diagram is redrawn and relocated, existing figures receive annotation and caption revisions, and the hyperparameter table gains settings for the prism model. New figures display runtimes, distance/size errors, spatial failures and FNO inputs/predictions, while new tables present external comparisons. The superposition diagram becomes Figure 7 through relocation rather than new scientific content.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning relative to neural operators, particularly FNO and DeepONet, explaining differences in source conditioning, discretisation and superposition. It adds extensive hypernetwork background and references supporting the FMM and prism experiments. The earlier Hamiltonian/Lagrangian-network comparison is removed, shifting the related-work emphasis toward operator learning and physical surrogates.

T1.justification: v2 Eq. 6 corrects v1 Eq. 5's formal approximation by evaluating the field at each query rather than summing over query locations. Section 6 adds mathematical reasoning about FMM precision, interior-source corrections and computational cost. The existing superposition argument and analytical dipole expression largely persist, with material relocated to Appendix B.

improvement.justification: v1 leaves practical scaling, external comparison and broader source geometries largely untested. v2 addresses these gaps through prism experiments, runtime measurements, FMM/FNO comparisons and detailed failure analysis, substantially strengthening the evidence and clarifying where the method loses accuracy. Added implementation details improve reproducibility. The comparisons remain specific to the documented baseline setups, and Table 2 loses useful uncertainty provenance, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and interpretability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same source-to-field hypernetwork framework and retain matching experiments and results. Their text, equations, figures, tables and supplementary material are readable and support a reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganisation.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds prism-source evaluations, runtime measurements, FMM and FNO comparisons, and failure analyses in Section 6 and Appendices C–E.

before.justification: v1 reports original magnetic-field and potential approximation experiments, including direct versus indirect prediction, single-to-multiple-source generalisation, training curves and numerical comparisons in Table 2.

results.title: Scalable physical source-to-field inference with hypernetworks

C1.justification: The original contribution of communication-efficient training with a shared initialization-time mask remains. V2 expands its main contributions to near-oracle mask recovery with sufficient client participation, larger-model scalability, and adaptation to unseen classes through a mask refresh. These additions in the introduction and conclusion extend the claimed capabilities beyond v1's static-setting contribution.

C2.justification: V2 develops structural alignment as a stronger explanation for shared-mask performance, adds minibatch-sufficiency and warmup/client-drift interpretations, and extensively argues for hardware-acceleration compatibility. Its new limitations section identifies continuous concept drift as a boundary requiring further adaptation. These materially extend v1's more tentative local-mask drift discussion and existing interpretation of permutation results.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-access link, the K=100 benchmark-client count, layer-specific Kaiming initialization details, explicit communication-accounting assumptions, and baseline adaptation information. Most optimizer, epoch, learning-rate, batch-size and partition details were already provided in v1 Appendix A.3. Conversely, v1's named COINSTAC deployment description and explicit deployment architecture list are no longer documented. These are targeted reproducibility changes.

E1.justification: The CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and TinyImageNet datasets and existing non-IID scenarios remain. V2 adds a bounded new scenario within CIFAR-10: training initially on classes 0–7, then admitting clients with previously unseen classes 8–9 (Appendix A.6). This extends coverage to novel-class arrival without adding another dataset or domain.

E2.justification: V2 Table 1 adds evaluated SparsyFed and Flash comparisons on CIFAR-10/100 Dirichlet partitions. FedPM is added to the CIFAR-100 comparison, including Figure 2(b), while its CIFAR-10 pathological result from v1 Table 1 is omitted. FedAvg and Random also gain entries in corresponding benchmark tables. These substantially expand and revise the actual comparator set.

E3.justification: V2 introduces ResNet-50 evaluation across 50–95% sparsity, an oracle-mask comparison using 1–400 minibatches, and a warmup control with 10 dense rounds evaluated at the same total 500 rounds. Its OOD protocol introduces held-out-class clients at round 225. These are substantial new evaluation designs; the original benchmark partition parameters and core training hyperparameters are retained.

E4.justification: V2 adds analyses testing minibatch sufficiency against a full-training-set oracle, sensitivity to initialization versus dense warmup, and adaptation after distribution shift. The earlier permutation, global/local random-mask, longer-training and heterogeneous-client analyses are largely retained or rearranged. However, v1 Appendix A.3's separate saliency-based local-mask experiment reporting 70.22% accuracy is removed.

E5.justification: V1's main accuracy tables contain point estimates. V2 adds explicit five-run reporting, ± quantities in Tables 1–2, random-seed information, and error bars or standard-deviation bands in mask analyses. TinyImageNet FOMO is identified as a single run that failed to converge. V1 already reported uncertainty for communication times. The new run-count disclosures do not establish that more runs were performed than in v1.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial results for ResNet-50, oracle-mask estimation, warmup and OOD adaptation; Table 3 reports 47.53% for SSFL versus 12.04% for DisPFL at 95% sparsity. Original headline SSFL benchmark accuracies remain unchanged. FedPM's reported CIFAR-10 Dirichlet accuracy changes from 57.30% to 46.44%, and SubFedAvg's CIFAR-10 communication figure changes from 278.8 to 346.6 MB. Deployment timing values are also revised, rather than merely replotted.

M1.justification: V2 adds one-shot OOD adaptation: clients recompute saliency using trained active weights and original initializations for inactive weights, then refresh the shared mask and resume training (Section 4.3, Algorithm 2). This substantially extends v1's fixed-mask procedure. The stated Algorithm 1 also changes initialization from averaging client initializations to server initialization, and model aggregation from equal averaging to data-size weighting.

P1.justification: The introduction, contribution list, method exposition and conclusion are extensively rewritten. The standalone preliminaries section disappears, much of the original related work moves to Appendix B, and experiments are reorganized into explicit benchmark and analysis subsections. The title and publication formatting also change. The narrative restructuring is substantial independently of added scientific content.

P2.justification: V2 redraws Figure 1, reorganizes the original dataset tables into partition-based tables, and replaces the communication-time table with a model-size plot. Existing convergence plots are merged, and client-performance plots move into a composite main-text figure. New oracle/OOD plots and ResNet-50, warmup and cost-analysis tables substantially change the visual presentation beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: V2 substantially updates positioning around dynamic, structured and initialization-pruning FL, discussing additional work such as SparsyFed, FedPaI and HeteroFL. Appendix B retains much of v1's historical survey while expanding sparse language-model coverage and acknowledging earlier related gradient-aggregation and neuroimaging work. This goes well beyond relocating references or updating bibliographic metadata.

T1.justification: The connection-saliency derivation remains mathematically equivalent despite substantial rewriting. V2 Appendices A.3–A.4 add computational-complexity and communication-cost derivations, including fixed-mask 4sP-byte transmission versus 8sP for COO and 4sP+P/8 for bitmasks. This is a limited analytical extension; the new oracle-mask convergence evidence is empirical, not a convergence proof.

improvement.justification: V1 provided little direct validation of minibatch sufficiency or the decision to avoid warmup, and omitted run counts for benchmark accuracies. V2 substantially addresses these gaps through oracle-mask and warmup experiments, uncertainty reporting, and broader baseline and larger-model comparisons. These strengthen support for the central design. The gains outweigh shortcomings, including removal of the local-saliency-mask experiment, absence of a no-refresh OOD control, and new numerical inconsistencies such as Table 3's 23.21-point gap being described as 24.39 points in the text.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SSFL despite the changed title. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable matching of retained, revised and added material.

after.justification: V2 retains original benchmark experiments and adds ResNet-50, oracle-mask estimation, warmup and distribution-shift results in Section 4 and Appendix A.

before.justification: V1 reports original federated classification experiments, mask analyses and geographically distributed communication-time measurements in Section 5 and Appendix A.

results.title: SSFL: Discovering Sparse Unified Subnetworks at Initialization for Efficient Federated Learning

C1.justification: v3 drops the explicit contribution of being first to explore the AL/OOD connection and elevates the existing latent-space refinement and self-balancing fusion to named contributions. Its headline OOD claim narrows from two first places and one second place to one first place and two top-three placements specifically for near-OOD. The conclusion expands its AL performance claim to eight benchmark settings.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly explains why the shared metric cannot independently solve open-set AL: informative unlabeled samples and OOD samples can be ambiguous. It adds discussion of top-k batch-diversity limitations, pretrained feature-space benefits, computational disadvantages, and why smaller reference subsets might remove outliers. These materially expand applicability boundaries and mechanism interpretations.

D1.justification: v3 adds project-page/code access information, SIMCLR initialization details, runtime hardware, full-cycle checkpoint sourcing, and UMAP construction details. These incrementally extend the existing experimental documentation. Most sigmoid parameters and search settings are retained and reformatted into tables; the linked resources' availability is not established by the PDFs.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN active learning and the same OpenOOD dataset pairings. The added pretrained-model and AL-checkpoint experiments change initialization and evaluation procedures within retained data and tasks. Open-set active learning is discussed but explicitly remains unevaluated.

E2.justification: v3 Tables 1 and 5 add SCALE, CombOOD, NNGuide, FeatureNorm, and RankFeat to the corresponding OpenOOD comparisons. The new pretrained CIFAR-10 comparison also evaluates PT4AL, TypiClust, and ProbCover alongside retained methods. These substantially broaden the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: Reported query sizes change from 5,000 to 2,000 for CIFAR-100 and from 1,000 to 500 for SVHN. Appendix B.1 changes CIFAR-10/SVHN training from learning rate 0.1 with multistep scheduling to 0.025 with cosine scheduling. New protocols include SIMCLR initialization, ResNet34, additional query budgets, AL-checkpoint OOD evaluation, runtime measurements, and aggregate benchmark rankings. These are reported setting changes, not proof that every retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds query-size sensitivity, medium-data and model-size analyses, a UMAP examination of unlabeled/OOD overlap, intermediate-cycle OOD evaluation, and runtime/subset-size tradeoffs. The earlier feature-enhancement plots and sigmoid/subset ablation remain in v3 Figure 11, Figure 12, and Table 3; their relocation is not additional evidence.

E5.justification: v3 introduces uncertainty bands in the full-cycle OOD plots and ± quantities in runtime tables, although their statistical meaning is not clearly specified. Appendix B.2 identifies three seeds for the new full-cycle experiment. Existing AL standard-error reporting and three-seed CIFAR OpenOOD averaging remain; no increase in repetitions for retained experiments is established.

E6.justification: Substantial new results accompany the expanded comparisons and analyses. Reported CIFAR-100 SISOMe near/far AUROC changes from 80.96/79.80 to 81.10/80.16, while NAC changes from 72.00/86.56 to 75.90/86.98. SISOMe's unchanged ImageNet near-OOD score of 78.59 falls from first to third with added comparators. AL curves are revised under changed settings, and the earlier OOD tables' classification-accuracy entries are removed.

M1.justification: The five components remain: multilayer coverage, KL-gradient feature enhancement, distance ratios, energy-score fusion, and sigmoid-steepness optimization. Class-wise subset selection is also retained. The revised explanations and evaluations of existing components do not establish an algorithmic change.

P1.justification: The introduction, motivation, related work, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Preliminaries move ahead of related work, experimental subsections are reorganized, and Appendix A becomes a larger collection of experiments with the original qualitative material retained as A.4. These changes exceed routine copyediting.

P2.justification: v3 changes the document layout, redraws the life-cycle diagram, adds several plots and runtime tables, and replaces main AL accuracy plots with differences relative to random selection. Separate OOD tables become consolidated comparisons, with far-OOD results moved to the appendix. Parameter lists become tables. Some presentation defects remain, including Figure 1's caption overlapping body text.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion substantially expands to open-set AL, DDU, pretrained AL approaches, and newer OOD methods. v1's broad assertion that existing methods had not been evaluated on both tasks is replaced by acknowledging such uncertainty approaches and distinguishing SISOM through shared metrics and the application life cycle. This materially revises its research positioning.

T1.justification: The formal AL/OOD setup, distance definitions, score equations, and sigmoid optimization remain substantively unchanged. Gradient notation is clarified, but no new theorem, proof, or mathematical derivation is introduced. Aggregate benchmark ranking is an evaluation change.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important gaps in v1 by directly testing OOD detection after AL training, measuring runtime and subset tradeoffs, broadening comparisons, and examining sensitivity to budgets and models. Its explicit open-set AL boundary also clarifies what the unified method supports. Reporting inconsistencies temper these gains: Appendix A.5 claims first place for CIFAR-10 far-OOD despite Table 5 showing FeatureNorm at 95.59 versus SISOMe at 94.74. Nevertheless, the added validation and clearer applicability substantially improve the paper overall.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SISOM research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite extensive reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds pretrained-model comparisons, sensitivity experiments, OOD evaluation of active-learning checkpoints, and runtime measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original active-learning experiments, OpenOOD evaluations, ablations, and feature-space analyses in Section 5 and Appendix A.

results.title: A Unified Approach Towards Active Learning and Out-of-Distribution Detection

C1.justification: Both versions claim a less restrictive state-constrained framework, convergence and policy dominance under stated assumptions, and strong StaCQ benchmark performance. Although v2's abstract explicitly says state-of-the-art, v1 already makes that claim in its discussion. Multi-step learning remains a prospective extension.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands applicability and failure discussions: deterministic versus stochastic environments, false reachability estimates at loose thresholds, tuning and critic-count fairness, and accumulated model error and computational costs for multi-step extensions. These qualify and explain the results beyond v1's largely forward-looking discussion.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a code-repository link and newly states the original maze's reward values, learning rate, discount, and convergence duration. Appendix G discloses evaluation every 5,000 training steps. Existing architecture, normalization, hyperparameter, hardware, and runtime details in Appendices B–D are largely unchanged.

E1.justification: The same 18 D4RL datasets and original maze example remain. Appendix H adds an idealized sparse-maze scenario with gaps that prevent one-step stitching but permit paths through non-dataset intermediate states. This modestly extends the illustrative scenario coverage, without adding a benchmark domain.

E2.justification: The benchmark comparator set remains BC, BCQ, TD3+BC, IQL, MBTS, Diffuser, and RAMBO. Appendix E retests existing comparators with different tuning and critic-count settings; POR is newly discussed but not evaluated.

E3.justification: Appendix E adds controlled designs using a fixed StaCQ hyperparameter across locomotion datasets and environment-tuned TD3+BC with four critics. Appendix F systematically varies three reachability norms and four thresholds. These substantially expand evaluation controls, while Appendix C retains the original benchmark settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds tuning and critic-count controls, reachability sensitivity tests on Walker2d-Medium and MediumExpert, learning curves across the benchmark datasets, and a two-step maze case study. These investigate confounding, failure conditions, training behavior, and stitching limitations that v1 did not analyze.

E5.justification: Both versions retain five-seed evaluation with 10 locomotion or 100 Antmaze trajectories. v2 explicitly identifies standard deviations in the new table captions and introduces shaded standard-deviation bands across training; v1's Table 1 leaves its plus/minus statistic unnamed. No increased seed count or formal significance testing is established.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises several StaCQ results, including Hopper-Random from 9.1 ± 0.9 to 17.5 ± 12.8 and the Antmaze total from 309.6 to 319.8; its baseline and OneStep scores remain unchanged. New controlled and sensitivity results substantially expand the evidence: Table 3 reports Walker2d-MediumExpert falling from 116.2 ± 1.5 to 6.7 ± 12.4 when the L-infinity threshold increases from 0.1 to 0.5. The original score revisions are not explained as same-procedure gains.

M1.justification: The specified StaCQ update now uses a target actor in the critic target and adds its soft update in Algorithm 1. The main actor loss changes from positive to negative lambda times Q, correcting its inconsistency with the stated maximization objective. These are local specification changes; the PDFs do not establish corresponding code changes.

P1.justification: Related work moves from Section 2 to Section 5, QA/QS terminology becomes QSA/QSS, and substantial portions of the introduction, related work, experimental discussion, and conclusion are rewritten. This is extensive narrative revision beyond adding the new scientific material.

P2.justification: v2 adds a reachability schematic, two experimental tables, a six-panel learning-curve figure, and a second maze comparison. The original maze figure is retained and renumbered. Journal formatting also changes typography, table spacing, headers, and algorithm placement throughout.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of POR and its relationship to IQL and state-constrained learning, citing Xu et al. (2022). It also adds Jin et al. (2021) and Shi et al. (2022) in the theoretical discussion. The broader positioning against batch-constrained and model-based approaches remains.

T1.justification: Appendix H expands v1's brief multi-step suggestion into a dataset-anchored two-step reachability definition and tentative value-update and policy-extraction equations. Section 7 also proposes a stochastic reachability definition. The original convergence assumptions, results, and proofs remain substantially intact; no completed multi-step convergence proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important weaknesses in v1's empirical support: Appendix E controls tuning and critic-count differences, while Appendix F tests the central reachability choice and exposes severe failures. Learning curves, clearer applicability limits, and added reproducibility information further strengthen the paper. Reporting remains imperfect, including conflicting per-environment versus per-dataset wording in Table 2, but this limited ambiguity does not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SCQL framework and StaCQ algorithm. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite reorganization and added material.

after.justification: v2 retains original maze and D4RL results and adds controlled comparisons, reachability ablations, and training curves in Appendices E–G.

before.justification: v1 reports original maze-navigation outcomes and D4RL evaluations of StaCQ and its one-step variant, including five-seed results in Table 1.

results.title: State-Constrained Offline Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The central contribution—learning conditional and marginal predictors through placeholder-based augmentation—remains unchanged. However, Section 5 strengthens the empirical claim from consistently achieving competitive performance in v1 to consistently outperforming conventional imputation and ensemble methods in v3, despite exceptions in the reported results.

C2.justification: v3 adds finite-data versus asymptotic interpretations of imputation, discusses applicability to modern multimodal models, and identifies SGD-based training as a boundary. It removes v1's explicit caveat about untested missing-pattern-specific models. Its new claim that Knockout consistently beats Knockout- overstates Table 3: with three missing features, MSE is 0.175 versus 0.163.

D1.justification: v3 discloses the 0.0741 regression knockout rate, exhaustive testing of 130 missingness patterns, additional feature dimensions, and the Food-101 training recipe. These improve documentation without establishing changes to retained experiments. Conversely, it removes the CPU-testing hardware detail, specific ADNI application instructions, and the retained tree results' site identification.

E1.justification: v3 adds text-image classification on UPMC Food-101 and controlled self-censored MNAR training scenarios, extending modality and missingness coverage. Conversely, v1's Buffalo Auto Arborist evaluation in Table S8 disappears. The prior Columbus results remain identifiable in v3 Table 5's ResNet-50 rows despite the omitted site label.

E2.justification: The regression comparison expands beyond the common baseline, missForest, and Knockout* to input dropout, zero imputation with indicators, MICE, MIWAE, supMIWAE, KNN, and linear-regression imputation. v3 also adds the out-of-support-imputation common baseline in mixed-input classification and Knockout* in the noisy-label comparison. Food-101 includes additional published comparator scores.

E3.justification: v3 retains the main 3,000-sample regression setting but adds 300-, 1,000-, and 15,000-sample evaluations, a self-censored MNAR protocol, and ViT-B-16 tree-classification configurations. Food-101 introduces a ResNet50/RoBERTa evaluation with its own training budget and validation split. Newly specified details of retained experiments do not establish that their procedures changed.

E4.justification: New analyses test training-data sensitivity, distinguishing observed MNAR missingness from induced masking, out-of-support imputation without Knockout training, and placeholder choice in noisy-label learning. The scalar placeholder sweep and structured-image placeholder analysis already existed in v1; their relocation or redisplay is not a new ablation.

E5.justification: v1 Table 2 explicitly identifies CIFAR variability as standard deviations; v3 Table 4 retains the same uncertainty values and five-run count but omits that identification. Otherwise, established repetition counts, Alzheimer's standard errors, and segmentation confidence intervals remain unchanged. There is no evidence of increased repetitions or new statistical testing.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial results for new comparators, MNAR experiments, training-size analyses, ViT configurations, and placeholder controls, while removing Buffalo results. Newly reported Food-101 accuracies are 92.7% versus 91.5% for the common baseline with both modalities, and 63.2% versus 47.5% with images alone. Existing main CIFAR scores and prostate AUCs are retained.

M1.justification: Both versions use independent random masking, placeholder substitution, the same supervised objective, structured masking, and distinct placeholders for induced versus observed MAR/MNAR missingness. v3 clarifies sampling and evaluates additional model configurations; its new Knockout- variant ablates an existing component rather than revising the proposed method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, experimental descriptions, and ADNI appendix undergo widespread rewriting. Placeholder guidance and comparator descriptions gain structured lists and expanded explanations; Section 5 becomes a broader Discussion. The main experimental narrative now explicitly develops analyses previously presented primarily in appendix figures.

P2.justification: v3 changes typography, author layout, spacing, and table organization throughout. Regression plots expand to three panels with larger comparator legends; the tree table gains backbone groups. New summary, ablation, and Food-101 displays are added, Buffalo's table is removed, and the Gaussian illustration and placeholder sweep move into the main text.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning against imputation theory and supervised missing-data research, including Josse, Bertsimas, Le Morvan, and Ipsen. It acknowledges closely related masking approaches by Neverova and Parthasarathy and Sundaram, and discusses modern multimodal and foundation models. These additions materially qualify the relationship to prior work.

T1.justification: v3 corrects reversed mask states in Section 2.2's marginalization identity and Appendix A.2's derivation. It adds a positive-denominator assumption and a discrete counterexample demonstrating failure of an in-support placeholder. These are localized mathematical corrections and additions; the principal marginalization argument and multitask decomposition remain.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evaluation of the unchanged method: its much broader regression comparisons address v1's limited comparator coverage, while controlled MNAR, training-size, and augmentation controls directly examine important assumptions. Corrected mask identities and closer engagement with prior work also improve the scientific argument. Dropping Buffalo results and the missing-pattern-specific baseline caveat reduces completeness, and the Table 3 interpretation overclaims superiority. Nevertheless, the expanded comparative and diagnostic evidence provides a substantial net improvement in the paper's support and assessability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Knockout method and corresponding experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including identifying relocated material.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds further simulations, ablations, model configurations, and text-image classification experiments on UPMC Food-101.

before.justification: v1 reports original regression and classification simulations and experiments on Alzheimer's forecasting, noisy-label learning, tumor segmentation, tree classification, and prostate cancer detection, including appendix results.

results.title: Knockout: A simple way to handle missing inputs

C1.justification: V2 elevates establishing an OSTTA benchmark to an explicit contribution in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion. The central claims about pioneering open-set single-image VLM adaptation, ROSITA's contrastive separation, continuous LayerNorm adaptation, and efficiency remain substantially intact. The new terminology and ReDUCe name do not themselves establish new scientific contributions.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's clustering explanations and brief memory/FPR limitations, v2 explains initial adaptation instability, contrasts ReDUCe with UniEnt, discusses LoRA tradeoffs, and analyzes reliable-sample quality. Section 6 explicitly acknowledges MNIST's limited realism and the absence of evaluation on streams containing no undesired classes. Appendix E adds a more specific account of difficulties on ImageNet-C and semantically similar classes.

D1.justification: Appendix B supplies configurations for four added baselines, including prototype handling, cache capacities, learning rates, and optimizers. Appendix C.5 specifies LoRA placement and ranks, and the dataset inventory adds DomainNet sample counts. Existing ROSITA settings remain unchanged. V2 removes v1's asset-license inventory and changes the code-access pointer from the project website to a direct repository link.

E1.justification: V2 adds DomainNet Clipart, Painting, and Sketch evaluations with MNIST, plus CCC/MNIST streams with gradual corruption changes. It also extends continual evaluation to CIFAR-100C and tests rapidly changing domains. These substantially broaden domain and temporal-condition coverage. Some earlier combinations, including VisDA/SVHN, no longer have reported results.

E2.justification: V1's main comparisons use ZS-Eval, TPT, TPT-C, and the MaPLe-based PAlign variants. V2 Tables 1–3 additionally evaluate (K+1)PC, UniEnt, TDA, and DPE on retained benchmarks. Appendix C.4 also adds DAF detector comparisons and crosses detector choice with UniEnt versus ReDUCe objectives.

E3.justification: V2 expands parameter-selection experiments to additional attention blocks, combined prompt/LayerNorm updates, LoRA ranks, and SGD/AdamW controls. It replaces the appendix's ViT-B/32 and ResNet-50 evaluations with CLIP and Open-CLIP ViT-L/14 settings, adds a 300,000-sample CCC protocol, and measures feature distances. Frequent-switching sample budgets are new, although Table 5 specifies 200 where the prose says 250. Main ROSITA hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds two previously unreported pairwise loss combinations, broader parameter and LoRA sensitivity studies, detector/objective controls, feature-separation measurements, and reliable-sample accuracy diagnostics. These test component necessity and failure mechanisms more extensively. Reliability filtering and neighbor-count analyses already existed in v1; their relocation or repetition is not counted as new analysis.

E5.justification: V1 Appendix B.1/Table 8 and v2 Appendix C.1/Table 9 report the same five-random-seed study, mean-and-standard-deviation practice, and numerical entries. V2 does not introduce additional uncertainty estimation or significance testing.

E6.justification: Shared main ROSITA scores largely remain unchanged, including 84.17 HM on CLIP CIFAR-10C/MNIST. V2 adds substantial benchmark, baseline, ablation, and diagnostic results. New comparators alter rankings: on CLIP CIFAR-100C/MNIST, (K+1)PC reaches 59.72 HM versus ROSITA's retained 57.34. Conversely, v1's detailed known/unknown accuracy tables, smaller-backbone results, and several MaPLe scenario results are removed.

M1.justification: Matching Equations 1–8 across versions shows the same proposed procedure: dynamic LDA identification, reliability filtering, two feature banks, pseudo-label and contrastive losses, and vision-encoder LayerNorm updates with fixed text classifiers. ReDUCe renames the existing objective, and desired/undesired replaces weak/strong OOD terminology. Alternative detectors and parameter choices are evaluated as controls rather than replacing ROSITA's procedure.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Problem setup and benchmarking move ahead of the method, parameter analysis becomes a separate main section, baseline exposition moves largely into Appendix B, and the analysis is reorganized into nine research questions. Terminology changes throughout, and the appendices are substantially reordered.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a different publication layout, relabels the framework diagram, expands the parameter-selection plot, and restructures comparison tables with additional rows and improvement annotations. A combined scenario table replaces detailed main-text continual results, while reliability results move from the appendix into the main text. New diagnostic tables accompany removal of detailed result tables and the MaPLe complexity plot.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning against training-free adaptation, prototype evolution, open-set entropy objectives, and LoRA, adding the corresponding TDA, DPE, UniEnt, and LoRA references alongside CCC and Open-CLIP. It develops explicit CNN-versus-VLM and ROSITA-versus-UniEnt/(K+1)PC distinctions. Several earlier general domain-adaptation and source-free-adaptation references are dropped.

T1.justification: V1 provides loss definitions and intuitive explanations; v2 adds explicit gradient analysis in Section 3.1 and Appendix A, including normalized-feature assumptions and derivations of attraction and softmax-weighted repulsion. This is substantive new mathematical analysis. However, Appendix Equations 13 and 15 omit the temperature factor present in Equation 9, and the undesired-sample gradient inconsistently uses K+ instead of K.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens comparative validation: v1 relied mainly on zero-shot and prompt-tuning baselines, whereas v2 includes adapted open-set and efficient alternatives and directly tests detector, objective, and parameter choices. Broader domain-shift evaluations and specific failure diagnostics further clarify applicability. These address important weaknesses in the original evidence. The gains are qualified by removal of detailed known/unknown accuracy results, the 200/250-sample inconsistency, gradient-normalization errors, and superiority wording that exceeds some new results. Nevertheless, the stronger controls and comparative evidence establish a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ROSITA by the same authors, despite the changed title and terminology. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison. Local reporting inconsistencies do not prevent comparison of the work overall.

after.justification: V2 retains original ROSITA experiments and adds benchmark comparisons, parameter studies, representation-distance measurements, and failure diagnostics.

before.justification: V1 reports original adaptation experiments, baseline comparisons, loss ablations, continual-domain evaluations, and five-seed results in the main text and appendices.

results.title: Efficient Open Set Single Image Test Time Adaptation of Vision Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion add claims about recovering bifurcation progression, distinguishing dynamical families under tested warps, and agreement with independent task-information diagnostics. Broad uniqueness and information-bottleneck conclusions are narrowed toward empirical geometric findings within the studied settings.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly interprets embedding entropy as geometric dispersion rather than direct representation information. It develops explanations distinguishing early-step label-irrelevant variability from later task-relevant structure, and adds substantive qualifications about non-invariance to smooth warps, descriptive clustering, and entropy distances not uniquely measuring representation quality.

D1.justification: Appendices A.1–A.10 substantially expand dataset statistics, preprocessing, sampling, embedding parameters, synthetic generation, and diagnostic procedures. Examples include t-SNE perplexity 50 and 2000 iterations, LLE/UMAP configurations, and explicit synthetic integration settings. These disclosures do not establish reruns of existing experiments. v1's promised future code release is removed without replacement access information.

E1.justification: v2 retains Area2Bump and HAR but adds controlled Hopf and Pitchfork synthetic datasets, dynamic-versus-static controls, and clean-versus-warped scenarios (Section 5.1; Appendix A.5). Label-corruption and sequence-masking experiments also introduce new test conditions on Area2Bump.
