These substantially expand documentation without establishing changes to retained experiments. Conversely, v1's GPU/timing information and explicit CLUSTER block-size disclosure are omitted.

E1.justification: v2 retains CLUSTER and both UPFD datasets, adds featureless Reddit Threads graph classification under structure attacks, and evaluates local single-victim CLUSTER attacks. These additions broaden the represented graph data and attack tasks beyond v1's global node-classification and graph-level node-injection evaluations.

E2.justification: v2 adds a single-random-perturbation baseline alongside the retained random-search attack, expands transfer comparisons with GPS and Polynormer and with GPS-GCN on CLUSTER, and evaluates Nettack in the local CLUSTER comparison (Figure 26). Nettack was cited but not evaluated in v1.

E3.justification: Reported attack-budget ranges expand from 15% to 50% on CLUSTER and from 50% to 100% on UPFD. New protocols include Reddit's stratified 75/12.5/12.5 split, local attack constraints, homophily measurement, and adversarial-training budgets and replay settings. The original datasets' splits, first-50-test-graph evaluation, and 125 attack steps remain.

E4.justification: The original component ablations and constrained CLUSTER analysis remain. v2 adds comparisons of SAN spectral-gradient alternatives, detailed transferability analyses, tests of whether injected graphs preserve node-centric homophily, and local-attack evaluations with different constraints (Appendix C). These address substantial additional questions about attack effectiveness and meaningfulness.

E5.justification: Both versions report attack averages and standard deviations over four random seeds, including the component-ablation tables. The added experiments and result rows do not introduce a different uncertainty-reporting practice, increased run count, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive architecture, Reddit Threads, transfer, local-attack, homophily, and adversarial-training results. Figure 7 newly reports much greater adversarial-training benefits for Graphormer than GCN. Table 3 adds SAN eigen-backpropagation results, including 54.4 ± 0.6% unconstrained CLUSTER accuracy with attention relaxation. Existing Graphormer/GRIT ablations are retained; rounding of old SAN values is not a result change.

M1.justification: v2 adds attack adaptations for GPS's gated message passing and Polynormer's sparse attention, plus an alternative eigenvalue-separation procedure enabling spectral backpropagation (Appendix F.2). It also introduces modified free adversarial training with separate attack/model passes and discrete perturbations (Section 7, Appendix D), substantially extending v1's attack framework.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and methodological exposition are extensively rewritten. Architecture descriptions move from v1's Appendix B into the main preliminaries, and v2 separates evaluation, attack results, adversarial training, related work, and conclusion into distinct sections. The narrative is substantially reorganized beyond the added scientific content.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two-column to single-column layout. Retained attack plots are redrawn with revised panels, axes, styling, and legends, and duplicated main-text ablations are consolidated in the appendix. New displays include the node-probability illustration, defense and transfer plots, homophily distributions, local-attack plots, and hyperparameter tables.

R1.justification: The central positioning as the first adaptive GT robustness study remains. v2 adds focused connections to free adversarial training, prior work on MPNN flexibility, Polynormer, and homophily-based unnoticeability, while removing several earlier positional-encoding and certification references. The existing related-work argument remains largely recognizable.

T1.justification: v1 states spectral perturbation approximations and refers readers elsewhere for repeated eigenvalues. v2 adds a discontinuity counterexample and explicit eigenspace-basis construction, derives a minimum-norm eigenvalue-separation optimization (Appendix F), and supplies architecture-specific complexity reasoning (Appendix G.3). Principle II also explicitly requires differentiability almost everywhere.

improvement.justification: The new hyperparameter tables and numerical procedures substantially reduce v1's reproducibility gaps, while broader architecture/task comparisons and local-attack and homophily checks strengthen validation. Section 7 and Figure 7 also add an empirically tested defense. These gains outweigh the loss of hardware/timing details and the explicit optimality caveat, although the broad robust-learning interpretation remains supported chiefly by Graphormer-versus-GCN experiments.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same graph-transformer robustness work, with matching core relaxations, node-injection formulation, and retained experiments. Their main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison despite the changed title and substantial expansion.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds results for further architectures, Reddit Threads, local attacks, homophily analyses, and adversarial training in Sections 6–7 and Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original attack results on CLUSTER and both UPFD datasets, including accuracy curves and component ablations in Section 5 and Appendix E.

results.title: Adversarial Robustness of Graph Transformers

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from NLG evaluation, instruction tuning and three reasoning benchmarks to a tuning-free hierarchy for text/image evaluation and four reasoning benchmarks. Turbo/Lite and approximately 7.7-fold efficiency become headline claims. Fine-tuning remains in an appendix but loses its central contribution status, and the earlier specific SummEval and GPT-3.5/GPT-4 improvement claims are replaced.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations for task-dependent differences between hierarchy and debate, guidance on peer count and chair strength, and interpretations of chair dependence on correct peers. Appendix G newly argues that SummEval's skewed ratings undermine its suitability. Limitations shift toward computational cost, weaker chairs, missing inter-peer discussion and untested modalities, while several configuration questions left open in v1 receive empirical discussion.

D1.justification: V2 adds API-provider information, task-specific generation limits, an AutoPrompt worked example, expanded task prompts and repository/PyPI links claiming public access. V1 only promised code after review. Conversely, v1's explicit fine-tuning split details and A100 hardware statement disappear. V2 also retains a future-release statement in Section 11, leaving its availability wording inconsistent.

E1.justification: V2 retains SummEval, TopicalChat, GSM8k and CSQA, adds ICQD caption evaluation and AGIQA image-generation evaluation, and adds AQuA multiple-choice algebra and BBH-DU date reasoning. StrategyQA is removed. Multimodal evaluation, only proposed as future work in v1 Appendix C, is now actually tested.

E2.justification: The reasoning comparison replaces ReConCile and GPT-4 rows with zero-shot CoT, Self Correction, Multi-Agent Debate and Multi-Agent Peer Review. New multimodal comparisons evaluate CLIPScore, ImageReward, PickScore and, on AGIQA only, X-IQE. G-Eval and Analyze-Rate remain NLG comparators, while the fine-tuning comparison drops its GPT-3.5 reference row.

E3.justification: SummEval evaluation expands from 200 selected samples to the full 1,600. The main peer models change from GPT-3.5, Gemini-Pro and Mixtral to Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-Nemo-12B and Gemma-2-9B, with GPT-4o-mini replacing the GPT-3.5 chair. New multimodal protocols use two VLM peers, a GPT-4o chair, 864 usable ICQD samples and 500 AGIQA samples selected for rating coverage. Cost, timing and threshold-based error evaluations are also introduced.

E4.justification: V2 adds peer-count/composition and weaker-chair ablations, aggregate peer/chair error analysis, ProTeGi optimization comparisons, score-versus-comment communication tests, SummEval distribution analysis and inference timing. V1's critic-strategy experiments, incremental component ablation and worked evaluation, fine-tuning and reasoning case studies disappear. Prompt ablations are substantially redesigned around TopicalChat.

E5.justification: V1 specifies two-run averaging for its prompt ablation but provides no uncertainty estimates or significance tests. V2 reports three-run averages for NLG and reasoning, adds ± values to reasoning Table 4, and reports paired t-test p-values in Appendix M. These are substantial reporting additions; the ± statistic is not clearly defined, and the PDFs do not establish an increase in runs for otherwise identical experiments.

E6.justification: Results are extensively replaced and expanded. TopicalChat average Spearman correlation changes from 0.597 in v1 Table 2 to 0.628 for Turbo and 0.579 for Lite in v2 Table 2 under changed models and protocols, not a matched-setting improvement. V2 adds multimodal results, including Turbo correlations of 0.497 on ICQD and 0.657 on AGIQA, and revises reasoning and TopicalChat fine-tuning results. StrategyQA, SummEval fine-tuning and critic-strategy results are removed.

M1.justification: V2 removes v1's optional critic module and its re-evaluation and weighting pathways. Appendix K explicitly adopts scores-only peer-to-chair communication instead of analyses plus scores; the GSM8k chair prompt likewise changes from reviewing solutions to receiving final answers. These substantially revise the supported information flow, although v2's equations still show comment-score pairs. Turbo/Lite largely name the n=20/n=1 settings already tested in v1.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten, and the main narrative is reorganized into methodology, experiments, results and analysis. SummEval results and fine-tuning move to appendices; limitations and related work are rewritten; prompts are reorganized by task. A reproducibility statement replaces the former potential-risks section.

P2.justification: V2 changes from a two-column layout to a single-column ICLR format and redraws the framework illustration around the hierarchy and Turbo/Lite variants. It adds a multimodal diagram and peer-scaling, error-analysis, rating-distribution and timing plots. Tables gain variant, cost and uncertainty structure. The critic diagram disappears, while v1 Figure 2's prompting schema is retained as v2 Figure 4.

R1.justification: Research positioning expands substantially into multimodal quality assessment, with CLIPScore, ImageReward, PickScore, HyperIQA and X-IQE, and into prompt optimization through OPRO, APE and ProTeGi. ReConCile changes from a central empirical comparator to an explicitly excluded baseline because of architectural differences in Appendix I. The positioning increasingly emphasizes hierarchy and efficiency relative to debate-based systems.

T1.justification: V2 Equations 1–4 and Algorithm 1 express the peer/chair evaluations, multiple responses and score averaging already described procedurally in v1 Section 2 and Appendix A. This adds notation and pseudocode, without new substantive mathematical assumptions, theoretical results, proofs or derivations.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses validation gaps: multimodal applicability is tested rather than merely proposed, SummEval uses the full test set, and peer-count, chair-strength and error analyses investigate configuration limits explicitly left open in v1. Broader reasoning comparisons and repeated-run reporting further strengthen assessment. These gains outweigh reduced fine-tuning documentation and remaining overclaims: notably, the claim that both variants beat NLG baselines is too broad, since Lite's SummEval average Spearman correlation is 0.447 versus G-Eval's 0.472 in Table 9.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ReFeR and retain the same peer-review-inspired framework and several benchmarks. Their main text, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial restructuring.

after.justification: V2 reports original text and multimodal evaluation, reasoning, fine-tuning and framework-analysis results in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original NLG evaluation, ablation, Mistral-7B fine-tuning and reasoning results, including Tables 1–10 and appendix case studies.

results.title: ReFeR: Improving Evaluation and Reasoning through Hierarchy of Models

C1.justification: The abstract, four listed contributions, and conclusion retain the main efficiency, performance, and robustness claims. The introduction newly asserts applicability to partially observable tasks using a student with memory and a teacher with full-state access, modestly extending the stated scope.

C2.justification: v2 newly states that clipping is unnecessary for forward KL but retained for potential reverse-KL, multiple-teacher use. It also qualifies the work's primarily fully observable setting and discusses potential applicability to partial observability. Appendix B.4 interprets the new PPO comparison as evidence for the value of teacher guidance.

D1.justification: Appendix A retains the preprocessing, architectures, hyperparameters, training budgets, and evaluation episode counts. Table 3's added environment-step row repeats information already given in v1's prose. The sb3-distill library and code-access link are unchanged.

E1.justification: The environment coverage, corrupted-teacher subset, and Procgen training/test scenarios are retained. The new PPO comparison reuses four Atari and four Procgen environments. Partially observable tasks are newly discussed but not evaluated.

E2.justification: v2 adds pure PPO without distillation as a substantive new control alongside the retained student-distill and teacher-distill baselines (Appendix B.4, Table 7). This evaluates reinforcement learning alone on larger student networks; v1 used PPO to train teachers but lacked this student comparison.

E3.justification: Principal relative-score summaries change from geometric means to geometric interquartile means, and distillation curves change from means to interquartile means. Table 6 also adopts human-normalized Atari reporting. The PPO-only comparison introduces an additional control, while the existing splits, architectures, training budgets, and action-selection settings in Appendix A remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendix B.4 removes the entire distillation component to test whether teacher guidance contributes beyond PPO alone, addressing a central component question absent from v1. The existing corrupted-teacher robustness and distillation-weight sensitivity analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v1 already reports five seeds and standard-deviation bands for teacher training. v2 adds 95% confidence intervals to the principal student-result tables and distillation curves, alongside revised interquartile estimators. Five seeds remain specified; the PDFs do not establish an increase in runs or explain the confidence-interval construction.

E6.justification: Aggregate results are extensively revised: Table 1's larger-student Atari PPD score changes from 1.25x to 1.10x under the new aggregation, while Table 5's individual scores remain identical. New Table 7 reports PPO versus PPD results, including 0.38x versus 1.16x on the four-Atari subset. Figures 9–11 add individual distillation curves. The overall row of Table 1 and Figure 2's numerical test-performance annotations disappear.

M1.justification: Equation 2 and Algorithm 1 retain the same PPO-plus-clipped-KL objective, student-generated rollouts, repeated minibatch updates, and critic training. Section 2 expands the explanation without changing the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites expand the method explanation, motivate benchmark selection, and revise Related Work. The new PPO subsection becomes Appendix B.4, shifting the retained Procgen analysis to B.5. The main section order, contribution list, and much of the experimental and concluding prose remain intact.

P2.justification: Figures 1, 2, and 6–8 are redrawn with uncertainty bands, markers, and revised legends and axes; Figures 9–11 are added. Table 1 and the Procgen comparison table are reorganized into stacked network-size blocks accommodating confidence intervals, and a new PPO comparison table is introduced. These substantially change the presentation of empirical evidence.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around prior combinations of reinforcement learning and distillation, adding discussion of COSIL, ADVISOR, TGRL, and Rajeswaran et al. The introduction acknowledges these predecessors, and Related Work contrasts their observability assumptions, objective combinations, and balancing strategies with PPD. v1's closest-work discussion primarily emphasized Schmitt et al.

T1.justification: The MDP formulation, gradient framework, optimization objective, and appendix algorithms retain their mathematical substance. Added notation and explanations unpack existing components without introducing a new formal derivation, theorem, or proof.

improvement.justification: The previously absent PPO-only control tests the central value of teacher guidance, while confidence intervals and individual learning curves substantially improve scrutiny of the empirical claims. Expanded discussion of closely related methods also clarifies the contribution. These gains outweigh reporting regressions: v2's Tables 2 and 6 give conflicting corrupted-Atari PPD summaries (0.64x versus 0.69x), and Figure 2 removes test-score annotations still referenced in the text.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Proximal Policy Distillation by the same author. All 19 pages of v1 and 24 pages of v2, including equations, figures, tables, and appendices, support comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and additionally reports a PPO-only comparison in Appendix B.4.

before.justification: v1 reports original distillation experiments on Atari, Mujoco, and Procgen, including network-size comparisons, corrupted-teacher experiments, and sensitivity to the distillation weight.

results.title: Proximal Policy Distillation

C1.justification: v1 centers its contribution on improving Prompt-DT. v2 broadens the claimed framework to other sequence-modeling architectures, explicitly featuring Reinformer, and adds a concrete claim of matching Prompt-DT with only 10% of the data on selected tasks. Architectural flexibility and component validation become explicit contributions in the introduction and conclusion.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations separating embedding quality from backbone priors, qualifies data efficiency under extreme scarcity, and acknowledges regularization failures on Point-robot. It discusses prompt-selection benefits versus overhead and explains Reinformer's additional inference cost. The earlier Meta-World language/RL domain-gap explanation disappears, and the stated model-size limitation changes to GPT-2 and Qwen2.5-0.5B.

D1.justification: v2 specifies LoRA targets in query/key/value projections, initialization and training of RL-specific layers and the prompt encoder, and explicit inference pseudocode. It adds A6000/Xeon hardware, timing and trainable-parameter information in Section 4.5/Table 8, updates hyperparameters, and supplies a source-code/configuration repository reference in Appendix A.

E1.justification: Within the retained few-shot continuous-control setting, v2 adds Point-robot goal navigation and removes Meta-World pick-place-v2. Cheetah-dir, Cheetah-vel, Ant-dir and Meta-World reach-v2 remain. This is a limited substitution in task coverage, distinct from the larger protocol changes.

E2.justification: Table 1 drops Prompt-Tuning DT and Prompt Diffuser, retains Prompt-DT, and adds Prompt-Rein, CORRO, CSRO and Meta-DT. Meta-DT also enters the reduced-data comparison, while its unregularized LPDT comparator disappears. Additional experiments introduce text-embedding-only controls and Prompt-EDT; v1's NLP text-regularization comparator is removed.

E3.justification: v2 reports Meta-DT/SAC data instead of v1's Prompt-DT datasets with TD3 Cheetah-vel and expert Meta-World collection. Initialization changes from DistilGPT2 to GPT-2, batch size from 16 to 8, and dataset fractions expand from 100%/10% to five levels down to 1%. Reported splits change: Table 9 gives 45/5 Cheetah-vel tasks, although Section 4.2 still says 35/5. Online prompt-selection and fixed-score timing protocols are also added.

E4.justification: v1 already contains regularization and reduced-data ablations. v2 substantially expands these and adds tests separating embedding-only language-model use from backbone initialization, GPT-2 versus Qwen initialization, alternative sequence models, random versus return-selected prompts, and computational costs (Sections 4.4–4.5). The earlier NLP text-regularization analysis is removed.

E5.justification: Both versions retain three-seed result tables with plus/minus values and shaded training curves. However, v1 Figure 2 explicitly specifies one seed, whereas v2 Figure 2 omits the curve-specific seed count. This reduces seed disclosure; it does not establish a change in the number of runs.

E6.justification: The main scores are substantially replaced under revised settings: for example, Table 1's LPDT-Classifier means change from 947.84 to 1121.68 on Cheetah-dir and from -31.57 to -55.15 on Cheetah-vel. These are not comparable-setting gains or losses. v2 adds extensive variant, data-fraction, prompt-selection and timing results, while removing pick-place scores, NLP text-regularization results and v1's per-task result breakdowns.

M1.justification: The initialization, LoRA and prompt-regularization framework remains, but v2 adds LPDT-Rein with state-return-action ordering, expectile return prediction and actions conditioned on predicted returns (Section 3.4). It also implements EDT-based and optional return-based prompt-selection variants. These extend the actual training and inference procedures.

P1.justification: The introduction, preliminaries and method explanations are substantially rewritten, and Algorithm 1 expands into training and inference pseudocode. Dataset and baseline sections are merged; expanded data-efficiency and ablation studies move into the main text; training curves move to the appendix. Terminology changes from unsupervised to contrastive regularization, with new code-availability and acknowledgment sections.

P2.justification: The main comparison table is transposed and expanded, with green/blue highlighting replacing bold-only rankings. New grouped ablation, architecture and computational tables replace the earlier presentation, including removal of per-task tables. Figure 2 is redrawn with four LPDT variants, revised axes and legends, and moved to Appendix E. Figure 1 remains largely unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 substantially updates positioning around Reinformer, Elastic DT, Meta-DT and DPDT, discussing architectural compatibility and differences in test-time adaptation or prompt selection. Related work also expands to return-conditioned learning theory and off-dynamics RL. These substantive additions go beyond the publication-metadata updates to retained works such as LaMo.

T1.justification: Section 3.4 adds mathematical definitions for the Reinformer input sequence, expectile return loss and augmented objective, Equations (3.8)–(3.10). Section 3.3 explicitly states the same-task batching assumption underlying contrastive pairs. Other core mathematics is largely retained or elaborated; neither version presents theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's regularization and two-size data checks through initialization controls, architectural extensions, broader data-scarcity tests and measured computational costs. Clearer implementation details and the code/configuration reference address substantial reproducibility gaps. These gains outweigh the loss of pick-place coverage and per-task breakdowns, although the inconsistent Cheetah-vel split and overstated text-embedding interpretation around Table 4 remain weaknesses. The improvement concerns evidence and documentation, not directly comparable performance gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LPDT research by the same authors. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support matching retained, revised and removed material.

after.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of LPDT variants, initialization and regularization ablations, prompt-selection experiments and computational measurements. Some baseline scores are attributed to other papers, but the LPDT results are original.

before.justification: v1 reports original LPDT experiments on MuJoCo and Meta-World, including per-task results, regularization ablations and reduced-data evaluations in Appendices D–E.

results.title: Pre-trained Language Models Improve the Few-shot Prompt Ability of Decision Transformer

C1.justification: v2 narrows the abstract's accuracy claim from consistently superior performance to competitive or better performance, and presents the remedy as a potential solution direction. The central synchronization-mismatch claim and headline bounds of approximately 50% fewer spikes, twice-faster inference, and 10% higher accuracy remain.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands explanations of scheduling, relative event order, and hardware dynamics (Section 5; Appendix A.5.1). It develops the training-cost versus asynchronous-robustness tradeoff using the constrained CIFAR-10 experiment and distinguishes projected dynamic energy from static-power effects (Section 4.6; Appendix A.11). These add substantive mechanisms and applicability limits beyond v1's brief discussion.

D1.justification: v2 supplies source-code access information absent from v1 and documents the CIFAR-10 architecture, hyperparameters, memory-driven adaptations, and momentum-noise settings (Table 6; Appendix A.10; Figure 11). It also expands input-encoding documentation. The repository's actual accessibility is not established by the PDFs.

E1.justification: v2 adds CIFAR-10 natural-color object classification to the retained neuromorphic digit, speech, and gesture tasks. This extends evaluation beyond event-stream datasets to static images supplied as continuous-valued currents in one timestep, materially broadening the represented data and input conditions.

E2.justification: Corresponding experiments retain the layered-training baseline and unlayered RS/MS approaches. The new CIFAR-10 comparisons reuse these approaches. Newly discussed methods such as the Yao et al. approaches are not evaluated as additional baselines.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a distinct CIFAR-10 protocol with a VGG-style model, single-timestep inputs, 150 epochs, batch size 64, and forward-group sizes 512 during training and 64 during testing (Table 6; Appendix A.10). It also adds synaptic-operation counts and energy projections using 26 pJ per operation, excluding static power. Settings for the original three datasets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The original hyperparameter and resource analyses are retained. v2 adds training-loss convergence comparisons for the three original datasets (Figure 10), plus CIFAR-10 inference-group-size sensitivity and momentum-noise stability analyses (Figures 7 and 12). These extend the existing analyses and identify unstable training at smaller momentum-noise values.

E5.justification: Both versions use the same 25th/75th-percentile bars for spike distributions in v1 Figure 2/v2 Figure 4. Neither reports repeated-training run counts or seeds, and v2 introduces no new confidence intervals, significance tests, or run-level uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: The original Table 2 scores and resource-use results are retained. New CIFAR-10 results report accuracies of 0.805 for layered execution, 0.183 for asynchronous execution of the layered-trained model, and 0.712 after asynchronous training (Figure 7). v2 also adds convergence findings and projected-energy entries, such as N-MNIST energy of 0.9155 versus 0.3454 microjoules for layered versus unlayered-RS models (Table 3).

M1.justification: Algorithm 1, unlayered backpropagation, and the RS/MS scheduling policies remain. The CIFAR-10 extension adapts the model to a convolutional VGG-style architecture with non-leaking IF neurons, continuous-valued inputs, and terminal membrane-potential classification instead of spike-count classification (Sections 3.2, A.4, A.10). These are limited procedural adaptations.

P1.justification: The introduction and methodological explanations are extensively rewritten, accelerator background moves into Related work, and timing and scheduling terminology receive expanded explanations. The short discussion becomes a substantially reorganized Discussion & Future outlook. These changes extend well beyond inserting new experimental content.

P2.justification: v2 adds synchronization and backpropagation diagrams, an input-encoding illustration, CIFAR-10 and convergence displays, an architecture diagram, and an energy table. It redraws v1's threshold illustration, rearranges retained plots and tables, moves the latency legend outside the panels, and adopts a different journal layout.

R1.justification: v2 adds a substantive comparison with Yao et al. (2024, 2025), contrasting burst-based approaches with removing synchronization barriers. It adds positioning around newer training methods, neuron models, and hardware, while removing several earlier asynchronous-simulation and synchronization references. This goes beyond the change from numbered to author-year citations.

T1.justification: Appendix A.4 extends the mathematical definition of the class logit c_i: for CIFAR-10 it is the terminal output-neuron membrane potential rather than the spike count. The existing backpropagation derivation, neuron equations, surrogate, loss expression, and linear complexity argument remain; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: The CIFAR-10/VGG experiment addresses v1's lack of validation beyond small fully connected models and exposes incomplete accuracy recovery and training instability. Clearer diagrams, implementation documentation, and code-access information substantially improve assessability. The energy projections explicitly state their assumptions. CIFAR-10 still falls below layered accuracy, and hardware-energy measurements and run-level uncertainty remain absent, but the broader evidence and clearer limits substantially strengthen the paper.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same asynchronous SNN simulation and unlayered-backpropagation study. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison despite the changed title and extensive revision.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds CIFAR-10 results, convergence analyses, and synaptic-operation and projected-energy results.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on N-MNIST, SHD, and DVS gesture, including accuracy, spike density, latency, hyperparameter sensitivity, and training resource use.

results.title: Exploring the Limitations of Layer Synchronization in Spiking Neural Networks

C1.justification: The central contribution remains set-based reinforcement learning for verifiably robust control. v2 additionally claims verifiability across different frameworks and quantifies perturbation tolerance as up to nine times that of standard reinforcement learning. It also explicitly claims empirical scalability to more complex locomotion tasks, extending rather than replacing the original contribution.

C2.justification: v1 discusses conservative policies and computational costs. v2 adds substantive qualifications: training alone does not guarantee robustness, Hopper results lack formal certification, verification requires known dynamics and bounded uncertainties, and model mismatch can invalidate safety guarantees. Appendix C also interprets how critic regularization affects contraction and convergence, expanding the explanation of the robustness-performance trade-off.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies benchmark time horizons, averaging over the last five agents in each training run, Hopper evaluation details and hardware, and code/video access pointers. The existing architecture and training-parameter table are retained. These additions improve documentation without demonstrating changes to the corresponding retained experimental settings.

E1.justification: v2 adds MuJoCo Hopper-v2 locomotion, substantially extending evaluation to more complex dynamics and larger state/action spaces. The original navigation, inverted-pendulum, and 1D/2D quadrocopter tasks remain; 'quadrotor' is a renaming, and the 2D task was already evaluated in v1's appendix.

E2.justification: v1 compares against PA-PC, Naive, and Grad. v2 adds evaluated MAD and RORL comparators in Figure 5, broadening comparison to maximum-action-difference attacks and conservative smoothing. RORL is explicitly excluded from the TD3 comparison; the appendix's 2D quadrotor plot retains the original comparator set.

E3.justification: v2 introduces verification across four toolboxes and empirical Hopper evaluation using 50 MAD-attacked trajectories and 200 trajectories with uniform perturbations. It also adds noiseless learning-curve evaluations. The reported verified-return formula changes its negative-reward sign convention from v1 Equation 30 to v2 Equation 12. Existing network sizes and tabulated training hyperparameters remain unchanged; newly stated horizons do not establish changed settings.

E4.justification: Beyond the existing weighting-factor comparisons and quadrocopter attack analysis, v2 adds actor/critic regularization sweeps with convergence histories, learning curves, verification-toolbox dependence tests, and attack-specific results for the inverted pendulum. These examine parameter sensitivity, training stability, and whether improved verifiability extends beyond CORA.

E5.justification: v1 states that experiments use five seeds and displays shaded bands without defining their statistical meaning. v2 explicitly reports means and 95% confidence intervals across five seeds. This improves uncertainty reporting without establishing an increase in the number of runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds MAD/RORL results, Hopper returns and runtimes, sensitivity and convergence results, and multi-toolbox verification outcomes. Table 1 reports CORA verification times of 423.45 seconds for the standard agent and 1.99 seconds for the set-based agent. The retained attack-return plots are also revised between v1 Figure 6 and v2 Figure 7. The original training-time values remain unchanged in v2 Table 2.

M1.justification: The SA-SC and SA-PC procedures retain zonotope propagation, the center-error plus diameter regression loss, weighted set-based policy gradients, and the actor-only simplification. The gradient factors are rearranged equivalently, and the expanded exposition does not establish a new method component or training procedure.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, method explanations, and evaluation narrative. It moves the probabilistic derivations into Appendix B, consolidates benchmark descriptions in Appendix C, brings the regression-loss proof into the main text, and introduces dedicated related-work and limitations sections. The presentation now emphasizes gradient sets and verified performance.

P2.justification: The paper changes from a two-column layout to a predominantly single-column journal layout. v2 adds set-propagation and gradient illustrations, verification and Hopper runtime tables, and numerous sensitivity and learning-history plots. Existing experimental figures are enlarged or restructured, while the probability-density illustration and 2D quadrotor results are relocated and relabeled.

R1.justification: The basic positioning against pointwise adversarial training remains. v2 adds discussion and citations concerning conservative smoothing, randomized smoothing, model-based certification, alternative verification tools, and reachset-conformant modeling. Much of the dedicated related-work section relocates earlier introductory material; Koller et al.'s preprint-to-publication update is the same underlying work.

T1.justification: The central loss derivations and expectation-preservation proof are retained, largely in v2 Appendix B. v2 adds a polynomial runtime bound and proof in Proposition 4, formulates the objective using adversary-dependent state visitation, explicitly restricts the expectation-preservation proposition to ReLU networks, and revises the sign in the verified-return expression. These are bounded additions and corrections to the existing theoretical framework.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central verifiability claim through additional robust-RL baselines, verification across four toolboxes, and sensitivity and convergence studies. Explicit confidence intervals and substantive limitations make the evidence easier to assess, especially the distinction between empirical Hopper robustness and formal certification. The Hopper runtime caption understates overhead—Table 4 reports 343.56 versus 44.70 seconds for SA-PC and PA-PC—but this limited weakness does not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and qualification.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same set-based reinforcement learning work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable, allowing content to be matched despite substantial reorganization and formatting changes.

after.justification: v2 retains original control experiments and reports additional baseline comparisons, verification-toolbox evaluations, Hopper-v2 experiments, and hyperparameter studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original control experiments, including verified-return curves, adversarial-attack evaluations, training runtimes, and the appendix's 2D quadrocopter results.

results.title: Training Verifiably Robust Agents Using Set-Based Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: v1 chiefly claims interpretable bias discovery and model diagnosis. v2 adds competitive or state-of-the-art debiasing performance as an explicit abstract and introduction contribution when SaMyNa is coupled with GroupDRO. The abstract also drops v1's 'first tool' novelty assertion. Training-time and inference-time diagnosis remain core claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive limitations concerning inherited captioner biases and human interpretation (Sec. 5.6), plus retraining and computational restrictions on automatic thresholds (Appendix F). It expands explanations of imbalanced embedding aggregation and B2T's filtering and sampling failures. The earlier explanation attributing stronger similarity scores to larger text encoders is dropped.

D1.justification: v2 supplies the exact captioning prompt, confidence-based selection of misclassified examples, preprocessing source, BAR GroupDRO hyperparameters, timing hardware and batch size, and human-survey instructions. E1.justification: The four image benchmarks and their classification tasks remain, including balanced Waterbirds and the existing ImageNet-A cases. The new 20-participant keyword-annotation study on three retained datasets adds a limited human-task and population extension (Sec. 5.4).

E2.justification: v2 adds a debiasing comparison against ERM, LISA, GroupDRO, George, JTT, CNC, LfF, DebiAN and B2T+GDRO (Table 1), largely using cited baseline results. Appendix F adds a randomized-label control. Captioning is reported as using one generic prompt instead of v1's dataset-specific prompts; this establishes a reported setting revision, without proving which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test removal of shared-feature subtraction, joint hyperparameter effects, captioner adequacy, B2T sample efficiency and failure cases, and randomized-label threshold calibration. The original aligned/conflicting accuracy diagnostic is removed. ViT, balanced-Waterbirds, nails-versus-mushrooms and k analyses already existed in v1; their relocation is not an addition.

E5.justification: Appendix F newly estimates a randomized-label null distribution and uses its maximum for class-specific thresholds, with distribution standard deviations reported. This adds statistical calibration. Plus/minus reporting already existed in v1 Table 12; v2's additional error-bearing rows do not establish a new uncertainty practice or increased runs. Neither version specifies run or seed counts.

E6.justification: v1 Table 1's vanilla subgroup accuracies disappear; v2 Table 1 adds GroupDRO results, including 90.60 and 90.62 worst-group accuracy on CelebA and Waterbirds, and 71.26 average accuracy on BAR. Human, captioner and B2T results are added. Existing keyword outputs also change, such as CelebA's woman score from 0.48667 to 0.39947. These are revised outputs under changed reported settings, not established same-setting gains.

M1.justification: The core discovery pipeline remains, but v2 adds CLIP-based subgroup pseudo-labeling followed by GroupDRO training (Sec. 4.3), substantially extending the procedure to mitigation. Appendix F introduces an optional randomized-label threshold-selection procedure. Section 3.2.5 also replaces explicit target-class keyword filtering with allowing users to disregard such keywords.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: existing ViT, balanced-Waterbirds, nails-versus-mushrooms and k analyses move into a new main-text analysis section, while visual feedback moves to Appendix A. Contributions and method explanations are rewritten and expanded, and the appendices are reorganized around comparisons, ablations, survey details and calibration.

P2.justification: v2 adds extensive comparison and human-study tables, caption examples, ablation plots and calibration histograms. It combines the Waterbirds and CelebA plots, redraws the pipeline diagram, incorporates existing heatmaps into Figure 1, expands the appendix heatmap examples, and introduces landscape result tables. Table 5 has a localized clipping problem.

R1.justification: B2T was already cited in v1, but v2 substantially expands positioning against it around validation requirements, captioning cost, keyword filtering and modality flexibility (Introduction and Appendix D). It revises the description from captioning the training set to the validation set. New references include Guimard et al.'s classifier-to-bias framework, margin-based noisy-label work, ClipCap and additional debiasing comparators.

T1.justification: v2 explicitly adds the binary-class symmetry argument: centered class embeddings point in opposite directions, producing opposite cosine scores and reversed keyword rankings (Appendices C.2.4 and D). The principal equations otherwise retain their mathematical substance; expanded averaging explanations and notation changes do not constitute new theory.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's lack of direct comparative validation through B2T comparisons and downstream GroupDRO tests, supplemented by human judgments, targeted ablations and explicit captioner limitations. These strengthen evidence for usefulness and interpretability despite removal of the original subgroup-accuracy diagnostic. Remaining weaknesses include unspecified run counts and overbroad superiority wording: Table 1 gives Waterbirds worst-group accuracy of 90.62 for SaMyNa versus 90.70 for B2T+GDRO.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SaMyNa, with matching core methods and benchmarks. Their main text and appendices support reliable comparison, including the rotated tables. Clipped BAR scores in v2 Table 5 are available fully in Table 25.

after.justification: v2 retains original bias-discovery experiments and adds debiasing results, direct B2T comparisons, a human annotation study, captioner comparisons and additional ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original keyword-discovery experiments, subgroup accuracies, visualizations, and appendix ablations on Waterbirds, CelebA, BAR and ImageNet-A.

results.title: Say My Name: a Model's Bias Discovery Framework

C1.justification: The central algorithmic and consistency contributions remain. v2 narrows the introduction's claim of absent continuous-exploration benchmarking to limited prior literature and adds explicit claims of no pre-training and small, constant cost per training trajectory.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking poorer higher-dimensional performance to reduced replay diversity, contrasts refreshed MetaGFN samples with fixed nested-sampling samples, and explains replay-frequency tradeoffs. The dependence on suitable low-dimensional collective variables and the alanine convergence failure case remain acknowledged.

D1.justification: v2 replaces the code placeholder with a specific MetaGFN repository address and supplies a nested-sampling implementation address. It adds Local Search reconstruction settings and higher-dimensional policy and grid-resolution details. Most existing implementation, hardware, and training-time information is retained and consolidated.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from three environments to five through new three- and four-dimensional grids with eight and sixteen modes. The retained two-dimensional grid also changes its mode coordinates from ±7 to ±10. The line and alanine-dipeptide environments remain.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates on-policy training, noisy exploration, and Thompson sampling. v2 Figure 5 adds Local Search GFlowNets to the comparisons and nested sampling to alanine dipeptide and the grid environments. Nested sampling is explicitly excluded from the line experiment.

E3.justification: Grid batch size changes from 64 to 128. New higher-dimensional experiments use longer trajectories, two-component policies, and coarser metadynamics grids. v2 also reports a common replay admission threshold of 10^-3, replacing v1's grid and alanine-specific thresholds of 10^-4 and 10^-10. These are reported setting revisions, without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix D.2 and Figure 8 add a line-environment sensitivity study varying replay-buffer and metadynamics frequencies. The earlier trajectory-regeneration/noise ablations, KDE exploration analysis, and alanine best/worst-run cases are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: The main comparisons retain means and standard-error bands over ten repeats. v2 removes v1's conflicting prose describing these bands as standard deviations and explicitly reports standard deviations over ten repeats for the new sensitivity plot. No increase in repeats for existing experiments or new significance testing is established.

E6.justification: v2 Figure 5 adds baseline and higher-dimensional results and revises the two-dimensional grid curves under changed settings. New findings include nested sampling outperforming MetaGFN on the three-dimensional grid with DB loss, while Figure 8 favors replay frequency 2. Alanine mode counts in Table 1 remain identical. Revised grid curves do not establish same-setting performance gains over v1.

M1.justification: The KDE-based Adapted Metadynamics procedure and MetaGFN's backward sampling, replay, and on-policy training remain unchanged. v2's Algorithm 2 matches v1's Appendix D Algorithm 3; regenerating trajectories was already the variant used in v1's main experiments.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites the exploration and collective-variable background, divides the method into dedicated subsections, and separates environment descriptions from results. Experimental appendices are reorganized into one Appendix D with common settings, while algorithm descriptions are integrated into their relevant sections.

P2.justification: v2 adds a metadynamics schematic and sensitivity plot, combines three separate performance figures into an expanded fifteen-panel Figure 5, and relocates the MetaGFN pseudocode into the main text. The paired alanine energy/KDE display is split between the main text and appendix, alongside extensive layout and typography changes.

R1.justification: The introduction substantially develops positioning against Sendera et al.'s off-policy diffusion-sampler training and gradient-based MCMC approaches. New references and discussion cover nested sampling, local credit assignment, and collective-variable learning methods. This changes the account of related research beyond bibliography formatting.

T1.justification: Definition 2.1(iv) adds an explicit requirement that reaching the sink be guaranteed within a bounded number of steps. Theorem 3.1, the appendix lemmas, and the core convergence argument are retained; most proof edits concern indices and coordinate notation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited comparative evaluation through two additional exploration baselines, harder grid environments, and a frequency sensitivity study. These results better establish both MetaGFN's advantages and its dimensionality limitations. Stronger research positioning and concrete code-access information further improve the paper, although the core theoretical argument remains largely unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MetaGFN work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments across five environments, additional baseline comparisons, and a new hyperparameter sensitivity study in Appendix D.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on the line, two-dimensional grid, and alanine-dipeptide environments, including repeated training runs and supplementary analyses in Appendices E–G.

results.title:
MetaGFN: Exploring Distant Modes with Adapted Metadynamics for
  Continuous GFlowNets

C1.justification: The convergence and generalized-smoothness claims remain, but v2 adds explicit claims of superior symmetric-estimator stochastic complexity and competitive classification performance. Its abstract and contributions also assert scalability on activation-heavy CNNs and Transformers with a flat memory footprint, substantially extending v1's synthetic-validation and comparable-cost positioning.

C2.justification: v2 develops an activation-storage explanation for memory advantages and interprets Omniglot results through adaptation budgets and inner-solver differences. Section 7 adds strong-convexity and hyperparameter-tuning limitations, while Appendix A gives perturbation-scale and regularization guidance. v1's limitations mainly concern solving two inner problems and the memory cost of automatic differentiation.

D1.justification: Appendix D adds architectures, query counts, learning-rate search information, regularization and perturbation values, conjugate-gradient settings, sequential execution, and GPU-memory measurement procedures. v1 mainly supplies quadratic formulas and synthetic settings. Some retained-experiment documentation is lost when v2 shortens Figure 1's caption, including its outer-GD and learning-rate-tuning explanation.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates only synthetic linear regression. v2 adds nonlinear MNIST-1D 3-way 5-shot classification and Omniglot 5-way 1-shot and 5-shot classification, substantially broadening the evaluated data and task requirements.

E3.justification: The new experiments introduce episodic classification protocols with 10 query examples per class for MNIST-1D and 15 for Omniglot, five adaptation steps, and neural-network configurations. They also introduce peak-GPU-memory measurements while varying ConvNet channels, Transformer embedding dimensions and sequence lengths; v1 evaluates synthetic gradient error and loss.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's inner-step and conjugate-gradient comparisons, Appendix A adds controlled studies of perturbation scale versus solver precision and regularization versus adaptation distance and conditioning. Figures 3 and 6 add resource-scaling analyses across model width and input sequence length.

E5.justification: v2 first reports five-seed averaging and ± uncertainty values for its Omniglot results in Table 2; v1 provides no repeated-run or uncertainty reporting. This addition is limited to that evaluation, and v2 does not identify whether its ± values represent standard deviations or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: v2 adds classification outcomes, including FO-B-MAML accuracies of 99.24±0.29% and 99.70±0.17% on Omniglot 1-shot and 5-shot tasks, respectively. It also adds MNIST-1D accuracy and memory results, ES-MAML curves, and memory and sensitivity findings in Figures 3–6. These are new outcomes, not same-setting improvements over v1 scores.

M1.justification: The perturbed inner objective, forward and symmetric finite-difference estimators, and Algorithm 1 are retained. v1 already introduces both estimators and anticipates the symmetric bias rate. v2 adds theory and specifies sequential subproblem execution, without establishing a changed underlying meta-learning procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, theoretical discussion and conclusion are substantially rewritten. v2 introduces a dedicated related-work section, divides experiments into several subsections, and reorganizes the appendices around new empirical analyses while retaining and relocating existing proofs and quadratic details.

P2.justification: v2 adds five figures and an Omniglot results table, enlarges Figure 1 and adds ES-MAML traces, and restructures Table 1 with separate forward/symmetric rows and total-complexity reporting. The TMLR format also changes typography, text width, headers and placement throughout the paper.

R1.justification: The new related-work section positions FO-B-MAML against Kwon et al.'s first-order bilevel method using solver independence and symmetric bias rates. Section 3.4 adds a substantive ES-MAML comparison based on informed versus random perturbations. These additions substantially expand positioning beyond v1's emphasis on MAML, FO-MAML, Reptile and iMAML.

T1.justification: v2 adds higher-order regularity assumptions and an explicit symmetric-estimator bias derivation in Appendix C.3, formalizing a rate anticipated in v1. It revises bias and smoothness statements and extends convergence analysis to stochastic gradients and task sampling, reporting leading stochastic complexities of O(ε^-6) and O(ε^-5.5) for the forward and symmetric estimators.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's reliance on one synthetic example through nonlinear classification, five-seed Omniglot results, measured memory scaling, sensitivity studies and implementation details. The symmetric-bias derivation also strengthens the analytical documentation. Omniglot baselines are not matched reruns, and the 'flat memory' claim overstates Figures 3 and 6, which show growth; nevertheless, the expanded practical evidence and reproducibility information provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FO-B-MAML research, with readable text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Retained material can be matched across revisions, including proofs moved from Appendix A to C and experimental details moved from B to D.

after.justification: v2 retains synthetic experiments and reports original classification, memory-scaling and hyperparameter-sensitivity results in Section 6 and Appendices A–B.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic linear-regression experiments measuring meta-gradient approximation error and optimization loss in Section 5 and Figure 1.

results.title: A New First-Order Meta-Learning Algorithm with Convergence Guarantees

C1.justification: The central contributions remain joint foreground/background grounding, identity preservation and multi-subject customization. v3 removes v1's explicit 'first work' and 'first attempt' novelty assertions, narrowing its stated priority claims.

The stated attention procedure changes from multiplicative masking of logits and output in v1 Eqs. 7-8 to additive zero/negative-infinity masking of logits without the final output mask in v3 Eqs. 4-5. This establishes a localized revision to the described computation, without establishing implementation changes.

Masked cross-attention becomes subject-grounded cross-attention, the preliminary section moves to Appendix A, and experiments are reorganized around single-subject, multi-subject and complex-layout evaluation, with additional appendix sections.

Essential training settings and specific limitations also improve reproducibility and interpretation. results.title: GroundingBooth: Grounding Text-to-Image Customization

C1.justification: V2's introduction explicitly extends the claimed benefits to cross-modal retrieval, particularly text-to-image retrieval. The central contributions of comparison-based finetuning, comparative prompting, classification improvements, and embedding arithmetic remain substantially unchanged in the abstract and discussion.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations linking prompting benefits to low confidence, synthetic-comparison errors to missing caption details, and limited visual-feature gains to predominantly text-encoder benefits. It also argues robustness to noisy comparisons and applicability at larger scales. These refine the earlier explanations and limitations without replacing their central interpretation.

D1.justification: Appendices B.3–B.4 add exact judging prompts, inputs, and scoring rubrics; Section 4.4 specifies 77-token retrieval truncation. Existing hyperparameters, compute disclosures, and code access remain. However, v2 removes v1's explicit SDXL two-encoder replacement description and names ViT-G/14 instead of ViT-L/14, leaving the generation setup less clearly reconciled.

E1.justification: V2 adds Flickr30k image-to-text and text-to-image retrieval, Spot-the-Difference captioning and text-to-image-pair retrieval, and ImageNet-A/ImageNet-R distribution-shift evaluations. These substantially expand actual task and test-distribution coverage beyond the retained classification and generation experiments.

E2.justification: The original CLIP, COCO-finetuned CLIP, and Rewrite-finetuned CLIP comparisons remain. New Tables 12–13 add IDC + CLIP and the reported IFDC and VACC reference baselines against IDC + PC-CLIP; the latter reference scores are taken from prior work. This is a localized expansion for image-difference tasks.

E3.justification: Table 5 replaces CLIPScore with GPT-4o-mini ratings on a 1–5 scale. Added protocols include retrieval and captioning metrics, a 300-example synthetic-data audit, linear probes using 100 labeled instances per class, and ViT-H/14 evaluations. Table 5 changes its image count from 8000 to 800, but v1 Appendix D.1 already specified 800, so an actual sample reduction is not established. V2 Appendix D.1 also retains the old CLIPScore description.

E4.justification: V2 adds filtering/noise ablation, natural distribution-shift tests, encoder assessment through linear probing, larger-model evaluation, confidence-versus-prompting-gain analysis, and a synthetic-data quality audit. These address robustness, mechanism, and applicability questions beyond the retained COCO-versus-CUB and contrastive-versus-MSE ablations.

E5.justification: Section 4.3 adds statistical estimation of the correlation between classifier confidence and comparative-prompting gains across five datasets. Existing five-seed mean-plus-standard-error reporting is retained. No confidence interval or significance test accompanies the new correlation.

E6.justification: Original classification, embedding-distance, and loss/data-ablation values are retained. New results include Flickr30k text-to-image R@1 of 64.88 for CLIP versus 69.80 for PC-CLIP, and captioning CIDEr of 41.17 versus 43.09 for their IDC variants. Tables 14–17 add filtering, shift, probing, and scale results. Table 5 replaces CLIPScore values 0.532/0.542 with judge scores 1.75/2.33; these different metrics do not establish a cross-version performance gain.

M1.justification: The main contrastive objective, comparison-generation procedure, and comparative-prompting rule remain unchanged. Appendix C.6 adds an evaluated full-finetuning variant that also updates the image encoder for linear probing, whereas v1's experiments update only the text encoder.

P1.justification: Most original prose and method exposition are retained, with localized clarifications, an added prompting example, and acknowledgments. Appendices A–C are reordered from generation/experiments/details to details/generation/experiments, and new experimental subsections are inserted. This is a limited narrative revision rather than a comprehensive rewrite.

P2.justification: V2 adopts TMLR typography and page layout, enlarges and relocates retained displays, and introduces boxed prompts. It adds seven experimental tables and a synthetic-quality histogram, while revising Table 5's metric label and caption. The original qualitative generation grids are retained and renumbered, not newly generated evidence.

R1.justification: Related work adds targeted discussion of image-difference captioning, citing Jhamtani and Berg-Kirkpatrick, Park, Guo, and Hu, and distinguishes PC-CLIP as incorporating differences into embeddings. References also expand for new benchmarks and comparators, while OpenCLIP and eDiff-I citations disappear. The overall research positioning remains similar.

T1.justification: The objectives and mathematical definitions in Equations (1)–(5), including difference-based classification and comparative prompting, are unchanged. No new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical validation through retrieval and image-difference tasks, while the synthetic-data audit and filtering ablation directly examine previously weakly tested supervision-quality assumptions. Probing, scale, and shift evaluations further establish the approach's scope. These gains outweigh localized reporting weaknesses, including inconsistent image-generation metric/encoder descriptions and occasional overstatements of mixed results in the new tables.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PC-CLIP and comparative prompting. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and matchable despite appendix reordering and substantial experimental additions.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds original retrieval, captioning, synthetic-data quality, robustness, linear-probing, and model-scale evaluations.

before.justification: V1 reports original difference-based and zeroshot classification experiments, embedding analyses, image-generation results, and appendix ablations.

results.title: Finetuning CLIP to Reason about Pairwise Differences

C1.justification: The introduction's main contribution and the conclusion broaden GenCAD from image-conditioned generation to both image- and sketch-conditioned generation. The abstract also shifts its superiority claim from precision and modifiability to conditional and unconditional generation. Reconstruction and the greater-than-15-fold retrieval claim remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations linking BrepGen's stronger MMD/JSD and the sketch model's higher FID to diversity tradeoffs, plus reasons for selecting four CSR layers and ResNet-18. These explanations accompany new evidence rather than establishing causal mechanisms. Existing limitations concerning vocabulary, invalid geometry, and clean isometric inputs remain.

D1.justification: v2 documents sketch creation and the ablation ViT's six attention layers, 16 heads, and patch size 32, and clarifies SOL-token handling. Appendix C removes component-class and normalization snippets. Core training and hardware details are retained, with the old Appendix D moved to E. The encoder ablation's image-versus-sketch labeling remains ambiguous.

E1.justification: v2 adds sketch-conditioned retrieval and generation alongside rendered-image conditioning. Section 3.2 describes 845,105 synthetic sketches made with Canny edges and Gaussian blur. This materially expands evaluated input conditions, although the underlying DeepCAD geometry remains unchanged and real hand-drawn sketches are not established as evaluated.

E2.justification: Table 3 adds evaluated BrepGen and ContrastCAD + RRE comparisons to DeepCAD and SkexGen, substantially expanding the principal generation comparison. BrepGen was cited but not included in this comparison in v1. The appendix comparison with One-2-3-45, Shap-E, and DreamGaussian is retained.

E3.justification: Section 3.2 revises the reported image count from 840,947 to 845,105 while retaining CAD train/validation/test counts. New experiments introduce sketch preprocessing and CSR-depth and encoder-architecture configurations. Existing training budgets, metrics, and point-sampling settings remain unchanged; the revised count does not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Appendix D tests CSR encoder/decoder depths of two, four, and six layers and compares ResNet-10/18/34 with ViT for retrieval. These provide quantitative architecture analyses absent from v1. Figure 13 also adds an Onshape feature-editing case study. Existing sequence-length analysis and failure examples are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report retrieval repetitions of 1000, 10, 3, and 3 for the four candidate-set sizes, with the same plus/minus reporting practice. New sketch and encoder-ablation rows extend that practice without introducing new uncertainty procedures, seed reporting, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Existing reconstruction, image-retrieval, generation, and FID values are retained. New sketch-generation results are COV 82.59, MMD 1.33, JSD 3.53, and FID 0.32; sketch retrieval at 2048 candidates is 60.77 ± 0.75. Added competitor rows give BrepGen the lowest reported MMD/JSD, 1.05/1.22. Tables 5–6 add architecture-ablation outcomes.

M1.justification: The four-stage CSR, contrastive encoder, diffusion-prior, and CAD-decoder procedure remains unchanged, as do its losses and selected architectures. Sketch experiments reuse this framework. Explicitly documenting prepending the SOL token clarifies decoding rather than establishing a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract is rewritten, one related-work subsection is removed, terminology and grammar receive localized edits, and pseudocode is shortened. A new ablation appendix shifts the training-details appendix lettering. Most explanatory prose and the main section sequence are retained, so this is not an extensive narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 substantially redesigns the title page and overview, combines the diffusion schematic's panels, and reorganizes large qualitative galleries into compact figures incorporating sketches. It expands comparison tables, adds two ablation tables and an editing figure, and adds a sketch FID bar. These are extensive visual changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 removes the neural-representation survey subsection and associated references, while adding works including DiffCAD, ContrastCAD, ViT, volumetric design, and reverse engineering. Section 5.2 now acknowledges existing CAD-model retrieval and confines the claimed gap to CAD-program retrieval. The overall generative-CAD positioning remains similar.

T1.justification: The CAD representation, objectives, and mathematical evaluation definitions are substantively retained. Replacing the parameter-vector length notation with Np is equivalent for the fixed-dimensional representation. Omitting the explicit standard Chamfer-distance formula does not establish a changed metric. Neither version supplies new theoretical propositions or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support: Appendix D supplies previously missing architecture ablations, Table 3 broadens competitor coverage and reveals performance tradeoffs, and Figure 13 demonstrates the claimed editability. Synthetic-sketch experiments provide evidence for the expanded input scope, while reorganized figures improve readability. Broad superiority wording and ambiguous image/sketch ablation labels limit precision, but do not outweigh these substantial gains in validation and assessability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GenCAD by the same authors. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds sketch-conditioned experiments, architecture ablations, and a CAD-editing demonstration.

before.justification: v1 reports original CAD reconstruction, image-based retrieval, and conditional and unconditional generation results in Section 5, with additional qualitative comparisons in the appendices.

results.title:
GenCAD: Image-Conditioned Computer-Aided Design Generation with
  Transformer-Based Contrastive Representation and Diffusion Priors

C1.justification: The central contributions remain broadcast notation and a decomposition built from it. v2 explicitly prioritizes notation and mathematical formalization, labels BD a preliminary, noncentral proof of concept, and disclaims empirical superiority. This qualifies the contribution without replacing its core.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly acknowledges that BD-generated synthetic data favor BD by construction, treats traffic results as preliminary, and discusses zero-denominator failures and unresolved initialization sensitivity. It also adds substantive guidance on when broadcast notation, explicit shape annotation, or Named Tensor Notation is preferable.

D1.justification: v2 supplies demonstration-code and traffic-data links, clarifies the SNR ground-truth target, adds Julia broadcasting examples, and provides operator-entry instructions in Appendix F. Experimental noise magnitudes, solver budgets, and repetition details remain unspecified.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates only a synthetic 32-by-32-by-32 tensor. v2 adds a real traffic-speed tensor of shape 32-by-21-by-24, substantially extending coverage beyond data generated by BD itself. The added normalization and blending examples are algebraic illustrations, not evaluated tasks.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparators remain canonical polyadic decomposition, Tucker decomposition, and tensor-ring decomposition. v2 extends this same comparator set to traffic data; the additional related-work discussions do not introduce experimentally evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: The new traffic experiment treats the original tensor as ground truth, adds Gaussian noise, and evaluates reconstruction SNR across model sizes. No revision to the existing synthetic evaluation protocol is stated. The explicit SNR formula primarily documents the previously used metric.

E4.justification: Neither version reports separate ablations, initialization-sensitivity tests, controlled robustness studies, or error analyses. v2 extends the reconstruction-versus-parameter comparison to traffic data without adding such an analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version specifies experimental repetition counts or random seeds, or reports confidence intervals, variability estimates, or significance tests. Both versions present performance curves without uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: v2 Figure 5(b) adds substantive real-data findings: BD generally lies between CPD/TRD and Tucker over much of the parameter range. Several synthetic BD values also change, including approximately 44.4 to 45.4 dB near 27,600 parameters, while the baseline curves and synthetic ranking persist. These are revised reported values, with no documented explanation for the revision.

M1.justification: The broadcast operator, BD and summed-BD models, least-squares objective, and ALS/HALS updates are retained from v1 Section VII in v2 Section 5. The explicit shape conventions and initialization cautions clarify the existing procedure without establishing an algorithm change.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the abstract and introduction, adds an explicit contribution list and conclusion, reorganizes operator properties and examples, and expands related work into thematic subsections. The appendices are reorganized, and the NumPy explanation is rewritten with parallel Julia examples.

P2.justification: The document changes from two columns to one, adds tensor-network diagrams in Figures 2-4 and 7, expands the performance figure into synthetic/traffic panels, and adds the operator-input Table 2. Existing diagrams and the symbol-conflict table are retained with relocation or redesign.

R1.justification: The brief related-work discussion becomes a substantive comparison with existing tensor products and notation systems, especially Named Tensor Notation in Section 6.3. New references cover tensor-network diagrams, normalization methods, einx, and TensorLy, materially expanding research positioning.

T1.justification: v2 adds the Cauchy-Schwarz norm bound and its proof in Theorem 3.1 and Appendix A, broadcast-operator identities in Appendix C, and formal tensor-network and Khatri-Rao relationships. The existing least-squares derivation is retained as Appendix D, rather than being a new proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the mathematical exposition and positioning through explicit shape conventions, a proved norm bound, unified normalization examples, and comparison with Named Tensor Notation. Construction-bias caveats and mixed traffic results also make the empirical interpretation better calibrated than v1's synthetic-only demonstration. These gains outweigh the localized fold/unfold inconsistency in Eq. (49), although experimental settings and uncertainty reporting remain incomplete.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same broadcast-product formalism and broadcast decomposition. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support a reliable comparison, including material moved or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: v2 Section 5.3 and Figure 5 report synthetic reconstruction results and an additional experiment using real traffic-speed data.

before.justification: v1 Section VII-C and Figure 2 report original synthetic-tensor reconstruction experiments comparing broadcast decomposition with CPD, Tucker, and tensor-ring decomposition.

results.title: Broadcast Product: Redefining Shape-aligned Element-wise Multiplication and Beyond

C1.justification: The central contribution remains a unified AR model for causal queries involving complex confounders and sequential actions. V3 narrows the abstract's 'any DAG' wording to 'a large class of DAGs', emphasizes queries beyond standard RL, and strengthens the introduction's comparison with prior work to a claim that all prior methods require fixed-length covariates and actions.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive explanations of randomized ordering as protection against overfitting, the flexibility gained by retaining later actions, and RL's failure on partial interventions because it optimizes a policy rather than modeling the remaining-action distribution. It interprets the new scaling and sensitivity results. Known-graph, observed-variable, and prefix limitations remain, with a new suggestion to impute unconfounded missing values using mask tokens.

D1.justification: V3 adds a project-code URL, clarifies BERT's final-token masking procedure, and documents the continuous-input embedding used for IHDP. Appendix A updates maze architecture, training, and hardware details, including the change from a 1080 Ti to a Tesla T4. Most chess and PeerRead training information is retained, although the PeerRead weight-decay selection rule is removed.

E1.justification: V3 adds IHDP, covering treatment-effect estimation with mixed numerical covariates and continuous outcomes. Maze evaluation adds queries conditioned on the starting row and environments with up to five spatial dimensions. V1's 6x6 red-versus-blue path scenario with a shifted exit distribution is removed; chess and PeerRead coverage remains.

E2.justification: V3 introduces a deep Q-learning offline RL comparator for maze queries; v1's 'offline' condition instead evaluated an AR model trained on policy-generated data. IHDP adds comparisons with NN, random forest, causal forest, and CRNET in Table 5. The chess MLP and PeerRead MLP/C-BERT comparators are retained.

E3.justification: The main maze experiment replaces randomized/optimal-policy mixtures with a fixed goal, distance-weighted starting positions, and an explicit stochastic movement policy. It evaluates exactly six moves and four-move prefix interventions, with revised model configurations and training budgets; dataset size changes from 50,000 per dataset to 10,000. PeerRead's stated buzziness definition adds 'embed'. IHDP introduces absolute/relative ATE-error evaluation on random train-test splits.

E4.justification: V3 adds controlled sensitivity studies of maze dimensionality and path length, PeerRead training-set size, and GPT model size. It removes the earlier maze policy-mixture analysis and 6x6 two-path case study. The right-versus-down Monte Carlo example is partly retained in Appendix B, and the chess distribution-shift experiment remains.

E5.justification: V3 first reports three-trial means and standard errors for DARCIE's PeerRead ATT estimates, adds uncertainty to training-size experiments, and reports IHDP means and standard errors across 30 random splits. The existing 1,000-repeat chess Monte Carlo reporting remains. Figure 10's caption says standard deviation while Appendix D says standard error, leaving its band definition ambiguous.

E6.justification: PeerRead Table 1 changes BERT's relative errors from 16/15/18% to 37/34/43%, and GPT's from 20/25/29% to 34/19/10%, reversing their ranking. These revised trial summaries accompany a changed reported buzziness definition, so they are not established same-setting gains or losses. V1's GPT point estimates also appear in v3 Table 3. New maze, sensitivity, and IHDP results substantially expand the evidence; IHDP ATE error is 0.1104 for DARCIE versus 0.1085 for causal forest. Chess Table 2 is unchanged.

M1.justification: Sequencification, the next-token likelihood objective, and Monte Carlo intervention estimators remain unchanged. Appendix E adds a feedforward embedding layer for continuous IHDP values, a limited input-processing adaptation. Expanded explanations of randomized topological ordering describe an existing procedure.
