P1.justification: V3 extensively rewrites the introduction, methodological explanations, experimental narrative, and conclusion. Related work moves from Section 5 to Section 2, and the framework receives a more detailed subsection structure, including a dedicated randomized-ordering explanation. The broader-impact statement is removed and acknowledgements are added.

P2.justification: V3 changes the document template and typography, redraws and combines the maze/chess illustrations, and replaces the main maze displays with AR/RL violin plots and heatmaps. It adds scaling and training-size plots and new tables. The right-versus-down display is reduced and moved to the appendix; the original PeerRead causal diagram and 6x6 illustrations are removed.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion expands substantially to longitudinal and continuous-treatment methods, including Frauen, Bica, Nie, and Zhu, and causal generative models from Xia and Rahman/Kocaoglu. Positioning now explicitly contrasts unified multi-query learning with componentwise generative modeling. References supporting possible non-prefix generation strategies are removed; publication-year updates to retained works are not substantive additions.

T1.justification: V3 Section 3.1 explicitly introduces unconfoundedness and positivity assumptions, including the requirement that p(a,x,y) be positive for all triplets. V1 did not formally state these assumptions. The principal likelihood, adjustment, and Monte Carlo equations remain equivalent, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens validation of the framework's claimed flexibility: v1 lacked a maze comparator, systematic scaling tests, and uncertainty for its main PeerRead estimates. The added comparisons, sensitivity studies, and IHDP evaluation make applicability and reliability easier to assess, while clearer exposition and a code link improve accessibility. These gains outweigh the removed maze case study and remaining reporting weaknesses: PeerRead's superiority language exceeds Table 1's support, and Figure 10 inconsistently labels its uncertainty bands.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same autoregressive causal-inference framework. The complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support matching retained, revised, and added content.

after.justification: V3 reports original results for those environments and adds maze scaling, PeerRead sensitivity experiments, and IHDP treatment-effect evaluation.

before.justification: V1 reports original maze, chess-endgame, and semi-synthetic PeerRead experiments, including additional results in Appendices B-D.

results.title: Deep Autoregressive Models as Causal Inference Engines

C1.justification: The central PC-framework and derivative-free EnKG contributions remain. The introduction drops v1's blanket statement that competing methods fail to produce reasonable Navier–Stokes predictions and reframes the contribution around superiority on difficult nonlinear tasks and computational efficiency relative to derivative-free methods with expensive forward models.

C2.justification: v2 replaces v1's blanket imaging-superiority statement with acknowledgment of DPG's advantages on linear tasks. It adds nonconvex/local-optimum qualifications, proposed smoothing and likelihood explanations for gradient-based comparisons, and interpretations of prior-quality sensitivity and solver failures. The existing posterior-uncertainty and ensemble-runtime limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link, benchmark-specific ensemble sizes, resource measurements, and gradient-baseline tuning details, including the guidance-search range and A100-40GB memory limitation. Table 2 newly explains that starred results exclude one or two unstable test cases. These are substantial disclosures; they do not establish changes to previously undisclosed settings.

E1.justification: Both evaluate the same four restoration tasks on FFHQ64/256, sparse noisy Navier–Stokes inversion, and GRMHD black-hole imaging. The reduced-data prior experiment uses the existing Navier–Stokes population and task, rather than adding dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds DiffPIR to FFHQ256 comparisons and DPS and PnP-DM to Navier–Stokes and black-hole comparisons (Tables 8–10). FFHQ256 DPS results are relocated from Table 1, not newly added. The FFHQ64 DPS comparator in v1 Table 5 is removed.

E3.justification: New protocols sweep guidance and diffusion-query budgets, train a weaker prior using one-tenth of the data for 15k steps, tune gradient-based comparators, and measure runtime and memory. Table 7 also changes both GSG methods' reported query budgets from 20,000 to 10,000 for FFHQ256 deblurring and phase retrieval; unchanged scores do not establish that these experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds guidance-scale and diffusion-query ablations, prior-quality robustness tests, covariance-trace checks of Assumption 3, and an EnKG–EKI error-versus-cost analysis. Existing ensemble-size analyses remain. The radial power-spectrum analysis in v1 Figure 3 is removed rather than relocated.

E5.justification: Both use sample standard deviations for Navier–Stokes results and best/worst-particle bands for ensemble-size analysis. v2 extends standard-deviation reporting to added comparisons and ablations, without reporting new seeds, repetition counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or a changed uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Core EnKG reconstruction scores remain unchanged, but Tables 8–12 add substantial results: DiffPIR achieves 22.20 versus EnKG's 20.06 phase-retrieval PSNR, and the weaker prior raises EnKG's relative L2 error from 0.120 to 0.169. New timings and failure outcomes are reported. Table 2 revises EnKG's total diffusion evaluations from 2695k to 3342k and SCG's forward evaluations from 512k to 384k; FFHQ64 DPS results disappear.

M1.justification: Algorithm 2 corrects the guidance summand's centered particle from x_i^(j) to x_i^(k), matching the ensemble member being summed. This changes the printed update formula, while the prediction step, ODE likelihood approximation, and correction design remain intact. The PDFs do not establish a corresponding implementation change.

P1.justification: The introduction's PC explanation is rewritten, background and related work are reorganized, and method and experimental interpretations receive substantial revisions. Separate limitations and conclusion sections are merged, and new appendix sections organize additional comparisons and robustness evidence. The changes extend beyond local copyediting.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a different publication layout and redraws Figure 1. Figure 3 replaces the spectrum panel with a cost–error comparison; Figures 5 and 6 expand into additional panels. Table 2 gains a runtime column, Tables 8–12 are added, and FFHQ256 gradient comparisons move into a separate table. Figure 7 is reformatted using the same examples.

R1.justification: The new related-work section substantially expands positioning against ensemble Kalman regularization/convergence research and earlier predictor-corrector diffusion methods. It distinguishes EnKG's forward-model correction from sampling schemes such as those of Song, Lezama, and Bradley–Nakkiran. Additional gradient-guidance and fast-sampling references extend the discussion, while several generic optimization references are removed.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 revises the central convergence argument: v2 introduces a multiplicative contraction bound, explicitly scopes Lemma 1 to correction iterations, and states Proposition 1's approximation after sufficient iterations. It also corrects Taylor-approximation reasoning and ensemble indices. Section 4.2 introduces Moore–Penrose treatment of singular covariance matrices, while Section 3 adds the linear-surrogate formulation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation and reproducibility through competitive gradient-based comparisons, sensitivity and prior-quality tests, and code, tuning, and resource disclosures. It also qualifies v1's unsupported blanket imaging-superiority statement. These address important evidence and reporting gaps. Removing the FFHQ64 DPS comparison and spectral analysis loses some evidence, and efficiency wording remains broader than Table 2's runtimes support, but the overall gains are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EnKG research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial additions and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds gradient-based comparisons, sensitivity analyses, prior-quality experiments, and computational measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-restoration, Navier–Stokes, and black-hole reconstruction experiments, including quantitative comparisons and appendix ablations.

results.title: Ensemble Kalman Diffusion Guidance: A Derivative-free Method for Inverse Problems

C1.justification: The central contribution remains malicious-prompt detection through unlabeled-data bootstrapping. V2's abstract and introduction add explicit robustness claims for lexical/syntactic variations and emphasize theoretical justification. The headline improvement changes from 13.21 percentage points over Perplexity to 5.39 over GPT-5.4 under different evaluations; the general superiority claim remains.

C2.justification: Section 3.3 introduces the explanation that classifier training suppresses nuisance variations missed by projection scoring. The layer interpretation changes from stronger upper-layer features on LLaVA to stronger intermediate-layer features on Qwen. V2 addresses v1's typography and distribution-shift limitations experimentally and adds substantive qualifications about benchmark-defined maliciousness, context-dependent labels, false positives, and deployment as one layer of defense.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-access link, dataset-count tables, validation-selection criteria, extensive baseline prompts, adaptive-attack settings, and deployment-mode explanations. Appendix J adds measured latency and memory overhead. The reported environment changes from Python 3.8.5/PyTorch 1.13.1/A6000 to Python 3.10.19/PyTorch 2.6.0/A100.

E1.justification: V1's ImageNet-based adversarial meta-instructions and XSTest-based visual jailbreak evaluation are replaced by mixtures using JailBreakV-28K, GPT4V-Caption, VLGuard, MLLMGuard, and MSSBench. V2 additionally evaluates abnormal benign inputs from MMMU and scenarios involving paraphrases, typographic instructions, and detector-targeted attacks.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated comparators including HiddenDetect, ASTRA, LlamaGuard3-Vision, LLaVAGuard, Ovis2-34B, InternVL3-78B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct. GPT-5.4 replaces GPT-4V in the main comparisons, and Appendix G adds GuardRank. The larger-backbone comparison also changes from Perplexity/MirrorCheck to HiddenDetect/ASTRA.

E3.justification: The main protocol changes from fixed-size mixtures at pi=0.01 to benchmark-specific mixtures at pi=0.005, with official or random 80/20 splits. Qwen 7B/72B replaces Phi-3 and LLaVA-13B coverage. Classifier training changes from 50 to 20 epochs, learning rate 0.05 to 0.005, and batch size 512 to 128. Validation becomes 100 labeled samples; new protocols include model-judged attack success and low-FPR detection metrics.

E4.justification: Beyond revised versions of existing layer, score, classifier, and benign-sample-count ablations, v2 adds benign paraphrase robustness, abnormal-input tests, same-source confounder controls, token-position/pooling comparisons, text-only controls, threshold sensitivity, pseudo-label quality, subspace alignment, and adaptive attacks. V1's smaller perturbation-radius sweep is removed; v2's white-box PGD experiment instead targets detector evasion.

E5.justification: Both main results tables report averages over five runs and use plus/minus uncertainty entries. V2 applies the same reporting style to additional results without introducing a different run-count policy, seed disclosure, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedure.

E6.justification: Most benchmark and ablation results are replaced under different conditions. For example, v1 reports 92.87 AUROC for LLaVA's meta-instruction average; v2 Table 1 reports averages of 93.00 for LLaVA and 94.79 for Qwen on new benchmark mixtures. New findings include 91.06 AUROC in the same-source control and 95.65/82.36 under typographic/white-box attacks. These are not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The centered, singular-value-weighted SVD scoring, pseudo-labeling, and classifier pipeline remain. Section 4.1 changes the classifier from a two-layer MLP with intermediate dimension 512 to a three-layer MLP with dimension 1024. This is a limited architectural revision rather than a new detection framework.

P1.justification: The introduction, problem formulation, method exposition, experimental narrative, and related work undergo extensive rewriting. V2 reorganizes the classifier discussion into a dedicated Section 3.3, moves qualitative analysis into Appendix B, and restructures the supplementary material. The title, author information, and terminology also change.

P2.justification: V2 retains the original projection sketch within an expanded three-panel Figure 2, reorganizes robustness and ablation plots, replaces qualitative displays, and redesigns the main comparison table with method categories and independent-detector groups. Numerous appendix tables and a threshold plot are added. The journal template also changes typography, headers, and author layout.

R1.justification: Section 5 substantially revises positioning around multimodal safety benchmarks, dedicated guard models, and activation-based detectors such as HiddenDetect and ASTRA. It expands distinctions from related representation/SVD approaches while removing much of v1's out-of-distribution-detection discussion and citations. These changes exceed bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: V2 adds Proposition 3.3 and Appendix K's covariance decomposition, alignment condition, top-k score-gap theorem, and proofs, substantially extending v1's mathematical definitions and intuitive SVD rationale. Definition 2.2 also changes maliciousness from prompts producing malicious outputs to an intention-based latent label and explicitly defines detection risk.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical support beyond v1's narrow optimization-based attacks, directly addressing its stated typography and distribution-shift limitations. Adaptive attacks, same-source controls, pseudo-label audits, and deployment metrics provide important checks on practical reliability. These gains outweigh the loss of earlier threat-specific results. Qualifications remain: some label-free wording conflicts with the disclosed labeled validation set, and Appendix K analyzes unweighted projection energy rather than directly proving properties of the implemented weighted score.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VLMGuard. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revisions to the evaluation.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark evaluations, robustness experiments, ablations, pseudo-label measurements, and computational-overhead results in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original detection experiments on LLaVA and Phi-3, including AUROC results, ablations, transfer evaluations, and attack-success measurements.

results.title: VLMGuard: Bootstrapping Malicious Prompt Detectors from Unlabeled Vision-Language Prompts in the Wild

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add superior MLP expressivity as an explicit theoretical contribution and extend the performance claim to distribution shifts. The claim of reproducing arbitrary target MLPs under rank conditions is substantially more specific than v1's informal statements about greater generality.

C2.justification: Appendix F.4 newly qualifies FS-Merge's advantage when models share initialization, noting that cheaper RegMean can perform similarly. F.6 identifies memory limitations preventing full FS-Merge evaluation on eight models. Existing core limitations remain. The new blanket robustness interpretation overstates Table 5: distillation has higher mean accuracy for Gaussian and shot noise in the CIFAR100/EuroSAT comparison.

D1.justification: v2 clarifies that BERT classification heads are trainable and documents model provenance, configurations and runtimes for added experiments. Tables 3–4 replace exact optimized-parameter counts with yes/no indicators. The code URL remains, but the footnote no longer states that models are available. Most original implementation details and hyperparameter grids are retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds CIFAR100-C corruption evaluation and merging across SUN397, Food101 and CIFAR100 (Tables 5 and 27), substantially extending input conditions and scene/food task coverage. The earlier MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, vision-classification and GLUE tasks remain; BERT coverage is not newly introduced.

E2.justification: Tables 3–4 add LoRA-based knowledge distillation at several ranks, providing a substantial parameter-efficient comparator to FS-Merge alongside full-model distillation. Existing MLP and BERT comparator sets remain in the appendices. Git Re-Basin is newly analyzed theoretically, not newly evaluated as an empirical baseline.

E3.justification: v2 introduces heterogeneous-pretraining, shared-initialization, five-severity corruption and eight-model evaluation protocols. The shared-initialization experiment uses average initialization. For the retained main four-model comparison, FS-Merge's reported rank changes from 32 to 24. The new large-dataset augmentation budget is inconsistent: Appendix F.5 states 100 augmented images per dataset, while Table 27 states 1000.

E4.justification: New analyses examine corruption robustness, dependence on pretraining strategy and shared initialization, and scaling to eight models. The original initialization, augmentation, local-versus-global and inner-feature analyses are retained; v1's Appendix H discussion becomes v2's G.3–G.5.

E5.justification: Table 5 newly reports means and standard deviations across five corruption severities. This measures cross-severity dispersion, not uncertainty across repeated training runs. The existing five-seed MLP experiments and three-seed BERT data-size error bars remain unchanged.

E6.justification: Tables 5 and 24–28 add substantial result blocks, while numerous retained scores change. For example, Table 1's FS-Merge accuracy changes from 84.52 to 85.83, and Table 3's DTD/EuroSAT per-task accuracy changes from 63.18 to 62.64. The BERT Average score for QQP/QNLI is corrected from 563.2 to 56.32. Results with changed ranks cannot establish same-setting performance improvements.

M1.justification: The merge/unmerge matrices, frozen source weights, reconstruction objectives, folding procedure and diagonal-plus-low-rank parameterization are retained. Sequential FS-Merge already appears in v1. The added evaluations use existing method variants.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial main-text passages are rewritten, and the attention-method explanation is condensed with details referenced in Appendix B. BERT evaluation gains a main-text subsection, the data-size subsection is integrated into vision results, and the conclusion becomes a broader discussion. Appendix discussions are also substantially reorganized.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a journal layout, redraws method schematics, expands captions and adds multiple experimental tables. Tables 3–4 gain LoRA rows and revised parameter columns; the main ViT-L table moves to the appendix, and a BERT subset is redisplayed in the main text. The existing data-size plots in Figures 4–7 are unchanged.

R1.justification: Appendix A adds an adapter/parameter-efficient-fine-tuning discussion and distinguishes FS-Merge from Wan et al.'s LLM knowledge fusion. Additional citations support corruption testing, new datasets, feature-rank assumptions and distillation. The established positioning relative to ZipIt, mode connectivity and model merging largely remains.

T1.justification: v2 adds Theorem 2.1 and Appendix H's definitions, expressivity theorem, proposition, separating example and proofs comparing FS-Merge with RegMean and Git Re-Basin under rank assumptions. v1 has no corresponding formal analysis. One new proof step needs correction: the displayed M in Eq. 26 has rank d, contrary to the following rank-at-most-r assertion when r is smaller than d.

improvement.justification: The main gain is substantially stronger empirical support for generality: LoRA-distillation comparisons, corruption tests, varied pretraining, larger tasks and eight-model merging address important gaps in v1's evaluation. The shared-initialization discussion also clarifies when cheaper methods suffice. These gains outweigh localized shortcomings, including Table 27's conflicting augmentation counts, Table 5's overbroad robustness interpretation and the rank error following Eq. 26; the added theory therefore requires correction.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FS-Merge research. Their main text, figures, tables, equations and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds corruption tests, alternative pretraining settings, larger-dataset evaluations and eight-model merging results.

before.justification: v1 reports original MLP, vision-transformer and BERT merging experiments, including accuracy measurements, data-size studies and appendix ablations.

results.title: Foldable SuperNets: Scalable Merging of Transformers with Different Initializations and Tasks

C1.justification: Locret-Q and over 2× prefill acceleration on query-driven tasks become explicit contributions. The abstract shifts its novelty claim from first comparable-model deployment on a single 4090 to first eviction framework compatible with chunked prefill. Applicability is narrowed from all transformer-based LLMs to decoder-only LLMs.

C2.justification: v2 explains vanilla Locret's weakness on query-dependent tasks and motivates query-aware eviction, while arguing that query-independent scoring suits multi-turn conversations. Appendix G distinguishes stabilizer requirements across retrieval and NLU tasks. Appendix M newly attributes throughput differences to system variation, although its consistently lower retaining-head throughput does not establish that explanation.

D1.justification: v2 expands reproducibility documentation with RULER backend and configuration details, extreme-context data construction, and conversation settings. It newly discloses pre-RoPE caching with continuous positional reassignment and SirLLM's CPU sorting operations. These disclosures do not establish changes to the original implementation; the original training recipe and code-access link remain.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained ∞Bench and L-Eval coverage, v2 evaluates query-dependent RULER tasks, English LongBench tasks, synthetic retrieval in approximately 10-million-token contexts, and multi-turn Rock-Paper-Scissors conversations. These substantially expand task requirements and input conditions.

E2.justification: v2 adds direct H2O and SnapKV comparisons in the scoring-consistency analysis, selected ∞Bench tasks, and RULER; SnapKV also appears in the budget sweep. PyramidKV is evaluated as a Locret combination. The original main benchmark comparator set remains unchanged.

E3.justification: New protocols include 128K RULER evaluation with separate prefill/decode measurements and a 6000-token Locret cache. RULER uses 500 examples per task except H2O, SirLLM, and vanilla Locret, which use 20. Additional protocols specify 50 extreme-context examples and 2000 conversation turns with different cache and stabilizer settings. Original main evaluation settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds local/global importance-consistency analysis, cache-budget and chunk-size sweeps, stabilizer sensitivity on QMSum, a retaining-head overhead ablation, and PyramidKV compatibility testing. Earlier training-data, head-width, retrieval-stabilizer, quantization, merging, and cache-pattern analyses are retained, often relocated.

E5.justification: Appendix M, Table 20 newly reports throughput as mean/standard deviation for inference with and without retaining heads. This adds explicit uncertainty reporting for a limited analysis; repetition counts, seeds, and significance-testing procedures are not provided.

E6.justification: Original main benchmark and RTX 4090 results are unchanged. New results include RULER scores of 75.54 for Locret-Q versus 72.97 for MInference, a LongBench average of 42.31 for Locret, and 100.00 on extreme-context retrieval, alongside new diagnostic and conversation results. New Tables 5 and 12 list Locret C.Debug as 29.71, unexplained against 27.92 in retained Table 1.

M1.justification: Section 4.4 introduces Locret-Q, which prepends query tokens when constructing training labels and during inference, enabling query-aware eviction. Appendix H also combines Locret with PyramidKV budget allocation. The original retaining-head architecture, losses, and base inference algorithm remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and method exposition are extensively rewritten. Query-driven evaluation replaces orthogonality as the third main experimental question; orthogonality moves to Appendix H and pseudocode to Appendix C. The title and conclusion change, and the appendices are substantially reorganized.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main layout, redraws the framework diagram, adds consistency and hyperparameter figures, and introduces numerous benchmark and diagnostic tables. Existing displays are relocated and restyled, including highlighted Locret rows. The original cache-pattern images and training curves are retained as Figures 7–9.

R1.justification: v2 substantially develops positioning around causal versus future-dependent scoring, streaming compatibility, and query-aware eviction, alongside its revised novelty claim. It adds substantive engagement with SnapKV, ShadowKV, DuoAttention, and PyramidKV, plus RULER and LongBench references, while removing several peripheral architecture and sparsity citations.

T1.justification: The cache-problem definitions, top-b theorem, and proof are retained from Appendix F as Appendix N. However, v2 removes Section 3.4's explicit cache/runtime memory bounds and corrects the training-label answer-token range from nq(d) ≤ p to nq(d) < p.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses gaps in v1's applicability evidence by exposing query-dependent failure, introducing and evaluating Locret-Q, directly comparing additional eviction methods, and testing sensitivity, extreme contexts, and multi-turn use. These targeted additions improve understanding beyond the unchanged main scores. Unequal RULER sample sizes, unexplained C.Debug discrepancies, and the overconfident timing interpretation weaken individual claims, but the clearer failure conditions and broader supporting evidence provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Locret and provide readable text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. The shared method, experiments, and appendix material can be matched reliably despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds RULER, LongBench, extreme-context retrieval, multi-turn conversation, sensitivity, and inference-overhead experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark accuracy, memory consumption, RTX 4090 throughput, training ablations, and cache-pattern analyses, including appendix results.

results.title:
Locret: Enhancing Eviction in Long-Context LLM Inference with Trained
  Retaining Heads on Consumer-Grade Devices

C1.justification: The central claims about combining weight standardization with channel attention, aggregation compatibility, and privacy utility remain. The novelty claim is narrowed: v1 says prior work had not designed heterogeneity-specific models and calls ANFR the first such broadly compatible method; v2 acknowledges FedConv and removes the conclusion's explicit 'first' claim.

C2.justification: v2 interprets baseline-tuned hyperparameters as yielding conservative performance estimates, discusses diminishing returns from increasing BN batch sizes, and adds accuracy/memory/latency tradeoffs relevant to resource constraints and stragglers. These extend the discussion while retaining the original channel-attention mechanism and DP-regularization interpretations.

D1.justification: v1 promises a future code release; v2 supplies a code-access link in the abstract. v2 also explicitly discloses the existing validation-based checkpoint-selection procedure and documents settings for the new training and profiling experiments, including profiler, batch size, mixed precision, and hardware information. Pretrained weights remain promised after acceptance.

E1.justification: Both versions use Fed-ISIC2019, FedChest, CIFAR-10, CelebA, and FedPathology for the same classification tasks, alongside ImageNet pretraining. The added experiments reuse this coverage; centralized controls, initialization choices, and hardware profiling change configurations rather than datasets or prediction tasks.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated FixBN comparisons on Fed-ISIC2019 and FedChest in Table 3; v1 only discussed FixBN as related work. Section 4.8 and Table 9 substantially broaden the architectural comparators to EfficientNetV2-Small, ViT-Small, ConvNeXt-Small, and FedConv-InvertUp, beyond the retained ResNet variants.

E3.justification: v2 adds doubled-local-step experiments, the nine-round FLamby protocol, random-initialization and centralized controls, final-round CIFAR-10 evaluation with batch size 64 and no gradient clipping, and CPU/GPU profiling. Section 4.1 also changes the stated CIFAR-10 client count from eight to five while retaining split-2 and the numerical table entries. This establishes a reported setting change without establishing that those experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained attention-module, CSI, attention-weight, and localization analyses, v2 tests sensitivity to local training steps, pretraining, benchmark hyperparameters, checkpoint selection, and FedChest batch size (Section 4.2; Appendices B and C.3). It also adds convergence trajectories and measured computational overhead, substantially expanding scrutiny of robustness and practicality.

E5.justification: Both versions state that results summarize three seeds using means and standard deviations. v2 adds limited seed disclosure by identifying an example run as seed 2024 in Figure 5. No increased independent-run count, new confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedure is established.

E6.justification: The original classification scores are retained, but substantial new results are reported. Examples include ANFR's 76.34 on Fed-ISIC2019 with doubled local steps and 83.20 on CIFAR-10 with random initialization. Broader comparisons also reveal exceptions to overall superiority: Table 9 reports 78.32 for FedConv-InvertUp versus 75.07 for ANFR-ECA on Fed-ISIC2019. These are added comparisons under specified conditions, not revised same-setting gains.

M1.justification: ANFR remains the combination of scaled weight standardization and channel attention within an NF-ResNet backbone. Attention placement and the SE, ECA, and CBAM variants are retained. Testing different depths and initializations does not introduce a new method component.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and interpretability discussion receive substantial editing. The formerly continuous method section becomes four named subsections, experiments are reorganized, and a new results appendix changes the appendix structure. The title and author information also change, and the standalone reproducibility statement is removed.

P2.justification: v2 adds seven tables and a four-panel convergence figure, expands the personalized-comparison table, and relocates the related-work matrix into the main text. The journal layout substantially resizes and reformats existing displays while retaining their image content. Table 10 also swaps the GFLOPs/GMACs headings relative to v1 Table 6 without changing the numerical entries.

R1.justification: v2 adds FedConv as directly relevant prior architectural work and revises the comparison matrix and novelty positioning accordingly. It also adds references for ViT, ConvNeXt, and EfficientNetV2 associated with the expanded evaluation. Most of the existing literature review and research positioning remain intact.

T1.justification: v2 omits v1's explicit definition of the sample-weighted global objective in Equation 1 while retaining the local objective and core normalization/channel-descriptor derivations. Section 3.3 adds an assertion that ANFR inherits the aggregation method's convergence guarantees, without supplying new assumptions, a theorem, or a proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical scrutiny: the added architectural competitors address v1's narrow comparator scope, alternative initialization and training protocols test dependence on the original setup, and measured runtime/memory support assessment of practical utility. Code-access information and checkpoint-selection disclosure improve reproducibility. Important caveats remain: Table 9 does not support blanket superiority claims, and the no-early-stopping experiment changes other settings simultaneously. Nevertheless, the added evidence substantially improves readers' ability to assess ANFR's strengths and boundaries.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ANFR architecture and share the core experiments, equations, and figures. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite changes to the title, authorship, and organization.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds architecture comparisons, alternative training protocols, sensitivity analyses, convergence plots, and computational measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification experiments across five datasets, differential-privacy results, attention-module comparisons, and class-selectivity and localization analyses.

results.title: An Architecture Built for Federated Learning: Addressing Data Heterogeneity through Adaptive Normalization-Free Feature Recalibration

C1.justification: The central three-principle framework and QMLE contribution remain. The revised introduction additionally claims empirical contributions from each principle and demonstrated scaling in enormous discrete action spaces, while identifying DDPG more explicitly as the primary comparison.

C2.justification: Section 5.3 adds practical interpretations connecting amortization to tolerance of small sampling budgets and reduced inference costs. Appendix D interprets the new scalability findings, while footnote 5 qualifies the MLE analogy by explaining that the reframed likelihood gradient alone does not define a meaningful optimization problem.

D1.justification: Appendix B.3 replaces a future code-release promise with a declared release and concrete repository link, adding Stable Baselines provenance and licensing information. Appendix D documents new ablation configurations. One ambiguity remains: D.3 retains Table 1's uniform ratio of 0.9 while specifying a categorical ratio of 1.

E1.justification: v1 already tests discrete and curriculum variants on Cartpole SwUp, Hopper Hop, and Walker Run. v2 substantially extends discrete-action coverage with three-bin versions of Finger Spin, Walker Walk, Quadruped Run, Humanoid Walk, and Dog Walk, reaching 38 dimensions and approximately 1.35 quintillion actions (Figure 10). The original continuous-control coverage remains.

E2.justification: v2 adds DQN as an evaluated comparator in the discrete-control architecture study (Figure 10), with its results attributed to Seyde et al. (2023) in Table 2. The original main-text and appendix comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Appendix D adds experimental designs comparing sampling budgets of 2 and 1000, controlling target and greedy budgets at 2 while removing learned predictors, and comparing sampled maximization against DQN's exact maximization on discretized tasks. These are new protocols; the original benchmark settings and Table 1 remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Section 5.3 and Appendix D systematically examine sampling sensitivity, the contribution of amortization, and architecture-related scalability. These substantially extend the retained bandit and appendix analyses. The DQN comparison jointly removes several principles, rather than isolating architecture alone.

E5.justification: Table 2 replaces QMLE's unspecified task-dependent '5 or 10' seeds with five for Dog and Humanoid tasks and ten elsewhere, and adds ten seeds for DQN. This clarifies reporting without establishing increased repetitions. Mean returns with one standard error were already reported in v1.

E6.justification: New Figures 8–10 report sampling-budget sensitivity, substantial degradation without amortization, and discrete QMLE performance alongside DQN's learning curves or computational failures. These substantially expand the empirical findings. All nine original figure graphics are retained unchanged, so the additions do not represent improved scores on the original comparisons.

M1.justification: Section 4, Algorithm 1, and the main architecture in Appendix B retain the same sampling, amortized maximization, Q-learning, and predictor-training procedures. The new ablation variants evaluate existing components without revising the proposed method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and selected explanations are revised, including clarification of complex action spaces and the illustrative experiment. Section 5.3 and an ablation appendix are inserted, but most existing prose and the overall argument sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a comprehensive journal layout with different typography, margins, headers, and author formatting. It adds three multipanel ablation figures, expands Figure 3's caption and the seed table, and relocates the original Figures 8–9 as Figures 11–12 without changing their graphics.

R1.justification: v2 adds Bellemare et al. (2017) for distributional learning and Hill et al. (2018) for Stable Baselines. It sharpens DDPG's role as the closest comparison, while retaining the positioning relative to QT-Opt, AQL, and earlier sampling-based maximization work.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and derivations remain substantively unchanged, with no new theorem or proof. Equation 14 adds an indicator for positive additional-sample counts, explicitly expressing the already-stated zero-sample reduction; it does not change the estimator under the usual empty-sum convention.

improvement.justification: Section 5.3 and Appendix D substantially address v1's limited direct testing of the principles through controlled sampling and amortization studies and broader discrete-action evidence. Concrete code-access information and clearer seed reporting also strengthen reproducibility. The DQN comparison confounds several components, and its sampling ratios are ambiguous, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gain in empirical support for the paper's central argument.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same QMLE work and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The original material can be matched reliably, including v1 Appendix D, which becomes Appendix E in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds sampling-budget, amortization, and architecture comparisons in Appendix D.

before.justification: v1 reports original QMLE control benchmarks, bandit experiments, and appendix demonstrations involving multiagent coordination and action-space curricula.

results.title: Learning in complex action spaces without policy gradients

C1.justification: The central claims remain that privacy sensitivity is concentrated in relatively few parameters and that adaptive sparsity tuning improves privacy-utility trade-offs. Compatibility with trained and already-defended models was already claimed and tested in v1. v2 foregrounds broader validation without replacing these core scientific contributions.

C2.justification: v2 replaces an unexplored-white-box limitation with measured residual vulnerabilities, explicitly distinguishes PAST's empirical protection from differential-privacy guarantees, and adds a hypothesized limitation concerning pretrained LLM knowledge. It also explains privacy-sensitivity migration and revises the sparsity interpretation from decreasing to increasing Gini, substantially refining mechanisms and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: Appendix F/Table 3 supplies model-specific hyperparameter ranges, Section 5 documents Opacus and the DP-SGD search grid, and CIFAR-10 split sizes become explicit. The basic optimizer, training budgets and hardware information are retained. Conversely, v1's instruction to detach adaptive weights from backpropagation is omitted.

E1.justification: The five datasets and classification tasks are retained. v2 Section 5 adds white-box gradient attacks and evaluation on especially vulnerable canary samples, substantially extending adversary-access and evaluated-population coverage. Additional model architectures alone do not constitute new dataset coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds MIST and SELENA to the CIFAR defense comparisons and evaluates DP-SGD in Figure 8a. Conversely, v1 Appendix B's direct loss-gap optimization comparator disappears. CCL is retained from v1's combined-defense experiment rather than newly introduced.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce SqueezeNet/MobileViT configurations, LiRA/RMIA with 32 inference models, AUC and low-FPR metrics, and a canary test with 500 members and 500 non-members. Cross-dataset P1 changes from using maximum attack advantage in v1 to average attack advantage in v2. Appendix F also describes lambda-then-alpha tuning, unlike v1's stated alpha-only tuning.

E4.justification: v2 adds inference-set size/composition sensitivity, shared-hyperparameter tests across architectures, alternative privacy proxies, within-layer sensitivity, privacy migration and an RMIA regularization ablation. Earlier CIFAR-100 and alpha/epoch analyses remain under new numbering. The direct-loss-gap ablation is removed, rather than relocated.

E5.justification: v1 provides no repeated-seed uncertainty analysis. v2 Appendix J and Table 4 report nine seeds and means with standard deviations for accuracy, attack AUC and P1 on CIFAR-10/ResNet-18, including P1 of 0.791 ± 0.006. This introduces explicit uncertainty reporting without establishing how many runs underlay v1.

E6.justification: v2 reports substantial new attack, architecture, DP-SGD, canary and robustness results. Its new white-box comparison reports gradient-mean attack AUC of 0.981 without defense versus 0.796 with PAST. Figure 2b changes from a decreasing to an increasing Gini trajectory. Revised cross-dataset P1 results use different aggregation and cannot establish same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Both retain module-normalized weighted L1 regularization and post-convergence tuning. However, v1's adaptive-weight equation uses an undefined G-tilde and gradients without absolute-value signs, whereas v2 Equation (6) explicitly normalizes gradient magnitudes. The PDFs do not establish whether this changes the procedure or corrects the earlier notation.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method exposition and results narrative undergo extensive rewriting and reorganization. Related work moves from the main text to Appendix A, a substantial Discussion section is introduced, and retained appendix material is reorganized alongside separate theory, settings and analysis sections.

P2.justification: The earlier P1 tables are replaced by Figure 5 bar charts, the CIFAR-10 comparison moves to Appendix H, and the dense module-level plot is regrouped into Figures 15-16. Numerous new plots and tables accompany extensive changes to axes, legends, captions and publication layout. Several retained results are therefore redisplayed rather than newly added.

R1.justification: The positioning around overparameterization, pruning and regularization remains largely intact. v2 adds references and targeted discussion concerning LiRA/RMIA, MIST/SELENA, differential privacy and worst-case privacy evaluation, and supplies attribution for CCL. Related work's relocation to Appendix A does not itself change the research positioning.

T1.justification: Unlike v1, v2 Appendices B-C contain formal propositions, a theorem and proofs. These include a Gaussian-loss argument relating the mean loss gap to attack advantage at fixed FPR, a Bayesian optimal-membership-inference derivation following cited prior work, and a posterior-distribution derivation. These additions substantially expand the mathematical rationale.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the assessment of privacy protection through LiRA/RMIA, vulnerable-canary and white-box evaluations, including explicit evidence of remaining weaknesses. Seed statistics, formal rationale and clearer applicability limits improve credibility and assessability. These gains outweigh losing the direct-loss-gap comparison and replacing precise P1 tables with bar charts. The changed P1 aggregation is not evidence of a performance improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PAST research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds attack evaluations, architecture comparisons, robustness analyses and repeated-seed measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original membership-inference defense experiments on five datasets, privacy-sensitivity measurements, ablations and runtime results, including appendix experiments.

results.title: Defending Membership Inference Attacks via Privacy-aware Sparsity Tuning

C1.justification: The four research questions and central claims remain: goal difficulty principally affects persuasion, guard personas strongly influence anti-social behavior, undesirable behavior can emerge without negative persona prompts, and some models fail role adherence. The expanded model sample and supplementary checks do not replace these headline contributions.

C2.justification: V3 adds model safeguards as an alternative explanation for unattempted escapes, whereas v1 emphasizes anticipated difficulty. It explicitly limits its agents to role-playing LLMs without memory or environmental interaction, discusses the prison scenario's realism, and interprets stricter scoring as showing that persuasion is harder to establish. Most existing limitations and persona-based interpretations remain.

D1.justification: V3 Table 1 specifies the GPT-4.1 snapshot and context length, and the text identifies annotator affiliations and roles. The code reference changes to an anonymized repository described as providing code and generated conversations. V1's separate reproducibility statement, including installation, database, and analysis-script guidance, is removed; existing prompts and open-model hyperparameters remain documented.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same prison environment, escape and additional-yard-time goals, five personality pairings, and risk/oversight conditions. V3's additional conversations extend model configurations within this coverage. Information-protection and policing scenarios are proposed future work, not evaluated tasks.

E2.justification: V3 adds GPT-4.1 to the evaluated roster of Llama3, Command-r, Orca2, Mixtral, and Mistral v0.2. The original five remain, and Mixtral and Mistral are still excluded from downstream behavioral analyses because of conversational failures, leaving four analyzed models instead of three.

E3.justification: V3 Appendix F.2 introduces an additional evaluation protocol that re-annotates previously successful conversations using clearer commitment requirements, excluding vague promises and unconfirmed supervisor referrals. The main permissive labels remain. The experimental total increases from 2,000 to 2,400 conversations, and the reported annotator panel increases from 13 to 15; the 19-message format and original decoding settings are retained.

E4.justification: V3 adds scenario-specific failure analyses (Tables 3–6), separates persuasion attempts from success conditional on attempting across personalities (Tables 8–12), and tests sensitivity to success definitions (Table 13). It also adds fractional-logit robustness checks for the bounded anti-social behavior outcomes, beyond v1's OLS analyses and existing temporal and Granger analyses.

E5.justification: V3 Table 7 adds Cohen's kappa for outcome and turn annotations, plus the mean and standard deviation of absolute turn disagreements, beyond v1 Table 3's disagreement counts. Fractional-logit checks add an alternative estimation procedure. Both versions already report ten repetitions per configuration, confidence intervals, standard deviations, and significance tests; no increase in repetitions is reported.

E6.justification: V3 adds GPT-4.1 outcomes and updates pooled estimates: the yard-time persuasion odds ratio changes from 9.31 to 35.07 after expanding the model pool, not as a same-setting performance gain. New Table 13 reports that stricter coding retains only 44 of 111 Llama3 yard-time successes and 4 of 118 GPT-4.1 successes. Detailed failure, conditional-success, and robustness results are also newly reported.

M1.justification: The toolkit architecture, shared/private prompt templates, role assignments, and conversation-generation procedure remain unchanged (v1 Appendices A–B; v3 Appendices B–C). Adding GPT-4.1 as an evaluated model and changing supplementary outcome scoring do not introduce a new simulation method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and substantial portions of the results and conclusions are rewritten. Conclusions move before limitations, the ethics statement becomes a broader-impact statement, the standalone reproducibility section disappears, and a new persuasion-results appendix reorganizes the supporting narrative.

P2.justification: V3 introduces ten additional tables and six fractional-logit figures, expands the annotation table with agreement statistics, and adds GPT-4.1 panels or series throughout existing displays. Figures and tables are extensively resized and relocated, and tighter line spacing changes the document layout beyond simple renumbering.

R1.justification: V3 substantially expands positioning around multi-agent security, emergent misalignment, social conventions, and agent definitions, citing works such as Hammond et al. (2025), de Witt (2025), and Ashery et al. (2025). It sharpens the distinction between hierarchical interactions and interactions among equals, engages SPE criticism through Le Texier (2019), and removes some older general AI background references.

T1.justification: The OLS specification, Granger restricted model, F-statistic, and stationarity discussion are mathematically equivalent across versions. V3 adds empirical estimation and annotation checks, but no new mathematical definitions, derivations, theorems, or proofs.

improvement.justification: V1 leaves the sensitivity of its permissive persuasion labels untested. V3 directly quantifies that important weakness: only 44 of 111 Llama3 yard-time successes survive stricter coding. Together with annotation-agreement statistics and fractional-logit checks, this substantially strengthens evidential transparency and robustness. The improvement is tempered by reporting inconsistencies, notably GPT-4.1 yard-time attempts disagreeing between Figure 2 and Table 8, and the removal of reproducibility setup guidance.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same zAImbardo study of guard–prisoner LLM interactions. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched across the revision.

after.justification: V3 reports 2,400 conversations across six LLMs, retaining the original empirical analyses and adding persuasion re-annotation, detailed outcome breakdowns, and robustness analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulations comprising 2,000 conversations across five LLMs, with human persuasion annotations, anti-social behavior measurements, and statistical analyses.

results.title: I Want to Break Free! Persuasion and Anti-Social Behavior of LLMs in Multi-Agent Settings with Social Hierarchy

C1.justification: The principal method, comparable-reconstruction-quality claim, and training-free motion claim remain. v2 removes the explicit first-use claim for image inverse problems and adds prominent memory/accessibility claims, including up to 77% lower memory and suitability for 8 GiB GPUs. Its conclusion further asserts an order-of-magnitude memory reduction, exceeding the unchanged table's evidence.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of prompt dependence, possible decoder effects in prior selection, and persistent errors when prompts mismatch target faces. It acknowledges motion-quality versus path-accuracy tradeoffs and the limited ImageNet FID reference size. These provide specific applicability boundaries beyond v1's general speed, performance, and future-domain limitations.

D1.justification: v1 promises a future code release; v2 reports public code and supplies its repository link. v2 also documents revised optimization parameters, an alternative prior source, and clean-fid features, preprocessing, and reference statistics. Hardware reporting gains an unresolved inconsistency: Section 4.1 says all experiments use RTX 3090, while Appendix E.5 retains A6000 measurements.

E1.justification: ImageNet/FFHQ super-resolution and Gaussian deblurring remain. Motion evaluation changes substantially: v1 illustrates hand-designed forward and zigzag paths, whereas v2 evaluates HumanML3D test motions with sparse conditioning at 5 of 196 frames. This introduces a distinct sparse-control scenario; the earlier motion demonstrations are no longer reported.

E2.justification: v2 adds OmniControl and Guided Motion Diffusion (GMD) as quantitative motion comparators in Table 3, providing external comparisons absent from v1's motion demonstration. The image comparison methods remain DPS, DDRM, PSLD, ReSample, and the Markov-process variant.

E3.justification: The main image evaluations expand from 100 to 1,000 images per dataset. Reported optimization settings change, including Adam to RAdam, learning rates, schedules, and the ImageNet super-resolution KL weight. v2 also introduces SSIM/FID/KID evaluation, quantitative sparse-motion protocols, and prompt/prior controls; the prior comparison uses 100 FFHQ images.

E4.justification: Appendices E.7-E.9 add tests of text conditioning, VQDiff-ITHQ versus CVQDiff-FFHQ priors, and prompt-related failure cases. Figure 2 expands the early-structure analysis through multiple conditional samples. The existing Markov-process and forgetting-coefficient analyses are retained, with revised examples.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for its results. Larger evaluation sets and additional metrics do not change the uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Tables 1-2 replace the image scores: for example, G2D2 ImageNet super-resolution changes from LPIPS/PSNR 0.349/23.20 to 0.340/23.82. Changed samples and optimization settings prevent interpreting this as a same-setting gain. v2 adds motion, prompt/prior, and SSIM/FID/KID results. The memory/time values in v1 Table 4 and v2 Table 5 remain identical.

M1.justification: The reported inner optimization changes from Adam to RAdam in Section 4.1 and Appendix E.2. The variational objective, Gumbel-Softmax relaxation, star-shaped sampling, and initialization strategy remain fundamentally unchanged. The star-decomposed distribution corresponds to v1's qsampling, rather than a newly introduced sampler.

P1.justification: The introduction and methodological exposition are extensively rewritten. Section 3 separates star-shaped noise, the decomposed distribution, and variational inference more explicitly, with expanded explanations and revised terminology. Ethics and reproducibility statements move into appendices, and the appendix structure is reorganized.

P2.justification: v2 substantially redraws Figures 2-3, adds prompt/prior/failure figures and motion/expanded-metric tables, and removes v1's motion Figures 6 and 14. Several retained image grids are relocated and enlarged. Typography, headings, and page layout also change throughout.

R1.justification: The existing related-work framework is retained. v2 adds a focused distinction from Feynman-Kac steering, a paragraph on applications across domains, and references supporting the motion comparators, alternative prior, optimizer, metrics, and prompt tuning. This extends the positioning without replacing its central relationship to continuous inverse solvers and discrete guidance.

T1.justification: Appendix D corrects important reasoning: the KL proof uses the decomposed joint, and Lemma D.1 replaces v1 Lemma B.3's unjustified Kronecker-delta return argument with successive marginalization. These substantively repair support for the retained method. However, v2's new transition-normalization condition uses (K-1)beta despite Eq. 2 containing K beta contributions per non-mask column.

improvement.justification: v2 repairs an important marginal-preservation proof and substantially strengthens validation through broader image sampling, quantitative motion comparisons, and analyses exposing prompt/prior dependencies and failures. These address weaknesses in v1's theoretical support and largely illustrative motion evidence. The gains outweigh new reporting defects, including the transition-normalization inconsistency, conflicting hardware statements, and an unsupported order-of-magnitude memory claim: Table 5 shows 4.7 versus at most 20.9 GiB. The improvement rests on stronger justification and more informative evidence, rather than the changed performance scores alone.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe G2D2 and have readable text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. The expanded and reorganized material in v2 can be matched reliably to v1.

after.justification: v2 reports original image reconstruction experiments, quantitative HumanML3D motion results, prompt and prior-model ablations, and failure cases.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet and FFHQ reconstruction experiments, graphical-model and forgetting-coefficient analyses, resource measurements, and qualitative motion-generation results.

results.title: G2D2: Gradient-Guided Discrete Diffusion for Inverse Problem Solving

C1.justification: The abstract expands the claimed demonstrated scale from 25 to 80 time series. The introduction shifts from finding global solutions to near-global solutions, and the conclusion replaces the finance claim of two-minute global optimality with a 20% gap in 30 minutes. These substantially revise scalability and attained-exactness claims while retaining eventual global convergence.

C2.justification: V3 introduces a substantive limitation concerning normalization and suitability for data with meaningful original scales. It interprets baseline weaknesses through their non-Gaussian or nonlinear modeling assumptions and discusses variability as dependent on computation time. The new finance interpretation explicitly acknowledges that preferring ExDBN's network is subjective because ground truth is unknown.

D1.justification: V3 newly identifies Gurobi and the main benchmark's 32 GB memory limit, and specifies autoregressive order two for the financial networks. Conversely, the numerical regularization settings supplied in v1's plot legends disappear from v3's redesigned plots. These are localized additions and losses in reproducibility information.

E1.justification: V3 adds ER-3-1-var, with Gaussian noise variances sampled separately for each variable from (0.6, 1.2). The ER/SF graph families, Krebs-cycle task, and 16-CDS dataset remain. V1's ER2-1-1 corresponds to v3's renamed ER-2-2, so that naming change does not add coverage.

E2.justification: V1's synthetic experiments directly compare only with DYNOTEARS. V3 adds evaluated LiNGAM and NTS-NOTEARS comparisons in Figures 1–2 and the scalability study. It also adds DYNOTEARS as an actual comparator within the finance application, displaying both methods' learned networks in Figures 6–7.

E3.justification: The evaluation changes from selecting the best ground-truth-based threshold separately for each method to using a fixed threshold of 0.15. G-score evaluation is dropped. New experiments include a runtime–accuracy study with 25 variables and 250 samples, and scaling to 30–80 variables with n = 5d, a 22-hour limit, and 128 GB memory. The main benchmark's 7200-second cap is retained.

E4.justification: V3 quantifies the three lazy-constraint variants already discussed in v1 through Table 2, and adds runtime–SHD curves and constraint-count diagnostics in Figures 3 and 5. It also reports a qualitative normalization-sensitivity test and substantially expands the finance case study through analysis of recovered graph structures.

E5.justification: Both versions specify ten seeds per synthetic experiment. V3 adds standard deviations and uncertainty bands to the earlier mean-and-worst-case reporting, and reports runtime means with standard deviations in Table 1. This expands uncertainty reporting without establishing an increase in repetitions.

E6.justification: V3 replaces and expands the synthetic results, removes G-score results, and adds runtime, scalability, and financial-network findings. Table 2 reports mean MIP gaps of 0.335, 0.344, and 0.346 for all-cycle, shortest-cycle, and first-cycle variants. The finance result changes from global optimality within two minutes to a 20% gap after 30 minutes; identical experimental settings are not established.

M1.justification: The documented L2 penalty changes from sums of edge indicators and unsquared lag weights in v1 Equation 11 to squared intra- and inter-slice weights in v3 Equation 13. This revises one objective component; the structural model and lazy cycle-cut algorithm remain. The PDFs do not establish whether implementation changed.

P1.justification: The introduction and problem formulation are extensively rewritten, with expanded variable definitions and a new MIQP tutorial. Data generation moves into the experiments section, the applications are reordered, and the title and regularization terminology change. These constitute substantial narrative restructuring beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: V1's three full-page figures organized by graph ensemble are replaced by SHD and F1 grids organized across ensembles and sample sizes. V3 adds runtime and scaling plots, constraint-count plots, two tables, and paired financial-network heatmaps. The author block, typography, and placement of figures within the text are also redesigned.

R1.justification: V3 substantially expands connections to optimization-based DAG learning through Manzour, Xu, and Jaakkola, and adds literature on scale-sensitive causal benchmarks, DBN history, and mixed-integer optimization foundations. The introduction consequently provides a broader account of competing approaches and their limitations than v1's predominantly application-oriented framing.

T1.justification: The mathematical definition of L2 regularization is substantively corrected between v1 Equation 11 and v3 Equation 13. The identifiability remark and underlying cycle-exclusion and convergence reasoning remain. The new MIQP and MIP-gap section mainly supplies standard background rather than new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens the evidence needed to assess ExDBN's accuracy–computation tradeoff through measured runtimes, standard deviations, time-budget analyses, and quantified lazy-constraint comparisons, which v1 largely lacked. It also supplies meaningful applicability limitations and qualifies the finance optimality claim. Missing per-setting regularization values and lingering L1/L0 terminology inconsistencies weaken reproducibility, but the expanded empirical support and more explicit qualifications provide a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ExDBN and retain the same core research problem and algorithm. All 12 pages of v1 and 16 pages of v3, including equations, plotted results, and end matter, support comparison. Neither supplied PDF contains an appendix.

after.justification: V3 reports original synthetic comparisons, scalability and runtime experiments, lazy-constraint evaluations, and learned financial networks, alongside the retained biomedical result.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic comparisons with DYNOTEARS in Figures 1–3 and ExDBN runtime and optimality-gap results for the finance and biomedical examples.

results.title: ExDBN: Learning Dynamic Bayesian Networks using Extended Mixed-Integer Programming Formulations

C1.justification: The central claims about latent-space interpretation, editing directions, and controllable augmentation remain. v2 extends its introduction/conclusion superiority claims to SeFa and removes v1's explicit claim that joint interpretable directions had never previously been found.

C2.justification: v1 inferred latent-space class proportions from codeword fractions. v2's Section 5.1 and Appendix A.1 show that diversity alone does not explain the horse class's roughly 25% allocation and that initialization with 8 or 16 codewords changes it, materially qualifying that interpretation. v2 also expands the geometric/MSE explanation and drops the assertion that a larger image pool alone establishes greater statistical significance.

D1.justification: v2 documents uniform dithering and the training loss, supplies SeFa semantic indices and layer ranges in Table 3, and updates the repository address. Conversely, v1's detailed reproducibility statement and code inventory disappear, although codebook-access statements remain. The PDFs do not establish that the underlying resources became unavailable.

E1.justification: Both versions use FFHQ, AFHQ, LSUN Cars, CIFAR10, ImageNet, and the same synthetic distribution domains. The added human ratings and initialization/sensitivity experiments evaluate retained data and editing tasks rather than introducing new application coverage.

E2.justification: SeFa, previously only cited, becomes an evaluated comparator across seven face-editing directions in Tables 1–2 and Figure 11, alongside GANSpace and LatentCLR. It also participates in the new human-ranking comparison, substantially extending the central comparative evaluation.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a 20-participant ranking study using 100 latent vectors, five per participant, with seven editing positions at sigma=2.67. It adds analyses using 10,000 vectors per CIFAR10 class and initialization/hyperparameter sweeps. The main qualitative illustration changes sigma from 2.5 to 4. The existing automatic evaluation retains 1,000 vectors and 41-image trajectories.

E4.justification: v2 adds random-versus-proposed initialization comparisons on 3D moons (Figure 4), CIFAR10 class-diversity and initial-codebook-size analyses (Appendix A.1), and systematic bitrate, batch-size, and learning-rate sensitivity tests (Appendix A.8). The earlier bitrate, class-transfer, and traveling-salesman analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions average automatic scores over 1,000 latent vectors without reporting repeated-training seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. New human-rank frequencies and class-diversity variances are descriptive results, not uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: All existing SFVQ, GANSpace, and LatentCLR numerical rows in Tables 1–2 are unchanged. New SeFa rows alter some rankings: its smile correlation is 0.46 versus SFVQ's retained 0.40. Figure 10 adds human-ranking outcomes favoring SFVQ on five directions, with comparable performance on rotation and gender. New appendix results document initialization-dependent class allocation and hyperparameter sensitivity.

M1.justification: The proposed norm-ordered initialization, 0.99/0.01 codebook expansion, adjacent-codeword editing directions, and BigGAN latent-space transfer remain unchanged. v2 explains existing SFVQ training more explicitly; alternative initial codebook sizes are experimental configurations rather than a replacement algorithm.

P1.justification: The introduction's contribution bullets become an integrated narrative, the method explanation expands into separate why/how subsections, and qualitative and quantitative comparisons receive separate sections. The reproducibility section is removed and appendices are reorganized. These changes substantially revise the exposition beyond routine language editing.

P2.justification: v2 adds Hilbert-curve, dithering, initialization, and geometric diagrams; human-ranking, class-diversity, and sensitivity plots; and a SeFa configuration table. Comparison tables expand and the qualitative comparison figure is replaced. Existing displays are reorganized within the journal layout, while the earlier ten-example gallery is no longer embedded.

R1.justification: Section 2 expands substantially beyond the earlier three-category overview, explaining supervised, linear/nonlinear, GAN-inversion, and diffusion-editing approaches and their relationship to this work. Numerous relevant works are added, including StyleSpace, Song et al.'s methods, and recent diffusion research, with an explicit distinction between the paper's GAN focus and diffusion editing.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 adds explicit mathematical definitions of the dithered codebook and nearest-sample quantization map, including uniform interpolation, in Equation (1). v1 described curve mapping verbally. This adds limited formal specification without introducing a theorem, proof, or new theoretical guarantee.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the retained method through human rankings, a substantive SeFa comparison, and tests of previously asserted hyperparameter robustness. Its initialization analysis also qualifies an important overinterpretation of codeword proportions, while fuller method explanations improve assessability. Losing the detailed reproducibility inventory and moving qualitative examples to an unavailable supplement reduces self-containment, but these drawbacks are outweighed by the stronger evidence and more informative analysis of central claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SFVQ study, and all included pages and appendices are readable. However, v1 includes ten qualitative comparison plates, while v2 references a separate 50-example supplement that is not supplied. Those galleries cannot be fully matched; the remaining material supports reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds SeFa comparisons, human rankings in Figure 10, and initialization and sensitivity analyses in Appendices A.1 and A.8.

before.justification: v1 reports original SFVQ experiments, quantitative face-editing results in Tables 1–2, and appendix experiments on class transfer, bitrates, and synthetic distributions.

results.title: Unsupervised Panoptic Interpretation of Latent Spaces in GANs Using Space-Filling Vector Quantization

C1.justification: Both versions claim unsupervised, dimension-wise self-explainable embeddings through structural disentanglement, introduce interpretability metrics and claim strong empirical performance. The revised abstract and conclusion make these claims more explicit, but the central contributions and their scientific scope remain the same.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly limits community alignment to one aspect of comprehensibility, discusses alternative interpretable structures, and explains attribution as marginal rather than exclusive responsibility under correlated dimensions. It also adds substantive interpretations of accuracy–interpretability trade-offs, regularization/depth effects and semantic coherence, considerably expanding v1’s qualifications and mechanism discussion.

D1.justification: v2 adds training and explanation-extraction pseudocode, DiSeNE hidden-size search details, DGLFRM hyperparameters and graph-explainer training/mask-conversion settings. It newly documents downstream attribute concatenation and Cora keyword preprocessing. These substantially expand reproducibility information; the code/data repository disclosure is retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds Tree-Cliques and Tree-Grids, extending synthetic evaluation to tree backbones and grid motifs. Appendix H also adds Cora multiclass topic classification and semantic analysis. The original real-world, biological and four synthetic datasets remain represented.

E2.justification: DGLFRM is added to the embedding comparisons in Tables 1–3 and the real-data link-prediction comparison. New Table 4 evaluates GNNExplainer and PGExplainer on GCN, GraphSAGE and GATv2 against DiSeNE explanations. These substantially broaden the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: v2 specifies plausibility evaluation on correctly classified test instances, whereas v1 describes averaging over test instances. New Table 4 evaluates only the most important embedding feature, unlike Table 3’s weighted aggregation. New protocols also include Pareto scoring, controlled regularization/depth sweeps and Cora multiclass evaluation. The principal train/test splits remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1’s dimensionality curves, v2 adds accuracy–interpretability Pareto analyses, sensitivity to entropy regularization and encoder depth, visual comparisons of global and local explanation subgraphs, and Cora topic/text case studies. These examine trade-offs, component sensitivity and semantic meaning that v1 did not analyze directly.

E5.justification: Both versions report averages over five runs and numerical uncertainty. Appendix D newly specifies standard errors from five independent runs and incorporates uncertainty into Pareto-dominance assessment. The reported run count remains five; no additional significance-testing procedure is introduced.

E6.justification: Existing values change: Table 2 reports DiSe-FCAE’s PPI overlap consistency as 0.934±0.003 instead of 0.548±0.001, and Table 3 changes GraphSAGE’s BA-Cliques classification plausibility from 0.016±0.004 to 0.160±0.004. The latter table also has a revised reported evaluation restriction. Substantial new results cover added comparators, tree benchmarks, Pareto rankings, sensitivity and Cora semantics.

M1.justification: The random-walk objective, attribution-based explanations, affiliation orthogonality, entropy regularization and FCAE/GAE encoders are retained. Identity inputs were already used in v1’s experiments; v2’s topology-only description and added pseudocode do not establish a changed learning procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are rewritten, method and metric explanations are extensively expanded, and plausibility is reorganized into explicit steps. Comprehensibility becomes Topological Alignment and structural faithfulness becomes connectivity preservation. The appendix is reorganized from A.1–A.4 into thematic sections A–H.

P2.justification: v2 adds Pareto plots, explanation subgraphs and correlation maps, sensitivity panels, semantic tables with word clouds, and algorithm displays. Existing tables gain comparator rows or task columns and are rearranged within a new journal layout. The original synthetic plots are retained and expanded as Figures A9–A12.

R1.justification: Section 3.3 substantially expands the metrics’ positioning relative to existing explanation accuracy, contrastivity, faithfulness and BAGEL plausibility measures. Additional literature supports the new disentangled baseline, graph explainers, computational scaling and topology-versus-attribute discussion. This extends research contextualization beyond the largely retained related-work taxonomy.

T1.justification: Appendix B adds a stepwise time/space complexity derivation and comparative complexity table. Appendix D defines Pareto coverage and efficiency, while Section 3.2 explicitly states the nonnegative-activation assumption needed for entropy. These supplement the formal framework; the original losses and interpretability metric formulas remain substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the interpretability claims through more relevant comparators, grid-motif tests, semantic examples, sensitivity studies and accuracy–interpretability analysis. Explicit limits on community-based comprehensibility and fuller implementation documentation address important weaknesses in v1. Some reporting inconsistencies remain: Table 2’s discussion still says DiSeNE loses on Cora despite its revised leading scores. This limits reporting precision but does not outweigh the substantial evidential and explanatory gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DiSeNE research work. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, allowing retained, relocated and newly added material to be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds benchmark comparisons, sensitivity analyses, Pareto analyses and qualitative explanation studies in Tables 1–4 and Appendices C–H.

before.justification: v1 reports original embedding-interpretability, link-prediction and node-classification experiments in Tables 1–3 and Appendix A.

results.title: Disentangled and Self-Explainable Node Representation Learning

C1.justification: The central solver, adaptive-conversion contribution, arbitrary-preference capability, and convergence order remain. v3 newly claims that its dependence on objective count is tighter than previous OMD bounds and optimal for offline learning. Preference-guided learning receives greater emphasis, but diverse-preference capability was already claimed in v1.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive qualifications about adaptive averaging's diversity-versus-optimality trade-off, objective-scale bias, approximate dominance evaluation, and iteration-versus-sample complexity.
