It also explains limitations of gradient-based comparator behavior and acknowledges that improved optimality need not improve accuracy parity. These go substantially beyond v1's discussion of training stability and fairness.

D1.justification: v3 adds a project-code access link, the 1000-epoch synthetic budget, additional baseline hyperparameters, disclosure of mini-batch losses for dominance comparisons, ablation construction details, and runtime measurements. Original hardware and many settings remain. Conversely, v1's explicit VLMOP2 formulas and dimension d=10 are no longer stated, leaving some benchmark details less self-contained.

E1.justification: Synthetic coverage expands from VLMOP2 alone to VLMOP2 plus F1-F6. v3 also adds a two-client CIFAR10 scenario with 0/90-degree rotations and multiple preference targets, extending beyond the retained ten-client MNIST/CIFAR10 fairness tasks with uniform preferences.

E2.justification: The retained VLMOP2 comparison gains STCH, ExcessMTL, MGDA, CR-MOGM, Moco, PMTL, EPO, and FERERO. The ten-client comparisons add EPO, FERERO, ExcessMTL, and AdaExcessMTL. Additional comparisons evaluate momentum-enhanced STCH and adaptive LS/TCH variants. These are evaluated comparators, not merely new citations.

E3.justification: v3 introduces hypervolume evaluation, a two-client evaluation over three preferences, ratio-based metrics, and dominance-evaluation controls using mini-batches, full training data, or validation data. The validation variant splits the test set into validation and testing halves. Appendix B.2 also changes the reported CIFAR10 local budget from one iteration to one epoch per round; this establishes a documentation-level protocol revision, not that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained PGD/EG comparisons, v3 adds lambda-step-size sensitivity (Figure 5), momentum-STCH comparisons (Table 4), adaptive-conversion component studies (Table 7), dominance-evaluation robustness (Table 8), and objective-ratio compatibility tests (Table 9). These substantially expand evidence about mechanisms and practical reliability.

E5.justification: The three synthetic seeds and ten federated-learning seeds remain unchanged. However, v1 Figure 4 presents seed-specific VLMOP2 solutions, whereas v3 Figures 6-8 present averages, supplemented by hypervolume means with ± values in Table 10. This changes how synthetic seed variability is reported without establishing additional runs or a new statistical estimation method.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive benchmark, baseline, ablation, hypervolume, and runtime results. For example, new Table 3 reports loss hypervolumes of 9.166 for OMD-TCH and 7.005 for AdaOMD-TCH. Most original federated-learning scores are retained. Malformed entries are also repaired: STCH CIFAR10 Rotation accuracy is printed as 6.320 in v1 Table 2 and 66.320 in v3 Table 11, a reporting correction rather than demonstrated performance improvement.

M1.justification: The core minimax formulation and adaptive weight-transfer conversion remain. However, v1 Equation (9) updates theta using newly computed lambda(t+1), whereas v3 Equation (4) uses lambda(t), changing the update procedure. v3 also implements optional ratio-normalized weight updates and applies adaptive conversion to LS, TCH, and ExcessMTL.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, conclusion, and substantial explanatory passages are rewritten around preference-guided multi-objective learning. Related comparisons are reorganized into Section 3.4, federated-learning experiments become four structured subsections, and expectation/high-probability results exchange main-text and appendix placement. Terminology and the title also change.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. Figure 2 expands its comparator panels, federated-learning figures are reorganized, and synthetic appendix plots become multi-problem grids. New comparison, hypervolume, runtime, and ablation tables are added; the original combined numerical table becomes six subtables in Table 11. Several original plots remain as relocated displays.

R1.justification: New Table 1 and Section 3.4 substantially expand positioning against prior OMD, gradient-manipulation, and preference-guided methods. Added references include Cortes et al.'s multi-objective framework, FERERO, Moco, CR-MOGM, and the approaches of Kamani and Momma. Existing LS/STCH relationships are retained within this broader comparison.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 substantially revises the convergence derivation to match the changed lambda indexing, removing additional terms and changing the reported dual-bound constant under the square root from 54 to 20. v3 expands the p-norm derivation and adds formal sampling and sample-complexity comparisons in Appendix A.3. Expectation and high-probability bounds already existed in v1; their relocation alone is not new theory.

improvement.justification: v1's general preference-guided claims were supported mainly by one synthetic problem and uniform-preference federated learning. v3 substantially strengthens that evidence through broader synthetic coverage, real-data preference evaluation, relevant competitors, and controlled ablations. Its discussion also exposes diversity and sampling trade-offs, while corrected tables and code-access information improve usability. Some benchmark details are omitted and local-update wording remains ambiguous, but these limitations do not outweigh the stronger empirical support and clearer applicability boundaries.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OMD-TCH/AdaOMD-TCH research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison despite substantial rewriting and expansion. Printing defects in v1's results table can be distinguished from extraction problems through visual inspection.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds synthetic benchmarks, preference-guided federated-learning results, ablations, and runtime measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original VLMOP2 optimization results and MNIST/CIFAR10 federated-learning experiments in Section 4 and Appendix B.

results.title: Adaptive Online Mirror Descent for Tchebycheff Scalarization in Multi-Objective Learning

C1.justification: The contribution shifts from RADT for Decision Transformer to a general REAG framework claimed to enhance DT, Reinformer, and QT. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion emphasize consistent improvements across DT-type architectures and explicitly present RADT as preliminary work. The central distribution-alignment and suboptimality claims remain.

C2.justification: New Appendix D explains harmful augmentation through limited occupancy overlap, heterogeneous replay data, and unreliable return estimates, and recommends alternatives or disabling relabeling. v2 also adds a clipping explanation involving estimation errors and QT regularization. The earlier explanation that consistency enforcement harms trajectory stitching is removed. These materially revise mechanisms and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: Appendix B.4 newly reports a 1000-rollout estimation budget, hardware, and CQL training costs of 2.48 target and 9.39 source GPU-hours. Conversely, v1's explicit DT hyperparameter table is replaced by references to the original backbone papers, and SAC checkpoint scores and XML modification listings disappear. DARA and CQL hyperparameter tables largely remain.

E1.justification: The three locomotion environments remain, but reported coverage contracts substantially. Random evaluations and all morphology-shift evaluations disappear. Walker2D and Hopper kinematic tests from v1 Figure 4 are removed, while the HalfCheetah kinematic scenario from v1 Figure 9 remains in v2 Table 11. BodyMass and JointNoise remain the principal shifts.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated Reinformer and QT baselines and their augmented variants, plus DFDT, H2O, and IGDF in Tables 8–10. The conventional algorithms and their DARA variants remain. Within the consistency ablation, the unaugmented DT control shown in v1 Figure 7 is absent from v2 Figure 5.

E3.justification: The reported Walker2D-Medium clipping interval changes from 0.9–2 to 0.9–1.25. The consistency ablation changes from backward reconstruction within context windows to reconstruction from an augmented initial return. New protocols compare Q predictions with 100 rollout trajectories and vary CQL regularization and target sample counts. Figure 1 also replaces summed ranks with normalized average ranks. These changes do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds Q-value accuracy checks, sensitivity to critic training, and empirical checks of the Gaussian approximation in Figures 6–8. Clipping and consistency analyses extend to three backbones. Conversely, v1's target-return sweep and empirical-statistics augmentation comparison disappear, alongside several dynamics stress tests. This substantially changes the questions investigated.

E5.justification: Five-seed averaging remains. v2 identifies the seeds, explicitly labels standard deviations, and adds 95% confidence intervals for the principal comparisons in Table 7. Figure 6 reports means and variances over 100 trajectories. These refine uncertainty reporting without establishing an increase in repeated training runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive results for additional backbones, comparators, and diagnostics while removing earlier evaluation entries. Retained scores also change: Walker2D Medium-Replay 1T BCQ changes from 62.567 to 60.638, and HalfCheetah Medium-Expert 1T AWR changes from 901.68 to 90.168 (v1 Table 1; v2 Table 8). Revised aggregate ranks use a different comparison pool and cannot be interpreted as direct performance gains.

M1.justification: The augmentation procedures remain DARA-based return relabeling and Gaussian mean–variance matching through Equations 4.1–4.4. CQL-based estimation and variance-ratio clipping already appear in v1. v2 renames the framework and applies it to Reinformer and QT without specifying a new augmentation mechanism.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, experimental narrative, and ablation discussion are extensively rewritten around DT-type frameworks. Terminology changes throughout from RADT to REAG. Detailed theory moves into the main text, references move before the appendices, and the appendix structure is reorganized with separate failure-analysis and additional-theory sections.

P2.justification: v2 adopts journal formatting and substantially redesigns the displays. Comparisons are organized around multiple backbones, v1's landscape results table is replaced by separate portrait tables, and several plots become grouped panels. Confidence-interval tables, Q-value curves, and histograms are added; earlier plots and the consistency pseudocode are removed.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands beyond DARC/DARA to discuss filtering, representation alignment, cross-domain optimization, and model-based approaches, including H2O, VGDF, BOSA, IGDF, SRPO, and MOBODY. v2 also cites DFDT and positions the earlier RADT study as a precursor to the broader REAG framework.

T1.justification: The original detailed sample-complexity result largely moves from v1 Appendix A into v2 Section 4.4, with its proof retained in Appendix A. Separately, new Appendix E introduces distinct source and target behavior policies, mixture-policy definitions, revised coverage assumptions, and Theorems E.4–E.6 with proofs. This materially extends the theoretical scope.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation beyond the single DT backbone through additional architectures and relevant comparators, checks key estimation assumptions, and explicitly analyzes cases where augmentation hurts. Appendix E also extends the analysis to differing behavior policies used in practice. These gains improve the support and qualification of the paper's conclusions, despite the loss of Random and morphology evaluations, several earlier ablations, and self-contained DT training details.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same return-augmentation research, with RADT renamed REAG in v2. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including the rotated results table in v1.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds evaluations involving Reinformer, QT, additional baselines, value-function diagnostics, and empirical return distributions in Section 5 and Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original MuJoCo experiments comparing DT, RADT, and baseline algorithms, together with dynamics-shift and component ablations in Section 5 and Appendix D.

results.title: Return Augmented Decision Transformer for Off-Dynamics Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion substantially reframe the empirical contribution. The explicit claim of state-of-the-art performance with a significantly smaller model and training dataset is dropped, while broad low-budget optimization performance and maintained synthetic accessibility become central claims. The proposed framework and interactive application contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explicit limitations concerning additive molecular growth, inability to remove or replace fragments, and unsuitable fixed-size optimization settings. It also explains fragment-size tradeoffs, conditioning-dimensionality effects, declining bonding success, and circumstances favoring MARS. These materially qualify v1's largely positive applicability discussion.

D1.justification: v2 adds a source-code repository reference, learning rate and scheduler settings, stopping patience, GP hyperparameter fitting, categorical relaxation/rounding, baseline tuning, and scaffold composition details. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation. Conversely, v1's explicit latent search bounds and 100-instance GP initialization are no longer stated.

E1.justification: The QED and KAT1 docking evaluation becomes a 20-oracle suite covering QED, rediscovery, similarity, multi-property optimization, structural modification, and predicted activity. KAT1 docking results are removed. Appendix A.2 adds training on ZINC250K fragments and mixed QM9/ZINC250K fragments; evaluation also introduces QM9 scaffolds alongside ZINC250K scaffolds.

E2.justification: v1 Table 2 compares against JT-VAE, Scaffold-GGM, DrugHIVE, LIMO, PGFS, and GP-MOLFORMER. v2 Figures 5–7 instead evaluate MARS, Graph-GA, Smiles-GA, Stoned, MolDQN, and SynFlowNet. Earlier methods remaining in related work does not preserve their participation in the reported comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 introduces common-scaffold, common-budget baseline comparisons and Top-10 learning curves instead of the earlier maximum/mean QED summaries. The input set becomes 37 QM9 and 63 ZINC250K scaffolds, and the 0.60 similarity threshold disappears. New protocols include baseline tuning, model-dimension comparisons, and SA analysis restricted to settings with at least 30 improved scaffolds.

E4.justification: The QED-only conditioning ablation expands to three oracles and adds random search to isolate LSBO's contribution. New analyses examine fragment sources, latent dimensions, two- versus six-dimensional conditioning, similarity changes, bonding success over iterations, and synthetic accessibility. The earlier training-fragment QED distribution is removed.

E5.justification: v2 newly specifies ten seeds, reports seed-averaged bonding rates, and displays error bars on benchmark curves; v1 lacks corresponding repetition and uncertainty reporting. The error-bar statistic is not defined, and neither confidence intervals nor significance tests are specified. This establishes new reporting, not an increase over a known earlier run count.

E6.justification: Earlier aggregate QED and KAT1 results are replaced by extensive benchmark and analysis results. For example, v2 Table 1 reports Top-10 QED scores of 0.930, 0.922, and 0.897 for LSBO+CVAE, RS+CVAE, and LSBO+VAE at threshold 0.5. The stated QM9 reconstruction accuracy changes from over 99% to over 90%. Changed metrics and scaffold populations prevent direct performance comparisons with v1.

M1.justification: Section 4.3.1 changes the reported GP kernel parameterization from one lengthscale symbol to separate continuous and categorical lengthscales. The BRICS-conditioned CVAE, default architecture, UCB search, similarity constraints, penalties, and Algorithm 1 otherwise remain intact. Newly documented acquisition optimization details do not establish a further procedural change.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is reorganized from separate QED and docking sections into a unified benchmark grouped by task and similarity constraint. Training gains separate dataset-selection and model-training subsections. The abstract, conclusion, and related work are substantially revised, with a dedicated limitations discussion and a reorganized, expanded appendix.

P2.justification: The original QED/docking summaries are replaced by extensive learning-curve grids, SA/RA plots, fragment comparisons, scaffold visualizations, and bonding analyses. Retained content is distinguishable: Figures 1–3 persist, the QED trajectories move from Figure 5 to Figure 8, and the application screenshot moves from Figure 10 to Figure 14.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially around Gao et al.'s sample-efficiency benchmark, strong genetic-algorithm baselines, MARS, GFlowNets/SynFlowNet, STONED, and concurrent GenMol research. SA/RA literature is also introduced. This shifts comparative positioning toward low-budget constrained editing and synthesizability assessment rather than mainly generative-model and scaffold-method comparisons.

T1.justification: The kernel definition in Section 4.3.1 now permits separate lengthscales for its continuous and categorical factors, whereas v1 writes both with one parameter. The optimization objectives, CVAE losses, and similarity definition otherwise remain substantively unchanged. No theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited evidence for comparative sample efficiency and synthesizability through common-budget baseline evaluations, broader ablations, predictive SA/RA checks, and explicit applicability limits. Added implementation details also improve reproducibility. Removing the KAT1 study loses direct docking evidence, and the abstract still mentions docking while error bars remain undefined. These shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial strengthening of the paper's central empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CLaSMO research, with matching core methods and retained illustrations. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite extensive experimental revisions.

after.justification: v2 reports original results across 20 optimization tasks, synthetic and retrosynthetic accessibility evaluations, and additional model and optimization analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original QED optimization, KAT1 docking simulations, CVAE reconstruction results, and a conditioning ablation.

results.title: Conditional Latent Space Molecular Scaffold Optimization for Accelerated Molecular Design

C1.justification: The principal contributions—learning calibration from response-consistency graphs and transferring across domains—remain. However, v2's introduction explicitly restricts applicability to correctness aligned with training data and excludes consistently incorrect training information, narrowing the stated scope.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly identifies a fundamental failure condition: consistently wrong responses can produce graphs resembling correct responses. It also adds explanations involving learned graph patterns, self-reflection failures, embedding-feature overfitting, and ROUGE sensitivity to answer length. The conclusion's earlier future-work discussion is replaced by emphasis on this consistency-versus-correctness limitation.

D1.justification: v2 specifies the ROUGE threshold of 0.3, supplies the labeling prompt, and states that baseline default hyperparameters were used. Appendix A now mentions GCN or GIN and both batch sizes, without identifying their experimental assignments. Conversely, explicit split sizes and v1's statement that supplementary materials provide model code disappear; actual code availability is not established by either PDF.

E1.justification: Evaluation expands from TriviaQA and CoQA to include TruthfulQA's longer factual answers and HotpotQA's multi-passage reasoning task. TruthfulQA also becomes an out-of-domain target in Table 3. These additions materially broaden the represented task requirements.

E2.justification: External baseline membership remains unchanged in the corresponding main benchmark and OOD comparisons. Appendix G newly evaluates two alternative GNN configurations against the proposed design: sentence-embedding node features and ROUGE-L graph weights. These constitute limited additions of comparison variants.

E3.justification: v2 reports evaluation across different train/validation splits, replacing v1's explicit first-4,000 training examples and equally divided 1,582 validation/test examples without specifying replacement sizes. It also introduces GPT-4 labeling for TruthfulQA and manual-label evaluation covering 600 questions per dataset on three datasets. The primary calibration metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Section 4.4 checks automatic labels against human judgments and reevaluates calibration using manual labels. Appendix G adds threshold sensitivity at 0.3 versus 0.5, sentence-embedding node-feature ablation, and ROUGE-L edge-weight ablation. Existing sample-size, layer-count, response-count, case-study, and visualization analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without an experimental repetition count. v2 newly states ten repetitions with different train/validation splits and adds ± reporting in Tables 1, 2, and 10. This substantially changes uncertainty reporting, although the meaning of ± is unspecified and an actual increase in run count cannot be established.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 revise existing scores and add two datasets: for Llama3/TriviaQA, 'Ours' AUROC/ECE changes from 0.84/0.025 to 0.864±0.002/0.035±0.004. The revised evaluation description limits direct performance interpretation across versions. New results include automatic-label accuracies of 0.96/0.92/0.89, manual-label comparisons, and ablation outcomes. Training-size results also change, while the original OOD table entries remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 3.1 adds an LLM-based correctness-labeling procedure alongside ROUGE-L, used for TruthfulQA. The similarity graph, cluster-membership node features, GNN prediction, and multiple-prompt procedure remain intact. The corrected cross-entropy equation does not establish a change to the implemented loss.

P1.justification: The abstract, substantial introduction passages, reliability-diagram discussion, and conclusion are rewritten or reorganized. Publication front matter replaces the preprint presentation, broader impacts receive a separate heading, and the appendix hierarchy changes from A.1–A.6 to standalone lettered sections. These editorial changes extend beyond inserting new experiments.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redrawn to expose embedding, clustering, graph construction, and prediction stages. Tables 1–2 expand to four datasets with uncertainty entries, five new tables are added, and the training-size table is placed beside Figure 3. Typography, front matter, and prompt boxes change substantially; the existing reliability and response-pattern plots are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references concerning internal-state confidence estimation, TruthfulQA, LLM judging, and training-data issues, while removing the He–Jiang survey and Huang rank-calibration references. It sharpens the distinction between learned consistency patterns and handcrafted graph statistics, while retaining the overall research positioning.

T1.justification: v2 Equation 8 corrects v1 Equation 7 by adding the missing logarithm to the positive-label term of binary cross-entropy. This repairs the stated objective underlying the accompanying consistency argument. The semantic-class formulation is retained, and no substantial new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical credibility by validating automatic labels against human annotations and confirming comparisons with manual labels, addressing an important unchecked dependency in v1. Broader task coverage, graph-component ablations, and explicit acknowledgment of consistently wrong answers further improve support and scope clarity. Missing split sizes, undefined ± values, and overly broad superiority statements remain weaknesses, but the new validation evidence provides a clear substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same graph-based confidence calibration work. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and corresponding methods, experiments, figures, and tables can be matched despite substantial additions and reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and reports additional benchmark evaluations, human-label validation, and graph-component ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original calibration experiments using Llama3 and Vicuna on TriviaQA and CoQA, including out-of-domain evaluations, sensitivity analyses, and appendix case studies.

results.title: Graph-based Confidence Calibration for Large Language Models

C1.justification: v1's central contribution is the feasibility of prompted LLM world models for web planning, with specialized training proposed as future work. v2 makes scalable world-model training a central contribution and claims that Dreamer-7B performs comparably to GPT-4o, with further gains from in-domain adaptation. The abstract and conclusion now present a substantially broader contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of training-data scaling, domain adaptation, Reddit's dense-layout limitations, and the usefulness of intrinsic evaluation. Its horizon discussion explains degradation through increasingly indistinguishable simulated trajectories. v1's representation-specific hallucination tradeoff, limited-discriminative-power explanation for Mind2Web-live, and dedicated limitations discussion are removed, including the explicit approximately $1-per-task cost qualification.

D1.justification: v2 adds data-source and filtering instructions, synthesis prompts, dataset composition, and detailed training recipes in Appendix C. These include 64 H100 GPUs, batch size 192, optimizer and learning-rate schedules, epoch budgets, and separate adaptation settings. Appendix D documents checkpoint selection. The original planning prompts are largely retained, while v1's approximate per-task API cost is omitted.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation on a 100-task Online-Mind2Web subset and training on over 3.1 million web interactions spanning approximately 1.2 million unique URLs. Appendix D also introduces a 44-task intrinsic action-discrimination evaluation. VisualWebArena and Mind2Web-Live remain covered.

E2.justification: v2 adds Qwen2-VL-7B and Qwen2-VL-72B as world-model comparators across the downstream benchmarks, plus GPT-4o-mini in the intrinsic evaluation. The reactive and tree-search comparison families remain, but v1's contextual reactive results for GPT-4, Gemini, Claude, GPT-4-turbo, and GPT-3.5-turbo are removed from the main comparison.

E3.justification: v1 describes the 910-task VisualWebArena benchmark, whereas v2 explicitly specifies its 233-task human-verified subset. Mind2Web-Live observations change from HTML to screenshots, and completion-rate reporting is dropped. v2 adds stratified Online-Mind2Web sampling with 30 easy, 40 medium, and 30 hard tasks, plus an intrinsic evaluation protocol with deviation-action filtering and checkpoint selection. These are substantial reported protocol changes, not evidence of same-setting performance gains.

E4.justification: v2 adds training-data scaling, domain-specific continual-training analyses, intrinsic-versus-downstream evaluation analysis, and a GPT-4o/Dreamer-7B case comparison. It replaces v1's joint state-representation and horizon study with a horizon study on Online-Mind2Web, removing the HTML/accessibility-tree comparison and task-difficulty breakdown. Simulation and self-refinement ablations remain with revised results; the two original appendix case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix D.3 newly estimates Pearson correlation between intrinsic task-level accuracy and Mind2Web-Live success rate, reporting 0.8455. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests; the addition is an association statistic, not evidence of improved run-level uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 Table 1 adds Online-Mind2Web success rates of 37.0% for GPT-4o WEBDREAMER, 35.0% for Dreamer-7B, and 26.0% for the reactive baseline, alongside extensive new training and intrinsic results. Reported VWA reactive/tree-search scores change from 17.7%/26.4% to 17.6%/26.2%, and Mind2Web-Live reactive success changes from 22.1% to 20.2%, under revised settings. Ablation values are revised, completion and difficulty-specific entries are removed, and the efficiency measurements are retained unchanged.

M1.justification: v1 implements world modeling through prompting and explicitly leaves fine-tuning to future work. v2 introduces an autonomous interaction-data synthesis pipeline and trains Dreamer-7B from Qwen2-VL-7B using next-token prediction of state-change descriptions, followed by domain-specific continual training. These substantially extend the method while retaining the core MPC planning loop.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and related-work discussion are extensively rewritten and condensed. The standalone preliminary section is incorporated into the method, analyses are reorganized around planning and training, and the separate limitations section disappears. The appendices gain an overview and contribution statement and are reorganized around retained prompts, training, intrinsic evaluation, and case studies.

P2.justification: v2 rebuilds the main results table into a method/world-model-by-benchmark layout, redraws the ablation chart, and replaces the joint representation/horizon plot. It adds a synthesis-pipeline diagram, scaling and data-distribution plots, training tables, intrinsic-evaluation displays, and a model-comparison example. The original schematic, efficiency tables, and two appendix case figures remain, with relocation or revised captions.

R1.justification: The reactive-agent, tree-search, and world-model positioning remains recognizable. v2 adds relevant training, perception, and benchmark references and revises its distinction from the same Chae et al. work: the contrast becomes small-scale in-domain training versus general world-model training, rather than trained models versus GPT-4o prompting. Publication-year and venue updates alone do not constitute new cited work.

T1.justification: The POMDP formulation and MPC selection rule remain substantively unchanged, with no new theorems or proofs. v2 Appendix D.2 introduces hierarchical definitions of pair-wise, state-level, and task-level correctness, including explicit treatment of tied scores. The gap-closing ratio gamma defined in v1 Table 3 is removed. These are limited changes to mathematical definitions.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the paper by addressing v1's deferred question of whether specialized world models can be trained effectively. Comparisons against the untrained backbone, additional online evaluation, scaling and adaptation studies, and a detailed training recipe provide meaningful empirical and reproducibility gains. There are material drawbacks: representation and difficulty analyses are lost, and GPT-4o's VWA total conflicts between Tables 1 and 3 (23.6% versus 23.2%), weakening the broad claim of surpassing GPT-4o. These shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial new support for trainable web world models.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe WEBDREAMER and provide readable main text, figures, tables, and complete appendices. The retained planning framework, prompts, and case studies can be matched despite substantial additions and revised experimental settings.

after.justification: v2 reports original evaluations across three benchmarks, trained Dreamer-7B results, scaling and domain-adaptation experiments, and an intrinsic evaluation in Appendix D.

before.justification: v1 reports original WEBDREAMER evaluations on VisualWebArena and Mind2Web-live, efficiency measurements, planning-horizon experiments, and component ablations.

results.title:
Is Your LLM Secretly a World Model of the Internet? Model-Based Planning
  for Web Agents

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution paragraph and discussion retain the same central claims: learned feature proposals, analytically solved output weights, latent refinement and regularization improve training of thin two-layer networks on small datasets. The additional evidence does not redefine the main contribution.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the categorical minibatching prohibition with a discussion of batch-dependent output weights and explicitly states the squared-loss restriction. Appendix B explains why jointly sampled output weights underperform. Section 4.2 qualifies support recovery by acknowledging off-support features, while Remark 1 discusses extension to vector-valued outputs.

D1.justification: Appendix C supplies settings that v1 left to the code: learning rates of 1e-4 for GFT/refinement and 1e-3 for neural networks, 100000 neural-network steps, epsilon=1e-7 and 1000 regularization samples. These are newly documented details; the code address, GPU and reported runtime remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate g1–g3, f1–f3, h1–h3 and the same six UCI datasets: Propulsion, Galaxy, Airfoil, CCPP, Telemonit and Skillkraft. The new appendices vary feature counts and training procedures on existing tasks, without adding data domains or test scenarios.

E2.justification: v2 adds F-Opt and Gaussian kernel ridge regression to each of Tables 1–3. Figure 1 additionally evaluates conventional neural-network training, previously absent from that comparison. Appendix B introduces fully sampled weights and noisy-gradient controls, substantially expanding the evaluated alternatives.

E3.justification: New settings include N=50 and N=200 in Appendix A, joint feature/output-weight sampling and noisy SGD with noise strength 0.1 times the step size in Appendix B, and a median-rule Gaussian kernel. Existing experiments retain their splits, metrics, regularization search and stated GFT training budget; Appendix C's disclosures do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's refinement comparisons and feature visualization, v2 tests direct feature optimization, sensitivity to feature count, replacing the analytic output-weight solve with joint sampling, and adding gradient noise. Appendices A–B and the expanded Figure 1 provide substantial new evidence about component necessity and optimization behavior.

E5.justification: Both versions report five-run mean test MSEs. Tables 4–6 extend the same reporting practice, without adding seed information, dispersion estimates, confidence intervals, significance tests or an increased repeat count.

E6.justification: Matched scores in Tables 1–3 and retained Figure 1 panels are unchanged. v2 adds F-Opt, kernel-ridge and neural-network visualization results, plus extensive width and ablation results in Tables 4–6. These also expose sensitivity: Table 5 reports Fourier GFT-r MSE 1.82 for f3 with d=10, M=200 and N=200, an added setting rather than a revised original score.

M1.justification: The proposed pipeline retains the linear output-weight solve, learned feature distribution, latent-space Adam refinement and total-variation regularization. GFT-p is renamed GFT-r. F-Opt's direct reduced-loss optimization was already described in v1; the new experimental controls do not revise the proposed GFT procedure.

P1.justification: v2 edits prose, replaces GFT-p/post-processing terminology with GFT-r/feature refinement, converts Example 1 into bullets and expands the explanation of compared methods. It adds Appendices A–C and updates author/publication information, while retaining the main section sequence and narrative.

P2.justification: Figure 1 expands from nine to twelve panels through a new neural-network row. Tables 1–3 gain comparator rows and are reflowed, while three new tables present appendix experiments. Best-score highlighting gains boldface, and publication headers are added.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds connections to extreme learning machines, Dunbar et al.'s adaptive random-feature work and implicit kernel learning, while sharpening distinctions from sparse feature selection and alternating updates. Kernel-regression and UCI references are also added. Publication updates for existing references do not represent new related works.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 newly states that the regularized solution of equation (6) converges to the minimum-norm solution of equation (5) as epsilon approaches zero. This adds a limited mathematical property; the core derivations remain unchanged and no new theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: The F-Opt comparisons and Appendix B controls address an important gap in v1 by directly testing the roles of learned proposals and analytically solved output weights. Width experiments and explicit implementation settings further strengthen empirical scrutiny and reproducibility. These are substantial gains, although five-run means still lack dispersion estimates and the newly exposed width-dependent failures receive little interpretation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete, readable versions of the same research work. Their methods, equations, experiments, figures and tables can be matched reliably. v1 ends with references; v2 additionally contains Appendices A–C.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and adds numerical baseline comparisons, feature-count experiments and ablations, including original results in Tables 4–6.

before.justification: Sections 4.2–4.4 report original feature visualizations, synthetic function approximation and UCI regression results in Figure 1 and Tables 1–3, alongside baseline results attributed to prior work.

results.title: Generative Feature Training of Thin 2-Layer Networks

C1.justification: The central claims about reference-matching bias, judgement ambiguity, and the benefits of NMR/DG remain. The corpus contribution is revised from 47,100 ratings and 471 listeners to 246,000 Hindi/Tamil ratings and 492 listeners; Section 7 reports 255,000 annotations including English. These revise the stated contribution's scale without redefining its central scientific claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations for near-tied Tamil rankings and inflated anchor scores, discusses objective metrics' perceptual and language limitations, and uses survey responses to interpret rater behavior. Section 7 explicitly acknowledges no significant English variance reduction. Limitations now discuss missing demographics and additional biases, although Appendix A.8 inconsistently retains the statement that English was not evaluated.

D1.justification: v3 adds an explicit MANGO dataset-access link and identifies TorchAudio-Squim for objective measurements. It also documents rater demonstration calls, iterative guideline development, demographic nonresponse, and institutional ethics approval. XTTS training information is relocated rather than newly introduced.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates Hindi and Tamil using IndicTTS. v3 adds English systems trained on LJSpeech and evaluations by native US English speakers, substantially extending language, corpus, and listener-population coverage (Section 7).

E2.justification: Standard MUSHRA and CMOS remain the comparison protocols, with FS2, ST2, and VITS as the principal evaluated systems. XTTSv2 and duplicated VITS already appeared in v1's extended test; its table is moved into v3's main text. The new objective metrics assess alignment with conventional MUSHRA rather than introduce additional baselines against the proposed variants.

E3.justification: Table 1 increases DG panels from 14 Hindi and 15 Tamil listeners to 20 each, and DG-NMR panels from 15 to 20 each. New protocols include English evaluations with 30 listeners rating 30 utterances, English CMOS with 15 listeners, and a focused Tamil FS2-versus-VITS CMOS test. Section 4.7 also introduces PESQ, STOI, and SI-SDR measurements.

E4.justification: v3 adds objective-metric alignment analysis, CMOS-derived preference breakdowns, an 89-participant post-evaluation survey, and Tamil and English fault-isolation analyses (Section 4.7; Appendices A.2, A.5, A.7). A focused Tamil CMOS comparison investigates the FS2/VITS ranking discrepancy. Existing sensitivity, rejection-rule, and extended-system analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report means, standard deviations, and 95% confidence intervals and use 1,000 subsampling trials for ranking sensitivity. v3 does not specify a revised uncertainty-estimation, seed, or significance-testing procedure. Larger listener panels and changed interval values affect settings and results.

E6.justification: DG and DG-NMR results are revised alongside the enlarged panels: Hindi DG-NMR ST2/VITS means change from 89.55/89.33 in v1 Table 4 to 84.97/85.68 in v3 Table 6, reversing their order. Original MUSHRA, CMOS, NMR, and extended-test scores are retained. v3 additionally reports English, objective-metric, preference, survey, and diagnostic results; these are added or revised findings, not same-setting TTS performance improvements.

M1.justification: The NMR, DG, and combined procedures remain unchanged, including the six error counts, three perceptual dimensions, and scoring weights and caps. Section 5 newly describes iterative development, but the documented procedures and appendix guidelines do not establish a method revision.

P1.justification: v3 substantially expands explanatory material through a new MUSHRA background subsection and extended discussions of scoring and results. It adds dedicated English and Future Work sections and reorganizes the appendices, including moving the extended-test material into the main text. Much of the original introduction and method wording remains.

P2.justification: v3 adds objective-metric, English-comparison, and preference tables; a survey display; Tamil/English diagnostic plots; and English rating distributions. Several existing distribution plots are redrawn, Figure 5 is revised, and the extended-test table moves from the appendix to the main text. These changes substantially expand and reorganize the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v3 adds supporting literature on naturalness, expressive evaluation, anchor limitations, objective metrics, and perceptual biases, including Shirali-Shahreza and Penn, Merritt et al. (2018), Kumar et al. (2023a), and Zielinski. The existing positioning as a critique and refinement of MUSHRA remains.

T1.justification: The scoring formulas in v1 Appendix A.3 and v3 Appendix A.6 are algebraically identical. Reordering the arguments of min(7, SP) and changing notation or equation layout do not change the mathematics. No new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: The English study directly addresses v1's explicit lack of English validation, while larger DG panels and targeted diagnostic analyses substantially strengthen assessment of the proposed protocols. Reporting the absence of significant English variance reduction also clarifies their limits. These gains outweigh incomplete editorial integration: Appendix A.8 still denies English evaluation, and Appendix A.5's 22% difficulty claim conflicts with Figure 9's 12% difficult plus 3% very difficult.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MUSHRA evaluation study and proposed variants. Their text, tables, figures, scoring formula, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial additions in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds English evaluations, objective-metric results, a participant survey, and further diagnostic analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original Hindi and Tamil listening experiments, including MUSHRA and CMOS scores, proposed-variant evaluations, and listener-sensitivity analyses.

results.title: Rethinking MUSHRA: Addressing Modern Challenges in Text-to-Speech Evaluation

C1.justification: The abstract, enumerated contributions, headline performance claims, and conclusion retain their substantive message. However, v2 removes the introduction's assertion that learnable synaptic delays capture only short-window patterns, narrowing the comparative claim motivating TSkips.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the skip-removal results as evidence that TSkips improve learned representations during training, and discusses differences between forward and backward spike activity. New discussion addresses historical-state storage, memory and energy costs, neuromorphic routing constraints, and deployment without delayed states. Section 4.6 also acknowledges the parameter-efficiency advantage of competing transformers.

D1.justification: v2 documents the zero-tensor inference control, its treatment of alpha on DSEC-flow, and per-run NAS-selected delays and positions. Existing hardware, optimizer schedules, neuron initialization, dropout, and detailed architecture tables are retained. Corresponding CIFAR10-DVS-specific skip placements and delays are not supplied.

E1.justification: v2 retains the four original datasets and adds CIFAR10-DVS object classification in Section 4.6. This extends coverage to a distinct recognition task and event streams with artificially generated temporal information from repeated camera movements.

E2.justification: DVS-Gesture Table 2 adds Streaming rollout SNN, cited as Kugele et al. (2021), with 0.8M parameters and 95.56% accuracy. The new CIFAR10-DVS comparison adds NDA ResNet18/VGG11 baselines, alpha-SSA, and SpikingResformer, alongside Spikingformer. The original optical-flow and speech comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 adds evaluation using large spiking ResNet18/VGG11 models with NDA augmentation, and controlled inference tests that replace delayed-state inputs with zeros. Table 12 additionally evaluates NAS searches producing seed-dependent delay and connection choices. The original datasets' stated splits, metrics, sequence lengths, and training schedules are retained.

E4.justification: Section 4.5 and Figure 8 add spike-activity analyses for two SHD examples. Appendices B.2 and C.2 test whether gains survive disabling temporal skips at inference, while Appendix D.2 examines robustness across NAS seeds. The earlier delay, placement, depth, energy, convergence, and operator analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v1 provides benchmark point estimates without reported seed counts or dispersion. v2 explicitly reports additional DSEC-flow NAS experiments across three random seeds, with mean AEE and standard deviation in Table 12. This introduces uncertainty reporting for that evaluation, without establishing repeated-run reporting for all benchmarks.

E6.justification: The original headline scores are retained, but v2 adds substantial results: CIFAR10-DVS backward-TSkips ResNet18 reaches 82.93% versus its 78.00% baseline; SHD backward-TSkips-1 scores 92.78% with skips disabled versus 93.64% enabled; and Table 12 reports seed-aggregated AEE. These are new evaluations, not improvements over v1 under unchanged conditions. New Table 6 reverses Mini/Micro labels relative to Table 1.

M1.justification: The core delayed connections, adaptive LIF neurons, alpha mixing, NAS procedure, and training algorithm are retained. Sections 4.5 and 5 introduce an optional deployment procedure that disables delayed-state propagation at inference. For DSEC-flow, Appendix B.2 explains retaining the alpha-weighted current-state contribution while zeroing the delayed contribution.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the order of the original methodological and experimental material are retained. v2 makes targeted explanatory rewrites, introduces Observations, Scalability, and Discussion sections, and reorganizes the supplement into Appendices A-D. Author information, citation style, terminology, and cross-references are also updated.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column format to a predominantly single-column journal layout, extensively resizing and relocating figures and tables. v2 adds the spike-activity Figure 8 and Tables 4, 6, 9, and 12. Existing plots and supplementary tables remain identifiable despite renumbering and reformatting.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds substantive discussion of streaming rollouts, SCTT temporal skips, and TTFS delayed connections. It replaces the blanket short-window characterization with distinctions involving configuration-search expense, synchronization, and evaluation scope. Section 4.4 also positions TSkips as complementary to DCLS-Delays. These changes materially refine the relationship to closely related research.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 changes the formal temporal constraint from t < Delta t < T to 0 < t - Delta t < T and explicitly specifies discrete time indices. This revises the admissible delayed-time condition. The principal equations and search-space calculation remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof appears.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps through inference-removal controls, three-seed NAS results, and evaluation on standard architectures for CIFAR10-DVS. Closer engagement with prior temporal-skip methods and explicit hardware limitations also improve scientific positioning and qualification of the claims. These are substantial gains beyond the retained headline scores. The inconsistent Mini/Micro labels in Table 6 and missing CIFAR10-DVS skip configurations limit precision and reproducibility, but do not outweigh the overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TSkips research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and supplementary sections are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds CIFAR10-DVS experiments, inference-time skip-removal analyses, spike-activity observations, and experiments across random seeds.

before.justification: v1 reports original optical-flow and classification experiments on DSEC-flow, DVS128 Gesture, SHD, and SSC, alongside ablations, convergence analyses, and energy estimates.

results.title: TSkips: Efficiency Through Explicit Temporal Delay Connections in Spiking Neural Networks

C1.justification: The introduction explicitly extends the contribution beyond RIS to REC and positions holistic masking with pixel-level DCL against architecture-dependent, CLS-based alternatives. This broadens the claimed applicability and sharpens the novelty claim, while the abstract's original RIS performance claims and the conclusion remain substantially unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations about preserving semantic anchors during text masking and the unfavorable accuracy/computation tradeoff of cross-distillation. It also interprets RefClef and REC results as supporting broader applicability. The existing limitations concerning ambiguous descriptions and difficult visual scenes are retained.

D1.justification: v2 describes the additional linguistic masking variants and acknowledges use of the NSML platform. However, it removes v1's two-A6000 hardware disclosure and measured 18.4-hour CARIS versus 16.7-hour MaskRIS training comparison. Appendix C's core implementation settings and the code-access link remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds segmentation evaluation on RefClef, extending beyond the three COCO-derived datasets, and adds Referring Expression Comprehension on RefCOCO (Table 3). These expand both represented data and task requirements beyond v1's segmentation coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds CM-MaskSD and MagNet. Table 2 adds DETRIS and a ReMamber-with/without-MaskRIS comparison; ReMamber previously appeared only in other comparisons. New REC comparisons evaluate EEVG, SimVG and C3VG, substantially broadening the comparator set.

E3.justification: The established RIS splits, metrics, image resolution and training recipe remain unchanged. Added experiments introduce REC evaluation using DetAcc and additional encoder configurations, plus comparisons varying masking regions, linguistic masking schemes and auxiliary distillation. These extend the protocol without replacing the existing RIS evaluation.

E4.justification: v2 adds object-centric versus context versus holistic image masking (Table 5), whole-word/span/POS-based text masking (Appendix Table C), and cross-distillation (Appendix Table D). Figure 8 adds three qualitative ablation examples. Earlier component, masking-ratio, patch-size and training-loss analyses are retained, sometimes relocated.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or statistical significance tests. Both present point estimates and training curves without uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: v2 adds RefClef results (75.21 oIoU for CARIS and 76.06 with MaskRIS), REC results, additional architecture comparisons and new ablation outcomes. Table 1 revises combined-training CARIS scores, including RefCOCO testA from 79.40 to 79.85 and RefCOCOg test from 69.75 to 68.73; corresponding MaskRIS scores remain unchanged. The earlier measured training times are removed.

M1.justification: The proposed random image masking, BERT-style text masking and shared-weight clean/masked prediction distillation remain unchanged. The corrected loss-weight equation preserves the default lambda of 0.5. Alternative masking and distillation schemes are evaluated as ablations; no changed core procedure is documented for the REC applications.

P1.justification: The contribution list, compatibility discussion and computational-cost discussion are revised, and a dedicated comparison section is added. The masking-ratio discussion moves into a reorganized appendix; affiliations, acknowledgments and citation style also change. Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column format to a single-column journal layout with extensively repositioned displays. v2 adds a comparison diagram and several tables, expands Tables 1–2 and the qualitative masking figure, rearranges the augmentation plots side by side, and moves the masking-ratio table into the appendix.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning against masking-based RIS research, especially CM-MaskSD and MagNet, through the introduction, related work, new Figure 2 and Section 4.4. It also adds literature supporting REC comparisons, RefClef and alternative text masking strategies.

T1.justification: Appendix Equation 5 changes from lambda times Ldist plus (1-lambda) times Lce to (1-lambda) times Ldist plus lambda times Lce. This resolves v1's contradiction with its statement that lambda=1 recovers CARIS. Other mathematical definitions and equations remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the paper by addressing v1's missing comparisons with closely related masking methods and adding targeted evidence about masking choices, distillation and applicability beyond the original RIS benchmarks. Correcting Equation 5 also removes a concrete mathematical inconsistency. These gains outweigh the loss of measured runtime and hardware information, although the added experiments remain sparsely specified and some Table 1 commentary is stale after the comparator and score updates.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MaskRIS. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and can be matched despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds RefClef results, referring expression comprehension experiments and further masking and distillation analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original segmentation results, robustness evaluations, component ablations and training analyses in Section 4 and Appendix A.

results.title: MaskRIS: Semantic Distortion-aware Data Augmentation for Referring Image Segmentation

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion add a central comparative claim of more accurate feature and graph-structure reconstruction, beyond v1's feasibility claim that graph data can leak. The research question shifts toward exploiting graph properties, while the introduction narrows the novelty claim from the first work to among the first.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations linking DLG's difficulties to feature–topology interdependencies. Appendix H attributes difficult feature reconstruction to absent direct node-level supervision and interprets higher multi-hop scores as successful topology reconstruction despite imperfect features. Most existing limitations and sensitivity interpretations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix H adds technical documentation that GSM-k evaluation aggregates neighborhoods using a randomly initialized GCN with at least k layers. Existing GLG optimizer, initialization, width, and regularization details are retained; moving pseudocode to Appendix A does not change their substance.

E1.justification: V2 extends evaluation to citation-network data through OGBN-Arxiv for Node Attacker 1 and adds Tox21 molecular graph reconstruction in Appendix H. The existing social, synthetic, MUTAG, COIL-RAG, and FRANKENSTEIN coverage is retained.

E2.justification: V1 discusses competing attacks without directly benchmarking them. V2 adds DLG comparisons across all seven attack settings in Tables 3–9. Tox21 comparisons additionally include GRAIN, TabLeak, DLG+A, and TabLeak+A in Tables 19–20.

E3.justification: The new Tox21 evaluation introduces GSM-0, GSM-1, GSM-2, and FULL metrics alongside RNMSE, AUC, and AP, including comparisons with adjacency information supplied to baselines. Settings for retained experiments, including model width, optimizer, batch sizes, and matching procedures, remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Table 19 adds a limited side-information analysis comparing DLG and TabLeak with their adjacency-informed +A variants. The existing regularization, network-width, batch-size, initialization, threshold, and graph-size/density analyses are retained, often relocated to appendices.

E5.justification: V2 Table 19 introduces asymmetric upper/lower uncertainty margins without defining their statistical meaning. Existing standard-deviation reporting and run counts remain: generally 20 runs and 10 for minibatch experiments. V2 explicitly calls the 20 runs independent, without reporting an increase.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive baseline, OGBN-Arxiv, and Tox21 results. Some retained values also change: GCN/GitHub joint node reconstruction AUC changes from 0.96±0.01 in v1 Table 4 to 0.99±0.04 in v2 Table 6. The PDFs do not explain whether these revisions reflect corrections or reruns; existing batch and TU-dataset results are retained.

M1.justification: The gradient-matching objectives, regularizers, projection and sampling procedures, and Algorithms 1–3 remain unchanged. The algorithms move to Appendix A; attacker suffixes a/b/c become G/N/GN. Molecular initialization and thresholding strategies already appeared in v1.

P1.justification: V2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: related work becomes Section 2, algorithms move to Appendix A, and neighborhood, batch, and sensitivity studies move to Appendix F. TU-dataset discussion is consolidated in Appendix G. Extensive prose revisions standardize reconstruction terminology and attacker names.

P2.justification: Seven main result tables gain separate DLG blocks, and the target-node table gains an OGBN-Arxiv column. New tables summarize method differences, threat models, and Tox21 results. Existing figures are retained but several move to appendices; TU adjacency-table panels change from stacked to side-by-side.

R1.justification: The new Related Work section substantively positions GLG against concurrent GRAIN, emphasizing their different requirements for node-degree information, and adds DAGER and graph-privacy literature. Table 1 provides a new method comparison, replacing v1's positioning as the sole first graph-gradient attack.

T1.justification: Propositions 1–6, their stated conditions, the label-extraction derivation, and proofs in Appendices B–E retain the same mathematical substance. V2 adds no theorem, proof, or substantive correction; the additional GSM metrics serve empirical evaluation.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses an important validation gap through systematic DLG comparisons and additional GRAIN/TabLeak benchmarks, substantially strengthening evidence for GLG's comparative value. Its treatment of concurrent work also improves novelty positioning. Some superiority statements exceed the results—GRAIN has higher GSM-0, and DLG wins certain GitHub feature comparisons—and Table 19's uncertainty margins are undefined. These limitations temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial gain in comparative validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GLG research and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Renamed attackers and relocated material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: Section 6 and Appendices F–H retain original experiments and add baseline comparisons and results on OGBN-Arxiv and Tox21.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix F report original feature and adjacency reconstruction experiments, including batch, sensitivity, and initialization studies.

results.title: Gradient Inversion Attack on Graph Neural Networks

C1.justification: v2 adds the conclusion that medical and non-medical base models perform similarly after fine-tuning. The three framework requirements, strong language-only baselines, LoRA's in-distribution advantage and absence of a consistent robustness winner remain. Greater abstract emphasis on shift-versus-method variability restates a conclusion already present in v1.

C2.justification: v2 adds specific qualifications about medical-knowledge and demographic biases in LLM judges, the predominantly radiological scope, and the framework's status as a research tool rather than a clinically deployable benchmark. Appendix E further explains generalization through related question patterns and recommends greater training-data diversity.

D1.justification: v2 supplies separate selected hyperparameters for the non-medical model, revised evaluator prompts, and explicit identification of LLaVA-Med with (IA)3 for the retained multimodal ablation. Dataset-processing instructions and code-access information remain substantially unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use English SLAKE, OVQA and MIMIC-CXR-VQA with the same medical VQA coverage. The new swapped-shift study changes which existing SLAKE modalities and question categories are held out, rather than introducing new data or task types. Corruption and combined OVQA shifts already appear in v1.

E2.justification: v2 adds LLaVA 1.6 as a non-medical comparator to LLaVA-Med 1.5 throughout the robustness experiments. Appendix B.1 also expands the evaluator comparison beyond Mistral and traditional metrics to models including Phi-3, Gemma, Qwen, LLaMA, Granite, Biomistral and Prometheus. The original fine-tuning and sanity-baseline sets remain.

E3.justification: Evaluation switches from Mistral to Gemma with revised closed-ended grading prompts, and the human study increases from 50 to 100 questions per dataset. New protocols evaluate LLaVA 1.6 and hold out MRI or Position categories in SLAKE instead of X-Ray or Size. Original dataset sizes, preprocessing and hyperparameter-search ranges are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds per-question image/no-image win-tie-loss analysis, comparisons among LLM judges, and a SLAKE ablation testing sensitivity to held-out categories. Appendix C.5.1 adds statistical examinations of robustness rankings and variability. The corruption study and multimodal-shift ablation are retained, not newly introduced.

E5.justification: New Appendix C.5.1 reports 100 bootstrapped robustness estimates per experiment, pairwise Welch tests with multiple-testing correction, and ANOVA F-values and p-values. These substantially extend v1's robustness uncertainty reporting. The existing three-seed PEFT means and standard deviations remain; no increase in training seeds is established.

E6.justification: Tables 14-19 revise scores and add non-medical-model results, alongside new evaluator, swapped-shift and statistical findings. For example, OVQA LoRA's open-ended question-type OoD score changes from 1.72 to 1.98 in Table 16. Because the evaluator changes from Mistral to Gemma, this is a replaced measurement, not a same-setting performance gain.

M1.justification: The framework's evaluator component changes from Mistral to Gemma. Appendix A.2 also revises closed-ended prompts to explicitly accept synonymous answers and additional irrelevant detail. The three requirements, hybrid exact-match/LLM scoring structure and fine-tuning methods remain.

P1.justification: The former framework-setup and separate fine-tuning-study sections become a unified Empirical Study with explicit R1-R3 validation subsections. Results discussion and conclusions are rewritten, and appendix dataset details move before hyperparameter searches. This substantially reorganizes the narrative beyond merely appending experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adds win-tie-loss charts, an expanded evaluator heatmap, non-medical-model plots, a significance matrix, a corruption-pipeline diagram and swapped-shift panels. Tables gain medical/non-medical subdivisions, qualitative examples move to the appendix, and the publication template changes typography and page layout.

R1.justification: v2 adds Gemma, Bahri et al. and Jeong et al., positioning its fine-tuned medical/non-medical comparison against Jeong's zero- and few-shot findings. Some contextual references, including Yoon et al. and Ma et al., disappear. The central positioning around three evaluation pitfalls remains.

T1.justification: The relative-robustness definition is unchanged, and neither version introduces theoretical propositions or proofs. The new bootstrap, Welch-test and ANOVA procedures are empirical statistical analyses rather than new mathematical theory.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation by comparing multiple judges on a larger human-rated sample, checking robustness findings with a second base model, and testing alternative held-out categories. These address v1's dependence on one evaluator and one backbone. Added statistical analyses and explicit applicability limitations improve assessability, although changed scoring prevents interpreting cross-version numerical differences as performance gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SURE-VQA. Their complete main texts, figures, tables and appendices support comparison, including matching relocated material and distinguishing changed evaluation settings.

after.justification: v2 reports these empirical studies with revised evaluation and adds LLM-evaluator comparisons, a non-medical base model, alternative held-out splits and statistical analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original fine-tuning experiments on three medical VQA datasets, a human-rater study, and corruption and multimodal-shift analyses.

results.title: SURE-VQA: Systematic Understanding of Robustness Evaluation in Medical VQA Tasks

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: auxiliary cross-modal alignment, instruction tracking, and improved sample efficiency and systematic generalization. Explicitly naming MiniGrid alongside BabyAI clarifies the existing two-benchmark scope.

C2.justification: v2 adds an explicit applicability discussion requiring textual instructions and modality embeddings. Appendix A.1 interprets the runtime penalty in relation to interaction efficiency, while A.2.3 explains the preference for episode-word similarity through its lower computational cost.

D1.justification: v2 documents conjunction-based parsing, replacement with mask tokens, and reward-threshold-based trajectory selection more explicitly. It also reports runtime estimates. Existing optimizer settings, learning rates, batch sizes, hardware, and code link are retained, with several settings relocated to Appendix A.

E1.justification: The five BabyAI levels and MiniGrid PutNear task are retained. v2 Figure 4 and Table 2 add RGB MiniGrid GoToObj and GoToDoor evaluations, extending task coverage within the existing gridworld domains.

E2.justification: v2 adds LISA as a comparator on GoToSeqS5R2 and OpenDoorsOrderN4 in Table 3. Figure 8 also adds BabyAI with instruction tracking but without CAREL as a control. The existing BabyAI and SHELM baselines remain.

E3.justification: v2 introduces convergence-budget comparisons with LISA using 100,000 demonstration trajectories and a timing protocol averaging FPS over 100,000 frames. Plotted training horizons extend from 20M to 30M frames for Synth and from 5M to 10M for PutNear. These substantially expand the evaluation design.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's pooling and instruction-tracking comparisons, Appendix A.2 adds loss-coefficient sensitivity, action-embedding removal, alternative tracking similarity scores, and instruction tracking without CAREL. Appendix A.1 adds computational-cost analysis, substantially expanding component-level and supplementary evaluation.

E5.justification: Both versions state two random seeds and show shaded learning-curve bands. v2 additionally reports numerical ± terms in Tables 2-3, but does not define their statistical meaning or establish an increase in run counts.

E6.justification: v2 adds LISA, additional MiniGrid, ablation, and runtime results, alongside revised learning curves. For example, Table 2 reports GoToDoor success of 83% ± 1% for SHELM + CAREL versus 50% ± 3% for SHELM at 1.5M frames. Table 4 newly reports average throughput of 420.17 FPS for CAREL versus 668.93 for BabyAI.

M1.justification: The core architecture, multi-grained contrastive objective, and instruction tracking are retained. However, the stated masking schedule changes from p = 0.8 tanh(2t/T) + 0.01 in v1 to p = tanh(t/T) in v2 Section 2.2.1, a limited procedural revision.

P1.justification: Much of the original prose and overall narrative remains intact. v2 expands method motivation and worked instruction-tracking explanations, separates the pseudocode, reorganizes experimental subsections, and moves optimizer details into an appendix.

P2.justification: v2 introduces four tables and four appendix analysis figures, separates the SHELM comparison into an expanded three-panel Figure 4, and revises existing plot axes and captions. The document also adopts a substantially different journal layout, including wider text and figure placement.

R1.justification: v2 adds Garg et al. on LISA, Yu on sample-efficient reinforcement learning, and Ladosz et al. on exploration. These support the new comparison and runtime discussion; the central positioning around adapting X-CLIP-style alignment to instruction-following RL remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Equation 12 changes normalization from 1/n to 1/N, resolving the mismatch with the declared N-pair batch; n denotes episode length. Appendix A.4 also supplies a formal POMDP definition and discounted-return objective. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: Appendix A.2 substantially strengthens component validation by isolating choices that v1 largely evaluated together. Runtime measurements expose the computational cost of sample-efficiency gains, and worked masking details improve reproducibility. These address important gaps in v1, although undefined uncertainty terms and unequal LISA training budgets limit the added comparative evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CAREL framework. Their text, equations, figures, and tables support reliable comparison. v1 has no appendix; v2's Appendix A is available and included in this assessment.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds benchmark comparisons, runtime measurements, and component ablations in the main text and Appendix A.

before.justification: v1 reports original BabyAI and SHELM experiments, including learning curves and instruction-tracking comparisons in Figures 2-3.

results.title: CAREL: Instruction-guided reinforcement learning with cross-modal auxiliary objectives

C1.justification: v1 foregrounds artificial nodes, universality under strict edge ordering and financial-task performance. v3 drops MEGA-GNN's universality contribution and foregrounds the neighbor-aware operator, stronger moment-based expressiveness and equal asymptotic complexity. Principal empirical claims extend to social networks. AML superiority is qualified through 17-of-18 comparisons against corresponding Multi-GNN variants and MEGA-PNA leading five of six datasets against all reported competitors.

C2.justification: v3 attributes gains more specifically to correct neighbor grouping and the concentration of illicit transactions on multi-edge pairs, and addresses parameter-count and efficiency explanations. Limitations now identify the moment-based theoretical scope and untested application domains, replacing v1's emphasis on evolving multigraphs. Appendix F also replaces v1's categorical dismissal of fairness concerns with substantive discussion of false positives, inherited bias, interpretability and human oversight.

D1.justification: v3 supplies a repository URL and states that code, preprocessing, training scripts and configurations are public, replacing v1's future-release promise. It adds software/CUDA versions, CPU/RAM specifications, timing boundaries, parameter counts, dataset statistics, temporal graph-construction details and R-GCNE settings (Appendices C–D). The original GIN/PNA hyperparameters and two-hop, 100-neighbor sampling remain largely unchanged; these disclosures do not imply wholesale experimental reconfiguration.

E1.justification: Beyond v1's AML transaction classification and ETH phishing detection, v3 evaluates Reddit, Wikipedia and MOOC user-state prediction and a synthetic per-neighbor-statistics regression task. It also includes AML Large HI/LI and ETH scenarios with artificially collapsed parallel edges. The added social domain, regression task and altered graph-input conditions substantially broaden coverage.

E2.justification: AML comparisons add plain GenAgg, R-GCNE, FraudGT, Multi-FraudGT and an edge-classification adaptation of DIAM (v3 Tables 16 and 20). ETH adds DIAM and Multi-FraudGT while dropping the reported ADAMM-GenAgg and Multi-GenAgg rows. JODIE participates in the new social-network comparison. GFP+LightGBM and GFP+XGBoost remain in Appendix E.1 rather than being removed.

E3.justification: New protocols include independently generated synthetic train/validation/test graphs evaluated by MAE, 60/20/20 temporal social splits evaluated by ROC-AUC, capacity-matched controls and neighborhood-size sweeps. AML PR-AUC reporting disappears. ETH splitting changes in the description from transactions in v1 Section 4 to nodes ordered by first transaction in v3 Appendix C.4, retaining 65/15/20 proportions. This is a reported protocol revision; unchanged overlapping scores do not establish a rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds synthetic aggregation diagnostics, ETH edge-collapse tests, AML random-grouping controls, capacity-matched comparisons, and empirical sampling-size, memory and training-cost analyses. Existing component ablations gain base-model comparisons and medium AML datasets but lose the ego-ID-only configurations. The port-permutation study is revised from Multi-GIN/Multi-PNA to Multi-PNA/Multi-FraudGT. These substantially expand tests of mechanism, confounding and scalability beyond v1.

E5.justification: Both versions report means and standard deviations across different seeds: five runs in v1 and at least five in v3, without establishing an increase for retained experiments. v3 adds a focused set of two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests across six paired AML dataset scores (Appendix E.4, Table 21). The comparison against the strongest non-MEGA baseline yields p=0.093.

E6.justification: Retained AML entries change between v1 Table 2 and v3 Table 16: MEGA-GIN Medium LI F1 changes from 39.03 to 46.05, and MEGA-GenAgg Small HI from 74.88 to 74.48. Multi-FraudGT now leads Small HI at 75.81. Extensive new task, control and resource results appear, while mixed-aggregator AML rows, GenAgg-based ETH rows and PR-AUC results disappear. These are reported result revisions, not established same-setting algorithmic gains.

M1.justification: The central two-stage, bidirectional architecture remains. v3 adds MEGA-RGCNE, combining PNA-style first-stage pooling with relation-specific transformations in the second stage (Appendix C.5). It also revises the written reverse-edge update to include the previous individual edge embedding, unlike v1 Equation 10 (v3 Equation 11). These are limited procedural extensions; the neighbor-aware terminology itself does not establish a new method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and method exposition are extensively rewritten around neighbor-aware aggregation. Related work moves from Section 5 to Section 2, while detailed limitations of existing methods move to Appendix A. Experiments are reorganized into diagnostic, social, financial, ablation and scalability sections, and the appendices are restructured. The title, authorship listing and publication header also change.

P2.justification: v3 redraws the aggregation illustration and introduces detailed layer diagrams and relational-model diagrams. The AML presentation shifts from v1's colored result table to main-text comparison plots with expanded appendix tables. ETH results are reformatted, component tables gain parameter counts, and new control/resource tables and scalability plots appear. Existing Multi-GNN/ADAMM illustrations are combined and relocated to the appendix.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially to DIAM, FraudGT, JODIE, relational architectures and their expressiveness, aggregation theory, and financial-crime applications.
