Appendix A develops the distinction and complementarity between relation-aware and neighbor-aware processing. Earlier universality/random-initialization and subgraph-method discussions are reduced. This changes the research positioning beyond bibliographic updates or moving the related-work section.

T1.justification: v1's conditional-universality theorem, unique-node-ID lemma and BFS proof construction are removed. v3 introduces formal single-stage and neighbor-aware operators and a new expressiveness theorem for sum/raw-moment aggregators, whose proof assumes a constant edge-feature coordinate. Its complexity analysis includes linear transformations and node activations, extending v1's aggregation-focused analysis. The permutation-equivariance proof and port-number proposition/counterexample are also revised.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the empirical explanation of why the method works. Random-grouping, edge-collapse and capacity-matched controls address important alternatives left unresolved by v1's benchmark and component comparisons. Broader evaluated competitors, social-domain validation, measured resource costs and concrete reproducibility information make the evidence more assessable. Statistical tests and substantive limitations also temper the claims. PR-AUC results are lost, and the changed ETH split description alongside unchanged scores remains unresolved, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the substantial gains in experimental support and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MEGA-GNN, retaining the two-stage multigraph aggregation framework and overlapping AML/ETH experiments. The complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial renaming and reorganization.

after.justification: v3 reports original financial and social-network experiments, synthetic node regression, controlled ablations, and runtime/memory measurements in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original AML edge-classification and ETH node-classification experiments, component and port-number ablations, and inference-throughput measurements, including supplementary results in the appendices.

results.title: MEGA: Message Passing Neural Networks for Multigraphs with EdGe Attributes

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: introducing MICL, proposing PTGM and IKD within MoInCL, and demonstrating improved continual learning across six multimodal tasks. The expanded experiments support these retained claims without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of task-recency effects, captioning interference, positive transfer, and IKD's shared-backbone regularization, together with interpretations of the new analyses. It explicitly excludes non-textual outputs and clarifies the replay-free scope. The explicit small-dataset limitation is replaced by a specific limitation concerning incomplete answer-space coverage from generated pseudo-QA pairs; broader-impact discussion is also added.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents offline pseudo-target generation, identifies the generators, and specifies 48GB GPU memory. Section 4.4.3 reports approximately 64 versus 45 minutes per AudioCaps training epoch and explains that the roughly 40% overhead excludes offline generation. These are additional disclosures; the original implementation settings are largely retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds MMLU evaluation of the backbone's general knowledge and reasoning capability (Section 4.4.5). The six image/audio/video captioning and QA datasets remain unchanged. Additional task orders rearrange this retained coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds BECAME and HiDe-LLaVA to the main comparisons and per-task forgetting tables, alongside the five original baselines. It also evaluates joint training as an upper-bound comparator. BECAME additionally joins the first-three-task comparison, formerly v1 Table 4 and now v2 Table 2.

E3.justification: The original splits, metrics, two task orders, and 1B setup are retained. New protocols include two additional orders, including strict modality/task-type alternation; an 8B backbone experiment; joint training; paired transfer evaluations; 0/50/100% instruction-corpus conditions; and zero-shot MMLU evaluation before and after continual-learning steps.

E4.justification: v2 introduces component-removal ablations for PTGM, IKD, and weight fusion, plus analyses of cross-task transfer, instruction-corpus sensitivity, computational cost, and general LLM capability retention. Appendix C tests challenging task-order robustness, and Figure 9 adds generated pseudo-QA examples. These substantially expand the diagnostic evidence beyond v1's forgetting trajectories and captioning example.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or statistical significance tests. v2's additional task orders and MMLU fluctuations across training steps do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive results for new comparators, ablations, transfer, sensitivity, MMLU, additional orders, and the 8B model. Original MoInCL scores remain unchanged, while PathWeave's numerical and qualitative outputs are revised; for example, Order 1 CIDEr changes from 33.35 to 34.20 in Table 1. HiDe-LLaVA becomes the highest-scoring continual-learning comparator on Order 2 QA accuracy: 46.15 versus EWF's 45.85 and MoInCL's 45.22.

M1.justification: PTGM, IKD, LoRA adaptation, weight fusion, Algorithm 1, and the three-round QA-generation prompts are retained. v2 clarifies pseudo-target generation and the architecture without establishing a changed algorithm. The additional 8B experiment tests the existing method.

P1.justification: Much of the original abstract, introduction, method description, and conclusion remains intact. v2 adds explanatory passages and a method-distinction subsection, gives experimental setup explicit subheadings, and reorganizes the appendix into Sections A–H with a contents list. The main narrative sequence is preserved.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column layout to a single-column journal layout. Existing comparison tables expand, eight new tables and Figure 9 are added, and Figure 2 explicitly displays instruction outputs. Figures 3–8 are rearranged into larger two-column grids on separate pages, rather than two figures per page.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands contemporary research coverage with Audio Flamingo, newer VideoLLaMA and Qwen-VL models, and continual-learning work including HiDe-LLaVA, SEFE, CL-MoE, and BECAME. New Section 3.6 explicitly distinguishes IKD from conventional distillation and identifies weight fusion as an adopted strategy rather than a primary contribution.

T1.justification: The mathematical task formulation, loss definitions, weight-fusion rule, and evaluation formulas are retained. Neither version supplies theoretical proofs or guarantees. The added scope and memory-free explanations clarify the existing formulation rather than introduce new mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1 through component ablations, challenging-order tests, and larger-model validation (Table 5 and Appendices C/E), substantially strengthening the empirical case. Cost disclosures and specific limitations also improve transparency. Reporting flaws temper these gains: HiDe-LLaVA's Order 1 CIDEr is 25.27 in Table 1, while Table 14 implies 53.33, and Section 4.4.1 overlooks its Order 2 QA lead. These issues weaken particular comparisons, but the added component and robustness validation still provides a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MICL setting and MoInCL method. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds component ablations, transfer and sensitivity studies, MMLU evaluation, additional task orders, and larger-model experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original six-task continual-learning experiments, including baseline comparisons, task-by-task performance and forgetting, and qualitative outputs in the main text and appendix.

results.title: Modality-Inconsistent Continual Learning of Multimodal Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction expand the central contribution from improved multi-instance sketch-to-image generation to controllable concept-art generation with paired isometric and terrain representations. Although v1 already illustrated downstream 3D reconstruction, the dual-representation terrain workflow becomes an explicit main contribution only in v2.

C2.justification: v2 explains the large-scene limitation through SDXL's 32-fold downsampling and adds segmentation/depth-estimation limitations for 3D assembly. Appendix B interprets layer-placement results through contour amplification and efficiency tradeoffs. The original energy-competition, noise, texture and base-model limitation discussions largely retain their meaning.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies expand-only self-attention modulation and the terrain-sharing parameters alpha=5 and gamma0=1. Appendix H substantially expands the previously brief 3D backend description with segmentation, heightmaps, texture and asset retrieval, and Unity assembly. Table 3 supplies memory and timing measurements, and the original code link is replaced by an official repository and maintained mirror.

E1.justification: T2I-CompBench changes from a suggested benchmark in v1 to actual evaluation of color binding, spatial relations and small-object numeracy in v2. v2 also demonstrates paired isometric and terrain-only outputs. Non-game scenes and 3D reconstruction examples already existed in v1; those broad domains are not new.

E2.justification: v2 Table 2 adds DenseDiff and T2I-Adapter to the custom-scene quantitative comparison; v1 included them only in qualitative comparisons. New Table 1 also includes Stable v3 and FLUX.1 reference scores, explicitly attributed to the benchmark source rather than newly run experiments. The original qualitative comparator set is retained.

E3.justification: The reported custom evaluation expands from 20 to 50 scenes. v2 introduces GPT-4V-generated square sketches with manually adjusted sizes, B-VQA and UniDet metrics, and a stated 300-prompts-per-metric benchmark protocol. New layer-placement experiments measure memory and latency. Core inference settings remain unchanged. The numeracy passage's 100 examples and omitted minimum resolution leave that protocol incompletely specified.

E4.justification: New Appendix B, Table 3 and Figure 12 test where dense tuning should operate across ControlNet and U-Net, examining visual artifacts, accuracy, memory and latency. Figure 18 extends the hyperparameter analysis to additional scenes. The earlier TopK histogram, grayscale checks and model-transfer studies are retained; moving the histogram into Section 5.4 is not a new analysis.

E5.justification: v2 newly states ten generated images per prompt for T2I-CompBench and explicitly labels three seed-specific examples in Figure 2. These are limited additions to sampling and seed disclosure, not evidence of increased repetitions for retained experiments. Neither version reports confidence intervals, dispersion estimates or significance tests.

E6.justification: Custom-scene scores change: T3-S2S global CLIP/user ratings move from 0.3497/3.88 in v1 Table 1 to 0.3491/3.79 in v2 Table 2, alongside the change from 20 to 50 scenes, so these are not same-setting performance comparisons. v2 adds T2I-CompBench results of 0.6872, 0.4256 and 0.6257 for color, spatial relations and numeracy, plus layer-cost measurements and terrain/3D outputs.

M1.justification: v2 Section 4.3 adds full-scene and empty-terrain generation branches connected by mask-guided feature sharing with a time-dependent blending schedule. This substantially extends the original single-image workflow. The core prompt-balancing and TopK feature-enhancement procedures remain unchanged despite renaming Characteristics Prominence to Characteristics Priority.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and introduction are reframed around concept-art and terrain generation. Section 3 is substantially rewritten and reorganized, method terminology changes, the overview structure is condensed, and the TopK appendix becomes Section 5.4. The limitations and backend descriptions are also extensively reorganized and expanded.

P2.justification: v2 adds the twin-branch diagram, benchmark and cost tables, layer-placement visualizations, and terrain columns in existing example grids. Attention/value visualizations gain annotations, main qualitative and ablation figures are rearranged into compact adjacent panels, and the 3D demonstrations are redesigned and expanded. These exceed simple renumbering or numerical table updates.

R1.justification: v2 trims the broad text-to-image background citations and adds targeted foundations for its analysis and backend, including query-key normalization, SENet, Segment Anything, Osprey and 3D reconstruction methods. Its central positioning relative to ControlNet, Dense Diffusion, layout control and Sketch2Scene remains substantially intact.

T1.justification: v2 Section 3 adds embedding-norm decomposition, bounds on projected key/value norms, and an approximate exponential attention-ratio derivation. These provide additional mathematical reasoning beyond v1's empirical motivation and standard attention equations, but do not constitute a new formal theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's narrow quantitative validation through the compositional benchmark, direct quantitative DenseDiff/T2I-Adapter comparisons, and layer-placement/cost ablations. Expanded implementation and limitation discussions also make the design easier to assess. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses: the numeracy setup is incomplete, Appendix E's six variants/120 sets are unreconciled with the expanded evaluation, and the new terrain branch receives qualitative rather than independent quantitative validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe T3-S2S. All 19 pages of v1 and 24 pages of v2, including their appendices, provide readable text, equations, figures and tables sufficient for comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original results on 50 custom scenes, an adapted T2I-CompBench evaluation, dense-tuning layer and cost experiments, and terrain-generation demonstrations.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-generation experiments, CLIP scores and user ratings for 20 custom scenes, module and hyperparameter ablations, and appendix transfer experiments.

results.title: T$^3$-S2S: Training-free Triplet Tuning for Sketch to Scene Synthesis in Controllable Concept Art Generation

C1.justification: v2 makes strong alignment without joint training and incorporation of additional modalities without adjusting existing models explicit central contributions. v1 instead motivates easy integration through rapid joint-training convergence. Claims of interpretable knowledge, efficient learning and comparable downstream performance remain, but the independence claim substantially strengthens the asserted modularity.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly acknowledges that current reasoning is limited to controlled, simpler domains and attribute/category concepts, and discusses integration with broader VLMs. Appendix A.5 interprets dimensionality results through expressiveness, geometric complexity and possible overfitting. The method discussion also adds substantive explanations of negative sampling and the different supervision required for attributes and categories.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link, an exact ViT checkpoint identifier, detailed concept inventories and overlap tables, and Unified-dataset construction counts and balancing instructions. Model-head documentation is expanded and revised. Conversely, v1's four-A100 hardware specification and explicit one-epoch joint-training configuration disappear. The added repository's availability cannot be verified from the PDFs alone.

E1.justification: v2 adds a Unified dataset pooling CLEVR, COCO and GQA, merging overlapping concepts across their domains. It also evaluates independently trained Chinese, Spanish and French description models alongside English and vision. These introduce pooled-domain and multilingual matching scenarios beyond v1's separate datasets and English descriptions. WordNet coverage is retained.

E2.justification: The original image-text matching and VQA comparator sets remain. However, the ResNet baseline's reported hidden widths change from 128/128 to 512/256. v2 also adds a dedicated alignment-efficiency comparison against CLIP, FLAVA and ViLT; these are existing comparators, not newly introduced baseline families.

E3.justification: Table 1 replaces attribute F1 with mAP, and Figure 2 replaces training-accuracy curves with validation accuracy/mAP sampled every 50 steps. New protocols include pretrained initialization and GPU-time measurements for alignment, independent multilingual training, and balancing the Unified dataset by capping CLEVR training samples at 91,667. Original dataset split conventions and basic pretraining budgets remain.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled dimensionality experiments at 24, 50 and 96 dimensions, initialization and training-time alignment diagnostics, and positive-versus-negative multilingual entailment heatmaps. These examine dimensionality sensitivity and whether independent projections align. The original pretrained-versus-fresh concept-space ablation is retained in Appendix A.4, rather than newly added.

E5.justification: v1 Table 1 and Figure 2 report two-sigma uncertainty over five trials. v2 removes those uncertainty values, shaded bands and corresponding trial-count statements from the main comparisons. Five-trial, two-sigma reporting remains for the relocated concept-space ablation in Figure 6. This establishes reduced reporting, not fewer experimental runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds Unified, multilingual, timed-alignment and dimensionality results, including 0.954 initial alignment accuracy in Table 2. Classification entries are revised, with mAP replacing F1, preventing direct comparison of those attribute scores. The proposed method's GQA matching entries change from 0.929/0.536 to 0.924/0.531 under the revised training description. VQA accuracy remains 96.5, and WordNet KL divergence remains 0.1308.

M1.justification: The core box embeddings, projection losses and inference rules remain. Joint training becomes explicitly optional in v2 Appendix B, which omits v1's optional concept-space updating during that stage. The reported ResNet projection architecture also changes from a three-layer MLP with 512/256 hidden units to the linear projection heads described in v2 Appendix D.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, discussion and conclusion receive extensive substantive rewriting and explanatory expansion. Joint training moves from the main method to Appendix B; the original ablation moves to Appendix A.4. Experiments gain alignment and modality-incorporation sections, downstream tasks are regrouped, and model documentation is reorganized into dedicated subsections.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redesigned from three training-accuracy panels into six validation panels. New timing plots, multilingual heatmaps and tables, dimensionality results and concept inventories substantially expand the displays. Table 1 gains Unified columns, the original ablation moves into the appendix, and the GQA probing table moves into the main discussion. Journal formatting also changes typography and page layout.

R1.justification: Related work substantially expands its treatment of concept bottleneck models, including Dominici et al.'s shared multimodal concept space, Lee et al.'s distillation approach, and hierarchical concept learning by Sinha and Kong et al. Additional multimodal, annotation and safety literature broadens the positioning. The earlier GlanceNets citation and discussion are removed.

T1.justification: The optional combined objective L'_joint = L_joint + beta L_C defined in v1 Section 3.3 is omitted from v2 Appendix B. Otherwise, the box-probability definitions, smoothing construction, KL objective and principal projection/joint equations remain mathematically unchanged. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 supports easy modality integration mainly through rapid joint-training convergence. v2 directly tests independent alignment and multilingual incorporation, while pooled-domain evaluation and dimensionality controls strengthen evidence for the central framework. Detailed concept inventories and explicit applicability limits improve assessability. Removing main-comparison uncertainty and hardware details is a material regression, but the new validation substantially strengthens previously under-tested central claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same concept-centric multimodal framework. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support matching retained, relocated and revised content.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds Unified-dataset evaluations, multilingual matching, alignment-efficiency comparisons and dimensionality experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification, image-text matching, VQA, concept-space ablation and WordNet fitting results.

results.title: A Concept-Centric Approach to Multi-Modality Learning

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes data-efficient factual injection competitive with RAG. v2 expands the main claims to multiple model families and sizes, wall-clock and parameter efficiency, and using injected knowledge for multi-hop reasoning. Its abstract claims PD can surpass RAG, while the conclusion qualifies independence from larger teachers by requiring a sufficiently capable base model.

C2.justification: v2 substantially develops the style-mismatch explanation through entropy/KL analyses, explicitly distinguishing correlation from causation. It adds interpretations of forgetting tradeoffs, small-model limitations, reverse-KL behavior, metric dependence, and unsuccessful knowledge injection. v1's stated difficulty obtaining competitive Bonito questions outside NYT is omitted.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds explicit access information for code, evaluation questions, and replication instructions. Appendix D expands implementation details with precision, sequence limits, gradient accumulation, LoRA alpha, Bonito temperature, and configuration-specific schedules. These improve documentation without establishing changes to previously undisclosed settings. v1's dataset-license and screening disclosure is absent.

E1.justification: The four Squadshifts domains remain. v2 adds HotpotQA multi-hop evaluation after single-document question training, six MMLU-Pro subjects for general-capability retention, and Tülu 3 instruction data for regularization. These substantially broaden training content and evaluated task requirements.

E2.justification: The original SFT, UFT, RAG, distractor-SFT, and oracle comparisons remain. v2 adds SFT to the temperature comparison (v1 Table 3 versus v2 Table 4), evaluates larger-expert SFT variants in Table 3, and introduces the non-instruction-tuned Llama-3-8B reference in the MMLU-Pro comparison.

E3.justification: v2 introduces Qwen model configurations, PD XL training with 200 questions and one epoch, HotpotQA-specific training budgets and ten-document retrieval, and alternative grading procedures. It also adds controlled time and LoRA-rank experiments. For the retained setup, the reported GPU count changes from four to one, and the question-temperature table changes from 0.25 to 1.5, matching v1's prose; these revisions do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's temperature and question-count studies, v2 adds expert/teacher-size comparisons, question-generator comparisons, wall-clock and LoRA-rank analyses, reverse KL, entropy/KL-based data stratification, forgetting tests, and grading robustness checks. The original question-count analysis is extended, while Appendix Q adds concrete failure cases.

E5.justification: Both versions specify three seeds, except for models not retrained, and report uncertainty as two standard errors of the mean. The added result tables largely continue this practice; no changed repetition policy or new statistical inference procedure is specified.

E6.justification: Most original Llama-3 scores remain, but v2 adds substantial Qwen, HotpotQA, retention, scaling, and alternative-grading results. Table 6 newly reports MMLU-Pro means of 34.0 for PD, 37.2 with regularization, and 37.9 for regularized PD XL. The retained Table 2 changes Reddit PD+RAG from 76.7 ±2.7 to 77.8 ±1.6, matching v1's appendix Table 4 rather than establishing a new performance gain.

M1.justification: The core teacher-context/student-without-context procedure remains. However, v2 adds an optional KL regularization objective on unrelated instruction-response pairs, implemented with equal proportions of knowledge-injection and Tülu 3 samples (Sections 2.5 and 4.6). This substantively extends training to preserve general capabilities. Appendix J also evaluates a reverse-KL variant.

P1.justification: The introduction, method explanation, related work, and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting. Limitations are integrated into the conclusion, experimental discussion is reorganized, and appendices are extensively restructured. The title and author list change, while the separate ethical-considerations and LLM-usage sections disappear.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from two-column to single-column layout. Figure 1 gains a PD XL bar, Figure 3 is extended and redrawn, and three additional ablation plots appear. Table 2 becomes a multi-model display, retained appendix tables are reorganized, and numerous new comparison and diagnostic tables are added.

R1.justification: v2 foregrounds the already-discussed context-distillation lineage and sharpens its distinction from Qi et al.'s structured knowledge editing and larger-model dependence. It adds citations concerning imitation limitations, forgetting, and new models and benchmarks. Much of Appendix C restates prior-work discussion already present in v1.

T1.justification: v2 makes the vocabulary sum explicit in the KL objective, adds the regularization definition and unrelated-data assumption, and introduces an expected-KL/mutual-information identity (Sections 2.2 and 2.5). This is a limited formal expansion without new proofs. The identity is asserted without the condition that the student distribution equals the teacher distribution marginalized over context.

improvement.justification: v1's evidence centered on one evaluated model, modified Squadshifts, and one LLM grader. v2 substantially strengthens generalizability and evaluation reliability through cross-family and multi-hop experiments, alternative grading, and explicit forgetting measurements, alongside better implementation and access information. Superiority over RAG remains metric-dependent, and the new mutual-information identity is insufficiently justified. Nevertheless, the broader validation and demonstrated retention tradeoffs provide substantial net gains in scientific and practical quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same prompt-distillation research despite the changed title and substantial expansion. The complete main texts and appendices are readable, and retained methods, equations, tables, and examples can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds Qwen evaluations, HotpotQA results, MMLU-Pro retention measurements, and extensive ablations and grading checks.

before.justification: v1 reports original knowledge-injection experiments, baseline comparisons, temperature and training-data ablations, and manual grading validation.

results.title: Efficient Knowledge Injection in LLMs via Self-Distillation

C1.justification: The abstract explicitly extends the demonstrated model scale from 8M to both 8M and 1B parameters and describes larger-model gains as improved performance more generally. AMICL, faster emergence of ICL, and residual value streams remain the central contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving auto- versus hetero-association, preservation of representations across layers, and strong IOI differences despite similar training losses. It proposes specific hippocampal ablation hypotheses and explicitly qualifies broader applicability through task-specific gains and unresolved scalability and cost trade-offs (Sections 6.1–6.3).

D1.justification: Section 5 adds substantial architecture, tokenizer, precision, optimizer, training-schedule, and IOI-Hard generation details. The code-access disclosure is retained. Some new schedule information conflicts internally: the prose specifies 500 warmup and 5,000 cooldown steps, while Table 4 gives 1% and 10% of a 40,000-step run.

E1.justification: Section 5 adds pretraining on English Nemotron-CC-HQ documents and evaluation on ARC, PIQA, OpenBookQA, and HellaSwag. IOI-Hard adds a distinct contextual retrieval scenario involving 25 sentences and multiple name, place, and object associations. The original synthetic tasks and TinyStories/IOI coverage remain.

E2.justification: The matched synthetic comparisons retain the classic Transformer and query/key residual variants. Language-model comparisons still use the classic architecture against residual values, including at 1B scale. Appendix B introduces separate architectural controls without expanding these head-to-head comparator sets.

E3.justification: New experiments use 1B-parameter models trained for 40,000 iterations on approximately 84 billion tokens, with batch size 512 and context length 4,096. Evaluation adds single- and five-shot benchmark accuracy and 1,000 generated IOI-Hard prompts. Appendix B also introduces one-layer control configurations; the original experiments' stated settings remain substantially unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendix B tests four one-layer architectures without learned value projections, varying ReLU depth and placement. These controls examine whether that simpler AMICL-inspired construction supports ICL and how architecture affects learning trajectories. The existing AMICL parameter sweeps and accuracy-threshold analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Section 5.2 adds a paired t-test using benchmark accuracies across training checkpoints, alongside correlation reporting. The original four-seed synthetic experiments and three-instance language-model reporting remain unchanged. Independent repeated-training uncertainty is not reported for the new 1B comparison.

E6.justification: New 1B results show gains concentrated on ARC and OpenBookQA, little change on PIQA and HellaSwag, and a clearer IOI-Hard advantage (Figures 5, 6, and 14). Original numerical tables are unchanged, but Figure 3's IC2 loss changes from rising above 12 to falling near zero. The unchanged IOI table also receives inaccurate new percentage summaries of approximately 590% improvement and 60% reduction.

M1.justification: The AMICL assignments and layer-to-layer query, key, and value residual operations remain unchanged. The 1B model applies the existing residual-values method in another model configuration; the value-projection removals are control experiments rather than revisions to the proposed method.

P1.justification: Previously continuous sections are reorganized into named subsections separating setup, architecture, evaluation, interpretation, limitations, and conclusions. AMICL motivation and the discussion receive extensive explanatory expansion. The 8M model is renamed a toy language model, and the appendix structure is reorganized around new background and controls.

P2.justification: v2 adds training and benchmark plots, four control-experiment figures, and two hyperparameter tables. Figure 3's loss panel is revised, including its vertical scale. Original appendix Figures 4–6 and Tables 3–4 are retained as Figures 11–13 and Tables 5–6, alongside substantial figure-placement and layout changes.

R1.justification: New Appendix A substantially expands the neuroscience background and positioning of associative memory models. The discussion adds connections to transformer memory and factual-recall research, including Bietti et al. and Nichani et al., and situates single-layer ICL relative to linear-regression work by Zhang et al. and Lu et al.

T1.justification: Section 2.2 changes the stated domain of AMICL's parameter a from positive reals to arbitrary reals, while retaining the tested range and chosen value. The equations remain mathematically equivalent, and no theorem or proof is added. Most additional reasoning is conceptual motivation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical support beyond synthetic tasks and four simple IOI templates in 8M models. The 1B benchmarks, harder contextual retrieval task, and failed architectural controls provide stronger evidence about applicability and design limitations. Explicit discussion of task-specific gains improves calibration. Checkpoint-based significance testing, missing independent 1B training repetitions, and reporting inconsistencies limit confidence, but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in empirical support and explanation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AMICL and residual attention stream research. Text, equations, figures, tables, and all appendices are readable. Retained material can be matched across section and appendix renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds 1B-parameter language-model evaluations, IOI-Hard results, and architectural control experiments in Appendix B.

before.justification: v1 reports original AMICL simulations, two-layer Transformer training experiments, and 8M-parameter language-model results on TinyStories and indirect object identification, including appendix sensitivity analyses.

results.title: Associative memory inspires improvements for in-context learning using a novel attention residual stream architecture

C1.justification: The abstract and principal introduction/conclusion claims remain: edge transport through the line expansion provides a complementary hypergraph clustering approach, particularly useful for large hyperedges and certain community structures. Added experiments and qualifications do not redefine the main contribution.

C2.justification: v2 replaces broad assertions of weak parameter sensitivity with substantial qualifications about weighting/aggregation interactions and extreme node-alpha instability. It adds explicit limits on transferring Ollivier-curvature theory and sign interpretability, explains runtime disadvantages for large node stars, and discusses threshold-dependent clustering granularity. Appendix C also reports numerical instability for p=2 on NTU2012.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly documents node-measure defaults, gives constructive synthetic hyperedge-sampling instructions, and specifies the new sensitivity experiments. It replaces the code/data pointer from OlympioH/Ricci_curv_hyp with AnonRicciHG/Ricci_curv_HG. The principal software packages and hardware description were already present in v1.

E1.justification: All seven real datasets and the synthetic clustering families remain. Synthetic cardinality coverage changes modestly: Figure 5 replaces cross-community sizes 2, 3, 4 and 5 with 2, 4 and 6. Several size-3 and size-5 scenarios remain in Appendix C, so their disappearance from the main figure is not wholesale removal.

E2.justification: The real-data NMI comparison retains Node2Vec, DGI, GRACE, S2-HHGR, TriCL and Modularity. v2 additionally compares Modularity against both Ricci methods for real-data runtime in Table 2; v1's computational comparison only contrasts the two Ricci methods.

E3.justification: The main NMI metric, 20 flow iterations, synthetic 100-node/two-community setup and main threshold-selection rules remain. New experiments introduce controlled parameter combinations, comparisons between label-optimal and graph/hypergraph-modularity thresholds, and 20-iteration runtime measurements on four real datasets. Explicit p=1 and alpha=0.5 values replace unspecified library defaults in the documentation, without establishing a change from the earlier implementation.

E4.justification: New Section 4.3 and Appendix C substantially expand sensitivity analysis beyond v1's brief assertions. Figures S.2-S.6 test p, alpha, weighting and aggregation interactions; Tables S.2-S.3 examine joint parameter effects on NTU2012; Tables S.4-S.5 quantify threshold-selection effects on NTU2012 and Zoo.

E5.justification: Section 4.1 changes the reported averaging from ten random hypergraph generations to five. Figure 5 newly displays shaded bands, although their statistical meaning is not defined. The synthetic timing experiment retains averaging over five initializations.

E6.justification: NTU2012's reported NMI changes from 82.3 to 76.3 for N-Ricci and from 80.9 to 77.6 for E-Ricci, reversing their ordering; other entries in the main accuracy table remain unchanged. Figure 5 is revised, and new runtime and sensitivity results substantially expand the findings. These revisions do not establish controlled performance gains or losses because the earlier defaults and changed synthetic settings are not fully matched.

M1.justification: The transport, aggregation, flow-update and trimming pipeline remains. However, v2 Equation 3 replaces the shared/nonshared alpha-split edge measure with normalized weights over the full star; the earlier alpha=0 construction survives as Equation 4 for Proposition 1. Section 3.1 also removes the inverse-summed hyperedge-contribution weighting option.

P1.justification: Most existing exposition and the main section sequence are retained, with local language corrections and expanded explanations. Dataset descriptions move from Section 4.2 to Appendix B, a dedicated hyperparameter section and Appendix C are added, and publication/contact text changes. This is limited reorganization rather than wholesale rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a substantially different publication layout and rebuilds Figure 5 from sixteen small panels into twelve larger panels with revised legends and shaded bands. It adds five supplementary figures, four analysis tables and a runtime table, while relocating dataset statistics and retaining the proof illustration as Figure S.1.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including Sreejith et al., Iyer et al., Tian et al., Cushing et al. and Van Der Hoorn et al., expanding discussion of alternative curvatures, line-graph clustering and graph-curvature convergence. The central positioning relative to earlier hypergraph and Ricci-flow methods remains.

T1.justification: v2 generalizes the displayed node-measure definition with distance decay p and revises the main edge-measure definition. Proposition 1 retains its recurrence and shared-edge exclusion assumption, expressed through Equation 4 rather than alpha=0. Appendix A adds distance-based optimality arguments and corrects the first transport target, without introducing a new theorem.

improvement.justification: Section 4.3 and Appendix C address an important weakness in v1: parameter-insensitivity assertions lacked systematic supporting evidence. The new analyses establish consequential parameter interactions and quantify practical threshold-selection losses, while runtime comparisons and explicit theoretical limitations make applicability substantially easier to assess. Fewer synthetic repetitions and undefined shaded bands remain weaknesses, but the gains in experimental support and qualification clearly outweigh them.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same hypergraph Ricci-flow clustering work. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable, allowing retained, relocated and newly added material to be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains original synthetic and real-data experiments and adds runtime comparisons and original hyperparameter and threshold analyses in Section 4.3 and Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic clustering experiments in Figure 5, Ricci-method results on real datasets in Table 2, and computational measurements in Figure 6.

results.title: Hypergraph clustering using Ricci curvature: an edge transport perspective

C1.justification: The introduction narrows the graph's stated role from a task-agnostic foundation illustrated by planning to downstream relational reasoning. It also reframes the novelty claim from handling hallucinations and ambiguities through path identification to identifying query-relevant subgraphs before reasoning. The three-stage contribution and up-to-21.3% improvement claim remain.

C2.justification: v2 expands the limitations beyond dataset-label quality to untested non-relational generalization, manual symbolic-rule construction, and latency/accuracy tradeoffs, with recommendations for choosing the two variants. New analyses distinguish path identification's benefits for LLM reasoning from its small effect on symbolic benchmark accuracy, and interpret multiple-path selection and computational efficiency.

D1.justification: v2 specifies depth-first search and documents new model settings and module-level resource consumption. It consolidates v1's conflicting temperature statements of 0 and 0.3 into 0.3, with GPT-5 defaults, without establishing that retained experiments changed. It removes the statement that code and datasets accompany supplementary materials and omits the full SPARTUN label-mapping list.

E1.justification: Both versions use StepGame, CLUTRR, SPARTUN Find Relation questions, and the Chinese kinship dataset, together with the synthetic extraction test and seven graph-noise scenarios. Additional backbones and analyses operate within this retained coverage.

E2.justification: The external baseline roster remains IO/Zero-shot, Few-shot, CoT, CoT-SC, and LLM-ASP. v2 adds internal comparison variants: PoT with path identification removed in Table 6 and shortest-path-only reasoning in Table 7. Figure 2 retains the earlier noise comparison under symbolic-reasoner-with/without-path-identification labels.

E3.justification: v2 substantially expands model configurations with Llama3-70B-Instruct, o1-mini, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, and GPT-5 at minimal and medium reasoning effort. It adds module-level latency and token measurements on GPT-4o StepGame k=3, plus path-removal and shortest-path controls. Existing benchmark sizes, preprocessing, and accuracy definitions are retained; these additions do not establish reruns of the earlier results.

E4.justification: New Table 6 directly tests removing path identification from both PoT variants. Appendix A.2/Table 7 analyzes path-count distributions and compares multiple paths against the shortest path alone. Table 25 adds an extraction-error example, and Table 26 introduces reasoning-error cases. The earlier extraction-prompt comparison and synthetic-noise analysis remain.

E5.justification: Tables 1–2 introduce paired McNemar significance annotations comparing the highest and second-highest accuracies, absent from v1. Single-trial reporting remains, with no newly reported repeated-run uncertainty or confidence intervals. The captions do not specify the significance threshold.

E6.justification: The earlier GPT-3.5, GPT-4-turbo, GPT-4o, extraction, and noise results are retained. v2 adds substantial backbone, cost, ablation, and error-analysis results. The new findings include exceptions to superiority: on o1-mini CLUTRR, PoT-LLM scores 58.5 versus CoT-SC's 64.6, while PoT-Symbolic scores 65.9 versus LLM-ASP's 20.2 (Table 2). These are newly reported configurations, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The default graph-extraction, path-identification, and reasoning pipeline is unchanged, as are the appendix prompt templates. Section 4.2 newly identifies the path-finding algorithm as depth-first search; this specifies an existing component rather than establishing a procedural change. Shortest-path and path-removal variants are experimental controls.

P1.justification: The document is substantially reorganized: dataset and backbone descriptions move into Section 5.1, the noise taxonomy moves to Appendix A.1, and appendix topics and prompt collections are reordered. The limitations are rewritten and placed before the conclusion. The introduction, problem definition, and results narrative are edited, and the title loses its Path-of-Thoughts prefix.

P2.justification: The two-column presentation becomes a single-column layout with a redesigned author block. Table 1 incorporates the former appendix GPT-3.5 results and adds Llama3; new tables display reasoning-model results, costs, ablations, and errors. Prompt tables are reordered and sometimes split. Figure 2 changes from stacked to side-by-side panels with revised legends while retaining its plotted results.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for Llama 3, o1, SymBa, and hierarchical cooperative task allocation, including limited discussion of automated rule generation and task decomposition. It refines the introduction's novelty positioning, while the substantive related-work comparison with prompting and neuro-symbolic approaches remains largely unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 2 introduces clearer notation for the context, question, and queried entities but retains the same problem definition and composition assumptions. Graph and path definitions remain substantively unchanged. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: Tables 6–7 substantially strengthen evaluation of the central path-identification contribution by directly testing its removal and restricting path selection, revealing both benefits and settings with little benefit. Computational-cost measurements and expanded limitations make efficiency and applicability more assessable. These gains outweigh the dropped code/data availability disclosure and remaining reporting weaknesses, including single-trial results and broad success claims that overlook counterexamples such as o1-mini CLUTRR in Table 2.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Path-of-Thoughts (PoT) research. Their main text, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and relocation of material.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds model evaluations, computational-cost measurements, path-identification ablations, and path-count analyses in Tables 1–7.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark accuracies, graph-extraction experiments, and synthetic-noise evaluations in Tables 1–2, Figure 2, and appendix Table 28.

results.title: Extracting and Following Paths for Robust Relational Reasoning with Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract and three principal contributions retain their central novelty and performance claims. Section 7 adds qualifications that GODA cannot synthesize expert-level performance from nonexpert data alone and requires latent representations for visual applications. These narrow the stated applicability without replacing the main contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations for return-prior superiority, dataset-dependent scaling benefits and Pen-Human failure, together with explicit expert-data and visual-input limitations. It also introduces a Maze2D explanation involving direct spatial-goal conditioning, although the documented conditioning remains RTG and timestep; this is an unsupported interpretive addition rather than an established input change.

D1.justification: v2 documents substantial implementation information for its extensions: 84×84×3 observations encoded into 50-dimensional representations, encoder freezing and head fine-tuning, and online augmentation of 1M samples per 10K interactions with a 1:1 real/synthetic ratio and changing goal parameters. Sensitivity-analysis procedures and weights are also supplied. Original denoiser hyperparameters, hardware and timing information are retained in Appendix B.

E1.justification: v2 adds Medium-Expert locomotion datasets, pixel-based V-D4RL Cheetah-Run at four data-quality levels, and online interaction scenarios for three Gym tasks. These expand represented data quality, observation modality and interaction conditions. The original Gym, Maze2D, Adroit and traffic-control coverage is retained.

E2.justification: The external augmentation baselines TATU, SynthER and DiffStitch remain unchanged in corresponding experiments. Table 6 adds four internal comparison variants removing either gated connection or only its gating, beyond v1's AdaLN/in-context comparisons. BC, DMG and SAC otherwise serve as new evaluation backbones using familiar unaugmented/SynthER controls.

E3.justification: Section 5 revises the reported diversity metric from L2 distance to average nearest-neighbor Min L2 Distance, with corresponding changes to Equation 11 and results. Added protocols include latent-space BC evaluation, DMG evaluation and online SAC over 100K interactions. The online experiment uses update-to-data ratios of 1 for vanilla SAC and 20 for both augmented methods, so that comparison has unequal update budgets.

E4.justification: v2 adds separate connection/gating ablations (Table 6), a reward-sensitivity investigation of Adroit failures (Appendix C.3, Table 10), and scaling-factor experiments across additional dataset-quality levels (Figure 10). These investigate component contributions and failure conditions beyond v1's analyses. Existing mixed-dataset and traffic-data-size studies are retained in Appendices C.5–C.6.

E5.justification: Appendix C.3 adds weighted-least-squares reward-sensitivity estimation and 95th-percentile statistical summaries. These are diagnostic estimates, not confidence intervals. The principal benchmark's five-seed declaration and existing ± and error-band reporting practices remain unchanged; no increase in runs or new significance testing is documented.

E6.justification: Original task-level Gym/Maze2D, Adroit and traffic-control scores are retained, but v2 adds substantial results for the new settings and analyses. For example, visual BC averages are 39.9±4.8 with GODA versus 37.5±3.5 with SynthER (Table 4). The Gym IQL GODA average changes from 54.7 to 66.2 because Medium-Expert rows are added, not because retained task scores improve. Distance values also change under the revised metric.

M1.justification: The original offline denoiser, loss and RTG/timestep conditioning remain unchanged. However, v2 adds a visual pipeline using BC pretraining, frozen encoders, latent-space augmentation and output-head fine-tuning (Section 4.1.2), plus an online procedure with periodic diffusion retraining, hybrid replay and changing goal schedules (Appendix C.2, Algorithm 2). These substantially extend the procedure.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the paper, moving related work, implementation details and selected existing analyses into appendices. Method explanations expand to distinguish training from sampling, provide worked goal-selection examples and explain algorithm stages. Experimental sections are reorganized around the expanded evaluations, beyond routine wording edits.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column to a single-column layout and substantially redistributes figures and tables. v2 adds a workflow diagram, goal-selection examples, new result tables and online/scaling plots, and redraws the diversity-distance panel. Several original ablation plots are retained unchanged but relocated; the mixed-dataset table's previously incorrect caption is corrected.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting visual offline RL, DMG, SAC and image-generation conditioning, and updates several introductory application citations. Its central positioning against SynthER and DiffStitch remains unchanged. Moving the largely retained related-work discussion to Appendix A is organizational rather than a substantive positioning change.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 corrects v1's RTG-offset reasoning: adding a constant to every RTG changes the terminal reward, not the first reward. v2 also revises the distance definition and introduces a Lipschitz-based reward-sensitivity definition and composite measure in Appendix C.3. The central method equations remain unchanged, and no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: Where v1 left individual gating contributions and the Pen-Human failure largely unexamined, v2 supplies component controls, sensitivity analysis and broader scaling tests. The explicit nearest-neighbor metric, clearer procedures and concrete applicability limits substantially improve scrutiny of the central claims. Unequal SAC update budgets and the unsupported spatial-goal explanation weaken parts of the added interpretation, but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GODA research. Their text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison, including material relocated into v2's Appendices A–C. v1 has no separately labelled appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds visual-observation, DMG, online SAC, component-ablation and reward-sensitivity results.

before.justification: v1 reports original GODA data-quality measurements, policy evaluations, ablations and traffic-control simulation results, alongside some baseline results attributed to prior work.

results.title: Goal-Conditioned Data Augmentation for Offline Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: V1 centers its contribution on structure-preserving low-rank tensor-gradient compression and optimizer-memory savings up to 75%. V2 makes combined sparse-plus-low-rank compression and a mixed-precision recipe central contributions, emphasizing highly turbulent PDE evaluation and total-memory savings exceeding 50%. This substantially redefines the claimed contribution and its supporting scope.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations linking sparse entries to localized outliers, low-rank factors to global structure, and sparse-first ordering to improved factor estimation. It also interprets update-frequency effects and half-precision optimizer degradation. Beyond v1's decomposition-overhead and rank-selection limitations, v2 discusses sparse-index costs, joint rank/sparsity selection and the need for full-precision optimizer states.

D1.justification: V2 substantially expands implementation and reproducibility information: COO storage and scatter reconstruction, precision allocation, dataset-pair construction, decomposition-update frequencies, detailed NS1024 training configurations, and A100/H100/H200 hardware. Appendix F adds profiling warmup, collection and allocation-classification details. The stated code location changes from an anonymous repository to the named TensorGRaD repository.

E1.justification: V2 adds highly turbulent Kolmogorov flow, described at approximately Re = 2×10^5 in Appendix A and labeled 10^5 in the main results. V1's Re = 10^3 Navier–Stokes data and the other PDE datasets remain. This substantially extends the dynamical regime tested; 1024×1024 resolution itself was already present in v1.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's uncompressed and matrix-GaLore comparisons, v2 evaluates GRASS-inspired structured-sparse tensor methods, including top-k, probability and random selection, and a randomized-SVD low-rank variant. The earlier tensor method becomes an explicit low-rank-only control for the hybrid method. These comparators appear in reported results, especially Tables 1–4 and 11.

E3.justification: V2 introduces full, Mixed-1 and Mixed-2 precision controls, sparse-density and composition experiments, and a new high-Re evaluation protocol. Appendix A specifies 1,577 training and 279 test pairs with temporal offset 256 and stride 4; Table 13 specifies a staged 256-to-1024 training schedule. These are new experimental settings, not evidence that retained benchmark results were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 retains earlier rank, matricization and timing analyses while adding gradient-reconstruction error distributions, sparse-versus-low-rank ordering and residual/additive comparisons, precision sensitivity, projection-update frequency and sparse-mask selection ablations. Figures 3 and 7 and Tables 2, 3 and 11 test substantial new questions about the hybrid method's behavior.

E5.justification: V1 Table 6 already contains ± values without specifying their interpretation or run count. V2 Tables 1 and 4 explicitly report means ± one standard error over three seeds, and Appendix F discloses three profiling repeats. Reporting remains uneven: Table 11 promises standard deviations but displays only point estimates. No increase in runs for retained results is established.

E6.justification: Earlier benchmark values are retained under Tensor low-rank labels in v2 Tables 5–10 and 12. Substantial new results include high-Re test L2 values of 16.82±0.18 for full-precision TensorGRaD versus 17.02±0.18 for Adam, both ×10^-2 (Table 1), and precision-dependent degradation in Table 3. These are newly reported conditions and findings, not same-setting improvements over v1's Navier–Stokes scores.

M1.justification: V1 uses Tucker-based low-rank gradient projection. V2 Algorithm 1 adds an unstructured sparse branch, compresses the residual with the low-rank branch, maintains separate Adam moments and combines their updates with scaling parameters. The earlier method remains as the low-rank-only component; the hybrid is a substantive procedural extension.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method exposition and results narrative are extensively rewritten around TensorGRaD. Setup and results are combined, substantial background and dataset descriptions move to appendices, and standalone implicit-regularization and applications sections disappear. Explicit limitations and broader-impact passages are added. This is substantial narrative restructuring beyond the method's renaming.

P2.justification: V2 adds a hybrid-method schematic, reconstruction-error plots, turbulent-flow snapshots and new precision/composition tables, while redesigning the main memory–accuracy displays. Existing material is also relocated: v1 Figure 2 becomes v2 Figure 8, and v1 Table 1 becomes v2 Table 6. Typography, spacing and table placement change substantially throughout.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning around GRASS, robust PCA, robust tensor decomposition and low-rank-plus-sparse recovery. It also distinguishes gradient compression from SLTrain's weight decomposition and Scatterbrain's attention decomposition. V1 primarily positioned its contribution against matrix GaLore and tensor-weight compression; several earlier citations and their associated discussion are removed.

T1.justification: V2 adds mathematical definitions of sparse supports, structured Cartesian-product masks and projection/back-projection operations in Section 2.2 and Appendix E. The principal stable-rank, FNO-reversibility and fixed-projection convergence results remain essentially unchanged across v1 Appendices H–J and v2 Appendices K–M. No corresponding new convergence proof for the full hybrid update is supplied.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation through sparse and low-rank controls, precision and composition ablations, a harder turbulent benchmark, explicit three-seed uncertainty and fuller reproduction details. These make the memory–accuracy trade-off considerably more assessable than in v1. Important qualifications remain: Table 1's 52-to-29 GB reduction is approximately 44%, despite the accompanying 55% claim, and the retained proofs address the low-rank component rather than the full hybrid method. These shortcomings limit the headline claims but do not outweigh the substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research lineage, with Tensor-GaLore extended and renamed TensorGRaD. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices support comparison, including matching retained experiments and proofs across relocation and renaming.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds high-Reynolds-number Navier–Stokes results, sparse/low-rank comparisons, precision experiments and additional ablations.

before.justification: V1 reports original FNO training experiments on Burgers, Darcy flow, Navier–Stokes and electromagnetic propagation, including accuracy, memory, rank ablations and execution times.

results.title: TensorGRaD: Tensor Gradient Robust Decomposition for Memory-Efficient Neural Operator Training

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion qualify the outperformance claim to say NDS matches or surpasses state-of-the-art OR methods. The four methodological contributions and the reported best performance in 11 of 12 main settings remain unchanged.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly acknowledges dependence on training data resembling test instances and discusses weaker transfer to 2000-customer problems. Appendix F adds the hypothesis that initial improvement helps training focus on difficult, higher-quality solutions. These provide targeted explanations and applicability qualifications without replacing the central interpretation.

D1.justification: V1 promises a future code release; v2 supplies an implementation link. New Appendix A documents baseline code/model sources, stopping rules, beam and batch settings, training choices, memory constraints, and the C++ SISRs reimplementation. V2 also specifies model input features and states that NDS hyperparameters were selected manually.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate CVRP, VRPTW, and PCVRP with 100, 500, 1000, and 2000 customers and retain the spatial-distribution and capacity coverage. The new runtime and size-transfer studies reuse this coverage; they change evaluation configurations rather than introduce new datasets or tasks.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds NeuOpt for CVRP100 and UDC for CVRP500/1000. It also introduces SGBS-EAS as a VRPTW100 comparator, where v1 compared NDS only with traditional solvers. These additions materially broaden the evaluated learning-based comparisons.

E3.justification: V2 adds original-stopping-rule versus wall-time comparisons and BQ beam-width-16 evaluations alongside the retained beam-width-64 setting. New studies use 100-instance runtime-sweep sets, budget-dependent PCVRP augmentation counts, and 500-customer models evaluated at other sizes. The original main NDS training and testing configurations remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds runtime sensitivity analysis in Section 5.3 and Appendix D, ASA hyperparameter sweeps in Appendix E, an ablation removing initial improvement steps during training in Appendix F, and size-transfer analysis in Appendix G. The original component ablations and spatial/capacity generalization tests are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-seed uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The additional evaluation runs examine different configurations rather than introduce statistical uncertainty reporting; the policy's random seed inputs are retained method components.

E6.justification: V2 adds baseline scores and substantial runtime, sensitivity, ablation, and transfer results while retaining the main NDS scores. For example, Table 4 newly reports CVRP2000 objective 57.63 using the 500-customer model versus 56.00 using the size-specific model. Table 1 also changes GLOP's reported CVRP2000 objective from 63.00 to 63.02 and gap from 9.79% to 9.82%.

M1.justification: The deconstruction policy, reinforcement-learning procedure, encoder/GRU decoder, greedy reconstruction, and augmented simulated annealing remain unchanged, including Algorithms 1 and 2. The added input-feature descriptions and separate depot/customer projection details disclose architecture information without establishing a changed method.

P1.justification: V2 moves and expands the problem descriptions into a dedicated Section 3, adds a method overview, and clarifies encoder, search, and evaluation prose. Terminology and publication headings are edited, but most existing methodological and experimental narrative is retained.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains configuration subrows and second-best underlining. V2 adds runtime, hyperparameter, and training-ablation plots plus Table 4, and adopts a different journal layout. Existing training curves are rearranged and relabeled, while rollout visualizations are retained and reordered rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to PARCO, UDC, and Toth and Vigo, extending discussion of heterogeneous routing and divide-and-conquer approaches. The broad positioning relative to construction and improvement methods remains intact; publication updates to existing references do not constitute additional research coverage.

T1.justification: The policy, reward/gradient, encoder, and annealing mathematics are retained, with no added theorem, proof, or substantive derivation. Section 3 expands background descriptions of the existing problems. Maximizing collected prizes minus travel cost is equivalent to v1's PCVRP minimization formulation.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the evidence behind the unchanged method: additional relevant baselines, runtime comparisons, hyperparameter tests, and a direct training ablation address gaps in v1's validation. Detailed baseline configurations and a code link improve reproducibility, while size-transfer results and qualified claims make applicability clearer. Statistical uncertainty remains unreported, but the gains in empirical support and transparency are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Neural Deconstruction Search for Vehicle Routing Problems. All 18 pages of v1 and 25 pages of v2, including their appendices, provide readable text, equations, tables, and figures supporting comparison.

after.justification: Section 5 retains original empirical results and adds runtime comparisons. Appendices E-G report new hyperparameter studies, a training ablation, and generalization across instance sizes.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original routing benchmarks, component ablations, generalization tests, and scalability measurements. Appendices A and B provide training curves and policy-rollout visualizations.

results.title: Neural Deconstruction Search for Vehicle Routing Problems

C1.justification: The central interface-influence contribution remains, but v3 expands its main claims to three preference models and cross-domain/stochastic settings. The introduction explicitly focuses applicability on sequential decisions, distinguishing single-step LLM RLHF. Introduction and conclusion add model-dependent transfer failures and unintended influence, qualifying the earlier practical-success narrative.

C2.justification: v3 introduces cognitive load and limited remaining improvement over control as explanations for unsuccessful regret transfer. It discusses intuitive rather than explicit computation, unintended influence toward regret, and environment-dependent benefits of question wording. These add substantive mechanisms and applicability boundaries; the earlier partial-return identifiability explanation remains.

D1.justification: v3 documents the space-domain rewards, transfer procedure, tunnel dynamics, and additional survey questions. Conversely, it removes v1 Appendix J.4's hardware specifications and PyTorch/scikit-learn versions. Existing learning hyperparameters, partition seeds, and the shared code/data access link remain.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates interventions within the deterministic delivery domain. v3 adds transfer from delivery-domain training to preference elicitation in a space domain with different rewards, and a delivery environment with stochastic tunnel transitions. These test cross-domain generalization and decisions with uncertain outcomes, substantially expanding scenario coverage.

E2.justification: The added stochastic study evaluates change-in-expected-return alongside regret, expanding the compared preference/reward-learning models beyond v1's partial-return/regret pairing. Comparator membership in the original studies is retained: full comparisons removed from the main plots remain in v3 Appendix K.4.

E3.justification: v3 adds separate training and elicitation domains and a stochastic evaluation, each with 10 subjects per condition. Section 5.1 changes normalized return from (Vpi - VU)/V* to (Vpi - VU)/(V* - VU). Reported PRIVILEGED counts change from 64/65/50 to 39/43/42 for partial return/regret/control, but appendix collection totals and subsampling remain unchanged; this does not establish an actual dataset reduction or rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds generalization tests under domain and transition changes, cognitive-load survey analyses explaining unsuccessful regret transfer (Appendix E.3), and analysis of unintended preference-model influence (Appendix I). The synthetic-preference identifiability experiment was already present in v1 Appendix J.6 and is retained in v3 Appendix K.6.

E5.justification: The ten partition seeds and original statistical analyses are retained. Whether accuracy testing changes is unresolved: v3 Table 1 specifies Wilcoxon tests outside PRIVILEGED, whereas Appendix J still specifies Fisher's exact test and retains earlier p-values. The table also marks transfer accuracy as p < 0.01, while Appendix J reports p = 0.049.

E6.justification: Substantial new results accompany the added studies. Transfer accuracy is 86.29% versus 60.0% for partial return and 72.58% versus 72.92% for regret, comparing intervention with control (Table 7). Stochastic-study accuracies are 69.4% versus 67.8% for change-in-expected-return and 61.2% versus 65.9% for regret (Table 9). Original accuracy tables and full learning curves remain unchanged. v3 Figure 13 also corrects v1 Figure 9's significance caption to partial return, p < 0.05.

M1.justification: The three intervention mechanisms and original deterministic procedures remain. v3 adds a QUESTION variant targeting change-in-expected-return in stochastic environments, using the new question 'Which path do you prefer to start with?' and the corresponding reward-learning likelihood. This is a limited adaptation rather than a replacement of the intervention framework.

P1.justification: The introduction and conclusion are substantially expanded and rewritten around sequential decisions, transfer, and conditional effectiveness. Related work becomes two subsections, the experimental narrative gains nested follow-up studies, and the appendices are reorganized. The standalone practicality appendix disappears as cross-domain applicability receives direct experimental treatment.

P2.justification: v3 adds an experiment-summary table, new task illustrations, learning and likelihood plots, and accuracy tables. Figure 2 becomes a deterministic/stochastic comparison. Main reward-learning plots are simplified to target-versus-control displays, while the original full comparisons move to Appendix K.4. These are substantial display and layout changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: New Section 2.2 substantially broadens positioning around preference measurement, survey design, annotator discretion, and normative aggregation, citing works including Treiman, Buyl, and D'Alonzo. Section 3.2 also relates change-in-expected-return to Marklund and Van Roy's bootstrapped-return model. This exceeds a limited citation update.

T1.justification: v1 presents regret through a deterministic-transition derivation. v3 defines general regret using the sum of V* - Q*, separately defines change-in-expected-return and its preference distribution, and distinguishes these models under stochastic transitions (Section 3.2 and Figure 2). This substantially extends the formal framework, although it adds no theorem or proof. The normalized-return definition is also corrected.

improvement.justification: v3 directly tests the cross-domain practicality question left as future work in v1 Appendix A, revealing both successful transfer and an important failure boundary. The stochastic study further tests whether interventions distinguish outcomes from decision quality. These additions substantially strengthen assessment of applicability, supported by clearer scope and corrected reporting. Conflicting participant counts and summary-table statistics, an overbroad claim that all training interventions improve reward learning, and removed hardware/software details remain weaknesses, but do not outweigh the stronger empirical examination.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research on influencing human preferences for RLHF. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching results moved between the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds cross-domain training, stochastic-environment experiments, and participant-survey analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports three human-subject experiments, analyses of collected preferences, reward-learning evaluations, and supplementary analyses.

results.title: Influencing Humans to Conform to Preference Models for RLHF

C1.justification: v1 centers its contribution on a novel hybrid architecture and broad superiority over general and hybrid MLLMs. v2 makes a systematic empirical study of MoVE design principles the primary contribution, presenting LEO as their integration and emphasizing comparisons within MoVE. The earlier claim of being the first hybrid-MLLM exploration for autonomous driving is removed.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations for overlapping-tile redundancy, interleaving's spatial benefits, independent alignment, and freezing encoders to avoid catastrophic forgetting. It discusses accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs and limited benefits from additional SFT data. Beyond v1's tile-budget limitation, it adds fixed-encoder/7B constraints and analyzes failures involving road markings and document relationships.

D1.justification: Appendices A.1–A.2 substantially expand evaluation documentation, including benchmark subsets, the 1,000-example LingoQA evaluation, and staged experimental controls. Efficiency inputs and distilled-model resolutions are specified. The abstract changes a promised release to stated code availability. However, v1's explicit pixel-unshuffle factors and LingoQA Scenery/Action training-data instructions are omitted; these omissions do not establish changed settings.

E1.justification: v2 adds MathVista evaluation for visually grounded mathematical reasoning. The original 13 general benchmarks remain represented in Appendix Table 13, and LingoQA remains included. Thus, the abstract's change from 13 to 11 benchmarks reflects the main comparison's scope, not removal of the original coverage.

E2.justification: v2 substantially revises the comparison sets: Table 4 adds DeepSeek-VL, SPHINX, MoME-X3, MouSi-X3, and Eagle-X3, while Table 7 introduces RADIO, RADIO2.5, and MoVE-KD-v1.1. Appendix Table 13 adds further general models. QwenVL, QwenVL-Chat, and Eagle-X4 comparisons disappear. MouSi-X2 matches the earlier Mousi comparator rather than constituting a new baseline.

E3.justification: v2 introduces controlled experiments varying tiling, encoder pairs, merging strategies, and fusion timing, with controls specified in Appendix A.2. It also adds Eagle-1.8M SFT variants, averages across eight benchmarks, and efficiency measurements, including a prescribed 1024-by-1024 image and generation prompt. These are new evaluation designs; the main LEO training recipe remains substantially unchanged.

E4.justification: The limited v1 ablations expand into systematic tests of four tiling strategies, four merging strategies, and pre/post-adaptation fusion across encoder pairs. v2 also adds training-data scaling, efficiency tradeoffs, and explicit failure cases in Appendix A.5–A.7. The original encoder-freezing and channel-fusion results are retained, but v1 Table 7's LingoQA tiling ablation is omitted.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates for its experimental results. v2's added averages aggregate benchmark scores rather than repeated trials.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive fusion, tiling, efficiency, scaling, and qualitative results, including LEO's MathVista score of 37.2. The original 13 LEO benchmark scores and LingoQA scores are retained. Instruct-BLIP's VizWiz value changes from 45.5 in v1 Table 1 to 34.5 in v2 Table 13. The separate MMMU test score and LingoQA no-tiling results disappear.

M1.justification: The final LEO architecture retains InternViT-300M and SAM-L, dynamic tiling with global context, pixel unshuffling, independent MLP projectors, tile-level token interleaving, and InternLM2-7B. v2 formalizes and evaluates these existing components; its expanded experimental variants do not establish a redesign of the proposed model.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around three investigative directions. A dedicated empirical-study section now precedes the LEO description. General-model comparisons and detailed ablations move into a new multipart appendix, substantially changing the narrative and document organization.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a single-column journal layout, redraws the overview and fusion diagrams, and reorganizes comparison tables. Main-text averages are paired with full appendix tables, and new efficiency and success/failure displays are added. The original tiling illustration and qualitative montage are retained under new figure numbers rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: v2 broadens related work to knowledge-distilled encoders and newer visual-understanding approaches, adding works such as RADIO, RADIOv2.5, MoVE-KD, and MoME. It repositions Eagle from a concurrent comparator to a preceding empirical study and explicitly frames LEO's fusion investigation as complementary. This changes research positioning beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: v2 adds tensor notation, projector mappings, and the standard autoregressive factorization in Equation 1 to describe the existing procedure. These are explanatory formalizations, with no substantive new mathematical assumptions, theoretical results, proofs, or derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central fusion-design claims.
