Where v1 relied heavily on comparisons between different published models and limited ablations, v2 directly compares fusion timing and merging choices across multiple encoder pairs. Efficiency measurements and concrete failure cases also make benefits and boundaries clearer. The omitted driving-tiling ablation and some lost implementation details are drawbacks, and uncertainty reporting remains absent, but the stronger controlled evidence provides a substantial net improvement in paper quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LEO research, despite the changed title and expanded scope. Text, figures, tables, and equations are readable. v1 ends with references and has no appendix; v2 includes a readable Appendix A.1–A.7.

after.justification: v2 retains original LEO evaluations and adds experiments on encoder combinations, tiling, fusion, training-data scale, and computational efficiency, including appendix results.

before.justification: v1 reports original LEO benchmark results, autonomous-driving evaluation, training and fusion ablations, and qualitative examples in Tables 1–7 and Figure 5.

results.title: Rethinking the Mixture of Vision Encoders Paradigm for Enhanced Visual Understanding in Multimodal LLMs

C1.justification: The central claim of the first adaptive soft-clustering pooling operator remains. The abstract shifts from broadly superior benchmark performance to preserving performance while producing compact representations. The conclusion extends the stated contribution to graph regression and sparse O(E) reconstruction, without replacing the principal adaptive-pooling claim.

C2.justification: v1 proposes heterophilic adaptation as future work; v2 documents underperformance on Multipartite and explains it through the model's homophilic architectural and loss biases. v2 also interprets hyperparameter sensitivity and explains dense/sparse memory and runtime tradeoffs, including reduced sampling efficiency as graph density increases. These substantially develop the applicability boundaries and limitations.

D1.justification: v2 adds dataset-specific selected hyperparameters in Table 11, hardware and timing information in Section 5.3, expanded forward-pass pseudocode, and GPU negative-sampling and dense-enumeration details in Appendix A. It also reports access through Torch Geometric Pool, supplementing the repository already linked in v1.

E1.justification: v2 adds Peptides-struct graph regression and Multipartite classification under explicitly heterophilic, adversarial connectivity. These materially extend task and environmental coverage. The earlier datasets remain covered; GCB-H, IMDB, and DD results move to Appendix C, Table 12.

E2.justification: Compared with v1 Table 2, v2 Tables 3 and 12 add evaluated graph-level comparators SEP, EigenPooling, and HOSC. Table 3 also adds a GNN without hierarchical pooling. The four node-clustering comparators remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Reported graph-level settings change substantially: early-stopping patience falls from 500 to 100 epochs, learning-rate plateau patience from 200 to 30, and KL annealing from 300 to 50 epochs. MolHiv changes from one 32-unit MP layer before and after pooling to two 64-unit layers on each side with dropout and batch normalization. v2 also expands the prior-hyperparameter grid and introduces additional pooling-ratio evaluations.

E4.justification: v2 adds prior-hyperparameter sensitivity experiments on Enzymes and Colors3, comparator pooling-ratio sweeps, and analyses of memory, epoch time, and training duration, including dense versus sparse BN-Pool. Multipartite provides an explicit heterophilic stress test. The earlier Cora and GCB-H qualitative analyses are largely relocated rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions report means and standard deviations. v2 newly specifies averaging over 10 folds for Table 5 and identifies dataset folds and weight initializations as sources of variation in Table 8. This adds limited statistical documentation; an increase in repetitions for retained results or a formal significance-testing procedure is not established.

E6.justification: The node-clustering scores are unchanged, but BN-Pool graph-level scores are revised: Colors3 changes from 93±1 to 99±0 and MUTAG from 91±8 to 88±7. Because reported settings also change, these are not controlled same-setting gains or losses. v2 adds substantial results, including Peptides-struct MAE of 0.255±0.001, Multipartite accuracy of 58±2, and new sensitivity, cluster-count, and resource measurements.

M1.justification: v2 Section 3.4.1 introduces a sparse BN-Pool variant that reconstructs observed edges and sampled nonedges instead of all node pairs, with normalization by their combined count. The reported dense auxiliary-loss normalization also changes from 1/N in v1 Equation 10 to 1/N² in v2 Equation 12. These change the training objective and computation while retaining the DP/SBM foundation.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the introduction, adds an explicit contribution list, and divides the method into more explanatory subsections. Much of v1's DP background, model details, and qualitative-result discussion moves from appendices into the main text. This is substantial narrative restructuring beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, with widespread figure and table relocation. v2 adds overview and GNN/SRC diagrams, redraws the BN-Pool schematic, expands the cluster-distribution display, and introduces several analysis tables. The earlier graph-result table is split between the main text and appendix; retained qualitative figures are incorporated into the main presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting additional pooling comparators, broader graph applications, KL annealing, and software availability. However, Section 4 retains essentially the same positioning relative to DiffPool, DGVAE, SB-VAE, and the IBP-based overlapping SBM. Publication updates to existing references do not constitute new related work.

T1.justification: v2 Equation 3 restores the missing alpha_DP multiplier on the base-distribution term in v1 Appendix A, Equation 15, correcting the DP predictive distribution. Section 3.4.1 also supplies the sparse-loss expression and its 2E-term complexity argument. Most DP background and the underlying variational derivation are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation through additional comparators, a no-pooling control, pooling-ratio sweeps, an explicit heterophilic failure case, and measured dense/sparse computational costs. These address important gaps in v1's evidence, while dataset-specific settings and clearer exposition improve auditability. Changed protocols prevent attributing revised scores solely to method improvements, and sparse-variant task accuracy is not separately reported, but the broader controls and documented limitations provide a clear substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BN-Pool research, with substantial overlap in the method and experiments. Their main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support a reliable comparison despite extensive reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds graph-regression, heterophilic classification, sensitivity, and computational-resource results in Section 5 and Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original node-clustering and graph-classification experiments in Tables 1–2, together with qualitative analyses in Appendix E.

results.title: BN-Pool: Bayesian Nonparametric Pooling for Graphs

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion now present integration with Gossip-SGD as a central contribution, broadening the work beyond private distillation-based collaboration. The original correlation-metric critique, MCG/CGS objective, reputation mechanism, and two-client theoretical claim remain.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly limits the two-client theorem's applicability, explains obstacles to extending it, and identifies partial participation as untested. It adds interpretations of gossip fairness, beta trade-offs, communication savings, and privacy/abuse risks. The new experiments also use correlation to support fairness while retaining Section 3's warning about correlation-based fairness.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a code-repository link, beta = 15 and R = 5 settings, and additional encrypted-loss, payload, and computational-overhead details. Most optimizer, learning-rate schedule, batch-size, hardware, and runtime information is unchanged and merely moved from Section 5.1 to Appendix F.

E1.justification: Both versions use CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Fed-ISIC2019, and the same two-client simulation tasks, including existing imbalance and label-flipping scenarios. The new experiments change algorithms, communication configurations, client counts, and evaluation procedures within this retained coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds Gossip-SGD, labeled DSGD, to the CIFAR comparisons in Tables 2 and 6. Its new Fed-ISIC2019 comparison evaluates standalone training and Gossip-SGD with complete, ring, and exponential topologies. The earlier FedAvg, VPDL, CFFL, RFFL, and CGSV comparisons remain.

E3.justification: The new medical evaluation uses 100 communication rounds, balanced accuracy on a pooled global test set, and Pearson correlation alongside MCG/CGS. Appendix G.7 adds 20-client Dirichlet(0.5) experiments, and G.9 tests five beta settings. Existing PDL training settings are retained and relocated to Appendix F.

E4.justification: v2 adds client-population scalability tests, Gossip-SGD topology and communication-frequency analyses, and a beta sensitivity study examining utility versus fairness. Existing label-flipping, imbalance, mean-estimation, and PDL threshold-sensitivity analyses largely carry over; moving the single-corrupted-client results into the main text is not a new analysis.

E5.justification: v2 adds Pearson correlation significance tests, including p = 0.0026 against a 0.05 threshold, and error bars or shaded bands in the medical figures. Their uncertainty definitions and neural-experiment run counts remain unspecified. The simulation reporting of 1,000 and 10,000 runs is unchanged.

E6.justification: Original CIFAR table values are retained, but substantial Gossip-SGD, medical, scalability, and sensitivity results are added. In the new medical comparison, Table 7 reports CYCle MCG/CGS of 23.79/10.94 versus 30.26/15.64 for complete-graph Gossip-SGD: lower spread accompanies lower mean gain. These are new comparisons, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: Section 4.4 and Appendix C introduce a Gossip-SGD adaptation using pairwise gradient alignment, a softmax reputation mapping, a dynamic mixing matrix, and Bernoulli communication masks. This substantially extends the procedure beyond distillation-based PDL; the original PDL algorithm is retained.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much existing method and proof prose remain. Localized rewrites expand the CaPriDe and theoretical explanations, implementation details move to Appendix F, and contents and notation guides improve navigation. Much of the document's expansion comes from new scientific content rather than wholesale rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds method and topology diagrams, medical learning curves and correlation charts, scalability plots, and a beta-sensitivity figure. Tables 2 and 6 expand to include gossip results, tables receive revised highlighting, and the manuscript adopts journal formatting. The old medical reputation snapshots are replaced by communication-frequency graphs, while the data-distribution heatmap is retained separately.

R1.justification: The positioning expands substantially into gossip optimization and communication topology, supported by newly cited work by Boyd, Koloskova, Xiao, and Ying, alongside FHE-acceleration references. Section 2 adds an explicit first-to-target-decentralized-fairness claim and a stronger distinction from Cronus. Publication updates to existing references are not counted as new works.

T1.justification: The fairness-metric argument and Appendix A mean-estimation bounds and proofs remain essentially unchanged; Theorem 4.1 principally brings the existing result into the main text. Appendix C adds formal consensus and mixing-matrix definitions and gossip-update derivations, without establishing a new general convergence or fairness guarantee.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence with an explicit Gossip-SGD extension, direct decentralized comparators, medical accuracy/fairness results beyond v1's reputation heatmaps, and scalability and sensitivity checks. Clearer theoretical limitations also improve the paper's scope. The gains require qualification: the medical results trade mean gain for lower spread, making some utility-preservation language too strong, and uncertainty reporting remains incomplete.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CYCle research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and matchable despite the expanded content and journal formatting in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds Gossip-SGD comparisons, medical accuracy evaluations, larger-client experiments, and additional sensitivity analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original CIFAR experiments, Fed-ISIC2019 reputation measurements, label-flipping and sensitivity studies, and two-client mean-estimation simulations.

results.title: CYCle: Choosing Your Collaborators Wisely to Enhance Collaborative Fairness in Decentralized Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, five introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same substantive claims about the three-part recipe, 24-GPU-hour meta-training, performance on unseen tasks, aggregate evaluation metrics and adaptive schedules. The added appendix evidence does not redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: v1 offers general production-readiness caveats. v2 adds concrete applicability limits: full Celo is unstable on AlgoPerf workloads, while Celo-Adam generalizes but falls short of tuned-baseline validation performance. Appendix A.6 interprets this as a need for more robust learned update rules and scaled meta-training. A.5 additionally discusses runtime overhead relative to Adam.

D1.justification: v2 specifies the mixed-augmentation sampling choices and ranges, discloses the MLP's 30 inputs, two four-unit hidden layers and two outputs, identifies V100 hardware for runtime measurements, and states the provenance of AlgoPerf baseline data. Existing implementation instructions and code access remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix A.6 adds evaluations on Fast MRI reconstruction, ImageNet classification, LibriSpeech speech recognition and WMT translation, substantially broadening represented datasets and tasks. These include Celo-Adam evaluations and reported full-Celo instability. The original four meta-training datasets and 17-task evaluation suite remain.

E2.justification: Schedule-Free AdamW becomes an evaluated comparator in the new AlgoPerf experiments, alongside the benchmark's tuned NAdamW baseline. Existing comparison sets remain unchanged. Table 5's change from 'pretrained-velo' to 'velo-4000' is a rename of the same comparator.

E3.justification: v2 adds meta-training horizons of 1K, 2K and 5K evaluated at 10K steps, a wall-clock-per-step benchmark, and AlgoPerf training/validation comparisons using task-specific metrics such as SSIM, accuracy, WER and BLEU. Appendix A.6 describes AlgoPerf's target-or-timeout convention. These are additional protocols; the original 2K-step evaluation remains unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's component and augmentation-presence ablations, Table 6 compares global, tensor and mixed augmentation across training stages. Appendix A.4 tests sensitivity to meta-training horizon and generalization to longer runs, while A.5 analyzes computational overhead. These substantially expand the questions investigated.

E5.justification: Appendix A.5 specifies 10 seeds per optimizer for the new runtime benchmark. Existing three-seed evaluation and meta-training disclosures remain unchanged; this is not an increase in their run counts. Table 7 reports point estimates without adding confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Tables 1–5 retain their values, including Celo's final-loss IQM of 1.20 and speedup IQM of 1.86. New results include augmentation-level scores, 10K-evaluation IQMs of 1.85 for Celo and 0.34 for VeLO-S after 5K meta-training, runtime measurements, and AlgoPerf curves and instability findings. These substantially extend results under new conditions.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1, global task augmentation, the LSTM scheduler, the MLP update rule and two-stage meta-training remain unchanged. Celo-Adam in the new AlgoPerf evaluation corresponds to v1's existing Adam-update ablation in Table 3a. The additional augmentation variants do not replace the proposed default procedure.

P1.justification: The title becomes 'Celo: Training Versatile Learned Optimizers on a Compute Diet.' v2 makes localized grammar and terminology edits, updates author information and acknowledgements, renames Section 8, and inserts appendix subsections. The existing methodological narrative and main document organization remain largely intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds augmentation and runtime tables, an unnumbered scaling chart, and two six-panel AlgoPerf figures. Figure 5 gains a missing method legend. Existing appendix Figures 9–15 are retained as Figures 11–17, with surrounding layout reflow. The new displays substantially expand the visual evidence.

R1.justification: Section 7 adds targeted citations and discussion of stronger learned-optimizer baselines, hybrid nowcasting, and Thérien et al.'s µLO within Maximal Update Parametrization. It explicitly positions µLO as complementary. AlgoPerf competition and NumPy references are also added, without substantially changing the paper's overall research positioning.

T1.justification: Appendix A.5 introduces a computational-cost derivation: 288 FLOPs per parameter for Celo's MLP and relative overhead of 48/B against a linear layer's forward/backward computation, excluding scheduler cost. The existing optimization equations and mathematical definitions are unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves evidence about practical applicability. v1's iteration-based speedups and smaller-task evaluations left runtime costs and larger-workload behavior largely untested. Appendices A.4–A.6 and Table 7 address these gaps, including negative evidence about Adam-relative overhead and full-Celo instability. The additional ablations strengthen support for design choices. Although broad headline claims remain and full-Celo AlgoPerf traces are omitted, the new measurements and explicit limitations materially improve empirical credibility and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Celo research and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Retained content can be matched reliably despite the changed title and appendix renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and adds augmentation-level, scaling, runtime and AlgoPerf results. Original Celo/Celo-Adam outcomes are reported even though the AlgoPerf baseline curves use competition data.

before.justification: Sections 5–6 and the appendices report original Celo meta-training, optimizer evaluations, component ablations and learned-schedule analyses.

results.title: Celo: Training Versatile Learned Optimizers on a Compute Diet

C1.justification: The central claim that memorized networks retain decodable generalization is retained. v2 adds contributions concerning alternative probes, computational cost, and improved network performance through MASC-based retraining. It also narrows the corrupted-subspace superiority claim by explicitly acknowledging the ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 exception at 20% corruption.

C2.justification: v2 adds manifold-based motivation, interpretations of differing probe behavior, explanations for retraining successes and failures, and a hypothesis linking stronger generalization to reduced latent memorization. Some new numerical interpretation is inaccurate: Section 7 describes Table 9's -92.46% relative error reduction as 92.46% fewer correct labels, although these are different quantities.

D1.justification: v2 provides a code-repository link and implementation details for the new experiments, including ResNet-18 training settings, logistic regression's optimizer, learning rate, batch size and epochs, KNN's neighbor count and distance, and the retraining pipeline. These materially expand reproducibility information beyond v1's existing model and hardware descriptions.

E1.justification: Both versions use MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet for image classification under random label corruption and post-hoc true-label access. ResNet-18, additional probes, and retraining change models or procedures within this coverage, without introducing new datasets or task requirements.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated comparisons against logistic regression, K-nearest neighbors, linear discriminant analysis, quadratic discriminant analysis, and nearest class mean (Section 5 and Appendix C). v1 compares principally against network predictions, early-stopping performance, and random-initialization controls; those existing comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: New retraining experiments reserve 20% of the original test set for layer selection and validation, evaluate on the remaining 80%, and use up to 30 additional epochs with patience 3; a separate experiment uses 10 epochs without early stopping. v2 also adds ResNet-18 layer evaluations, probe-training protocols, and computational-cost and relabeling-error metrics. These additions do not establish changes to the retained experiments' protocols.

E4.justification: v2 replaces the Tiny ImageNet-focused PCA variance sweeps with comparisons of 99%, 75%, 50%, 25%, and one principal component across multiple model-dataset pairs. It adds computational-cost analyses, relabeling error decomposition, and retraining trajectories. Conversely, v1's dropout analyses in Appendix A.11 are removed; the early-stopping and random-initialization controls remain.

E5.justification: Appendix D newly reports five MASC runs using seeds 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50, summarized with means and 95% confidence intervals for PCA sensitivity. These runs use a fixed trained network. The broader practice of averaging three trained instances and displaying their ranges is retained, rather than replaced by five independent training runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds findings on probe accuracy and computational cost, PCA sensitivity, and mixed retraining outcomes. New ResNet-18 results include MASC trailing the model by 0.28 percentage points at 20% corruption (Table 6). The MLP-MNIST random-initialization control curve also changes between v1 Figure 10 and v2 Figure 23. Dropout results disappear, while corresponding retained base-model accuracy rows remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The PCA-based minimum-angle classifier remains substantively unchanged, but v2 introduces a substantial retraining procedure: select a layer using validation accuracy, relabel the training set with its MASC predictions, and further train the existing network. This extends the method beyond representation probing (Sections 3.4 and 7).

P1.justification: The introduction, contributions, related work, and discussion are substantially rewritten. Algorithms move into the main Methods section, latent memorization moves to Appendix H, and the appendices are reorganized by topic. The terminology consistently distinguishes generalization to true labels from performance on corrupted labels.

P2.justification: v2 adds explanatory schematics for the setting and retraining pipeline, redraws the MASC geometry illustration, expands model-comparison panels, and introduces probe, sensitivity, cost, and retraining displays. Summary tables are expanded and reorganized, early-stopping figures move into the main text, and dropout panels are removed.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion and citations for MentorNet, co-teaching, early-learning regularization, and manifold-based motivation, while removing references and discussion concerning Maini's localization work and Feldman's memorization studies. The central positioning against earlier probing and weight-rewinding research remains.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 adds an explicit distributional setup with i.i.d. sampling, separate clean and corrupted-label distributions, and evaluation relative to the clean target distribution. This supplies formal assumptions and definitions for the previously informal setting; no theorem, proof, or new theoretical guarantee is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence by addressing v1's missing alternative-probe comparisons and extending sensitivity analysis, while testing retraining and documenting failures. Clearer methods and additional implementation information improve assessability and reproducibility. These gains outweigh the loss of preliminary dropout evidence and localized interpretation errors, including Section 7's misreading of Table 9.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MASC research, with matching authors, methods, and experiments. Their main texts, algorithms, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds ResNet-18 experiments, alternative-probe comparisons, computational measurements, PCA sensitivity tests, and retraining results.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments measuring model and MASC accuracies under label corruption, including random-initialization controls, optimizer comparisons, and dropout experiments.

results.title: Decoding Generalization from Memorization in Deep Neural Networks

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction broaden the central performance claim from outperforming structural pruning to outperforming both pruning and MoE-construction techniques. Detailed analysis becomes an additional stated contribution. The original claims about uncovering experts without updating pretrained weights and jointly learning routing and expert configurations remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking the modest VO-routing benefit to small head dimensions and poor head-pruning performance to distorted attention features. It also discusses temperature robustness, recommends fewer than 16 experts, and qualifies comparable throughput by sufficiently large batch size. Existing interpretations of expert semantics and width allocation are retained.

D1.justification: The abstract adds a code-availability statement and repository address. New comparisons disclose training-token budgets and the matched-iteration fine-tuning setting for LLaMA-MoE. The detailed module configurations, optimizer settings, GPU allocations, and data-processing instructions already present in v1 remain substantially unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluated BoolQ, SciQ, TruthfulQA, and MMLU benchmarks in Tables 5–6 and Figure 10, substantially broadening task coverage beyond the original language-modeling and five commonsense benchmarks. The original training datasets and evaluation coverage are retained.

E2.justification: Tables 4–6 add evaluated LLaMA-MoE, G-MoEfication, LLaMA-MoE-v2, and CMoE comparators, including multiple configurations and fine-tuned variants. This introduces a substantial direct MoE-construction comparison group. The original structural and semi-structured pruning comparators remain represented.

E3.justification: Alongside the retained zero-shot protocols, v2 introduces 32-shot BoolQ, 5-shot WinoGrande and MMLU, 25-shot ARC-c, and 10-shot HellaSwag evaluations. It also introduces throughput measurements at batch sizes 512, 1024, and 1536. These are additional evaluation designs; the original default 10,000-iteration training setup remains unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained loss, dataset, and expert-count analyses, Table 13 tests local embeddings, head pruning, removal of VO routing, and temperature sensitivity. Figure 4 adds aggregate expert-utilization analysis, Figure 10 examines the MMLU accuracy–parameter trade-off, and Table 15 examines throughput scaling with batch size.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run summaries, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The retained expert-width boxplots describe variation among experts rather than uncertainty across experimental runs.

E6.justification: Original benchmark values are retained, including LLaMA-2 rows relocated from Table 3 to Table 12. v2 adds substantial MoE, MMLU, ablation, and throughput results: Table 13 reports 56.07 for full ToMoE versus 44.99 for head pruning, and Table 15 reports 2360.38–2919.45 tokens/s across batch sizes. Section 4.3 also incorrectly redescribes the unchanged 3.14-point advantage over ModeGPT-Alpaca as '3.14 times'.

M1.justification: The core architecture, expert construction, routing, and frozen-weight training remain the same. However, Section 3.4 changes the load-balancing probability calculation from explicitly defined softmax in v1 to GSmax in v2 without explaining whether this represents a changed calculation or inconsistent notation. An actual loss modification cannot be established reliably.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the abstract, condenses the introductory background, edits method explanations and notation, updates author information, and removes the Impact Statement. The main section sequence and much of the existing method and appendix prose remain intact.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a two-column conference layout to a single-column journal layout with substantially different front matter and table placement. v2 adds comparison and ablation tables and new plots, moves part of Table 3 into appendix Table 12, and combines v1 Figures 5–6 into v2 Figure 6.

R1.justification: v2 expands positioning against contextual sparsity through Deja Vu, CATS, and structured-sparsity work, and broadens dense-to-MoE discussion and comparisons through MoEfication, generalized MoEfication, LLaMA-MoE-v2, and CMoE. This substantially expands the prior-work context for its unified expert-construction and router-training claim.

T1.justification: New Appendix F derives the effective query–key width from overlapping binary pruning masks, showing that it reaches the allocated width K only when the masks coincide. This adds a focused mathematical justification to the qualitative concern already stated in v1 Appendix A.2.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important gap in v1: a dense-to-MoE method was evaluated mainly against pruning. Direct MoE comparisons, component validation, and measured throughput materially strengthen the evidence for its contribution. These gains outweigh new reporting problems, although the broader superiority claim needs qualification: Table 6 reports 57.40 for ToMoE versus 59.61 and 59.31 for LLaMA-MoE-v2, with very different training-token budgets. Those results support an efficiency–accuracy trade-off.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ToMoE. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated results between v1's Appendices A–E and v2's Appendices A–F.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds MoE comparisons, additional benchmarks, component ablations, and inference-throughput measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original ToMoE perplexity and zero-shot evaluation results, loss and dataset ablations, and expert analyses in the main text and appendices.

results.title: ToMoE: Converting Dense Large Language Models to Mixture-of-Experts through Dynamic Structural Pruning

C1.justification: v1 presents a novel three-package ASD pipeline as a principal contribution; v2 makes SCT sparsity detection the primary contribution and treats coloring and differentiation packages as supporting infrastructure. This substantially narrows the contribution framing and adds GNNs to the claimed application scope, while retaining the one-off computation and large-speedup claims.

C2.justification: v2 expands brief control-flow/GPU caveats into specific unsupported operations, explanations of unsafe sparsity underestimation, and memory-allocation and block-sparsity limitations. New solver discussions explain conditioning, precision, and JVP-count tradeoffs. The GNN discussion also acknowledges that different AD backends may partly explain its speedup.

D1.justification: v2 documents overload code generation and correctness checks, extension hooks, alternative sparsity representations, and coloring/decompression details. It supplies new GNN and solver configurations and replaces the anonymous repository reference with a named repository and archived release citation. These substantially expand documentation without establishing changes to the original implementation.

E1.justification: v2 adds node classification using an implicit GNN on simplified synthetic chains (Section 5.2), and extends Brusselator evaluation to Newton linear-system solves (Appendix G.2). These introduce downstream tasks beyond derivative construction. The original Brusselator, PGLib, and convolutional examples remain.

E2.justification: The original Symbolics/SCT and dense-AD/ASD comparisons remain. v2 additionally evaluates VJP-based GMRES against sparse direct solves for GNN differentiation, and lazy-JVP and materialized-Jacobian BiCGStab(l) against direct Newton solves. These substantially expand the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: The new GNN protocol uses 10-node chains, 100 input features, 16 hidden units, and one positive and one negative training chain, reporting loss and test accuracy against time. Its iterative and direct arms use Zygote and ForwardDiff respectively. Newton-step timing also introduces a new protocol; the original benchmark grid, hardware, and derivative backends remain.

E4.justification: v2 Figure 2 adds an explicit runtime-component breakdown examining the sparsity-detection bottleneck. Figure 5b adds a local sparsity example alongside the retained global convolution patterns. These are limited diagnostic additions beyond v1's aggregate timing comparisons and global-pattern illustrations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars. Parenthetical timing-table values remain speedup ratios, and the new GNN curves show epochs without uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Brusselator timings are revised: at N=192, unprepared ASD changes from 10.4 seconds in v1 Table 6 to 4.62 seconds in v2 Table 4 under the same stated grid and backend. v2 adds solver timings, runtime components, and GNN curves reporting nearly twofold faster epochs. All 41 PGLib rows in each full results table are unchanged.

M1.justification: The operator-overloaded tracers, local/global classifications, tensor overloads, and detection–coloring–differentiation pipeline are retained. Configurable sparsity representations already appeared in v1 Appendix A.5. v2 expands implementation documentation and applies the approach to additional evaluations without establishing a changed SCT algorithm.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contributions, and software narrative are extensively refocused around SCT. Applications move into the introduction; Hessian theory and experiments move into appendices; implementation material becomes organized subsections on representations, tensor overloads, and limitations. This is substantial restructuring beyond simply adding experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adds runtime-breakdown and GNN-training figures, expands the convolution figure with a local-pattern panel, and restructures the Brusselator table with Newton-solver columns. Duplicate main-text Brusselator-pattern and selected PGLib displays disappear while their appendix content remains. Captions and code-listing presentation are also revised.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of Lohoff and Neftci's Graphax approach, implicit-GNN literature, and additional coloring and solver references. Separate companion papers now document the differentiation interface and coloring package. Some citations, including AbstractDifferentiation, disappear, but the historical account and operator-overloading lineage remain largely intact.

T1.justification: v2 replaces gradient and Hessian sparsity equalities with upper bounds, adds a cancellation counterexample, and restores the missing minus sign in the implicit derivative formula. Appendix C adds formal compression/coloring conditions, although its greedy star-coloring wording conflicts with its own definition. The original tracing derivations otherwise remain.

improvement.justification: v1's efficiency evidence centers on derivative construction. v2 addresses the important downstream-use gap through Newton and GNN solver comparisons, adds bottleneck diagnostics, corrects central mathematical statements, and documents concrete failure conditions while preserving the Hessian evidence. These substantially strengthen usefulness and credibility. The toy GNN's different AD backends limit causal attribution, and the new coloring primer contains a local inconsistency, but these limitations do not outweigh the gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SCT-based automatic sparse differentiation work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching Hessian material moved into v2's appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical benchmarks and adds runtime decomposition, Newton-step solver timings, and implicit-GNN training and test results in Section 5 and Appendix G.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendices A.8–A.9 report original timing experiments for sparsity detection and Jacobian/Hessian computation on the Brusselator and PGLib problems.

results.title: Sparser, Better, Faster, Stronger: Sparsity Detection for Efficient Automatic Differentiation

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statement and conclusion retain the same central claims: calibrated, gradient-free initialization, closed-form optimal adapters and strong low-bit fine-tuning performance. Specifying 2-bit in the abstract and clarifying that initialization is gradient-free refine wording without materially redefining the contributions.

C2.justification: v2 newly interprets calibration-size stability as supporting practical deployment and explains comparable LoftQ initialization time through fewer SVDs balanced against costlier quantization. It also develops resource-efficiency implications from measured costs. The earlier interpretation of robustness across quantization group sizes is removed.

D1.justification: Table 10 newly documents initialization time and peak GPU memory, including CLoQ's 0.7 hours/9 GB for Llama2-7B and 1.5 hours/13 GB for Llama2-13B. v2 also describes LoftQ's five default alternating iterations. Code access and existing implementation details remain unchanged; Appendix A still provides hyperparameters only for Llama2.

E1.justification: The represented datasets and tasks remain WikiText-2, GSM8K/Math10K, the four arithmetic benchmarks and eight commonsense benchmarks. The mixed-training experiment recombines already represented math and commonsense data. Additional model families, calibration counts and sequence lengths change experimental settings within this coverage.

E2.justification: ApiQ was discussed but not evaluated in v1. v2 adds ApiQ-lw and ApiQ-bw to the Llama2 WikiText/GSM8K comparison and ApiQ-bw to arithmetic and commonsense comparisons. These substantial additions introduce a closely related competing initialization method while retaining the previous comparators.

E3.justification: v2 adds Llama3-8B and Mistral-7B configurations, mixed Math10K-plus-5K-commonsense training, calibration-size sweeps from 32 to 256, and fine-tuning sequence lengths from 256 to 2048. It also evaluates initialization duration and peak GPU memory. Existing default settings, splits and Appendix A hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of mixed-domain training, calibration-size sensitivity, sequence-length sensitivity and initialization efficiency (Tables 6 and 8–10). It removes v1's group-size analyses (Tables 4–5) and the Hadamard initialization variant from the adapter-factorization ablation. The remaining factorization comparisons are retained.

E5.justification: v1 provides no repeated-run counts or uncertainty estimates. v2 Table 4 reports CLoQ's Llama3 arithmetic accuracies averaged over five random runs with standard deviations. This reporting is limited to that configuration; no increased run count is established for retained experiments.

E6.justification: Shared Llama2 entries in v1 Tables 1–3 remain numerically unchanged in v2 Tables 3, 1 and 5. Substantial results are added for ApiQ, additional models and new analyses, while group-size and Hadamard results disappear. New Table 4 reports arithmetic averages of 59.0±0.34 for CLoQ versus 57.4 for ApiQ-bw. Table 5 also exposes exceptions to superiority: 4-bit Llama2-7B commonsense averages favor ApiQ-bw, 84.7 versus 84.2.

M1.justification: The MagR/OPTQ quantization, activation-weighted objective, two-SVD initialization and adapter fine-tuning remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 now explicitly includes Gram-matrix regularization already described in v1. The new pseudoinverse discussion concerns theoretical solutions rather than a changed experimental procedure.

P1.justification: Most introductory, methodological, concluding and appendix prose is retained. v2 revises result discussions around ApiQ, adds experimental discussion blocks, introduces the AltMin abbreviation and updates author and acknowledgment text. The overall section organization remains largely stable.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the predominantly two-column layout with a single-column journal format and substantially reformats the title block, equations and tables. Comparison tables are expanded and reordered, new experimental tables are added, and group-size tables are removed. Figures 1–2 retain identical image content.

R1.justification: v2 adds contextual references including PiSSA, OLoRA, RoseLoRA, Eckart–Young, Llama3 and additional quantization and initialization research. It supplements the computational comparison with LoftQ, while retaining the principal positioning against LoftQ, LQ-LoRA and ApiQ.

T1.justification: Theorem 3.1 and its proof remain unchanged. v2 adds a mathematical discussion extending the optimality condition to rank-deficient activations and supplies a pseudoinverse-based solution, supplementing the original full-rank treatment.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important evidential gaps by evaluating the closely related ApiQ baseline, testing additional model families and measuring previously unquantified initialization costs. Sensitivity experiments further strengthen the method's empirical support. These gains outweigh the loss of group-size and Hadamard ablations, although reporting remains imperfect: Table 4 supports a 1.6-point Llama3 arithmetic advantage over ApiQ-bw, whereas the prose claims 2.1 points. Overall, the central effectiveness and efficiency claims have substantially stronger direct evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CLoQ research. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete Appendix A are readable and matchable despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds model evaluations, ApiQ comparisons, sensitivity experiments and initialization-resource measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original language-modeling, arithmetic-reasoning and commonsense-reasoning experiments, together with quantization and initialization ablations.

results.title: CLoQ: Enhancing Fine-Tuning of Quantized LLMs via Calibrated LoRA Initialization

C1.justification: The central contribution remains inference-time safety through augmented latent MDPs. v3 qualifies the headline guarantee as relative to the supplied cost model and sufficiently large penalties, and changes categorical safety wording to an aim in the abstract and conclusion. The introduction also adds a claim of decoding cost comparable to beam search.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly discusses dependence on cost-model quality, including bias, dataset artifacts and false positives. It interprets independent judging as evidence against cost-model overfitting and develops latency and parameter trade-off explanations. These materially expand applicability boundaries and interpretation beyond v1's efficiency and jailbreaking caveats.

D1.justification: v3 adds checkpoint links, bfloat16 precision, a minimum 64 GB memory description and vLLM information for the latency study. However, it replaces v1's named V100 GPUs and CUDA 12.4 with unspecified internal hardware. The approximately 0.7-billion-parameter critic and its training hyperparameters are retained.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates only PKU-SafeRLHF. v3 adds HEx-PHI's harmful-instruction evaluation and HH-RLHF's human-preference prompts. HH-RLHF also supplies critic-training data for the HEx-PHI evaluation, substantially expanding the represented data and evaluation coverage.

E2.justification: The principal BoN, beam-search, ARGS and RE-Control comparator families and their safety variants are retained. v3 Tables 5–6 additionally evaluate Beam Search Lag. + Freq., a frequency-based diversity variant absent from v1's comparisons.

E3.justification: v3 standardizes main comparisons at N=128 and changes the reported ARGS sample count from 20 to 128. It adds Vicuna-7B and Llama3.1-8B-Instruct configurations, including QRM reward/cost evaluation, independent-judge win rates and a generation-versus-evaluation latency protocol. These are substantive changes in reported evaluation design, without establishing which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 expands v1's limited N/λ comparisons into systematic multiplier and search-parameter sweeps in Tables 5–7. It adds Pareto analyses, independent-judge checks of cost-model dependence, and latency decomposition. The earlier qualitative response examples are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions report reward values with ± spreads and display result distributions. v3 adds no explicit seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests or explanation of those spreads. Additional result rows and judge win/tie/loss counts do not establish a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Tables 3–9 add substantial benchmark and analysis results. In Table 2, the PKU/Alpaca critic entry changes from reward 6.81 and safety 91.04% to 6.50 and 94.46%. Timings are extensively revised, and Table 2 drops average-cost entries. Changed settings and hardware disclosure prevent interpreting all numerical differences as same-setting improvements.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 changes the stated outer-loop count from D/K to D/d, using beam depth rather than retained beam count. It also explicitly documents the penalized-policy updates already described in v1. Safety-state augmentation, critic objectives and the main search strategy remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten, related work moves from Section 6 to Section 2, and background subsections are consolidated. A proof roadmap is added, the experimental appendix is reorganized, and the broader-impact statement moves to Appendix E. These changes materially restructure the narrative.

P2.justification: The main text switches from two columns to one. Figure 1 becomes a fuller algorithm pipeline, and Figure 2 replaces separate runtime plots with four model panels encoding runtime by color. New Pareto and judge figures accompany expanded, reorganized tables; the qualitative examples are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: Appendix A substantially broadens the safety-alignment literature, adding dual-objective optimization, model editing, cross-model steering, self-evaluation and paired-model decoding approaches, including Safety Arithmetic, Stream Aligner and InferAligner. The principal novelty positioning remains, but it is situated against a considerably wider body of work.

T1.justification: The latent-MDP definition, principal assumptions, Theorems 1–2 and Appendix B's Bellman and convergence arguments retain their mathematical substance. The new main-text proof outline summarizes reasoning already present in v1's appendix; notation and assumption-wording refinements do not introduce a new guarantee.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens v1's narrow validation through additional datasets and models, parameter sensitivity studies and independent judging. Explicit cost-model qualifications also make the safety claims more defensible. These gains outweigh weaker hardware disclosure and new reporting inconsistencies, although conflicting Beaver beam-search entries in Tables 2 and 5 limit confidence in some quantitative conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe InferenceGuard, with matching central formulations, algorithms and theoretical results. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support a reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v3 reports original experiments across PKU-SafeRLHF, HEx-PHI and HH-RLHF, including model comparisons, parameter sweeps, independent-judge evaluations and latency measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original PKU-SafeRLHF experiments using Alpaca-7B and Beaver-7B, including reward, cost, safety rates, inference times and generated-response examples.

results.title: On Almost Surely Safe Alignment of Large Language Models at Inference-Time

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: online implicit PRMs trained from outcome labels, elimination of dedicated PRM pretraining, compatibility with multiple RL algorithms, and improved efficiency and reasoning performance. The headline performance and data-efficiency claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation of the method through Appendix C's discussion of reward parameterization, loss normalization and reward shaping. It adds interpretations concerning limited benefits from larger PRMs and reduced relative overhead for long responses. Appendix A newly states the 32B experimental boundary and shorter ablation budgets; the earlier Zero-training saturation discussion is retained.

D1.justification: v2 adds hardware specifications, component-level timing, CPU-offloading information and resource budgets for new comparisons. Existing training hyperparameters and preprocessing instructions remain. v1's public project/model/data link is removed, while v2 instead states that code is provided in supplementary material.

E1.justification: v2 adds AIME 2025 evaluation in Table 5. Additional comparisons use MATH training data and the DeepScaleR training setting in Appendices B.6–B.7. The original seven benchmarks and documented SFT/RL data collections remain, with coverage still centered on mathematical and coding reasoning.

E2.justification: v2 adds a reproduced VinePPO comparison and comparisons with DeepScaleR checkpoints in Tables 6–7, substantially extending the evaluated alternatives beyond the existing RL algorithms. VinePPO was only cited in v1. DeepScaleR comparisons use reported results and an estimated training curve; the original comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce 800 rollout steps, 16 responses per prompt instead of four, and 3B/7B/14B reward models with a fixed 7B policy. Additional protocols include matched 96-step RhoMath-1.1B training, 330-step training with an 8k response limit under the DeepScaleR setting, and avg@16 evaluation at temperature 0.3. The original main-experiment settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial tests of whether gains persist with more training and rollouts, whether reward-model capacity matters, and whether CE versus DPO PRM training changes performance. Runtime profiling also examines computational overhead. Earlier filtering, initialization, reference-model, single/double-forward and Zero analyses are retained, including relocated appendix material.

E5.justification: Table 12 newly reports avg@16 evaluation, adding explicit averaging over 16 sampled responses for AIME 2024 and AMC. This does not establish repeated independent RL training runs. The disclosed SFT seed remains 42, and no new confidence-interval or significance-testing procedure is documented.

E6.justification: The original main and RL-algorithm tables retain their scores, but v2 adds substantial scaling, timing, model-size, loss-choice and avg@16 results. For example, Table 6 reports 18.8% versus 18.4% validation accuracy and 1.22 versus 13.94 hours for PRIME versus VinePPO at 96 steps. These are newly reported experiments, not improvements to the unchanged original scores.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and the default implicit-reward, advantage-estimation and policy-update procedures remain unchanged. Appendix C.2 introduces and tests an alternative DPO loss for updating the PRM, while retaining CE as the default.

P1.justification: The document is extensively reorganized: imitation warmup moves into Appendix D; reference-model, single/double-forward and Zero studies move into Appendix B; detailed alternative advantage formulas also move out of the main text. v2 adds limitations, ethics, reproducibility and theoretical-discussion sections, alongside prose compression and author-list changes.

P2.justification: Numerous displays are relocated and resized, including v1 Figure 1 becoming appendix Figure 12 and v1 Table 3 becoming appendix Table 4. v2 adds scaling plots, runtime and comparison tables, and loss-ablation displays. Figure 17 presents the existing dense-versus-sparse comparison against wall time; retained plots also receive caption and legend revisions.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to DeepScaleR, Rho-1, potential-based reward shaping and maximum-entropy RL, and removes the Meta 2024 reference. Appendix C clarifies relationships to DPO and entropy-regularized RL. The main positioning around scalable online dense rewards remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix C adds a soft-Q expression, mathematical reasoning about cancellation of prompt-dependent reward offsets, and a potential-based reward-shaping argument at gamma=1. These extend the justification of the existing formulation; the original advantage equations remain, and no substantial new theorem-and-proof development is supplied.

improvement.justification: v2 materially strengthens the central efficiency argument, which in v1 relied mainly on training-step counts, through runtime profiling and a matched VinePPO comparison. Longer-training, larger-rollout and PRM-size/loss studies also address important robustness gaps. These gains outweigh limited shortcomings: DeepScaleR comparisons use estimated curves and different hardware/budgets, Table 2 implies approximately 28% overhead rather than the stated 24%, and direct public resource access information is reduced.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PRIME. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching material moved between the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and adds original scaling, runtime, reward-model-size, loss-function and baseline-comparison results.

before.justification: v1 reports original RL training results, seven-benchmark evaluations and ablations, including Tables 2–3 and Figures 3–13.

results.title: Process Reinforcement through Implicit Rewards

C1.justification: The central contribution remains iterative internalization of human hints without requiring expert demonstrations. The abstract and conclusion extend the explicit empirical outperformance claim from ToolQA to ToolQA and OfficeBench, including the new 90.3% OfficeBench result, without redefining the methodological contribution.

C2.justification: New Section 6 and Appendix A discuss human-supervision scalability, annotator expertise, required overlap in tool usage, training-time tool information, and reliance on ground-truth checks to identify failures. They explicitly acknowledge that cross-domain sequential training was not tested. Appendix C.3 also adds explanations of dropout through attention preservation, data augmentation, and easier hint internalization.

D1.justification: v2 adds extensive initial and corrective hint listings, OfficeBench tool and preprocessing documentation, reviewer-model identity, LoRA precision/layer coverage/merging details, and hardware and training times. A first-page footnote newly states that code and checkpoints are available. Much existing training information is relocated to Appendix E; exact ToolQA split counts and the explicit exact-string-match description from v1 are omitted.

E1.justification: v2 adds training and evaluation on 286 OfficeBench tasks spanning six applications and workflows requiring one to three applications. These non-templated document, spreadsheet, email, and calendar workflows substantially extend coverage beyond ToolQA. The six ToolQA groups and HumanEval/GSM8K evaluations remain.

E2.justification: Matched comparisons retain the Llama-3.1-70B prompt baselines, DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o, and cross-entropy training on successful trajectories. OfficeBench extends the same comparator set to another benchmark. The new dropout and balancing experiments vary components of MNM rather than introduce separate baseline methods.

E3.justification: OfficeBench introduces a 67/3/30 training/validation/test split and its own training schedule, including four teacher trajectories per task and seven epochs in Round 1. New ablations vary dropout and balancing. Existing ToolQA descriptions also change: filter counts become 15/21 instead of 14/18, and held-out templates are described as a three-way 60/10/30 split rather than a shared training/validation template pool plus test templates. These reported revisions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix C.3 adds direct tests of two previously unablated components: dropout rates 0.5, 0.7, 0.9, and 1.0, and training with versus without data balancing, on both benchmarks. Coding and reasoning skill-retention checks also cover OfficeBench-trained agents. The earlier held-out-template and cross-entropy analyses are retained.

E5.justification: For held-out ToolQA tasks, v1 reports one DeepSeek-V3 trial without uncertainty, whereas v2 reports three trials and adds standard errors (v1 Table 4; v2 Table 5). The general mean-and-standard-error reporting practice remains, and GPT-4o remains a single-trial comparison.

E6.justification: New OfficeBench results include Round 3 MNM success of 90.3%, compared with GPT-4o at 89.9% and DeepSeek-V3 at 86.9%. v2 also adds ablation results, OfficeBench token counts, and skill-retention scores. The headline ToolQA results remain unchanged. Held-out DeepSeek-V3 entries are revised under three-trial reporting, such as Yelp changing from a single-trial 78.2% to a mean of 84.9%; this is not a demonstrated same-setting model improvement.

M1.justification: The ReAct/Python architecture, iterative hint distillation, LoRA updates, probabilistic hint dropout, and data balancing are already present in v1. v2 specifies forward KL and additional implementation details, but does not establish a new algorithmic component. OfficeBench applies the existing procedure to another task domain.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is substantially reorganized around two benchmarks, with detailed training descriptions moved from Section 5.3 into Appendix E. v2 introduces a main discussion section and reorganizes the appendices around limitations, results, efficiency, training, tools, preprocessing, and hints. Existing task examples and broader-impact material are relocated, while much introductory and methodological prose is retained.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main text from two columns to one, substantially reflows figures and tables, and displays the prompt structure as a numbered listing beside Figure 2. It adds OfficeBench and ablation tables, expands the existing coding/reasoning and token-usage tables, and introduces extensive formatted hint listings. Figures 1–4 are retained rather than replaced by new scientific figures.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including Lost in the Middle, CLIN, AVATAR, OfficeBench, Pomerleau, and Sarch et al. It adds a substantive distinction from Sarch et al.'s abstraction-level feedback for vision-language agents. The related-work organization and claimed novelty of extending context distillation to interactive LLM agents remain.

T1.justification: The state and policy definitions, LoRA update equations, and Algorithm 1 are substantively retained. v2 explicitly states the direction of the existing KL objective but adds no new derivation, theorem, or proof. Its new applicability conditions are qualitative limitations rather than formal theoretical assumptions.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's ToolQA-centered evidence through distinct OfficeBench workflows and ablations of two important components. Detailed hints, implementation disclosures, and explicit applicability limitations materially improve reproducibility and interpretation. Some reporting weaknesses remain: the OfficeBench advantage over GPT-4o is narrow, and Table 9 implies approximately 14–17% of baseline input-token usage, inconsistent with the stated 7–10%. The broader validation and improved transparency outweigh these limitations; the improvement does not depend on the unchanged headline ToolQA scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Memento No More study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial expansion and reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds OfficeBench evaluations, component ablations, and further benchmark and efficiency measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original ToolQA experiments, held-out-template evaluation, coding and reasoning benchmark results, and a cross-entropy training comparison.

results.title: Memento No More: Coaching AI Agents to Master Multiple Tasks via Hints Internalization

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions add the claimed first private sliced Wasserstein autoencoder procedure as a central contribution. The conclusion also introduces the claim that the approach consistently matches or surpasses comparable Wasserstein-based methods, extending v1's claims about generality and privacy–utility preservation.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive computational limitations concerning Jacobian memory, GPU efficiency and small-batch bias in Remark 4.5 and Appendix G. Appendix E.6 explains the role of shared randomness, while Appendix F qualifies poor baseline performance as potentially attributable to the privacy correction or implementation. Earlier class-size and general-Wasserstein limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents the autoencoder architecture, group and batch counts, Python/JAX implementation, absence of JIT compilation, GPU hardware, runtimes and subbatch Jacobian computation. These substantially expand reproducibility information. Table 2's approximately one-tenth batch fractions conflict with the retained one-fifth description, leaving that setting ambiguous.

E1.justification: v2 adds MNIST and Fashion-MNIST image reconstruction, latent representation and generation experiments. This substantially extends v1's exclusively synthetic coverage; the existing synthetic fairness and circle-matching tasks remain.

E2.justification: Appendix F adds an evaluated Rakotomamonjy and Ralaivola (2021) baseline using Greenewald et al.'s (2024) privacy correction; v1 discussed this comparator without reporting its experimental results. This addition concerns the circle-matching experiment. Section 5.3's reference to Sebag et al. is a literature comparison, not another baseline evaluated here.

E3.justification: The added image experiments introduce a convolutional autoencoder protocol with a six-dimensional latent prior, Adam, 5,000 updates, batches of 600 and 100 projection directions. The new circle baseline uses 15 directions versus 50 for the proposed method. These are added experimental protocols; the retained fairness results do not establish rerunning under changed settings.

E4.justification: Appendix E.6 and Figure 16 add a focused robustness analysis of the statistical-parity classification experiment across random seeds, including paired private-minus-non-private loss trajectories. This tests whether the observed similarity depends on randomness. The previous fairness-weight and privacy-budget sweeps are retained.

E5.justification: v1 reports training curves without repeated-seed variability. v2 documents shared seeds for initialization, batches and Gaussian noise across fairness configurations, and adds a 10-seed analysis reporting means and bands of plus or minus two standard deviations. This introduces substantive uncertainty reporting without establishing how many runs originally underlay v1.

E6.justification: Figures 2–3 and 5–7 add image reconstructions, generated samples and latent-space results at epsilon values infinity, 10 and 5 with delta 10^-5. Figures 16 and 18 add repeated-seed loss results and circle-baseline outcomes. The original fairness and circle results are retained as Figures 8–15 and 17, rather than demonstrating improved same-setting performance.

M1.justification: Section 5 adds a concrete private sliced Wasserstein autoencoder adaptation, combining reconstruction with latent matching to a public prior and generating samples by decoding that prior. This extends the applications implemented in v1 while retaining its gradient estimator, clipping, Gaussian perturbation, subsampling and privacy accounting.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion are substantially rewritten around two applications. The deep-learning framework moves from Section 5 to Appendix B, detailed fairness material moves to Appendix E, and proofs and the sliced extension are redistributed. This substantially changes the narrative and document organization.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, and the visual presentation is extensively rebuilt. v2 adds autoencoder and computation diagrams, image-result displays, uncertainty plots, a baseline figure and two tables. Main-text fairness illustrations are consolidated, while their detailed results remain in the appendices.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted references on corrected slicing-mechanism privacy, private transport-map estimation and efficient private gradient computation. Greenewald et al. (2024) materially qualifies the closest baseline's privacy analysis. Most existing optimal-transport and fairness positioning is retained, with the extended fairness discussion moved to Appendix A.

T1.justification: The central sensitivity theorem, its proof and the counterexample for general Wasserstein losses are retained. Section 5.1 adds the combined reconstruction/prior-matching sensitivity bound for private autoencoders, and Remark C.2 supplies an explicit derivation of the clipped Jacobian's spectral-norm bound.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's synthetic-only validation through image experiments and addresses unreported run-to-run variability with a paired 10-seed study. The implemented baseline and detailed architecture/computation disclosures further improve empirical support and reproducibility. Image-method comparisons remain qualitative, and the batch-size inconsistency limits reproducibility, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Wasserstein-gradient privacy framework. Their complete main texts, figures, equations and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains these experiments and adds MNIST/Fashion-MNIST autoencoder results, a baseline experiment and a repeated-seed analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic experiments on private fair classification, regression, representation learning and distribution matching in Section 7 and Appendices B–C.

results.title: Learning with Differentially Private (Sliced) Wasserstein Gradients

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets, and central conclusion retain the same claims: learning pseudo physics from limited data improves operator learning without requiring known governing equations. The novelty claim and five-benchmark-plus-fatigue scope remain. The initial-condition caveat added to the conclusion already appeared in v1 Appendix C.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands limitations concerning difficult multiscale PDEs, spurious learned relationships, correlated grid samples, resolution dependence, and the distinction between predictive surrogates and discovered physical laws. It also interprets the new sequential-pipeline, robustness, and timing results and clarifies that residual regularization does not supply additional labeled pairs.

D1.justification: v2 adds an implementation-release link, specifies centered finite differences, identifies the RTX 4090 workstation used for timing, and documents the new robustness preprocessing. The extensive original hyperparameter settings are moved from Appendix A.7 into Section 5 without substantive changes. Table 12 reports runtime values but does not specify their units.

E1.justification: The five PDE benchmarks and fatigue-modeling task are retained. Coverage expands within existing benchmarks to shifted input distributions for Advection and Nonlinear Diffusion, and sparse, noisy observations for Nonlinear Diffusion. The more general PDE settings discussed in Section 6.1 are not evaluated.

E2.justification: v2 Table 6 adds SINDy-to-FNO and learned-phi-network-to-FNO sequential pipelines on Darcy Flow and Nonlinear Diffusion. SINDy was previously discussed but not evaluated. Existing FNO, DONet, PI-FNO, and architectural-ablation comparisons remain.

E3.justification: The original benchmark settings are retained, but substantial new protocols are introduced: sequential training with generated data; test kernel length scales of 0.15 versus training 0.25 for Advection and 0.10 versus 0.20 for Nonlinear Diffusion; and subsampling to 400 values, adding 5% Gaussian noise, then Gaussian-process interpolation back to 128-by-128 grids.

E4.justification: Section 5.2 adds tests of sequential versus joint learning, distribution-shift robustness of both the physics surrogate and PPI-FNO, sparse/noisy-data robustness, and training-time overhead. These substantially extend the existing architecture, derivative-order, loss-weight, learning-curve, and rich-data analyses, which are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five evaluations with randomly resampled training sets and report means with standard deviations. Additional result tables continue that reporting style. The new discussion of correlated grid samples and effective sample size introduces no corresponding uncertainty estimator, significance test, or revised repetition count.

E6.justification: All eight v1 tables retain their numerical entries in corresponding v2 tables. New Tables 6, 9, 10, 12, and 13 add pipeline, robustness, and timing results. For example, shifted Advection with 80 examples gives errors of 0.6471 for PPI-FNO and 0.6484 for FNO; noisy Nonlinear Diffusion with 30 examples gives 0.0504 and 0.0606, respectively.

M1.justification: The evaluated surrogate architecture, losses, and alternating procedure in Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. New Section 6.1 proposes adaptations for coefficient, initial-condition, and boundary-condition inputs, including a contrastive residual objective and a boundary-enforcing formulation. These are untested methodological extensions, not demonstrated changes to the benchmark implementation.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is reorganized into predictive-performance and ablation subsections. Hyperparameters and pointwise-error analysis move from the appendices into the main text, alongside a substantial new Discussions and Limitations section. Core introductory passages remain largely intact, but the document structure and explanatory treatment change extensively.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a two-column conference layout to a single-column journal layout, with extensive relocation and resizing of tables and figures. Panels from v1 Figures 3 and 6 are regrouped into v2 Figures 8 and 9. Five new tables and two new distribution-shift heatmap figures supplement the retained displays.

R1.justification: Five references are added for approximation theory, finite differences, learning theory, and PixelCNN. The new SINDy comparison further develops the distinction between explicit equation identification and flexible learned PDE representations. The principal positioning relative to neural operators, PINO, and cycle consistency remains.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 adds finite-difference error and grid-size scaling, universal-approximation arguments, and VC-dimension/sample-complexity statements. Section 6.1 adds generalized PDE formulations and reasoning about avoiding a trivial zero residual through a contrastive objective. The original mathematical formulation remains, without a new PPI-NO-specific convergence or generalization proof.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps through sequential-pipeline comparisons, distribution-shift and noisy-data tests, and measured computational overhead. These expose both persistent benefits and sharply reduced gains under harder conditions. The expanded limitations substantially improve interpretation of the unchanged main results. Although the proposed general-PDE extensions remain unvalidated and timing units are missing, the added evidence and qualifications make the method's benefits, costs, and applicability substantially easier to assess.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PPI-NO work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across substantial relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds sequential-pipeline comparisons, distribution-shift and noisy-data experiments, and training-time measurements.

before.justification: Section 5 and the appendices report original evaluations of PPI-FNO and PPI-DONet on five PDE benchmarks and fatigue modeling, including ablations and prediction visualizations.

results.title: Pseudo-Physics-Informed Neural Operators: Enhancing Operator Learning from Limited Data

C1.justification: The central contributions and claims about likelihood versus prior misspecification remain. The claimed empirical scope expands to practical applications, while the conclusion replaces v1's two-step diagnostic recommendation with a more qualified assessment emphasizing unresolved obstacles to practical deployment.

C2.justification: v2 Section 6 explains that comparing predictions with noisy observations can penalize successful noise removal, qualifying v1's recommendation to diagnose robustness using SSDD followed by PPD. It adds substantive limitations concerning label-free hyperparameter selection, interpretability, and failure of majority-domain alignment to protect rare misspecified observations.

D1.justification: New appendices document Ricker architectures and search ranges, decision-model networks and training budgets, empirical-data selection, cleaning thresholds, and Mahalanobis-based test-set classification. NNPE standardization and image-noise scaling are explicitly documented. One reproducibility inconsistency remains: Gaussian adaptation data number 48,000 in Section 5.2 but 49,000 in Appendix B.4.

E1.justification: v2 adds contaminated Ricker population-dynamics inference and diffusion-model inference on empirical Implicit Association Test data. These introduce temporal ecological simulations and human response-time modeling beyond the retained Gaussian and MNIST/USPS denoising coverage.

E2.justification: The matched benchmarks retain the same comparison participants: NPE, NNPE, NPE-MMD, NPE-DANN, and the analytic posterior for Gaussian inference. The new applications reuse the neural comparator set. NNPE standardization and noise scaling concern experimental settings.

E3.justification: Denoising evaluation changes from observed images seen during adaptation to a separate unseen test set. Gaussian test sets increase from 100 to 1,000, with posterior samples increasing from 100 to 5,000; denoising samples increase from 10 to 100. PPD changes to RMSE with denoised/resimulated references, and v2 adds NLL, C2ST diagnostics, and a 50-trial-per-method tuning protocol.

E4.justification: v2 adds systematic Ricker hyperparameter sensitivity analyses, t-SNE examinations of summary-space alignment, and real-data analyses of cleaning and prior–posterior convergence. Conversely, v1 Figures B6–B8, which directly measure approximation distances to the analytic posterior, are removed. The existing Gaussian domain and regularization analyses remain.

E5.justification: Gaussian reporting changes from averages over three runs to medians over ten runs, explicitly because extreme failures distort means. Ricker analyses introduce Gaussian-process trend estimates with 95% predictive intervals. Denoising retains its existing three-run mean and standard-deviation reporting.

E6.justification: New findings include Ricker calibration–error trade-offs and NNPE's advantage on misspecified human response times, where UDA provides no comparable benefit. Retained results also change: Table 1 reports likelihood-scale NPE-MMD NRMSE at lambda = 0.1 as 0.323 in v1 versus 0.189 in v2. These are replaced results under revised evaluation conditions, not a same-setting performance gain.

M1.justification: The NPE-MMD and NPE-DANN procedures, objectives in Equations 3–7, and gradient-reversal mechanism remain unchanged. Task-specific network configurations and hyperparameter exploration extend evaluation without introducing a new proposed method component.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is reorganized around four studies and three families of metrics.
