Appendix metric explanations gain corresponding subsections, retained results passages are rewritten, and the short conclusion becomes an extended Discussion covering mechanisms, regularization, practical measurement, and future work.

P2.justification: v2 adds a method schematic, hyperparameter-response plots, t-SNE panels, and empirical-data figures, while removing the direct analytic-posterior distance panels. Existing plots and tables are relocated and recaptioned, including switching the introductory scatterplot scenario. Typography, author layout, headings, and page composition are also substantially reformatted.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands the cited context to ecological dynamics and cognitive decision modeling, including Ricker, Wood, Greenwald, Ratcliff, and Project Implicit literature. It also adds UDA validation, recent SBI misspecification, and Bayesian model-comparison connections. Positioning against Huang and Swierc remains largely unchanged; Huang's year correction does not identify a new work.

The main theoretical content—the UDA bound, typical-set definition, posterior targets, objectives, and Appendix A definition of amortization—remains unchanged. No new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses substantial gaps in evidence for amortized generalization and practical robustness through unseen-image evaluation, larger posterior samples, systematic tuning analyses, and a real-data application exposing an important failure mode. Its discussion also qualifies the earlier diagnostic recommendation by recognizing the problem with noisy PPD references. These gains outweigh the loss of direct analytic-posterior distance plots, although omitted high-lambda results and inconsistent Gaussian budget reporting remain weaknesses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison, including matching the retained Gaussian and denoising experiments across renumbering.

after.justification: Sections 5.1–5.4 and Appendix B report original results for the retained benchmarks, Ricker-model hyperparameter exploration, and empirical human decision-making data.

before.justification: Sections 5.1–5.2 and Appendix B report original Gaussian inference and image-denoising experiments, including quantitative results and sensitivity analyses.

results.title: Does Unsupervised Domain Adaptation Improve the Robustness of Amortized Bayesian Inference? A Systematic Evaluation

Runtime scaling measurements and the weak-label comparison introduce additional procedures, including negative-learning loss and resampling partially labeled examples.

The error-rate optimization analysis was already in v1 Figure 10, while noise and class-imbalance tests are retained rather than newly introduced.

E6.justification: V2 adds Products-10K, RoBERTa-Large, weak-label, and runtime results; Table 3 reports total times of 2.31 minutes for CSQ+Cost(Ent) and 2.29 for CQ+Ent. BADGE cost-weighting changes from no improvement in v1 Appendix D to reported gains in v2. M1.justification: The two-stage query, conformal candidate construction, calibration procedure, error-rate optimization, and cost-weighted acquisition formula are retained. Expanded pseudocode and grid-search disclosure clarify the existing method; additional backbones and changed hyperparameter settings concern evaluation.

P1.justification: The overall section sequence and much of the prose remain. V2 rewrites selected method and analysis passages, promotes several appendix analyses into the experimental narrative, reorganizes appendices, and replaces the brief additional-experiments pointer with an in-depth analysis subsection. Journal front matter and acknowledgments are added, and the impact statement is removed.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from two-column preprint formatting to a single-column journal layout. Multiple figures are relocated or redrawn, axes and legends are revised, Table 2 expands across acquisition methods and rounds, and new runtime and experimental displays are added. Candidate examples gain explicit visual grouping, while v1's separate Figure 12 is omitted.

R1.justification: V2 adds a focused realistic-cost-model discussion citing Settles, Arora, Wallace, and Herde, alongside references for partial-label methods and new experimental components. The central positioning against n-ary queries and prior conformal-prediction work remains. Consolidated duplicate references do not represent removed research coverage.

T1.justification: Equation (7) changes the optimization domain from (0,1) to [0,1), formally admitting the conventional-query corner case already discussed in v1. This corrects a mathematical inconsistency without adding a new theorem. Theorem 3.1, its proof, and Appendix C's derivation remain substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the central efficiency claim. Runtime measurements address computational overhead left unmeasured in v1, and the weak-label comparison directly tests the value of follow-up queries. Products-10K experiments provide broader evidence for scalability and pretrained-model compatibility. These gains, together with clearer cost-model qualifications, outweigh the limited loss of detailed code-use guidance. The assessment does not depend on treating the revised headline percentage as a same-setting performance improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CSQ research. Their main text, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original classification experiments, ablations, noise and imbalance tests, and an annotation-time user study.

results.title: Enhancing Cost Efficiency in Active Learning with Candidate Set Query

C1.justification: The central framework and state-design contributions remain. v2 narrows v1's concluding claim of significant superiority for all weighted cost combinations to significant improvements for several trade-offs, and explicitly scopes the abstract's advantage to imbalanced/exponential costs. The state-design study becomes a separately enumerated contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive qualifications about approximately Markovian states, engineered-feature dependence, training overhead and inability to isolate RL from learning objectives and parameterization. Calimera+ and alternative-cost results refine explanations of the advantage and its boundaries. New sensitivity interpretations and nonstationarity discussion replace v1's concluding emphasis on reduced interpretability.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies the default discount factor of 1, ten confidence bins, uniform transition sampling, and settings for added classifier experiments. It reports computation times with five threads and changes the code-access reference from an anonymous repository to the author's GitHub repository. Most original architecture, optimizer and split details are retained.

E1.justification: Reported benchmark coverage contracts from 31 datasets—20 UCR and 11 Monash—in v1 Section 6.1 to 30—19 UCR and 11 Monash—in v2 Appendix A.1. The omitted UCR dataset is not identified. The additional sensitivity experiments retain these archive-based classification tasks.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's subsampled-series/noise augmentation and delayed-reward checks, v2 adds feature-removal ablations, full-series inputs, alternative rewards, discount/network sensitivity, encoding/classifier/sampling robustness and runtime analysis. The Calimera+ control examines feature-related explanations, while Appendix E adds selected-instance trigger-score and cost analyses at two sampling resolutions.

E5.justification: Both versions already use bootstrap intervals, Wilcoxon tests and Holm correction. v2 Figure 2 explicitly identifies the pairwise plots' bands and bars as 90% bootstrap intervals, previously unspecified for those plots, and Table 2 explains undefined p-values when all observations tie. Neither version specifies repeated-run or seed counts.

E6.justification: Figure 4's mean costs change, including Alert 6.70 to 6.92 and Calimera 7.97 to 8.22; the changed benchmark prevents interpreting these as same-setting deterioration. New findings include no significant separation under linear/balanced costs and improved Calimera+ rankings that generally remain below Alert+. Extensive sensitivity/runtime results are added, while v1's state-space p-value table is removed.

M1.justification: The default offline DDQN procedure, incremental-cost reward, five-feature state and model-selection strategy are retained; Alert★ becomes Alert+. Appendix D.2 adds optional reward objectives R2/R3 based on hindsight-optimal costs or triggering times, extending the framework's training variants.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Separate problem, information and literature sections become a consolidated background; the methodology gains dedicated pipeline, buffer, reward and training subsections. Dataset and implementation material moves to Appendix A, and the results narrative is reorganized around state design and comparison.

P2.justification: The paper changes from two-column to single-column presentation, redraws the pipeline diagram and removes v1's decision-boundary heatmaps. v1's main and appendix pairwise plots are merged into v2 Figure 2. New state-space/runtime tables and extensive sensitivity/case-study figures are added; the Pareto ordinate is corrected to one minus normalized misclassification cost.

R1.justification: The literature treatment is substantially refocused from v1's broad handcrafted/RL taxonomy, including shapelets and sequential-testing approaches, toward separable, classifier-agnostic triggering and prior RL reward designs. v2 adds offline-RL, imitation-learning and representation references and explicitly distinguishes Alert from classifier-dependent Earliest/SNP architectures.

T1.justification: v2 formally defines the new R2/R3 reward objectives and revises Calimera's stated cost difference from minFutureCost_t minus minFutureCost_(t+1) to minFutureCost_(t+1) minus Cost_t. Expanded standard DDQN equations explain the retained algorithm. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: The feature-matched Calimera+ control, alternative-cost evaluation and classifier/sampling robustness studies substantially strengthen evidence for the central contribution. The linear/balanced null result and explicit attribution caveats make v2's conclusions more defensible, while runtime measurements expose the training-cost trade-off. The unexplained benchmark reduction and removal of earlier state-space p-values weaken continuity, but the gains in controlled evidence and applicability assessment are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Alert research, with Alert★ renamed Alert+. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on 30 datasets, including retained comparisons and additional controls, sensitivity studies, runtime measurements and qualitative analyses in Section 5 and Appendices B–E.

before.justification: v1 reports original Alert experiments on 31 datasets, including baseline comparisons, state-space studies and delayed-reward experiments in Section 6 and Appendix A.

results.title: Alert: Learning Trigger Functions for Early Classification of Time Series using Deep-RL

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: model-agnostic interaction importance, distribution-free confidence intervals, efficient minipatch estimation, and higher-order extensions. The revised abstract's pairwise-first wording clarifies a scope already present in v1.

C2.justification: The central interpretation changes from isolating only a pairwise component to capturing all interaction terms containing that pair. Accordingly, v1 calls pair (1,2) null in the three-way scenario, whereas v2 interprets its detection as expected signal. v2 also removes the assertion that LOCO must be nonnegative and softens the claim of solving correlated-feature importance to a promising strategy.

D1.justification: Section 4.1 newly specifies cross-validation for selecting fixed hyperparameters, use of baseline implementations as supplied, and ReLU/hidden-layer details for MLPs. It also clarifies KRBF as an RBF-kernel support-vector model. These improve implementation disclosure without establishing changes to previously unspecified settings; hardware and dataset-source information largely remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the synthetic regression/classification families and the two real-data tasks. v2 adds detection under extreme feature correlation of 0.99, beyond v1's 0.3 and 0.9 scenarios (Figures 1B and A1B). The reduced cocktail sample and feature counts do not establish a new domain or task.

E2.justification: Table A1 newly compares FaithSHAP with iLOCO-MP on Car Evaluation. Conversely, the scenario (iii) panels comparing H-Statistic, FaithSHAP, and Iterative Forest disappear from the comparative simulation figures. These baseline methods remain in scenarios (i) and (ii); their renamed legends do not represent new methods.

E3.justification: New Figure 1A introduces N=10,000, M=10/100/500, 200,000 minipatches, and a three-hidden-layer MLP. The cocktail study changes from 15,972 records and 200 ingredients with a kernel regressor and 30,000 minipatches to 5,934 records and 100 ingredients with a three-hidden-layer MLP and 20,000 minipatches. The appendix also revises the stated autoregressive parameter from 0.9 to 0.8; this documents a setting change without establishing that retained curves were rerun.

E4.justification: Figures 1A and A1A substantially expand validation by comparing second- and third-order iLOCO across feature dimensionalities, replacing the earlier isolated third-order demonstration. Correlation-sensitivity analysis also expands. However, v1's minipatch-size sensitivity comparison (Figure A6) and raw-score-versus-SNR diagnostic (Figure A7) are removed.

E5.justification: Section 4.2 and Figure 4 change from marginal intervals described as controlling false coverage rate to reported Bonferroni-adjusted intervals, retaining alpha=0.1. Both versions specify 50 replicates for coverage studies. v2 no longer states v1's 20-replicate count for detection curves; this is reduced reporting, not evidence that fewer runs were performed.

E6.justification: v2 adds dimensionality-dependent second-/third-order detection results and Car Evaluation rankings, while removing scenario (iii) baseline results and two diagnostics. Cocktail results are replaced under changed data/model settings: Figure 4 now highlights pairings such as Lime Juice–Rum rather than Triple sec–Agave syrup. Table 1 changes FaithSHAP's two largest-setting entries from '>6 days' to 'Not Supported'; these are not measured runtime improvements.

M1.justification: Section 2.4 changes the generalized score's coefficients from (-1)^(|S|-|T|) to (-1)^(|T|+1), excluding the empty subset. This corrects the sign for even-order interactions and makes the general formula agree with the retained pairwise definition. The pairwise score and Split/MP estimation algorithms otherwise remain substantively unchanged.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, metric explanation, and empirical narrative undergo extensive rewriting. Section 4.1 now presents metric validation before comparative evaluation, with clearer inference-target explanations elsewhere. The former Appendices D–F are consolidated into a unified theoretical appendix, and supplementary empirical material is reorganized from Appendix G into Appendix E.

P2.justification: The figure presentation is substantially redesigned: expanded validation becomes Figure 1, comparison grids lose their scenario (iii) rows, and coverage plots receive revised markers, legends, and ticks. Figure 4 replaces crowded vertical plots with two horizontal 15-interaction displays. Appendix figures are reorganized, two diagnostics disappear, and Table A1 is added.

R1.justification: The introduction and related work substantially broaden positioning through epistasis applications, functional ANOVA foundations, additional LOCO/inference literature, and named interaction approaches including Integrated Hessians, regression-based methods, local attribution, and SPEX for LLMs. This replaces the earlier shorter, more generic treatment and adds distinctions between model-specific, local, and model-agnostic interaction methods.

T1.justification: Proposition 1 replaces v1's claim that population iLOCO equals the isolated interaction function with expected squared contributions from all terms containing the selected pair, using MSE for regression and absolute error for Bernoulli classification. Appendix D replaces the earlier separate derivations with an arbitrary-order Proposition 2, independent-feature sufficient conditions in Proposition 3, and inclusion-exclusion proofs. The higher-order sign correction and clarified minipatch inference target further revise the mathematical account.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves the central theoretical and empirical coherence: Proposition 1 and Appendix D replace the isolated-component argument with explicit variance-contribution results and general proofs, while the simulations' interpretation now acknowledges higher-order contributions to pairwise scores. Clearer inference targets and reported Bonferroni adjustment also strengthen the presentation of inference. Removing the minipatch sensitivity study, omitting the detection replicate count, and leaving a sign inconsistency in Appendix D's pairwise example are drawbacks, but they do not outweigh the correction of the central interpretation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same iLOCO research, with matching authors, methods, and applications. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical studies and reports revised interaction-validation experiments, cocktail analyses, and a new Car Evaluation ranking comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original interaction-detection simulations, confidence-interval coverage studies, computational timings, and analyses of Car Evaluation and Cocktail Recipe data.

results.title: iLOCO: Distribution-Free Inference for Feature Interactions

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: connecting RMDS to Bayesian nonparametric inference, introducing hierarchical covariance models including the coupled-diagonal model, and identifying regimes where these improve OOD detection. The additional evidence does not redefine those claims.

Section 4 newly interprets the log K gap as aggregation across plausible clusters, and Appendix D discusses computational tradeoffs. The existing Gaussian-assumption and overfitting limitations remain substantially unchanged.

D1.justification: V2 documents the CIFAR feature source and dimensions, dataset-specific tied-model prior choices, typical convergence in about ten EM iterations, and the provenance and inherited classifier accuracies of leaderboard comparisons. E1.justification: V2 expands beyond synthetic data and ImageNet-1K to CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 as in-distribution tasks. Appendices K-L evaluate reciprocal CIFAR and Tiny ImageNet near-OOD scenarios, plus MNIST, Places365, SVHN and Textures far-OOD scenarios. The original coverage is retained.

V2 specifies covariance of class means for the tied model's CIFAR prior, versus data covariance for ImageNet, and evaluates raw versus whitened/rotated CIFAR features. These extend experimental settings; retained ImageNet protocols, synthetic settings and accuracy/AUROC metrics remain unchanged.

Appendix M adds Independent RMDS to the ImageNet dimensionality sweep, directly testing independent covariance estimation against hierarchical sharing in high dimensions. The original ImageNet preprocessing ablation, synthetic sweeps and score-correlation analysis are retained.

E5.justification: V2 introduces parenthesized variability estimates throughout the CIFAR tables. Table 4 explicitly identifies standard deviations across three ResNet18 training runs with different seeds; Table 6 also reports parenthesized variability. V1 provides no corresponding seed or uncertainty reporting. This does not establish additional runs for the retained ImageNet results.

E6.justification: The original ImageNet results remain numerically unchanged in v2 Tables 2-3, including coupled-diagonal near-OOD AUROC 80.98 and tied-model far-OOD AUROC 92.70. New CIFAR-10 results give the full model 90.63/93.50 near/far AUROC versus RMDS 89.83/92.42 under W&R preprocessing. CIFAR-100 instead shows coupled-diagonal performance below RMDS. Added leaderboard entries and Figure 7's high-dimensional Independent RMDS collapse further expand the findings.

M1.justification: The tied, full, diagonal and coupled-diagonal Gaussian DPMMs retain their priors, scoring procedures, EM estimation and numerical integration. The whitening/rotation procedure is also unchanged. New experimental configurations do not introduce a new method component.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main section sequence are retained. Changes include localized explanations and rewrites, renamed and expanded experimental appendices, revised cross-references, an added author and updated acknowledgments. These do not amount to a wholesale narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a different journal layout and title/author presentation. Table 1 becomes a three-benchmark summary, while the original ImageNet table moves to Appendix J as Table 3. The revision expands comparison tables, adds CIFAR Tables 4-7, introduces a preprocessing flowchart and an additional dimensionality figure, and relabels the retained correlation plot.

R1.justification: V2 adds references supporting CIFAR/ResNet experiments, ASH, ReAct, SCALE, ReweightOOD and the expanded mathematical argument. Related work more explicitly states the post-hoc scope. The positioning relative to RMDS and earlier Bayesian nonparametric approaches remains stable; the author-year citation conversion is stylistic.

T1.justification: V1's heuristic Proposition 2 is replaced by Proposition 4.2 with explicit sub-Gaussian assumptions, a relative-covariance operator norm and a high-probability delta + log K bound. V2 adds an extended proof in Appendix E and computational complexity analysis in Appendix D. The proposition uses (C-d)/2, but the appendix conclusion inconsistently retains C/2-d.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the empirical basis for judging when the models help. CIFAR/ResNet18 evaluations, preprocessing controls, seed variability and the real-data Independent RMDS comparison address v1's reliance on one real-data benchmark and backbone, revealing both benefits and failures. The explicit theoretical bound and cost discussion add useful specificity, although Appendix E's inconsistent constant scaling still requires correction. The broader, more diagnostic evidence provides a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds CIFAR-10/100 evaluations and further analyses. These are distinct from the additional baseline scores explicitly attributed to the OpenOOD leaderboard.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic simulations, ImageNet/OpenOOD evaluations, covariance analyses, dimensionality experiments and preprocessing ablations.

results.title: A Bayesian Nonparametric Perspective on Mahalanobis Distance for Out of Distribution Detection

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction describe the 24-fold saving more precisely as a pretraining-instance budget reduction, explicitly comparing 10M with 240M instances, rather than broadly equating it with computational cost. The central claims that aligned dataset selection can outperform mixtures and that misaligned additions can harm performance are retained.

C2.justification: v2 interprets alignment as transferable across backbone types and supervised/denoising objectives, and adds an effective-rank explanation for information loss through pooling. Section 5 changes the ID/OOD distinction from domain-or-label differences to target-property differences. Appendix B documents feature-extractor-dependent QM9 ranking exceptions, while Appendix A softens the earlier blanket assertion that additional epochs cannot compensate for fewer samples on misaligned datasets.

D1.justification: Appendix D newly specifies the classes used for balanced sampling: molecular formulas for ANI-1x/Transition-1x and bulk structures for OC20/OC22, with equal sampling per class. Table 3 adds configuration-specific A100 GPU-day measurements. Existing GemNet batch sizes, learning rates, checkpoint selection, validation-subset size, and code-access information remain essentially unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds inorganic-material force prediction on OMat24's rattled-300-subsampled split, extending the energy/force evaluations beyond the earlier molecular targets. It also adds a denoising pretraining task on the existing upstream data. The four upstream datasets and earlier molecular and OOD benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: v2 Table 2 adds budget-matched Joint (Balanced) and Joint (Temperature) comparators to the large GemNet-OC-L experiment; these were absent from v1 Table 3. The original JMP references and small-backbone comparator membership are retained. Changing 'Mixed' to 'Joint' is a rename.

E3.justification: v2 adds a 0.5M-sample point to the budget sweep, evaluates 31M- and 87M-parameter EquiformerV2 configurations, and introduces a paired effective-rank protocol using 5k, 10k, and 15k graphs with standardized node-level and pooled features (Appendix C). The original main budget of 2M samples over five epochs and existing GemNet settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds backbone-type and pretraining-objective analyses, replaces the single alternative JMP feature-extractor check with a multi-checkpoint EquiformerV2 study, and adds effective-rank evidence about pooling. v1's random-sampling CSI plot and JMP-extractor plot are removed. Appendix C also introduces a ten-repeat bootstrap procedure reporting mean effective ranks. These are substantial additions to statistical reporting; v1 does not specify a previous seed count from which an increase could be established.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces earlier scores with multi-seed estimates: ANI-1x changes from 5.4 to 5.2 ± 0.2 on rMD17, 5.13 to 5.39 ± 0.26 on SPICE, and 2.9 to 3.1 ± 0.1 on QM9. The OOD and epoch-versus-data tables retain their numerical results.

M1.justification: v1 trains GemNet-OC models using energy/force supervision. v2 additionally trains EquiformerV2 backbones and introduces a DeNS denoising-pretraining variant using noisy atomic coordinates (Sections 4.4 and 4.6). These substantially expand the model and training-objective variants, while the central CSI-based dataset-selection procedure remains intact.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled around pretraining alignment, with substantial rewrites of related work, experimental explanations, and takeaways. CSI design discussion moves from Section 3.2 into reorganized appendices devoted to feature extractors, representations, and class balancing. Terminology is revised throughout, including 'relevance' toward 'alignment' and 'mixed' toward 'joint' pretraining.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one column, and figures and tables are extensively reformatted. The budget table becomes a multi-panel curve figure, Figure 1 changes from a grid to a horizontal arrangement, and Table 1 gains an OMat24 column and uncertainty entries. New architecture/objective tables and appendix plots accompany removal or replacement of earlier metric-design displays.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds substantial distribution-similarity positioning, including KL, JS, MMD, Fréchet ChemNet Distance, and GuacaMol. It explicitly distinguishes CSI's 3D cross-domain alignment purpose from earlier chemistry applications of FID. The pretraining discussion also develops distinctions between 2D, equilibrium-focused, and non-equilibrium methods, including DeNS.

T1.justification: The formal optimization equations, computational-budget definition, and Fréchet-distance formulation are substantively unchanged. Appendix C states the standard entropy-based effective-rank formula for an empirical diagnostic; it does not introduce a new theoretical result, proof, or derivation.

improvement.justification: v1's central evidence relied on one trained backbone family and molecular ID tasks that all favored ANI-1x. v2 meaningfully tests dataset selection through OMat24, where OC20 wins, and extends validation to EquiformerV2 and denoising pretraining. Three-seed uncertainty reporting, stronger representation analyses, and discussion of closely related chemical-distance metrics substantially improve credibility and positioning. Some earlier metric ablations disappear, and Appendix A retains errors such as calling 5.4 better than 5.1, but the overall evidential gains are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CSI-based pretraining dataset-selection study, despite the changed title and formatting. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds OMat24 evaluation, EquiformerV2 and denoising-pretraining results, and feature-representation analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original pretraining and fine-tuning experiments in Tables 1–5, alongside CSI, sampling, and representation analyses.

results.title: On the Importance of Pretraining Data Alignment for Atomic Property Prediction

C1.justification: The central claims that no model consistently dominates and that benchmarking needs greater rigor are retained. The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion now explicitly restrict these claims to supervised LTSF, with foundation models excluded from the empirical claim's scope.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning insufficient benchmark diversity, computational costs of architectural complexity, and simple baselines' competitiveness on Exchange. Section 6 adds concrete limitations concerning fixed horizons across domains, sensitivity to implementation and search choices, and the exclusion of foundation models. These extend v1's shorter alternative-view discussion.

D1.justification: v2 replaces the promise of a future code release with a stated repository location. It documents additional baseline settings, iPatch decoder details, and the efficiency-profiling procedure and hardware, including an RTX 4090 and AMD EPYC processor. Most original preprocessing and HP-search information is retained or relocated.

E1.justification: Forecasting coverage remains the same 14 datasets across five domains, with horizons 96, 192, 336, and 720. The benchmark-diversity audit and synthetic-input efficiency profiling do not add forecasting datasets or task requirements.

E2.justification: S-Mamba, xLSTMTime, and ModernTCN join the main comparison and the comparison with iPatch. Appendix H adds ARIMA and LOCF, labeled CLOF in Tables 12–13. The ranking-sensitivity comparisons also include TimeMixer, which was absent from v1's corresponding exclusion plots.

E3.justification: v2 replaces selected dataset/horizon exclusions with 5,000 uniformly sampled subset configurations. It introduces efficiency metrics and a composite score, with profiling over 1,000 synthetic-input iterations at batch size one. New baseline settings include MAE loss for xLSTMTime and a separate ModernTCN width grid. The original models' 40-trial search budget and documented grids are retained.

E4.justification: The limited exclusion examples in v1 Sections 4.1–4.2 become a systematic ranking-sensitivity analysis in v2 Section 4.1. v2 also adds an audit of benchmark diversity by domain, sampling frequency, and variate count, plus performance–efficiency analyses with and without MotorImagery. The earlier dataset-pattern, PCA, and HP-search stability analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v2 adds score distributions and plus/minus summaries across sampled benchmark configurations. It replaces v1's all-pairs sign-test reporting with a focused iPatch–iTransformer comparison and explicitly reports the expanded Friedman comparison for MAE. Three final training seeds, the two-search stability check, and the underlying Friedman/sign-test procedures remain unchanged.

E6.justification: New baselines and efficiency measurements substantially expand the results. Existing scores also change: in Table 2, TimeMixer's horizon-averaged Exchange MSE changes from 33705.21 to 0.550, and PatchTST's BeijingAir MSE from 0.8643 to 0.578. iPatch's Exchange results are revised in Appendix H. These are revised reports, with their causes undocumented, rather than established same-setting performance gains. The expanded comparison also changes aggregate rankings and Friedman results.

M1.justification: iPatch retains cycle-based patching, successive variate and temporal attention, and the same MLP ordering (v1 Section 5.2; v2 Section 4.5). The added output-reshaping and channel-wise decoder description documents the existing architecture without establishing an algorithmic change.

P1.justification: The narrative is extensively reorganized and rewritten. Dataset-guided model selection moves from v1 Section 6 into v2 Section 3; the statistical-testing and iPatch material moves into Section 4.5; HP details are consolidated in Appendix C. Recommendations and limitations become substantially revised dedicated sections.

P2.justification: The two-column conference presentation becomes a predominantly single-column journal layout. New benchmark-diversity and ranking-distribution figures accompany expanded radar and violin plots. Tables are restructured, mean and minimum full results are separated, efficiency tables are added, and the old pairwise-win matrix is removed. Boxed model summaries and recommendations further change the presentation.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands its positioning as independent confirmatory research, adding literature on unreliable benchmarking across machine-learning fields. It incorporates GIFT-Eval, additional architecture families, and more extensive discussion of foundation-model and LLM forecasting limitations. These are substantive additions beyond bibliographic publication updates.

T1.justification: Section 4.6 introduces the mathematical definition of the composite efficiency-weighted score ξ, including baseline normalization, metric directionality, weighting, and calibration reasoning. The existing iPatch mathematics, dataset-statistic definitions, and statistical-test formulas remain substantively unchanged; no new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence behind the benchmarking critique: broader architectural and simple-baseline comparisons address v1's restricted comparator coverage, while 5,000 sampled configurations replace a few selected exclusion examples. Section 4.6 and Appendix I quantify computational trade-offs that v1 explicitly left outside scope. Clearer applicability limits and code-access information also improve the paper. Unexplained score revisions and substantial reproduction gaps for ModernTCN and xLSTMTime in Table 9 remain weaknesses, but the broader, more diagnostic evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same benchmarking study and retain the iPatch example. All 20 pages of v1 and 29 pages of v2, including appendices, provide readable text, tables, figures, and equations sufficient for comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original forecasting experiments and adds evaluated baselines, randomized ranking-sensitivity analysis, and computational-efficiency measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original forecasting experiments across 14 datasets, hyperparameter-search stability experiments, and evaluations of iPatch, including detailed results in Appendix H.

results.title: There are no Champions in Supervised Long-Term Time Series Forecasting

C1.justification: The central contributions remain LuCA, sparse final-CLS adaptation through TOSCA, the stability–plasticity argument, and the headline accuracy and efficiency advantages. The continual-post-training framing and additional evidence do not materially redefine these scientific claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations connecting sparsity to reduced feature overlap and explaining why adaptation before calibration improves class geometry. It interprets task-wise and EuroSAT findings as evidence of plasticity and robustness. Appendix A.2 newly discusses lower IN1K average accuracies as an efficiency–adaptability tradeoff; dependence on pretrained-model generalization was already acknowledged in v1.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a code-repository link, explicitly identifies sigmoid calibration, and clarifies classifier optimization in Algorithm 1. Hardware and principal hyperparameters are retained. Conversely, it omits v1's explicit class-shuffling seed and statement that all methods use identical training/testing splits.

E1.justification: v2 adds a dedicated EuroSAT satellite-imagery classification scenario with ten classes, extending evaluation to an explicitly different image domain while retaining the six original benchmarks. Table 3 and Figure 5 report this additional coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 1 and A add RanPAC across all six retained benchmarks and HiDePrompt on CIFAR, CUB and ImageNet-R with both backbones. Both also enter the runtime comparison. RanPAC was cited but not evaluated in v1; HiDePrompt is not evaluated on the other benchmark columns, which contain dashes.

E3.justification: v2 adds per-task accuracy evaluation, module-selection accuracy against ground-truth task identities, cosine-similarity comparisons and feature-separation diagnostics. EuroSAT uses B0 Inc2. Existing backbone choices, training budgets and hyperparameters remain unchanged. The stated VTAB class count changes from 100 to 50, matching v1's plotted range without establishing that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds direct investigations of single-token plasticity, satellite-domain robustness, module decorrelation under different regularization strengths, feature geometry and entropy-based routing reliability (Tables 2, 3 and B; Figures 5–7). The original hyperparameter and component-order ablations remain; LuCA_r becoming TOSCA_r is a rename.

E5.justification: Both versions state five random-seed runs and retain mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting in the main benchmark tables. However, v2 removes v1's explicit class-order seed of 1993. There is no documented increase in repeated runs or addition of confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include CUB task-wise average accuracy of 97.6% and EuroSAT task-wise average accuracy of 99.3% for TOSCA, alongside new baseline and diagnostic results. Retained TOSCA entries also change: ImageNet-R/IN21K final accuracy is revised from 78.28 to 79.28 in Table 1, and OmniBenchmark/IN1K from 78.65 to 79.65 in Table A. Other shared table entries remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Both versions use an adapter followed by a calibrator, one sparse module per task on the final CLS representation, a frozen backbone, cross-entropy plus l1 regularization, and entropy-based module selection. Expanded inference explanations and more explicit pseudocode do not establish a changed procedure.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, methodology discussion and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Neuroscience motivation moves into the introduction, theoretical underpinnings move to Appendix A.1, terminology changes throughout, and the experimental narrative is reorganized into more focused subsections, including a separate discussion of the existing joint-training comparison.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 2, 3 and B and Figures 5–7, expands existing benchmark tables and plots with additional comparators, and revises legends and captions. The LuCA diagram is redrawn, and the document adopts journal typography, headers and wider layouts. These are substantial display changes beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: v2 adds HiDePrompt, EuroSAT and two sparse/online continual-learning references, and expands discussion of the already-cited RanPAC. It removes the squeeze-and-excitation analogy and citation, plus references to NISPA and continual prune-and-select. Positioning shifts toward foundation-model continual post-training while most related-work coverage remains.

T1.justification: The background prompt objective in Equation (2) changes its optimization variables from prompts, keys and the feature extractor to prompts, keys and classifier W, correcting its inconsistency with the frozen-backbone description. TOSCA's theoretical statements and Equations (10)–(11) are retained in Appendix A.1; no new proof is added.

improvement.justification: v1 mainly supported its orthogonality, routing and single-token plasticity claims through aggregate accuracy and basic ablations. v2 directly investigates these properties through task-wise results, representation analyses and Appendix Table B, while adding a dedicated satellite-domain test and stronger comparator coverage. This substantially strengthens empirical scrutiny of the central design. Some formalization and experimental-detail gaps remain, and the class-order seed disclosure is lost, but these limitations do not outweigh the targeted evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LuCA/TOSCA research despite the changed title and publication format. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable matching.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds EuroSAT evaluation, task-wise accuracy, representation analyses and module-selection measurements in the main text and appendix.

before.justification: v1 reports original six-benchmark experiments, runtime and parameter comparisons, and component and hyperparameter ablations, including additional results in Appendix A.2.

results.title: Unlocking [CLS] Features for Continual Post-Training

C1.justification: V1's abstract and conclusion emphasize inherent adversarial robustness without robust training. V3 reframes the contribution as a security analysis, narrows the abstract's robustness claim to standard white-box attacks, attributes the behavior to gradient obfuscation, and makes vulnerability under alternative attacks an explicit contribution.

C2.justification: V1 already discusses attenuation and vanishing gradients, but v3 interprets the new attack failures as evidence of gradient masking rather than general security. It adds a spectral-bias/low-pass scrubbing hypothesis and explains implicit differentiation's fixed-point versus finite-trajectory mismatch. Applicability limitations are revised, while the conclusion's explicit clean-accuracy tradeoff is dropped.

D1.justification: V3 replaces the promise of future code release with a repository location and an availability statement. It newly documents L2 gradient clipping at 1, damped inverse-Hessian calculations, and classifier depths in the runtime discussion. These are additional disclosures; the PDFs do not establish that the retained experiments changed accordingly.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and voxelized ModelNet10 classification under the same image and voxel perturbation domains. AutoAttack and BPDA extend testing on existing data without introducing new datasets, populations, modalities or task requirements.

E2.justification: V3 adds AutoAttack to the MNIST/Fashion-MNIST accuracy comparison in Table 1 and evaluates BPDA in Table 2. Table 3 also compares AutoAttack component timings with the proposed attacks. The existing ViT, CNN, autoencoder and voxel-classifier baselines remain.

E3.justification: V3 extends the evaluation design with BPDA's identity approximation for the backward derivative of the INR optimization mapping and sequential AutoAttack testing. Section 4.5 introduces cumulative component-runtime comparisons against 100-step suite attacks. These are new testing procedures; the previously stated training, preprocessing and perturbation-budget settings are retained.

E4.justification: Section 4.4.2 adds a diagnostic BPDA experiment testing whether apparent robustness survives bypassing gradient masking. Section 4.5 adds a detailed AutoAttack efficiency comparison. The existing activation-amplification, attack-bound sensitivity and latent-space analyses remain; moving Figure 6 into the main text does not constitute a new analysis.

E5.justification: V3 specifies five random restarts for the new BPDA evaluation, adding randomized repetition information absent from v1. These are attack restarts, not reported independent training runs or uncertainty estimates. No new confidence intervals or significance tests are introduced, and the existing shaded amplification plots are retained.

E6.justification: The original Table 1 scores and ModelNet10 table values are unchanged. New results include AutoAttack accuracies of 0.44 and 0.05, and BPDA accuracies of 0.076 and 0.159, for MNIST and Fashion-MNIST respectively at a 32/256 bound, plus Table 3 timings. V1 Appendix B.1.1's autoencoder accuracies of 98.8% clean and 11.28% robust are omitted.

M1.justification: The five original attacks—Full PGD, TMO, BOTTOM, ICOP and implicit differentiation—and BVA are retained. Expanded threat-model explanations and newly disclosed implementation details do not establish procedural changes to these methods. AutoAttack and BPDA enter as additional evaluations; the implicit-gradient formula correction is addressed under T1.

P1.justification: V3 retitles the paper and extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, implicit-differentiation explanation and discussion. It introduces dedicated threat-model and mechanism sections, consolidates the conclusion and limitations, and relocates much of the computational analysis to Appendix C. These constitute substantial narrative and structural revisions.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, with widespread figure resizing and relocation. Figure 1 replaces duplicated parameter-space panels with the intended parameter-versus-signal-space comparison. Table 1 gains AutoAttack columns, new BPDA and runtime tables appear, and Figure 6 moves from the appendix into the main text. Figures 2–10 otherwise retain their graphical content.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially beyond weight-space learning to gradient obfuscation, equilibrium models and adversarial purification. V3 positions the work against Athalye et al., Yang et al., DiffPure and robustness-trained INRs from Luo et al., while adding AutoAttack references and newer neural-functional learning work. This materially changes the security context and novelty positioning.

T1.justification: V3 Section 3.4.5 adds a Taylor-expansion derivation and an explicit Hessian-invertibility assumption. Equation 5 corrects the inverse-Hessian and mixed-derivative multiplication order shown in v1 Equation 3. This is a localized mathematical correction and expansion of the existing implicit-differentiation analysis; Section 4.4 supplies empirical reasoning rather than a new robustness theorem.

improvement.justification: V1's central robustness claim relied on its proposed attack suite. V3 adds AutoAttack and especially BPDA results exposing severe vulnerabilities, then narrows the abstract's claim and explicitly identifies gradient masking. This substantially improves the evidence underlying the paper's central security assessment, supported by the corrected derivation and additional reproducibility information. The discussion still mislabels BPDA as gradient-free despite defining a gradient approximation, and retains some overbroad robustness wording, so the improvement does not resolve every interpretive problem.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same INR classifier attack study despite the changed title and format. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V3 retains the original empirical results and adds AutoAttack accuracy, BPDA robustness and comparative runtime measurements in Tables 1–3.

before.justification: V1 reports original adversarial classification experiments on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and ModelNet10, activation and latent-space analyses, and computational measurements in Section 4 and the appendices.

results.title: Adversarial Attacks in Weight-Space Classifiers

C1.justification: v1 principally claims a framework and four datasets suitable for mathematical language-model training. v2 adds claims of state-of-the-art mathematical retrieval performance and demonstrated benefits even for previously mathematically pretrained BERT models, alongside pretrained-model releases.

C2.justification: Sections 7–9 and Appendix C add interpretations of complementary pretraining benefits and challenging-negative effects, while acknowledging the advantage of task-related pretraining. Beyond v1's parsing caveats, v2 discusses unsupported notations, LaTeX-only applicability, possible incorrect falsifications and the need for systematic output-error analysis.

D1.justification: Appendix C adds software versions, hyperparameters, eight-A100 hardware, training-time estimates, checkpoint identifiers, and training/evaluation code locations. Appendix B.1 newly specifies SymPy filtering calls. An MT upvote criterion is also newly documented, although Sections 6 and 8.2 inconsistently apply it to answers versus questions; the PDFs do not establish that the existing datasets were regenerated.

E1.justification: Using the retained MF, MT, NMF and MFR datasets, v2 adds actual training on masked-token and formula-pair tasks and evaluation of name-to-formula and formula-to-formula retrieval. v1 reports dataset generation and corpus analysis, with these learning applications only proposed. The source corpora and 71-identity collection remain unchanged.

E2.justification: v1 contains no model-baseline experiment. v2 evaluates BERT, MathBERT from Shen et al. (2021), and MPBERT against MAMUT-pretrained variants in Table 6, with checkpoints identified in Table 16. Table 21 additionally compares MPBERT variants using random or fixed negative examples.

E3.justification: v2 introduces retrieval protocols with 250 positive examples per identity, ten times as many negatives, ten-epoch fine-tuning, validation-F1 model selection, and classification and ranking metrics. It adds MLM-only pretraining controls and an NMF-Split evaluation using 49/11/11 training/validation/test identities with a frozen encoder. These are new experimental designs, not revisions to v1 model experiments.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained NMF generation analysis, Appendix C.4 adds evaluations by falsification count, substitution type, text versus formula input, and mathematical identity. It also tests challenging versus random negatives, changing versus fixed negatives, and generalization across identities excluded from fine-tuning.

E5.justification: v2 newly reports averaging five fine-tuning runs with different seeds and using different identity partitions across the five NMF-Split runs. This adds repeated-run reporting, but no standard deviations, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: The original dataset counts and Figure 5 findings are retained, while extensive model results are added. In v2 Table 6, MAMUT-MPBERT-MLM achieves NMF-FT/MFR-FT F1 scores of 87.6/80.6, compared with MPBERT's 79.9/74.0. Table 21 reports NMF-FT F1 of 79.9 with changing challenging negatives, 24.6 with random negatives and 74.4 with fixed challenging negatives. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over v1 scores.

M1.justification: EquVG and FalseVG remain substantively unchanged, but Appendix C.1 introduces a substantial model-training extension: mixed MLM/NSP training, mathematics-aware masking for MT, and 300 additional mathematical tokens for BERT. These implemented training components go beyond v1's suggestions of possible dataset uses.

P1.justification: Existing sections retain their order and mostly their wording, with localized copyediting, acronym expansions, explanatory additions and publication-header updates. The new material receives separate Experiments, Discussion, Limitations and Appendix C sections; the retained narrative is not extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v2 adds results and supporting tables, pretraining and tokenization diagrams, and a per-identity performance plot (Table 6, Tables 16–22 and Figures 6–8). Existing workflow diagrams gain icons and colored symbol highlighting. Earlier example tables and Figure 5 are retained, with renumbering and relocation distinguished from new displays.

R1.justification: The related-work narrative largely remains intact. v2 adds Shen et al.'s distinct MathBERT work while retaining Peng et al., connects substitution to alpha-conversion through Nederpelt and Geuvers, and adds supporting training and retrieval references. Section 8 further explains how notation diversity complements existing datasets' problem diversity.

T1.justification: No substantive theorem, proof, formal assumption or derivation is added or revised. The alpha-conversion connection is conceptual explanation, and Appendix C.3 supplies standard evaluation-metric formulas rather than new theoretical results.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's lack of downstream validation through model comparisons, MLM-only controls and challenging-negative ablations, while adding reproducibility information and explicit limitations. Evidence remains confined to generated retrieval tasks, and reporting defects remain: Table 20's MathBERT difference is inconsistent with its displayed accuracies, and Figure 8 retains an unfinished caption. These defects limit confidence in particular details but do not outweigh the substantial gain in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MAMUT framework and generated datasets. The main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial additions in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains those analyses and adds original model-training and retrieval results in Section 7, with ablations and further evaluations in Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original dataset-generation statistics in Table 5 and empirical analysis of falsification strategies and symbol substitutions in Appendix B.3 and Figure 5.

results.title: MAMUT: A Novel Framework for Modifying Mathematical Formulas for the Generation of Specialized Datasets for Language Model Training

C1.justification: v1 centers its contribution on the first competitive pure Transformer architecture. v2 reframes the contribution as two Transformer-centric families, makes iterative tokenization a principal contribution, and explicitly claims PrimusV2 reaches parity with stronger CNNs including ResEnc-L and MedNeXt.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly defends beneficial CNN–Transformer combinations, explains the stronger tokenizer's role, and acknowledges increased convolutional dependence and token-overlap risks for masked pretraining. It also qualifies retained ablations with a RoPE-error disclosure and adds clinical-applicability arguments from timing. Section 2.2 becomes more categorical about stable performance gaps excluding data scarcity as the limitation.

D1.justification: v2 specifies the new tokenizer's kernels, strides, channels, and residual-block arrangements, plus timing hardware and crop settings. Tables 12–14 newly disclose a legacy 3D RoPE permutation error. The code pointer changes from an author-hosted Primus branch to the nnU-Net project's Primus documentation; existing training hyperparameters and preprocessing tables are largely retained.

E1.justification: The same nine development/test datasets and the AMOS-CT, KiTS19, and TotalSegmentator-BTCV diagnostic coverage are retained. Appendix F measures random-crop runtime and extrapolates to illustrative clinical volumes; it does not evaluate additional clinical datasets or segmentation tasks.

E2.justification: The main benchmark expands from six comparison methods in v1 Table 6 to eleven in v2 Table 7. MedNeXt-L, UNETR++, SwinUNETR-v2, SegMamba, and VisionxLSTM are newly evaluated, substantially strengthening comparison across CNN, Transformer, state-space, and recurrent architectures.

E3.justification: The core cross-validation splits, preprocessing plans, and training budgets remain unchanged. v2 adds controlled tokenizer comparisons, memory measurements at 50% and 80% masking, and encoder timing using 160-cubed crops with batch size one, excluding preprocessing. The main benchmark now restricts L configurations to development datasets.

E4.justification: New tokenizer ablations compare four alternatives with and without Transformers, testing the tradeoff between accuracy and Transformer dependence (Table 6). v2 also extends dataset-size analysis to Primus-L, adds qualitative segmentation examples, and investigates memory and inference-time feasibility. The earlier Appendix C and E analyses largely remain.

E5.justification: Appendix F newly reports runtime estimation using the median of 100 forward passes. Existing three-seed introspection and CKA comparison procedures are retained; no increase in training repetitions or new segmentation confidence intervals is reported.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive PrimusV2 and baseline results: Table 7 reports average DSC of 81.43 for PrimusV2-M, 81.48 for ResEnc-L, and 81.72 for MedNeXt-L. Original Primus scores are also revised, and its L-model test-set averages are omitted while fold-0 appendix results remain. Table 13 replaces the unfinished KiTS23 Primus-L/4 entry with 84.79. Memory and runtime results are newly reported.

M1.justification: v2 introduces PrimusV2 alongside Primus. Its iterative tokenizer replaces the single patch projection with convolutional residual downsampling, creating overlapping, more expressive tokens before the Transformer. This changes a central architectural component rather than merely documenting the original model more fully (Sections 3.2–3.4).

P1.justification: Substantial portions of the introduction, diagnostic discussion, method description, and conclusions are rewritten. Method subsections are consolidated, the narrative is reorganized around Primus and PrimusV2, and Appendices F and G are added. These changes exceed routine wording edits.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a single-column journal layout, transposes and expands Table 1, redraws the architecture diagram, expands the benchmark table, and adds tokenizer and timing tables plus qualitative Figure 4. Figure 2 gains a Primus-L panel. The smaller-token results remain in Appendix C despite removal of their separate main-text summary table.

R1.justification: Appendix B's historical review is largely retained. v2 extends positioning to state-space and xLSTM competitors and adds references including UNETR++, DINOv3, V-JEPA, Chameleon, and clinical-timing work. Purity-based novelty is qualified as Transformer-centric design, while the central research motivation remains.

T1.justification: Appendix F adds a simple analytical runtime model based on the number of 160-cubed crops, prediction time per crop, and a deadline-based applicability criterion. The UNet-index definition and Appendix E's CKA/HSIC equations remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central empirical argument through tokenizer-removal controls and comparisons against stronger, newer baselines (Tables 6–7). These provide evidence addressing v1's small-lesion weakness and performance gap to strong CNNs while demonstrating a measurable Transformer contribution. Explicit convolutional tradeoffs and error disclosures improve transparency. Retained RoPE-error-affected ablations and clinical claims based only on encoder timing remain limitations, but do not outweigh the stronger experimental support and more precise architectural positioning.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the Primus research work. Their complete main texts, tables, figures, equations, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial additions and reformatting in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds PrimusV2 experiments, further baseline comparisons, tokenizer ablations, and computational measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original Transformer-removal experiments, Primus development ablations, cross-validation segmentation results, and representational-similarity analyses.

results.title: Primus: Enforcing Attention Usage for 3D Medical Image Segmentation

C1.justification: The central Tabby/Plain contributions and abstract's 44% improvement claim remain. v2 adds Claim 5 about generalization to unseen strings, expands the introduction's Plain improvement claim from 5/6 to all eight datasets, and updates the conclusion's parity claim from 3/6 to 5/8 datasets.

C2.justification: v2 adds a hypothesis linking GPT-2 versus Llama performance to relative output-head size, explicit privacy and computational limitations, and tokenizer-dependent boundaries on novel-string generalization. It also clarifies that efficiency implementations remain future work. These substantially expand v1's discussion of applicability and mechanisms.

D1.justification: v2 documents batch-end backpropagation, additional dataset links, SDMetrics and attack-implementation references, RTX A6000 runtime hardware, and the string experiment's data-generation recipe and hyperparameters. The code-access information and retained experiments' learning-rate values remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from six to eight tabular datasets through Magic gamma-ray classification and Shoppers purchase prediction. Appendix E.5 adds a distinct scenario involving novel, high-cardinality Code and ID strings. Existing datasets, including nested Glaucoma JSON, remain.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds CTGAN+, CLLM, TabSyn, TabDiff, and Forest Diffusion; Appendix E.1 also reports HARMONIC results. Within the Glaucoma comparison, Table 4 newly includes CTGAN, Forest Diffusion, and Tab-DDPM alongside the retained Base and Tabby models.

E3.justification: Existing benchmark settings remain, but v2 adds Shape, Trend, Wasserstein distance, a 50-attack membership-inference evaluation, and runtime benchmarking. Appendix E.5 introduces one-epoch Llama 3-8B training on 5,000 generated rows and evaluation of 1,000 samples. The runtime sample count is inconsistent: Appendix E.1 specifies 100, whereas Table 12 specifies 10.

E4.justification: v2 adds direct privacy-leakage testing, computational-cost comparisons, and a controlled case study testing string-format validity, novelty, and duplication. These address questions beyond v1's DCR analysis. Existing architecture ablations, model-size analyses, and per-column training trajectories are retained.

E5.justification: v2 Appendix E.6 removes v1 Appendix E.5's explicit statement that learning-rate selection uses 'one run.' Main-result three-run averaging, model-size two-run averaging, and existing uncertainty displays remain. This is reduced run-count disclosure, not evidence of additional runs or a changed uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Matched benchmark tables retain the original scores, while v2 adds extensive dataset, comparator, fidelity, privacy, runtime, and string-generation results, including 1,000/1,000 valid Codes and 999/1,000 valid IDs. The scaling plot changes Pythia-14M Base/MH values from approximately 0.85/0.86 in v1 Figure 5 to 0.86/0.82 in v2 Figure 7, matching unchanged Table 3. Revised AUP scores concern the expanded comparison, not a same-setting performance gain.

M1.justification: Column-specific experts, weight initialization, Plain serialization, sequential column processing, and nested-data and architecture variants are retained. The explicit deterministic-routing formula and batch-end backpropagation statement clarify the existing procedure without establishing a method revision.

P1.justification: The title, affiliations, terminology, glossary, and several explanatory passages are revised. Limitations, a broader-impact statement, and the new generalization subsection are added, while the main narrative and section sequence remain largely intact.

P2.justification: Comparison tables expand substantially, Table 2 gains a best-count column, and new metric, privacy, runtime, and example tables are introduced. Performance-profile presentation changes, the scaling plot is redrawn and moved from Figure 5 to appendix Figure 7, and the loss plot moves from Figure 6 to appendix Figure 8.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for additional synthesis methods, privacy evaluation, subword tokenization, and the new datasets. Related work broadens its diffusion discussion, but retains the central positioning of Tabby as an architecture modification complementary to existing training techniques. Curated LLM was already cited in v1.

T1.justification: The existing architecture and evaluation mathematics are retained, with no added proofs, theorems, or revised formal assumptions. Section 2.1's new indicator-function expression restates the previously specified column-to-expert mapping. Additional standard metric descriptions concern evaluation rather than new theoretical results.

improvement.justification: v2 closes important validation gaps through broader comparator coverage, direct privacy attacks, computational-cost measurements, and controlled novel-string testing. Explicit privacy and efficiency limitations also improve the paper's qualification of its claims. New reporting defects temper these gains: Table 6 includes a 0.52 discrimination score despite the metric's maximum of 0.5, and runtime descriptions disagree on 10 versus 100 samples. These weaken specific additions but do not outweigh the substantially more informative empirical assessment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Tabby architecture and Plain training technique. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds results for two tabular datasets, additional baselines, privacy attacks, runtime, distribution metrics, and a controlled string-generation experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthesis experiments on six tabular datasets and Glaucoma JSON, plus architecture ablations, model-size comparisons, and training-loss analyses.

results.title: Tabby: A Language Model Architecture for Tabular and Structured Data Synthesis

C1.justification: The central VQ-based self-play contribution remains. However, v2's conclusion adds substantive claims that self-play itself drives the gains beyond the VQ architecture, that VQEL achieves complete vocabulary use and lower concept-message entropy, and that performance compares favorably with both REINFORCE and Gumbel-Softmax. V1 primarily claimed REINFORCE superiority, controllability and reduced collapse without isolating self-play's contribution.

C2.justification: V1's explanations connecting commitment weight and channel capacity to exploration difficulties are removed. V2 introduces explanations based on sender codebook initialization, attributes the CelebA sender-only shortfall to the frozen pretrained encoder, and identifies receiver-only pretraining as a failure condition in Appendix B. It also qualifies the relationship between communication accuracy and topographic similarity.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies GRUs, baseline temperature implementation, search ranges and a 100-epoch baseline versus 50+50-epoch VQEL schedule; v1 provided only an illustrative equal-budget example. However, v2 removes v1's EMA decay, stale-code threshold, selected commitment weights, 100-step reward-baseline description and validation-checkpoint selection rule. Reproducibility documentation therefore changes substantially in both directions.

E1.justification: V2 retains Synthetic Objects, dSprites and CelebA and adds ShapeWorld, including evaluation on held-out color-shape combinations. This is a focused extension of synthetic visual and compositional coverage within the retained referential-game task.

E2.justification: V1 evaluates only REINFORCE as an external baseline, although it discusses Gumbel-Softmax. V2 actually evaluates straight-through Gumbel-Softmax with learned temperature alongside REINFORCE throughout Tables 1–5. Adding this central alternative substantially strengthens the comparator set.

E3.justification: V2 adds active vocabulary fraction, topographic similarity and conditional concept entropy to the evaluation. It retains only vocabulary size 10 and message length 4, removing the smaller-channel setting, and changes candidate-count evaluations from the original table settings to curves spanning 2–512 candidates. The stated fixed sampling temperature becomes a searched parameter, and new freezing and no-self-play controls expand the evaluation design.

E4.justification: V2 adds a direct test of self-play versus VQ architecture alone (Table 3), sender update and agent-role comparisons, and cosine-versus-Euclidean analysis (Appendix A). Appendix B investigates receiver-only pretraining and its failure. Conversely, v1's commitment-weight, message-length and vocabulary-size sensitivity studies in Figures 4–6 are removed rather than relocated.

E5.justification: Both versions report values with ± terms, but v2's candidate-count curves omit the uncertainty previously shown alongside candidate-count accuracies in v1's tables. V1's explicit mean-and-standard-deviation sensitivity plots also disappear. V2 mentions different seeds for initializing the two agents, which does not establish additional repetitions; neither version specifies repeat counts.

E6.justification: Results are substantially replaced and expanded. For CelebA with 100 candidates, v1 Table 3 reports 67.6% for VQEL after mutual play versus 58.2% for REINFORCE; v2 Table 1 reports 0.91 for sender-pretrained VQEL with RL versus 0.93 for REINFORCE, while both-agent pretraining reaches 0.94 in Table 2. These are revised settings and variants, not established same-setting gains. New metric and ablation results accompany removal of the smaller-channel and sensitivity results.

M1.justification: The core three-module VQ architecture remains, but v2 introduces substantive training variants: freezing the sender, combining reinforcement learning with a language-preserving self-play objective, and pretraining the receiver or both agents. Section 4.4 also specifies cosine codebook matching for the main experiments, whereas v1 specifies Euclidean matching. These extend the procedure beyond the original self-play followed by sender reinforcement learning.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and emergent-language related work are extensively rewritten. V2 reorganizes the method into numbered module subsections and pseudocode, separates experimental setup from results, and structures results around agent roles with two appendices. Terminology changes from Text to Message modules, and the title and author information are revised.

P2.justification: V1's separate architecture diagrams are merged and redrawn as v2 Figure 1, and a new generator/codebook diagram appears as Figure 2. Dataset-specific accuracy tables become tables organized around training variants and multiple metrics; candidate-count curves are added, the unique-message chart is revised, and sensitivity plots disappear. The page template and text width also change substantially.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands and reframes the motivation around Language of Thought and Inner Speech, adding Fodor and Alderson-Day–Fernyhough alongside newer emergent-language and evaluation literature. General linguistic references used in v1 disappear. Its comparison with Carmeli et al. also changes: v2 describes inference-only quantization, omitting v1's acknowledgment of their training-and-inference quantization setting.

T1.justification: V2 adds the mathematical definition of the GS-ST baseline's learned inverse temperature (Equation 9) and explicitly specifies reward as negative receiver contrastive loss, where v1 leaves the loss-or-accuracy reward ambiguous. The core VQ and contrastive-loss mathematics is otherwise largely equivalent and reorganized; neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses two important weaknesses in v1: the absence of an evaluated Gumbel-Softmax comparator and the inability to distinguish self-play's contribution from VQ architecture alone. The added baseline and Table 3 control substantially strengthen the central empirical argument, while Appendix B documents a useful failure boundary. Removed hyperparameter details and sensitivity studies, together with conclusion-level generalizations broader than the reported successes, remain material drawbacks. Nevertheless, the new comparisons and controls make the main contribution substantially better supported and assessable.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VQEL research despite changes to the title and presentation. All 17 pages of each version, including equations, figures and tables, support comparison. V1 has no appendix; v2 includes readable Appendices A and B.

after.justification: V2 reports original experiments on four datasets, including self-play variants, a no-self-play control and the additional experiments in Appendices A and B.

before.justification: V1 reports original referential-game experiments on Synthetic Objects, dSprites and CelebA, including performance comparisons and hyperparameter sensitivity results.

results.title: VQEL: Enabling Self-Play in Emergent Language Games via Agent-Internal Vector Quantization

C1.justification: v2 elevates inherent zero-shot harmonization and a novel texture-preserving personalization technique to explicit contributions, alongside the retained insertion method and dataset. Its conclusion extends validation claims to real scenes. The abstract replaces the claimed 0.5 PSNR/0.15 SSIM advantage with a 2.0 dB PSNR advantage against the revised comparison set.

C2.justification: v2 expands v1's scattered color and texture failure observations into explanations of IC-Light-induced albedo changes, texture oversmoothing, ambiguous illumination and unsupported dynamic scenes (Appendix D). It adds a camera-pose-noise hypothesis for missing real-scene shadows and discusses the tradeoff between shadow realism and background similarity (Appendices B–C, J).

D1.justification: v2 supplies LoRA, refinement, cropping and shadow settings, real-capture instructions, new baseline adaptations, original SceneNet identifiers, and code/project hyperlinks. However, v1's explicit initial DN-Splatter training and regularization settings and per-scene prompt list are omitted. Reproducibility information is substantially revised, with both additions and losses.

E1.justification: v2 retains the ten synthetic scenes and tiny real-image cup dataset, but adds captured real 3D insertion scenes involving a toaster, fabric bin and chair (Section 4.1; Table 7). This extends evaluation from synthetic 3D environments to real reconstructions, beyond the existing 2D real-image demonstration.

E2.justification: The main comparison expands from TIP-Editor and R3DG in v1 to those methods plus Copy-Paste, Latent Bridge Matching and Instruct-GS2GS in v2. All three additions participate in the reported synthetic comparisons, not merely citations or evaluations on the new real dataset.

E3.justification: Reported settings change substantially: class-preservation images decrease from 200 to 32, rough personalization increases from 500 to 1,000 iterations, and 3DGS optimization changes from 20,000 to 3,000 steps including refinement. v2 also modifies TIP-Editor settings, adds cropped PSNR and shadow/background metrics, and revises the stated DTIS definition to compare image and text feature differences. SSIMpart is retained under the name SSIMcropped.

E4.justification: v2 adds texture-preservation and shadow ablations, quantitative shadow analysis, cropping-strategy comparisons, failure cases and diffusion-backbone sensitivity experiments (Section 4.4; Appendices B–D, K–L). Backbone tests cover SD1.5–2.1 in 3D and extend through SD3.5 in 2D. Existing personalization, IC-Light and DDS analyses remain, while v1's explicit mean-initialization ablations are removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Additional scene averages and result tables in v2 do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Table 1 reports revised synthetic PSNRpart averages: D3DR changes from 8.863 to 11.966, TIP-Editor from 8.205 to 6.960, and R3DG from 8.406 to 8.598. These accompany revised methods/settings and are not controlled cross-version gains. v2 adds real-scene, shadow and component results, and reports 40 rather than 50 minutes for D3DR in Table 2.

M1.justification: v1 uses one personalized diffusion model followed by 2-step-DDS. v2 introduces two LoRA-personalized models, an additional image-conditioning convolutional branch for texture preservation, SDEdit refinement, and optimizable scene-shadow parameters with pruning (Sections 3.2–3.5). These substantially change the architecture and optimization procedure.

P1.justification: The title, introduction, method explanations and conclusion are extensively rewritten. The cup experiments are integrated into the method explanation, baseline configurations move to an appendix, and the appendices are reorganized around evaluation, limitations and implementation. These are substantial narrative and structural changes beyond adding experiments.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the two-column layout with a single-column journal layout, redraws the pipeline, restructures the main results into dataset averages with separate appendix tables, and consolidates qualitative comparison grids.
