It adds displays for personalization, model variants, failures, cropping and optimization schedules. Existing cup and SDS illustrations are also rearranged.

R1.justification: v2 positions the work as discovering another hidden zero-shot capability of diffusion models. It adds substantive discussions of LBM, Instruct-GS2GS and complementary language-guided placement through PlaceIt3D, plus references supporting texture personalization and rectified-flow adaptation. This substantially broadens v1's positioning around DDS, TIP-Editor and R3DG.

T1.justification: The original SDS/DDS formulation is retained apart from notation. Appendix H adds rectified-flow definitions and corresponding SDS/DDS expressions, while Section 3.5 formalizes the assumption that affected scene Gaussians can only darken. These provide a limited extension of the mathematical setup; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v1's 3D evaluation was synthetic-only, used two comparators and showed unresolved texture failures. v2 addresses texture preservation with a dedicated component and ablations, adds real-capture evaluation and a copy-paste control alongside additional competitors, and documents failure mechanisms. These substantially strengthen validation and explanation. Mixed shadow/background scores (Tables 3–4), omitted reproduction details and changed experimental settings limit some conclusions, but do not outweigh those gains.

A1.justification: Despite the changed title, both PDFs describe D3DR for diffusion-guided 3DGS object insertion. All 20 pages of v1 and 34 pages of v2, including appendices, are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original synthetic and real 3D insertion results, component ablations, shadow evaluations, diffusion-model comparisons and personalization experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic 3D insertion experiments, real-image cup editing, baseline comparisons, timing measurements and ablations.

results.title: Diffusion Models are Secretly Zero-Shot 3DGS Harmonizers

C1.justification: The central scientific contributions remain an information-theoretic definition of leakiness, ALL as its adversarial deep-learning approximation, and validation across AES, ECC and RSA implementations. Expanded comparisons and stronger descriptions of benchmark breadth support these retained contributions without materially changing their scientific scope.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands v1's scattered qualifications into explicit limitations of oracle assessments, DNN tests, template attacks, computational cost, tuning, synchronization and evaluation on cropped traces (Appendix F). New ablations also support interpretations concerning regularization, smoothing and the mixed usefulness of mask conditioning, materially refining explanations of ALL's gains and applicability.

D1.justification: V1 already supplied code access and hyperparameter tables. V2 adds ALL and evaluation pseudocode, a linked self-contained implementation, detailed comparator adaptations, dataset sizes and DPAv4/OTP processing disclosures, and A6000 runtime measurements. These substantially expand reproducibility information, although Algorithm 4's mask expression conflicts with its stated unocclusion convention.

E1.justification: The six real datasets and four simulated AES perturbation scenarios remain. V1's separate mixed-order and redundant first-order toy experiments are replaced by a scenario combining redundancy with multiple second-order leaking pairs (v2 Section 5.1 and Appendix E.1), changing a limited part of the synthetic coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds actual evaluations of OccPOI, m-Occlusion and second-order m-Occlusion, including tuned-window variants, alongside the retained statistical and attribution baselines. V1 discussed the related Yap and Schamberger methods but did not benchmark them. These additions substantially expand comparison with closely related approaches.

E3.justification: V2 replaces oGMM agreement with an SNR-based oracle and adds template-attack evaluation using selected features. Training settings and selection procedures also change: supervised ASCAD training increases from 10k steps to 20k/40k, and ALL selection changes from reverse occlusion alone to a composite criterion. These are substantive protocol revisions, not merely additional documentation.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's toy demonstrations and synthetic parameter sweeps, v2 adds controlled ablations of heavy input dropout, cooperative versus adversarial training, mask conditioning and smoothing (Appendix E.3.7). It also adds real-data learning-rate and budget sensitivity analyses and hyperparameter-search distributions. The earlier joint synthetic budget sweeps are replaced by fixed-budget simulations.

E5.justification: Both versions report benchmark means and standard deviations over five seeds. V2 adds median, quartile and whisker summaries of hyperparameter-search outcomes (Figures 20–21) and explicitly describes error-bar-based grouping of best results. These extend statistical reporting without establishing an increase in repeated-run counts.

E6.justification: Numerical results are extensively revised and expanded. For example, ALL's ASCAD-fixed reverse-occlusion score changes from 125.5 ± 0.4 in v1 Table 6 to 126.4 ± 0.2 in v2 Table 13. V2 additionally reports template-attack results, new toy outcomes, ablations and runtimes. Changed methods and settings prevent interpreting these as controlled version-to-version performance gains.

M1.justification: The constrained mutual-information objective and adversarial classifier/mask framework remain. V2 replaces the unbiased REBAR gradient estimator with biased CONCRETE at fixed temperature 1 (Section 4.2 and Appendix D.4), a localized but substantive change to the training procedure.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the introduction, background, method explanation and experimental narrative, including a clearer attacker/defender explanation. It reorganizes the appendices around notation, background, related work, derivations, experiments and limitations. This exceeds renumbering or expansion solely through new scientific content.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to a single-column layout. V2 redraws the method and causal diagrams, adds notation and architecture displays, introduces a consolidated main results table, and substantially reorganizes experimental graphics. Many of v1's individual baseline and occlusion-curve grids are replaced by summary tables and diagnostic plots.

R1.justification: Sections 3 and 4.3 and Appendix C substantially develop the relationship to prior methods, including their differing objectives and computational costs. Newly cited Egger et al. (2022) informs the white-box oracle and positioning of ALL as complementary to expert analysis. Yap and Schamberger were already cited in v1; their expanded treatment is not a new citation.

T1.justification: The main proposition and corollaries establishing the mutual-information formulation are retained from Appendix B.2 to D.2. V2 revises the conditional-information convergence argument using a bounded chain-rule sum, changes the gradient-estimator derivation to CONCRETE, and adds computational complexity bounds in Table 15. The central theoretical framework remains intact.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important weaknesses in v1's validation by evaluating closely related methods and testing whether regularization, smoothing or particular ALL components explain the gains. Complementary attack evaluation, runtime measurements and explicit limitations substantially improve the evidence and its interpretation. The biased gradient relaxation, acknowledged comparator contamination and Algorithm 4's inconsistent mask convention remain drawbacks, but the expanded controls and transparency provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ALL research work. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V2 reports original synthetic and real-dataset evaluations, component ablations, sensitivity experiments and runtime measurements in Section 5 and Appendix E.

before.justification: V1 reports original toy experiments, simulated AES experiments and evaluations on six real leakage datasets, including quantitative results in Tables 4–6.

results.title: Learning to Localize Leakage of Cryptographic Sensitive Variables

C1.justification: The introduction and conclusion strengthen the central contribution from separated sufficient and counterexample regimes to a sharp boundary at 1.75/L within the convergence interval. The gradient-flow and gradient-norm claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: V1 explicitly leaves the interval (1/L,1.75/L] unresolved; v3 removes this central limitation and interprets the convexity and possible non-convexity regimes as complementary. Questions about sustained concavity and other optimizers remain. V3 also adds intuition connecting gradient norms with objective decreases for sufficiently small steps.

D1.justification: The numerical illustration's disclosed function, step size and initialization are unchanged. Neither version adds implementation instructions, software or hardware details, or code and data access information.

E1.justification: The quadratic demonstration in Figure 1 is unchanged. No datasets, evaluated tasks or additional simulation scenarios are introduced.

E2.justification: Neither version reports empirical comparisons against other optimization methods. The cited mathematical results serve as theoretical background, not evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Figure 1 retains f(x)=x², step size 0.1, initialization x0=3 and the same displayed iterations. The revised theorem's step-size bound is not an experimental protocol change.

E4.justification: No ablations, robustness experiments or supplementary empirical analyses are added or removed. Theorem 2's analytical counterexample is retained, and Appendix A contains proofs rather than additional experiments.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated runs, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or other statistical uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Figure 1 retains the same numerical trajectory and decreasing objective curve; no empirical result entries change. The strengthened step-size guarantee is a theoretical result, assessed under T1.

M1.justification: Both versions analyze the same constant-step gradient descent update and gradient-flow equation. The larger provable step-size range changes the guarantee, not the optimization procedure.

P1.justification: V3 adds Moslem Zamani to the author list and makes localized explanatory and wording revisions in the introduction, preliminaries, proof exposition and conclusion. The section sequence and Appendix A organization remain recognizable and largely unchanged.

P2.justification: V3 changes typography, heading styles, title and author arrangement, page rules and spacing. The single-column organization and two-panel Figure 1, including its axes, legend and caption content, are retained; neither version contains tables.

R1.justification: Both versions cite the same four works by Bartle and Sherbert, Iserles, and Nesterov. The positioning that optimization-curve convexity has not previously been systematically studied is retained; citation formatting changes only.

T1.justification: Theorem 1 extends guaranteed convexity from 0<η≤1/L to 0<η≤1.75/L through a new weighted-inequality proof, matching the retained counterexample above 1.75/L. Theorem 3 repairs its positivity argument using contradiction, and Theorem 6 corrects the gradient-flow derivative to the negative squared gradient norm. Appendix A retains Theorem 8's statement while explicitly adapting and expanding the earlier monotonicity proof.

improvement.justification: V3 resolves the explicitly open interval (1/L,1.75/L] with a proof that matches the existing counterexample boundary, substantially completing the paper's central theoretical answer. Corrections to Theorems 3 and 6 and fuller appendix reasoning also improve mathematical reliability. No material loss offsets these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs contain the same research work, with corresponding definitions, theorems, Figure 1 and Appendix A. The complete text, equations and visual material support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: Figure 1 retains the numerical gradient-descent trajectory and objective values for the same quadratic example. The retained simulation qualifies, although the main contributions and appendix remain theoretical.

before.justification: Figure 1 presents an original illustrative numerical trajectory of gradient descent on f(x)=x², with step size 0.1 and initialization x0=3. This small simulation accompanies otherwise theoretical contributions.

results.title: Are Convex Optimization Curves Convex?

C1.justification: The principal architectural and forecasting contributions remain. v2 removes the introduction's specific 600%/20%/50% advantage claims and short-term-superiority wording, while strengthening the uncertainty contribution to explicitly claim empirically calibrated estimates. These refine the contribution claims without redefining the work.

C2.justification: v2 adds a regular-grid limitation concerning irregular geometries and explains temporarily higher StFT-F errors through distributional modeling and prediction variance. It also interprets the scale-count results as saturation and the coverage results as near-90% calibration. These are substantive but bounded additions to the retained interpretation of the method.

D1.justification: v2 adds DPOT hyperparameter ranges, explicit GPU-hour budgets, profiling batch size, and patch configurations for the scale sweep. Most existing implementation details remain. However, it omits v1 Appendix C's instruction to normalize residuals by their standard deviations; this is lost reproducibility information, not evidence that normalization was discontinued.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same three physical systems with the same domains, variables, and data-generation conditions in Appendix A. The added ablations, profiling, and coverage measurements use retained datasets. PDEBench appears as baseline provenance, not as an additional evaluated dataset.

E2.justification: v2 adds AR-DPOT, described as an AFNO variant, to Table 1 and trajectory comparisons across all three systems. It becomes the strongest external comparator on plasma MHD and shallow-water. FNO, ViT, and the BubbleML-modified U-Net remain; the UNetb label does not identify a new comparator.

E3.justification: The stated training rule changes from running sufficient epochs to imposing equal A100 budgets of 24 hours for plasma/Navier-Stokes and 48 hours for shallow-water. This is a reported protocol revision, without evidence establishing reruns. New evaluations measure coverage over the first 20 plasma and 10 shallow-water predictions and profile tokenizer variants at batch size 20. Existing splits and five-snapshot forecasting inputs remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds overlapping-tokenizer accuracy/cost ablations, a one-to-four-scale sensitivity study, computational tradeoff analysis, and quantitative uncertainty-calibration checks in Appendices B-D. These test previously unexamined component benefits and operating characteristics. The hierarchy/frequency-path ablation already existed in v1 Appendix B and is retained, including its numerical results.

E5.justification: v2 adds empirical coverage at nominal 90% and 95% confidence levels, including aggregate and variable-specific reporting in Tables 2, 10, and 11. The stated uncertainty band changes from 3σ in v1 Figure 4 to σ in v2 Figure 3. The existing 50 prediction samples per step and 100 stochastic trajectories are retained; additional independent training runs are not reported.

E6.justification: All 50 retained Table 1 values are identical; v2 adds ten DPOT entries rather than improving existing StFT scores. Substantial new results include tokenizer errors of 0.0986 without overlap versus 0.0307 with overlap on plasma, three/four-scale errors of 0.0385/0.0391, computational measurements, and coverage statistics. At nominal 90%, reported average coverage is 89.4% for plasma and 89.5% for shallow-water.

M1.justification: The coarse-to-fine hierarchy, dual processing paths, overlapping tokenization, summed block predictions, and rectified-flow residual correction are retained. Splitting Algorithm 1 into two algorithms and clarifying conditioning do not establish a changed procedure; v1 already documented time conditioning in Appendix C.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and method explanations are extensively revised. Overlapping tokenization moves into the StFT-block explanation, experimental setup gains labeled subsections, and the results narrative is reorganized around ablations and additional analyses. Existing experimental-details and visualization appendices move from C/D to E/F.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main layout from two columns to one, merges the architecture diagrams into an expanded Figure 1, and adds a patch-subdivision illustration. It reorganizes existing plots and uncertainty panels, introduces logarithmic error axes, adds DPOT to visual comparisons, restructures ablation tables, and adds coverage and computational displays.

R1.justification: v2 adds references and discussion concerning DPOT, P2C2Net, PDEBench, and plasma/probabilistic PDE research, while dropping the Kossaifi tensorized-FNO discussion. The central positioning against U-Net-style hierarchies and existing generative approaches remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The autoregressive decomposition, rectified-flow interpolation and loss, scale-contribution measure, and Appendix A governing equations retain their mathematical substance. Explicit flow-time arguments and revised indices clarify the existing formulation. Neither version supplies new theorems or proofs relative to the other.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of central contributions: the previously unablated tokenizer is tested, scale selection is examined, a stronger DPOT comparator is included, and visual uncertainty evidence is supplemented with measured coverage. These address important evidential gaps in v1. The gains outweigh the omitted residual-normalization instruction and reporting inconsistencies, although calibration checks cover only early prediction windows and Figure 10's DPOT FLOPs disagree with Table 9, limiting the corresponding conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same StFT/StFT-F research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds DPOT comparisons, tokenizer and scale-count ablations, computational measurements, and uncertainty-coverage results.

before.justification: v1 reports original forecasting experiments on plasma MHD, Navier-Stokes, and shallow-water systems, including quantitative comparisons, uncertainty visualizations, and ablations.

results.title: StFT: Spatio-temporal Fourier Transformer for Long-term Dynamics Prediction

C1.justification: The abstract and central architectural contributions are retained. The conclusion qualifies v1's claim that AIKAE 'outperforms' IKAE to 'performs equally or better,' modestly narrowing the claimed performance advantage.

C2.justification: V2 interprets augmentation benefits as clearest on the larger ECL and Traffic datasets, with similar IKAE/AIKAE performance elsewhere. It adds a numerical-conditioning caveat to algebraic invertibility, an overfitting explanation for excessive augmentation, and a regularization explanation for enforcing augmentation linearity. These substantially expand the discussion of mechanisms and applicability limits.

D1.justification: New Appendices C–D document dataset characteristics and split sizes, data-loading code provenance, NICE coupling networks, nonlinearities, the augmentation MLP widths [256,128,32], parameter counts and search ranges. E.2–E.3 additionally disclose architecture and training controls for retained experiments. These are substantial reproducibility additions; the experiment-code link is unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the four ETT datasets, ECL, Traffic, Weather and Exchange, plus satellite forecasting on Fontainebleau and Orléans. The added studies use this existing coverage; stochastic modeling is discussed without experiments.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain the same competing methods: iTransformer, PatchTST, TimesNet and DLinear in Table 1, persistence in the extended table, and the existing comparator sets in the lookback, RevIN and satellite experiments. The new sensitivity studies concern internal configurations and ablations.

E3.justification: V1 reports fixed training hyperparameters, with batch sizes 4 for ETT and 32 otherwise. V2 Appendix D reports per-dataset, per-horizon searches over coupling-layer counts {3,4}, widths {128,256} and batch sizes {4,128,512}. This substantively revises the reported model-selection protocol. New hyperparameter, augmentation-size and loss-weight sweeps also introduce additional experimental controls.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained encoder/RevIN ablation and lookback study, v2 adds initialization sensitivity, learning-rate and architecture sensitivity, and ECL/Weather prediction cases in E.4–E.6. F.1–F.2 directly test how augmentation dimension and enforcement of augmentation linearity affect satellite forecasting.

E5.justification: V1 reports a fixed initialization for the main forecasting benchmark and five-instance averages without dispersion for satellite experiments. V2 Table 6 adds means and standard deviations across five separately trained initializations for IKAE and AIKAE on ECL and Weather at all four horizons. The existing satellite averaging practice remains unchanged.

E6.justification: Many IKAE/AIKAE scores change in Table 1 and the extended table under the revised tuning protocol. For example, Weather at horizon 720 changes from AIKAE MSE/MAE 0.363/0.354 to 0.317/0.333; this is not a same-setting method improvement. V2 also adds substantial sensitivity and ablation results. External baseline scores, satellite Table 2 and the original RevIN ablation scores are retained.

M1.justification: The main AIKAE architecture, delay embedding and assimilation procedure remain unchanged. Limited methodological additions include an explicitly untested stochastic IKAE variant with a variance encoder in Appendix B and weighted linearity-loss variants evaluated in F.2. These do not replace the principal deterministic method or its default loss.

P1.justification: The seven-section main narrative and much of its wording are retained. V2 makes targeted explanatory and grammatical revisions, moves stochastic-modeling discussion into Appendix B, and reorganizes the expanded appendices. The added scientific material does not amount to a wholesale rewrite of the existing paper.

P2.justification: V2 adds multi-step and delay-embedding schematics, a hyperparameter-sensitivity figure, two forecasting case-study figures, and tables for dataset characteristics, seed variability and satellite ablations. Existing displays are retained or relocated under new numbering. These additions substantially expand the visual explanation and presentation of evidence.

R1.justification: V2 adds references on flow conditioning, linear forecasting and channel independence, including Lee et al., Toner and Darlow, and Han et al., plus activation-function references. The overall research positioning remains stable. Several other reference changes are publication metadata updates for already cited works.

T1.justification: Appendix B extends the existing change-of-variables discussion with Gaussian uncertainty propagation and a stochastic latent formulation. F.2 introduces the weighted linearity objective in Equation 23, and Section 3.1 adds a nullspace condition to the augmentation discussion. The principal Koopman and assimilation equations remain unchanged, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves reproducibility through Appendices C–D and strengthens evidence for the augmentation mechanism through capacity and loss ablations, sensitivity studies and five-seed uncertainty reporting. It also qualifies important interpretations and numerical-invertibility claims. A stale E.2 statement still links its unchanged ablation scores to the revised Table 1, and changed tuning limits direct interpretation of score gains. Nevertheless, the added methodological transparency and targeted validation provide a clear substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AIKAE research. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: V2 retains original forecasting and assimilation results and adds initialization, hyperparameter, augmentation-size and linearity-loss experiments in Appendices E–F.

before.justification: Sections 5–6 and the appendices report original time-series forecasting, satellite data-assimilation, ablation and lookback-length results.

results.title: Augmented Invertible Koopman Autoencoder for long-term time series forecasting

C1.justification: v1 principally claims granular, scalable behavior explanations demonstrated across three environments. v2 adds explicit claims of reward-free operation without underlying-policy access, priority as the first explanation approach based on unsupervised behavior segments, and superiority over trajectory-level baselines in fidelity, human preference, and cluster coherence.

C2.justification: v2 adds mechanism arguments about state-action inputs and delayed token shifts, interprets larger fidelity gaps against random assignments as behavioral distinctiveness, and attributes MiniGrid's weaker structural scores to the baseline's LSTM encoder. It also distinguishes geometric clustering quality from human interpretability and expands limitations concerning hand-crafted similarity measures. The earlier noisy-transition and ambiguous-cluster limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 Appendix B adds batch sizes, A100 hardware, explicit decay schedules, sequence padding/truncation, three-layer MLP/CNN behavior-cloning architectures, neighboring-label smoothing, and per-cluster training sample counts. These substantially expand implementation documentation; the PDFs do not establish whether newly described smoothing was newly implemented. v1's total sequence-count entries are omitted, while the public-code access information remains unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 retains HalfCheetah, Seaquest, and MiniGridTwoGoalsLava while adding pen-expert-v1, extending coverage to dexterous manipulation. It also introduces human behavior-description and explanation-selection tasks, substantially broadening evaluation beyond automated environment experiments.

E2.justification: Deshmukh et al. (2024), discussed but not experimentally compared in v1, becomes an evaluated comparator in v2 Tables 3–5. v2 also adds random-segment and random-cluster controls, raw state-action clustering, and direct k-means on learned embeddings as evaluated alternatives.

E3.justification: v2 introduces human-study protocols with 15 participants, description-similarity and preference metrics, structural clustering metrics, and fidelity evaluation over 200 actions from 20 episodes. Retained settings also change: Seaquest sequence length drops from 60 to 30 and codebook size from 128 to 64; MiniGrid maximum sequence length changes from 50 to 40. Tables 2 in v1 and 8 in v2 additionally report revised lambda values. These establish reported protocol changes without establishing which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The existing ablations are substantially reworked: MiniGrid occupancy bars become reconstruction-loss and occupancy curves across four environments, while the MiniGrid cluster-count-versus-lambda plot is replaced by structural-quality curves across three environments. v2 Appendix A also adds tests of learned representations versus raw inputs and spectral clustering versus direct k-means.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seeds, repeated-run counts, error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests. v2's human confidence ratings measure participants' subjective confidence, rather than uncertainty in the reported experimental estimates.

E6.justification: v2 adds human-study, fidelity, structural-quality, and clustering-ablation results in Tables 2–7, alongside Pen results and revised sensitivity curves. For example, HalfCheetah human preference is 81.3% for the proposed method versus 13.9% for Deshmukh et al.; its fidelity error is 0.36 versus 0.05, favoring the baseline on raw error. These are newly reported evaluations, not demonstrated same-setting performance gains over v1.

M1.justification: The VQ-VAE, spectral clustering, and MSE/cross-entropy attribution pipeline is retained. However, Section 3.2 changes graph weights from Count + lambda * distance^2 to (1-lambda) * Count + lambda * distance^2, altering the relative weighting of temporal and spatial information.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, retained method explanations, experimental narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Human evaluation and quantitative assessment receive dedicated subsections. The appendices are reorganized from behavior results/ablations/training to ablations/training/cluster visualization, and the impact statement is removed.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a single-column layout, adds an end-to-end pipeline diagram, and relocates an edited version of the original architecture figure to Appendix B. Graph insets disappear from retained rollout figures; attribution examples and appendix cluster panels are redesigned. New Pen figures and comparison tables, revised ablation plots, and expanded table structures substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially expanded and repositioned around offline, reward-free, post-hoc explanation. New comparisons discuss LAPO, Genie, EDGE, StateMask, RICE, HIGHLIGHTS, AOC, and XRL evaluation surveys. Several earlier references and discussions, including high-fidelity behavior modeling, reward decomposition, and offline skill graphs, are removed.

T1.justification: The formal graph-weight definition gains a (1-lambda) coefficient on transition frequency, and v2 explicitly specifies lambda in [0,1], allowing a distance-only endpoint. The quantization, training-loss, Laplacian, and attribution equations otherwise retain their substance. Neither version provides theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's central validation gap by supplementing author-interpreted visual examples with human judgments, baseline and random-control comparisons, component ablations, and fuller implementation details. This materially strengthens empirical grounding and reproducibility. The gains are tempered by fidelity-superiority wording that overreaches Table 4's raw errors, unexplained structural-score differences between Tables 5 and 7, and continued absence of uncertainty estimates. These weaknesses limit the conclusions but do not outweigh the substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same behavior-discovery and attribution framework. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, and figures, are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original results across four environments, two human-study tasks, quantitative baseline comparisons, and expanded ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original segmentation and attribution results on three environments, plus codebook-size and graph-weight ablations in Appendix B.

results.title: Behaviour Discovery and Attribution for Explainable Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The central contribution remains PA-based robustness assessment without supervision, including model selection. v2 modestly qualifies its compliance claim: the introduction presents deliberately nonformal ideal properties and says PA 'better complies,' while the conclusion emphasizes reliable scoring rather than explicitly asserting consistency with the desiderata.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly acknowledges difficulty separating covariate shift from sampling noise. Section 4.2 changes the interpretation from PA being more suitable than AFR_T to the measures providing complementary insights. It also adds interpretations of the new attack results and further justification for Adam; the finite-hypothesis and uniform-prior limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 reports approximate beta-optimization time of tens of minutes on one GPU and adds AutoAttack implementation information. It clarifies training from scratch, resampling across shortcut configurations, and epoch-wise model selection without establishing changes to the retained experiment. Existing code links remain; Figure 1's revised caption no longer specifies the earlier simulation size of 1000.

E1.justification: Section 4.1 and Appendix F add ImageNet evaluation, extending adversarial coverage from CIFAR-10 to higher-resolution, 1000-class images. CIFAR-10 also gains APGD-CE, APGD-DLR, and FAB attack scenarios. DiagViB-6 and the appendix IMDB experiments are retained.

E2.justification: AFR_T remains the comparison measure. The six CIFAR-10 model/defense families, ERM/IRM/LISA discriminability comparison, and ERM/IRM model-selection comparison are unchanged. ImageNet uses four already represented model/defense families; the added attacks generate evaluation conditions rather than competing robustness measures.

E3.justification: New protocols evaluate 10,000 randomly selected ImageNet validation images processed at 256 × 256 pixels and introduce AutoAttack procedures. Appendix F specifies bounds of {2,4,8,16,32}/255 for CIFAR-10 and {2,4,8}/255 for ImageNet. Existing PGD/FMN budgets and domain-generalization splits remain. Section 4.1 inconsistently writes denominator 225, whereas Appendix F and the figures use 255.

E4.justification: Appendix F substantially extends robustness testing across attack families, perturbation bounds, and attacked-sample proportions. These analyses examine whether PA/AFR discrimination and rankings persist under substantially more successful attacks. The earlier confidence-distribution, IMDB perturbation, and feature-alignment analyses remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Existing predictive-confidence standard errors and dataset-seed descriptions are retained. v2 introduces no repeated-run counts, new uncertainty-estimation practice, confidence intervals, or significance tests for the added evaluations.

E6.justification: Figures 14–18 add substantial PA and AFR_T results for the new attack conditions and ImageNet. They show, for example, weak models reaching minimum PA at partial adversarial ratios and different ranking transitions under AFR_T. Previously reported plotted data and all three tables are unchanged; these additions are not same-setting performance improvements.

M1.justification: The Gibbs-posterior construction, factorized agreement kernel, optimization over beta, and PA-based model selection remain unchanged. The new background discussion and replacement of score notation R with S do not introduce a different procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, methodological exposition, experimental explanations, discussion, and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting. v2 adds a Background subsection, reorganizes the PA explanation, and replaces 'metric' with 'measure' throughout. These changes extend beyond the prose needed to report new experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adds five multipanel figures, Figures 14–18. Figure 7 is enlarged and rearranged into five rows of paired plots, Figure 2 moves from the introduction to methodology, and Figures 1–2 receive expanded captions. Existing plotted data and table contents are retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds substantial positioning within the PA literature, tracing Approximate Set Coding, the similarity approach, Gibbs-posterior variants, and earlier applications. Section 3.1 distinguishes the original framework from this robustness adaptation. Additional references cover that lineage, annealing, AutoAttack/FAB, and ImageNet.

T1.justification: The maximum-entropy derivation, posterior factorization, agreement formula, and three stated properties retain the same mathematical content. Appendix A preserves the proofs, with notation changes rather than substantive corrections or new theoretical results.

improvement.justification: The APGD/FAB stress tests and ImageNet evaluation substantially strengthen the empirical basis for PA's robustness-assessment claims. They address v1's restricted adversarial validation by testing stronger attacks spanning broad failure rates and a much larger classification setting. Clearer PA research positioning and more qualified interpretation also improve the paper. The new attack-bound inconsistency limits protocol precision but does not outweigh these substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Posterior Agreement robustness framework. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and matchable; v2 retains Appendices A–E and adds Appendix F.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds APGD/FAB evaluations on CIFAR-10 and APGD evaluations on ImageNet in Appendix F.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulations and experiments on CIFAR-10 adversarial robustness, DiagViB-6 domain generalization and model selection, and IMDB perturbations, including appendix analyses.

results.title: Rethinking Robustness in Machine Learning: A Posterior Agreement Approach

C1.justification: The abstract and central introductory/concluding claims remain the same: combining Python world-model synthesis with hierarchical abstractions improves planning and learning efficiency. The conclusion retains the 24.5-fold API-usage reduction claim. New experiments expand support without redefining these main contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of initialization traps, overgeneralization of death-avoidance rules, and differences between object-oriented exploration and GPT-o1's repetitive behavior. It proposes maintaining alternative world models. Demonstrated transfer across visually distinct games in v1 becomes a future-work possibility in Section 4.5, although Section 4.2 still retains the Baba is AI success statement.

D1.justification: v2 documents the new WorldCoder comparison's MCTS depth, request cap, and curriculum matching, and specifies that the full-PDDL baseline is manually constructed without learning or revision. Existing API settings, the code-access link, and Appendix A's initialization and revision prompts remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Sections 4.7–4.8 add two KekeCompetition levels requiring sacrifice of controlled characters and a ten-level custom box-clustering game with lethal cherries. These introduce distinct task requirements. Baba is AI coverage remains reported in Section 4.2 despite removal of its dedicated transfer section.

E2.justification: v2 adds EMPA to the reported VGDL comparison in Table 3, a fully specified PDDL/Fast Downward baseline to the runtime comparison in Table 4, and WorldCoder to the BabyAI/Minigrid comparison in Table 7. v1 primarily compares against GPT-o1 and TheoryCoder's own ablation.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce environment-step and learning-efficiency metrics, token accounting, a 500-environment-step budget, and a matched WorldCoder curriculum with MCTS depth 30 and 50 API calls per level. A failure case is tested through 25 calls. The original six-call benchmark allowance and 500-second planning timeout remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds gameplay heatmaps for KekeCompetition levels 11 and 13, initialization-failure observations, two challenging failure cases, and a custom-game test addressing possible training-data contamination. These substantially extend diagnosis beyond v1's planning and prompting ablations. The dedicated transfer illustration is removed, although its broad outcome remains mentioned.

E5.justification: Section 4.7 newly discloses qualitatively that repeated runs sometimes become stuck. It supplies no run count, seeds, failure frequency, or uncertainty estimates. Runtime averaging over five runs was already reported in v1 and is retained; an increase in repetitions is not established.

E6.justification: v2 adds EMPA step/success results, FD runtimes, and WorldCoder comparisons: Table 7 reports 69,402 tokens and 100% success for TheoryCoder versus 388,861 and 83% for WorldCoder. Figure 15 adds four API calls across ten custom-game levels; Section 4.7 reports two failures, one after 25 calls. Original API-call totals persist; reversed Sokoban level/runtime ordering does not establish a same-setting performance gain.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 removes v1's model-predicted next-state assignment from the environment-execution loop before storing actual transitions. This is a limited pseudocode correction; both versions already describe collecting real environment transitions. The hierarchical planning architecture, synthesis/refinement procedure, and Appendix A prompts remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Related work gains numbered subsections, while the introduction and method exposition are shortened by removing travel and household examples and repetitive PDDL explanations. New experimental subsections are integrated, and publication and author-role text changes. Most existing prose and the main section organization are retained.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the empirical displays with new comparison tables, an FD column in the runtime table, a learning-efficiency chart, gameplay heatmaps, failure illustrations, and custom-game screenshots/results. It also replaces the BabyAI screenshot and removes v1's transfer figure. These changes extend beyond renumbering and page reflow.

R1.justification: v2 adds references and discussion concerning Guzdial et al.'s game-engine learning, Ruoss et al.'s LMAct benchmark, Minigrid, and Sutton et al.'s temporal abstraction framework. The principal positioning within theory-based RL, program synthesis, and bilevel planning remains intact.

T1.justification: The classical-planning formulation, abstraction definitions, and Equations 1–4 retain their mathematical substance. The added learning-efficiency formula is an adopted evaluation metric credited to prior work, not a new theoretical development. No proofs or formal guarantees are added.

improvement.justification: v2 materially addresses v1's limited comparative validation through relevant WorldCoder and full-PDDL baselines, environment-step comparisons, a custom-game test, and concrete failure cases. These strengthen evidence for the contribution and clarify its limits. Sparse uncertainty reporting, conflicting transfer language, and an apparent Figure 6/Table 3 inconsistency remain: the Push Boulders efficiency bar is about 0.021, whereas the stated formula and table imply 4/236, about 0.017. Despite these weaknesses, the stronger comparisons and explicit failure evidence provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TheoryCoder under the same title and authors. The complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and Appendix A are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds comparator evaluations, behavioral analyses, failure cases, and a custom-game experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original TheoryCoder evaluations on grid-world games, including API usage, task success, planning-time ablations, and model-transfer results.

results.title: Synthesizing world models for bilevel planning

C1.justification: The central contributions remain Corrupted Degradation Disparity and fairness-aware SAM. However, v2 explicitly limits the current scope to binary sensitive attributes, removes the introduction's highest-worst-group-accuracy claim, and consistently claims one metric instead of the conclusion's earlier reference to degradation and promotion-fairness metrics.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning medical-domain applicability, backbone robustness, and the conclusion that corruption disparities are not solely attributable to imbalance. It explicitly discusses binary-sensitive-attribute and metric-choice limitations, deferring intersectional validation. The asymmetric-noise discussion also distinguishes improved degradation fairness from potentially worse accuracy parity.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands sparse implementation documentation by specifying PyTorch, Ubuntu, CPU/RAM/GPU hardware, defaults c = 1 and rho = 0.05, the additional backbone variant, and a source-code access link. These are newly disclosed reproducibility details, not evidence that the earlier experiments used different defaults.

E1.justification: v2 retains the facial-attribute datasets and transfer tasks, adds CheXpert pleural-effusion classification with gender as the sensitive attribute, and evaluates FairFace under unequal corruption severity across demographic groups. These substantially broaden the application domain and test conditions. Intersectional evaluation remains future work.

E2.justification: GroupDRO and MSAM are newly evaluated in the retained CelebA and FairFace comparisons in Tables 1–3, substantially expanding the fairness and robustness comparators. Existing comparator membership is retained, including SAM, GroupSAM, and FairSAM in the cross-dataset experiments.

E3.justification: Beyond v1's ResNet-18 evaluations, v2 introduces a DINOv3 backbone identified as ViT-S/16 distilled, asymmetric Gaussian severity assignments of level 4 versus level 5, and grids over rho = 0.01–0.10 and c = 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2. These are added evaluation configurations; the PDFs do not establish revisions to the retained experiments' settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds sensitivity studies testing dependence on perturbation radius and group-weight budget (Tables 7–8), plus asymmetric-corruption tests across two backbones (Tables 5–6). The earlier snow-severity analysis and CelebA/LFW transfer analyses remain, rather than being newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions state that experiments use three runs and omit standard deviations from the main comparisons. v2 introduces explicit mean ± standard deviation reporting in the sensitivity tables. No increased run count, confidence intervals, or significance testing is documented.

E6.justification: v2 adds baseline results and the medical, asymmetric-corruption, and sensitivity results in Tables 4–8. GroupDRO changes Table 2's accuracy-disparity ranking: 0.0080 versus FairSAM's retained 0.0395. Table 3 adds accuracy-disparity entries and corrects Vanilla's subgroup degradation from 0.2088 to 0.2008. Existing FairSAM benchmark scores and the cross-dataset results are retained.

M1.justification: v1 Sections 3.2–3.3 and v2 Sections 4.2–4.3 retain constrained instance reweighting, equal per-group weight budgets, and the weighted-gradient per-batch perturbation. Expanded explanations and mathematical corrections do not establish a different training or inference procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and methodological prose receive extensive editing. Related work moves from Section 5 to Section 2, the method gains explanatory paragraph headings, experiments receive a more differentiated structure, and a dedicated Discussion section is added. These changes substantially reorganize the narrative.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column format to a single-column journal layout. Tables expand from five to ten, existing comparisons gain rows, and FairFace gains an accuracy-disparity column. v1's scatter figure is removed, while its severity bar chart survives as v2 Figure 1. The transfer tables are relocated and reformatted.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially around distribution shift, adversarial fairness, and the distinction from natural corruption, with additional GroupDRO, WILDS, and related citations. A new subsection discusses fairness in language and diffusion models, and intersectional references support the limitations discussion. The earlier Khani–Liang noise-regression discussion is removed.

T1.justification: Equation 11 corrects the Taylor expansion by restoring the gradient–perturbation inner product and using an approximation sign. v2 also removes the positive-definite description of the low-rank Hessian and introduces a worst-case pairwise degradation-disparity definition for intersectional groups in Equation 17. No new theorem or proof is provided.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's narrow validation and sparse implementation documentation through additional comparators, medical-image and asymmetric-corruption evaluations, parameter sensitivity evidence, and implementation/access details. Mathematical corrections and explicit applicability limits also improve the paper. New numerical inconsistencies temper confidence in exact scores—for example, Table 4 reports FairSAM aggregate corrupted accuracy of 0.8034, exceeding both subgroup accuracies, 0.8013 and 0.7984. Nevertheless, the broader comparative evidence and improved transparency provide a substantial overall gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FairSAM research. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and end matter support comparison. Neither supplied PDF contains a separately labelled appendix.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and reports additional CheXpert, asymmetric-corruption, backbone, baseline, and hyperparameter-sensitivity results.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification experiments on CelebA and FairFace, corruption-severity analyses, and transfer experiments between CelebA and LFW.

results.title: FairSAM: Fair Classification on Corrupted Image Data Through Sharpness-Aware Minimization

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: independent subject-consistent generation without subject-specific tuning or reference images, contrastive pseudo-word learning, and potential extensions beyond single human subjects. Additional experiments support these existing claims.

C2.justification: Appendices C–E substantially expand interpretation: they explain the preference for MSE over perceptual losses, interpret interpolation and neighbor results as meaningful identity structure, and discuss hyperparameter tradeoffs. They also qualify segmentation reliability by the clean portrait setting and explicitly identify thorough multi-subject evaluation as future work.

D1.justification: Appendices B and D supply previously unspecified architecture and training settings, including an eight-layer MLP, 256-dimensional codes and 5,000 steps, plus hardware/runtime, filtering, LLM prompts and licensing information. The abstract now reports code and weights as available. Conversely, v2 omits v1's explicit description of fine-tuning the face-trained model on 10K cat/dog images.

E1.justification: Section 4.5 adds training and generation with LSUN car images, extending v1's human and cat/dog coverage. CelebA, Portraits, Scenes and the two-person generation scenario are retained.

E2.justification: v1's multi-subject Figure 6 shows only CoCoIns; v2's additional Figure 12 compares it with Consistory and StoryDiffusion in that setting. Comparator membership in the original Portraits and Scenes experiments remains unchanged.

E3.justification: The original 1K-prompt Portraits and Scenes protocols remain intact. Appendix C adds FID evaluation using 10K images from Scenes repeated ten times, with each method's own base generator as reference, plus fixed-noise latent analyses using 100 codes. Appendix D adds a 100-image segmentation audit. These supplement the original evaluation.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component ablations, v2 compares MSE and DreamSim losses, tests sensitivity to background weight and negative-distance schedule parameters, and examines latent interpolation and pseudo-word neighbors (Tables 9–12; Figures 8–9). The segmentation audit adds another diagnostic check, substantially broadening analysis of the method.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seed-based variability, confidence intervals or significance tests. The new random-code and segmentation samples are evaluation designs, not uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 1–5 retain their numerical values. New Table 8 reports FID values of 9.2 for CoCoIns, 13.3 for Consistory and 15.2 for StoryDiffusion, each against its own base model. Tables 9–12 and Figures 8–13 add loss comparisons, sensitivity findings, latent-space behavior and generation results, substantially expanding the evidence without changing the original benchmark scores.

M1.justification: The mapping network, pseudo-word insertion, frozen generator, masked contrastive loss, background preservation and negative-distance weighting schedule remain unchanged. Appendix B discloses implementation choices; the DreamSim variant in Appendix C is an ablation rather than a replacement method.

P1.justification: v2 polishes the main prose, standardizes terminology such as 'generations,' updates the title/front matter and reverses the order of the extension paragraphs. Appendices A–F organize additional explanations, while the original main narrative and section sequence remain largely intact.

P2.justification: The document switches from two columns to a single-column TMLR layout, with extensively reformatted tables, captions and figure placement. The original multi-subject and general-concept figures exchange numbers, the latter gains a car row, and Tables 6–12 and Figures 8–13 introduce substantial new displays.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to LSUN and Prompt-to-Prompt and expands the comparison of approach categories in Appendix A/Table 6. The main related-work taxonomy and novelty positioning remain unchanged; bibliographic corrections and citation-style changes are presentational.

T1.justification: Equations 1–9, the masked-distance construction and weighting schedule remain mathematically equivalent. The appendices add empirical and explanatory material, without new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs or derivations.

improvement.justification: Appendices B and D address important reproducibility gaps by specifying the training configuration and data preparation. The added loss, sensitivity and latent-space analyses substantially strengthen support for design choices while preserving the original results. These gains outweigh the reduced specificity of animal fine-tuning details. Uncertainty reporting remains absent, and the new FID evidence measures proximity to each method's own base distribution rather than quality against a common reference.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CoCoIns work, with readable text, equations, tables and figures that support reliable matching. The supplied v1 ends with references; v2 additionally contains Appendices A–F.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds FID evaluation, loss and hyperparameter comparisons, latent-space analyses and generated examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original generation experiments, quantitative comparisons and ablations in Tables 1–5, plus human, animal and multi-subject examples.

results.title: CoCoIns: Consistent Subject Generation via Contrastive Instantiated Concepts

C1.justification: V1 headlines new best-known two-deletion sizes at lengths 12, 13 and 16 and previously unknown optimal constructions. V2 emphasizes a proof of concept and VT rediscovery, acknowledges known non-uniqueness of short optimal codes, and qualifies multiple-deletion superiority against stronger graph solvers. Compute allocation, harmful summary-code co-evolution, deduplication's importance and quaternary-code construction become central contributions.

C2.justification: V2 distinguishes VT complements from constructions outside every VT class and discusses rediscovery versus memorization. It adds explanations for reasoning and co-evolution failures, interprets joint optimization as regularization, and analyzes the contributions of discovered heuristics. The retained exponential-scaling limitation is developed into specific encoder requirements, limited theoretical understanding and potential use as short inner codes.

D1.justification: V2 adds model-specific hyperparameters, computational-cost tables, batching and prefetch settings, immutable-graph documentation and graph statistics. Appendix A revises evaluator allocation from two CPU cores to one and timeout from five minutes to 30 seconds. The code-access statement changes from a promised FunDCC release to a stated DistributedFunSearch release. Conversely, v1's extensive verbatim prompt appendix is removed.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates binary deletion-correcting codes. V2 adds quaternary single-edit-correcting codes covering insertions, deletions and substitutions, searching lengths 6–9 and reporting results through length 11. Binary two- and three-deletion evaluation extends through length 18. Three-deletion evaluation and single-deletion checks through length 25 already existed in v1.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated OnlineMIS, ReduMIS and Gurobi comparisons, explicit Helberg–Ferreira construction results, and DoDo-Code for quaternary codes. V1 principally compares against VT sizes, Landjev–Haralambiev search results, a trivial lexicographic baseline and cited minimum-degree results. Random greedy existed in v1 Appendix J but now participates in the principal benchmark tables.

E3.justification: Main single-deletion searches change from a 400K-function limit with early stopping and 20K additional functions to 500K iterations. V2 introduces $120 inference-budget comparisons, a primary top-50 mean normalized-gap metric, and held-out evaluation of a function selected on search instances instead of per-length maxima across functions. Qwen3/Gemma 4 configurations and direct three-deletion optimization add further protocols; three-deletion testing itself is retained.

E4.justification: V2 adds extensive reasoning-on/off and code/summary/reflection/co-evolution ablations across Qwen3 and Gemma 4, plus individual removal of six heuristics from a discovered two-deletion function (Appendix F). Existing deduplication, graph-input, scoring and prompt analyses are revised. The GPT-4o mini comparison and random-greedy code-size distribution analysis from v1 are removed.

E5.justification: V1 already includes three repeated default runs, variability across islands and min-max ranges across discovered functions. V2 makes three seeded runs standard and reports across-run mean/min-max bands, including pooled 12-run and 9-run reasoning comparisons. Appendix A adds throughput mean ± SD over four measurement windows and run-level variability in computational costs.

E6.justification: Results are substantially replaced and expanded. For two deletions at length 16, v1 Table 4 reports a maximum of 204 across joint-search functions; v2 Table 2 reports 200 for its selected joint function and 215 for both KaMIS solvers. Changed selection and search conditions prevent interpreting 204 versus 200 as a same-setting decline. New results include quaternary size 40,604 versus DoDo-Code's 36,368 at length 11, and findings against reasoning and summary-code co-evolution.

M1.justification: The core greedy construction, island-based evolution, output-hash deduplication and reset scheme remain. V2 adds per-instance normalized-gap feedback to few-shot docstrings and implements summary, reflection and joint summary-code evolution variants with reasoning enabled or disabled (Section 5.2). These are procedural adaptations within the existing framework.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Method steps become numbered subsections, experiments are reorganized around correction tasks and ablations, Limitations becomes Scalability, and a Conclusion is added. Several separate appendices are consolidated, with much of the earlier hyperparameter evidence retained in condensed prose.

P2.justification: The presentation is substantially redesigned: solver-oriented comparison tables, cost-versus-gap plots with uncertainty bands, and computational-cost, hyperparameter and graph-statistics tables replace much of the earlier display structure. Overlap histograms, numerous prompt listings and several tuning plots disappear. The existing VT-equivalent function listing moves from v1 Figure 6 to v2 Figure 3.

R1.justification: V2 substantially repositions the work around scientific program discovery and inference-compute allocation. It adds discussion and citations concerning AlphaEvolve, ShinkaEvolve, OpenEvolve/CodeEvolve, classical graph solvers, DoDo-Code and low-redundancy deletion constructions. It also explicitly contrasts its distributed implementation with existing systems and develops the connection to inner codes, while pruning much of v1's broader application survey.

T1.justification: VT equivalence was already argued in v1 Appendix H. V2 Appendix E substantially rewrites the proof into separate priority and lexicographic-order claims: a conflicting VT word can have equal or one-higher priority, replacing v1's equal-priority argument. This changes mathematical reasoning, not merely presentation. V2 Appendix C also adds verification costs to the retained exhaustive-search complexity analysis.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical credibility. Its graph-solver comparisons expose limitations missing from v1's record-size claims, while selected-function held-out evaluation and repeated-run ablations provide stronger support for generalization and search-design conclusions. Appendix F also supplies direct evidence about discovered mechanisms. Removing detailed prompt listings weakens self-contained reproducibility, but the improved comparisons, uncertainty reporting and more carefully qualified claims outweigh that loss.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work by Weindel and Heckel. All 40 pages of v1 and 31 pages of v2, including their appendices, provide readable text, equations, figures and tables supporting a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original code-construction experiments, graph-solver comparisons, reasoning and prompting ablations, component analyses and computational measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original evolutionary-search experiments, constructed code sizes, prompt and hyperparameter comparisons, throughput measurements and repeated-run results.

results.title: LLM-Guided Search for Deletion-Correcting Codes

C1.justification: v2 broadens the abstract's superiority claim from Chamfer distance to shape similarity and physical-validity metrics, and removes the introduction's explicit 'first approach' assertion. The model, dataset and fitting contributions remain, with template-specific training now explicitly emphasized.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly discusses per-template retraining, capture/template mismatch and occlusions, collision-removal tradeoffs, and smoother material-optimized fittings at slightly worse target distance. It revises the subdivision interpretation toward negligible shape changes and topology-sensitive physical metrics, and explains HOOD/ContourCraft failures through their flat-rest-shape assumption.

D1.justification: v2 newly states code/data availability and supplies project and dataset access links. It adds exact corpus sizes, material initialization, fitting preprocessing and PyTorch3D implementation information. Conversely, it removes HOOD's stretching-to-Lame conversion, explicit baseline mesh sizes and the separate 50-step ablation specification. The main training recipe remains.

E1.justification: Appendix B extends the previously dress-only simulated coverage to a separately trained T-shirt model, evaluated on an unseen sequence. This is a bounded garment-design extension within the same deformation task; the AMASS-driven dress and 4DHumanOutfit fitting tasks remain.

E2.justification: ContourCraft is added to the evaluated comparison methods in Table 2 and Figure 3. HOOD and MGDDG remain; the comparator expansion is limited to one additional method.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 expands the combined-unseen test into separate unseen-shape, motion and material tests plus an all-unseen test. Seven shape/physical metrics replace the original three, including revised surface sampling. Subdivision becomes an added evaluation variant rather than the default subdivided evaluation. Captured-data fitting changes from four sequences to two with fixed-versus-optimized material conditions.

E4.justification: v2 adds latent-noise diversity examples, fixed-versus-optimized material fitting, a five-pose extension of the existing motion-conditioning analysis, and a seam-processing ablation. It removes the guidance ablation. The mesh-resolution analysis is retained and revised in Table 3 rather than simply deleted with v1's Table 4.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, statistical confidence intervals, significance tests or experimental uncertainty estimates. v2's varying-noise examples illustrate generative diversity rather than introduce statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The comparison and ablation results are extensively replaced and expanded. v1 Table 2 reports D-Garment CD of 2.395 cm; v2 Table 2 reports four test groups, including all-unseen ECD of 0.19 under revised conditions, so these are not direct performance gains. New T-shirt and longer-history results appear. Fitting changes from four sequence curves to material-strategy curves with 90th-percentile distances of 2.14 and 2.34 cm.

M1.justification: The generation backbone remains, but the fitting procedure changes substantially. v2 replaces Chamfer-plus-Laplacian fitting with robust Chamfer, an explicit collision penalty and additional normal-consistency and edge-length regularization, and introduces joint material/latent optimization (Sections 3.2 and 5.4). v1's optional temporal/collision-guided sampling branch is omitted.

P1.justification: v2 retitles the paper, revises the abstract and portions of the introduction, related work and experimental narrative, and changes terminology to emphasize physical grounding. The main section sequence remains, with a broader-impact statement and appendices added.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to predominantly single-column layout. Comparison and ablation tables are substantially restructured; baseline and fitting figures are replaced or expanded. New diversity, template/capture, T-shirt and seam figures are added, while the resolution analysis is merged into the main ablation table.

R1.justification: The existing positioning is extended with ContourCraft and additional simulation literature, including graph-network simulators and NeuralClothSim. New fitting/data references include Barron and GarmentCodeData, while Esser and Wallace references disappear. The central distinction between pose-dependent modeling and dynamic simulation remains.

T1.justification: Localized mathematical definitions change: v1's integral curvature error is replaced by an edgewise RMS dihedral-angle error, and v2 defines additional physical metrics in Section 5.1. The fitting objective is also revised. Neither version contains a theorem/proof framework; the principal diffusion training equations remain.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for physical conditioning: separate generalization tests, broader physical measurements, ContourCraft comparisons and targeted appendix analyses address limitations of v1's combined-unseen evaluation. Explicit template restrictions and fitting tradeoffs also improve claim calibration. Although HOOD setup details disappear and captured-sequence coverage shrinks from four to two, the stronger experimental design and clearer applicability boundaries outweigh these losses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe D-Garment and retain the same core model and dress dataset. Text, equations, tables and figures are readable throughout. v1 ends with references; v2 additionally contains readable Appendices A–D.

after.justification: v2 reports original simulation and captured-data experiments, with additional T-shirt results and pose-history and seam-processing analyses in the appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original garment simulations, baseline comparisons, ablations and fitting results on captured 4DHumanOutfit sequences in Section 5.

results.title: D-Garment: Physically Grounded Latent Diffusion for Dynamic Garment Deformations

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion broaden the stated scope of demonstrated effectiveness to wave propagation and shock problems. The central architectural contributions, frequency-aware loss, and up-to-50% parameter-saving claim remain. Rollout stability is more prominent in the abstract but was already claimed and investigated in v1.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive discussion of remaining shock-related errors, degradation during resolution transfer, patch-size and cutoff tradeoffs, and computational overhead. Appendix M distinguishes parameter efficiency from execution efficiency by acknowledging roughly 3.3-fold slower training and inference than base FNO in the reported comparison. These materially clarify practical limitations.

D1.justification: Appendices B, M, and O substantially expand data preparation, baseline configurations, batch sizes, hardware, and timing procedures. v2 specifies the H100 benchmarking environment and explains measured versus extrapolated trajectory runtimes. It also adds project-page access information and clearer 3D patch specifications; the PyTorch/NumPy implementation basis is retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds compressible Navier-Stokes turbulence, Wave-Gauss acoustic propagation, and the compressible Euler four-quadrant Riemann problem, extending evaluation to additional turbulent, wave, and shock phenomena. Appendix L also introduces actual zero-shot spatial super-resolution tests; v1 only discusses that capability.

E2.justification: Transolver is added to the retained Kolmogorov Flow and Diffusion-Reaction comparisons. The TRL3D comparison expands beyond v1's FNO, U-Net, and CNextU-Net to include LSM, differential-kernel NO-LIDK, and reported FNO/TFNO results from The Well. Appendix M additionally compares runtime with Athena++.

E3.justification: The main TRL3D configurations change from 18 to 12 global modes; LOGLO-FNO also changes from 48 to 52 channels and from learning rate 0.0044 to 0.0040. New protocols include time-averaged rollout windows, cross-resolution evaluation, controlled component/patch-size experiments, and hardware timing benchmarks. These extend beyond newly disclosed settings.

E4.justification: v2 replaces the Kolmogorov component-ablation tables in v1 Appendix K with fuller TRL3D loss/HFP isolation studies. It adds patch-size sensitivity, adaptive-noise and radial-cutoff ablations, TRL3D mode sensitivity, super-resolution robustness, and shock-error visualizations. The existing attention/SPHERE study and much spectral and correlation analysis remain.

E5.justification: v1 does not report seed-based experimental uncertainty. v2 Appendix N reports four-seed comparisons with 95% confidence intervals; Appendix K adds repeated-run means and standard deviations, including five-seed cutoff tests. Runtime measurements also gain repetition counts and uncertainty. Appendix K.5 explicitly discloses excluding one unstable run from its three-run summary.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive benchmark, ablation, super-resolution, uncertainty, and runtime results while largely retaining the original Kolmogorov and Diffusion-Reaction scores. New Wave-Gauss results favor LSM on nRMSE but LOGLO-FNO on mid/high-frequency errors. TRL3D scores are replaced under revised configurations, so their numerical differences do not establish same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The architecture, adaptive noise, SPHERE loss, and optional attention-fusion variant remain. However, Section 3.2 and Appendix D.2 revise the radial-loss normalization from 1/(Nx Ny Lx Ly) to (Lx/Nx)(Ly/Ny). This changes the general loss definition, although both pseudocode versions set Lx=Ly=1, making their implemented factors equivalent.

P1.justification: Much existing prose and the overall narrative remain. v2 clarifies tensor notation, expands metric explanations and the symbol glossary, reorders parameter-budget subsections, moves Algorithm 1 into the appendix, and separates main-text ablations from detailed appendix results. These are targeted editorial and structural refinements rather than wholesale rewriting.

P2.justification: Main comparison tables are redesigned as compact metric summaries, with full tables placed in Appendix G.2. v2 enlarges and relabels the architecture diagram, restyles equations and tables, and adds shock maps, sensitivity plots, super-resolution/timing tables, and confidence-interval figures. Existing spectral and correlation figures are largely retained and reformatted.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Poseidon, Transolver, Athena++, and Schwarz et al. on frequency bias. Appendix A more explicitly distinguishes patchwise spectral convolution and HFP from NO-LIDK. The broader related-work narrative and identification of NO-LIDK as the closest comparator remain.

T1.justification: Equation 3 specializes the general input-dependent local kernel to a convolutional kernel depending on x-y. Algorithm 1 corrects the formal radial aggregation and indexing, alongside the revised loss normalization. Appendix F's complexity derivations remain; the expanded descriptions of existing metrics do not constitute new theoretical results.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens component attribution, empirical breadth, uncertainty reporting, and transparency about computational costs—important gaps in v1's support for accuracy and efficiency claims. Sections 5 and Appendices K–N provide the decisive gains. Some limitations remain: the noise analysis excludes an unstable run, and the claim of best results on all TRL3D metrics conflicts with LSM's lower one-step vRMSE in Table 5. These shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial improvement in evidence and practical qualification.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LOGLO-FNO and provide readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices. Retained material can be matched across the substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds experiments on three further PDE problems, component ablations, super-resolution, computational cost, and variability across runs.

before.justification: v1 reports original neural-operator experiments on Kolmogorov Flow, Diffusion-Reaction, and Turbulent Radiative Layer 3D, including quantitative comparisons and appendix analyses.

results.title: LOGLO-FNO: Efficient Learning of Local and Global Features in Fourier Neural Operators

C1.justification: The central claims of parallel, evaluation-free posterior stacking and improved posterior approximation remain. v3 adds inexpensive ELBO-bias mitigation as a contribution in its outline and conclusion, replacing v1's deferral of debiasing to future work. Its introduction also explicitly limits the intended operating regime to approximately ten dimensions or fewer.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands applicability and limitations: inherited GP dimensional scaling, when ordinary MCMC is preferable, incomplete neuronal-posterior accuracy, and dependence of runtime advantages on likelihood cost. It explains that capping leaves residual bias and does not remove the bias-producing optimization mechanism. These qualifications and practical interpretations go well beyond v1's brief bias warning and overhead discussion.

D1.justification: v3 supplies Algorithm 1, weight initialization and softmax details, coordinate-transformation handling, entropy sample counts of 20 during optimization and 100 afterward, Adam learning rate 0.1, and processor/RAM specifications. It also reports filtering counts, provides an S-VBMC Python-package link, and revises neuronal model/data attribution. These are substantial reproducibility disclosures, without proving corresponding implementation changes.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the 2D clustered GMM, 2D narrow ring, five-parameter neuronal model, and six-parameter multisensory model using participant S1. The noiseless and Gaussian-noise scenarios remain the same. New analyses reuse these problems; revised neuronal-data attribution does not establish different task or population coverage.

E2.justification: v3 retains single-run VBMC and BBVI with 50 or 500 mixture components, while adding uniform Naive Stacking throughout the main comparisons and optimized posterior-only stacking in Appendix A.3.1. Tables A.3–A.4 confirm their participation. These controls substantially strengthen comparisons against simpler ways of combining the same VBMC outputs.

E3.justification: v3 reports an additional eligibility requirement, maximum component variance below 5, beyond v1's convergence requirement, and selects the first 100 eligible runs. Added analyses use true-log-joint Monte Carlo checks and define total parallel runtime as the slowest of 40 VBMC runs plus stacking. The main likelihood budgets, noise settings, and accuracy metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds controls testing whether weight optimization improves on averaging and whether component-level optimization improves on posterior-level optimization. Figures 6–7 diagnose expected-log-joint bias and compare two capping heuristics against Monte Carlo estimates. Appendices A.3.2 and A.4.1 add total-runtime and convergence-failure analyses. v1's run-count curves, noise comparisons, and posterior examples were already present.

E5.justification: The reported stacking repetitions increase from ten to twenty per stack size. Medians with interquartile ranges are replaced throughout by medians with 95% confidence intervals computed using 10,000 bootstrap resamples. Both versions use 100 retained VBMC runs; v3's newly disclosed attempted and excluded run counts do not establish how many attempts v1 required.
