E6.justification: v3 adds substantial results for Naive Stacking, posterior-only optimization, debiasing, total runtime, and filtering, while revising existing VBMC/S-VBMC estimates. For example, noiseless-ring S-VBMC with ten runs reports median delta-LML of 0.15 in v1 Table A.1 and 0.034 in v3 Table A.3. Changed selection and repetition protocols preclude treating this as an isolated algorithmic gain. Figure 7 newly shows capping containing bias growth.

M1.justification: The original component-weight optimization remains, but Section 5.2 introduces a substantive output correction: capping the estimated expected log-joint using either run-level or component-level medians. Appendix A.3.1 also introduces a variant optimizing only whole-posterior weights. The expanded softmax and Jacobian descriptions document implementation; they do not independently establish changes to the original algorithm.

P1.justification: v3 extensively reorganizes and expands the narrative. Background, algorithm, and experiments receive dedicated subsections; related work, model descriptions, metrics, BBVI details, overhead, and bias material move from appendices into the main exposition. A substantial discussion section and reorganized technical appendices replace the earlier compact structure, alongside extensive explanatory rewriting.

P2.justification: The synthetic-results figure is redesigned from two rows overlaying noise conditions into four separate condition rows with additional comparator displays. v1's synthetic posterior illustration and overhead figure move into the main text as v3 Figures 2 and 5. New bias and ablation figures, runtime/filtering tables, expanded comparison-table rows, revised captions, and a different document layout substantially change presentation.

R1.justification: The brief related-work paragraph becomes a substantially expanded positioning discussion. v3 adds historical stacking references such as Wolpert (1992) and Yao et al. (2018), additional divide-and-conquer and federated inference literature, and an explicit contrast with direct Bayesian-quadrature approaches including Osborne, Gunter, and Adachi. Existing distinctions from variational boosting and parallel MCMC are retained and developed.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds a substantive mathematical treatment of run-specific coordinate transformations, deriving consistent stacked densities, entropy calculations, and expected-log-joint corrections. Section 5.2 formally defines the capped estimators. The identical-posterior example explaining selection-induced bias already appeared in v1 Appendix A.8 and is retained in v3 Section 5.1; it is not a new theoretical result.

improvement.justification: v1 left ELBO debiasing unresolved and lacked controls separating optimized stacking from simple aggregation. v3 addresses these important gaps with Naive Stacking and posterior-only comparisons, direct Monte Carlo bias checks, and an empirically evaluated correction. Detailed algorithm and transformation documentation, filtering transparency, and clearer applicability limits substantially improve reproducibility and interpretability. The correction remains heuristic and leaves residual bias, but those acknowledged limits do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and technical completeness.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same S-VBMC research. All 24 pages of v1 and 38 pages of v3, including appendices, equations, tables, and figures, support comparison without material reading gaps.

after.justification: v3 reports original benchmark results and additional stacking comparisons, bias-correction experiments, runtime measurements, and convergence-filtering outcomes.

before.justification: v1 reports original posterior-approximation experiments on two synthetic and two neuroscience problems, including numerical results, posterior visualizations, and computational timings.

results.title: Stacking Variational Bayesian Monte Carlo

C1.justification: v1 principally claims convergence to controllable neighborhoods in O(epsilon^-2) iterations. v2's Contributions explicitly adds accuracy-dependent function-evaluation guarantees: O(epsilon^-4) for unconstrained variance-reduced optimization and O(epsilon^-6) for the constrained case, together with a Goldstein-stationarity guarantee. It also foregrounds general covariance analysis and explicitly identifies the objective setting as deterministic.

C2.justification: New Section 3.4 explains oracle accuracy and evaluation-cost tradeoffs, noise amplification through smoothing, and the implications of covariance and norm choices. It explicitly leaves noisy-feedback theory and second-order optimality open. Remark 5 adds discussion of coercive objectives and unbounded constraint sets, substantially expanding applicability and limitation analysis.

D1.justification: v2 documents the added covariance constructions, noise distributions, sampling counts, and smoothing settings, and reports function-evaluation costs for alternative oracles. Original implementation and dataset-access information remains. The new covariance experiment has a reporting inconsistency: Section 4.3 specifies 5,000 iterations, while Figure 3 shows a longer trajectory.

E1.justification: The original datasets and five application areas remain. Section 4.3 adds least-squares scenarios with additive noise on function evaluations, extending the input environment beyond v1's fixed measurement perturbations without introducing another dataset or application domain.

E2.justification: GDA and DS remain the least-squares comparators, and DS remains the poisoning and classification comparator. New Section 4.3 adds comparisons among forward, backward, and central-difference oracle variants and between single-direction and variance-reduced ZO-EG.

E3.justification: Original benchmark protocols are retained. New Section 4.3 introduces controlled covariance configurations, one versus 100 sampled directions, and smoothing parameters of 10^-5 and 10^-4. Appendix C adds numerical bound evaluations over 500 randomly selected parameter configurations for each theoretical setting.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained illustrative examples and lane-merging MVI check, v2 adds systematic investigations of covariance conditioning, oracle choice, output noise, sample count, and smoothing strength in Section 4.3. Appendix C additionally investigates covariance selection through numerical bound minimization. These substantially expand the examination of sensitivity and robustness.

E5.justification: v2 newly specifies five-run averaging for the covariance experiment and three-run averaging for the noisy-oracle experiments. The original ten-run means and standard deviations in Table 1 and twenty-run poisoning averages remain unchanged. No new confidence-interval or significance-testing practice is introduced.

E6.justification: Original benchmark results remain unchanged, including Table 1 times of 0.39, 0.21, and 24.56 seconds for ZO-EG, GDA, and DS. Added results show better convergence for condition-number-one covariance choices, advantages of central differences under stronger noise, and benefits from increased sampling and smoothing. Appendix C reports numerical support for condition-number-one bound minimizers.

M1.justification: The two-stage Gaussian ZO-EG core remains. v2 adds backward and central-difference oracle options, iteration-dependent batch sizes, and the B^-1-preconditioned variant in Appendix E, Algorithm 3; projections also use B-weighted geometry. Variance reduction itself already appeared in v1, Appendix C.

P1.justification: The overall section order and much existing prose remain. v2 expands the contribution explanations, moves variance-reduction Algorithm 2 from Appendix C into Section 2.2, and adds dedicated discussion subsections. Author affiliations and acknowledgments also change; the revision is primarily scientific expansion rather than wholesale narrative rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 3–5 for covariance and noisy-oracle studies and displays the new Algorithm 3. The original seven figures and Table 1 retain their content, with relocation and renumbering where necessary. The overall typography, table style, and page layout remain similar.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted references concerning alternative oracles, second-order optimality, coercivity, and mathematical background, including Malladi et al., Jin et al., and Daskalakis and Panageas. It also revises descriptions of prior works' stochastic, deterministic, and constraint settings. The central positioning around zeroth-order optimization under weak MVI assumptions remains.

T1.justification: v2 substantially revises the analysis using weighted primal and dual norms, explicit covariance eigenvalues, and condition-number-dependent assumptions and bounds. It adds variance-reduction theorems and accuracy-dependent query complexity, revises the constrained stationarity residual, and supplies corresponding proofs. New Appendices C and E develop covariance-selection reasoning and bounds for the preconditioned variant.

improvement.justification: v1 largely left the accuracy-dependent cost of variance reduction implicit. v2 supplies explicit batch-size prescriptions, function-evaluation bounds, and supporting derivations, making a central computational tradeoff assessable. Covariance analysis, controlled robustness experiments, and clearer applicability limits further strengthen technical completeness and practical interpretation. The localized iteration-budget inconsistency in Section 4.3 limits reproducibility of that experiment but does not outweigh these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ZO-EG research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial expansion and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds covariance and noisy-oracle experiments in Section 4.3 and numerical bound-selection investigations in Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original numerical experiments on toy functions, robust least squares, data poisoning, breast-cancer classification, and lane merging.

results.title: Min-Max Optimisation for Nonconvex-Nonconcave Functions Using a Random Zeroth-Order Extragradient Algorithm

C1.justification: The central novelty, original accuracy and speedup claims, and inverse-design contribution remain. The Introduction and Discussion add claims of robustness to noisy supervision and effective low-resolution hybrid training, including cavity-flow applicability with a qualification that this case requires data.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of physics losses suppressing noise fitting, random sampling reducing fixed-grid overfitting, and physics-only training failing for cavity flow. Section 2.3 clarifies that exact gradients refer to the computational graph, while Appendix G discusses nonsmooth components and higher-order residual instability. Conversely, the explicit statement that Poisson hybrid training was harder to tune is dropped.

D1.justification: Appendix C.3 adds cavity-flow architecture, optimizer, scheduler, training budget, sampling grids, and loss-component details. v2 also discloses smooth activations such as GeLU and lists Transolver tuning dimensions. Original experiment configurations and code-access information are retained, mostly through relocation; the activation discussion does not establish a switch from ReLU.

E1.justification: v2 adds incompressible Navier–Stokes lid-driven cavity flow at Reynolds number 500, predicting velocity and pressure over a specified time interval. It also adds noisy Burgers supervision as a distinct training scenario. The original four problem families remain.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Transolver with finite-difference physics losses to the Burgers comparison, reporting PDE residual 3.01e-2 and relative L2 error 7.47e-2. Existing PINO and Meta-PDE/FEniCS comparisons remain. Other newly discussed Transformer methods are cited rather than evaluated.

E3.justification: New protocols vary Burgers supervision resolution and Gaussian noise levels, and independently vary Poisson data and physics sampling counts. Cavity-flow experiments introduce a 3D FNO configuration, fixed versus randomly sampled training points, and separate test grids of 32×32×16 for PDE residuals and 64×64×50 for data loss. Original experimental settings are largely retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds hybrid-training data-efficiency studies for Burgers and Poisson, noise robustness comparisons, and cavity-flow ablations examining loss composition, sampling density, and fixed-grid generalization. The existing radius/weight-function ablation, derivative comparisons, and timing analyses are retained or relocated, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: The matched runtime comparison retains means over 200 instances and minimum–maximum shading in v1 Figure 4 and v2 Figure 7. Neither version reports independent training-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. New tables continue reporting point estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 4, 5, 7, and 10 add substantial results on data efficiency, noise, and cavity flow, alongside the new Transolver row. For example, at 50% noise, Table 5 reports true-solution relative L2 errors of 4.39e-2 for Autograd and 6.08e-2 for finite differences. Matched original tables retain their values. v1's airfoil forward-validation error of 0.0146 is omitted, while inverse-design coefficients remain unchanged.

M1.justification: v2 introduces ReLoBRaLo adaptive loss weighting for cavity-flow training; v1 discussed adaptive weighting only as future work. The core mollification strategy and mGINO composition remain. The changed mathematical distance definition is not reflected in the appendix pseudocode, so an implementation change there is unconfirmed.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is extensively reorganized into problem-description, comparison, and analysis subsections. Problem descriptions and the radius ablation move from appendices into the main text, methodological explanations expand, and future directions become a separate extended discussion. Language and terminology are also edited throughout.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from two-column to single-column layout. v2 combines the kernel and weight illustrations in Figure 1, splits v1 Table 4 into Tables 6 and 9, relocates appendix figures, and removes duplicate displays. It also adds initial-condition and cavity-flow illustrations and new analysis tables, including color-coded results.

R1.justification: v2 adds a dedicated discussion of Transolver/Transolver++, Unisolver, and PDEFormer, expands the positioning of physics losses relative to hard constraints, and connects future extensions to multiscale CNN, GNN, and FNO training. These additions substantially broaden research positioning beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: Section 3 changes d from squared normalized distance, ||x-y||^2/r^2, to ||x-y||_2/r while retaining weight formulas (9)–(12), changing their mathematical definitions. However, v2 Appendix D still specifies squared distances. The kernel differentiation identity and point-cloud finite-difference derivation are retained; no new proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence about when physics-informed training helps and fails. Tables 4, 5, 7, and 10 test noisy supervision, separate data sparsity from physics sampling, and expose cavity-flow failures under physics-only or fixed-grid training—questions not adequately tested in v1. The Transolver comparison and clearer organization further improve assessability. These gains outweigh the omitted airfoil forward-error value and the localized inconsistency between the revised weight definition and retained pseudocode.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same mollified graph neural operator research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds cavity-flow experiments, noise robustness tests, data-efficiency analyses, and an evaluated Transolver baseline.

before.justification: v1 reports original Burgers, nonlinear Poisson, hyperelasticity, and airfoil inverse-design experiments, including comparative errors, timing results, and ablations.

results.title: Enabling Automatic Differentiation with Mollified Graph Neural Operators

C1.justification: A central advertised theoretical guarantee is narrowed: the contribution schematic in Figure 1 replaces linear strong equivalence with 6-strong equivalence and the corresponding sixth-power SW bound. The conclusion also replaces preservation of geometric properties with reliance on Euclidean geometry. The proposed metric families and broad application claims remain.

C2.justification: V2 explains the practical compactness assumption and identifies unrestricted weak equivalence as conjectural. It adds interpretations of runtime bottlenecks and projection-count trends. For barycenters, it acknowledges loss of prominent input features and nearly unimodal intermediates, limits the toy example to computational feasibility, and interprets DSMW outputs as smoothed counterparts of SW point clouds.

D1.justification: V2 documents Sinkhorn regularization epsilon=0.1, explicitly states the clustering fit range k=2–9, and explains the ten-iteration stopping interval. It replaces v1's direct implementation repository link with a statement that code is supplementary and the repository will be available upon acceptance. That supplementary code is not contained in the supplied PDFs.

E1.justification: Figure 2 replaces two four-mode synthetic populations with six-mode populations, extending cluster-number detection to another ground-truth cluster count. CIFAR10, MNIST and their application tasks remain unchanged. The larger runtime configurations are setting changes rather than new task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds entropically regularized MW, computed using Sinkhorn iterations, to the actual runtime comparison in Table 1. V1 compares only MW, MSW and DSMW there. The application comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: V2 revises the reported MSW stopping rule to average changes across component pairs, retaining the 10^-3 threshold and ten-iteration interval. It adds runtime configurations with 1,000–10,000 components at d=50 and dimensions 1,000–3,000 at K=10, and reports projection counts. The stopping-rule revision does not establish that retained timings were recomputed.

E4.justification: Tables 2–3 extend scaling analyses and examine how projection counts vary with component count and dimension. The entropic-MW comparison additionally tests whether accelerating the outer transport removes the runtime bottleneck. The retained barycenter images receive new discussion rather than a new experimental analysis.

E5.justification: V2 explicitly identifies the timing summaries as mean plus-minus standard deviation; v1 displays unexplained plus-minus values. The original ten-pair runtime setting is unchanged, and no increased repetition count, confidence interval or significance test is reported.

E6.justification: V2 substantially extends the central efficiency evidence with entropic-MW timings and new runtime/projection-count tables. For example, DSMW takes 0.16 seconds at d=50, K=10,000 and 6.90±3.21 seconds at d=3,000, K=10; MSW exceeds 60 seconds in both settings. Figure 2 adds six-cluster convergence outcomes. Original Table 1 timings and CIFAR10/MNIST result images are retained, so these are added results rather than same-setting performance improvements.

M1.justification: The MSW, SMW and DSMW constructions, Algorithms 1–2, and DSMW quantization and barycenter optimization procedures are retained. The Gaussian-barycenter formula is mathematically corrected, but the PDFs do not describe a new construction or changed implementation.

P1.justification: V2 separates Numerical Analysis from Experiments and Applications, moving the existing application subsections into Section 5 and the conclusion into Section 6. It adds localized explanations, standardizes mathematical notation, edits affiliation text and removes the acknowledgements. Most existing prose and narrative order are retained.

P2.justification: Table 1 becomes a four-panel comparison, and Tables 2–3 add scaling displays. Figure 1 receives revised equivalence labels; Figure 2 replaces two examples and adds explanatory labeling; Figure 3 gains axis labels without changing its curves. Barycenter captions expand, while the remaining result imagery and overall visual organization are retained.

R1.justification: The single-cell application citation changes from Yachimura et al. (2024) to Lin et al. (2023), which was already cited elsewhere, and the Yachimura reference is removed. Positioning relative to the independently developed Nguyen mixture-distance papers remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Equation 3 replaces a linear Wasserstein/SW bound with exponent 1/[p(d+1)]. Theorem 3.2 consequently changes SMW ≤ C_P DSMW to SMW ≤ C_P DSMW^(1/6), with a revised proof using Jensen's inequality; Proposition 3.7 now bounds SW_2^6. V2 also corrects the moment definition and changes the Gaussian-barycenter formula from an unsquared Wasserstein objective to W_2 squared.

improvement.justification: The decisive gain is correction of an overstated central theoretical guarantee in Equation 3, Theorem 3.2 and Proposition 3.7, with a revised derivation. The entropic baseline, larger-scale timing evidence and explicit barycenter limitations also improve support and qualification of the conclusions. Removing the direct code link and introducing an unresolved citation placeholder reduce accessibility and polish, but do not outweigh these substantial scientific improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, methods and applications. All 22 pages of v1 and 23 pages of v2 support comparison through readable text, equations, tables and figures. Neither supplied PDF contains a separate appendix.

after.justification: V2 retains original application experiments and reports additional runtime and convergence results in Tables 1–3, alongside revised synthetic clustering results.

before.justification: V1 reports original runtime experiments, synthetic clustering results, CIFAR10 distortion comparisons, and MNIST-based quantization and barycenter experiments in Table 1 and Figures 2–6.

results.title: Slicing the Gaussian Mixture Wasserstein Distance

C1.justification: The central claim that noisy-label HPO enables more realistic and fair benchmarking remains. V2 refocuses RQ1 on identifying the best evaluated criterion and RQ2 on comparing approaches under that criterion, while foregrounding the ensemble framework in the introduction and conclusion. This refines the contribution's emphasis within the same research objective.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations involving double-dipping and class-specific bias to motivate its posterior construction. It also explicitly distinguishes selecting configurations from estimating their true generalization risk, retaining the need for clean test labels. Further qualifications address unequal computational costs, unexplored validation budgets, and potentially better untested ensemble subsets.

D1.justification: V2 clarifies how def-data transfers general hyperparameters while retaining approach-specific defaults, specifies an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X for timing measurements, and revises the reported run-accounting formula from 116,025 to approximately 151,900 runs. The existing code link and principal cluster hardware disclosures remain. The revised accounting does not independently establish additional executions.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate mgc, label-me, dopanim, reuters, and spc with the same seven label variants each. The revision from '35 datasets' to '5 datasets, each with 7 variants' clarifies existing coverage; no new domain, task, or label-noise scenario is introduced.

E2.justification: The evaluated selection-criterion comparison expands from nine to eleven criteria, replacing accuracy-based alternatives with the revised aggregation-level and crowd-level posterior criteria. The same 13 LFC approaches remain after matching abbreviations, but mv and the ground-truth reference newly receive ens results where v1 Table 5 reported N/A.

E3.justification: The candidate pool changes from 50 sampled configurations to 50 plus the default configuration. The stated default training length changes from 50 epochs in v1 Table 4 to 30 in v2 Table 3. New analyses introduce loss-reduction, win-rate, and Kendall correlation measures. Splits, architectures, and fivefold validation remain unchanged; these reported revisions do not establish wholesale reruns.

E4.justification: V2 adds a sequential ensemble-member removal ablation in Table 7, Kendall rank-correlation distributions in Figure 7, pairwise win-rate analyses in Figures 10 and 12, and a computational-overhead case study in Figure 8. These examine ensemble composition, ranking agreement, comparison consistency, and practical cost beyond v1's average-rank analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions report five test weight initializations and mean-plus-standard-deviation appendix results. V2 additionally reports standard errors for aggregate ranks, loss reductions, and ensemble ablations in Tables 4, 5, and 7 and associated plots. It does not report an increase in repeated test runs or introduce significance testing.

E6.justification: The appendix results are substantially revised and expanded. For example, mgc-worst-2 ens loss for geo-reg-w/geo-w is replaced from 56.87±0.80% in v1 Table 5 to 49.93±1.42% in v2 Table 8. V2 Table 4 newly reports ens's aggregate 5.15-percentage-point reduction against def. These are results under revised criteria/settings, not controlled cross-version gains. Dataset statistics also change, including label-me-rand-v aggregation noise from 23.7% to 25.0%.

M1.justification: Section 3.4 replaces direct accuracy-weighted aggregation and loss weights with a posterior-based framework using uniform class priors, simplified worker likelihoods, MAP aggregation, and posterior-confidence weights. Learned aggregation now uses logarithmic odds weights rather than accuracy itself. The ensemble retains rank aggregation but combines seven individual risk criteria instead of five.

P1.justification: The introduction, methodological exposition, experimental discussion, and recommendations are extensively rewritten. V2 introduces consistent hyperparameter-selection terminology, shorter approach names, structured paragraph headings, and a hierarchical explanation of criteria. It reorganizes the appendices around inference, theory, and experiments and adds broader-impact and acknowledgement sections.

P2.justification: V1's main ranking heatmaps are replaced by aggregate tables and loss-reduction plots with error bars. The criterion catalogue becomes a hierarchy diagram, and the HPO diagram is redrawn. V2 adds correlation, runtime, win-rate, and ablation displays, reorganizes table groupings, and substantially changes typography and page layout.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations supporting default-setting fairness, double-dipping, Borda rank aggregation, Kendall correlation, metalearning, and societal impacts. Table 1 adds early-stopping comparisons and the existing dopanim study as a survey row. The central positioning around the lack of systematic noisy-crowd-label HPO remains; the Wei citation's year update identifies the same work.

T1.justification: V2 introduces a posterior/Bernoulli formulation and Appendix B's three propositions with proofs concerning prior bias, confusion-probability bias, and MAP equivalence to logarithmically weighted majority voting. It also adds a stepwise worst-case complexity analysis in Table 6. V1 contains risk and inference definitions but no corresponding propositions or complexity analysis.

improvement.justification: V1 supports its ensemble recommendation mainly through average-rank comparisons. V2 substantially strengthens that evidence with loss effect sizes and standard errors, component-removal ablations, pairwise comparisons, and measured overhead, while clarifying the need for clean test labels to assess actual generalization. These additions improve the paper's evidential basis and practical interpretation. An unresolved reporting discrepancy—the default changing from 50 to 30 epochs while all def scores remain identical—limits protocol certainty, but does not outweigh the substantial analytical improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe crowd-hpo by the same authors. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revisions and reorganization.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendices B–C report original benchmark results, ensemble ablations, rank-correlation analyses, and runtime measurements.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix B report original benchmarking experiments involving 13 learning-from-crowds approaches and 35 dataset variants, including test losses over five weight initializations.

results.title: crowd-hpo: Realistic Hyperparameter Optimization and Benchmarking for Learning from Crowds with Noisy Labels

C1.justification: The central contribution remains efficient, unified restoration without external prompts. The abstract revises parameter/FLOP savings from approximately 82%/85% to 84%/80%. The conclusion more explicitly restricts the model's scope to degradations covered by current all-in-one benchmarks, refining the earlier broad 'any image' framing.

C2.justification: v2 introduces a multi-environment, degradation-invariant representation interpretation and connects training-distribution balance to the learned reconstruction prior. Appendix E adds substantive limitations concerning globally uniform corruption, degradation concentrated in one domain, and reduced global-modeling flexibility. It explicitly excludes unrestricted restoration of arbitrary degradations; v1 primarily discussed component complementarity and dataset imbalance.

D1.justification: Appendix A and Table 11 supply dataset counts, training budgets, Adam settings, loss descriptions, crops, augmentation, batch size, GPUs and explicit Tiny/Small configurations largely absent from the supplied v1 PDF. Code availability changes from promised to stated available. These improve documentation without proving implementation changes. Reproducibility remains limited by conflicting epoch counts between A.1 and A.2.

E1.justification: v2 adds zero-shot underwater enhancement on UIEB, extending evaluation to a distinct real-world domain. Its CDD11 comparison also expands from two triple-degradation scenarios in v1 Table 5 to eleven single, double and triple combinations in v2 Table 3. The principal three- and five-degradation benchmarks and unseen CSD evaluation remain.

E2.justification: The main three- and five-degradation comparator sets remain. However, the CDD11 comparison adds WGWSNet and WeatherDiff and removes TransWeather; CSD adds MoCE-IR-S, and the complexity comparison adds full-sized MoCE-IR. v1's extensive single-task comparison table disappears, although its PromptIR/AnyIR deraining comparison survives in v2's capacity analysis.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include Tiny/Small configurations, depth and prompt controls, fusion-weight alternatives, and training-data rebalancing using approximately 90% of the original samples. Appendix A specifies evaluating the five-degradation checkpoint on 890 UIEB images without fine-tuning. These are additional experimental designs; newly disclosed settings alone do not establish changes to retained experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds capacity and prompt-removal controls in Table 9, spatial-only versus frequency-only versus fixed/learnable fusion in Table 10, and data-distribution sensitivity in Table 12. Appendix B adds PCA and t-SNE representation analyses. The earlier component ablations, channel-activation analysis and SVD analysis remain, rather than constituting new analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions report unexplained plus/minus quantities for FLOPs, without run counts, seeds, restoration-score uncertainty or significance tests. v2 changes these values and adds rows but does not introduce a different uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces AnyIR's 32.83 dB average with 32.80/32.86 for Tiny/Small. Table 2 revises PromptIR's average from 29.15 to 29.72 dB. Table 6 replaces AnyIR's 6.29M parameters/19G FLOPs with 5.74M/26G and 8.51M/39G configurations. Numerous underwater, CDD11, ablation and timing results are added, while most single-task entries disappear. These are not established same-setting gains. v2 Table 2 reports Tiny's average as 30.71, although its five scores average approximately 30.55.

M1.justification: The skip-split architecture, attention pathway, GatedDA and spatial-frequency fusion procedure remain substantially unchanged. As written, Algorithm 1 adds a small constant delta inside the standard-deviation square root. Newly disclosed losses and the learnable fusion weight do not establish changes from v1's unspecified implementation choices.

P1.justification: The introduction and method explanation are substantially rewritten around inverse problems and degradation-invariant learning. The former method overview becomes separate preliminaries and framework subsections, experimental organization changes, and appendices organize protocols, analyses, additional results, limitations and broader impact. These constitute extensive narrative restructuring beyond simply adding experiments.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column conference layout to a single-column journal layout. The overview moves from Figure 1 to Figure 4, and retained figures are resized or rearranged. New diagrams, underwater examples and appendix visualizations appear; the CDD11 table expands to eleven scenarios, and tables gain model-variant rows and second-best highlighting.

R1.justification: Sections 2-3.1 substantially expand positioning through four architectural paradigms, multi-environment learning, and explicit comparison with expert routing. New references include the Jiang et al. survey, Tang et al.'s unified restoration work and Perceive-IR; numerous single-task and peripheral references disappear. Publication updates to retained works are not treated as new citations.

T1.justification: New Section 3.1 explicitly defines the degradation observation model and four encoder-decoder mapping paradigms, adding a limited mathematical formulation of the problem and architectural distinctions. No theorem, proof or formal generalization guarantee is added; the principal attention and fusion equations are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central efficiency and generalization argument: Appendix A supplies previously missing implementation information, Tables 9-10 test capacity and fusion alternatives, and expanded CDD11/UIEB evaluations and Appendix E better establish applicability and boundaries. These gains outweigh the loss of most single-task comparisons and reporting defects, notably the incorrect Tiny average in Table 2, stale five-degradation discussion and conflicting epoch counts. Those defects limit confidence in exact figures, but the added validation and documentation materially improve the paper's assessability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AnyIR, with matchable algorithms, experiments and figures. All supplied pages are readable, including v2 Appendices A-F. v1 ends with references despite mentioning separate supplementary material; newly supplied appendix content is assessed as newly documented evidence.

after.justification: v2 retains original restoration experiments and reports additional underwater evaluation, model variants, ablations, data-balancing results and inference-time measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original restoration experiments, unseen and mixed-degradation evaluations, efficiency measurements, component ablations and feature analyses.

results.title: Any Image Restoration via Efficient Spatial-Frequency Degradation Adaptation

C1.justification: The unified-model and competitive generation/prediction claims remain. v3 adds improved small-molecule conditional control as an explicit headline contribution and sharpens the novelty claim around alternating attention during both pretraining and fine-tuning. OOD prediction, representation learning and peptide-design benefits were already claimed in v1.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive limitations concerning shared-capacity trade-offs, restricted model scale, fixed descriptors and uncertain transfer to other modalities. It interprets temperature-dependent fidelity/diversity trade-offs, qualifies OOD superiority as statistically nonsignificant, and treats peptide perplexity as balancing plausibility and novelty rather than simply requiring minimization. Extended discussion also addresses continuous-property tokenization and future molecular-interaction modeling.

D1.justification: v3 adds a code-repository link and extensive reproducibility disclosures: dataset access information, peptide filtering and construction, hardware and precision, sequence padding, gradient clipping, task-specific fine-tuning settings, layer freezing, sampling runtime and acceptance counts. Appendices E–H substantially extend v1's shorter implementation appendix. These are documented details and access claims; external resource availability was not verified.

E1.justification: v3 adds property-conditioned small-molecule generation targeting QED, SA and logP, plus MOSES evaluation. Peptide pretraining expands to general-purpose Peptipedia/UniProt sequences, while the downstream study focuses on MIC-conditioned design instead of separate AMP-classification and MIC arms. GuacaMol, MoleculeNet and Lo-Hi coverage is retained.

E2.justification: v3 adds task-specific non-joint Hyformer controls to conditional generation, Lo-Hi and representation probing. Conditional generation compares against MolGPT and GraphGPT variants, while MOSES includes additional comparators such as HMM, NGram and LatentGAN. Conversely, the Uni-Mol without 3D comparison in v1 Table 2 is removed from v3 Table 5.

E3.justification: Reported pretraining settings change substantially: GuacaMol augmentation decreases from 10x to 2x, batch size increases from 512 to 1024, warm-up increases from 2,500 to 5,000 steps, and the larger-model budget increases from 200K to 250K iterations. Generation changes from top-k=25 at temperature 1.0 to top-k=10 across three temperatures. Peptide evaluation replaces entropy/Jaccard metrics with diversity, fitness and additional prediction oracles. These reported revisions do not establish which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 directly tests joint training through non-joint controls for conditional generation, OOD prediction and probing. It adds temperature sensitivity, conditional-sampling acceptance analysis and per-target ClinTox F1 analysis. The original augmented/unaugmented generation comparison disappears, and the nine-molecule qualitative example is replaced by temperature-specific and property-conditioned examples. The PCA representation analysis is retained.

E5.justification: v3 adds parenthesized uncertainty estimates to GuacaMol generation results and reports peptide means and standard deviations over 100 bootstrap iterations. It introduces 95% significance qualifications for predictive comparisons, explicitly noting that Lo-Hi differences are not significant. The three-seed reporting already present for MoleculeNet and Lo-Hi remains; no increase in those run counts is established.

E6.justification: New conditional-generation, MOSES and non-joint-control results substantially expand the evidence. Lo-Hi Hyformer means change, including KDR-Hi from 0.689 to 0.701 and Sol-Hi from 0.600 to 0.640, changing the latter's ranking relative to Chemprop. GuacaMol and peptide result sets are replaced under revised settings. Retained MoleculeNet prediction scores and existing probing rows are unchanged; revised scores should not be interpreted as controlled version-to-version gains.

M1.justification: The reported 50M backbone depth changes from 8 layers in v1 Table 6 to 12 in v3 Table 7. The central alternating-attention mechanism, training losses and generation-then-filtering procedure remain unchanged. The added conditional-sampling pseudocode elaborates the existing procedure.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and substantial experimental discussion are rewritten. Retained experiments are reorganized into synergistic benefits, standalone generative/predictive performance and peptide design. Conclusions become a discussion with limitations, and the appendices are reorganized into separate discussion, notation, proofs, benchmark definitions, implementation and additional-experiment sections.

P2.justification: v3 adds conditional-generation and MOSES tables, restructures the generation and peptide tables, and introduces shaded comparison rows. Figure 2 is redrawn with the separate conditional amino-acid distribution panel removed. The original molecule plate is replaced by multiple temperature and conditioning plates. The architecture diagram is retained, and the identical PCA plot moves from Figure 4 to Figure 9 within a substantially revised journal layout.

R1.justification: v3 expands positioning to include 3D molecular generators and UniGEM, explicitly distinguishing their scope from SMILES-based joint modeling. Appendix B provides a substantive comparison with the already-cited Dong et al. alternating-attention work, emphasizing supervised objectives and use during fine-tuning. Additional peptide-data and evaluation references broaden the supporting literature beyond bibliographic formatting changes.

T1.justification: v1's conditional-sampling lemma and mismatched point/threshold proof are replaced by the event-conditioning identity in v3 Equation 12. Appendix D.1 adds a softmax-Jacobian lemma and masked-attention corollary. This is a limited formal addition, and Corollary D.2 incorrectly identifies j<t as masked although its stated causal mask excludes j>t.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the evidence for synergies that v1 largely inferred from comparisons with different models. Direct non-joint controls, especially conditional generation in Tables 1–3, address that weakness; Table 1 reports average MAD of 0.018 versus 0.059 for the non-joint variant. Multiple peptide oracles, bootstrap uncertainty, explicit limitations and fuller implementation details further improve assessment and reproducibility. Removing the no-3D Uni-Mol comparison loses useful evidence, and the gradient corollary contains an indexing error, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial empirical and documentation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Hyformer, with matching core methods and identifiable corresponding experiments. Text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are sufficiently readable for comparison, including the image-only appendix figures.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds conditional molecule generation, non-joint controls, MOSES evaluation and revised peptide experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original Hyformer results for molecular generation, property prediction, representation probing, hit identification and antimicrobial peptide generation, alongside qualitative appendix analyses.

results.title: Synergistic Benefits of Joint Molecule Generation and Property Prediction

C1.justification: The abstract's central convergence-ordering and conditioning claims remain. A fourth introductory contribution and the expanded conclusion extend the claims to finite-sample full-batch and stochastic settings, distinguishing NGD superiority with tuned rates from sandwich ordering with equal small rates.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands applicability qualifications: the unknown transient before asymptotic bounds apply, local versus nonlinear discrete-time behavior, and exact versus approximate Fisher information. Section 4.1 corrects the perturbation interpretation from the Fisher matrix to its inverse. The conclusion adds a conditional route toward K-FAC guarantees and discusses the limits of extending the results beyond the simplex.

D1.justification: The new experiments document empirical-frequency target construction, uniform mini-batch sampling, a learning-rate decay formula, and numerical learning rates in Tables 1–2. Reproducibility remains limited because the dataset size, batch size, stopping tolerance, and decay parameter are unspecified; no code or data access information is added.

E1.justification: The task remains KL minimization over synthetic discrete distributions. Section 5 adds a target-access scenario in which optimization uses finite observations rather than exact target probabilities; no real-world dataset or separate application domain is introduced.

E2.justification: The comparisons retain Euclidean gradient methods in η and θ coordinates against natural gradient, including their corresponding stochastic versions. K-FAC appears only in future-work discussion and is not evaluated.

E3.justification: v2 adds n = 10 simulations and finite-sample discrete-time protocols, including full-batch and mini-batch updates. Section 5 compares equal small learning rates with individually tuned rates and measures convergence by the maximum iterations across 100 initializations to a fixed tolerance. These are new protocols, not documented reruns of the retained continuous-time experiments.

E4.justification: Figures 9 and 11 add substantial learning-rate sensitivity analyses for full-batch and stochastic optimization, testing when NGD's advantage emerges. Figures 6–7 also examine whether the convergence ordering persists at higher dimension. The earlier curvature analysis and nonconvexity counterexample are retained, with the latter relocated.

E5.justification: Both versions report variation across 100 random initializations, and v2 extends this convention to additional experiments. Neither introduces seed identifiers, confidence intervals, significance tests, or a new uncertainty-reporting practice. The new maximum-iteration statistic serves as a performance metric rather than an uncertainty estimate.

E6.justification: The original n = 2 convergence findings remain. New n = 10 flow results report rates approximately 16.239, 0.099, and 1.974 for η-GD, θ-GD, and NGD. Under the newly tuned empirical settings, Table 1 reports 29, 12, and 2 iterations respectively; Table 2 reports 41, 20, and 3 for stochastic updates. These are added results, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The original GD/NGD framework and Fisher geometry remain unchanged. Section 5 adds empirical-target and mini-batch stochastic adaptations, with explicit update equations and a decaying learning rate, rather than replacing the underlying method.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized: main-text proofs move into Appendix C, the former nonconvexity appendix moves into Section 3, and references precede the appendices. Explanations of convergence and limitations expand, and a dedicated empirical section is inserted before the conclusion.

P2.justification: The five original figures are retained and rearranged, including the nonconvexity plot becoming Figure 2. v2 adds Figures 6–12 and three tables covering higher-dimensional behavior, empirical trajectories, learning-rate sensitivity, and theory–experiment correspondence. Typography, captions, and page layout are also extensively reformatted.

R1.justification: Bullo's Lectures on Network Systems is removed together with the LaSalle-based argument in Appendix A. The remaining cited works and principal research positioning are retained; venue and bibliographic updates do not represent new references.

T1.justification: v2 materially revises assumptions and proofs. Theorem 7 requires a uniform perturbation margin below 1, correcting v1 Theorem 4.3's pointwise bound. Appendix A's Theorem 9 restricts v1's arbitrary-initialization reverse-KL result to sufficiently small initial divergence and replaces its global argument with local reasoning. Theorem 3's proof also revises the compactness argument and explicitly establishes the local T = 0 case. Other proofs are largely relocated.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important theoretical deficiencies through the uniform stability margin in Theorem 7 and the appropriately restricted reverse-KL theorem in Appendix A. The new experiments directly test learning-rate-dependent comparisons in finite-sample and stochastic settings, while expanded limitations clarify what the theory establishes. These provide substantial gains in rigor and evidential support, although the experiments remain synthetic and incompletely specified for reproduction.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work by Datar and Ay. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and relocated material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains those simulations and adds higher-dimensional experiments and finite-sample full-batch and stochastic optimization results, including Tables 1–2.

before.justification: v1 reports original numerical simulations of gradient flows, including measured convergence rates over 100 random initializations in Section 3 and Figures 2–4.

results.title: Convergence Properties of Natural Gradient Descent for Minimizing KL Divergence

C1.justification: The abstract, five introductory contributions, and conclusion largely retain their original claims. v3 more explicitly defines the mobile-centered scope and positions its contribution through mobile-specific comparative analysis, including the quantitative benchmark comparison highlighted in Table 1.

C2.justification: New Sections 4.6, 5.3, and 6.4 substantially develop design trade-offs and limitations: perception latency, persistent memory, specialization versus generalization, shallow annotations, unrealistic task scenarios, and unreliable automated judging. Section 7 adds a more detailed security and ethical analysis and connects future directions to the new performance synthesis.

D1.justification: v3 identifies sources and backbone configurations for the new score compilation and expands technical summaries of surveyed systems, including model sizes and training pipelines. These improve documentation without establishing new implementations or changed experimental settings. The existing GitHub collection remains the same resource.

E1.justification: New resources such as JEDI, LearnGUI, and Mobile-Bench-v2 are surveyed rather than used in newly conducted training or testing. Table 11 adds reported scores on benchmarks already discussed in v1, rather than establishing new experimental task coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates a proposed agent against experimental baselines. Table 11 introduces a literature-based comparison of existing systems, but no baseline set for evaluating the paper's own method is added or revised.

E3.justification: Section 6.3 introduces aggregation rules for the new performance comparison: averaging ScreenSpot mobile text/icon scores, macro-averaging GUI-Odyssey results across four splits, and distinguishing AndroidControl single-step success from AndroidWorld task success. These are reporting and aggregation choices, not evidence of experimental reruns.

E4.justification: No new ablations, sensitivity experiments, robustness tests, or empirical case studies are reported. The expanded discussions of benchmark brittleness, interruptions, and evaluation failures are interpretive analyses rather than newly executed tests.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for an original evaluation. Table 11 supplies point scores without adding uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v3 adds a substantial numerical comparison in Table 11, absent from v1: examples include UI-R1 at 90.2 on ScreenSpot, UI-TARS-72B at 88.6 on GUI-Odyssey, and Mobile-Agent-v3 at 73.3 on AndroidWorld. These are newly reported literature-derived results, not same-setting improvements over v1. Existing DigiRL and DistRL numerical claims are retained.

M1.justification: The contribution remains a survey and taxonomy, without a newly proposed operational agent. Added descriptions of systems such as Mobile-Agent-v3 and ZeroGUI concern cited methods, not changes to an algorithm introduced by this work.

P1.justification: The narrative gains a standalone related-work section and comparative synthesis subsections following the framework, modeling, and resource reviews. The future-directions section is extensively rewritten around trade-offs and capability gaps, producing substantial structural change despite retention of much earlier descriptive prose.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column presentation, expands the taxonomy and milestone figures, and enlarges existing survey tables. Eight new tables provide comparisons, performance summaries, limitations, and security classifications; Figure 11 adds an automated-evaluation diagram. Many earlier displays remain under new numbering.

R1.justification: v3 adds a dedicated Related Work section and survey-comparison table, substantially expands coverage of 2025 agents and security research, and explains why selected desktop and web methods inform phone automation. This materially strengthens and revises the survey's positioning beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: The POMDP states, actions, transition probabilities, and observations in v1 Section 3 are retained in v3 Section 4. No new theorem, proof, substantive mathematical definition, or derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's predominantly descriptive treatment by adding structured comparisons of architectural and modeling trade-offs and detailed diagnoses of dataset and evaluation weaknesses. Sections 4.6, 5.3, and 6.4 make the survey more useful for choosing approaches and identifying research gaps. Table 11 also provides a useful numerical overview, although its heterogeneous models and single-step versus whole-task metrics limit the broad claims about RL superiority and online/offline performance. Those limitations temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains in analytical depth.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same survey and retain its central taxonomy and conceptual framework. Text, tables, figures, and references support comparison. Neither supplied PDF contains a separately labeled appendix.

after.justification: Section 6.3 describes calculating averages for Table 11 but also says performance data comes primarily from existing studies. It does not distinguish newly computed analysis results from reproduced scores, leaving the originality of this quantitative synthesis uncertain. No new model experiments are identified.

before.justification: v1 surveys existing research. Numerical findings, including the DigiRL and DistRL improvements, are attributed to cited studies; no original empirical study is reported.

results.title: LLM-Powered GUI Agents in Phone Automation: Surveying Progress and Prospects

C1.justification: The title, abstract and contribution bullets replace explicit physics and physical-knowledge framing with parameterized model knowledge and object-centric motion knowledge. This modestly narrows the contribution's characterization. The central three-stage refinement claim, complex-motion benefits and headline comparison between 1.5B- and 13B-parameter models remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of Stage 1's scene and camera priors, depth-based occlusion handling, motion conditioning versus textual guidance, and confidence values as condition indicators. It also interprets PMP as a general motion denoiser. Existing limitations largely move unchanged to Appendix D, leaving its long-video future-work statement unreconciled with Section 5.1's new demonstration.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies shared PMP training across categories, pose-MSE supervision, the annotated dataset's approximately 55% human/15% animal/30% general-object composition, and absence of target poses in the original preference study. It also documents long-video window stride, overlap and blending. These are useful additions to documentation; the existing annotation pipeline and project-access information remain.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained Panda-70M subset, daily-activity evaluations and TikTok dances, v2 evaluates general video generation on VBench++, motion transfer on DAVIS, and standalone human-motion refinement on HumanML3D and KIT-ML. It also demonstrates 128-frame generation. These substantially broaden the evaluated data and task requirements.

E2.justification: v2 adds comparisons with video generators including Wan2.1, DynamiCrafter, Step-Video-TI2V, Gen-4-I2V and Magi-1; DAVIS comparators MotionClone, ImageConductor and Go-with-the-Flow; and motion-generation comparators MotionDiffuse, ReMoDiffuse and MoMask. Disco is removed from the dance-results table, although its dataset split remains in use. The original SVD and HunyuanVideo preference comparisons remain.

E3.justification: v2 introduces Wan2.1 backbone evaluation, VBench++ metrics, DAVIS motion-transfer metrics and Top-1/2/3 R-Precision evaluation. Its efficiency experiment reduces Stage 1 resolution to one quarter, frames from 16 to 8, and denoising steps from 50 to 32. New occlusion ratings exclude responses without interactions. The former Stage 1/Stage 3 comparison is described as without/with PMP, without establishing whether the control or experiments actually changed.

E4.justification: v2 adds an efficiency-versus-quality preference study (Table 8), sensitivity to three confidence encodings (Table 9), prompt and motion-strength examples (Figure 11), and an occlusion case study and targeted preference evaluation (Figure 6, Table 4). The original mesh analysis is retained in Appendix C. The relabeled PMP study retains the earlier stage-comparison scores and is not additional numerical evidence.

E5.justification: Both versions report seed 42 for the main paired-generation study and three raters per pair. v2 adds studies using descriptive scores and preference percentages but introduces no repeated-run uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests.

E6.justification: The full-motion TikTok row changes from SSIM 0.842 and FVD 137.53 in v1 Table 2 to 0.864 and 121.26 in v2 Table 5; target-pose FVD remains 130.14, and image-only FVD 136.43 is added. New benchmark and ablation tables substantially expand reported findings. Runtime changes from 77 to 49 seconds under reduced Stage 1 settings, rather than an unchanged evaluation configuration.

M1.justification: The three-stage pipeline, conditioning channels and perturbation-based prior training remain; PPPM is renamed PMP. v2 adds a long-video inference extension using motion interpolation/extrapolation and overlapping 32-frame clips with blended boundaries (Section 5.1), which v1 left to future work. Newly stated MSE supervision does not establish a changed training objective.

P1.justification: v2 reorganizes the manuscript by moving detailed dataset construction, the mesh analysis and limitations into Appendices B–D, and restructuring the main experimental narrative around PMP. Stage 1 receives substantial explanatory expansion. The title and PPPM/PMP terminology change throughout, and the appendix gains a broader-impact section.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column layout to a single-column journal format. Figure 4 adds paired SVD comparisons; the stage visualization is rearranged into without/with-PMP pairs; and new benchmark tables, occlusion examples, long-video examples and conditioning visualizations are introduced. Existing mesh and architecture figures are retained and relocated or renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 substantially extends positioning into direct motion generation, motion-transfer systems and newer video backbones, citing and discussing methods such as MoMask, MotionDiffuse, Go-with-the-Flow and Wan2.1. Section 4.2 newly contrasts direct motion models' scene and camera limitations with motion extracted from video generators. The original related-work discussion is largely retained.

T1.justification: The diffusion equations, parametric-mesh definitions and 21-point general-object representation are retained, with some mathematics reformatted or relocated. Neither version provides theoretical propositions or proofs, and v2 adds no substantive formal derivation.

improvement.justification: v1's broad applicability claims rested mainly on SVD preference studies and a dance benchmark. v2 substantially strengthens their support through evaluation with another backbone, general-video and motion-transfer benchmarks, standalone motion refinement, and targeted efficiency and sensitivity tests. Added training details also improve assessability. These gains outweigh the unresolved relabeling of the stage comparison as a PMP ablation and the appendix's inconsistent long-video limitation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ReVision research. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched despite the changed title, terminology and organization.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds VBench++, DAVIS, HumanML3D and KIT-ML results, alongside new user studies and ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original video-generation experiments, MTurk preference studies, TikTok dance-generation scores and comparisons between generation stages.

results.title: ReVision: Refining Video Diffusion with Explicit 3D Motion Modeling

C1.justification: The central stationary FPR guarantee is narrowed from ASAT generally to the calibration-safe variant, with v2 explicitly stating that the experimental algorithm does not instantiate Proposition 1. The abstract also distinguishes stationary FPR control from transient violations during nonstationary adaptation. The central adaptive-scoring contribution remains.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly separates empirical safety of the practical algorithm from the theoretical guarantee and identifies reuse of training samples for calibration as an unresolved theoretical issue in Appendix C, Remark 1. D1.justification: Appendix D.5 documents the new simulation's Gaussian means of 5.5 and -6, standard deviation of 4, linear scoring function, horizon, and exact parameter grids. Existing architecture descriptions, optimizer choices, and grid-search hyperparameters are retained.

E2.justification: The evaluated FSFT, FSAT, binary-classifier, and scoring-function comparisons are retained. Several names are corrected to match existing plots: for example, the ImageNet prose changes MSP/KNN to KNN/MDS, which were already the methods displayed in v1 Figure 15, now v2 Figure 14.

E3.justification: The new Gaussian study uses a linear scorer, 100,000 time steps, and separate sweeps of alpha, p, and gamma, reporting feasibility time and annotation counts alongside FPR/TPR. Existing benchmark settings are retained. V2 explicitly states that experiments use the practical algorithm, not the newly analyzed calibration-safe variant.

E4.justification: Appendix D.5 adds a targeted sensitivity analysis testing how FPR tolerance, labeling probability, and OOD prevalence affect safety, TPR, cold-start duration, and annotation cost. The existing window-size and update-frequency analyses remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Existing experiments retain five repetitions with means and standard deviations. The new sensitivity table reports five seeds and uncertainty values, extending the existing repeated-run reporting practice without changing replication or uncertainty estimation for retained results.

E6.justification: The retained benchmark plots show unchanged results. New Table 4 adds simulation outcomes: at alpha=0.05 and p=gamma=0.2, reported FPR is 4.23 ± 0.21% and TPR is 87.41 ± 0.63%; increasing p from 0.05 to 0.40 increases mean human annotations from 36,235 to 59,535. M1.justification: V2 introduces calibration-safe Algorithm 3: a newly trained scorer is calibrated exclusively on subsequent samples and deployed only when its threshold constraint becomes feasible, while the previous scorer remains active. This substantially changes calibration and deployment for the analyzed variant. Separately, the stated model-selection criterion changes from adding to subtracting twice the DKW margin in Section 3.2 and Appendix B.

Algorithm 1 moves from Appendix B into the main text, an appendix contents list is added, title and author information are updated, and acknowledgments are removed.

P2.justification: V2 applies document-wide TMLR typography and front-matter formatting and rearranges displays. Figure 1 replaces digit/clothing illustrations with MRI examples, the former comparison Figure 2 becomes Table 1, and Algorithm 3 and the three-part sensitivity Table 4 are added. Existing performance plots are preserved, with several captions corrected.

The DKW citation changes from Nadaraya (1965) to Dvoretzky et al. (1956), and the Ren/Kirichenko references disappear. The central positioning as online adaptation beyond fixed scoring remains.

It adds three token-usage figures, reference-solver tables and the hint-results table, while relocating existing runtime and library figures into the appendix.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves the evidential basis and calibration of the paper. This implements an extension only proposed as future work in v1; the principal local-temperature interpolation and posterior-inference procedure remain.

P1.justification: The main section structure and much existing prose remain. Local rewrites clarify temperature terminology and mathematical notation, update the abstract and conclusion, and introduce appendix navigation. Former Appendix C becomes Appendix E after the new dataset and DKL appendices.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial table displays for timing, objective ablation, n-body/UCI results, and DKL accuracy and speed. Existing figures and tables are retained with updated captions and placement; Figures 7–8 are grouped together, and the temperature and lengthscale histograms exchange Figure 9–10 numbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for UCI, Girard and Hutchinson trace estimation, Plummer softening, and SciPy. The main positioning against derivative variational GPs and kernel interpolation remains. The SoftKI reference's preprint-to-publication update represents the same cited work.

C1.justification: V1 claims general upper and lower bounds and tight minimax rates through entropy conditions; v2 centers its contribution on lower bounds under Construction 7. Main-text optimality comparisons become qualified. The abstract also replaces the claim of near n^(-1/2) rates for merely convex boundaries with near n^(-1) rates for convex-Lipschitz boundaries, under changed assumptions.

C2.justification: Section 1.4 now explains that Barron bounds match prior upper bounds asymptotically in high dimension, while Hölder bounds match at α=1 and differ substantially for small α. Convexity is described as suggesting faster optimal learning rather than establishing it. The noiseless and worst-case caveats remain, while v1's limitation concerning unavailable covering-number estimates is removed with the old proof framework.

D1.justification: The new figure captions disclose concrete plotting choices, including explicit baseline functions, d=2, α=0.4, and M=200 or M=80 in Figure 2. E4.justification: The empirical margin illustration is retained, with no added ablations, robustness tests, sensitivity studies, or error analyses. Figures 2–4 explain mathematical constructions rather than test additional empirical questions.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for its empirical illustration. The revised minimax proofs do not introduce empirical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Figure 1 retains the same empirical plots and findings: strong margins for the illustrated MNIST and Fashion-MNIST classes and a weaker margin for CIFAR-10. No empirical scores or experimental result entries are added or removed; the changed analytical rates are addressed under T1.

V2 explicitly takes the minimax supremum over classifier–distribution pairs and adds regularity and margin-exponent restrictions. The Hölder two-sided rate n^(-αγ/(αγ+d-1)) becomes a lower bound n^(-γ/(γ+d-1)) for 0<α≤1 and γ≥α. Barron lower-bound logarithmic factors disappear, and general convex functions are replaced by convex-Lipschitz functions with a different bound.

improvement.justification: V1's Lemma 11(S3) uses a positive-density separation step that its margin upper bound does not justify. V2 replaces this central weakness with explicit hard distributions, margin checks, local separation bounds, and an Assouad argument in Appendices A–C. Its qualified main-text optimality comparisons also improve precision. Coverage is narrower, and the abstract still claims convex-Lipschitz optimality beyond the demonstrated lower bound, but the reconstruction substantially strengthens the paper's theoretical foundation.

before.justification: Figure 1 reports data-analysis outcomes on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10: principal-component embeddings, fitted SVM boundaries, and predicted class probabilities. These constitute original empirical illustrations within an otherwise theoretical paper.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical analyses and adds Llama/Minitron experiments, causal role validation, linear probes, robustness quantification, and sensitivity studies.

results.title: Distilled Circuits: A Mechanistic Study of Internal Restructuring in Knowledge Distillation

The expanded experiments support these existing claims without materially redefining them.

It acknowledges that SPIDER's vector library performs best in that comparison. Conversely, v1 Appendix D.2's explanation of declining Darcy GP success through overfitting is removed.

These disclosures substantially expand reproducibility information, although v1's CPU and runtime statement disappears, and the newly stated zero-flux Darcy boundaries conflict with the claimed steady state under positive constant forcing.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained three systems, v2 evaluates a scalar 3D reaction-diffusion equation with SO(3) symmetry (Appendix C.4) and turbulent channel flow with velocity and pressure fields from the Johns Hopkins Turbulence Database (Appendix D.2). E2.justification: v2 adds the compact-library PySINDy** comparator to the existing Boussinesq and reaction-diffusion comparisons (Table 4), D-CIPHER on Darcy flow (Table 6), and scalar- and vector-library SPIDER comparisons on channel flow (Table 10). The SPIDER results are reused from the cited work, not reported as new baseline runs. The original comparators remain.

New protocols include a 32-cubed 3D simulation with 1% noise and a temporal training/test split, plus a six-threshold filtering sweep. Newly specified settings for retained simulations are additional disclosure, not evidence that those experiments changed.

These are interquartile ranges, despite being called confidence intervals; the stated repeat count remains 100.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises PySR's Darcy prediction error from 0.187 to 0.114 and SI's Boussinesq complexity from 13 to 15. Substantial new results include 3D SINDy success probabilities of 0.51 versus 1.00 for SI, D-CIPHER and channel-flow equations, and filtering success ranging from 0.36 to 1.00. Noisy-data curves also change under revised parameter-selection settings, so they are not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Appendix C.5 adds a concrete D-CIPHER adaptation: invariant differential operators construct its derivative dictionary, while fundamental invariants constrain its learned right-hand side. The original algorithms, linear symmetry constraints, Sparse PCA step, and symmetry relaxation remain; Sparse PCA was already documented in v1 Appendix C.2.

P1.justification: The main-text and appendix organization is substantially reworked: related work moves into Section 2, Sparse PCA explanations and GP-budget discussion move into the main narrative, and broader impacts move before the references. The appendices are reorganized around expanded experiments and a dedicated comparison section. Much original mathematical prose remains, but the explanatory structure changes considerably.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a different journal layout and adds a prolongation illustration, an auto-tuned WSINDy figure, and tables for uncertainty ranges, 3D results, D-CIPHER, channel flow, and filtering sensitivity. Existing tables gain comparator rows. The GP-budget plot moves from v1 Figure 5 to v2 Figure 3; several other figures are retained with renumbering.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds substantial coverage of neural operators, surrogate models, and coarse-grained dynamics. New Appendix D positions the framework against EquivSINDy, symmetry regularization, and SPIDER, explaining restricted equivalence and differences in symmetry and algorithm scope. D-CIPHER and additional WSINDy literature also enter the discussion; this exceeds citation relocation or bibliographic updating.

T1.justification: Appendices A.2 and A.4 add a worked rotation-prolongation calculation and a characteristic-equation derivation of SO(2) ordinary invariants. Appendix D.1 also states the framework's equivalence to EquivSINDy in the restricted time-independent ODE setting. The central invariant-completeness and linear-subspace propositions and their proofs are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the framework's generality through higher-dimensional experiments and broader comparisons. The filtering and WSINDy sensitivity studies expose practical failure conditions that v1 left largely untested, while fuller positioning and dispersion reporting make the evidence easier to assess. These gains are substantial despite reporting problems: quartiles are mislabeled as confidence intervals, WSINDy tuning commentary is inconsistent, and the newly specified Darcy boundary conditions require reconciliation with the claimed forced steady state.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same symmetry-invariant equation-discovery framework. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison after matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds results on 3D reaction-diffusion, channel flow, D-CIPHER integration, and parameter sensitivity. Its SPIDER comparison numbers are explicitly attributed to prior work.

before.justification: v1 reports original equation-discovery experiments on Boussinesq, Darcy flow, and reaction-diffusion data, including repeated trials, prediction errors, and noise and symmetry-breaking studies.

results.title: Discovering Symbolic Differential Equations with Symmetry Invariants

C1.justification: v2 drops the introduction's assertion that corruption adaptation for VLMs has not been explored and reframes the problem around domain-shift methods' over-specialization. The central contribution remains UnInfo's uniformity-aware, information-balanced encoder adaptation; its three main components and headline accuracy-improvement claim are retained.

C2.justification: v2 acknowledges that regularized mutual-information optimization can rival UnInfo and attributes improvements to combined components rather than uniformity alone. It adds substantive qualifications concerning small-batch estimation, i.i.d. sampling, continual-adaptation interference, and the confounded encoder-versus-embedding ablation. Performance discussion shifts toward consistency relative to No-adapt despite stronger competitors.

D1.justification: v2 supplies an exact pretrained-checkpoint link, names the four tuning corruptions, explains clean-data-based threshold selection, and explicitly documents once-per-sample batched evaluation. Appendix D specifies spherical transport costs and the POT implementation for the existing EMD analysis. Most optimizer settings and the existing code link remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds CIFAR10-C and CIFAR100-C, lower ImageNet-C corruption severities, and sequential corruption streams for continual adaptation. These substantially broaden the represented data and input conditions. ImageNet and ImageNet-A/R already appeared in v1; their additional adaptation results do not introduce new datasets.

E2.justification: DMN, Mint, and BATCLIP enter the retained ImageNet-C/C-bar comparisons and efficiency table in v2. DMN was previously discussed but not evaluated. Mint and BATCLIP provide competing encoder-updating approaches absent from v1's comparisons; Appendix E.6 additionally evaluates BATCLIP with LoRA.

E3.justification: The stated main checkpoint changes from DataComp-1B in v1 Section V-B to LAION-2B in v2 Section 5.2. Identical retained benchmark means do not establish whether experiments were rerun. New evaluation configurations include OpenAI ViT-B/32, SigLIP, and continual adaptation without resets using learning rate 0.0001.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's component ablations and sensitivity plots, v2 tests mutual-information objectives, fixed versus dynamic balancing, batch size, encoder versus embedding updates, and LoRA versus LayerNorm with teacher controls. Appendix E also adds hyperparameter-selection checks, continual-adaptation analysis, and prediction-imbalance analysis of collapse.

E5.justification: v2 adds per-result ± uncertainty values throughout the primary accuracy and ablation tables, where v1 reported means alone. Both versions already specify three random-seed runs and include uncertainty in some efficiency/sensitivity displays; no increase in runs is established. The accuracy tables do not clearly identify what their ± quantities represent.

E6.justification: Shared primary benchmark means remain unchanged, including UnInfo's 27.10% and 36.13%. Added Mint results of 29.14% and 38.06% remove UnInfo's leading average ranking. Entropy-only ablation means change from 0.10% on both datasets to 0.22% and 0.29%. The Gaussian-noise weight trajectory changes in Figure 3→4, and extensive additional benchmark and analysis results appear.

M1.justification: The proposed UnInfo algorithm retains the same entropy and uniformity losses, mutual-information-based balancing, image-encoder LoRA updates, EMA distillation, and teacher inference.
