Algorithm 1 moves to Appendix B. Newly evaluated alternative losses and parameter updates are experimental ablations, not replacements for the proposed method.

P1.justification: The overall section sequence and much existing exposition remain recognizable. v2 condenses the abstract, edits and expands explanations, consistently substitutes image corruption for sensor degradation, reorganizes related-work paragraphs, swaps qualitative and efficiency subsections, and relocates pseudocode into the expanded appendix.

P2.justification: The document changes from an IEEE-style two-column layout to a single-column format. Tables are extensively reformatted with angled headers and uncertainty entries, sensitivity panels become side by side, and numerous experimental tables and analysis plots are added. The original overview and embedding visualization remain, while the weight-trajectory figure is revised.

R1.justification: v2 substantially revises positioning by adding encoder-updating corruption methods such as Mint, BATCLIP, CLIPArTT, and WATT, including Mint's conceptual relationship to uniformity. Related work is organized along episodic/cumulative and frozen/updating-encoder axes, replacing v1's predominantly frozen-encoder comparison narrative.

T1.justification: Section 3 revises the data-processing argument: v1 treats H(Z|X) as constant because the encoder is deterministic; v2 instead explicitly assumes small fluctuations and describes decreasing embedding entropy as likely. This changes the mathematical assumptions and reasoning without introducing a new theorem or proof framework.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses a major weakness of v1's evidence by comparing against competing encoder-updating methods and testing broader datasets, models, and failure conditions. The additional loss and parameter ablations, uncertainty reporting, and explicit limitations substantially strengthen assessment of when and why UnInfo works. Remaining problems include the unexplained checkpoint-description change and overbroad superiority wording: BATCLIP does not exceed UnInfo on ImageNet-C-bar, despite the accompanying generalization.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UnInfo research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds benchmark, model, severity, continual-adaptation, and ablation experiments, including Appendix E.

before.justification: v1 reports original prompting experiments, adaptation benchmarks, component ablations, sensitivity analyses, and computational measurements.

results.title: Uniformity First: Uniformity-aware Test-time Adaptation of Vision-language Models against Image Corruption

C1.justification: The central conditional-NOT, hypernetwork, and GSA contributions remain. V2 newly claims the first comparison of NOT with established solvers for GSA and explicitly includes conditional image generation among its contributions. Its conclusion drops v1's assertion of maintaining theoretical guarantees, with convergence and approximation guarantees instead identified as future work.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations of normalization methods' effectiveness for images and explicitly limits extrapolation from MNIST to large-scale image generation. It also identifies missing convergence and approximation analysis. Conversely, Section 5.2.2 removes v1's caveat that neural and simplex cost magnitudes may not be comparable, while retaining Figure 5.

D1.justification: V1 promises future code/data release; v2 states release and supplies a repository link. V2 also discloses the stratified 80/20 climate split, 10,000 IAM evaluations, automatic mixed precision, and CondOT comparison configurations. These materially expand reproducibility information, while Appendix A.1's existing hyperparameters remain unchanged. Repository availability was not externally verified.

E1.justification: V2 adds noise-to-image generation conditioned on all ten MNIST classes, beyond v1's unconditional digit-2-to-digit-3 transport experiment. This substantially extends demonstrated conditional-task coverage into images. Although Section 4.3 mentions continuous attributes, Table 1 explicitly identifies the reported MNIST experiment as having no continuous conditioning input.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds CondOT Default and CondOT Adapted as evaluated comparators on climate damages and RICE50+ GSA; v1 only discussed CondOT without reporting its scores. The existing conditioning alternatives and simplex reference remain. CondOT is explicitly excluded from MNIST evaluation.

E3.justification: New comparisons introduce parameter- and epoch-matched CondOT configurations, retaining CondOT-specific optimization and contrasting discretized versus mixed conditioning. The added MNIST experiment uses class-conditioned generation evaluated with FID and classification accuracy. Existing experimental settings are retained; the newly stated climate split and IAM sample count are disclosures rather than established protocol changes.

E4.justification: V2 extends component ablation into conditional image generation, testing removal of pretraining, shared embeddings, and alternative conditioning mechanisms. Table 1 and new Figure 6 add quantitative evidence and visible artifact comparisons for these choices. The earlier unconditional ablations and appendix implementation analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both versions retain the 1,000 climate bootstrap replicates, climate uncertainty intervals, appendix distribution plots, and GSA estimator. V2 adds no repeated-training run counts, seeds, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates for its new comparison scores.

E6.justification: Existing Figure 3 and climate/IAM Table 1 scores are retained. New CondOT Default/Adapted entries report climate Wasserstein distances of 0.322/0.255 and IAM correlations of 0.025/0.389, alongside unchanged proposed-method values of 0.170 and 0.942. New conditional MNIST results include FID 2.509 and accuracy 1.000. These are added comparisons and task results, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The hypernetwork, encoder-decoder architecture, discrete embeddings, positional encoding, pretraining losses, and alternating optimization remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 and Appendix A.1 retain the same procedure. The added MNIST application uses already-supported convolutional architectures and conditioning.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, background, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Background becomes four subsections; applications and experimental setup are separated from results; and a computational discussion section is added. Method explanations are substantially expanded, although the appendix prose is largely retained.

P2.justification: V2 adopts TMLR typography, headers, and a wider layout, with enlarged and repositioned existing displays. Table 1 gains CondOT columns, a MNIST results block, and an expanded caption; new Figure 6 presents a multirow digit-generation comparison. V1's appendix Figures 6–8 remain as Figures 7–9.

R1.justification: V2 adds flow-matching and rectified-flow context, additional application references, and more specific discussion of conditional OT flows' optimization and input-distribution restrictions. The central positioning as a flexible conditional extension of NOT remains. Wang's 2025 publication corresponds to the already-cited 2023 work, rather than a distinct new method.

T1.justification: The OT formulations, conditional objective, assumptions, and Appendix A.3 sensitivity-index definition and estimator remain mathematically unchanged. V2 repeats existing GSA definitions and properties in Section 4.2; this does not introduce a new theorem, derivation, or proof.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation: direct CondOT comparisons address v1's lack of an evaluated external conditional-OT baseline, and conditional MNIST ablations test the central conditioning claims beyond scientific data. Added experimental disclosures and the reported code/data release improve reproducibility information. These gains outweigh localized regressions, particularly removal of the GSA cost-magnitude caveat despite unchanged Figure 5 and ambiguity about MNIST attribute conditioning.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Neural Conditional Transport Maps, with matching authors, mathematical framework, and retained experiments. Text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A.1–A.5 are readable and support comparison despite extensive expansion and reformatting.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and adds evaluated CondOT baselines and quantitative and qualitative class-conditional MNIST generation results.

before.justification: V1 reports original architecture and conditioning ablations, synthetic-distribution and MNIST transport results, climate-damage generation, and RICE50+ sensitivity analysis, including supplementary results.

results.title: Neural Conditional Transport Maps

C1.justification: V2 adds downstream classification improvement as an explicit introduction contribution and conclusion. V1's main empirical claims concern probability quality, useful expert priors, and sample efficiency, while acknowledging that downstream benefits remain unquantified. The new claim substantially extends the asserted practical contribution.

C2.justification: V2 adds an autoregressive-bias explanation for FullDist, interpretations of downstream gains, and a qualification that MLE wins with sufficiently abundant synthetic data. It acknowledges the DeepSeek-V3 exception to SepState's advantage. V1's dedicated limitations discussion, including inference-cost and expert-validation caveats, is removed.

D1.justification: Appendices B–C newly document base-2 logarithms, epsilon smoothing at 1e-8, handling states absent from the top-20 token candidates, additional model versions, reasoning effort, and classification prior-strength selection. These materially expand implementation information. The code repository address is unchanged; several additions disclose details rather than demonstrate changed implementations.

E1.justification: The 80-network bnRep coverage remains. V2 adds downstream classification on HouseVotes84, PhDArticles, Pokemon, Titanic, CAD1, CAD2, Covid, Puffin, and Trajectories. This substantially extends evaluation from recovering probability distributions to predicting target labels on observed datasets.

E2.justification: V2 adds a direct chain-of-thought classification comparator and expands probability-estimation comparisons with Claude/Gemini FullDist variants and DeepSeek-V3 controls. Figure 2 and corresponding appendix plots remove GPT-4o-mini Random and MLE entries from those comparisons, although MLE remains in EDP experiments. FullDist and uniform-prior updating already existed in v1.

E3.justification: V2 introduces stratified 80/20 classification splits, macro-F1 evaluation, Hill Climbing and Naive Bayes structures, full/20/10-sample parameter estimation, and development-set selection of prior strength. It also adds four LLM configurations and fixed-count sampling per CPT row. These extend the protocol; newly documented KL implementation details alone do not establish changed experiments.

E4.justification: Appendix D adds EDP checks with DeepSeek-V3, Gemini, and Claude and an additional per-CPT-row sampling analysis. Reasoning-model comparisons and existing state/parent subgroup analyses broaden the diagnostic evidence. Conversely, v1's linear-pooling comparison and its explicit prompt-style, additional-context, and chain-of-thought robustness discussion are removed.

E5.justification: V2 adds five-run averaging and empirical standard deviations for low-resource classification results in Table 2. The original pilot using up to five LLM samples and subsequent single-sample inference policy remain. No confidence intervals or formal significance tests are added.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 add extensive classification outcomes absent from v1: for example, GPT-4o EDP averages 0.70 macro-F1 versus MLE's 0.63 under Hill Climbing with 10 samples. Expanded plots add model results, including DeepSeek-V3 favoring FullDist, and revise EDP distributions and rankings. These are new or revised reported results, not established same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: V2 removes linear pooling as an EDP fusion option, retaining the existing pseudocount update with renamed notation. Per-state querying and normalization are preserved as SepState, formerly EPK. FullDist also existed in v1; its promotion into the methodology does not establish a new algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, methodology, and conclusion are substantially rewritten around expert priors and a two-stage pipeline. EPK becomes SepState, FullDist is integrated into the method exposition, subsection organization changes, and the KL and setup appendices exchange order. This exceeds terminology cleanup.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redesigned to show extraction followed by empirical-count fusion. V2 adds classification tables and additional EDP plots, redraws comparison plots with consistent method colors, and compresses the description and prompt diagrams into column layouts. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering or numerical updates.

R1.justification: V2 sharpens the contrast with Huang and Feng around shallow binary networks and unavailable gold probabilities. It adds classification, chain-of-thought, and new-model references while removing the standalone parameter-learning discussion and several supporting citations. The central positioning as probabilistic knowledge extraction for real-world BNs remains.

T1.justification: V2 Appendix B adds an explicit definition of normalized epsilon-smoothed distributions and their strict-positivity property. The BN-KL decomposition and derivation are unchanged, moving from v1 Figure 6 to v2 Figure 5. The added CPT-KL formula formalizes the averaging metric already described in v1.

improvement.justification: V1 explicitly left downstream usefulness untested; v2 substantially addresses that gap through nine classification datasets, two structures, two LLMs, and repeated-run variability reporting in Tables 1–2. Broader model checks and clearer implementation details further strengthen the paper. The removed limitations discussion and some overstated performance claims are drawbacks, and low-data tests still use full-data structures and additional development data. Nevertheless, the new task-level evidence provides a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Bayesian-network parameterization work. Their text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices A–E are readable and support comparison despite substantial rewriting, renaming, and reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original Bayesian-network experiments and adds classification results on nine datasets, additional LLM evaluations, and repeated-run results in Appendix D.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments on 80 Bayesian networks, including probability estimation, combining LLM priors with sampled data, and analyses by node states and parent counts.

results.title: Extracting Probabilistic Knowledge from Large Language Models for Bayesian Network Parameterization

C1.justification: The central UGPP formulation and fully unsupervised frozen-GNN prompting contributions remain. v2's introduction strengthens the comparative claim from outperforming baselines 'in most cases' to consistently outperforming methods with full label access. Its conclusion also explicitly qualifies applicability to a shared source/target label space.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly interprets adversarial regularization as target-side stabilization, with source compatibility supplied indirectly by the frozen model and confidence filtering. It adds substantive discussion of confirmation bias, calibration, access to unlabeled data, computational tradeoffs, and the distinction from LLM reasoning. The new limitations paragraph explains why a frozen head cannot generally accommodate new target classes.

D1.justification: v2 adds measured training and inference times with evaluated node counts in Table 21 and clarifies validation-based disabling of ineffective regularizers. The PyTorch implementation, RTX 3090 hardware, principal hyperparameter grids, and code-access statement are retained. These are limited additions to technical documentation.

E1.justification: v2 adds BBBP and BACE molecular graph datasets and Cornell, Texas, and Wisconsin node datasets while retaining the original coverage. It also adds cross-dataset transfer, a stress test with reindexed target categories, and evaluation without distribution shift (Section 4.5 and Appendix A.6.3), substantially broadening the tested populations and scenarios.

E2.justification: Beyond the retained comparators, v2 evaluates DAGPrompt, PRONOG, and GCOPE in Tables 9–10 and SOGA and GraphCTA in Table 14. The SFDA comparators are explicitly adapted to freeze their encoders and train their prediction heads; these are not evaluations of unrestricted full-model adaptation.

E3.justification: v2 introduces sorted source/target partitions with graded shift severity, category reindexing with a three-output frozen head, GraphGPS and GATv2 backbones, and an additional comparison allowing supervised baselines to fine-tune their decoders. New diagnostics measure MMD, pseudo-label accuracy, ECE, and runtime. The original main-experiment splits and tuning grids are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained ablations and embedding analysis, v2 adds graded-shift sensitivity, cross-dataset and category-transfer stress tests, source-performance retention, no-shift controls, computational-cost analysis, MMD diagnostics, and confidence-threshold/calibration analysis. These test robustness and mechanism questions largely unexamined in v1.

E5.justification: Both versions specify 10 dataset seeds and five model initializations per seed, totaling 50 runs, and mix results with ± reporting and point estimates. No new confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures are specified. The added calibration study evaluates predictive reliability rather than changing sampling-uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for new datasets, comparators, transfer settings, runtime, and reliability diagnostics; for example, Table 1 newly reports UGPrompt's GCN BACE F1 as 64.6±1.9. Most original scores remain. One retained entry changes: GraphPrompt's 50%-label CiteSeer clustering-shift IMP moves from +1.6 in v1 Table 7 to -1.6 in v2 Table 12 despite unchanged F1 values.

M1.justification: The core unsupervised architecture and three losses remain unchanged. The few-shot pseudo-label loss changes from summing over the full batch B in v1 Equation 8 to unlabeled samples Su in v2 Section 4.4. Algorithm 2's body also switches from returning scores to argmax labels, although its output header still says scores. The PDFs do not establish corresponding implementation changes or reruns.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, and introduction are substantially rewritten around source-free, parameter-efficient adaptation. Related work moves from v1 Section 2 to v2 Appendix A.1, the experimental and appendix organization expands, and terminology systematically distinguishes 'source-trained' from general 'pre-trained' models. These changes substantially revise the narrative and structure.

P2.justification: Tables 1–2 expand with new dataset columns, Figure 2 is redrawn with logarithmic axes, revised legends, and additional datasets, and numerous new comparisons and diagnostics receive dedicated tables. Journal formatting changes typography, margins, headers, and table styling. The original framework, embedding, and higher-label-budget figures are largely retained.

R1.justification: v1 distinguishes UGPP from source-free adaptation mainly in an appendix. v2 explicitly positions it as a restrictive prompting instance within SFDA in the introduction and problem formulation. It substantially expands engagement with recent graph prompting, graph SFDA, and PEFT through DAGPrompt, PRONOG, GCOPE, SOGA, GraphCTA, and LoRA, beyond merely relocating related work.

T1.justification: The few-shot loss definition changes its summation domain from B to Su and its confidence comparison from strict to inclusive (v1 Equation 8; v2 Section 4.4). The formal UGPP assumptions, core unsupervised objectives, and complexity bound otherwise remain equivalent. No new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens assessment of the central adaptation claim: comparisons with decoder-finetuned prompting and adapted SFDA methods address v1's restricted comparison regime, while MMD and calibration diagnostics test previously mostly intuitive mechanism arguments. Explicit label-space limitations improve applicability guidance. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses: superiority language exceeds the new evidence—DAGPrompt leads on five of seven datasets in Table 10—and v2 introduces an inconsistent IMP sign in Table 12.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UGPP problem and UGPrompt framework despite the changed title. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds benchmark comparisons, transfer experiments, runtime measurements, and pseudo-label reliability diagnostics.

before.justification: v1 reports original graph and node classification experiments, distribution-shift evaluations, ablations, and embedding analyses in the main text and appendix.

results.title: Freeze, Prompt, and Adapt: A Framework for Source-free Unsupervised GNN Prompting

C1.justification: The introduction adds a theoretical contribution: explaining dataset-size scaling for kernel methods at fixed, low diffusion noise. The abstract and central claims about generalization before memorization, early stopping and the hierarchical phase diagram retain their previous scope.

C2.justification: Section 3.3 adds a spectral interpretation of memorization time, interprets agreement under feature learning as extending beyond fixed kernels, and links batch-size independence to optimization steps rather than repeated exposures. Section 5 distinguishes diffusion memorization from noisy supervised regression. The conclusion removes v1's explicit limitation concerning explanation of the law for deep, time-dependent diffusion architectures.

D1.justification: Appendix E documents the added experiment's ReLU activation, single hidden layer, width 8192, data dimension, initialization regimes and optimization conditions. Existing Appendix A hyperparameters, hardware information and code-access links are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix E adds Gaussian-distributed vectors in 64 dimensions for empirical-score fitting at fixed diffusion noise. This is a limited synthetic extension; the existing image, language and hierarchical-grammar coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in the existing experiments is unchanged. The new NTK and feature-learning initializations are controlled conditions in the scaling analysis; the cited random-feature results are theoretical comparisons, not newly evaluated benchmark baselines.

E3.justification: Appendix E introduces a distinct controlled evaluation protocol: fixed-noise score fitting with a one-hidden-layer network, NTK versus mean-field initialization, noise and dataset-size sweeps, and full-batch versus stochastic gradient descent. Figures 14–16 cover P=128–2048 and batch sizes B=8–128. Existing diffusion-experiment settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Figures 14–16 add substantial diagnostic analyses testing the predicted noise and dataset-size scaling, its persistence under feature learning, and sensitivity to batch size. These directly investigate the mechanism and robustness of the central memorization-time law; v1 lacks these analyses.

E5.justification: Existing error-bar displays and statistical reporting are retained. Appendix E adds no reported seed counts, repeated-run summaries, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Figures 14–16 newly report memorization times consistent with linear dependence on dataset size, inverse dependence on noise standard deviation under both initializations, and approximate batch-size independence. These are new findings in the Gaussian setting. Existing results and Figures 1–13 remain unchanged, including CIFAR-10 FID 5.4 with 0% copies.

M1.justification: The early-stopping proposal and existing diffusion-model training and sampling procedures are unchanged. Appendix E introduces analytical and experimental probes of score learning, rather than a revised generative method.

P1.justification: Related work moves from Section 1.1 to Section 5, the conclusion is renumbered, and Section 3.3 gains a theoretical-support discussion. Local wording and explanatory edits accompany these changes, but most existing prose and the main experimental narrative are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 14–16 with paired panels, rescaled-axis plots, insets and legends for the new experiments. Existing Figures 1–13 retain their graphical content, with limited caption edits and changes to placement and surrounding text flow.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning through explicit comparison with Bonnaire et al.'s random-feature analysis, earlier Gaussian-approximation learning, and supervised double descent and benign overfitting. It adds relevant kernel and mean-field references while retaining the earlier cited works.

T1.justification: New Appendix E develops a kernel-operator scaling argument using separated Gaussian components, localized score-mode ansatz functions and Rayleigh quotients, obtaining tau_mem proportional to P/sigma^nu. It distinguishes ReLU NTK and random-feature exponents. Section 2 also corrects the empirical distribution by inserting the missing 1/P normalization.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly lacked an explanation for its central memorization-time scaling law. v2 substantially strengthens that argument through a kernel scaling derivation and controlled tests of noise, dataset size, initialization and batch size in Appendix E. Removing the explicit deep-architecture limitation weakens qualification, since the new theory addresses a restricted setting. Nevertheless, its assumptions remain stated, and the added explanatory and diagnostic evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, central claims and original experiments. The text, equations, figures and appendices support reliable comparison, including the new Appendix E in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds numerical score-learning experiments on Gaussian data in Appendix E, Figures 14–16.

before.justification: v1 reports original diffusion-model experiments on CIFAR-10, CelebA, text8, LAION-10k and Random Hierarchy Model data, including results in Appendices B–D.

results.title: Bigger Isn't Always Memorizing: Early Stopping Overparameterized Diffusion Models

C1.justification: The central claims of adaptive budgeting, explicit user control, and difficulty-aware two-stage training are retained. V2 additionally claims robustness under hyperparameter variation in the introduction; its abstract and conclusion otherwise preserve the original contribution scope.

C2.justification: V2 adds localized interpretations: initial Easy-tag bias is attributed primarily to format learning during SFT, prompting failures are linked to instruction-following limitations, and binary difficulty categories are justified by control simplicity and reliability. It also interprets the new ablations and sweeps as supporting reward complementarity and robustness.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies the default difficulty threshold as 0.625 and supplies exact baseline and difficulty-aware evaluation prompts in Section 4.1. These disclosures do not establish changes to the existing experiments. Software, hardware, optimizer details, and the promised future code release remain unchanged.

E1.justification: DeepMATH training and evaluation on AIME2024, AIME2025, MATH500, and GSM8K are retained. The additional experiments vary model size, rewards, and prompting within the existing mathematical task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds the evaluated S1.1-7B-PE prompting baseline in Figure 4(b), reporting response lengths under a requested 500-token limit. The existing comparison methods remain, with renamed rows and corresponding 14B configurations.

E3.justification: V2 adds matched 14B training/evaluation, reward-removal experiments, reward-weight combinations, and difficulty-threshold sweeps over 0.625, 0.5, and 0.375. It also tests prompted 500-token limits and qualitatively reports a 1000-token test. Previously stated data budgets, metrics, and decoding settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds individual reward ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity tests, comparison with prompted length control, and response-length distributions by predicted difficulty. It also expands final difficulty-tag proportions into trajectories during RL, directly examining how difficulty judgments develop.

E5.justification: Both versions average AIME2024 and AIME2025 performance over eight independent runs. V2 adds no seed reporting, confidence intervals, significance tests, or other uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: The original 7B results in Tables 1–2 remain unchanged. V2 adds extensive results under new conditions: AdaCtrl-14B achieves 34.58% accuracy with 15173.21 tokens on AIME2024, while 7B reward ablations yield 17.08% without calibration reward and 15.42% without length reward. Hyperparameter, prompting, and distribution analyses add further findings; these are additional results rather than same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The two-stage training procedure, Easy/Hard control interface, rollout-based difficulty estimation, three reward components, and GRPO objective remain unchanged. The 14B experiments extend model-size settings without introducing a new algorithm or architecture.

P1.justification: The introduction and substantial portions of the method/results narrative are rewritten. The separate tag-interface subsection is integrated into cold-start training, RL subsections are consolidated, and controllability moves from analysis into main results. Terminology shifts from length-trigger tags to difficulty-aware tags.

P2.justification: V2 removes the opening summary chart, redesigns the retained example and training diagrams, expands Tables 1–2, and adds Tables 3–4. Final tag-proportion bars become training trajectories, with new prompting and distribution plots. The retained training curves also change their step-axis scale from 0–640 to 0–80 without explanation.

R1.justification: V2 adds Wei et al.'s chain-of-thought work and two Hongru Wang et al. papers, while removing the ThinkPrune citation. The introduction more explicitly contrasts uniform compression with brittle fine-grained prompting. Most related-work discussion and the overall novelty positioning remain intact; duplicate-reference consolidation does not remove those works.

T1.justification: Equations 1–7 retain their mathematical substance. Renaming reasoning traces from r to p and distinguishing the KL coefficient as beta-prime are notation refinements. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs.

improvement.justification: V1 lacked individual reward ablations and sensitivity tests and evaluated only a 7B backbone. V2 substantially strengthens validation through separate reward-removal controls, threshold/weight sweeps, and matched 14B comparisons, while disclosing previously missing prompts and the default threshold. Reporting weaknesses remain: some mode-comparison claims overgeneralize Table 2, and the training-step axis changes unexplained. These issues limit precision but do not outweigh the substantial gains in testing the method's components and robustness.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AdaCtrl research. All pages, equations, tables, and figures support comparison. Neither supplied PDF contains an appendix.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds 14B experiments, hyperparameter sweeps, reward ablations, and further analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original model-training and evaluation results, including accuracy, response lengths, controllability experiments, and training dynamics.

results.title: AdaCtrl: Towards Adaptive and Controllable Reasoning via Difficulty-Aware Budgeting

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the central claims about probabilistic spatial feature inversion and its two applications. The introduction expands the explicit contribution list to claim demonstrated generalizability across ConvNeXt stages and robustness to corrupted inputs.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation of applicability and failure conditions: it discusses intermediate representations' reduced sensitivity to pixel deviations and failures to reproduce severe noise and contrast corruption. Appendix A.5 adds arguments about pretrained diffusion efficiency while acknowledging resolution differences and possible incomplete RCDM convergence. The original limitations paragraph is retained.

D1.justification: v2 adds RCDM weight/code provenance and training resources, intermediate feature-map dimensions, and suggested uniform control settings. The main FeatInv training recipe and code link remain. Reproducibility still has ambiguities: selected model-specific settings are not explicitly tabulated, and Appendix A.5 describes a FeatInv batch size of two while Section 2 states eight.

E1.justification: v2 adds ImageNet-A natural adversarial images and ImageNet-C corruption scenarios, substantially extending evaluation beyond ordinary ImageNet images and the already-used BAID dataset. ImageNet training and BAID coverage are retained; the additional concept examples remain within existing ImageNet coverage.

E2.justification: v1 discusses Bordes et al.'s approach without evaluating it directly. v2 Appendix A.5 and Table 4 introduce RCDM as an evaluated competing inversion method, using supplied ResNet50 weights and an independently trained ConvNeXt variant. This materially expands comparison beyond FeatInv variants and the MiniSD baseline.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes tuning from FID-based selection of fixed guidance scales to model-specific control-strength and guidance selection using classification agreement. Tables 1 and 3 change spatial cosine-similarity aggregation from median to mean. Added protocols include one-epoch intermediate-layer training, control/guidance sweeps using one image per class, and native-resolution versus resized RCDM evaluation.

E4.justification: Appendix A.2 replaces the ConvNeXt guidance-only FID/cosine-distance analysis with joint control-strength/guidance analyses across three backbones. v2 also adds intermediate-layer analyses, different-seed reconstruction examples, ImageNet-A/C robustness tests, and four additional concept-steering case studies. The earlier BAID and spatial-composition analyses are retained, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly states that the main evaluation generates one sample per feature map and adds qualitative variation across different random seeds in Appendix A.3. The five matched-seed reconstruction pairs used by FeatInv-Viz remain unchanged. Neither version reports confidence intervals, significance tests, or quantitative uncertainty estimates for the benchmark results.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 revise many results: unpooled ResNet50 top5/top1 agreement changes from 87%/63% to 91%/70%, while unpooled ConvNeXt FID changes from 7.14 to 8.20. These are revised results under changed settings, not established same-setting gains. v2 also adds RCDM, intermediate-layer, and corruption results, plus aggregate BAID results and ImageNet-A agreement of 71%/38%.

M1.justification: The frozen MiniSD backbone, ControlNet conditioning, convolutional feature encoder, noise-prediction objective, and FeatInv-Viz procedure remain unchanged. The intermediate-layer experiments reuse the existing procedure with layer-specific dimensions; control and guidance tuning changes concern experimental settings.

P1.justification: Most existing prose, including the abstract, methods, conclusion, and limitations, remains closely matched. v2 clarifies faithfulness terminology, creates a dedicated robustness subsection, reorganizes appendices, and moves BAID and spatial-composition discussion into the main text. These are localized revisions rather than a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the guidance line plot with control/guidance heatmaps and adds intermediate-layer charts, seed-variation grids, corruption plots and image panels, an RCDM comparison table, and further concept visualizations. Existing BAID and spatial-composition figures move into the main text. The document also adopts a different publication layout.

R1.justification: v2 adds Preechakul et al.'s diffusion autoencoders and distinguishes their global latent codes from spatial feature conditioning. It also adds the ImageNet-A/C references and expands the discussion of the already-cited RCDM approach. The central novelty positioning remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The concept-subspace decomposition and mathematical operations in Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. No new theorems, proofs, or formal assumptions appear. The added description of faithfulness is informal, while the cosine-aggregation revision concerns evaluation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation by adding a direct competing-method comparison and systematic tests of intermediate layers, adversarial images, and corruption severity. These address v1's limited evidence about comparative effectiveness and where faithful reconstruction fails. Unequal RCDM resolutions, possible incomplete convergence, and reporting inconsistencies—including calling lower RCDM FID values higher—temper the conclusions, but the added validation and concrete failure boundaries provide a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FeatInv work. Their main text, tables, figures, algorithm, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including material relocated between the appendices and main text.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds RCDM comparisons, intermediate-layer experiments, ImageNet-A and ImageNet-C evaluations, and reconstruction-variability analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet reconstruction experiments, cross-model evaluations, encoder and guidance ablations, BAID reconstructions, and feature-manipulation demonstrations.

results.title: FeatInv: Spatially resolved mapping from feature space to input space using conditional diffusion models

C1.justification: The central claims remain layer-dependent redundancy, training-free selective Jacobi acceleration, superlinear and finite convergence, and up to 4.7× acceleration with little generation-quality loss. The new experiments support the existing generality claim. The added 'discrete' terminology clarifies the finite-cascade setting already studied.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning initialization insensitivity, architecture-dependent layer selection, memory savings from avoiding KV storage, reconstruction consistency, and GAN/diffusion tradeoffs. The original undertraining and training-optimization limitations remain. Its new claim of preserving 'strict bijective consistency' is stronger than the reported nonzero reconstruction errors directly establish.

D1.justification: v1 promises code release upon acceptance; v2 supplies a project-code URL. Table A2 newly documents batch sizes, sequence lengths, and AFHQ architecture alongside retained CIFAR settings. The appendices also identify the nflows implementation, MAF training/evaluation settings, and the diffusion checkpoint, substantially expanding reproducibility information.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates image generation on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and AFHQ. v2 adds binary MNIST generation and Boltzmann-distribution approximation for a high-temperature 2D Ising model, substantially extending coverage beyond the original image domains. It also evaluates image reconstruction on the retained datasets.

E2.justification: The sequential and uniform Jacobi baselines remain in Table 1. v2 adds an evaluated CIFAR-10 comparison with the baseline labeled FastGAN and DDIM at 20 steps in Appendix E.5/Table A6, extending comparisons from decoding alternatives to distinct generative-model families.

E3.justification: The main TarFlow protocol remains unchanged. New protocols include eight-layer MAF experiments, 3,000 reverse-KL training epochs and 100,000 evaluation samples for Ising, 20-step DDIM, round-trip reconstruction MSE, and memory measurement at batch size 16. The dependency analysis also adds L2 distance. Newly disclosed TarFlow configurations do not establish changes to its existing experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds zero/Gaussian/previous-layer initialization ablations, quantitative dependency analyses at additional masking offsets, reconstruction-error tests, and per-layer iteration, runtime, and memory analyses. These substantially extend robustness and mechanism validation. The original full convergence plots are retained as Figure A2 rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions report maximum deviations across three CIFAR runs in Table 1 and average TarFlow timing over ten runs. v2 introduces no new seed-reporting practice, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedure; its additional results principally use point estimates.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in Table 1 are unchanged. v2 nevertheless adds substantial results: 15.7× Ising and 18.4× binary-MNIST acceleration, reconstruction MSEs of 0.00636/0.00313/0.00122, memory usage of 5.2 versus 7.8 GB, and cross-model and runtime-breakdown results. Figure 1 also changes its reported dependency curves and replaces its CIFAR-10 panel with CIFAR-100.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and the TarFlow procedure retain the same Jacobi updates, stopping rule, and sequential first layer. Appendix E.3 extends the layer-selection policy for MLP-based MAF: without KV caching, Jacobi decoding is applied to every layer. This is a limited procedural adaptation.

P1.justification: v2 edits the title, author information, prose, and terminology, including replacing image-specific 'patches' with 'sub-variables'. It rewrites the preliminaries, folds experimental settings into Section 4, and regroups appendices with a notation guide. The overall motivation-method-evaluation narrative and most section sequencing remain.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a different publication layout, redraws Figure 1 with dual metrics, adds an initialization chart, six appendix tables, and new diagnostic and reconstruction figures. The full original Figure 4 moves to Figure A2 while the main text shows two panels; original Figures 6–7 become Figures A7–A8. These changes substantially reorganize visual presentation.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion and principal novelty positioning remain largely unchanged. v2 adds Zhong et al. (2020) for its GAN comparison and contextualizes results against GANs and diffusion models. TarFlow's updated publication information and the switch to author-year citations do not constitute new cited research.

T1.justification: The convergence propositions and proof strategies are retained. v2 replaces the proof's C1-diffeomorphism assumption with continuous differentiability and corrects inconsistent K-versus-L finite-convergence statements. Appendix D adds an argument that both implementations have O(L²) memory complexity. These are localized mathematical corrections and additions.

improvement.justification: v1's empirical support was confined to TarFlow and lacked direct reconstruction and resource diagnostics. v2 addresses these gaps with another architecture, a non-image sampling task, initialization and reconstruction tests, and detailed inference profiling and reproducibility information. These additions substantially strengthen validation of generality and practical behavior while retaining the original main results. The reconstruction appendix overstates exact bijective preservation, but that qualification does not outweigh the broader evidential improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same selective Jacobi decoding work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, proofs, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds MAF experiments, initialization tests, reconstruction measurements, resource analyses, and comparisons with other generative models.

before.justification: v1 reports original TarFlow experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and AFHQ, including inference comparisons, dependency analyses, convergence measurements, and stopping-threshold ablations.

results.title: Accelerating Inference of Discrete Autoregressive Normalizing Flows by Selective Jacobi Decoding

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the central novelty, two-variant denoising contribution, and independence from noise-model knowledge. The revised discussion adds an explicit claim of practical scalability to OGBN-Arxiv, including execution where several competing methods encounter memory limits.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation of graph-dependent influence approximations, baseline behavior on sparse versus dense graphs, split sensitivity, overlapping classes, and computational scalability. It also positions DeGLIF as complementary preprocessing for noise-robust learners. The overlap-specific relabelling interpretation remains uncertain because Tables 8 and 10 report identical values for different scenarios.

D1.justification: v2 discloses torch.linalg.inv usage, dataset-dependent weight decay, and the sampling strategy underlying the original splits. It adds architectures, clean-node budgets, splits, and data modifications for new experiments, plus measured resource costs. Code access changes from an anonymous short link to an explicitly identified GitHub repository; the PDFs do not establish changes to repository contents.

E1.justification: v2 adds OGBN-Arxiv, PubMed, and the heterophilic Roman-Empire dataset, substantially extending graph size and structural coverage. Appendix E.2 also adds class-imbalanced and overlapping-class Cora scenarios. The original datasets and binary variants remain.

E2.justification: TSS joins the retained main benchmark comparator set in v2 Table 2 and receives additional comparisons under its preferred split. DirGNNConv is newly evaluated as the standalone comparator for Roman-Empire in Table 16. The original main-table comparators are retained.

E3.justification: The original main benchmark settings remain, but v2 introduces separate full-split TSS comparisons, group-removal experiments using 100 subsets per group size, and runtime/memory evaluations. New benchmark protocols include 400 clean nodes and hidden dimension 64 for OGBN-Arxiv, and a 50/25/25 split with DirGNNConv for Roman-Empire. Macro-F1 evaluation is also added.

E4.justification: v2 adds empirical checks of influence additivity and behavior without strict convergence, class-imbalance and overlap stress tests, split-sensitivity comparisons, and the TSS hybrid analysis. These examine previously untested assumptions and failure conditions. Existing clean-set-size, repeated-denoising, backbone, and threshold analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report five-run means and standard deviations. v2 additionally introduces average-rank analysis and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests comparing both DeGLIF variants against TSS and RTGNN in Section 5, substantially expanding statistical support for comparative claims. Appendix E.1 also introduces Pearson-correlation estimation for influence validation.

E6.justification: The original main-table and binary results are retained apart from equivalent rounding. v2 adds substantial results for TSS, hybrid training, influence validation, runtime, and new scenarios. For example, Table 14 reports 36.7±3.6 for DeGLIF versus 31.6±2.7 for GCN at 50% pairwise noise on OGBN-Arxiv; these are newly evaluated results.

M1.justification: The influence calculation, two noisy-node detectors, and relabelling rule remain unchanged. Section 5.4 adds a concrete hybrid variant that replaces the second-stage GCN with TSS, extending the training pipeline within the existing framework.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: related work moves from Appendix D into Section 7, computational complexity becomes a dedicated section with a new appendix discussion, and a notation guide and assumption remarks are added. Experimental interpretation and discussion are extensively revised, alongside document-wide terminology and citation-style edits.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn, v1 Tables 2–3 are transposed and consolidated into v2 Table 2, and the two main threshold figures are merged. The original relabelling table becomes prose, retained appendix plots are resized or relocated, algorithms are reformatted, and numerous new experimental tables are introduced.

R1.justification: The principal novelty positioning and most original related-work discussion remain. v2 adds TSS, new dataset/backbone references, and literature on Hessian-vector methods and influence-approximation limitations. It also emphasizes complementing existing noise-robust methods through hybrid training.

T1.justification: Theorems 1–3 and their Appendix C proofs are essentially retained. v2 explicitly extends the stated applicability to stationary points with invertible Hessians, derives the relabelling-weight bound, and adds an i.i.d.-sampling rationale for expected-risk claims. Section 6 and Appendix D add complexity and inverse-Hessian-vector-product formulations.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1 through empirical validation of the influence approximation, comparisons under alternative splits, and measured scalability on larger and heterophilic graphs. These additions materially strengthen assessment of reliability and applicability while preserving the original results. Identical entries in the new imbalance and overlap relabelling tables weaken that particular analysis, but the broader validation gains remain substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DeGLIF research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds benchmark, robustness, influence-validation, hybrid-model, and runtime results in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: Sections 4–5 and Appendix E report original node-classification experiments on Cora, Citeseer, Amazon Photo, and binary variants, alongside denoising and sensitivity analyses.

results.title: DeGLIF for Label Noise Robust Node Classification using GNNs

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution statement redefine the allocator as a strict refinement of token-level allocation and newly claim lower quantization error under the same bit budget. They explicitly extend the contribution to from-scratch pretraining. The abstract also recasts 4.3× as throughput speedup over FP32, adds a 1.33× wall-clock claim over AQ-SGD, and narrows the memory claim to avoiding activation-cache overhead. The 3–4-bit and SGD-rate claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations involving within-token heterogeneity, group-size/metadata tradeoffs, and pipeline bubbles. v1's dedicated early-pretraining limitation is removed, while Appendix D qualifies the 8B run through its limited tokens-per-parameter budget. Appendices G–H add low-bit applicability boundaries and attribute the long-horizon NaN event to backward fixed-point precision, reporting recovery at 10 bits.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands reproducibility information: default allocation/group sizes and the 80/20 precision split, contiguous uint8 packing, approximately 4.41 transmitted bits per element including metadata, profiling settings, and detailed pretraining architecture and optimizer parameters. Appendix H documents gradient scaling and checkpoint recovery. These disclosures go well beyond v1's short training-settings appendix, although no new code-access resource is provided.

E1.justification: v1's C4 pretraining experiment is replaced by SlimPajama-6B pretraining, and Appendix D adds mathematical-corpus pretraining on Proof-Pile. HellaSwag and MBPP evaluation disappear. MMLU is removed from the main downstream comparison but remains in the group-size ablation, so its coverage is not wholly removed. The four fine-tuning/instruction-tuning datasets and Math-7K verification remain.

E2.justification: The main FP32/FP16, AQ-SGD, and original-Qwen comparators remain. Appendix H newly evaluates NAIVE-4bit against TAH-Quant-4bit for backward gradients. Newly cited methods such as QuaRot and SpinQuant are not evaluated baselines; likewise, Appendix D explicitly says AQ-SGD is only included in the legend, not executed.

E3.justification: The pretraining protocol changes from Qwen2.5-3B/C4 for 6,000 iterations to LLaMA-3.2-1B/SlimPajama training through approximately 6B tokens, with PP=4, sequence length 4096, batch size 256, and held-out perplexity checkpoints. A separate 8B-model protocol and controlled micro-batch/precision sweeps are added. v2 also reports four or eight pipeline stages instead of uniformly eight, changes the downstream average's benchmark composition, and documents an actual backward-precision increase from 8 to 10 bits after instability.

E4.justification: The original group-size, adaptive-allocation, and Hadamard ablations remain. Appendices E–H add throughput sensitivity to micro-batch size and bandwidth, outlier-threshold sensitivity, INT4/INT3 ratio comparisons, an INT2 failure test, and backward-gradient stress tests. The long-horizon NaN investigation adds a concrete failure analysis absent from v1.

E5.justification: v2 adds curves labelled ePDF to the existing quantization-error histograms and specifies a 300-step rolling-mean estimator for pretraining loss in Table 1. These are limited additions to statistical summaries. Neither version supplies repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or a significance test supporting v2's statistically indistinguishable wording.

E6.justification: New results include 6B-token validation perplexities of 20.64 versus 20.67 for TAH-QUANT and FP16, and step-600 backward-quantization losses of 2.52 versus 6.04 for TAH-Quant-4bit and NAIVE-4bit. C4 and several downstream result entries disappear. Retained downstream scores and GPT-2 throughput values are unchanged; the SFT average changes from 60.9 to 59.32 because benchmark membership changes. The unchanged throughput table gives 4045/751, approximately 5.39× at 100 Mbps, inconsistent with v2's stated maximum of 4.3×.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 changes a central component: v1 assigns one precision to every tile belonging to a token, whereas v2 ranks channel-window allocation tiles and permits different precisions within one token. The new allocation size A defaults to the quantization group size G; A=C recovers token-level allocation. This changes the allocation procedure, while retaining group quantization and the pivot-Hadamard transform.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much existing prose remain. Targeted rewrites affect the abstract, contributions, allocation explanation, evaluation discussion, and conclusion; computational overhead receives its own subsection. Evaluation instructions move from the table caption into Appendix B, additional appendices are organized by study, and writing/impact disclosures and an additional author are introduced.

P2.justification: v2 consolidates the retained convergence and runtime panels into Figure 2 and merges the two component-ablation figures into Figure 3. It redraws Figure 1 with density overlays and revised axes, narrows the downstream table, and adds a pretraining table, a two-panel pretraining figure, and six supplementary experimental tables. This substantially changes the presentation of the evidence beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds positioning against Subspace Networks, QuaRot, and SpinQuant, distinguishing parameterization constraints and inference rotations from activation communication during training. Additional citations support slow-network settings and the pretraining token-budget discussion. MMLU, HellaSwag, and MBPP references are removed. The broader research positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: The convergence assumptions, theorem, corollary, and Appendix C proofs remain substantively unchanged after matching renumbering. v2 adds computational-complexity bounds for pivot selection, entropy ranking, and Hadamard application in Section 3.4, and formalizes allocation tiles and the A=C special case. These are limited mathematical additions, not a new convergence proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's explicitly acknowledged weak pretraining validation through a 6B-token from-scratch experiment with held-out perplexity and an additional 8B-model check. The sensitivity tests, disclosed backward-gradient failure, and implementation details materially improve evidence about applicability and reproducibility. These gains outweigh the narrower downstream comparison, although unsupported statistical-equivalence language and the throughput-speedup inconsistency limit the strength of some claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TAH-QUANT. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial additions and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and reports additional pretraining, throughput-sensitivity, low-bit quantization, and numerical-stability experiments in the main text and Appendices D–H.

before.justification: v1 reports original training-loss curves, throughput measurements, downstream benchmark scores, quantization-error measurements, and component ablations.

results.title: TAH-QUANT: Effective Activation Quantization in Pipeline Parallelism over Slow Network

C1.justification: The central failure-mode diagnosis and lower-bound remedy remain. v2 adds an abstract claim of a seven-percentage-point worst-class advantage over AUTO and makes empirical Pareto-frontier membership a conclusion claim, refining v1's broader assertions of outperforming existing methods.

C2.justification: v2 adds regime-dependent bias–variance explanations, discusses when small clipping bounds can help, and explains AUTO's advantage with very limited tuning trials. It distinguishes demographic parity from predictive accuracy and explicitly identifies tuning overhead as a limitation. The conclusion also replaces v1's assertion that DP inherently enforces unfairness with a more qualified distinction between privacy guarantees and accuracy disparities.

D1.justification: v1 promises a future code release; v2 supplies a repository link. v2 newly identifies the BoTorch sampler, AUTO's stability constant, and model-specific runtimes, including revised tabular timing. Conversely, v1's explicit gender-balancing statement for Adult/Dutch is omitted; this changes documentation without establishing an actual preprocessing change.

E1.justification: v2 retains the four original datasets and adds CelebA eyeglasses classification with gender-specific evaluation (Section 4.1, Figure 3). This extends coverage from handwritten digits, clothing, and census records to natural face images and demographic disparities in attribute prediction.

E2.justification: v2 adds AUTO to the retained image and tabular comparisons, including DP-HPO experiments. Appendix C.1 additionally evaluates FairDP against the existing methods on Adult and Dutch using group accuracy and demographic parity. Constant and unbounded adaptive clipping remain.

E3.justification: v2 adds demographic-parity evaluation and fixed-lower-bound controls. The tabular privacy-budget set changes from {0.1, 0.2, 0.5} to {0.05, 0.1, 0.2}, and AUTO receives a tabular learning-rate grid extending to 50 (Table A3). DP-HPO curves also use different reported total privacy budgets, preventing direct same-budget performance comparisons.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's illustrative trajectories and hyperparameter heatmaps, v2 adds an Adult accuracy-sensitivity analysis (Figure A1), tests fixed CLB = 0.1 against tuning (Appendix C.2), and adds Skewed MNIST/CelebA training trajectories (C.4). Appendix C.3 also expands micro-versus-macro accuracy analysis beyond the earlier Skewed MNIST heatmaps.

E5.justification: The reported DP-HPO averaging decreases from 20 runs in v1 Figure 4 to 10 runs in v2 Figure 5. Standard-error reporting and ten-run optimal-hyperparameter comparisons remain. Table A1 clarifies the tuning summaries as ten random seeds with twenty trials per tuning run.

E6.justification: Retained numerical results are revised: bounded clipping's Skewed MNIST ResNet-18 macro/worst-class accuracy at epsilon = 2 changes from 94.32%/71.41% in v1 Table 5 to 94.11%/68.87% in v2 Table A4. v2 also adds CelebA, AUTO, FairDP, fixed-bound, and demographic-parity results. DP-HPO curves change, although conflicting endpoint budgets in v2 Figure 5 and Table A7 limit their interpretation.

M1.justification: Algorithm 2 retains the normalized gradient update, noisy gradient-count query, exponential clipping-bound adaptation, and lower-bound constraint. The newly evaluated fixed CLB = 0.1 variant uses an existing parameter setting; it introduces no new clipping component or update rule.

P1.justification: v2 reorganizes Methodology, moves dataset preprocessing from Appendix A into Section 4.1, restructures the experimental appendices, and substantially rewrites results discussion and conclusion. Terminology shifts throughout toward disparate impact and accuracy parity, while algorithms gain explanatory annotations.

P2.justification: The principal accuracy-versus-budget line plots are redesigned as joint-performance scatter panels, with expanded line-plot comparisons appearing in the appendix. v2 adds CelebA, demographic-parity, sensitivity, and trajectory displays, expands result tables, and revises heatmap captions and axes. The journal layout also replaces the earlier wrapped figures and algorithms.

R1.justification: v2 substantially broadens positioning through AUTO and FairDP comparisons and reconciles its findings with prior small-clipping results using bias–variance reasoning. New discussion cites Rehn et al. (2026), Barocas et al. (2023), and Defrance and De Bie (2025) to contextualize clipping regimes and fairness trade-offs.

T1.justification: Lemma 3.1 expands Gaussian-mechanism composition from unit sensitivities to arbitrary sensitivities Delta1 and Delta2, retaining the original formula as a special case. The applied privacy theorem remains unchanged, and no substantial new proof development is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation through alternative clipping/fairness baselines, demographic-parity evaluation, CelebA, and direct tests of tuning sensitivity and a fixed lower bound. These address important gaps in v1's comparative evidence and practical tuning claims. Reporting weaknesses temper the gains: DP-HPO uses fewer runs, and Figure 5's Fashion-MNIST endpoint epsilon = 116.8 conflicts with Table A7's 13.370. Nevertheless, the broader comparative and diagnostic evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same bounded adaptive clipping work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, despite some internal reporting inconsistencies.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on five datasets, including CelebA, expanded baseline comparisons, sensitivity studies, and training-trajectory analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original mean-estimation experiments and private image/tabular classification results on four datasets, including hyperparameter analyses in Appendix B.

results.title: Mitigating Disparate Impact of Differentially Private Learning through Bounded Adaptive Clipping

C1.justification: The central probabilistic-INR, individualized prediction and single-training claims remain. The abstract narrows comparisons to existing INR approaches and qualifies order-of-magnitude improvements as occurring on several datasets. The conclusion replaces the broad inference-efficiency advantage with the more specific claim of fixed inference time independent of gradient adaptation.

C2.justification: v1 already discussed stronger competitors in some settings and long-horizon outliers. v2 substantially extends interpretation through architectural-complexity tradeoffs, calibration behavior, decoder and likelihood explanations, and explicit limitations concerning informative missingness and a single global latent representation. It also distinguishes evaluated in-distribution generalization from unevaluated foundation-model and out-of-distribution settings.

D1.justification: v2 adds an anonymous code link and repository-based data/dependency instructions in its reproducibility statement. It newly specifies the Laplace output parameterization, covariate binning, temporal pooling, AdamW use and configurations for added experiments. The existing detailed split, hyperparameter and hardware disclosures largely remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The underlying datasets are retained, but v2 adds joint multivariate forecasting on Electricity, Traffic and Solar-H, requiring multiple series to be modeled together (Section 4.1.5). Appendix B.3 also adds Electricity forecasting with partially observed history, extending the previously fully observed forecasting scenario.

E2.justification: CSDI is added to univariate and multivariate imputation comparisons and downstream HAR classification. Appendix A.13 introduces evaluated TV-VAE decoder baselines, while A.8 adds a TimeFlow variant trained with randomly sampled observation ratios. The original comparison methods remain.

E3.justification: Existing splits and principal univariate settings are retained. Added protocols include enlarged networks for joint forecasting, randomized TimeFlow training, decoder and likelihood controls, and NLL/90% coverage evaluation. Missing-history forecasting uses shared test masks but different training exposure: TV-INRs receives a missing-history curriculum while baselines train on full histories. B.3 lists a 0.2 observation ratio where Table 29 lists 0.3.

E4.justification: v2 adds Fourier-frequency ablations, comparisons against direct MLP decoders, predictive calibration analysis, forecasting-error histograms, missing-history robustness tests and Laplace-versus-Gaussian sensitivity analysis (A.12–A.13 and B.1–B.4). These test architectural necessity and failure mechanisms beyond v1's existing covariate and TimeFlow missingness analyses.

E5.justification: v2 introduces quantitative predictive-uncertainty evaluation, explicitly labeled 5th–95th percentile bands and detailed best-model-versus-comparator significance tables. Welch's test at alpha=0.05 was already documented in v1. Conversely, v1's explicit three-training-seed statement disappears; this is a loss of reporting detail, not evidence that fewer runs were performed.

E6.justification: The original main benchmark values are retained, while substantial new results cover CSDI, joint forecasting, ablations, calibration, missing-history robustness and imputation latency. Small existing values also change: TimeFlow's Electricity MAE at L=2000, training ratio 1.0 and testing ratio 0.5 changes from 0.25084 to 0.25284 (v1 Table 11; v2 Table 13). New Table 33 marks sparse-P12 comparisons of C-TV-INRs against SAITS and TV-INRs as nonsignificant, unlike v1's significant-superiority claim.

M1.justification: Section 3.1 corrects the stated training rule from minimizing to maximizing the same ELBO. The Transformer, latent-variable, hypernetwork and INR pipeline remains intact. Newly specified Laplace outputs and covariate binning clarify implementation; they do not establish a redesigned method or rerun of existing experiments.

P1.justification: The introduction, contributions, related-work passages, method instructions and experimental narrative undergo substantial rewriting. v2 adds an explicit pipeline summary, reorganizes appendix material and introduces dedicated reproducibility and limitations sections. These changes materially reshape the explanation and navigation beyond simply appending results.

P2.justification: v2 expands comparison tables and the classification figure with CSDI, adds numerous analytical tables and an error-distribution figure, and redraws prediction examples with percentile bands. Main-table highlighting changes from significance/comparability to best/second-best means, the dataset summary moves to the appendix, and the document adopts journal formatting.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion and citations for CSDI, LSCD and temporal INR foundation models, plus references supporting missing-data mechanisms, masked training and Fourier features. This broadens and qualifies the existing research positioning without replacing its central relationship to INR, hypernetwork and amortized-inference work.

T1.justification: Appendix A.9 adds componentwise complexity reasoning under the assumption L is much larger than embedding and latent dimensions, yielding stated time and memory bounds of O(NL²E) and O(ML²). v2 also removes the earlier equality that incorrectly defined the absent-index set as all indices. These are bounded analytical additions and corrections, without new central theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked direct validation of the INR decoder's contribution and quantitative assessment of its probabilistic predictions. v2's targeted decoder/Fourier ablations, calibration measurements and explicit failure analyses substantially strengthen architectural justification and expose applicability limits, including serious interval undercoverage. Different training curricula and inconsistent ratios weaken the missing-history comparison, and the lost seed-count statement reduces transparency, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the broader gains in validation and qualification.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Temporal Variational Implicit Neural Representations by the same authors. All 22 pages of v1 and 36 pages of v2, including appendices, tables, equations and figures, support comparison despite substantial additions and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, multivariate forecasting, ablations, uncertainty evaluation and missing-history experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original imputation, forecasting, downstream HAR classification and computational timing experiments in the main text and appendices.

results.title: Temporal Variational Implicit Neural Representations

C1.justification: Both versions retain the same central contributions: nine OR environments, Gym/OmniSafe integration, and empirical diagnosis of safe RL limitations under complex constraints. v2 explicitly calls the work a benchmarking and diagnostic study, clarifying rather than changing its original contribution.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the brief overall discussion with extensive interpretations by algorithm class, linking behavior to trust-region updates, replay-based estimation, and discontinuous constraint landscapes. It adds qualifications about scalarization favoring high-violation policies and deterministic coverage. ASU is now interpreted as failing feasibility despite reasonably competitive rewards.

D1.justification: New Section 4 documents the small CMDP wrapper, external JSON instance specifications, and extension through inheritance. Further details include stochastic failure sampling, inventory-policy trigger bounds, and runtimes for added methods and scenarios. The repository access information and hardware remain the same.

E1.justification: The nine task families remain. Evaluation adds stochastic compressor failures through SchedMaintEnv-v1 and removes the GTEP scenario without transmission lines. Standard GTEP, multi-bus unit commitment, and ASU evaluations are retained despite changes in placement.

E2.justification: FOCOPS, SACLag, and SACPID join the original five algorithms in the retained comparisons. Appendix C.3 also evaluates classical (s, S) and (r, Q) inventory policies against the RL reward results, substantially broadening the comparison methods.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 replaces v1's cost-filtered best/worst selection with Pareto identification and normalized scalarization over 101 preference weights. It specifies a cost threshold of 25 for reasonable optimality and introduces a perfect-information optimization upper bound for stochastic maintenance. Evaluation remains based on 10 episodes.

E4.justification: v2 adds reward–safety preference sensitivity analyses in Figures 3 and 13 and compares deterministic versus stochastic maintenance behavior. Constraint-wise diagnostics expand to eight algorithms. Conversely, v1's blending disable/none ablations and generation-expansion analysis without transmission are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions describe standard-deviation bands for training curves. Unlike v1's mean-only evaluation tables, v2 Table 4 explicitly reports standard deviations for selected stochastic-maintenance results. The 10-episode evaluation count is unchanged; additional independent training runs are not established.

E6.justification: The original algorithms' retained deterministic evaluation values are unchanged, but substantial results are added for three algorithms, stochastic maintenance, and inventory heuristics. New SACLag results on GridStorageEnv are reward −68690.5 and cost 0.03, supporting its revised solvability classification. The (r, Q) policy obtains reward 10948.9 versus OnCRPO's retained 7598.66. Results for the removed variants disappear.

M1.justification: The benchmark gains a localized environment-model extension: SchedMaintEnv-v1 uniformly samples compressor failure times from MTTF, MTTF−1, and MTTF−2 at episode initialization (Appendix A.8). The deterministic version remains, and no new learning algorithm is proposed.

P1.justification: The environment overview is reorganized to cover all nine families, a dedicated implementation section is introduced, and the results discussion is extensively rewritten around multi-objective evaluation and algorithm classes. Evaluation tables and supplementary discussions are reorganized into separate appendices.

P2.justification: v2 adds eight environment schematics, evaluation bar charts, Pareto-score plots, and comparison and summary tables. Earlier evaluation tables are consolidated into a rotated appendix table, existing plots expand to eight algorithms, and several variant plots are removed. These substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for SAC, PID constraint control, FOCOPS, and Powell's sequential-decision framework. Table 1 and Appendix D expand comparisons with OR-Gym and SustainGym, including interfaces and observation/action dimensions. The central positioning around industrial constraints beyond existing benchmarks remains unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 introduces a formal normalized scalarized score for Pareto comparisons and a stochastic failure-time assumption. Appendix A also revises state-set definitions, including equipment in STN and restricting observed inventory to main supply-chain nodes. Most environmental equations remain equivalent, and no new theorem or proof appears.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the benchmark's evidential value through broader algorithm comparisons, an evaluated stochastic scenario, and classical inventory reward references that challenge the learned policies. Explicit reward–safety analysis and implementation documentation address important evaluation and usability gaps. Removing blending and topology ablations reduces diagnostic coverage, scalarized winners can remain highly infeasible, and classical-policy costs are unreported. These limitations temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SafeOR-Gym and the same nine core environment families. Their main text, appendices, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renamed material.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds evaluations of further RL algorithms, stochastic maintenance, and classical inventory policies.

before.justification: v1 reports original training curves, evaluation rewards and costs, constraint-violation analyses, and runtimes for five safe RL algorithms.

results.title: SafeOR-Gym: A Benchmark Suite for Safe Reinforcement Learning Algorithms on Practical Operations Research Problems

C1.justification: The abstract changes from claiming comparable unimodal performance to claiming outperformance on several unimodal as well as multimodal tasks. The central contributions—early fusion through a single encoder, combined training objectives, and multimodal datasets and evaluations—remain the same.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly limits TGIT findings to learning transformation families represented during training, acknowledges FuseLIP-S's weaker classification/retrieval performance, and qualifies MMM as an additional benefit rather than the sole explanation for gains. Appendix B distinguishes tokenizer fidelity from token-budget scaling and interprets the new controls. Additional discussion addresses inference-cost amortization and specific risks from caption-generated data and spatial-localization capabilities.

D1.justification: V2 clarifies positional embeddings across the concatenated sequence, cosine-similarity retrieval, category-level mean top-1 accuracy, and the 80-template ImageNet evaluation. It explicitly advertises code and dataset release, whereas v1 advertises code and models. Existing training hyperparameters and asset links are retained; the PDFs alone do not verify external resource availability.
