E1.justification: Training and evaluation retain the same dataset and task coverage, including CC3M/CC12M, generated multimodal tasks, Visual Genome, HQ-Edit, MMEB, OpenImages tasks, ImageNet, and SugarCrepe. V2's unimodal-task table aggregates previously evaluated MMEB subtasks rather than introducing new coverage.

E2.justification: V2 substantially expands the controlled comparisons with TiTok-SigLIP-BMLF and small/base SigLIP-MLF variants using frozen pretrained encoders (Tables 14–15). These examine alternatives absent from v1. Pretrained SigLIP and VLM2Vec are retained comparisons moved from v1 Table 11 to v2 Table 5, not new baselines.

E3.justification: New protocols independently cross tokenizer and transformer sizes at a fixed 128-token budget, supply TiTok tokens to late fusion, pretrain and freeze SigLIP backbones before multimodal training, and train with MMM alone. Main training budgets remain unchanged. V2 also corrects OI-Crop's main-text description from five to four same-image negatives, matching v1 Appendix A.4 rather than establishing an actual dataset change.

E4.justification: Appendix B adds substantial analyses separating tokenizer fidelity from encoder size, testing tokenizer pretraining as an explanation for gains, evaluating frozen backbones, checking the necessity of contrastive loss, and examining unimodal performance separately (Tables 13–17). Existing loss and hard-negative ablations remain. The CC3M-trained per-transformation TGIT breakdown is removed; the CC12M-trained breakdown remains.

E5.justification: V1 reports benchmark point estimates without training-seed uncertainty. V2 Table 10 reports means and standard deviations across three different training seeds for FuseLIP-B and SigLIP-BMLF on CC3M+MM across nine benchmarks. V1's training-run count is unspecified, so an increase from a particular earlier count cannot be inferred.

E6.justification: V2 adds results for the new controls, seed averages, and unimodal aggregates. For example, Table 14 reports 69.3% TGIT for TiTok-SigLIP-BMLF, and Table 16 reports 0.2% VQA for MMM-only FuseLIP-S. Main Table 3 scores remain identical. V2 removes the CC3M per-transformation TGIT scores and corrects OI-Crop random chance from 1.0% to 10.0% in the relocated fine-tuning comparison.

M1.justification: The proposed frozen TiTok tokenizer, shared bidirectional transformer, token concatenation, final-token embedding, combined SigLIP/MMM objective, and hard-negative procedure remain unchanged. V2 clarifies their operation; the newly tested configurations are experimental controls rather than revisions to the proposed method.

P1.justification: The overall section sequence and much of the prose remain. V2 edits wording and explanations, folds Setup into Experiments, moves MMEB fine-tuning and external-model comparisons from Appendix B into the main results, relocates Limitations into Discussion, and adds Broader Impact. These are bounded reorganizations within the existing narrative.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a different publication layout, redraws the architecture diagram, condenses Figure 2, and redisplays an existing horizontal-flip example as main-text Figure 3. It adds several analysis tables, introduces zero-shot markers, relocates and compresses the fine-tuning table, reduces Table 4 to CC12M results, and reorders appendix displays. These changes extend well beyond pagination.

R1.justification: Related work adds VisualBERT, UNITER, recurrence-enhanced retrieval, newer multimodal-LLM embedding work, and DALL-E, while explicitly distinguishing embedding research from other early-fusion applications. Some citations, including DreamSim and EVA-CLIP, disappear. These are targeted positioning updates; the central relationship to CLIP, SigLIP, FLAVA, and MagicLens remains.

T1.justification: The SigLIP, multimodal SigLIP, MMM, combined-objective, and modality-gap formulations are unchanged. V2 adds explanatory qualifications but no new substantive mathematical definitions, assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs.

improvement.justification: V1's attribution of gains to early fusion left tokenizer quality and pretraining insufficiently separated from architecture. V2's controlled experiments in Tables 13–16 substantially address that gap, while Table 10 adds evidence about training stability. Clearer TGIT applicability boundaries also improve interpretation. The lost CC3M transformation breakdown and small unexplained cross-table discrepancies, such as FuseLIP-B TGIT being 93.9 in Table 13 versus 94.3 in Table 3, are drawbacks, but the stronger evidence for the central argument provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FuseLIP and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete Appendices A and B. Content can be matched despite substantial reformatting, renumbering, and relocation.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds original experiments on tokenizer and encoder configurations, comparison models, loss components, and training-seed variability.

before.justification: V1 reports original model evaluations, hard-negative and loss ablations, runtime measurements, and appendix experiments on compositionality, modality gaps, and fine-tuning.

results.title: FuseLIP: Multimodal Embeddings via Early Fusion of Discrete Tokens

C1.justification: The introduction narrows the empirical contribution from consistently outperforming state-of-the-art defenses to outperforming baselines on generation while remaining competitive on classification. The abstract foregrounds recovery and convergence theory, but the central adaptive-purification contribution remains.

C2.justification: v2 adds a conceptual extension from classification theory to prompted VQA and generative VLMs. Appendix D introduces explanations linking semantic richness to threshold selection, threshold/step-size combinations to premature stopping or over-purification, and scheduler variation to recovery behavior. The original image-only limitation and hallucination interpretation are retained, with relocation.

D1.justification: v2 adds a source-code access link, detailed BPDA identity-gradient implementation and EOT averaging instructions, calibration and component timing, and further experimental configuration information. It specifies A100 40G hardware and H100 use for hallucination/jailbreaking, replacing v1's blanket A100 description. Previously disclosed diffusion hyperparameters are mainly relocated into the main text.

E1.justification: v2 adds MNIST and ImageNet-Sketch evaluations, resolution/long-tail distribution-shift scenarios, targeted-caption attacks on MiniGPT-4, and L2-bounded threats. The retained classification tables are relabeled from ImageNet1K to ImageNet-R without numerical changes; the PDFs do not establish whether that reflects corrected identification or different experiments.

E2.justification: Matched comparisons retain TeCoA, FARE, JPEG-DL, DiffPure, and CLIPure. Additional evaluations use existing defenses or no-defense controls, sometimes restricting the comparator subset for new settings. AttackVLM supplies additional attacks, rather than a new competing defense.

E3.justification: New protocols include targeted-caption matching with CLIP scores, 16/255 captioning attacks, L2-bounded VQA attacks, PSNR/LPIPS fidelity measurements, batch-one overhead measurements, and fixed-depth DiffPure controls. Appendix D varies calibration sizes and scheduling strategies. Original settings largely persist; D.5's stated default step size of 0.10 conflicts with 0.01 elsewhere, so an actual default change is unresolved.

E4.justification: Beyond retained backbone and captioning threshold/step-size ablations, v2 adds quantitative fidelity analysis, under-/over-purification comparisons, and robustness checks under additional threats. Appendix D substantially expands threshold sensitivity testing across calibration sizes, domains, tasks, and encoders, and adds scheduler comparisons. Relocated adaptive-attack results are not new analyses.

E5.justification: v2 Appendix D.1 newly reports three random seeds across calibration sizes and a threshold estimate of 0.958 ± 0.003. v1 lacks this uncertainty reporting. The meaning of the ± quantity is unspecified, and comparable repeated-run uncertainty is not added to the main performance tables.

E6.justification: Matched original tables retain their numerical scores, but v2 adds substantial results in Tables 5, 7, and 9–16 and Figure 5. For example, the new MF-ii comparison reports average CLIP scores of 0.730 without defense versus 0.465 with DiffCAP; new fidelity measurements report OF-COCO PSNR of 29.03 for DiffCAP versus 24.27 for DiffPure. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over v1 under identical settings.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 retain cumulative noise injection, consecutive-embedding similarity stopping, threshold calibration, and reverse denoising. The explicit shared-noise assumption concerns the theoretical analysis; alternative schedulers are evaluated as ablations without replacing the proposed default procedure.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the abstract and contribution presentation, swaps related work and preliminaries, moves adaptive attacks and the captioning threshold ablation into the main analysis, and moves the principal classification comparison into the appendix. Author statements and a dedicated hyperparameter appendix substantially reorganize the narrative, although much technical prose is retained.

P2.justification: The document adopts a different publication layout and extensively rearranges displays. The old threshold plot becomes main-text Figure 2 with explicit axis labels, qualitative examples are enlarged, and classification and adaptive-attack tables change placement. Ten genuinely new tables and a new VQA sensitivity figure substantially expand the visual evidence.

R1.justification: v2 adds DiffPAD to the purification discussion and references for MNIST, ImageNet-R, ImageNet-Sketch, and LPIPS. Positioning against adversarial training and fixed-time purification remains substantially unchanged. Numerous venue updates and consolidated duplicate references represent bibliographic maintenance rather than newly cited research.

T1.justification: Lemma 1 and Theorem 2 explicitly acquire a shared-Gaussian-noise coupling condition, clarifying their formal scope. Appendix B.3 replaces v1's flawed monotonicity argument with an auxiliary-function argument using H(t) = beta(t)^2 − 2C_beta(1 − alpha(t)). This substantively repairs the reasoning supporting the central decreasing-bound result.

improvement.justification: v2 repairs a central proof argument and makes its coupling assumption explicit. Quantitative fidelity comparisons and systematic threshold tests address important gaps in v1's support for faithful, reliably adaptive purification; expanded attack evaluations and implementation information further strengthen the paper. These gains go beyond unchanged headline scores. Remaining ImageNet-label inconsistencies and conflicting default step-size statements limit clarity and reproducibility, but do not outweigh the substantial improvements in mathematical reasoning and empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DiffCAP research, with matching algorithms and substantial shared experimental content. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, references, and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds targeted-attack, perceptual-quality, distribution-shift, and hyperparameter evaluations in the main text and Appendices C–D.

before.justification: v1 reports original captioning, VQA, classification, and ablation results, plus adaptive-attack, hallucination, and jailbreaking evaluations in Appendix B.

results.title: Diffusion-based Cumulative Adversarial Purification for Vision Language Models

C1.justification: v2 expands the headline contribution into a modular framework accommodating prior CBM relationship structures, adds computational-efficiency claims, and emphasizes effectiveness with very limited concept supervision. Its abstract claims operation without additional computational overhead. The conclusion also qualifies leakage avoidance as occurring in specific scenarios, narrowing v1's broader leakage-free characterization.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations connecting CCI with intervenability and stronger regularization with scarce concepts. It attributes ineffective propagation to inversion problems and weak parent–child influence, recommending direct-concept interventions (Appendices A.3 and E.4). It also proposes an optimization explanation for side-channel benefits. Conversely, v1's explicit warning that misaligned expert reasoning can constrain performance is removed.

D1.justification: v2 replaces the promise of code release upon acceptance with a concrete repository hyperlink. It adds exact profiling hardware, timing and memory instrumentation, execution controls, and numerical handling for inversion. Most existing implementation documentation remains; the approximate training durations and total compute estimate in v1 are removed. The linked repository's availability cannot be verified from the PDFs alone.

E1.justification: The datasets, image populations and classification targets remain unchanged. v2 adds a limited-concept-supervision scenario on CUB by removing entire concept groups (Figure 9, left), extending incomplete-concept evaluation beyond the fixed iFMNIST setting.

E2.justification: v2 evaluates C2BM and CGM with discovered and supplied graphs on FMNIST and CelebA, and adds CBM+SC across the retained benchmarks (Table 2; Figure 6; Appendix E.2). These substantially expand the actual comparator set. Ground-truth-concept and CREAM-without-side-channel results already existed in v1's appendices. The black-box row is removed from the appendix hard-versus-soft comparison.

E3.justification: Appendix D now states that ResNet-18 uses no pretrained weights and describes CelebA training as 200 epochs rather than early stopping with a 200-epoch cap. Selected CelebA CREAM settings change from dropout 0.8 to 0.1 and total latent dimension 512 to 75. New experiments introduce controlled CPU/GPU profiling and propagation with dC=1. These are reported protocol revisions; they do not establish which earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses relating CCI to intervention effectiveness, removing CUB concept groups, comparing interventions with and without side-channels, propagating indirect-concept interventions, and substituting a discovered CelebA graph (Figures 8–9; Appendices E.2, E.4 and E.6). These test substantial new questions. Existing group interventions, leakage ablations and dropout, dimensionality and depth studies are retained or relocated.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five seeds and report means and standard deviations. v2 additionally specifies averaging computational measurements over 20 iterations after five burn-in iterations (Appendix E.1). This adds a measurement-repetition protocol, without indicating an increase in training seeds or a new general uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Many retained results change: CUB CBM task accuracy is 62.03±0.51% in v1 Table 1 and 73.76±0.32% in v2 Table 2; revised settings prevent treating this as a controlled performance gain. cFMNIST H-CREAM accuracy changes from 88.18±4.92% to 91.29±0.73% in the appendix comparison. v2 also adds comparator scores, runtime and memory results, missing-concept findings, and the finding that indirect-concept propagation yields almost no accuracy benefit.

M1.justification: v2 adds an intervention-propagation procedure: invert concept activations, recover preceding latent activations, then propagate forward to update other concepts and task predictions (Section 4.2; Appendix A.3). This substantially extends v1's CREAM interventions, which directly replace concept predictions for task inference. The underlying splitter, masked networks, joint loss and side-channel regularization remain.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Related Work moves from Section 4 to Section 2, leakage and the side-channel receive dedicated subsections, and the experimental narrative and Appendix E are reorganized. These are substantial editorial and structural changes beyond inserting new experiments.

P2.justification: v2 changes the document template and typography, recolors reasoning graphs, expands and restructures tables, and adds intervention and efficiency displays. Existing CCI and dropout plots are combined with new panels, and correlation heatmaps switch from signed to absolute values with revised color scales. Several appendix results move into main-text displays.

R1.justification: v2 adds Parisini et al. on leakage, removes the Alvarez Melis–Jaakkola and Lakkaraju–Bastani references, and sharpens comparisons with CGM and C2BM concerning graph restrictions, computational cost and side-channel interpretability. Table 1 maps prior approaches' relationship structures into CREAM. Most cited work is retained; C2BM's publication update is not a new work.

T1.justification: New Appendix A.3 derives the conditional softmax inverse and discusses conditions for recovering exogenous activations, including dimensionality, nonzero weights and activation-range restrictions. This is a localized mathematical extension. The graph masks, training objective, leakage definition, CCI formula and CCI threshold derivation already appear in v1.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation by directly comparing against closely related graph-based CBMs previously only discussed, testing side-channel controls and scarce-concept settings, and documenting unsuccessful intervention propagation with explicit limitations. Computational measurements and a code-access link improve auditability. Some claims remain overstated: the abstract's no-overhead wording conflicts with Table 3's 1.82–2.46× CBM-relative GPU runtimes on FMNIST/CUB. Nevertheless, the broader comparisons and clearer empirical boundaries provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CREAM research work. The complete main texts and Appendices A–H are readable, including equations, tables and figures, and retained material can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on the retained datasets, including expanded baseline comparisons, computational measurements, concept-removal experiments and intervention-propagation tests.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on both FMNIST variants, CUB and CelebA, including accuracy, interventions, leakage and appendix ablations.

results.title: Towards Reasonable Concept Bottleneck Models

C1.justification: The central contribution remains progressive optimization for more accurate sparse-view inverse physics without architectural changes. v3 adds explicit claims of computational efficiency and physical interpretability relative to MASIV, and reframes the headline mechanism around physics-guided geometry refinement. The research objective and principal contribution remain recognizable.

C2.justification: v3 qualifies full-joint optimization failure by material complexity and argues that coupled parameters make future-trajectory accuracy more informative than individual parameter errors. It also explains velocity-first scheduling and attributes smaller Spring-Gaus transfer gains to fixed anchor connections and limited spatial flexibility. These substantially extend interpretation; the original simulation-cost and nondifferentiability limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendices C–D and Table 9 newly document 40K initialization iterations, the 3K/37K initialization breakdown, batch sizes, comparator configurations, and GSO stress formulations. Conversely, v1's project/demo link and explicit cosine-schedule details are omitted. Documentation expands substantially, although Table 9 specifies 40K GIC appearance-refinement iterations while Appendix C states 30K.

E1.justification: v3 retains the Spring-Gaus synthetic and real-world datasets and PAC-NeRF materials, while adding GSO evaluation covering 12 object shapes. Table 7 also introduces monocular and two-view reconstruction conditions beyond v1's three-view and ten-view evaluations, expanding the tested observation conditions.

E2.justification: v3 adds MASIV to the Spring-Gaus comparison, Vid2Sim and a constitutive-model-aligned GIC variant to GSO comparisons, and Spring-Gaus to PAC-NeRF elasticity comparisons. It also adds Sequential+ and cyclic controls and broadens full-joint comparisons. Conversely, the retained ten-view evaluation compares against GIC without v1's PAC-NeRF and Spring-Gaus comparator results.

E3.justification: Reported post-initialization training budgets change: Spring-Gaus uses 100/100 iterations instead of 100/100/100, while PAC-NeRF Newtonian training changes from 50/50/300 to 100/250. v3 introduces sequential/cyclic control protocols and GSO comparisons with aligned stress formulations. The original three-camera selection and real-world 14-frame training/6-frame testing split remain.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's limited optimization diagnostics, v3 systematically compares sequential, joint, progressive, and cyclic strategies; tests Stage 1 parameter choices across materials; measures initial-geometry and camera-view sensitivity; and evaluates adaptation to the Spring-Gaus framework. Tables 3 and 6–8, Figure 4, and Appendices A–B substantially strengthen analysis of scheduling, robustness, and applicability.

E5.justification: Both versions report means and standard deviations across PAC-NeRF scenes within material categories. v3 extends that reporting convention to additional comparisons but introduces no repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Changed deviation values are result changes rather than changes in statistical practice.

E6.justification: Numerous existing results are replaced: three-view Spring-Gaus ProJo4D mean CD changes from 0.97 to 1.60 and PSNR from 22.77 to 22.30; real-world mean PSNR changes from 36.60 to 38.30. These accompany a revised optimization procedure and are not same-procedure gains or losses. v3 also adds GSO, baseline, and ablation results while removing detailed per-object ten-view results.

M1.justification: v1 successively optimizes velocity, velocity plus materials, and finally all parameters, keeping geometry and appearance fixed until Stage 3. v3 instead optimizes geometry and appearance jointly with velocity in Stage 1, then adds material parameters for full joint optimization in Stage 2. This substantially changes the central optimization procedure, as confirmed by Table 1 and the optimization equations.

P1.justification: The abstract, later introduction, related work, and motivation undergo substantial rewriting, including an explicit contribution list. Separate initialization, full-joint, and progressive-method discussions are reorganized into the revised Section 3. Results gain a dedicated ablation section and appendices, while limitations are consolidated into the conclusion.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn for the revised stages; optimization plots are reorganized and expanded with Figures 4 and 7. Tables are substantially restructured, with new GSO, ablation, and training-configuration displays and a condensed camera-view comparison replacing the detailed dense-view grid. PAC-NeRF qualitative panels change, v1's real-world image comparison disappears, and the document adopts a different publication layout.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially revised around Vid2Sim, MASIV, Simplicits, and neural constitutive modeling, with a new connection to curriculum learning over parameter space. The dedicated discussion distinguishing inverse estimation from generative dynamics is removed, along with several associated references. This changes research positioning beyond citation-format updates.

T1.justification: Appendix D adds explicit mathematical definitions of the different Kirchhoff stress formulations used by PAC-NeRF/GIC and Vid2Sim/Simplicits, absent from v1. This is a limited formal addition supporting the GSO comparison. Neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs for progressive optimization.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's limited direct validation of its optimization rationale through scheduling controls, material-wise Stage 1 ablations, and tests on another framework. New MASIV/Vid2Sim comparisons and GSO material-formulation controls strengthen assessment of competitiveness and applicability. Expanded implementation details also help reproducibility. Reporting weaknesses remain, including swapped introductory parameter-error labels relative to Table 2, conflicting GIC refinement budgets, and removal of real-world qualitative examples. These drawbacks do not outweigh the substantial improvement in support for the central contribution.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ProJo4D and provide readable text, equations, figures, and tables supporting a reliable comparison. v1 ends after its references; v3 additionally contains Appendices A–D, which were included in the comparison.

after.justification: v3 reports original benchmark results and expanded experiments, including GSO evaluation, optimization ablations, camera-view sensitivity, and analyses in Appendices A–B.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction, future-state prediction, and physical-parameter estimation experiments on synthetic and real-world data, including Tables 2–4 and optimization diagnostics in Figure 3.

results.title: ProJo4D: Progressive Joint Optimization for Sparse-View Inverse Physics Estimation

C1.justification: v2 adds shared multi-task representations, computational reuse, and sample efficiency as central contributions in the abstract, introduction, and discussion. It qualifies v1's broad emphasis on minimal nonlinearity being often optimal by identifying low-data and switching-dependent settings where sparse nonlinearity is advantageous.

C2.justification: v2 shifts the explanation of fully nonlinear failures from overfitting/over-approximation toward optimization instability and learned linearization. It adds computational-reuse interpretations and specific limits on extending dynamical interpretability to modern architectures. However, Section 4.4's claim of chance-level linear performance on the rodent task conflicts with A.4.5, which retains successful task-only linear models and approximately 87% joint-model accuracy.

D1.justification: v2 adds a dedicated Reproducibility section providing a study-specific experiment/dataset repository; v1 only linked upstream AL-RNN implementation code. It also documents the new cognitive-task construction and the activation placement and causal implementation of the S4/Linear Transformer variants. The repository's availability is reported by the PDF.

E1.justification: v2 adds an 11-task cognitive suite involving pro/anti responses, delayed matching, selective attention, and go/no-go decisions under joint training (Section 4.5; Appendix A.3). It also adds variable-delay copying, which changes recall timing requirements (A.4.3). The original datasets remain, including the relocated rodent experiment.

E2.justification: v2 adds direct LSTM and GRU comparisons on Addition, Copy, sMNIST, and Speech Commands in Table 2, substantially expanding v1's comparisons among AL-RNN configurations. Tables 2–3 add activation variants. Figure 27 separately compares fully linear, standard, and sparsely nonlinear configurations within S4 and Linear Transformers.

E3.justification: New protocols include multi-task training with 20, 50, or 500 samples per task, Jensen-Shannon comparisons of task representations, and additional latent-size/regularization controls (Figures 5 and 17). Appendix A.1.3 also changes the stated audio sequence-length comparison from 16k to 784 steps; this documentation change does not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's bitcode and manifold analyses, v2 adds activation comparisons, training-loss and gradient diagnostics, train–test checks for overfitting, and best-run analyses (Tables 2–3; Figures 14, 17–18). It also adds digit-specific eigenspectra, stroke-aligned switching, multi-task representation consistency, and architecture-transfer analyses (Figures 9, 11, 24, 27).

E5.justification: v1 already reports ten-seed standard deviations and some SEM-based uncertainty. v2 adds an IMDb Welch's test (t = -1.34, p = 0.20), SCAN mean absolute deviation in Figure 18c, and explicit five-run aggregation for multi-task experiments. There is no reported increase in the retained experiments' ten-seed counts.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial multi-task, variable-delay, activation, and architecture results. Table 2 adds Copy accuracies of 54 ± 12% for LSTM and 69 ± 7% for GRU, alongside 92 ± 3% for ReLU AL-RNN. Figure 18 additionally reports that the best individual Addition model is fully nonlinear, qualifying the earlier emphasis on its poorer aggregate performance.

M1.justification: The core AL-RNN recurrence, regularization, and decoding framework remain. v2 extends the activation choices beyond ReLU to GeLU, tanh, and hardtanh, and implements final-layer-only nonlinear variants of S4 and Linear Transformers (Section 3; Figure 27). These are limited architectural extensions.

P1.justification: The abstract, method exposition, and discussion undergo extensive rewriting, with revised terminology and a new title. Detailed classification, contextual-integration, and rodent analyses are redistributed into a reorganized appendix, while multi-task learning becomes a main section. The later discussion also contains a nearly duplicated paragraph.

P2.justification: v1's appendix model schematic becomes an expanded main Figure 1; IMDb and sMNIST displays are merged into v2 Figure 2. Contextual and rodent figures move to the appendix. v2 adds three tables and numerous diagnostic and multi-task figures, expands existing panels, and adopts a different publication layout.

R1.justification: v2 expands related work to Legendre Memory Units and hybrid sequence architectures, and adds references supporting multi-task motifs, linear attention, and piecewise-linear approximation. The central positioning remains repurposing the existing AL-RNN for mechanistic analysis. Several other reference changes are publication-metadata updates rather than new works.

T1.justification: Appendix A.4.1 adds Proposition 1 and a formal impossibility proof for linear AL-RNNs solving masked addition. It derives the affine input–output mapping and shows that fixed coefficients cannot implement mask-dependent selection. v1 asserted this limitation without the corresponding proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's largely descriptive case: activation and hyperparameter controls, optimization diagnostics, and train–test analyses test alternative explanations for sparse nonlinearity's benefits. Multi-task experiments establish important data-dependent boundaries, while the addition proof and study-specific code-access information improve support and reproducibility. The contradictory rodent-task summary and limited baseline-setting details temper these gains, but the stronger evidence and more qualified explanations provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AL-RNN study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite the changed title and substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds multi-task learning, variable-delay recall, baseline comparisons, and additional diagnostic experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original AL-RNN experiments on classification, memory, contextual integration, SCAN, and joint modeling of rodent behavior and neural recordings.

results.title: Uncovering the Computational Roles of Nonlinearity in Sequence Modeling Using Almost-Linear RNNs

C1.justification: The central efficiency conclusion changes substantially. v1 emphasizes AR's batch-scaling advantage and FM speed obtained by sacrificing quality; v3's introduction, Table 1 and conclusion emphasize FM's advantage in most tested cases, limiting AR's advantage to large batches and short sequences. The summary also qualifies AR control adherence with accumulated-error susceptibility.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations involving representation compression, conflicting controls and accumulated errors, and possible memory-bandwidth limits on AR inference. It also cautions that adapted representation configurations may be suboptimal and that the observed EnCodec advantage does not establish general superiority. The original 400M-model limitation is retained.

D1.justification: v3 identifies VGGish for FAD and the HTSAT-base CLAP variant, links the backbone configuration, and discloses parameter contributions from skip connections, conditioning projections and embeddings. It also documents controls used in the new runtime ablation. Existing preprocessing, normalization, optimizer settings and inpainting pseudocode are largely retained.

E1.justification: v1 explicitly avoided MusicCaps; v3 evaluates the existing models on it in Appendix F and characterizes its data in Appendix A. This extends evaluation from curated proprietary audio to heterogeneous public recordings while retaining the training sources and core music tasks.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain AR, EnCodec-based FM, VAE-based FM, and the supervised/zero-shot inpainting alternatives. MusicCaps reuses the existing comparator set. Appendix F quotes MusicGen's previously reported FAD rather than newly evaluating it.

E3.justification: v3 introduces matched-length/frame-rate experiments, reconstruction evaluation using SI-SNR, ViSQOL and log-MSD, and runtime tests across durations and model depths. Appendix K controls attention and sampling overheads; Appendix I measures entropy over 100 prompts. The revised runtime plot reports batch latency instead of v1's per-sample latency, although the prose remains inconsistent.

E4.justification: v3 adds substantial diagnostic evidence: separating sequence-length effects from representation frame rate, checking reconstruction quality, quantifying dataset quality, examining entropy under temporal conditioning, and varying transformer depth to investigate runtime overheads. These extend v1's sampling-step and training-configuration sensitivity analyses.

E5.justification: New Appendix A reports CE, PQ and CLAP values with ± quantities across datasets, without defining the dispersion measure. The human study's 95% confidence intervals and approximately 250 judgments per cell remain unchanged; additional training runs or seeds are not reported.

E6.justification: Tables 2–5 and the original Euler-sampling results retain their values. v3 adds extensive results, including MusicCaps 25 Hz FAD scores of 4.10 for AR, 5.53 for EnCodec-based FM, and 4.58 for VAE-based FM, plus reconstruction, duration, entropy and model-depth measurements. The runtime throughput curves also change; these should not be interpreted as established same-setting speed improvements.

M1.justification: The core AR/FM architectures, objectives, representations, temporal conditioning, and inpainting algorithms are retained. FM skip connections already appeared in v1. Removing cross-attention and using argmax in v3 Appendix K are experimental controls, not revisions to the principal methods.

P1.justification: The principal section order and much of the original prose remain. v3 makes focused language and explanation edits, reorganizes the conclusion under explicit subheadings, adds a broader-impact paragraph, and renumbers existing appendices around new material. Publication headers are also added.

P2.justification: v3 adds frame-rate/duration, entropy and model-depth/runtime figures, alongside dataset-quality, reconstruction and MusicCaps tables. It redraws the runtime plot with different latency units and batch coverage, and redesigns Table 1 from three columns to two with a limitations row. Several original displays are retained or relocated.

R1.justification: Targeted references and discussion are added for FM–diffusion connections, memory-bound AR inference, dataset selection and architectural choices. The main related-work organization and comparative positioning remain intact. Stable Audio's publication update represents the same cited work.

T1.justification: Section 5.4 adds an approximate runtime derivation using batch size, sequence length, latent dimension, GPU parallelism and FM step count to contrast AR and FM complexity. This is a limited analytical addition; the existing mathematical formulation and algorithms remain substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the comparison by testing representation-related confounds, adding public-benchmark evidence, and establishing important boundaries on the runtime conclusions. These address weaknesses in v1's evidence and attribution. The gains are tempered by inconsistencies: Section 5.4 retains throughput values that disagree with Figure 5, and Table 7's 100 Hz PQ/CE values disagree with Table 2. These localized problems do not outweigh the stronger diagnostic evidence and more qualified conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same controlled comparison of autoregressive and flow-matching music generation. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds MusicCaps evaluation, reconstruction measurements, entropy analysis, and further runtime and frame-rate experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, runtime measurements, training-configuration experiments, and a human study of inpainting.

results.title: Auto-Regressive vs Flow-Matching: a Comparative Study of Modeling Paradigms for Text-to-Music Generation

C1.justification: The central signal-identification, stability, and application claims remain, including the abstract's average 10% improvement claim. v2 newly foregrounds gains extending to gradient boosting and the contribution of individual components. v1 discussed application beyond random forests primarily as a future extension.

C2.justification: v2 refines explanations of overfitting and correlated-feature bias, and distinguishes costly model refitting from efficient inference with fixed GLM coefficients. Its limitations now acknowledge incomplete ensemble-configuration coverage. Figure 7's interpretation is also qualified from general superiority to competitiveness, emphasizing advantages at low PVE.

D1.justification: v2 adds the 16-CPU-core runtime configuration and discussion of parallel computation across trees. Most RF and GLM settings move from v1 Appendix B into Section 4, but the previously stated logistic solver='saga' detail is omitted. Both PDFs retain links to the same implementation and experimental repositories.

E1.justification: The twelve real datasets and principal evaluation tasks remain unchanged. However, Section 4.1 replaces the pure interaction response with an additive-plus-polynomial-interaction response, revising the synthetic signal structure being recovered. Larger samples and additional ensemble configurations do not themselves introduce new dataset coverage.

E2.justification: Figure 5 adds Local MDI to the subgroup comparison, previously containing LIME, TreeSHAP, and global OLS. Table 2 also includes Local MDI when ranking each ablated variant, whereas v1 compares each variant against LIME and TreeSHAP. These are comparator-membership changes independent of the LMDI/Local MDI naming changes elsewhere.

E3.justification: Semi-synthetic sample sizes change from {150, 500, 1000} to {300, 500, 1000}, and the Linear+LSS response expands from three terms to five. v2 adds full-dataset evaluations reaching 72,000 observations, alternative RF and boosting configurations, and runtime experiments varying leaf size and ensemble size. Section 5 also revises its stated sample sizes and retention range to match settings already plotted in v1's stability appendix; this correction alone does not establish a changed experiment.

E4.justification: Section 6 and new Appendix F extend component ablations with sensitivity to forest size, minimum leaf size, and gradient boosting. Section 9 adds runtime-scaling analyses, while Appendix D.3 tests whether feature-selection findings persist beyond downsampling. These substantially extend the original component, correlation, and application analyses.

E5.justification: The corresponding experiments retain 30 synthetic runs, 50 correlation runs, 20 real-data runs, and 15 stability runs, with standard-error reporting. Stability still compares five RF fits with different seeds. The new result tables introduce no stated new uncertainty-estimation or significance-testing procedure.

E6.justification: Benchmark curves, ablation ranks, and counterfactual values are revised. For example, LMDI+'s House 16H counterfactual distance changes from 7.8 to 7.6, while Higgs changes from 18.1 to 18.2 in v1 Table 3 versus v2 Table 4. New ensemble, full-dataset, and runtime results substantially expand the evidence. Revised synthetic results use changed response functions or sample sizes and do not establish same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 retains the expanded node/raw-feature representation, regularized GLM, coefficient-product attributions, zero scores for unused features, and averaging across trees. Gradient boosting is newly evaluated without a distinct attribution procedure. The stump-formula correction aligns the equation with the node-supported construction already described in v1.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and contribution list, MDI-bias explanations, local-attribution motivation, and discussion receive broad rewriting and expansion. Implementation details move into the main experimental section, runtime analysis becomes a separate section, and the appendices are reorganized to accommodate full-dataset results and ensemble ablations.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a different journal layout with revised typography, margins, headers, and author presentation. Table 2 becomes a component checklist, five additional tables display ensemble, runtime, and full-dataset results, and multiple plots receive revised axes, legends, or comparator curves. Existing appendix maps and application illustrations are retained rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: Research positioning expands substantially through the PCS framework, explicit treatment of Sutera et al.'s Local MDI, MAPLE, permutation-based global importance, and additional attribution-evaluation and stability literature. These additions change how the contribution is situated relative to existing methods and methodological principles, beyond the switch to author-year citations.

T1.justification: Equation 3 replaces threshold-only indicators with explicit membership in the left and right child nodes. This corrects the displayed stump function so it is zero outside the split node. Proposition 1 and Appendix A's mathematical formulation remain substantively unchanged; no new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked quantitative runtime comparisons and experimental validation beyond its default RF configuration and capped real-data evaluations. v2's ensemble checks, full-dataset evaluations, and timing studies substantially strengthen evidence for practical applicability while revealing computational tradeoffs with TreeSHAP and LIME. The corrected stump equation and fuller treatment of relevant prior work further improve rigor. These gains outweigh the limited reproducibility loss from omitting the previously specified logistic solver.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Local MDI+ research work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revision and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and reports additional ensemble-configuration, full-dataset, and runtime results.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic and real-data experiments on feature identification, stability, ablations, counterfactuals, and subgroup discovery, including supplementary results.

results.title: Local MDI+: Local Feature Importances for Tree-Based Models

C1.justification: The core contributions remain diffusion-generated views for cross-view MAE, consistency metrics, and multi-anchor masking, with improvements over CropMAE and a narrower gap to video-based methods. v2 emphasizes diffusion-model selection in its headline contribution, but that use was already claimed and demonstrated in v1 Appendix A.4.1.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive qualifications concerning Lumos pretraining and possible data leakage, the comparability of 3D-pretrained CroCo, and the computational impracticality of video diffusion. New analyses motivate hypotheses about parameter-scaling difficulties and why classifier filtering may sacrifice useful diversity. These extend the original limitation concerning uncontrolled generated variations.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a project-code link, specifies the feature space for nearest-neighbor image selection and the 4–48-frame sampling interval, and documents synthetic-image resolution and storage. It also adds detailed optical-flow training settings and expanded resource comparisons. Existing optimizer, hardware, and default training disclosures are retained; the new compute reporting inconsistently labels eight-GPU elapsed hours as GPU hours.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates downstream representations only through video label propagation on DAVIS, VIP, and JHMDB. v2 Appendix A.4.5 adds optical-flow estimation, training WAFT on FlyingChairs and FlyingThings and evaluating transfer to KITTI. This substantially extends task and data coverage.

E2.justification: v2 Table 6 adds evaluated CroCo v1 and v2 baselines, including different model sizes; v1 cited CroCo but did not report these comparisons. Table 10 also adds a CropMAE Real+Synthetic control. These additions broaden comparison to 3D-pretrained methods and directly test a synthetic-data alternative, while retaining the original baselines.

E3.justification: Table 1 increases the stated consistency-evaluation sample from 500 to 5,000 images and video-frame pairs. New protocols include two-stage WAFT training with 50K/100K iterations and zero-shot KITTI evaluation, larger-model experiments, and bag sizes of six and eight. The filtering experiment removes 20.4% of training instances while holding training iterations fixed. Original default pretraining and label-propagation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds synthetic-data CropMAE controls, parameter-versus-patch scaling, DINOv2-based consistency checks, classifier-based quality assessment and filtering, and bag-size/masking sensitivity studies. The existing Gen-SIS/RCG analysis is extended with Lumos rather than newly introduced. The comparative pose visualization in v1 Figure 3 is removed, although CDG-MAE-only qualitative examples remain.

E5.justification: The original three-seed means and standard deviations, and the single-seed four-anchor results, are retained unchanged in v2 Table 5. Table 15 reuses existing uncertainty estimates and extends the single-seed exploratory reporting practice. No increased repeated-run budget, new uncertainty estimator, confidence interval, or significance test is reported.

E6.justification: Original headline label-propagation scores are retained, but substantial new results cover CroCo, Lumos, scaling, filtering, robustness, and optical flow. For example, v2 Table 12 reports Stage-2 KITTI endpoint error/F1 of 3.70/11.50 for CDG-MAE versus 3.81/11.75 for CropMAE. Table 14 reports slightly lower scores after filtering. Table 1 consistency values also change under the enlarged sampling protocol, rather than establishing same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The proposed procedure retains offline diffusion-generated views, a shared ViT encoder, masked multi-anchor cross-attention, and pixel reconstruction loss. Additional generators, filtering experiments, and downstream WAFT evaluation test configurations or applications without revising the default CDG-MAE algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and related-work prose are substantially revised and tightened. Diffusion-model selection and computational analysis move into dedicated main-text sections, while the appendix is reorganized around expanded supplementary studies. The title and publication presentation also change.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the overview diagrams, removes the comparative pose figure, consolidates earlier diffusion-selection and multi-anchor tables, and adds displays for resource comparisons and new analyses. Previously adjacent tables and appendix visualizations are redistributed and resized within a different document layout. Retained plots and examples are distinguishable from genuinely new displays.

R1.justification: v2 adds references and discussion for Lumos, video-diffusion alternatives, optical-flow pipelines, and classifier-based analysis. It also explains CroCo's distinct 3D-pretraining context. The principal positioning relative to CropMAE, SiamMAE, and self-supervised diffusion remains stable; citation-format changes and duplicate-reference cleanup do not constitute substantive additions.

T1.justification: The GS, LS, and NPS definitions and the substantive encoder, decoder, and reconstruction equations remain unchanged. Distinguishing mask-token notation in Equation 8 clarifies the existing procedure. Neither version introduces theoretical propositions or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support: the synthetic-data CropMAE control addresses a previously untested alternative explanation, optical-flow transfer extends validation beyond label propagation, and backbone, filtering, and scaling studies test important assumptions and limits. Added access and implementation information improves reproducibility. The inconsistent compute units and single-seed exploratory results limit some conclusions, but do not outweigh the substantial gain in controlled and diagnostic evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CDG-MAE research despite the revised title. The complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, and figures, are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds optical-flow evaluation, synthetic-data controls, scaling experiments, and generated-view quality and robustness analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original view-consistency measurements, CDG-MAE training experiments, ablations, and evaluations on DAVIS, VIP, and JHMDB, including additional appendix experiments.

results.title: CDG-MAE: Cross-view Masked Modeling using Diffusion Generated Views

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes scalar Gaussian mean estimation and algorithm heterogeneity. v4 explicitly claims feasibility in two theoretical settings and adds heterogeneous downstream risk functions as a contribution. Its abstract frames large-dataset benefits more cautiously as potential savings in repeated curation within a cost-sharing model.

C2.justification: v4 adds explanations for nonmonotonic dependence on contamination and filter effectiveness, and conjectures why Tiny ImageNet shows a weaker price signal. It expands the applicability discussion for cost-sharing conditions and identifies sample modification, particularly token editing in language modeling, as outside the current sample-removal framework.

D1.justification: v4 adds a stated public code link, filtering pseudocode, and model/scoring-function mappings in Appendix E. It documents new experimental configurations, replaces Adult tuning tables with defaults and neural-network settings, and revises reported GPU usage from 200 to 250 hours. Appendix G expands dataset access/licensing information and changes the CIFAR-10 license statement.

E1.justification: v4 adds CIFAR-10N with human annotation errors, Tiny ImageNet with 200 image classes, and BAF fraud classification with fairness objectives (Section 5.2; Appendices D.3 and D.6). Adult and CIFAR-10 label-noise and shortcut coverage remain, with shortcut experiments moved to the appendix.

E2.justification: v4 Table 1 adds evaluated Confident Learning-based and oracle filters alongside the default filter. Figure 5a adds a no-prefiltering comparator to the Gaussian experiment, absent from v1 Figure 1a. The quantile, z-score, SDO, and earlier alternative shortcut filters remain.

E3.justification: Adult changes from 14 tuned robust/brittle model instances to seven models using library defaults and a fixed neural-network configuration; its label-noise metric changes from accuracy to macro-F1. New protocols include a wider CNN and different regularization range for Tiny ImageNet, and seven Random Forest learners with different fairness weights for BAF.

E4.justification: v4 adds sensitivity analyses for oracle effectiveness and Confident Learning-based filtering, and extends learner-diameter analysis to label noise (Appendices D.4, D.5, D.8). Existing shortcut diameter, alternative-filter, and loss-reweighting studies are retained. The original default-filter learner-specific shortcut profiles in v1 Figures 6 and 7b are omitted.

E5.justification: Both versions specify eight repetitions and standard errors for Gaussian mean estimation, and repeated-run averages with error bars for classification. v4 extends uncertainty reporting to new comparisons, including Table 1, without introducing a changed run count, seed policy, or statistical testing procedure.

E6.justification: v4 adds substantial benchmark and filter-comparison results. For example, Table 1 reports CIFAR-10 high-heterogeneity prices of 2.2% (s.e. 0.2) for default filtering and 2.0% (s.e. 0.2) for CL-based filtering. Adult results are replaced under revised settings. Gaussian-risk values and the plotted quantile/z-score ordering also change between v1 Figure 1a and v4 Figure 5a without an explained protocol change.

M1.justification: The original minimax framework remains, but v4 adds learner-specific accuracy/fairness objectives and integrates subgroup sampling controlled by three parameters (Section 5.2, Algorithm 2). Section 4.2 also introduces an oracle filter parameterized by removal fraction and effectiveness. These extend the objectives and procedures; Algorithm 1 primarily formalizes existing filtering.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Theory is reorganized with major proofs in the main text; Gaussian experiments and shortcut descriptions move into Appendix D. The supplementary material is extensively restructured, and new algorithm and applicability discussions reshape the narrative beyond simple renumbering.

P2.justification: v1's twelve-panel Figure 2 is split and rearranged into v4 Figures 2 and 6. Selected learner-specific plots move into main-text Figure 1, while new comparison tables, benchmark plots, sensitivity plots, and pseudocode displays are added. Adult hyperparameter tables and some shortcut profiles disappear, alongside extensive journal-format layout changes.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds substantive comparisons with distributionally robust optimization, multi-distribution learning, and the price of robustness. Appendix E connects LARP's filtering structure to LAION and C4 curation. New Confident Learning and fairness references support additional methodological relationships; the original first-framework novelty claim remains.

T1.justification: The Gaussian/Huber-contamination result becomes a theorem for strictly smooth distributions under strong contamination, retaining the Gaussian bound as Corollary 4.5. v4 adds the oracle PAC-style Theorem 4.6 and general utility conditions in Corollary 5.2, replacing v1's mean-specific Appendix D argument. The original cost-sharing lemma is retained as Theorem 5.1.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens support for LARP's generality beyond v1's narrow theoretical setting and synthetic-corruption benchmarks. Broader guarantees, natural annotation errors, alternative filters, and conflicting fairness objectives test important aspects of the central argument. Explicit cost-sharing conditions, pseudocode, and a stated code release also improve scrutiny and reproducibility. Unexplained Gaussian-result revisions and omitted shortcut profiles limit parts of the evidence, but do not outweigh these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LARP framework and share identifiable methods, experiments, and theoretical results. All 24 pages of v1 and 34 pages of v4, including appendices, were readable; figures and equations could be checked visually.

after.justification: v4 reports original experiments throughout Section 5 and Appendix D, including retained studies and new BAF, CIFAR-10N, Tiny ImageNet, and filtering comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original Gaussian mean-estimation simulations and Adult/CIFAR-10 experiments, including learner-specific results and supplementary analyses in Appendix C.

results.title: LARP: Learner-Agnostic Robust Data Prefiltering

C1.justification: V2 qualifies the introduction's performance claim with 'among the evaluated methods' and explicitly confines the conclusion's selector-performance finding to mTSBench. The central contributions—benchmark scale, joint detection/selection evaluation, and substantial selection gaps—remain unchanged.

C2.justification: The new Practical Takeaways section explains selector weaknesses through coarse dataset-level features and recommends caution with top-1 recommendations. Additional discussion interprets domain and anomaly-characteristic dependence. Appendices C/G introduce substantive annotation-quality limitations, dataset-specific concerns, and qualifications about interpreting detector agreement, substantially expanding v1's narrower limitations.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents the top-7.5% anomaly-score threshold, clarifies use of official splits and the fallback anomaly-free training segment, and specifies that semi-supervised detector runtimes include training and inference. It also replaces the front-page repository link with a project-site address. These disclosures do not establish changes to previously unspecified settings.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same 344 time series from 19 datasets. New subgroup analyses and case studies reuse this coverage. Revised PSM and SWAN-SF descriptions and domain labels do not establish replacement of the evaluated data.

E2.justification: V2 adds fixed-choice PCA and an Ensemble averaging all 24 detectors' anomaly scores to the model-selection comparison in Table 2. PCA previously appeared as a detector, but not as a comparator in this table. The three selectors and Oracle, Near-optimal, and Random baselines remain.

E3.justification: Table 2 expands from 12 to 13 metrics by separating F1 from Max-F1; the earlier F1 entries are retained under Max-F1. V2 also adds ranking-depth and stratified evaluations. The short-anomaly cutoff changes from fewer than 2 points in v1 Appendix D to fewer than 20 in v2 Appendix E, although the corresponding heatmap retains its entries; rerunning is not established.

E4.justification: V2 substantially expands analysis of selector failure conditions: Tables 3–5 examine anomaly ratio, anomaly duration, and application domain, while Figure 6 examines ranking depth. New Appendix C compares annotation salience and detector predictions on selected series. The earlier dimensionality and extreme-anomaly-length analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report means and standard deviations across evaluated time series. The additional grouped tables extend that reporting practice without introducing repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, significance tests, or a new uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial results for the new baselines, subgroup analyses, ranking curves, case studies, and dataset-specific detector runtimes. Table 2 reports PCA AUC-ROC of 0.697 versus Orthus's retained 0.672. The original selector F1 values 0.292/0.381/0.386 reappear as Max-F1, alongside separate F1 values 0.135/0.222/0.222; these are not evidence of same-setting deterioration. Most matched earlier benchmark results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The detector pool, three model-selection algorithms, and documented adaptations remain unchanged. V1 Appendices C/E correspond to v2 Appendices D/F. The added PCA and Ensemble comparisons are evaluation baselines, without a revision to the benchmark's existing algorithms.

P1.justification: V2 revises the abstract and local wording, corrects several dataset descriptions, and adds a Practical Takeaways section. Broader Impact moves from Appendix F into the main text, and appendices are reorganized around the new case studies. Most existing exposition and the main narrative sequence are retained.

P2.justification: The paper adopts a substantially different publication template and front matter. Table 2 gains columns and a metric row; Tables 3–5 and Figures 6, C.1, and C.2 introduce new displays. The detector-runtime chart becomes a combined average-bar and dataset-heatmap figure. Several retained figures and tables are also relocated.

R1.justification: V2 adds Wu and Keogh (2023) when discussing benchmark flaws, removes Orion/Sintel from Table 1 and the references, and explicitly distinguishes its multivariate benchmark from the already-cited univariate selection study by Sylligardos et al. The broader research positioning remains stable.

T1.justification: The mathematical problem formulation, anomaly-scoring notation, and proxy-performance argmax selection rule remain equivalent. Neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs. The Max-F1 explanation clarifies an empirical metric rather than adding a mathematical development.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important gaps in the benchmark's practical interpretation: Table 2 tests fixed PCA and a simple ensemble against selectors, while the new subgroup analyses and annotation case studies reveal conditions under which aggregate conclusions need qualification. Explicit thresholding and timing details further improve transparency. Section 4.2 incorrectly says Ensemble trails MetaOD, contrary to most Table 2 entries, but this localized error does not outweigh the substantial gains in comparative evidence and limitations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same mTSBench work and contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices. Retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering, with no material reading gaps.

after.justification: V2 retains these original empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, stratified analyses, ranking curves, and qualitative prediction case studies.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations of 24 anomaly detectors and three model selectors on 344 time series, including performance, ranking, runtime, and anomaly-length analyses.

results.title: mTSBench: Benchmarking Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection and Model Selection at Scale

C1.justification: The central contributions remain joint MAE/LoRA co-adaptation, improved discriminative vision performance over MAE and direct frozen-LLM fusion, and an attention-based account of background robustness. The renamed method, softened state-of-the-art wording, and additional supporting experiments do not materially redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations involving overfitting under full LLM fine-tuning, optimization difficulties with two blocks, semantic maturity at deeper insertion points, and semantic priors acting as regularizers under attribute shifts. Appendix F also develops the training-versus-inference cost distinction and applicability tradeoff beyond v1's brief latency warning. These are substantial new explanations and qualifications.

D1.justification: v3 adds a code-availability statement, LoRA alpha and learning-rate scheduling details, and inference FLOP/memory figures. Reported pretraining time becomes approximately 35 hours for LAVIE versus 30 for the baseline, replacing v1's approximately 30 hours for both. Exact MLP-control projection dimensions are removed, while most existing training and hardware details remain.

E1.justification: v3 adds video object segmentation on DAVIS-2017 and ImageNet-E evaluation covering edited backgrounds, object sizes, positions, and directions. These introduce temporal prediction and additional controlled distribution shifts. ImageNet-Segmentation coverage already existed in v1's appendix and is not a new task.

E2.justification: v3 adds a fully trainable LLaMA-block comparator against frozen and LoRA-adapted alternatives in Table 6. The corresponding component-ablation table drops v1's supervised-only comparator rows, although those methods remain in Table 1. The MLP and randomly initialized LLM controls are retained; merging or renaming them does not introduce new baselines.

E3.justification: Added experiments vary LLM family and size, source-block index, block count, insertion depth, LoRA rank/alpha, and attention configuration. DAVIS evaluation introduces region-similarity and contour-accuracy metrics. These substantially expand the experimental designs, while the retained 800-epoch MAE and 100-epoch fine-tuning budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds tests of full fine-tuning versus LoRA, alternative LLMs and layers, multiple blocks, LoRA hyperparameters, RoPE/causal attention, and insertion depth. New paired background-swap visualizations and ImageNet-E analyses further examine robustness. Conversely, the earlier component ablations' ImageNet-C results disappear.

E5.justification: v1 already includes a ten-seed ImageNet-1K analysis with reported 99% confidence intervals and a three-seed supervised-LoRA comparison. v3 removes the ten-seed analysis but broadens three-seed mean/standard-deviation reporting through Tables 1, 3, and 12–15; the supervised-LoRA standard-error table remains. Section 4's blanket seed-0 statement conflicts with several appendix captions.

E6.justification: Table 1 changes the MAE baseline/proposed-method ImageNet-1K summaries from 83.2/83.6 to three-seed means of 83.11/83.63, rather than establishing a same-setting performance increase. v3 adds extensive DAVIS, ImageNet-E, and ablation results and updates segmentation summaries. COCO mask scores and ImageNet-C ablation entries disappear, while COCO box scores and ImageNet-9 results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The proposed procedure retains the ViT encoder, projected LLM block, query/value LoRA adaptation, joint MAE reconstruction objective, bidirectional attention, RoPE removal, and downstream fine-tuning. Renaming LUViT to LAVIE and testing alternative configurations do not change the default method.

P1.justification: v3 retitles the paper, consistently renames the method, numbers the method subsections, reorganizes the dense-prediction discussion, and restructures Appendix B. Existing multimodal discussion moves into Appendix C.3, while the contents pages and societal-impact section disappear. Together with substantial experimental and interpretive paragraph revisions, this exceeds a limited language edit.

P2.justification: The journal template changes typography and layout throughout. Tables are substantially restructured: classification gains reproduced-baseline rows, dense prediction combines benchmarks, and existing ablation tables are consolidated. v3 redisplays two earlier saliency examples in the main text, adds paired background-swap visualizations and new experimental tables, and removes the ten-seed uncertainty plot.

R1.justification: New Appendix C.4 positions LAVIE as complementary to robust ViT approaches including RVT, FAN, and MedViT. References also expand for the new datasets, LLMs, and feature-hierarchy discussion, while Picard and Lacoste references disappear with their associated sections. The central positioning relative to LM4Vision, gradient coherence, and multimodal models remains.

T1.justification: v1's attention equations use WQ WK-transpose divided by sqrt(d), omitting the input features. v3 corrects them by defining Q = XWQ and K = XWK and using QK-transpose divided by sqrt(dk), in Section 5 and Appendix A.1. This is a mathematical correction; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the unchanged method's empirical justification by directly testing previously untested adaptation and architectural choices, checking alternative LLMs, and extending evaluation to video and controlled attribute shifts. Broader uncertainty reporting and quantified inference costs improve assessment of reliability and practicality. These gains outweigh the loss of the ten-seed confidence-interval analysis and some earlier results/details, although conflicting seed descriptions and significance claims without a reported formal test remain weaknesses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete and readable, including their appendices, equations, tables, and figures. They describe the same research work, with LUViT renamed LAVIE in v3; retained and relocated material can be reliably matched.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and reports additional DAVIS-2017, ImageNet-E, architectural ablation, and repeated-seed results.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification, robustness, COCO detection and segmentation experiments, component ablations, attention analyses, and repeated-seed experiments.

results.title: Enhancing Self-Supervised Visual Representation Learning via Low-Rank Adapted LLMs

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same central contributions: representation-level drift evaluation, targeted memory realignment, and FR-like performance with lower resource requirements. The revised conclusion incorporates CLEAR-10 evidence without materially redefining these core claims.

C2.justification: v1 offers brief future-work remarks about detection. v2 Section 6 substantially develops detector dependence, false alarms, contaminated buffer references, gradual or mixture drift, adversarial concealment, and loss of relevant submodes during replacement. Appendix B additionally interprets weaker natural-drift benefits and ER-ACE’s poorer comparison with FR.

D1.justification: The anonymous implementation link is replaced by a named GitHub repository, now explicitly advertised as providing code and benchmark datasets. CLEAR-10 construction details are added. The original hyperparameter settings are retained and moved from Appendix B to Appendix D; repository contents were not externally verified.

E1.justification: v2 adds CLEAR-10 evaluation using natural temporal changes between early and late image buckets, extending coverage beyond the retained synthetic transformations of four vision benchmarks. This substantially broadens the represented drift conditions.

E2.justification: Corresponding original experiments retain ER, ER-ACE, DER++, SER, and CLS-ER, with the same Vanilla and Full Relearning comparisons. The new CLEAR-10 and backbone studies reuse subsets of these methods; no comparator is removed from a retained experiment or newly introduced.

E3.justification: The original evaluation settings remain intact. Appendix B adds a CLEAR-10 protocol excluding BACKGROUND, combining buckets 1–2, shifting recurring classes to buckets 9–10, and using five two-class tasks with a 1000-sample buffer. Appendix C adds ResNet-152 and ViT-S evaluations with ER and a 5000-sample buffer.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds dedicated tests of whether AMR generalizes across deeper convolutional and transformer architectures. Appendix B adds detector-failure and sensitivity analysis, including limited benefits from relaxing the KS threshold and improved detection with MMD. Existing buffer-size, transformation-severity, feature-space, and efficiency analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v1 reports three-run averages and unidentified ± quantities; v2 explicitly labels these quantities as standard deviations. Shared results retain the same reporting values and run count. CLEAR-10 also reports three-run averages, while the new backbone table provides point estimates without uncertainty or a stated run count.

E6.justification: All 280 matched main-table entries are unchanged between v1 Tables I–II and v2 Tables 1–4. New Tables 5–6 add substantial results under additional conditions: CLEAR-10 ER achieves 51.50% FAA with AMR versus 47.53% with FR, whereas ER-ACE achieves 53.00% versus 59.33%. Backbone experiments also add new results, rather than same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: Appendix B adds feature-space MMD detection for CLEAR-10 after finding the original uncertainty-based KS detector insufficiently sensitive. The central flush-and-resample AMR procedure remains unchanged. Algorithm 1 expands the replacement operation already described in v1.

P1.justification: Most existing introduction, method, theory, and experimental prose remains closely matched. Local revisions expand Algorithm 1, rewrite the conclusion and future-work discussion, and add related-work subheadings. References move before the appendices, while the original hyperparameter appendix becomes Appendix D.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column IEEE layout to a single-column TMLR layout, with substantially enlarged and rearranged figure panels. The two combined results tables become four dataset-specific tables, and hyperparameter displays are consolidated. Figures 15–16 and Tables 5–6 are added; original figure contents are retained.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially through discussions of adaptive plasticity, recent drift-detection methods, and the distinction from test-time adaptation. Added examples include PromptFusion, SD-LoRA, BECAME, MCD-DD, and DriftLens, alongside citations supporting CLEAR and MMD.

T1.justification: The problem formulation, mathematical definitions, four theorems, and their proofs are retained. The new MMD discussion is descriptive and introduces no new formal derivation or theoretical result.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1’s synthetic-drift, ResNet-18-only validation through natural temporal data and additional architectures. More decisively, it exposes the original detector’s failures and documents mixed CLEAR-10 outcomes alongside detailed applicability limits, making practical claims more assessable. CLEAR-10 shifts are mild, and backbone results lack uncertainty reporting, but the added validation and explicit failure analysis materially improve the paper’s evidential grounding and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AMR framework. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching retained material across the substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds original CLEAR-10 experiments and evaluations with ResNet-152 and ViT-S in Appendices B–C.

before.justification: v1 reports original drift-adaptation experiments, accuracy and forgetting results, computational comparisons, and transformation-severity experiments in Appendix A.

results.title: Holistic Continual Learning under Concept Drift with Adaptive Memory Realignment

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion are unchanged, and the introduction retains the same contribution list: semantic emergence without trainable input embeddings, universal visual embeddings, representational interference, and released implementations. New controls and visualizations support these existing claims rather than redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: v4 extends the original orthographic-versus-semantic interference explanation into a conflict between token discrimination and semantic proximity, including gradient imprinting and the sufficiency of arbitrary fixed identifiers. It also explains the existing visual clusters through pixel density and PCA, and contextualizes the SmolLM comparison through differing training-data volumes. The explicit scale and modality limitations in Section 6.3 remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v4 substantially expands implementation disclosure: n-gram extraction and Unicode allocation, layer/head counts, rotary embeddings, untied output weights, parameter breakdowns, and the repetition mapping for 16-dimensional controls. It also specifies training/validation token counts, gradient accumulation, evaluation intervals, and final-checkpoint selection. These details improve reproducibility without themselves establishing changes to previously unspecified settings; repository and model access links remain the same.

E1.justification: v1 Figure 5 includes SQuAD evaluation results, which disappear from v4's reported evaluations, although SQuAD-v2 remains training data. The principal Wikipedia languages, multilingual tokenizer coverage, MMLU, ARC, and CommonsenseQA remain represented.

E2.justification: Beyond the retained trainable-embedding baseline, v4 evaluates sequential 16-bit identifiers and random 64-, 256-, and 1024-dimensional embeddings, each with corresponding PCA/normalization variants. Figure 4 also adds SmolLM and SmolLM2 at 135M and 360M parameters. These substantially expand the comparator set; the GPT-2 score mentioned in prose is contextual rather than a newly reported controlled comparison.

E3.justification: The reported setup changes from 0.2B/0.4B/0.5B models with 65,536- or 131,072-token vocabularies to approximately 0.3B models with 65,536 tokens. The stated training corpus changes from approximately 9B to 4B tokens, and maximum batch size changes from 16 to 18. The new representation analysis also introduces a 70-word, seven-category activation-probing protocol.

E4.justification: v1 visualizes input embeddings but lacks nonvisual frozen controls. v4 adds ablations testing visual information, embedding dimensionality, and PCA/normalization through sequential-index and random embeddings (Sections 3.1 and 5.4). Figures 8–11 additionally examine the authors' trained models across input embeddings, attention projections, and early and late Transformer blocks.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. v4's additional initialization variants and training trajectories do not constitute uncertainty estimation across replicated runs.
