E6.justification: v1 reports MMLU scores of 22.29 for best_bvv_ru and 11.37 for its trainable counterpart; v4 reports 23.81 for Model_UNI_GLIF and 12.54 for Model_unfrozen under different model and data settings, so these are replacement results rather than same-setting gains. v4 adds comparator and ablation scores, internal-layer findings, and Appendix B's numerical loss/perplexity trajectories, while removing the earlier size/language-specific results and SQuAD score row.

M1.justification: The proposed glyph-rendering, resizing, PCA, normalization, and freezing pipeline remains unchanged. The expanded tokenizer description documents the existing vocabulary family; the new index and random embeddings serve as experimental controls rather than replacing the proposed visual method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. Editorial changes include organizing tokenizer construction into three subsections, expanding selected explanations, removing a repetitive discussion paragraph, and adding headings for the new analyses and appendices. The revision is not a wholesale rewrite of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v4 replaces the two-column presentation with a single-column layout and substantially redesigns the experimental displays: combined model curves, revised benchmark heatmaps, and new multi-panel activation and ablation figures. The unchanged input-embedding plots are enlarged and relocated. The model inventory moves to Appendix A with revised rows and columns, and Appendix B adds a numerical training table.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds previously absent, directly relevant glyph/pixel research by Salesky et al., Wang et al., Dai and Cai, and Liu et al. It explicitly positions the work against trainable or auxiliary visual features used for downstream tasks, substantially expanding discussion of the closest prior research. SmolLM/SmolLM2 references are added, while the ERNIE and ALBERT bibliography entries are removed.

T1.justification: Neither version presents formal theorems, proofs, or a developed mathematical theory. The retained embedding construction is mathematically unchanged; the new interference explanations and representation analyses are qualitative arguments and empirical investigations.

improvement.justification: v4 addresses an important weakness of v1 by adding nonvisual frozen controls that help distinguish visual information from freezing and identifier sufficiency. Internal-layer probes examine semantic emergence beyond the input-only visualizations, while substantially fuller implementation details make the experiments easier to assess and reproduce. The narrower model-size and evaluation coverage is a tradeoff, and uncertainty reporting and causal validation of interference remain absent. Nevertheless, the better experimental controls and transparency provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same frozen visual Unicode embedding research. All eight pages of v1 and nineteen pages of v4 are readable, including figures, tables, and v4's Appendices A and B. v1 has no appendices.

after.justification: v4 reports original training and benchmark results, initialization ablations, internal-layer visualizations, and numerical training trajectories in Appendix B.

before.justification: v1 reports original tokenizer comparisons, model training curves, benchmark scores, and embedding visualizations in Figures 1–7.

results.title: Emergent Semantics Beyond Token Embeddings: Transformer LMs with Frozen Visual Unicode Representations

C1.justification: Both versions claim that Global TopK and cross-reconstruction create aligned sparse concepts across models and modalities, achieve approximately 0.80 Jaccard alignment, and enable localization and retrieval. v2's explicit USAE comparison supplies new evidence for the retained superiority claim without changing the central contributions or claimed capabilities.

C2.justification: v2 expands interpretation through reconstruction-direction asymmetry, reasons for retaining separate stream activations, and qualifications on label purity as an interpretability proxy. Appendix F.3 identifies foreground bias and failures on background queries beyond v1's detailed-part example. Computational-cost caveats and a new Broader Impact discussion further expand applicability and misuse considerations; the taxonomy-depth interpretation is removed.

D1.justification: New Appendices A.4–A.5 document cached-feature training, H100 runtimes, the USAE implementation, matched hyperparameters, and USAE-specific settings. Appendix C specifies additional encoder checkpoints, feature extraction, and preprocessing. These substantially improve reproducibility documentation without establishing changes to retained experiments. The code link remains unchanged, while the explicit NMSE normalization formula is lost.

E1.justification: Both versions use Open Images and MS-COCO for the same image/text representation, attribution, segmentation, and retrieval tasks, including external-query examples. The additional encoder combinations change model configurations, while label purity and background-localization examples extend evaluation within existing coverage.

E2.justification: USAE changes from a discussed prior method in v1 to an evaluated comparator for activation consistency, concept alignment, probing, and segmentation, as well as the new purity and reconstruction comparisons. Existing Local TopK, DETR, and CLIP comparisons are retained. This substantially expands direct comparison with the principal competing method.

E3.justification: v2 introduces purity evaluation using top-10, 25, 50, 100, and all examples, variance-weighted R² reconstruction evaluation, and encoder combinations containing up to ten streams. Reported Jaccard evaluation narrows from taxonomy depths 0–5 to depth 5. Existing SPARC training budgets, splits, probe procedures, and downstream evaluation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds analysis across purity subset sizes and encoder compositions, and extends localization failure analysis with scene-object, facial-feature, and background queries in Figures 26–30. The taxonomy-depth sensitivity analysis is removed. Original latent-count, sparsity, cross-loss, and learning-rate sweeps remain, with the latter two moved to Appendix B.

E5.justification: v2 adds standard errors over latents for Jaccard alignment and label purity, and over tasks for probe losses. v1 reports these retained alignment and probe results without uncertainty. The fixed training seed and task-specific split seeds remain unchanged; the PDFs do not establish additional independent training runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results: USAE Jaccard is 0.2166 versus the retained SPARC value of 0.8018, and new purity and reconstruction tables provide direct comparisons across configurations. The new matrices include unfavorable SPARC outcomes, such as negative Swin reconstruction R² in Table 10. Original segmentation and retrieval scores remain; the Global-plus-cross CLIP-image probe loss changes from 0.5355 to 0.5354, and depth-0–4 Jaccard entries disappear.

M1.justification: The stream-specific affine encoders and decoders, aggregated-logit Global TopK selection, ReLU, reconstruction objectives, and auxiliary dead-neuron handling remain unchanged. v2 clarifies why streams retain separate activation magnitudes and condenses the loss equations without establishing a different SPARC procedure.

P1.justification: v2 substantially condenses the introduction and training-objective explanation, rewrites concept-alignment exposition, and reorganizes the empirical narrative. Retrieval moves from Section 4.5 to Appendix G, while cross-loss and learning-rate subsections move to Appendix B. These are meaningful structural and explanatory revisions beyond the added scientific content.

P2.justification: v2 adds purity and reconstruction tables, an encoder inventory, and five failure-case figures. Existing comparison tables gain method columns, USAE rows, or uncertainty formatting; the Jaccard table replaces hierarchy-depth columns with a single depth-5 summary. Retrieval displays and two ablation plots move to appendices, while original qualitative images and ablation plots are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of BatchTopK and citations for the additional encoders and R². The central positioning against USAE and earlier concept-alignment approaches remains substantially unchanged. The Burns reference's update from preprint to conference publication identifies the same work rather than a new citation.

T1.justification: Appendix A.4 adds an asymptotic derivation: with fixed batch size and comparable feature dimensions, SPARC costs O(M²Ld) per batch versus USAE's O(MLd). The central model mathematics remains equivalent, although v1's explicit NMSE definition is omitted. The added standard R² formula does not constitute a new theoretical result.

improvement.justification: v1 criticizes USAE without directly evaluating it. v2 resolves this central evidential gap through documented, matched-budget comparisons, while broader reconstruction tests, uncertainty reporting, and explicit failure cases strengthen credibility and applicability assessment. Reproducibility documentation also improves substantially. Losing coarser-depth alignment results and the explicit NMSE definition reduces some detail, and the new reconstruction results do not support uniform superiority, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SPARC and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and extensive appendices. Renumbered and relocated material can be matched reliably across versions.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds evaluated USAE comparisons, label-purity measurements, reconstruction matrices, runtime measurements, and localization failure cases.

before.justification: v1 reports original concept-alignment, probing, segmentation, retrieval, and ablation results on Open Images and MS-COCO, plus qualitative appendix analyses.

results.title: SPARC: Concept-Aligned Sparse Autoencoders for Cross-Model and Cross-Modal Interpretability

C1.justification: The principal reconstruction-performance claim remains. However, the introduction adds a substantial theoretical contribution: transformers can express the Bayes-optimal substitution-only algorithm, and near-optimal-loss estimators must approximate its predictions. v1 claimed a scaling-law explanation through a simplified linear model, without these transformer-specific claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds specific applicability limits and mechanism interpretations beyond v1's general distribution-shift caveat. These include failed extrapolation beyond training lengths, ambiguity with misclustered two-read inputs, attention-based rejection of incorrect traces, and explanations of positional errors. It also discusses autoregressive inference costs and explicitly leaves gradient-descent convergence theoretically unresolved.

D1.justification: v2 adds context lengths and early-stopping information, detailed baseline architecture descriptions, the Chandak preprocessing and experiment-selection pipeline, and inference hardware, batching, and timing details. Conversely, it omits v1's explicit pretrained-model and test-dataset links while retaining the code link. This changes access documentation without establishing that those resources became unavailable.

E1.justification: v2 adds the Chandak et al. nanopore dataset, evaluating six experiments with 117-nucleotide originals (Appendix I). It also adds mixed-source misclustered inputs and empirical substitution-only reconstruction scenarios. The original synthetic lengths and Noisy-DNA and Microsoft datasets remain.

E2.justification: The main classical and specialized neural baseline set is retained. The prompted-model comparison adds GPT-5 and chain-of-thought variants alongside GPT-4o mini (v1 Appendix C.3; v2 Appendix J.3). The substitution-only study also introduces comparison against Bayes-optimal loss.

E3.justification: Reported test counts change from 15,843 to 15,696 for Noisy-DNA and from 5,235 to 5,109 for Microsoft. Table 1 changes Microsoft's fine-tuning batch size from 52 to 25 and weight decay from 0.1 to 0.001, and Noisy-DNA dropout from 0.3 to 0.1. New experiments add variable-length training, decoding controls, fine-tuning-data fractions, and hardware-normalized throughput protocols.

E4.justification: Beyond retained noise, cluster-size, alignment-target, and scaling analyses, v2 adds misclustering robustness, sequence-length extrapolation, decoding and input-order sensitivity, pretraining ablation, and fine-tuning-data efficiency. Appendix D adds sequence-pattern and positional error analyses and expands attention inspection across layers; Appendix M.5 adds confidence and representation probes.

E5.justification: v2 newly reports three-seed averages with standard-deviation bands for principal TReconLM plots, specifying that fine-tuning runs share a pretrained checkpoint. Appendix N clarifies that table deviations concern test examples and table results use seed 100. It also reports 20 permutation evaluations with variability, binomial tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction, and repeated inference-timing measurements.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for the new dataset, robustness tests, ablations, inference costs, and substitution-only analyses. Existing tables also change: DNAformer's synthetic N=7 Levenshtein distance is corrected from 1.83e-1 to 1.83e-2 (v1 Table 2; v2 Table 5). Noisy-DNA's reported advantage over ITR changes from 13% to 14.7%, but revised samples and fine-tuning settings prevent interpreting this as a same-setting improvement.

M1.justification: The default decoder-only transformer, cross-entropy training, and greedy reconstruction remain unchanged. Appendix B newly introduces evaluated inference variants using beam search and per-position majority voting over reconstructions from up to ten trace-order permutations. These are limited alternative procedures rather than a redesign of TReconLM.

P1.justification: The seven-section main narrative and much existing exposition remain. v2 tightens prose, revises the contribution summary, subdivides robustness and theory discussions, moves detailed Noisy-DNA preprocessing into Appendix G, and reorganizes the appendices. These are editorial and structural refinements alongside the larger scientific additions.

P2.justification: Figure 3 gains a misclustering panel, the alignment-target figure incorporates decoding variants, and the single attention heatmap becomes a layer-by-layer grid. New displays cover errors, misclustering, the Chandak dataset, throughput, and confidence. Existing plots gain uncertainty displays, while tables gain context-length information and columns for neural baselines already plotted in v1.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to Chandak et al., Benjamini-Hochberg, Cover, and Tsybakov, and removes Holenstein et al. The main research positioning remains stable. Related-work descriptions receive limited revisions, including describing DNAformer's dynamic-programming postprocessing as optional rather than required.

T1.justification: v2 adds a quaternary substitution-channel optimality derivation, a two-layer transformer construction for majority voting, and a theorem relating excess cross-entropy to total-variation distance, with proofs in Appendix M. These substantially extend v1's linear-model analysis. Proposition 1's concentration coefficient also changes from 6 to 12, and its proof corrects sample-size denominators from n to N.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support through quantified seed variability, realistic misclustering tests, pretraining and data-efficiency ablations, another real-data evaluation, and explicit failure boundaries. These address important gaps in v1's evidence about reliability and practical applicability. Expanded implementation documentation also helps reproducibility. Omitting direct model and dataset links is a limited drawback, outweighed by these gains; updated performance numbers alone do not establish improvement because some evaluation settings changed.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TReconLM and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The expanded v2 can be reliably matched to v1 across relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains original reconstruction experiments and adds empirical results on misclustering, decoding, pretraining, data efficiency, another real dataset, inference cost, and substitution-only reconstruction.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic and real-data reconstruction experiments, scaling experiments, and supplementary comparisons and analyses.

results.title: Trace Reconstruction with Language Models

C1.justification: The three central contributions remain equivariant long-range message passing, the LOREM architecture, and experiments probing short-range limitations. V2's discussion adds a specific claim of competitive force accuracy and better energy predictions on the larger ADAPT benchmark, and explicitly confines adaptation-free operation to architecture hyperparameters while allowing dataset-specific training tuning.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly frames the work as a proof of concept and explains why aggregate errors on heterogeneous datasets can obscure contributions from long-range physics. Appendix D adds qualifications about numerical precision and the imperfect relationship between validation error and qualitative cumulene curves. The earlier limitations concerning distance decay, naive quadratic evaluation, and inadequate benchmarks remain.

D1.justification: V1 promises a future code and data release; v2 states that code, data, configurations, and trained models are available in a specified Zenodo archive. V2 also supplies float32 training information, more detailed PET settings and model counts, tuning procedures, and hardware and training-time information for the added experiments. These substantially expand documented reproducibility.

E1.justification: The five original benchmarks are retained. Appendix J adds ADAPT silicon point-defect configurations with 24 dopant elements and 52 dopant pairs, substantially extending the evaluated materials coverage. Appendix E also introduces periodic NaCl, CsCl, and Cu2O supercells for runtime evaluation.

E2.justification: SpookyNet is added to the MgO and NaCl comparisons in Table 1. The new ADAPT comparison includes ADAPT Small/Large, MatterSim, and several pretrained MACE variants alongside retrained MACE. CACE's renaming to CACE-LES represents the same retained comparator.

E3.justification: V1 specifies LAMB throughout; v2 specifies ADAM except for cumulene and changes the MgO energy-loss weight from 100 to 1000. PET's cumulene settings also change, including batch size 32 to 16, attention layers, and learning-rate scheduling. New protocols include the inner 4000/500 tuning split, runtime scaling measurements, additional error metrics, and ADAPT evaluation on 100 held-out trajectory starting structures.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained cutoff, message-passing-depth, and SN2 analyses, Appendix F systematically compares no long-range block and long-range orders l=0,1,2 across four benchmarks. Appendix E analyzes runtime scaling and long-range overhead, while Appendix H tests whether tuning and early stopping on the reported validation set affect conclusions. These address substantial new questions about mechanism, efficiency, and evaluation robustness.

E5.justification: V2 newly discloses two LOREM training seeds, reporting the better run in the main table and the alternative run in Tables 11–12. Runtime measurements are averaged over ten repetitions. This adds limited repeated-run reporting without confidence intervals or formal significance tests; it does not establish that v1 used fewer runs.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises existing scores: LOREM biodimer energy RMSE changes from 0.459 to 0.222 meV/atom, and CACE/CACE-LES MgO energy RMSE from 0.735 to 0.071. PET now leads cumulene RMSE with 3.205 meV/atom and 46.905 meV/Å versus LOREM's 3.309 and 50.084, reversing v1's ranking under revised training settings. Substantial new runtime, ablation, tuning, seed, and ADAPT results are also reported.

M1.justification: The equivariant-charge aggregation and overall short-range/long-range architecture remain recognizable. However, Appendix D changes the default parameter count from 953,870 to 1,021,198 despite retaining the listed architecture hyperparameters, and v1's initial-layer normalization exception disappears. The PDFs do not establish whether these reflect implementation changes or corrections to the description.

P1.justification: The abstract, background, related work, method explanations, and discussion undergo extensive rewriting. Ewald summation moves from Section 4.1 into the background, spherical operations are consolidated in Appendix A, and the experimental narrative and appendices are reorganized. These are substantial explanatory and structural changes beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: V2 changes typography, margins, headings, and front matter; revises the architecture diagram's labels and legend; adds a SpookyNet column and second-best highlighting to Table 1; and adds an optimizer column to Table 3. New runtime, ablation, robustness, and ADAPT displays substantially expand the visual presentation. The original cutoff-study Figure 6 is matched to Figure 10 rather than counted as a wholly new analysis.

R1.justification: V2 adds targeted references and discussion concerning multilevel summation, ADAPT, tensor-product body order, and optimization or normalization methods. Its positioning as an equivariant extension of physics-inspired Ewald message passing remains intact. Many other reference changes merely restore dates or update publication metadata.

T1.justification: Section 2 and Appendix A add explicit mathematical definitions of feature spaces, rotation actions, equivariant linear maps, and weighted Clebsch–Gordan tensor products beyond v1's brief operation list. The inverse-power aggregation, spherical norm, and background-charge invariance argument are retained; no new central theorem or proof replaces them.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the central mechanism: Appendix F isolates equivariant charges within LOREM, and Appendix E supplies runtime evidence absent from v1. The inner-split check, larger ADAPT evaluation, and detailed reproducibility statement address important earlier evidence and documentation gaps. Two-seed testing remains limited, and Appendix H's 'nearest other' rows omit SpookyNet despite Table 1, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial overall gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LOREM research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original LOREM evaluations and adds runtime measurements, representation-order ablations, validation-protocol checks, alternative-seed results, and silicon point-defect experiments.

before.justification: Section 6 and the appendices report original LOREM energy and force evaluations, cutoff and message-passing experiments, and numerical invariance checks.

results.title: Learning Long-Range Representations with Equivariant Messages

C1.justification: The abstract qualifies the earlier broad privacy benefit as an observed empirical improvement and explicitly claims competitive downstream accuracy and AUROC for mixed-model synthesis. Partitioned generation, computational feasibility and mixed-model synthesis remain the central contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix B introduces substantial interpretation of partitioning as information fragmentation, explains the non-equivalence of noise-strength parameters, and limits the comparison to random concatenation rather than the complete framework. v2 also develops requirements for end-to-end privacy accounting and discusses realistic adversarial applicability. The earlier warnings about non-private validators, partition-aware attacks and selection bias remain.

D1.justification: Appendices A.2 and C.2 newly disclose a 100-iteration limit, typical fourfold oversampling, and typical random-forest settings of 5–20 estimators and depth 10–15. These are additional details rather than established setting changes. Conversely, v2 removes the hardware specifications and dataset-license column. The repository and dataset links were already supplied in v1.

E1.justification: The eight benchmark datasets and their tasks remain unchanged in Table 1. v2 adds noisy-input scenarios in Appendix B and a controlled two-variable example with ground-truth marginal inputs in Appendix C.2, providing limited additional synthetic test conditions.

E2.justification: Table 3 and Figure 8 expand the mixed-model comparison to include TabDiff, ARF, TVAE, CTGAN, ADS-GAN and TabDDPM. CTGAN appeared elsewhere in v1 but was absent from this comparison. Appendix B additionally evaluates Gaussian noise, random replacement and column-wise shuffling as alternatives to partitioning.

E3.justification: New protocols include three perturbation schemes at five strengths and a 250-sample controlled experiment using ground-truth marginal samples to isolate validator effects (Appendices B and C.2). The original benchmark splits remain unchanged. Table 3 also relabels accuracy differences as F1 differences, although the appendix still describes accuracy; the PDFs do not establish whether this involved recomputation.

E4.justification: Appendix B adds sensitivity comparisons testing whether ordinary noise injection reproduces partitioning's effects. Appendix C.2 adds a controlled analysis of distributional distortion caused by unoptimized versus optimized validators. The earlier correlation, validator-choice, calibration and threshold analyses are retained, with much of v1 Section 4.4 moved into Appendix C.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly states that random seeds were left unlocked and specifies ten repetitions for Table 3. The table newly marks statistically indistinguishable results using 95% confidence intervals. Existing standard-deviation and standard-error reporting largely persists; these disclosures do not establish increased run counts.

E6.justification: Table 3 expands from 12 to 25 result rows, while Figures 7–8 add TabDiff mixtures and broader baseline results. Eleven retained table rows preserve their numbers; the DPGAN–synthpop row changes, including epsilon risk from 0.048(7) to 0.14(3). New noise and validator-distortion findings appear in Figures 10 and 13. The correlation study replaces its PCA panel with AUROC results.

M1.justification: Column partitioning, separate generators, validator training on authentic and shuffled joins, and iterative acceptance and reshuffling remain unchanged. TabDiff supplies another instance of the existing interchangeable-generator design. The expanded implementation discussion does not establish a revised algorithm.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and background are revised, and the experimental narrative gains an extensive roadmap and more descriptive subsections. Implementation details move to Appendix A, validator analyses to Appendix C, and metric explanations to Appendix D. The conclusion becomes a discussion, with additional impact and materials statements.

P2.justification: v2 adds validator and noise diagrams, new comparison plots and the distribution-distortion visualization. Table 3 is expanded and reformatted from landscape to portrait with metric groupings and significance styling. Existing plots gain revised labels and directional arrows; the validator comparison changes from a grid to vertically stacked panels.

R1.justification: v2 adds contemporary generator and benchmark references, alongside foundational differential-privacy and private-covariance work. It explicitly acknowledges prior partitioning-related efficiency benefits. The established positioning relative to conditional generation, federated learning and record linkage remains largely intact.

T1.justification: The framework definitions and computational-scaling arguments are retained across the corresponding sections. There are no new substantive assumptions, theorems, proofs or derivations. The added noise formulas specify experimental perturbations.

improvement.justification: The broader contemporary-baseline comparisons substantially strengthen the previously narrow evidence for mixed-model utility–privacy tradeoffs. The controlled experiment in Figure 13 isolates an important validator failure mechanism, while clearer empirical-privacy qualifications improve claim precision. These gains outweigh the loss of hardware and license details. Accuracy/F1 terminology remains inconsistent, and the added noise comparison is explicitly inconclusive, but neither limitation negates the substantial improvement in empirical support and diagnostic depth.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DGM framework, algorithm and benchmark suite despite the changed title. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, and relocated material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds generator comparisons, noise-injection experiments and a controlled validator study, including results in Appendices B and C.

before.justification: Sections 4.1–4.4 report original synthetic-data experiments, timing measurements, simulations and validator analyses, with results in Table 3 and Figures 2–9.

results.title: Disjoint Generation of Synthetic Data

C1.justification: The central survey contribution and what/when/how framework remain. v4 qualifies the work as a guiding synthesis of an emerging field, emphasizes autonomy as the defining distinction, and softens categorical ASI-precursor language in the introduction and conclusion.

C2.justification: v4 substantially expands interpretations and limitations: operational boundaries and autonomy levels, distinctions between self-play and imitation, benchmark coverage gaps, obstacles to fair comparisons, personalization/privacy trade-offs, and evolution-specific model, memory, and tool risks. Sections 7.3 and 8.3 provide much more concrete qualifications and mitigation guidance than v1.

D1.justification: New worked examples disclose source-attributed configurations and resource information, including backbone models in Table 11 and EvoAgent's reported A100 hardware and training times in Table 10. The survey repository link remains unchanged, and no new implementation or data release is documented.

E1.justification: Neither version actually conducts training or evaluation on datasets. DS-Bench, EvaLearn, AutoEnv, and other additions expand surveyed literature, rather than the work's experimental dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates baselines against a proposed method. v4 Table 11 newly collates published comparisons, but does not introduce an experimental baseline evaluation by this work.

E3.justification: Beyond v1's broad assessment categories, v4 Section 7.2.4 and Table 10 specify proposed protocols covering state resets versus persistence, per-task and cumulative budgets, retention probes, OOD evaluation, and cost and safety measures. These are substantive evaluation-design recommendations, not evidence of rerun experiments.

E4.justification: v4 Table 10 adds a focused literature-based case study checking EvoAgent against the proposed long-horizon protocol, identifying supported features and missing retention, cost, and safety reporting. Neither version reports original ablation or robustness experiments.

E5.justification: Neither version reports run counts, actual seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests for an original evaluation. v4 recommends seed logging and criticizes limited repetitions in cited benchmarks, without adding uncertainty estimates to its reported comparisons.

E6.justification: v4 adds substantial quantitative literature synthesis through Tables 5, 10, and 11 and Section 7.1.6. For example, Table 11 newly lists GSM8K scores of 90.5%, 90.8%, and 94.6% for ADAS, AFlow, and ScoreFlow with GPT-4o-mini. These are newly tabulated cited results under partially matched settings, not v1-to-v4 performance gains.

M1.justification: Neither version proposes an implemented agent algorithm or model. Expanded descriptions of existing methods and new operational inclusion criteria do not change a proposed computational procedure.

P1.justification: Evaluation is reorganized into goal-specific metrics and coverage-gap subsections, while safety is rewritten around emergent risks and mitigation strategies. Positioning and methodological explanations are extensively expanded, the contents pages are removed, and the title and citation style change.

P2.justification: v4 adds five tables covering costs, coverage gaps, protocols, comparative performance, and deployment safeguards; revises Figures 1, 3, and 4; and expands several captions. Existing metric and horizon-comparison tables are retained and renumbered within the new journal layout.

R1.justification: v4 adds substantial historical positioning through genetic algorithms, genetic programming, Sims, and NEAT, alongside newer memory, self-play, and safety literature. Section 2.2 also replaces v1's overly categorical lifelong-learning distinction with a discussion acknowledging replay and episodic memory.

T1.justification: v4 Section 7.1.2 corrects the transposed task/time indices in the forgetting and backward-transfer formulas to match the stated definition of J_i,t. The POMDP formulation and evolution/objective equations (1)-(3) remain unchanged; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: Operational inclusion criteria, the corrected lifelong-learning comparison, historical grounding, and substantially stronger evaluation and safety analysis address important conceptual and practical weaknesses in v1. These gains outweigh localized problems in the new quantitative material: notably, Table 10 incorrectly calls 21.80% to 30.29% a 105.9% relative gain, although those values imply about 38.9%.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same self-evolving-agent survey, with matching core taxonomy and equations. Text, tables, figures, and references support reliable comparison. Neither supplied PDF contains an appendix.

after.justification: v4 remains a survey. Its new numerical examples and comparative tables synthesize cited studies, while the evaluation protocols are recommendations rather than original experimental results.

before.justification: v1 surveys existing systems and benchmarks. Its performance statements are attributed to prior work; it reports no original empirical study.

results.title: A Survey of Self-Evolving Agents: What, When, How, and Where to Evolve on the Path to Artificial Super Intelligence

C1.justification: The central contributions remain intact. However, the discussion narrows cropping's superiority from 'all evaluations' in v1 to 'all evaluation modalities' in v2, accommodating the newly reported task-level exceptions while retaining the overall augmentation, rapid-adaptation and late-layer claims.

C2.justification: V1's assertion that the last layer always performs best is qualified by penultimate-layer peaks for dropout and for cropping on STS/classification. V2 discusses objective–evaluation misalignment and adds specific limitations concerning training duration and MTEB training only on ICLR. It also withdraws the caption's claim that whitening improves untuned MPNet.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies period-based sentence splitting, SentenceTransformers normalization and normalization differences between evaluations, and adds the RoBERTa checkpoint. The removed projection-head report also removes its architecture dimensions. Main hyperparameters, hardware and code-access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Table 1 expands from 12 tasks across four MTEB modalities to 19 across five. Seven classification tasks add sentiment and intent/domain recognition coverage, including AmazonPolarity, Banking77 and IMDb. The six datasets used for in-domain representation evaluation are retained.

E2.justification: V2 adds dropout-tuned MPNet to Figure 4b's layerwise comparison and includes untreated BERT/RoBERTa controls in new Table S1. The main off-the-shelf comparator membership in Tables 1–2 remains unchanged.

E3.justification: New evaluation settings include train/test logistic regression with 100 maximum iterations, controlled fine-tuning experiments with BERT and RoBERTa, and layerwise MTEB evaluation using unnormalized embeddings. The block average now covers five modalities. Existing MPNet training settings and kNN splits are retained; normalization disclosures alone do not establish rerunning existing experiments.

E4.justification: New Table S1 tests whether augmentation rankings generalize across backbones. Expanded Figure 4 and new Figure S3 examine layerwise quality across augmentations and MTEB modalities. Conversely, v1's explicit projection-head ablation and its finding of no consistent benefit disappear.

E5.justification: Both Table 2 captions retain the same approximate ±1 percentage-point uncertainty based on binomial standard deviation. Neither version reports additional seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: V2 adds classification, backbone and layerwise results. Its 51.8% cropping average versus v1's 48.7% reflects expanded benchmark coverage, not a same-setting gain. Existing Table 1 BGE-base/BGE-large values are exchanged. Pre-fine-tuning whitening accuracy with cosine distance changes from 46.9% to 18.5% in v1 Table S2 versus v2 Table S3, reversing the reported benefit.

M1.justification: The two-sentence cropping procedure, dropout pairing, mean pooling, cosine InfoNCE loss and in-batch negatives are retained. BERT/RoBERTa experiments apply the existing procedure; newly disclosed preprocessing details do not establish a method change.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites and reorganizes related work into three subsections, revises the abstract and introductory framing, reworks the layer discussion and introduces a separate Limitations section. Training without pre-training moves from Section 3.3.4 to Section 3.4.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains a classification block, new Table S1 presents backbone comparisons, Figure 4 expands from two to three panels, and Figure S3 is added. Figures 1 and 3 move from text-wrapped placements to standalone displays, while captions and supplementary layouts are revised.

R1.justification: Related work substantially expands to distinguish encoder and generative embedding models, instruction tuning and newer contrastive approaches. Added works include E5, GTE, CoCondenser and NV-Embed. Section 4 explicitly positions the layer findings relative to Skean et al. (2025); these additions extend beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: The InfoNCE objective and appendix metric formulas remain mathematically unchanged. Neither version provides theoretical results or proofs, and v2's added mechanism discussion is conceptual rather than a formal derivation.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the evidence behind the broad conclusions by testing additional backbones and a previously omitted task family. Its expanded layer analysis exposes exceptions to final-layer optimality, improving the conclusions' calibration, while clearer limitations and implementation disclosures aid interpretation. Losing the explicit projection-head check and leaving some numerical revisions unexplained are drawbacks, but the broader tests and more qualified conclusions provide a substantial overall gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same cropping-versus-dropout study. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across revisions and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and adds classification benchmarks, BERT/RoBERTa experiments and further layerwise evaluations.

before.justification: V1 reports original contrastive-training experiments, MTEB scores, in-domain classification results and ablations in the main text and appendices.

results.title: Cropping outperforms dropout as an augmentation strategy for self-supervised training of text embeddings

C1.justification: The abstract and main contributions retain the same OOPE, spectral lower-bound and FW claims. V3 newly asserts that the fixed-design setting was previously unstudied (Section 3). Its conclusion also explicitly qualifies minimax matching by the well-/poorly-explored regimes and additive constants, qualifications already present elsewhere in v1.

C2.justification: V3 pinpoints the unresolved intermediate-regime bound gap to a uniform eigenvalue bound (Remark 4.12), extending v1's general confidence-width explanation. It interprets the new FW experiments through approximation costs, sparse-support savings and insufficient exploitation time at short horizons. The fixed-design and no-drift restrictions remain.

D1.justification: Section 6 adds explicit parameter tables, a random-partition recipe for offline allocations, and initialization details for warm-started LinUCB and LinTS. These improve experimental documentation. The PDFs still provide no code-access instructions or numerical solver specifications.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate synthetic spherical linear bandits with Gaussian reward noise. V1 explicitly includes rank-deficient offline coverage: five supported arms in ten dimensions. V3's reported experiments use larger, full-dimensional random supports and do not retain that explicit missing-directions scenario. No new application domain or external dataset is introduced.

E2.justification: V1's empirical figures contain only OOPE under different offline-data quantities. V3 adds online phased elimination (Figure 1), warm-started LinUCB and LinTS (Figure 2), and direct OOPE-versus-OOPE-FW comparisons (Figures 3–4). The warm-started methods were previously discussed theoretically but not experimentally compared.

E3.justification: V1 evaluates a modification that reuses all offline and previous online data with phase-dependent weighting; v3 states it implements Section 4's prescribed OOPE. Dimensions, arm counts, horizons and offline allocation procedures also change. New experiments include fixed-spectrum effective-dimension sweeps across multiple horizons and dimensions (Tables 2–5).

E4.justification: Beyond v1's offline-data quantity and coverage studies, v3 investigates whether Frank-Wolfe improves OOPE and how that comparison depends on effective dimension, horizon and ambient dimension (Figures 3–4). This adds substantial sensitivity analysis of the approximation's benefits and failure regimes.

E5.justification: V1 displays variability through boxplots without specifying repeat counts. V3 explicitly reports 50 runs per horizon and mean-regret confidence intervals; Figure 1 specifies 95% intervals. This changes statistical reporting but does not establish an increase over v1's unstated run count.

E6.justification: The original boxplot results are replaced by new results under different settings. Figure 2 shows OOPE outperforming LinTS and outperforming LinUCB at longer, but not the shortest, horizons. Figures 3–4 add FW gains and performance reversals across regimes. These are new findings, not same-setting performance improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The principal OOPE and OOPE-FW procedures remain unchanged. V3 adds a horizon-free adaptation using increasing horizons, full restarts and recomputed offline weights/effective dimensions (Remark 4.7), plus optional preliminary exploration to satisfy the offline-sample condition (Section 3).

P1.justification: Most prose and proof structure is retained. V3 separates stationarity and fixed-design assumptions, adds focused explanations, rewrites the conclusion and moves the expanded experiments into Section 6. Author information and publication headers are also updated.

P2.justification: The two appendix boxplot figures are replaced by four main-text figures featuring regret curves, comparator legends, confidence intervals and a three-panel sensitivity analysis. V3 also adds bounds-summary Table 1 and experimental-parameter Tables 2–5, substantially changing the visual presentation.

R1.justification: V3 adds Besson and Kaufmann (2018) for the doubling-trick extension and newly positions the fixed-design setting as previously unstudied. The related-work survey and other cited works are essentially retained.

T1.justification: V3 adds a horizon-free regret argument and a quantified additional-regret bound for preliminary exploration. The effective-dimension definition, principal upper/lower bounds and Appendix A/B proofs remain substantively unchanged. New Table 1 summarizes existing bounds rather than introducing new theoretical results.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens empirical validation: v1 tests a data-reusing modification without algorithm baselines, whereas v3 reports the prescribed OOPE procedure, relevant comparisons, repeated-run uncertainty and both favorable and unfavorable FW regimes. This addresses important gaps between the theoretical contributions and their empirical support while retaining the proofs. These gains outweigh losing the explicit rank-deficient experiment, although evaluation remains synthetic and Figure 2 does not support uniform superiority at every horizon.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OOPE/OOPE-FW research. Their text, equations, figures and appendices support comparison. The proof appendices are retained; v1's experimental Appendix C is replaced by v3's Section 6.

after.justification: Section 6, Figures 1–4 report original simulations comparing OOPE with online phased elimination, warm-started LinUCB/LinTS and OOPE-FW.

before.justification: Appendix C, Figures 1–2 report original synthetic linear-bandit simulations measuring regret under different offline-data quantities and coverage.

results.title: Regret minimization in Linear Bandits with offline data via extended D-optimal exploration

C1.justification: The central contributions remain differentiable-distance penalization, oracle-based randomized exploration, computationally efficient two-stage training, and constrained/adversarial generation applications. The abstract explicitly identifies the existing one-stage efficiency comparison, and the conclusion emphasizes both methods without materially redefining the contributions.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation through explanations of PDM/NAMM distribution mismatch, joint optimization versus fine-tuning and forgetting, baseline-induced variance reduction, and constraint-dependent computational overhead. The principal limitations already existed in v1 Appendix C and are relocated. The explicit statement that thickness FID worsens is removed, although Table 3 retains the adverse values.

D1.justification: v2 adds per-experiment training times, practical starting recommendations for lambda, t0, and N2, and clearer descriptions of comparator requirements and subspace information access. These extend documentation; the reported GPU, experiment-specific parameter table, and code-access link are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same five synthetic cases, MNIST brightness and thickness constraints, and adversarial generation for MNIST/LeNet-5 and CIFAR-10/ResNet-50. The new fine-tuning and gradient analyses operate within existing synthetic tasks.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated NAMM and PDM baselines across the synthetic cases in Table 2, PDM for MNIST brightness in Table 3, and a fine-tuned FM comparator in Appendix C.1.1. NAMM and PDM were cited in v1 but did not participate in these comparisons. This substantially broadens the empirical comparison set.

E3.justification: v2 adds a controlled with/without-baseline evaluation using fixed model parameters at each epoch and gradient-norm/variance measurements, plus absolute training-time comparisons across methods. Existing data splits, generation sample counts, SWD/FID evaluations, and tabulated FM-DD/FM-RE hyperparameters are retained.

E4.justification: New Appendix C.1.1 compares joint optimization with fine-tuning and examines distribution distortion. Appendix C.1.2 adds an ablation testing whether baseline subtraction reduces gradient noise, while Table 4 quantifies comparative training costs. These substantially extend analysis beyond the retained parameter sweeps and adversarial noise controls.

E5.justification: Figure 6 introduces gradient statistics computed from 100 repetitions of an epoch with model parameters fixed. This adds a statistical estimation procedure; the existing 100-generation-trial averaging and synthetic mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting remain unchanged. The PDFs do not report an increase in independent training runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds NAMM/PDM scores, fine-tuning results, runtime measurements, and gradient curves. MDM's Box SWD changes from 0.2764 ± 0.0874 to 0.1431 ± 0.0747. Between v1 Table 8 and v2 Table 9, Gaussian-noise norms change from 5.59 to 5.47 for MNIST and 10.94 to 11.15 for CIFAR-10; CIFAR-10 accuracy changes from 84.1% to 82.3%. Original headline FM-DD/FM-RE scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Appendix C.1.2 introduces and tests an FM-RE gradient-estimation variant that subtracts a constant baseline b=1 from the terminal constraint indicator. The core FM-DD objective, two-stage FM-RE procedure, and sampling algorithms remain unchanged; the adversarial-generation adaptation was already documented in v1.

P1.justification: v2 removes 'Efficient' from the title, edits the abstract and explanatory passages, expands the conclusion, and adds hyperparameter guidance. It moves the adversarial formulation and limitations into the main text and renames the experimental appendix from D to C. Most section ordering and existing prose remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 adds fine-tuning and gradient-diagnostic figures and a training-time table, expands comparison tables, and visually groups existing adversarial examples. The TMLR format changes front matter, headers, typography, and display placement, including placing Figure 2 beside Table 3. The combined display and layout revision is substantial.

R1.justification: v2 adds Uehara et al. (2024) and explicitly distinguishes joint optimization from reinforcement-learning-based fine-tuning. It expands discussion of the already-cited PDM and clarifies NAMM's differentiable-distance requirement. The broader positioning against reflection and mirror-map approaches remains intact.

T1.justification: Appendix B adds a derivation showing that a state-dependent baseline has zero expected score-function contribution and gives the corresponding unbiased gradient expression in Equations 22–23. The original propositions and proofs are otherwise substantially retained, with clarified trajectory notation.

improvement.justification: The NAMM/PDM evaluations address an important gap in v1's comparisons with methods applicable beyond simple convex constraints. The gradient-baseline proof and ablation, fine-tuning comparison, and runtime table substantially strengthen assessment of optimization behavior and practical trade-offs. Although v2 softens discussion of the unchanged thickness-FID disadvantage, its numerical evidence and principal limitations remain disclosed, yielding a clear net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FM-DD/FM-RE research. Their main text, equations, proofs, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including content moved between the appendices and main text.

after.justification: Section 6 and Appendix C report original generation and adversarial-image results, alongside additional baseline comparisons, training-time measurements, and gradient diagnostics.

before.justification: Sections 6.1–6.3 and Appendix D report original synthetic-generation, constrained MNIST-generation, and adversarial-image experiments, with distributional metrics, constraint violations, and classification results.

results.title: Constraint-Aware Flow Matching via Randomized Exploration

C1.justification: The introduction replaces the contribution claim of 'almost no local/global structure trade-off' with a claim of a 'state-of-the-art trade-off,' qualifying the asserted benefit. The central contribution of combining t-SNE locality with PCA global structure and the claim of superior benchmark performance remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explicit qualifications concerning absent theoretical guarantees, runtime overhead, CIFAR10 difficulties, and UMAP's strengths under clustering-based metrics not evaluated here. Appendix B also explains the scaling choice and gradient-induced shrinkage. Earlier limitations concerning reference-embedding bias and dataset-dependent regularization remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A documents the added datasets' sampling and preprocessing, including Mammoth coloring through agglomerative clustering and Fashion MNIST rescaling before PCA. Code links now identify the tmlr branches. Hardware and the reported CNE training budget remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Table 1 expands coverage from seven to eleven datasets, retaining all previous datasets and adding Mammoth, Landsat Satellite, Fashion MNIST, and CIFAR10. These introduce 3D shape, remote-sensing, clothing-image, and object-image settings beyond the earlier predominantly biological benchmark.

E2.justification: The main benchmark retains the same competing algorithms. However, the new alignment comparison in Table S1 evaluates least-squares scaling, translation-adjusted scaling, full Procrustes alignment, and no scaling against default DREAMS; these comparator configurations were absent from v1.

E3.justification: Reported initialization changes from unit-standard-deviation PCA or approximately scale-10 MDS coordinates to first-coordinate standard deviation 10^-4. Default DREAMS regularization changes from 0.1 to 0.15, and the decoder default from 0.01 to 0.005. New protocols include alignment controls, runtime accounting including reference-embedding computation, and a k sweep from 1 to 200.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained CNE-versus-decoder analysis, v2 adds tests of scaling, translation, rotation, and gradient propagation in Appendix B; runtime comparisons in Appendix C; and sensitivity to the neighborhood size used for evaluation in Appendix F. These directly examine previously untested design choices and evaluation robustness.

E5.justification: Both versions specify means and uncertainties across four random seeds. v2 additionally identifies the runtime error bars as standard deviations in Figure S2, whereas v1 does not identify its uncertainty statistic. This is a limited reporting clarification, not evidence of increased run counts.

E6.justification: v2 adds results for four datasets and the new supplementary analyses, while replacing several retained-dataset scores: for example, DREAMS on Tasic changes from 0.91 to 0.88 in Table 2 under revised settings. These are not same-setting performance changes. Some new results have unexplained cross-display differences: FMNIST DREAMS-MDS scores 0.87 in Table 2 but 0.83 in Figure S14.

M1.justification: Equation 2 changes the reported regularization penalty from lambda times the squared discrepancy to lambda/n times that discrepancy. The underlying t-SNE-plus-global-reference framework, norm-ratio scaling, and CNE/decoder variants remain. This is a limited objective revision; the PDFs do not establish whether it corrects documentation or changes implementation.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most explanatory prose remain recognizable. v2 makes local language corrections, expands selected explanations, adds publication and affiliation text, and reorganizes the appendix into separately titled sections rather than v1's three subsections.

P2.justification: Figure 3 and the CNE comparison expand into two-row displays, and Tables 1–2 accommodate the added datasets. New displays cover alignment, optimization trajectories, runtime, score contours, and neighborhood sensitivity, alongside four new embedding grids. Figure 1 also moves onto the opening page.

R1.justification: Related work adds EmbedOR, UMATO, and Cluster and Embed, alongside new references supporting Procrustes analysis, evaluation qualifications, and dataset sources. These extend the context without substantially changing DREAMS' positioning relative to StarMAP and SQuadMDS-hybrid.

T1.justification: Appendix B adds a focused mathematical analysis: an alternative least-squares scaling factor, its relationship to norm-ratio scaling through Cauchy–Schwarz, and gradients with and without differentiating through the scale factor (Equations 6–9). The existing background mathematics remains, and no general performance guarantee is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the method beyond v1's predominantly biological benchmark. The added domains, controlled scaling tests, neighborhood sensitivity analysis, and runtime measurements address important gaps in generality, design justification, and practical evaluation. Clearer limitations further improve interpretation. Unexplained differences between some appendix scores and Table 2 weaken numerical clarity, but do not outweigh these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DREAMS method and retain identifiable corresponding experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support a reliable comparison despite the expanded scope in v2.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on eleven datasets, together with scaling and alignment ablations, runtime measurements, and neighbor-count sensitivity results.

before.justification: v1 reports original embedding experiments on seven datasets, quantitative comparisons in Table 2, and additional variant evaluations and visualizations in the appendix.

results.title: DREAMS: Preserving both Local and Global Structure in Dimensionality Reduction

C1.justification: The central claim—solver-independent unsupervised MIP representations supporting multiple downstream tasks—remains. v5's conclusion extends claimed applicability to preliminary MIP-to-SAT transfer and qualifies FORGE as a step toward a foundational model. Replacing 'warm-start prediction' with 'search guidance' largely clarifies the existing variable-hint application rather than introducing a different central contribution.

C2.justification: Section 7 adds specific limitations concerning training scale, unexplored code semantics, solver integration and untested downstream applications. The appendices add interpretations of codebook insensitivity, covering/packing directions and cross-domain transfer. v5 also discusses the accuracy/computation tradeoff against strong hand-crafted features and distinguishes FORGE's sharing across problems from Cai et al.'s sharing across tasks, substantially refining the account of generalization.

D1.justification: Most hardware, learning rates, epochs and solver budgets were already disclosed and move to A.7. New details include Gurobi v12.0.3, equal BCE/triplet weighting, explicit PS-Gurobi retraining, and GPU-driven exclusion of very large training instances. A.1 and A.6 document baseline and SAT features. The stated release expands from code/pretrained weights to datasets, fine-tuned models and ready-made benchmark embeddings; availability is not independently verified.

E1.justification: v5 adds strIPlib evaluation across ten named optimization families, solver-configuration prediction using SCIP, and SAT/UNSAT-aware clustering on G4SATBench (A.2, A.5–A.6). This substantially expands task and domain coverage beyond the original optimization experiments. Figure 3 also changes the displayed difficulty groups, although its legend disagrees with the retained category list in Section 4.

E2.justification: v5 adds the Hutter et al. (2014) hand-crafted feature baseline to clustering and directly evaluates Cai et al. (2025a)'s multitask model for solver configuration (Figure 8; Table 3). These introduce substantive external comparisons absent from v1's experiments. The original mean-readout, label-propagation, Gurobi, Li et al. and PS-Gurobi comparisons remain; the random-feature PS-Gurobi control moves to Appendix A.8.

E3.justification: Section 4 changes the reported clustering test size from 1,050 to 1,000 instances. Added protocols include 500 strIPlib instances, codebooks ranging from 500 to 10,000 entries, embedding-arithmetic controls fixing graph size and solving difficulty, SCIP configuration evaluation, and 1,400 Hard SAT formulas grouped by problem type and feasibility. These substantially extend evaluation design; the original Gurobi time limits and principal training budgets are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix A.3 adds codebook-size sensitivity analysis, A.4 tests whether embedding arithmetic reflects covering/packing relationships, and A.6 compares unchanged MIP features with SAT-adapted features to isolate feature specialization. These address new questions about representation behavior and transfer. The pretraining-versus-scratch comparison and PS-Gurobi random-feature control already existed in v1; relocating the latter is not a new ablation.

E5.justification: Both versions average clustering NMI over ten k-means runs, and v1 Figure 3 already displays ± uncertainty terms. v5 extends that reporting convention to additional results without documenting a new uncertainty-estimation procedure, increased run count or seed policy. Appendix A.3's significance statement supplies no identifiable new test procedure.

E6.justification: Figure 3 changes mean-readout NMI from 0.087 to 0.726 and FORGE NMI from 0.843 to 0.953; changed sample counts and plotted categories prevent treating these as same-setting gains. New results include static-feature NMI 0.991, codebook sensitivity, SAT-transfer NMIs 0.76 and 0.77, and configuration runtimes—for example, 801.21 seconds for Cai et al. versus 670.95 for FORGE on CA. Original integrality-prediction errors and displayed solver-gain percentages are retained.

M1.justification: The GraphSAGE/vector-quantization backbone and pretraining losses remain unchanged. The reported search-guidance procedure changes from top-5% positive candidates to top-decile candidates and describes separate negative-anchor neighborhoods; hard-negative selection changes from proximity to the positive variable to proximity to the anchor. Appendices A.5–A.6 add configuration-prediction heads and a SAT-specific input-feature variant using unchanged pretrained weights. These are limited adaptations of the existing framework.

P1.justification: v5 extensively rewrites the introduction and experimental narrative, consistently reframes warm starts as search guidance, merges numerical-results subsections into task descriptions, moves setup details to A.7, and splits related work between Section 6 and A.9. The former conclusion becomes a structured limitations/future-work discussion. These are substantial changes to the existing document's organization and exposition.

P2.justification: v5 adds static-feature, strIPlib, embedding-arithmetic and SAT plots plus three tables. Existing diagrams and solver plots are enlarged or relabeled, and Figure 3 is replotted with changed categories and axis labels. The original three-way PS-Gurobi plot is retained as Figure 14 while a two-method view appears in Figure 7. Typography, margins and figure placement are extensively revised.

R1.justification: Beyond relocating existing related work, v5 substantially expands positioning around GNN expressivity and foldable MILPs, hand-crafted instance features, algorithm selection and portfolios, online neighborhood search, and optimization-to-SAT transfer. New relevant works include Hutter et al.'s feature studies, Chen et al.'s MILP representation analysis, G4SATBench and Pal and Kadıoğlu's transfer work. Bibliographic duplicates and publication updates do not account for this substantive expansion.

T1.justification: Appendix A.4 adds explicit covering/packing problem formulations, the vertex-cover/independent-set complement relation, and mathematical definitions of embedding centroids, difference vectors and translations in Equations 6–9. The original model losses and triplet-loss equation remain unchanged. No new theorem or proof establishing FORGE's capabilities is supplied; the GNN expressivity discussion summarizes prior work.

improvement.justification: v5 substantially strengthens evaluation of the central general-purpose representation claim. The strong hand-crafted comparator, additional optimization and SAT domains, third downstream task and codebook ablation address important gaps in v1's validation; explicit limitations also better qualify the foundational-model framing. The revised clustering account remains insufficiently reconciled: Section 4 reports 1,000 instances and 21 groups, Figure 3 lists 20 groups, and A.3 uses 1,050 instances. Despite this reporting weakness and sparse statistical-test details, the broader, more discriminating evidence provides a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FORGE research. Their text, equations, figures and tables support reliable comparison, including all nine appendix subsections in v5. v1 has no appendix.

after.justification: v5 retains original empirical evaluations and adds appendix experiments on static features, strIPlib, codebook size, embedding arithmetic, solver configuration and SAT transfer.

before.justification: Sections 4–5 report original clustering, integrality-gap prediction, solver-guidance and PS-Gurobi augmentation experiments.

results.title: FORGE: Foundational Optimization Representations from Graph Embeddings

C1.justification: v1 claims that no existing black-box approach supplies both global and local uncertainty and presents Geometric Suspicion as the first sampling-based black-box local method. v2 removes these broad priority claims and emphasizes a unified geometric alternative to existing graph-based approaches. This substantially narrows the claimed novelty, while retaining the overall detection and correction contributions.

C2.justification: v1 emphasizes deferral for high-dispersion batches and correction for intermediate hallucination rates. v2 substantially reframes the discussion around semantic distributions, limitations of single-vector representations, and confidently wrong models with little response diversity. It interprets Qwen3-8B/TriviaQA failure through the scarcity of correct alternatives and adds explanations connecting the component metrics to Degree and Eccentricity.

D1.justification: Appendix B.3 newly identifies the adapted UQ-NLG baseline code, the entailment variant using DeBERTa-Large, and an eigenvalue threshold of 0.7. Appendix C documents reproduction details for the new ablations, including PCA handling and archetype-count constraints. The original embedding model, optimization steps, and main hyperparameters are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use CLAMBER, TriviaQA, text-only ScienceQA, MedicalQA, and K-QA for the same ambiguity-detection and question-answering tasks. The new analyses reuse this coverage; sample-size sweeps and changes to filtered-subset reporting concern evaluation design rather than new datasets or tasks.

E2.justification: v1 Table 2 compares Geometric Suspicion selection with default greedy responses. v2 adds Degree and Eccentricity as competing local uncertainty methods across four QA benchmarks and four LLMs, substantially expanding direct comparative evaluation. The global comparators—Semantic Volume, Semantic Entropy, and p(true)—are retained.

E3.justification: v2 adds per-question AUARC evaluation and replaces Table 2's absolute hallucination rates and separate mid-valid subset reporting with ΔH/AUARC comparisons. Appendix C introduces controlled sample-count, PCA-dimension, and archetype-count sweeps, including subset-specific PCA refitting and fixed-basis truncation. The original dataset construction, default hyperparameters, and validation split remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendix C tests sensitivity to response count, embedding dimension, and archetype count for local and global uncertainty. Appendix E adds an analysis relating correction performance to available correct responses. Figure 3 replaces two illustrative cases, while the earlier mid-valid performance breakdown disappears. The existing Appendix D component-selection analysis is retained.

E5.justification: Table 2 changes its stated uncertainty convention from standard errors to standard deviations across runs. Appendix C introduces 30 within-question subset resamples for the sample-count analysis and explains aggregation; Figure 5 adds a quadratic fit with a 95% confidence interval. Both versions retain three main experimental runs, so this does not establish an increase in that run count.

E6.justification: v2 adds baseline and AUARC results, ablation results, and the corrective-potential relationship, while removing absolute hallucination rates and mid-valid results from Table 2. Some proposed-method values change: Qwen3-8b/MedicalQA ΔH is 7.4 percentage points in v1 and 8.0 in v2 under the revised scoring rule. Global Table 1 and the Appendix D Mann–Whitney results remain numerically unchanged.

M1.justification: The final Geometric Suspicion aggregation changes from summing component ranks in v1 Eq. 6 to combining empirical right-tail probabilities using Fisher's method in v2 Eqs. 7–8. This changes the response-ranking rule but is a localized refinement: the three component metrics, archetypal analysis, global volume score, and minimum-score selection remain.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution statements, local-method explanations, and discussion are substantially rewritten. The theorem moves from the appendix into the methodology, case-study interpretation moves into the results, and the proof and experimental appendices are reorganized. These alter the narrative structure beyond simply appending new experiments.

P2.justification: Table 2 is reorganized from dataset-grouped hallucination-rate breakdowns into model-grouped method comparisons. Figure 3 is redrawn using UMAP instead of t-SNE, with new annotations and two replacement examples. v2 also adds five ablation tables and Figure 5's regression plot; the earlier appendix tables are retained as Tables 8–9.

R1.justification: The new Semantic Space Confidence discussion positions the method against Semantic Density and the already-cited Lin et al. work's Degree/Eccentricity methods, substantially revising its relationship to prior local uncertainty research. Bhardwaj et al. and Han et al. are newly cited for long-form representation and factuality limitations. Lin's changed citation year does not represent a newly added work.

T1.justification: The entropy–volume theorem, assumptions, corollary, and proof retain their mathematical substance; moving the theorem into Section 3.3 is not new theory. v2 revises the formal suspicion-score definition and adds Appendix F's time and memory complexity arguments, O(Tnd'K) and O(nd'+nK+Kd').

improvement.justification: v2 addresses v1's lack of established local-method comparisons through Degree/Eccentricity evaluations, adds parameter-sensitivity and corrective-potential evidence, and narrows the first-of-kind novelty claim. These substantially strengthen validation and clarify the main contribution's scope. Removing absolute hallucination rates and the mid-valid breakdown loses useful detail, and no direct ablation establishes that Fisher fusion improves on rank summation, but the overall gain in evidential support and qualification is substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. All 17 pages of v1 and 20 pages of v2, including appendices, are readable, and the methods, equations, tables, and figures can be matched across revisions and relocations.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark experiments and adds local-method comparisons, parameter ablations, and an empirical analysis of corrective potential in Appendices C and E.

before.justification: Tables 1–2 report original hallucination-detection and response-selection experiments across four LLMs. Appendix D reports original analyses supporting the component metrics.

results.title: Geometric Uncertainty for Detecting and Correcting Hallucinations in LLMs

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add convergence-rate analysis as an explicit central contribution, linking rates to approximation fidelity and LDS stability. Case studies are now presented as validation of theoretical predictions, extending v1's central claims beyond unification and heuristic guidance.

C2.justification: v2 removes v1's broad dismissal of Jacobi for Markovian models and replaces Table 1's convergence-based ordering with approximation order. Interpretations now accommodate Jacobi's favorable GRU behavior and distinguish approximation accuracy from LDS stability. Appendix C.2 adds explicit local-basin conditions and limitations of the convergence bound.

D1.justification: Appendix E documents the new diagonal experiment's zero trajectory initialization and dimensions, the GRU diagnostic configuration, and the Langevin step-size settings. These are limited reproducibility additions. The existing JAX/Equinox implementation, H100 hardware disclosure, stochastic diagonal estimator, and code-access information are retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds the synthetic diagonal-LDS scenario x(t+1) = alpha x(t), testing contraction dynamics distinct from the retained permutation, GRU, and Langevin settings (Appendix C.4). The existing application coverage remains; the additional Langevin parameter sweep stays within that coverage.

E2.justification: Jacobi is newly evaluated alongside sequential evaluation, Picard, quasi-Newton, and Newton in all three main case studies (v1 Figures 1–3 versus v2 Figures 2–4). Previously it was discussed theoretically but omitted from these comparisons. This substantially expands the central solver comparisons.

E3.justification: Existing experiments retain the residual tolerance of 5e-4 and batch size 16. New protocols include a D=2, T=100 diagonal-LDS test measuring iterations to trajectory error below 1e-5, D=8/T=1000 GRU diagnostics, and Langevin step sizes 1e-5, 1e-4, and 1e-3 at D=2, 4, and 8.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled Jacobi-versus-Picard contraction analysis (Figure 7), diagnostics connecting GRU Jacobians and convergence factors to solver behavior (Figure 8), and Langevin step-size sensitivity (Figure 10). These substantially strengthen mechanism and sensitivity analysis. v1's mixture-component analysis is retained as v2 Figure 9.

E5.justification: Figure 8 newly shows cross-seed distributions of inverse-Jacobian norms and convergence factors, exposing variability beyond v1's median performance curves. The existing ten-seed reporting and five timed repetitions per seed remain unchanged; no increased replication, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported.

E6.justification: New results show Jacobi achieving GRU speedups while requiring approximately T iterations for S5 and Langevin problems (Figures 2–4). Figures 7, 8, and 10 add contraction trajectories, Jacobian diagnostics, and a Picard/Newton timing reversal as Langevin step size increases. These materially extend the reported findings.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and the intended Newton, diagonal quasi-Newton, Picard, and Jacobi procedures are retained. Hutchinson diagonal estimation and clip-ELK already appear in v1 and remain in v2. Expanded explanations and convergence analysis do not introduce a new algorithm.

P1.justification: The introduction, method explanations, case-study narratives, and related-work discussion are substantially rewritten. The former Section 2.5 summary is condensed, and the narrative becomes framework, convergence analysis, then empirical validation. Existing experimental and related-work appendices move to E and F, alongside new C and D; author and publication information also changes.

P2.justification: v2 adds a parallel-scan schematic and three substantial analytical figures (Figures 1, 7, 8, and 10). Table 1 gains a parallelization column, and the main experimental plots gain Jacobi curves, revised legends, captions, and some axis ranges. Existing appendix illustrations and the mixture-component plot are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands historical and theoretical positioning through Bellen and Zennaro, Gander and Vandewalle, Kelley, and Lu et al., among others. It acknowledges earlier parareal frameworks, narrows the LDS-unification novelty claim to the machine-learning community, and explicitly positions its convergence analysis as extending prior results.

T1.justification: v2 adds a Lipschitz-based error bound and proof (Proposition 3), a Jacobian-difference norm identity (Lemma 1), and an exact Picard inverse-norm formula and proof (Lemma 2), with supporting Appendices C–D. Existing group-word and R-convergence propositions are retained and renumbered. The Picard summation's lower index is also corrected from 1 to 0.

improvement.justification: v1's method-selection advice was largely heuristic and broadly dismissed Jacobi without evaluating it. v2 adds an explicit convergence bound with limitations, direct comparisons correcting that guidance, and diagnostic and sensitivity experiments supporting more conditional recommendations. These changes substantially improve scientific support and practical reliability, although the bounds remain conservative and do not establish exact wall-clock rankings.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LDS framework and core case studies. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original simulation results and adds Jacobi comparisons, a diagonal-LDS simulation, GRU Jacobian diagnostics, and Langevin step-size experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulations measuring convergence iterations and wall-clock time for S5 word problems, randomly initialized GRUs, and Gaussian-mixture Langevin dynamics, including an appendix experiment varying mixture components.

results.title: A Unifying Framework for Parallelizing Sequential Models with Linear Dynamical Systems
