E6.justification: v3 adds the empirical results in Figures 7–8 and Table 2. These include target-dependent reversals between biased and unbiased weighting. Table 2 reports average Pass@256 of 74.4 for Skew-R, 73.3 for Pass@K-mixed and 72.5 for GRPO, while average Pass@1 favors GRPO. v1 has no corresponding performance results.

M1.justification: The existing REINFORCEK, RLOOK, GRPOK, mixed, Skew-R and entropy-shaped updates are retained. Section 5.3 additionally instantiates the power-surrogate family F(u)=u^q/q, producing advantage scaling by rho_hat^(q-1) and adjustable emphasis on hard or easy examples.

P1.justification: v3 substantially revises the introductory and forward-engineering exposition, adds a roadmap and notation summary, and reorganizes practical considerations. The detailed biased-scaling discussion moves to Appendix C.3, while related work becomes a standalone section. Numerous retained passages are condensed or clarified.

P2.justification: v3 adds a framework schematic, unified algorithm table, two empirical figures and a benchmark-results table. All five original analytical plots remain; notably, v1 Figure 4 moves to Appendix C.3 as Figure 6. Figure sizing, captions and the opening-page layout also change.

R1.justification: The new Related Work section acknowledges Davis and Recht's independent surrogate-objective analysis and connects the framework to conditional stochastic optimization, explicitly relating its update to Hu et al.'s biased stochastic-gradient method. This substantively expands research positioning alongside new experimental-resource citations.

T1.justification: v3 adds the general weighted-gradient equivalence result and proof in Section 5.3, the PPO-versus-surrogate derivation in Appendix A, and the RLOOK unbiasedness proof in Appendix B.3. It also corrects algebraic factors in the arcsine identity and Skew-R/incomplete-beta derivations from v1 Appendices B–C.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the central theoretical argument through a general equivalence result, an unbiasedness proof and corrections to earlier algebra. New controlled experiments, implementation details and clearer research positioning further support the framework. The experiments remain preliminary and lack uncertainty estimates; the Table 2 discussion also overstates Skew-R at K=128, where it scores 67.9 versus Pass@K-mixed's 68.7. These limitations temper the empirical conclusions but do not outweigh the theoretical and explanatory gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures and appendices are readable, allowing retained material to be matched across revisions and relocations.

after.justification: Appendix D reports original model-training experiments on synthetic arithmetic and real mathematical reasoning tasks, with outcomes in Figures 7–8 and Table 2.

before.justification: v1 contains derivations, proofs and plots of analytically defined gradient weights and surrogate functions. It reports no original experimental, simulation or data-analysis outcomes, including in its appendices.

results.title: Advantage Shaping as Surrogate Reward Maximization: Unifying Pass@K Policy Gradients

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: reconstructing useful thinking-trace proxies, improving open-model raters through SFT, and refining codebooks to improve human alignment and cross-model agreement. The added experiments support these retained claims.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly qualifies the shared-bias explanation for reduced inter-rater agreement as a hypothesis rather than asserting bias reduction. It also adds interpretations about the necessity of traces, architecture generalization, generalist generators, and data efficiency. The substantive limitations and future directions in Section 5 remain unchanged.

D1.justification: The supplied SFT hyperparameters, refinement prompts, and dataset-processing details are retained. Codebook access instructions change from the GitHub repository in v1 Appendix D to an anonymous repository's codebook directory in v2 Appendix E, while the main GitHub reference remains. This establishes changed access instructions, not verified resource availability.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same five datasets and eight rating dimensions: HANNA stories, student essays, SummEval summaries, Chinese-to-English WMT translations, and HelpSteer2 responses. The additions vary models and trace budgets within this existing coverage.

E2.justification: V2 Table 4 adds a ratings-only SFT comparator, addressing an important alternative to trace-augmented training absent from v1. Appendix Tables 9–10 also add GPT-4o-generated trace variants alongside the existing DeepSeek and gpt-oss variants in both application comparisons.

E3.justification: V2 substantially expands experimental conditions through a DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B base model, ratings-only training, GPT-4o trace generation, sampling coverage at k values from 1 to 32, and four instruction/rubric trace-budget combinations. The original filtering, metrics, early stopping, LoRA settings, and main k=16 configuration remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds an ablation testing whether traces contribute beyond SFT alone (Table 4), sampling-coverage analysis (Figure 5), and trace-quantity sensitivity analysis (Table 8). Appendix A additionally examines architecture generalization and the need for specialized reasoning generators. The original refinement-component and post hoc ablations remain as Tables 5–6.

E5.justification: Section 3.3 retains the same paired t-tests, one-sided bootstrap tests, and significance reporting. V2 adds no run or seed counts, confidence intervals, or new uncertainty-estimation procedures; additional significance-marked results follow the existing practice.

E6.justification: All numerical entries and significance markers in v1 Tables 1–5 remain in v2 Tables 1–3 and 5–6 after matching metric order. Substantial new results include ratings-only SFT averaging tau=0.191 versus 0.281 with DeepSeek traces, Llama-based SFT increasing average tau from 0.151 to 0.216, and GPT-4o trace variants averaging 0.237 for SFT and 0.339 for codebook refinement. Figure 5 and Table 8 add utilization and sensitivity findings.

M1.justification: The rejection-sampling procedure, first-matching-trace selection, SFT objective, and two-stage instruction/rubric refinement remain unchanged. The post hoc explanation alternative already appears in v1. Additional model evaluations do not document a new algorithmic procedure.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main section sequence are retained. V2 makes localized explanatory edits, inserts a new SFT-ablation paragraph and an additional-results appendix, adds acknowledgments, and removes the placeholder CCS text. Existing appendix content moves from A–D to B–E without substantial rewriting.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the two-column draft layout with a single-column publication layout, redraws Figure 3 with concrete examples, adds the sampling plot and five tables, and reorders metric columns. New Figure 6 visualizes the unchanged Table 3 results. Figures, codebook examples, and prompt boxes are extensively resized and relocated.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds reasoning-distillation references covering medical questions, software engineering, finance, cybersecurity, and general-purpose trace datasets such as Synthetic-1 and OpenThoughts. This locally broadens the literature discussion while retaining the same positioning of codebook refinement as the distinctive second application.

T1.justification: The definitions of latent and reconstructed traces, label-matching filter, augmented dataset, and SFT loss in Equation 1 are mathematically unchanged. Neither version contains additional theorems, proofs, or substantive derivations absent from the other.

improvement.justification: The added ratings-only SFT control addresses an important missing comparison in v1, substantially strengthening evidence that thinking traces contribute beyond generic fine-tuning. Architecture, generator, and sensitivity experiments further strengthen validation while preserving the original results. Some new appendix wording is imprecise: Table 8 shows a nonmonotonic trace-quantity trend, and Table 9 evaluates GPT-4o-generated traces in a Qwen-based rater despite wording suggesting GPT-4o itself is fine-tuned. These limitations temper individual interpretations but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in experimental support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research framework and retain matching methods, datasets, and experiments. All pages, including appendices, are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and added analyses.

after.justification: The original empirical results remain, supplemented by a ratings-only training control, additional model evaluations, and sampling and trace-quantity analyses.

before.justification: Sections 4.3–4.5 and Tables 1–5 report original fine-tuning, codebook-refinement, inter-rater agreement, and ablation results.

results.title: Through the Judge's Eyes: Inferred Thinking Traces Improve Reliability of LLM Raters

C1.justification: The scientific claims in the abstract, contribution bullets and conclusion retain their scope: broad zero-shot imputation evaluation, covariate integration, and the TabPFN-TS accuracy versus MoTM efficiency trade-off. New experiments support these retained contributions.

C2.justification: V2 corrects the Figure 2 interpretation by explicitly identifying MoTM's third-place average rank and lack of significant difference from SAITS. It also adds substantive explanations of feature sensitivity, harmful covariates under sparse sampling, incomplete-covariate limitations and compute-dependent deployment choices.

D1.justification: V2 adds a paper-specific code-availability link, NuwaTS implementation access and its 96-step workaround, explicit ablation configurations, and selected SAITS hyperparameters. Existing pretrained-model sources, hardware disclosures and main training settings are retained.

E1.justification: The 33 main univariate datasets, four daily/weekly datasets and three covariate datasets are retained. Figure 12 adds six-hourly-to-hourly reconstruction examples on Wind-France and PV-France, introducing a regular sparse-input scenario. Incomplete or asynchronous covariates are discussed but not evaluated.

E2.justification: V2 substantially expands the reported comparisons through Table 3: MOMENT's qualitative exclusion rationale becomes an explicit quantitative comparison, alongside newly included NuwaTS and cubic spline interpolation on eleven datasets. The original main-benchmark comparator set remains unchanged.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce five temporal-encoding configurations and a SAITS grid over model widths 128/256/512 and one to four layers, selected by validation MAE across four masking scenarios. V2 also documents NuwaTS evaluation using 96-step segments. These are additional protocols; the original benchmark settings remain intact.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained missingness and sampling-rate analyses, Appendix D tests dependence on temporal features, Appendix F examines SAITS tuning and accuracy–training-time sensitivity, and Figure 12 investigates sparse-grid reconstruction with covariates. These address substantial new robustness and methodological questions.

E5.justification: V2 adds Mean (Std) summaries to existing MAE, WQL and low-frequency results, plus shaded bands in Figure 13. These expand statistical reporting, but neither repeated-run counts nor seeds are supplied, and the bands' construction is unspecified.

E6.justification: Original per-dataset benchmark scores are unchanged, but v2 adds extensive competitor, feature-ablation, tuned-SAITS and sparse-grid results. Aggregate entries also change: low-frequency BRITS and Linear means move from 0.525 and 0.510 to 0.531 and 0.512 respectively, despite unchanged underlying rows (v1 Table 8; v2 Table 9).

M1.justification: The core TabPFNv2-based TabPFN-TS and pretrained-INR/ridge MoTM procedures remain unchanged. Alternative encodings are ablation controls; incomplete-covariate handling is discussed as possible extensions rather than changes to the evaluated main pipeline.

P1.justification: V2 revises the main-results discussion, removes redundant model descriptions from Appendix A.3, adds appendix subdivisions and acknowledgements, and updates author/publication information. Most existing prose and the main narrative structure remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds four substantive tables covering additional baselines, feature ablations and SAITS tuning, plus two figures for sparse-grid examples and tuning sensitivity. Existing tables gain statistical summary rows, and figures and tables are relocated within the revised layout.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations concerning time-index modeling, ImputeINR, Imputeformer, temporal feature engineering, NuwaTS and TabPFN 2.5. It replaces the critical-difference-diagram citation with Demšar (2006). These broaden context without redefining the central novelty claim.

T1.justification: Appendix D.1 adds explicit mathematical definitions of alternative temporal feature maps for the ablation, including daily-only, index-only and random-period encodings. The original feature map and WQL equations remain unchanged; no theorem, proof or theoretical guarantee is added.

improvement.justification: Feature ablations and validation-selected SAITS tuning address important missing controls in v1, while additional competitors and covariate failure examples strengthen the benchmark's evidential support and applicability boundaries. Some added summaries require reconciliation, including TimeMixer++ at 0.677 in Table 6 versus 0.681 in Figure 1. These reporting problems limit precision but do not outweigh the substantial gains from testing previously unexamined explanations for the headline results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TabPFN-TS and MoTM imputation benchmark. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, temporal-feature ablations, sparse-grid examples and SAITS tuning experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original imputation benchmarks, probabilistic predictions, covariate experiments and runtime comparisons, including daily/weekly evaluations in Appendix C.

results.title: Are Time-Indexed Foundation Models the Future of Time Series Imputation?

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion narrow the central claim from merging methods generally failing to transfer to LLMs to difficulty improving general capabilities through heterogeneous, potentially conflicting checkpoints. TIES is recast from catastrophic degradation to limited gains under tuning. Task Arithmetic remains the preferred approach.

C2.justification: New explanations attribute Task Arithmetic’s stability to normalized averaging and TIES’s sensitivity to trimming and sign consensus limiting cancellation. Section 5 interprets the domain controls as evidence about heterogeneity, while Section 3.1 explicitly frames Model Stock’s use as a stress test beyond its intended setting. These materially revise mechanisms and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v1’s promised code release becomes a repository link in v2. Appendices C and F newly disclose normalization, float16 evaluation, automatic batching, absence of chat templates, and exact few-shot counts. Appendix E supplies specialist checkpoint identifiers and task lists. These materially improve documentation without establishing that newly disclosed inference settings changed.

E1.justification: Appendix E adds a distinct evaluation scenario using curated medical and mathematical specialists for Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B. It tests preservation of domain capabilities through within-domain and joint-domain merging. The original checkpoint pools and sixteen-benchmark coverage remain; the new task suites draw on subsets of existing benchmarks.

E2.justification: Matched comparisons retain Task Arithmetic, TIES-Merging, Model Stock, TSV-Merge, Iso-C, TA+SB, and TIES+SB. Appendix E reuses these methods with base-model and individual-expert references. Newly cited works do not become additional evaluated merging algorithms.

E3.justification: New protocols include a joint TIES density–scaling grid, normalization-disabled Task Arithmetic controls, extension of the normalized scaling sweep to λ=10, and three-expert domain merges versus six-expert joint merges. Revised main TIES/TIES+SB evaluations specify λ=0.1; v1 did not separately state their scaling coefficient.

E4.justification: Appendices C–E substantially expand tests of why merging succeeds or fails: normalization controls, scaling-versus-update-norm analyses, global and layerwise task-vector alignment, and structured domain-mixing comparisons. The original density and boosting-threshold sweeps are retained as Figures 17 and 18, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions use fifteen matched checkpoint subsets at intermediate merge sizes, one all-twelve merge, and standard deviations across sampled subsets. No new seed-reporting practice, confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-run uncertainty procedure is introduced.

E6.justification: TIES and TIES+SB results are substantially replaced. At n=12, the average success-rate/reported-improvement entries change from 0/-4.32 to 75/+0.13 in Table 1 and from 0/-8.67 to 100/+0.36 in Table 3. These are revised evaluations, not established gains under identical settings. Appendices C–E also add normalization, alignment, and domain-retention findings.

M1.justification: The evaluated merging algorithms and their principal procedures remain unchanged. Appendix C documents normalization as an existing configuration and tests normalization/scaling variants; it does not introduce a new merging algorithm or establish a change to the original method implementation.

P1.justification: The abstract and much of the introduction are rewritten, research questions are reformulated, and results, discussion, and conclusion narratives are revised around in-the-wild merging. Appendix C becomes a structured explanation with four subsections, and new appendices and a broader-impact statement extend the document structure.

P2.justification: v2 adds normalization and joint-sensitivity plots, global and layerwise alignment heatmaps, domain-comparison bar charts, and Tables 4–6. Figure 11 gains an extended scaling axis; retained displays are resized or relocated, and Table 2’s caption is expanded. Earlier density and boosting figures remain under new numbering.

R1.justification: v2 removes the assertion that merging methods had not been evaluated on LLMs and distinguishes its general-capability objective from prior domain-specialist retention studies. New references include He et al.’s MergeBench, Cohere et al.’s Command A, and Roth et al. This substantially changes positioning; publication updates to retained references are bibliographic changes only.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(11) are retained. Equation (12) spells out the weighted-average normalization that v2 says was already enabled. This implementation explanation and the qualitative cancellation arguments do not introduce a substantive theoretical derivation, formal assumption, theorem, or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central comparison by investigating scaling and normalization behind the earlier TIES failures, reporting tuned results, and narrowing broad LLM-failure claims to heterogeneous merging. Domain controls and explicit implementation/evaluation details improve evidential support and reproducibility. Section 5 still overstates causal certainty when attributing failures specifically to heterogeneity, but the correction of the central comparison and its interpretation provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same model-merging study. The original experiments, equations, checkpoint lists, and appendix figures can be matched despite retitling and substantial additions. Text extraction and visual inspection support reliable comparison, including the appendices.

after.justification: v2 reports retained and revised benchmark results, plus new normalization controls, task-vector alignment measurements, and domain-specific merging experiments in Appendices C–E.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations across four base models and sixteen benchmarks, including merge-size comparisons, taskwise results, and hyperparameter ablations in Tables 1–3 and Appendices B–C.

results.title: A Systematic Study of In-the-Wild Model Merging for Large Language Models

C1.justification: The alignment and causal-swap claims remain, but v2's abstract and conclusion add multi-hop applicability and a mechanistic account of grokking. Section 6.3 claims the first SAE-based step-wise binding probe of multi-hop grokking. The conclusion replaces v1's broad world-model, agent, and robotics framing with relation completion and representation-learning dynamics.

C2.justification: v2 introduces the interpretation that stable concept binding precedes observable generalization, and uses ablations to distinguish the roles of supervision, decorrelation, and pretraining. Its limitations replace v1's single-hop restriction with explicit boundaries concerning GPT-2 scale, synthetic templates, small ontologies, indirect-question failures, and uncertain transfer to symbolic-ID settings.

D1.justification: v2 adds Code & Data access information, the full paraphrase-generation prompt, two-hop construction and training details, hyperparameter-selection disclosures, and the 1,000-example swap sample size. However, it removes earlier specifics about decoder initialization and value-head dimensions. The PDFs establish the added resource pointers, not their external availability.

E1.justification: v2 adds two-hop relation composition over 20 relations and 60 entities, extending v1's six-relation biography recall to intermediate-entity prediction and sequential reasoning. Appendix A.4 also reports an exploratory test of indirect LLM-generated paraphrases, excluded from the main evaluation. The reported biography birth-city inventory expands from 8 to 50 cities.

E2.justification: The traditional unsupervised SAE comparator is retained. v2 additionally evaluates supervised linear-probe steering in the two-hop comparison in Figure 8. G-SAE is discussed as related work but is not an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: Reported single-hop settings change substantially: the free-feature bank decreases from 100,000 to 10,000, SAE stage lengths change from 50/100 to 100/500 epochs, and questions are reassigned between training and held-out templates. v2 also introduces a 4,000/4,000 two-hop split and configuration-specific best-alpha ablation comparisons. These are reported protocol changes; the PDFs do not establish that retained results were rerun under every revised setting.

E4.justification: v2 adds loss-component ablations testing alignment, orthogonality, and value supervision, plus a Stage-1 ablation testing reconstruction, sparsity, and binding quality (Tables 6–7). Section 6.3 and Appendix I add checkpoint-based analyses of binding and delayed generalization. Appendix A.4 adds qualitative paraphrase stress testing. The repeated Stage-1 discussion in Appendices G and H describes one analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports explicit repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or between-run uncertainty estimates. v2's newly stated averaging over 1,000 swap examples is sample-size disclosure, not a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds 100% binding at both two-hop steps, a two-hop swap peak of about 8%, and ablation and grokking results. Table 6 reports swap success of 0.847 for the full model, 0.053 without alignment, and 0.046 without orthogonality, each at its selected alpha. The fragmentation/concentration curves are revised, failed-swap category retention is corrected from 74.7% to 75.3%, and v1's separate 91.2% value-head accuracy report disappears. These are not uniformly comparable before-and-after performance gains.

M1.justification: The frozen-backbone SAE, dedicated concept slots, auxiliary value heads, and core objectives remain. v2 adds step-wise supervision for two-hop outputs: aligning r1 when predicting the intermediate entity and r2 when predicting the final entity. This is a limited procedural adaptation. Removing the independence term from the displayed total loss does not establish its removal from the implemented method, since v1 already skipped it at its reported scale.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes and rewrites the narrative: objectives and training move into Section 3, experimental setup becomes part of Section 4, results separate into single-hop and two-hop sections, and qualitative swaps move to Appendix F. The conclusion and limitations are rewritten, an ethics statement is added, and author and title-page text changes.

P2.justification: v2 revises the overview graphic, redraws the fragmentation/concentration plots, compresses retained plots into smaller panels, and restructures the template table into training/held-out columns. It adds two-hop diagrams, comparison curves, binding heatmaps, grokking plots, and ablation tables. The original qualitative swap table and schematic are relocated to Appendix F rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: v2 substantively expands positioning around supervised SAEs and grokking: it contrasts AlignSAE with concurrent G-SAE and distinguishes its step-wise analysis from other SAE studies of emergence. It also adds dataset attribution to Allen-Zhu and Li and Du et al., and connections to grokked-transformer research. Several earlier general interpretability and steering references are removed.

T1.justification: v2 revises the mathematical fragmentation/concentration definition to use concept-slot activations rather than the full latent vector. Appendix D.3 also changes the formal swap-success criterion from matching relation labels to matching the target relation's gold answer value, consistent with the intended main-text evaluation. No theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: The component and curriculum ablations provide substantial evidence for design choices that v1 largely asserted, while the supervised comparator strengthens the control evaluation. Two-hop experiments directly address v1's stated single-hop limitation, and clearer scope and reproducibility information improve assessment. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses: two-hop swap success peaks at only about 8%, the grokking mechanism remains interpretive, and Appendix D.1 still describes latent overwriting while Section 4.4 and Appendix D.3 specify additive steering.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AlignSAE and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The retained material can be matched reliably despite substantial reorganization and added experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains original single-hop experiments and adds two-hop binding and steering results, component and curriculum ablations, and training-dynamics analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original GPT-2 biography experiments, including layer-wise concept binding, comparisons with an unsupervised SAE, swap interventions, and error analyses.

results.title: AlignSAE: Concept-Aligned Sparse Autoencoders

C1.justification: The central contribution is redefined from combining trajectory packing with memory retrieval to dynamically controlling compression through spatial relevance. V2's conclusion explicitly locates the contribution in compression-rate allocation rather than spatial scoring itself. Efficiency claims are also qualified: v1's conclusion describes retention without increased computational cost, whereas v2's abstract reports 16% diffusion-inference overhead plus additional selection cost.

C2.justification: V2 replaces v1's simulator-only limitation, which conflicted with its RECON experiment, with specific limitations involving occlusion, camera-pose availability, and localization errors. Appendix E adds an interpretation linking excessive compression to information loss. Section 6.5 also qualifies computational efficiency through candidate-dependent selection costs, replacing the earlier emphasis on marginal overhead and reduced memory.

D1.justification: V2 fills substantial documentation gaps through Appendices B–D: metric implementations, training/test trajectory counts, RECON eligibility, preprocessing, VAE/backbone configuration, optimizer settings, training and fine-tuning budgets, and H100 hardware. Section 4.2 also specifies overlap sampling and scoring weights. These are largely newly disclosed details; v1's omissions do not establish that all underlying settings changed.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Minecraft LoopNav ABA/ABCA tasks at navigation ranges 5, 15, 30, and 50, plus real-world RECON navigation. Revised history lengths and rollout analyses change procedures within this retained coverage; RECON was already evaluated in v1 Section 6.4.

E2.justification: Oasis, Mineworld, DIAMOND, and NWM remain the main comparators, and packing-only continues as Nearest Frame Packing. V2 adds the retrieval-only control to the rollout curves and replaces NWM with packing/retrieval variants in Figure 3. Its retrieval control uses four FoV-ranked frames, representing WorldMem/Context-as-Memory mechanisms within the shared backbone. The RECON comparison drops Packing only (v1 Table 3; v2 Table 4).

E3.justification: V2 equalizes component-ablation context budgets at four frames, changes packed configurations from 19 to 22 visible frames, and changes RECON's initial history from 20 to 80 frames. It extends plotted rollout windows, adds FVD to RECON and component comparisons, and adds pooled evaluation over 144 LoopNav rollouts. Table 1 also revises Mineworld's reported context from 15 to 32 and DIAMOND/NWM from 4 to 32, while retaining their means; this does not establish reruns.

E4.justification: Beyond revising the existing packing/retrieval ablations and extending rollout curves, v2 adds camera-pose-embedding removal and temporal/spatiotemporal compression studies (Appendix E). It also measures selection runtime against candidate count (Table 6) and checks whether FVD rankings persist when all 144 trajectories are pooled (Appendix G). These substantially broaden the mechanisms and limitations tested.

E5.justification: V1 reports point estimates. V2 systematically adds means and standard deviations across evaluation trajectories for SSIM, LPIPS, PSNR, and DreamSim in the main comparisons and ablations, while reporting FVD as a single set-level distance. This substantially expands variability reporting, but neither PDF establishes repeated-training-run counts or uncertainty across seeds.

E6.justification: WorldPack results are extensively replaced: Table 1's ABCA-5 SSIM changes from 0.35 to 0.44, whereas ABA-15 SSIM changes from 0.48 to 0.38, under revised method/context settings. Tables 2 and the RECON table also change, and new ablations and pooled FVD results are added, including WorldPack's 608 versus baseline 872 in Table 13. Efficiency findings change from reduced memory usage to approximately 12% greater usage; these are revised-configuration results, not same-setting gains or losses.

M1.justification: V1 combines recency-oriented packing with eight retrieved frames selected using a position/orientation score. V2 replaces this with Monte Carlo field-of-view overlap and a temporal penalty, using spatial rankings to allocate compression rates, including the uncompressed slots. The practical configuration changes from 19 frames in a 2.84-frame-equivalent context to 22 frames in a four-frame context (Section 4).

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, method narrative, ablation discussion, limitations, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Separate retrieval and packing subsections become a unified spatially-aware-memory section. The appendix is reorganized into Sections A–G, and the LLM-use disclosure moves there from the main text. These are substantial narrative and structural revisions.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn around geometric selection and compression, Algorithm 1 is added, and Figure 3 uses new rollout examples and comparator rows. The ABA-5 bar-chart comparison becomes Table 3; rollout plots change windows, axes, and legends. Numerous training, ablation, and evaluation tables are added, alongside broader typography and page-layout changes.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands related work and positions WorldPack as unifying FramePack-style compression with WorldMem/Context-as-Memory retrieval, explicitly attributing spatial scoring to prior work. It adds discussion and citations concerning adaptive tokenization, newer world models, drift correction, and pose estimation. V1's positioning primarily emphasized transferring frame compression into world modeling.

T1.justification: The core mathematical definitions change substantially. V1 Equations 4–9 define a Gaussian-weighted position/direction score without explicit FoV; v2 Equations 6–7 define normalized viewing-frustum intersection volume and a temporal penalty. The separate recent/retrieved-frame allocation in v1 Equations 10–11 becomes spatial-priority allocation in v2 Equations 4–5. The diffusion preliminaries and CDiT complexity argument remain unchanged; neither version supplies theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves reproducibility and support for the proposed mechanism. Algorithm 1 and Appendices B–D address major documentation gaps, while equal-context-budget component comparisons, new ablations, trajectory variability reporting, and pooled FVD strengthen experimental interpretation. Computational costs and applicability limitations are more explicit. RECON loses its packing-only control, and changed settings prevent interpreting revised scores as direct performance gains, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the substantial gains in transparency and evidential support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe WorldPack by the same authors, retaining the CDiT backbone and LoopNav/RECON evaluations despite substantial revisions. All pages, equations, figures, tables, and appendices were readable and support comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports revised WorldPack experiments and original pose-embedding, compression, runtime-scaling, and pooled-FVD analyses in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original WorldPack results on LoopNav and RECON, component ablations, rollout analyses, and computational measurements. These extend beyond the baseline results attributed to prior work.

results.title: WorldPack: Dynamic Frame Compression for Long-context Video World Modeling

C1.justification: The central claims remain specialized variance reduction for UDA, conditional optimality of the MMD stratification objective, and improved discrepancy estimation and target accuracy. Changing three benchmarks to four expands supporting evidence without redefining the core contribution.

C2.justification: v1 calls the post-training discrepancy analysis inconclusive and suggests a noise-floor explanation. v2 interprets the identical appendix results as indicating optimization stabilization rather than deeper minima. It also adds interpretations concerning T robustness, computational overhead, and diminishing kernel-clustering benefits at larger batches. Section 4 limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 newly supplies wall-clock training times and their aggregation procedure in Table 3, and revises the documented batch-size search range. Architecture, optimizer, kernel, training budget, and algorithmic trial settings remain documented as before; no new code or data access instructions appear.

E1.justification: Section 3 adds Office-Home: 65-category object classification across Art, Clipart, Product, and Real World images, evaluated over 12 transfers. This substantially extends task and visual-domain coverage beyond the retained medical, acoustic, and dog-breed benchmarks.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds CDAN + SDAT and CDAN + ELS while removing AFN. The other UDA baselines and the main sampling comparators remain, making this a targeted revision of the comparison set.

E3.justification: Section 3 changes the batch-size search from k drawn as 2^Uniform(3,5.5) to 2^Uniform(3,7). Figure 4 extends testing from k = 40 to 256. New protocols evaluate final accuracy across five T values and aggregate wall-clock times across splits, hyperparameters, repeats, and both adaptation losses.

E4.justification: The component ablation now covers substantially larger batches. New Table 4 tests whether reclustering frequency affects final accuracy, supplementing the retained variance-trajectory analysis. New Table 3 compares computational costs across samplers and datasets. These additions materially expand practical robustness and efficiency analysis.

E5.justification: Section 3 changes the stated number of seeded experimental repetitions from three to five. Both versions describe varying hyperparameter, initialization, and split seeds and report accuracy means with standard errors; no new significance-testing framework is introduced.

E6.justification: Accuracy results are extensively updated under revised settings: MMD + VaRDASS changes from 90.4±1.5 to 92.0±0.5 on Humpbacks and from 72.4±2.2 to 71.6±2.2 on Spawrious. These are not identical-setting performance changes. Office-Home, runtime, T-sensitivity, and baseline-by-split results are added. Appendix C omits the previous splitwise ERM sampler ablations; Appendix D values remain identical.

M1.justification: The MMD/CORAL stratification objectives, dynamically weighted kernel clustering, greedy assignment algorithm, and periodic reclustering procedure remain unchanged. The default T = 100 is relocated into the experimental settings, not replaced.

P1.justification: Experimental discussion receives localized revisions, Section 5.1 adds a short follow-up paragraph, and publication and review information is added. The principal section order, appendix organization, and most method and theory prose are retained.

P2.justification: Empirical displays are substantially reorganized: Tables 1–2 expand, runtime and T-sensitivity tables are added, and Figure 4 receives extended axes and revised styling. Appendix C changes from stacked split blocks to method-by-split matrices and adds Office-Home. The other figures and Appendix D table retain their content.

R1.justification: References are added for SDAT, ELS, Office-Home, Napoli and White's 2024 data-balancing work, and their 2026 follow-up; the AFN reference is removed. Brief discussion connects diverse sampling to balancing and introduces the follow-up. The existing 2024 citation becomes 2024b without changing the cited work.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, assumptions, Lemma 1, Theorems 1–4, and derivations are unchanged. Appendices A and B retain the same proofs and equations despite moving to later pages.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens practical evaluation by supplying previously missing runtime measurements and final-accuracy sensitivity to reclustering frequency (Tables 3–4). Broader task coverage, revised adversarial comparisons, and additional repetitions strengthen empirical validation. These gains outweigh the less cautious mechanism interpretation of unchanged Appendix D results, which does not itself establish that trajectory stabilization causes the accuracy benefits.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VaRDASS and contain readable main text, figures, tables, algorithms, equations, and Appendices A–D. Relocated and reformatted material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on four datasets, alongside variance simulations, runtime measurements, reclustering sensitivity results, and appendix breakdowns.

before.justification: v1 reports original variance simulations, algorithm comparisons, and adaptation experiments on Camelyon17, Humpbacks, and Spawrious, including appendix results.

results.title: Variance Matters: Improving Domain Adaptation via Stratified Sampling

C1.justification: v1 presents the framework as learning formally safe, safety-certified controllers. v2 restricts the invariance guarantee to an idealized setting without approximation errors and explicitly states that the learned barrier is not formally verified. This materially narrows the central safety claim while retaining the offline-learning and empirical-performance contributions.

C2.justification: v2 explains how function approximation, finite data, and learned dynamics can invalidate closed-loop guarantees, and discusses relaxing safety constraints for QP feasibility. It also qualifies v1's favorable interpretation of tau approaching one: optimistic stochastic outcomes can make extreme expectiles brittle, with the new MuJoCo evidence supporting tau=0.9.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly identifies tau=0.9 for main experiments, documents the boat dynamics and constraints, and names implementation sources for the additional baselines. Conversely, Table 11 removes v1 Table 8's shared Adam, learning-rate 10^-3, and ReLU specification. Existing hardware and architecture details are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix D adds boat navigation with state-dependent river drift, static obstacles, and bounded actuation. AGV collision avoidance and all five existing MuJoCo velocity-constrained tasks remain, making this a limited extension of domain coverage.

E2.justification: The new boat comparison in Table 9 evaluates CPQ, WSAC, CDT, and C2IQL alongside several retained competitors. These four additional methods substantially broaden the evaluated comparator set; the original AGV and MuJoCo comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: New protocols sweep four expectile values on three MuJoCo tasks and evaluate dynamics models trained for 50% and 25% of the standard budget, measuring prediction error on sampled state-action pairs. Existing dataset sizes, architectures, rollout metrics, and main evaluation sample counts are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained AGV ablations, v2 adds learned-barrier geometry across six expectiles, reward/cost sensitivity to expectiles on MuJoCo, and direct dynamics-underfitting tests with measured prediction errors. These substantially strengthen analysis of the central learning mechanism and sensitivity to model inaccuracies, previously investigated mainly through action noise.

E5.justification: Existing five-seed evaluations, reported uncertainties, standard-error description, and rollout percentile bands are retained. The boat comparison follows the existing five-seed practice; no new uncertainty estimator, significance test, or increased repeated-run count is reported.

E6.justification: Existing main results and Tables 1–6 are unchanged, but substantial new findings appear. Table 7 favors tau=0.9 over 0.99 on three MuJoCo tasks; Table 8 reports 96.32% safety with quarter-trained dynamics; Table 9 reports boat safety of 97.56±0.13% versus 88.43±0.59% for the strongest listed baseline, BC+NCBF. These are additional results, not demonstrated improvements over v1 under identical settings.

M1.justification: Equations 9–10 and Algorithm 1 replace separate behavior-barrier training and explicit action-support gathering with direct expectile updates using a target bootstrapped from B_theta at the observed next state. Appendix A.3 also introduces a slack-penalized QP. These substantially revise the specified training and control procedures; the PDFs do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

P1.justification: There are targeted rewrites of the abstract, positioning, methodology, and limitations, plus new appendix subsections and a boat appendix that shifts Experimental Details from D to E. Affiliations and publication information change, but most prose and the overall narrative structure are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds the six-panel expectile visualization and Tables 7–9. The environment illustration moves from main-text Figure 2 to appendix Figure 5, while existing plots and tables are retained and reflowed. Publication headers and the shortened Algorithm 1 alter presentation without a comprehensive redesign.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for WSAC, C2IQL, and conformal-prediction-based verification. Section 2.3 refines positioning around offline policy learning and using learned dynamics only during inference. The broader related-work survey remains largely unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical target/loss definitions in Equations 9–10 are revised, and Equation 22 introduces a formally specified relaxed QP. The finite-difference lemma and proof and the expectile definitions in Appendices A.1–A.2 are retained; no new learned-controller certification theorem is supplied.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses a central credibility problem: v1's formally safe-controller framing becomes an explicit distinction between idealized invariance and empirical safety of an unverified learned controller. The revised training specification and targeted expectile and model-fidelity experiments substantially improve assessment of the method's behavior and limitations. Additional boat comparisons strengthen empirical support. Missing slack-penalty settings and removed baseline optimization details leave reproducibility gaps, but these do not outweigh the substantial gains in claim accuracy and validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same V-OCBF study. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and equations, tables, and figures can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds boat-navigation comparisons, MuJoCo expectile experiments, and dynamics-model accuracy analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original AGV and five MuJoCo simulation evaluations, controller comparisons, and network-size, disturbance, and expectile ablations.

results.title: V-OCBF: Learning Safety Filters from Offline Data via Value-Guided Offline Control Barrier Functions

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retreat from prominent claims about benefiting from partially labeled datasets, and the conclusion explicitly leaves experimental validation of that benefit to future work. Resource-efficiency wording is also softened. The central contributions of discrete, end-to-end selection and joint multi-task prediction remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive qualifications about generalization to unseen cells rather than unseen patients, patient-specific confounding, sparse-panel task tradeoffs and the need for shared biological structure. It acknowledges that multi-task learning is not always optimal and partial-label benefits remain untested. New stability discussions interpret variable gene identities through functional redundancy and stabilization of a core panel.

D1.justification: New Appendix A.3 documents software packages, SMOTE, Random Forest settings, optimizers, architectures, batch sizes, learning rates, temperature schedules and sparsification schedules, including Tables 11-15. v2 also clarifies split granularity and F1 averaging and supplies a code-access link. These are substantial disclosures, not evidence that previously reported experiments were changed or rerun.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate VISp and COVID-PBMC with the same supervised targets and gene-panel size ranges. The added classifier, stability and marker/GO analyses examine the existing data and selected panels, without introducing a new prediction population, domain or input scenario.

E2.justification: The main comparisons add YOTO (FS only), which predicts with a Random Forest trained on YOTO-selected genes, while retaining all six original baselines. Appendix A.2.1 additionally evaluates multi-task Random Forest variants of Seurat and Seurat v3.

E3.justification: v2 substantially extends the evaluation design with isolated panel evaluation, matched-architecture single-task versus multi-task controls, a larger-capacity condition, and multi-task Random Forest comparisons. It also introduces gene-overlap, GO-rank concordance and cross-size containment protocols. The original 80-20 split and 1000-epoch budget remain; cell-level splitting and macro-F1 are newly clarified, not demonstrated protocol changes.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained selection-module ablation, v2 tests panel quality separately from classifier choice and multi-task learning separately from model capacity. Sections 4.4.6-4.4.7 add seed stability, known-marker enrichment, functional concordance and panel nestedness analyses; Appendix A.2.1 examines single-task versus multi-task baseline classifiers.

E5.justification: Existing benchmark reporting retains means and standard deviations across seeds 0, 1 and 2. Section 4.4.6 newly introduces Fisher's exact test, with an odds ratio and p-value for marker enrichment. This adds inferential reporting without establishing an increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for FS-only prediction, controlled multi-task comparisons, baseline classifier variants and biological stability. Most matched benchmark entries remain unchanged, but VISp F1 at 32 genes changes from 84.8 ± 0.0 in v1 Table 5 to 82.7 ± 2.7 in v2 Table 6. New Tables 2-3 show FS-only YOTO outperforming integrated YOTO on VISp, but not COVID-PBMC, contrary to the added prose.

M1.justification: The learned gene scores, differentiable ranking, straight-through binary selection, progressive sparsification, shared encoder and task-specific losses remain unchanged. The added Random Forest evaluation and architecture controls test the existing method; the implementation appendix does not establish a revised core algorithm.

P1.justification: The main section order and much existing prose are retained, with targeted rewrites, expanded explanations and additional experimental and implementation subsections. Author/publication information expands and acknowledgments disappear. v2 also introduces a duplicated abstract sentence and an unfinished '[...]' phrase in Section 4.4.6.

P2.justification: Figure 1 adds a feedback arrow, Figure 2 adds the FS-only series, and new Figures 4-5 visualize overlap, GO concordance and nestedness. Comparative tables gain pipeline columns, FS-only rows and revised highlighting; new ablation and implementation tables substantially expand the displays. The original class-distribution figure is retained as Figure 6.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting multi-task learning, SMOTE and biological marker validation, including Kurin, Liu, He, Chawla and Tasic. It qualifies PERSIST's end-to-end status in Table 1 and clarifies the relationship to Grover et al.'s ranking operator. The main related-work narrative and nearest comparison remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix A.3 adds an explicit mathematical specification of the exponential subset-size annealing schedule in Equations 8-9, where v1 described progressive annealing qualitatively. This is a limited formalization: the core ranking, masking and loss equations remain unchanged, and no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's missing implementation specifications and limited evidence isolating gene-panel quality and stability through Appendix A.3, classifier controls and new robustness analyses. Explicit limits on patient generalization and partial-label claims also improve scientific qualification. These gains outweigh localized reporting and editing problems, including the duplicated abstract text and the COVID-PBMC FS-only claim contradicted by Table 2.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same YOTO research work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison; retained material can be matched across renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds classifier controls, multi-task ablations, gene-selection stability analyses and biological enrichment results.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix A report original classification experiments on VISp and COVID-PBMC, including baseline comparisons and a selection-module ablation.

results.title: You Only Train Once: Differentiable Subset Selection for Omics Data

C1.justification: V1 claims variance-optimal estimation, transport minimization in γ-Stein geometry, and improved efficiency without sacrificing generation quality. V2's abstract, contributions and conclusion narrow these to a variance-suppression bound, idealized geometric/spectral mechanisms, and empirical evaluation under an explicit protocol. This materially reduces the claimed guarantees and generality.

C2.justification: V2 extends the existing continuum-analogy caveat to its double-well, geodesic and NFE interpretations, and treats GSC as a heuristic rather than an optimality certificate. It explains rank weights as an ordering device rather than calibrated density estimates, acknowledges fidelity costs, and limits practical benefits in light of the weak clean-target results.

D1.justification: V2 Appendix D supplies substantially more reproducibility information: training-mixture composition, autoencoder and flow architectures, optimizer and training duration, weighting and Jacobian parameters, solver settings, retrieval-bank size, and metric sample counts. It also adds a code-availability statement. Most are newly disclosed details; the PDFs do not establish that previously unspecified settings changed.

E1.justification: The principal CIFAR-10 task shifts from v1's stated clean-data training to a robust-target task using an inlier/outlier-class mixture and evaluation against held-out inlier-class images. This substantially changes the represented training population and generation target. The double-well, 20D ring, and Gaussian-contamination scenarios remain; v2 also reports a complementary clean-target rerun.

E2.justification: V2 adds one targeted comparator, FM+Jac, to the main quantitative comparison and decoded-sample gallery. V1 compares standard FM with γ-FM variants without this explicit-smoothing control. The optional γ-FM+Jac combination is mentioned but has no reported comparison results.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a matched-budget comparison with decoded-image FID, Recall and Coverage, fixed-step midpoint sampling, and validation-FID-informed selection instead of GSC alone. New experiments vary batch size from 128 to 1024 and dimension from 32 to 256. The main γ sweep drops γ=4. Newly disclosed architecture and training details do not establish changes to previously unspecified settings.

E4.justification: V2 adds diagnostics of distance concentration and weight stability across dimensions and batch sizes (Appendix C.1), trained-model minibatch ablations and clean-target checks (Appendix D.1), and density/weight/radial analysis of the ring example. The existing neighbor-count ablation and contamination stress plot remain. The original autoencoder reconstruction diagnostic is removed.

E5.justification: V2 first reports three-seed means and standard deviations in Table 4, identifies seeds 42, 1042 and 2042, and adds error-bar plots. V1 supplies point results and timing averages without corresponding training-seed uncertainty. This establishes new reporting, not an increase from a known v1 run count.

E6.justification: Table 1 is replaced: v1 reports γ=1 achieving inlier MMD 0.0126 versus FM's 0.0481, whereas v2 reports γ=1 with worse FID than FM (61.198 versus 59.063) and higher inlier MMD (0.000773 versus 0.000609). These are different settings, not cross-version performance changes. V2 also adds proxy/batch results and reports little clean-target advantage; the γ=4 result disappears.

M1.justification: The weighted-CFM framework remains, but v2's experimental implementation uses rank-based, quantile-scaled and clipped weights rather than v1's exponential distance-based proxy (Appendices C.1 and D). Shared-time batching is now explicit; v1 does not establish whether its batches mixed times. V2's Algorithm 1 still displays the exponential rule, leaving an implementation-description inconsistency.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, experimental narrative and conclusion are substantially rewritten. V2 separates latent-flow setup from a new evaluation subsection, reorganizes and expands the experimental appendices, and revises theoretical explanations to distinguish formal results from mechanisms. Cross-references and supporting document sections are also updated.

P2.justification: V2 redesigns Table 1, adds Tables 3–4 and Figures 3 and 7, replaces the ring visualization with density/weight/speed/radial panels, redraws the GSC curve, and replaces the sample gallery to include FM+Jac. Margins and figure placement change substantially. The double-well, contamination and NFE graphics are retained despite renumbering or revised captions.

R1.justification: V2 adds Eguchi (2025) and explicitly identifies prior density-powered Stein-operator work in Section 3.4. The broader positioning relative to flow matching, optimal transport and escort geometry remains. Added bibliography entries for spectral-bias papers already cited in v1 complete references rather than introduce new research coverage.

T1.justification: The propositions, proofs, and Appendix A largely remain. V2 changes the diffusion flux from p∇p^γ to p^γ∇p and restores the density factor in the final roughness functional (v1 Eq. 20 to v2 Eq. 21). The flux revision fixes the double-well equation's γ=0 limit, but v2 Eq. 9 retains an incompatible 1/γ prefactor.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves the paper's experimental scrutiny and transparency through an explicit smoothing comparator, fidelity/diversity metrics, three-seed sensitivity results, and detailed implementation reporting. Its acknowledgement of fidelity trade-offs and weak clean-target gains corrects important overstatements in v1. The weighting-rule inconsistency and newly introduced diffusion-prefactor error remain material weaknesses, but the clearer evidence and narrower claims provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same γ-Flow Matching work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including material moved or renumbered between versions.

after.justification: V2 reports original synthetic and CIFAR-10 results, including FM+Jac comparisons, decoded-image metrics, and additional proxy and minibatch sensitivity experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic-flow and latent CIFAR-10 experiments, contamination tests, sampling-efficiency results, and a neighbor-count ablation.

results.title: Implicit geometric regularization in flow matching via density weighted Stein operators

C1.justification: The abstract expands the contribution beyond the original CTRNN demonstrations to diverse cognitive tasks, path integration, and feedforward networks. It also qualifies preference for the training noise as approximate and dependent on sufficiently large training noise, refining the original emphasis on matching the training level.

C2.justification: Sections 3.5 and 4 substantially expand the saturation-versus-coupling explanation and distinguish training stabilization from generalization benefits. v2 discusses applicability beyond rectifying, fixed-point networks and updates the remaining limitations to include unexplored limit-cycle dynamics and the unquantified relative regularization effectiveness of noise-in versus noise-out.

D1.justification: Appendices A-B add MLP architecture, regularization and optimizer settings, cognitive-task sampling and encoding choices, and path-generation distributions, boundary handling, and trial lengths. Appendix A also newly states that experimental code is supplied as Supplementary Material, although its availability cannot be verified from the PDFs alone.

E1.justification: v2 retains function computation, maze navigation, and regulation, while adding six cognitive tasks: ReactPro/ReactAnti, MemoryPro/MemoryAnti, and DelayPro/DelayAnti. It also adds two-dimensional path integration, extending coverage to stimulus-response rules, memory, delayed responses, and position estimation from movement cues (Sections 2.2.3-2.2.4).

E2.justification: The corresponding function-computation comparisons retain noise-in and noise-out networks and their noise-level controls. The added MLP and tanh experiments investigate architectural dependencies rather than introduce competing benchmark methods. Cited task implementations are not newly evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds training-noise sweeps beyond the original function-computation setting (Figures 2b and A2), plus protocols for the new experiments. These include 15,000 cognitive-task training batches with doubled sampling of memory tasks, 100-step path-integration trials, and 20,000 MLP training batches (Appendices A-B). Settings for the retained experiments are largely unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test dependence on training-noise magnitude, rectification through ReLU versus tanh, recurrence through feedforward MLPs, and initialization through repeated training runs (Figures 2b, 3e, 6b, A1-A2). These substantially extend the original fixed-point prediction and ReLU regulator analyses.

E5.justification: Figure A1 newly reports four independent training runs with different initializations and noise seeds, displaying their individual error curves. v1 already reported error standard deviations and 300-sample Monte Carlo estimation, but lacked this across-training-run evidence. No confidence intervals or significance tests are introduced.

E6.justification: v2 adds cognitive-task, path-integration, MLP, tanh-regulator, training-noise, and replication results. New findings include zero-noise preference at sufficiently low training noise and sharper preference but worse optimal error as training noise increases (Figure 2b). The original principal curves are retained; these are additional results under expanded conditions, not same-setting performance improvements.

M1.justification: The central CTRNN update rules, noise-in/noise-out formulations, and fixed-point procedure are retained. v2 adds a feedforward adaptation with two 100-unit hidden layers and extends the single-neuron regulator from ReLU to tanh (Appendices A and B.5), introducing model variants without redesigning the central approach.

P1.justification: v2 reworks the abstract, several Results passages, and Future work, substantially expanding the mechanistic explanation. The Discussion is reorganized from two subsections into four covering regularization, broader relevance, stochastic resonance, and future work. The overall Methods/Results and Appendix A-C framework is retained.

P2.justification: Figure 2 gains a training-noise panel, Figure 3 expands from two to five panels, and Figure 6 gains a full tanh comparison. New appendix Figures A1-A2 display replication and noise-out sweeps. Figures 4-5 are rearranged, and Figure 4's noise-axis label is corrected from variance to standard deviation.

R1.justification: v2 adds literature on path integration and noise-dependent biological computation. Noise-out models are now grounded in prior neuroscience work rather than introduced solely for didactic purposes, and Koren et al. (2025) motivates an energy-efficiency qualification. The central positioning relative to stochastic resonance remains.

T1.justification: Equation 4 corrects its first branch condition from x >= 0 to x <= 0, repairing the overlapping conditions in the piecewise Ornstein-Uhlenbeck example. The principal fixed-point reasoning and Appendix C objectives remain unchanged; no substantial new proof framework is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited evidence for generality and repeatability through path-integration, cognitive-task, feedforward, tanh, training-noise, and repeated-run tests. These additions establish meaningful applicability boundaries and qualify the training-noise-matching claim. Expanded implementation details and discussion improve assessability. The gains outweigh localized reporting problems, including Section 4.1's reversed noise-in/noise-out label and Appendix B.5's nonnegative setpoint range despite negative tanh setpoints in Figure 6b.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same noise-preference study and retain identifiable methods, experiments, and analyses. Their complete text, figures, equations, and Appendices A-C are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds cognitive-task, path-integration, feedforward-network, activation-function, and training-run experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original trained-network experiments on function computation, maze navigation, and single-neuron regulation, together with numerical fixed-point analyses.

results.title: Paradoxical noise preference in RNNs

C1.justification: v1 explicitly distinguishes its information-flow analysis objective from reducing network size and uses pruning primarily for evaluation. v2 makes post-training pruning the central problem and contribution throughout the title, abstract, introduction, problem statement, and conclusion. It also explicitly limits the evaluated models to small-to-medium sizes and introduces a claim about hybrid scalability.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking SparseGPT's uneven performance to convolutional spatial coupling and training objectives, interprets the seed experiments as evidence of stability, and questions the suitability of the standard SynFlow iteration budget. Its expanded discussion addresses measured computational costs and hybrid mitigation. It also explains that CIFAR-100 adversarially trained models were excluded because of substantial accuracy loss.

D1.justification: v1 refers to training details in an appendix absent from the supplied PDF. v2 Appendices A.2-A.4 provide optimizer, learning-rate, weight-decay, PGD, normalization, and layer-level architecture details. v2 also adds a project code URL, a SparseGPT implementation pointer, and runtime/memory information. These improve documented reproducibility without establishing that previously unspecified settings changed.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate image classification on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100. Additional training configurations and sensitivity experiments retain these datasets and task requirements.

E2.justification: v1 compares against magnitude pruning, SNIP, and SynFlow. v2 adds the post-training Hessian-based SparseGPT baseline to the benchmark and weight-decay comparisons, including the Tanh plots whose legends show its participation. SynFlow is removed from the Tanh comparisons, substantially revising the comparator set across existing experiments.

E3.justification: The stated calibration sizes and pruning without retraining are retained. v2 expands CIFAR-100 evaluation from one ReLU model to three configurations, explicitly covering two CE learning rates and WD. New protocols compare aggregation rules, test SynFlow with 5, 50, and 100 iterations, measure computational resources, and evaluate hybrid pre-pruning with an accuracy-loss threshold of 0.025.

E4.justification: v2 adds minimum/mean/maximum ranking ablation (Figure 5b), calibration-selection and model-initialization sensitivity (Figure 8), hybrid scalability analysis (Figure 9), and SynFlow iteration sensitivity (Appendix A.10). Existing component, calibration-size, weight-decay, and per-layer analyses are retained or relocated. Additional appendix panels supply evidence that v1 sometimes mentions without including.

E5.justification: v1 provides no repeated-run or uncertainty reporting. v2 Section 6.3.5 tests three calibration sets and three model initializations, reporting mean pruning curves with minimum-to-maximum envelopes across the three models. This introduces an explicit uncertainty-reporting practice, although its coverage is limited to the CIFAR-10 CE ReLU setting.

E6.justification: v2 adds SparseGPT results, an expanded CIFAR-100 configuration comparison, aggregation and seed findings, and computational measurements; it removes Tanh SynFlow curves. New findings favor minimum aggregation and report improved SynFlow performance with five iterations. Within v2, Table 1 reports 1060.574 seconds per example for curvature versus 675.012 for the hybrid, with peak memory increasing from 13493.0 to 17201.2 MB.

M1.justification: The core inverse-weight graph, activation-dependent curvature, and minimum-based parameter ranking are retained. Section 7 adds an evaluated hybrid variant that first performs magnitude pruning to an accuracy-loss threshold and then applies curvature pruning to the remaining parameters.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around pruning. Implementation becomes Section 5.5; Algorithm 1 and the proof move to Appendices A.5-A.6; Tanh comparisons and per-layer discussion move into organized appendix sections. These are substantial narrative and structural changes beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: The original combined benchmark Figure 3 is reorganized into a ReLU comparison and appendix Tanh Figure 10, with revised legends and comparator curves. Per-layer and Tanh weight-decay displays move to the appendix. v2 adds aggregation, seed-variation, hybrid, and iteration-sensitivity plots, additional supplementary panels, and the runtime/memory Table 1.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially refocused around pruning at initialization versus post-training pruning, adding SparseGPT, Kumar et al.'s information-theoretic pruning barriers, and Wang et al.'s gradient-flow pruning work. The earlier robustness/OOD motivation and several information-flow and learning-based pruning references are removed. This accompanies a substantive repositioning as a graph-based post-training pruning approach.

T1.justification: The background probability definition changes from proportional weighting in v1 Definition 3 to explicit exponential normalization in v2 Definitions 2 and 4. Section 5.5 also corrects v1's self-referential shortest-path recurrence with a layer-recursive min-plus expression. Proposition 1 and its proof are retained, with the proof moved to Appendix A.6 and its probability distributions explained more explicitly.

improvement.justification: Relative to the supplied v1, v2 substantially strengthens assessability by supplying missing training and architecture details, adding a relevant post-training comparator, testing ranking and baseline-budget choices, reporting variation across runs, and quantifying computational costs. These address important reproducibility and validation gaps. The seed study remains narrow, and the hybrid reduces runtime while increasing peak memory, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidence and transparency.

A1.justification: The authors, neural-curvature construction, proposition, and overlapping experiments identify the same research despite the title change. Both PDFs are readable, but v1 ends with references on page 21 despite referring to appendices. Earlier supplementary details therefore cannot be fully compared with v2's Appendix A.

after.justification: v2 retains original pruning results and reports additional baseline comparisons, aggregation and seed experiments, and runtime and memory measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original pruning experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100, together with component, calibration-size, weight-decay, and per-layer analyses.

results.title: Post-Training Neural Network Pruning using Graph Curvature

C1.justification: The central contributions remain the same: diffusion paths benefit annealed sampling; first-order stochastic transitions offer limited gains; deterministic maps can approach second-order performance; and inaccurate learned log-densities undermine practical BGs. V2 changes their implementation and supporting evidence without replacing these core claims.

C2.justification: V2 strengthens the density-bottleneck interpretation using controlled experiments and revises the mode-blindness discussion to distinguish target-dependent tSM behavior and DiffCLF's partial success. Appendix C.1 newly qualifies the correction through Gaussianity, truncation error, and possible failure at dimensions at most 10. These are substantive mechanism and applicability qualifications.

D1.justification: V2 newly provides code-access information. Tables 2–4 document expanded search grids, initialization schemes, and selected hyperparameters, while Appendix D.2 explains shared-model selection. Appendices B.4 and C.1 add detailed scheduling and shared-probe estimator instructions. These materially expand reproducibility information beyond v1's smaller parameter table and general descriptions.

E1.justification: V2 adds non-Gaussian ManyWell targets in dimensions 16, 32, and 64, extending evaluation beyond v1's Gaussian mixtures. The 32-dimensional ManyModes benchmark also changes from 16/32/64 modes to 4/16/64 modes. Both versions retain the one-dimensional density-path case studies.

E2.justification: V2 adds DiffCLF+DSM to the evaluated density-learning objectives. Across the main AIS/SMC/RE comparisons, first-order stochastic baselines switch from EI to DDPM beta kernels; Figure 18 additionally compares both. V1's second-order DDPM is renamed DDPM-2, which alone is not a new comparator.

E3.justification: Fixed logarithmic tempering schedules become target-specific Lambda-optimal schedules, K=16 is dropped, and RE defaults to base rather than score-informed initialization. Training changes from K-specific networks and sampling-based hyperparameter selection to shared networks selected using density diagnostics; standalone DSM receives 2,000 rather than 1,000 epochs. V2 also adds log-normalizer evaluation and replaces TwoModes absolute weight error with direct weight estimates.

E4.justification: Figure 4 introduces exact-density/learned-score controls. Appendix D.4 adds scheduling, EI-versus-DDPM, and multi-step-transition comparisons, plus direct VP/VE invertibility and penalty-estimator diagnostics. These substantially revise the analysis suite: v1's local-MCMC-step and swap-period studies disappear, and its final-sampling hyperparameter sweeps are replaced by component-error investigations.

E5.justification: The main sampling experiments still use eight runs. V2 adds a dedicated metric-calibration experiment with 128 independent repetitions and explicit mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting (Figure 8). It also introduces boxplots for direct mode-weight and log-normalizer estimates, expanding distributional reporting without establishing an increase in the main experiment run counts.

E6.justification: V2 adds ManyWell, DiffCLF, log-normalizer, and diagnostic results while removing many detailed Gaussian-mixture panels and runtime results. Under its revised procedures, Figure 3 reports much closer agreement between Hutchinson-based and Hessian-based RE than v1. The RE-initialization findings also change from broadly beneficial score-informed initialization to mostly neutral or mixed effects. These are revised results under changed conditions, not isolated same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The implicit-midpoint framework remains, but v2 substantially revises its stochastic Jacobian treatment: ordinary Hutchinson estimation becomes Hutch++, and a penalty correction modifies importance weights and MH acceptance probabilities. Appendix C.1 also specifies shared probes for RE swaps. These change the implemented sampling procedure, rather than merely explaining v1.

P1.justification: The abstract is rewritten, several experimental discussions are clarified and streamlined, and discrete-time material moves from Appendix A.2 to B.4. Supplementary results are organized more thematically. Nevertheless, the seven-section main structure and much of the background, related-work exposition, and existing proofs remain recognizable.

P2.justification: Figure 3 combines TwoModes and ManyModes panels and removes its runtime row. Figure 4 expands the objective panels and changes control hatching. Extensive appendix grids give way to consolidated plots, boxplots, and new diagnostic figures; hyperparameter tables are expanded substantially. These are extensive display changes beyond renumbering or numerical updates.

R1.justification: V2 adds substantive references and discussion for DiffCLF, Hutch++, penalty corrections, and concurrent work by Hoffmann et al., while removing the pseudo-marginal justification cited in v1. Most of the related-work framework remains intact. Publication-year and venue updates for retained works do not constitute new research positioning.

T1.justification: New Appendix C.1 develops Gaussian-noise assumptions, a Bessel penalty transform, and variance-symmetry conditions for corrected MH transitions. This replaces v1's unsupported inference that unbiased log-determinant estimates automatically preserve sampling guarantees. Appendix B.4 also revises discretization formulas and introduces communication-barrier reasoning. The original implicit-midpoint lemmas and proofs are largely retained.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the empirical foundation: optimized tempering improves baseline fairness, exact-density/learned-score controls better test the proposed failure mechanism, and ManyWell addresses the Gaussian-only scope. Reproducibility information also improves. Important caveats remain: the runtime panel and detailed result grids are removed, and v2 Equation (35) gives gamma^2/N where the preceding penalty definition implies gamma^2/2. That inconsistency limits confidence in the mathematical repair, but does not outweigh the substantial improvement in experimental support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–D support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material and renamed methods.

after.justification: V2 reports original Gaussian-mixture and ManyWell experiments, controlled density-error investigations, and additional numerical diagnostics.

before.justification: V1 reports original sampling experiments on TwoModes and ManyModes, learned-density evaluations, and extensive appendix ablations.

results.title: Diffusion-based Annealed Boltzmann Generators : benefits, pitfalls and hopes
