C1.justification: The central claims remain that naive fine-tuning can underperform random initialization and that model-agnostic TACO bridges generalizable and instance-specific optimization with negligible additional overhead. The expanded task and backbone lists broaden supporting evidence without materially redefining these already broad claims.

C2.justification: v2 reframes the mechanism from potentially escaping poor local minima toward favorable initialization and faster attainment of better optima. It adds interpretations of compute scaling versus COExpander and the MIS RRG-10 exception, suggesting more updates could close that gap. The existing limitations paragraph is unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link, clarifies that model-specific random initialization can supply perturbations, and documents MIS generation, loss, learning rate, and SP settings. It also gives ConsFormer adaptation budgets and timings. Existing hardware and MVC/MC implementation details remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds MIS on 1,000-node random regular graphs, training on degree 20 and evaluating degrees 5, 7, 10, and 20. It also adds MaxCut on GSET across graph sizes from 800 to at least 3,000 nodes. These expand task requirements and graph populations beyond the retained MVC/MC coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated COExpander configurations on Twitter/COLLAB MVC and MC, plus PGD comparisons on Twitter. The new MaxCut comparison includes ConsFormer and fine-tuning alongside reported baselines such as SDP, RUNCSP, ECO-DQN, ESCORD, ANYCSP, and OR-Tools. Original comparator sets remain present.

E3.justification: Added experiments introduce substantial new protocols: MIS uses 3,000 training graphs, 50 evaluation graphs per degree, and approximation ratios normalized by theoretical upper bounds; MaxCut uses ConsFormer with 100 adaptation steps and percentage gaps to best-known cuts. COExpander comparisons add configuration sweeps and one-/three-step TACO settings. Retained MVC/MC protocols are unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond retaining the original sensitivity and seed-budget analyses, v2 adds best-versus-average seed comparisons and tests perturbations before adaptation versus during gradient updates, including their combination. Table 15 also adds a full random-initialization control. These investigate selection effects and alternative explanations for TACO's gains.

E5.justification: Appendix B.4 adds performance averaged across all eight input seeds alongside best-seed performance, changing the reported statistical aggregation. Existing seed counts and plus/minus reporting remain; neither additional independent training runs nor new confidence intervals or significance tests are established.

E6.justification: Original table values are retained, while v2 adds substantial results for COExpander, MaxCut, MIS, seed averages, and PGD. For example, Table 7 reports an 800-node MaxCut gap of 0.80% for TACO versus 0.98% for fine-tuning and 0.91% for reproduced ConsFormer; published ConsFormer is better at 0.31%. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over v1 scores.

M1.justification: Standard TACO's shrink-and-perturb initialization and online parameter reuse remain unchanged. Appendix B.6 introduces an optional TACO-PGD combination that also injects perturbations during gradient updates, a limited procedural extension rather than a redesign.

P1.justification: The introduction and method exposition are condensed, the motivating failure-mode discussion moves into renamed Section 2.3, and Appendix B gains descriptive subsections. Publication information and acknowledgments are added. Most prose and the overall section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual presentation with COExpander and MaxCut comparison tables, MIS trajectory figures and results, and seed-average and PGD tables. Existing figures and tables are retained, with relocation and renumbering; the sensitivity table gains a control row and expanded caption.

R1.justification: New references and discussion connect the experiments to COExpander, ConsFormer, perturbed gradient descent, MIS bounds, and additional MaxCut methods. Positioning relative to shrink-and-perturb, Meta-EGN, and test-time adaptation remains essentially unchanged. Publication-metadata updates do not constitute new related work.

T1.justification: Appendix B.5 adds an explicit MIS loss definition: a negative node-selection sum plus an edge-conflict penalty. This is a limited formal addition adopted from prior work. Existing CO, MVC, and MC formulations remain, and no new theorem, proof, or convergence guarantee is provided.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the model-agnostic claim, previously supported only by closely related EGN backbones, through ConsFormer/MaxCut and additional MIS experiments. COExpander comparisons and seed/perturbation controls also address important evidential gaps. Some new wording overstates uniform superiority over COExpander, and MaxCut gains concern the weaker reproduced ConsFormer baseline rather than its published scores. These qualifications limit the conclusions but leave a substantial overall improvement in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TACO research work. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original MIS, ConsFormer/MaxCut, COExpander, seed-averaging, and perturbed-gradient experiments. Some comparison scores are explicitly attributed to prior work.

before.justification: v1 reports original MVC and maximum-clique experiments, including static, distribution-shifted, and dynamic evaluations, optimization trajectories, and hyperparameter analyses.

results.title: Test-Time Adaptation for Unsupervised Combinatorial Optimization

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion shift from a novel alignment strategy that unlocks scaling laws toward a systematic granularity-calibration study that recovers a positive scaling trend. The contributions also add spatial pooling and multi-layer fusion, replacing the earlier emphasis on establishing shared human/model hierarchical granularity.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking pooling gains to foreground dilution and attention propagation, and fusion gains to complementary representations with diminishing returns. It also interprets the new channel and subject analyses. Section 4.2 newly identifies the test-split layer sweep as exploratory, materially qualifying how selected-layer results should be interpreted.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link, discloses retrospective test-based layer exploration and fixed InternViT L28 use in Tables 1–2, specifies pooling heads and the central patch region, and explains joint-modality UMAP fitting and channel-group construction. Reported hardware changes from RTX 3090 to RTX A6000. These substantially expand reproducibility information beyond the retained architecture and optimizer details.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate THINGS-EEG and THINGS-MEG, with the same participant populations and intra-subject and leave-one-subject-out image-retrieval tasks. The added studies vary splits, channel subsets and model components within this retained coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 retain the same external comparators: NICE, ATM, Neural-MCRL, UBP and NeuroBridge on EEG, and UBP and NeuroBridge on MEG. The new Figure 4 introduces local pooling comparisons, including center-only averaging and shared spatial weighting alongside adaptive attention heads. The original encoder comparison is retained.

E3.justification: Appendix B.2 adds a 74-concept validation holdout and validation-loss checkpoint selection; B.4 adds seven channel configurations with a stated 30-epoch budget. The reported MEG training set changes from 1,854 to 1,654 concepts, acquisition rate from 1000 to 1200 Hz, and bandpass from 0.1–100 to 0.1–40 Hz. These are documented protocol revisions, without evidence establishing that the retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds pooling and fusion ablations, validation-split robustness, regional/full-channel comparisons, subject-wise optimal-layer analysis, and scaling sensitivity to total versus prefix parameter counts. The original encoder, projector, training-dynamics, UMAP and retrieval-case analyses remain, several relocated to the appendix.

E5.justification: Five independent seeded runs remain specified in both versions, and v1 already reports scaling correlations and significance. v2 adds explicit SEM reporting for pooling and validation comparisons and mean ± standard deviation across ten subjects for the channel analysis. No increase in repeated-run counts is documented.

E6.justification: The numerical results in Tables 1–2 and 4–6 are unchanged. New Figure 4 reports 90.8% Top-1 accuracy for four-layer fusion and 91.3% for fusion with adaptive pooling, compared with the retained 82.6% single-layer configuration. These are additional configurations, not revised same-setting scores. New robustness analyses add further findings, and Section 4.4 corrects ViT-H/14's reported peak depth from 35.5% to 32.3%, matching Table 4.

M1.justification: v1 uses a single pooled intermediate representation. v2 adds learnable spatial and sample-adaptive pooling, plus multi-layer fusion that independently trains neural encoders and averages their retrieval similarity matrices (Sections 4.7–4.8). These extend the procedure substantially; the original projections and contrastive objective remain.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, several result discussions and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. Results gain a semantic-focused/implicit/explicit alignment organization. Former Sections 4.7–4.8 move to Appendices B.9 and B.3, while pooling and fusion become main-text sections.

P2.justification: v2 merges v1 Figures 3–5 into a composite Figure 3, relocates the encoder and projector figures, and adds pooling/fusion and four robustness-analysis displays. Figure 1's labels are revised, and the journal template changes title, typography and page layout. The appendix retrieval montages are retained rather than newly added cases.

R1.justification: Sections 2.2–2.3 substantially expand positioning around prior hierarchical brain alignment and representation granularity, including Wen, Seeliger and Tu (2018), Lu (2026), Bau (2017) and Raghu (2021). The revised framing explicitly builds on prior multi-layer/non-final-layer alignment findings, narrowing the earlier novelty positioning; some intrinsic-dimension and noise references are removed.

T1.justification: The mathematical problem formulation, projection and contrastive-loss equations, relative-depth formula and concept-accuracy definition are retained. Neither version supplies theoretical proofs, and v2's additions are procedural or empirical rather than new formal mathematical results.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked the validation, channel-selection and parameter-count controls now supplied in Appendices B.2 and B.4–B.6. These substantially strengthen the central empirical finding, while clearer prior-work attribution, selection disclosures and the narrower scaling-trend claim improve transparency and scientific scope. Pooling/fusion ablations provide useful additional methodological evidence. The validation study addresses checkpoint selection, however, and does not establish independent layer selection; optimal-layer results remain exploratory.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Shallow Alignment research. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across reorganizations.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds pooling, fusion, validation-split, channel-selection, subject-consistency and scaling analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original EEG/MEG retrieval experiments, layer-wise evaluations, encoder and projector ablations, and qualitative analyses.

results.title: Deep Models, Shallow Alignment: Uncovering the Granularity Mismatch in Neural Decoding

C1.justification: V1 makes broad claims about generalization measures across IID/OOD regimes and their usefulness for robustness. V2 restricts its conclusions to controlled CIFAR-10-C/P shifts and the studied CNN architectures, adds decision-level selection as a central contribution, and emphasizes leading individual sharpness/input-gradient signals alongside close, architecture-dependent family results.

C2.justification: V2 removes v1's speculative transfer-learning flatness explanation and broad deployment recommendations. It distinguishes association, local reliability, and selection utility; explains why minimizing a generalization gap need not maximize accuracy; and adds substantive limitations concerning eligibility filtering, dependent candidate sets, perturbation sequences, information budgets, and threshold-sensitive calibration findings.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents the 80/20 source training/validation split, metric provenance and logging fields, candidate filtering and deduplication, and selector support. Appendix B.1.1 details CIFAR-10-P sequence handling, including 10,000 sequences of 31 frames for the stated Gaussian-noise cell and cell-level aggregation. These disclosures substantially expand reproducibility information without proving that existing splits or loaders changed.

E1.justification: V2 removes the PACS/VLCS natural-domain experiments and the appendix's DistilGPT2/Wikitext-103 language-modeling experiment. Evaluation is consequently concentrated on CIFAR-10 and its corruption/perturbation targets, substantially reducing domain and task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated training-accuracy/loss and clean-validation-accuracy/loss baselines, Random, and Oracle references for decision selection, plus residualized calibration comparators. Its appendix sign-error plots also include full AIC/TIC/WAIC alongside their bias terms, whereas v1's corresponding plots show the bias terms. ATC is discussed but explicitly not evaluated.

E3.justification: V2 adds clean-to-shifted degradation targets and decision protocols with fixed selector directions, architecture–sweep–target candidate sets, a source cross-entropy eligibility threshold, normalized regret, and top-k hit rates. Appendix C.3.7 introduces held-out proxy-selection folds. The printed learning-rate grids also change, including NiN's unscaled 3.2 becoming 3.2×10^-2 for SGD; this does not establish that training was rerun.

E4.justification: V2 expands sign-error analyses to batch-size/dropout axes and clean-to-shifted targets. It adds eligibility-threshold, severity, architecture, and cross-shift transfer checks, plus source-statistics and residualization ablations testing whether calibration contributes beyond source fit. V1's conditional-mutual-information analysis and language-model axis-sensitivity study are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions list CIFAR seeds 0–4, but v2 newly reports bootstrap 95% intervals for granulated scores, selection regret, paired contrasts, and residual associations. It specifies resampling units, including 10,000 bootstrap samples for proxy selection, and qualifies dependence limitations. These additions do not establish increased training repetitions.

E6.justification: V1 has no decision-regret results. Under v2's restricted candidate-pool protocol, Table 1 reports normalized regret of 0.132 for sharpness.magnitude.init, 0.178 for clean validation accuracy, and 0.206 for ECE. V2 adds extensive transfer, residualization, and sensitivity results, changes Figure 1's correlation summaries, and removes the DomainBed, language-model, and conditional-mutual-information results. These are new or revised findings, not demonstrated same-setting training-performance gains.

M1.justification: The CIFAR classifiers and training objectives are retained. V2 introduces source-loss/error-residualized ECE/MCE selector variants in Appendix C.4.2. Appendix A.2 also changes the stated CNN path.norm computation from channel-wise propagation to summed log Frobenius norms; this is a specification revision, without establishing whether earlier implementations were changed.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, discussion, and limitations are extensively rewritten. The experimental narrative is reorganized into correlation, local reliability, and decision-level evaluation, and the appendices are rebuilt around CIFAR-specific diagnostics. This is a substantial narrative revision beyond terminology and renumbering.

P2.justification: V2 changes the main text from two columns to one, restructures sign-error figures into target-specific architecture panels with additional axes, and adds split correlation views and numerous selection/uncertainty tables. DomainBed and language-model displays disappear, while retained figures receive revised organization and expanded captions.

R1.justification: Jiang et al. and Dziugaite et al. remain the principal foundations. V2 adds Garg et al. (2022), explicitly distinguishing ATC's unlabeled-target accuracy estimation from source-only ranking, and adds Hendrycks et al. (2020) and Naganuma et al. (2022). References supporting the removed natural-domain and broader model context are dropped.

T1.justification: V2 removes the normalized conditional-mutual-information score K(mu) defined in v1 Appendix C.2 and introduces formal residualization definitions in Equations 57–59. It also corrects the reliability-diagram formula from a sum to a bin average by adding 1/M. Most existing margin, sharpness, and PAC-Bayes mathematics remains unchanged.

improvement.justification: V1's model-selection recommendations rely largely on correlations. V2 substantially strengthens their evaluation through direct selection comparisons, source-fit controls, uncertainty reporting, and threshold sensitivity checks, while narrowing conclusions to the evidence. Tables 25 and 49–52 expose why calibration association does not establish stable incremental selection value. Removing natural-domain and language-model experiments reduces breadth, and the new estimates remain exploratory, but the stronger empirical scrutiny and clearer interpretive boundaries resolve an important evidence-to-conclusion gap.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same generalization-measure benchmark, retaining the CIFAR-10/C/P experiments and six measure families despite a changed title and scope. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original CIFAR-10/C/P correlation and sign-error results, together with decision-level selection, sensitivity, cross-shift transfer, and calibration-residualization results.

before.justification: V1 reports original hyperparameter-sweep experiments on CIFAR-10/C/P, PACS, and VLCS, plus conditional-dependence analyses and a DistilGPT2/Wikitext-103 experiment in the appendices.

results.title: Generalization Measures under Controlled Covariate Shift: A Regime-Aware Benchmark

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: balanced checkerboard sampling, combined within- and between-scale conditioning, competitive ImageNet generation with few steps, and performance governed largely by total steps across several scale ratios. The additional experiments support these existing claims.

C2.justification: V3 adds explanations involving training budgets and KV-cache use for benchmark differences, distinguishes direct AR-VQ comparisons from contextual non-VQ results, and develops an information-redundancy explanation in Appendix E. Appendices A and C qualify the higher-resolution findings and discuss geometric distortions without conclusively attributing them to checkerboard sampling.

D1.justification: Appendix A documents transfer initialization, the ten-epoch schedule, and exact higher-resolution scale lists; Appendix D specifies CFG=1.5 for its entropy statistics. Core optimizer, hardware, training, and code-access information remains. Replacing the explicit validation-set description with 'standard reference set' makes that detail less precise.

E1.justification: Appendix A extends evaluation from 256×256 to 512×512 class-conditional ImageNet generation, adding a higher-resolution scenario. The dataset, conditioning task, and application domain remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains the original comparators and adds DiT-XL/2, MAR-L, GtR, and xAR as contextual non-VQ comparisons. Figure 4(c) adds a trained random-within-scale-order comparator. Figure 6 newly compares entropy with PAR and RandAR, which previously participated only in the benchmark comparison.

E3.justification: New settings include a random-order control, L-model scale/step sweeps, and ten-epoch transfer training from 256 to 512 resolution with revised scale progressions. Existing 256-resolution training budgets, metrics, and CFG sweeps remain. Section 4.1 replaces 'full ImageNet validation set' with 'standard reference set'; this wording does not establish whether reference data changed or experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V3 adds a direct checkerboard-versus-random-order ablation, extends scale/step sensitivity analysis to 512 resolution and the L model, compares baseline entropy profiles, and presents geometric failure cases in Appendix C. Conversely, it removes the brief unsuccessful output-head MLP experiment reported in v1 Section 3.3.

E5.justification: V1 reports CFG-sweep error bars and entropy quartiles. V3 additionally reports standard errors, standard deviations, one-tailed t-tests, and significance thresholds for adjacent-step and midpoint entropy changes in Tables 3–4. Both versions already specify 10,000 entropy samples; the additions do not establish more independent training runs or seeds.

E6.justification: New results include random-order FID 6.01 versus checkerboard 5.32 in Figure 4(c), four contextual benchmark rows, 512-resolution and L-model curves, baseline entropy profiles, statistical results, and failure images. The original Checkerboard-L Table 1 FIDs of 2.72, 2.83, and 2.79 and the RoPE results remain unchanged. The additions therefore expand evidence rather than demonstrate improved performance over v1.

M1.justification: The progressive scan algorithm, blockwise autoregression, input mixture, token embeddings, cross-entropy objective, and RoPE formulation remain unchanged. The random-order model is an experimental control; the additional resolution experiments do not establish a change to the proposed method.

P1.justification: V3 locally rewrites and tightens introductory, related-work, and method prose, adds an autoregression-background subsection and broader-impacts section, and switches to author-year citations. The main narrative and section sequence remain largely intact; the new appendices chiefly contain additional evidence and discussion.

P2.justification: The document is globally reformatted. Table 1 gains a method/tokenizer column and comparator groups, Figure 4 gains panel (c), and Figure 6 gains baseline panels. Figures 9–11 and Tables 3–4 are new. Existing plots and sample images are retained but resized or relocated, including a dedicated page for Figure 8.

R1.justification: V3 adds xAR discussion and bibliography entries for xAR, Flow Matching for Generative Modeling, and Flow Straight and Fast. Positioning relative to PAR, RandAR, and scalewise autoregression remains substantially intact. DiT, MAR, and GtR were already cited in v1, although their benchmark rows are new.

T1.justification: Algorithm 1 and the input-mixture and RoPE equations are retained. The new autoregressive probability factorization is background exposition, while Appendix E offers heuristic conditional-dependence reasoning. Neither introduces a new formal assumption, theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical revision.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens evidence for the central design and scaling claims: the random-order control directly tests the ordering choice missing from v1, and Appendices A–B extend validation beyond the original small-model, 256-resolution analysis. Entropy tests, failure examples, and explicit transfer limitations improve assessability and transparency. These gains outweigh limited reporting drawbacks, including the less explicit reference-set description and misleading 'lower FID' wording in Section 4.2.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same progressive-checkerboard image-generation work. Their text, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support comparison. V1 has no appendices; v3 adds Appendices A–E.

after.justification: V3 retains those original experiments and adds a random-order comparison, higher-resolution and large-model evaluations, failure examples, and entropy statistics.

before.justification: V1 reports original ImageNet generation results, scale/step experiments, RoPE ablations, and entropy measurements from the proposed models in Section 4.

results.title: Progressive Checkerboards for Autoregressive Multiscale Image Generation

C1.justification: The central claim changes from a normalized representation-space likelihood to a spherical subdensity with an associated variational bound. The abstract and introduction replace the claim of outperforming comparable one-class anomaly baselines with broader OOD validation. Competitive representation learning and feature-wise uncertainty remain central contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations connecting uncertainty statistics to class geometry and likelihood factorization to collapse prevention. Removing KL is now interpreted through partial learning and seed-dependent instability rather than uniformly failed representations. The conclusion newly distinguishes representation-space uncertainty from calibrated downstream predictions and removes the earlier ImageNet-gap tradeoff discussion.

D1.justification: Appendix A substantially expands implementation specifications with the exact MLP structure, activations, bias choices, initialization, variance transformation, and ImageNet variance centering. Test-time posterior-mean scoring is explicit. Appendix C.4 adds GH200 hardware, batch size, precision, FLOP-counting tools, profiling procedures, and memory-extrapolation information.

E1.justification: One-class CIFAR-10 anomaly detection is replaced by full-CIFAR-10 in-distribution training and external OOD evaluation against CIFAR-100, Tiny ImageNet, MNIST, SVHN, Textures, and Places365. Tiny ImageNet representation-learning experiments are also added. CIFAR-100 and STL-10 were already evaluated in v1's ablations.

E2.justification: v2 adds reproduced VI-SimSiam comparisons and reported OpenOOD comparisons with MSP, ReAct, KNN, and ViM. The one-class comparison containing GEOM, DROCC, Deep SVDD, SimpleNet, PANDA, and CutPaste disappears. Rot+Trans, GOAD, and CSI remain under the new OOD task; the ImageNet comparator set remains unchanged.

E3.justification: Representation training changes from MoCo-v2 to BYOL augmentations, weight decay from 5e-6 to 5e-4 with exclusions, and default ν from 3 to 1. The 800-epoch comparison changes k-NN from k=30 to k=20 and permits method-specific baseline recipes. The new OOD protocol uses 200 epochs and separate near/far AUROC aggregates instead of ten one-class evaluations.

E4.justification: v2 adds posterior-geometry analysis, factorized-versus-standard likelihood diagnostics, Monte Carlo sample ablations, isotropic-versus-diagonal posterior tests, and compute profiling. The projection-head experiment and joint β-by-ν anomaly sweep disappear. Tail and loss-component ablations are revised, with the directional-only and radial-only configurations removed.

E5.justification: Three-run averaging already appears in v1. v2 extends standard-deviation reporting to the representation comparisons and retained ablations, adds uncertainty bands to OOD curves, and explicitly identifies non-finite-run exclusions and single-run diagnostics. The PDFs do not establish an increase in the existing three-run count.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces ImageNet top-1 accuracy of 65.6 ± 0.4% with 68.2 ± 0.3% under revised training. The 90.3% one-class AUROC is removed, while the new OpenOOD task reports 92.4 ± 0.2%. Revised ablations show partial collapse at ν=50 on CIFAR-10/100, unlike v1. Changed methods and protocols prevent interpreting these as controlled gains over v1.

M1.justification: The directional loss changes from an ambient Student-t density on normalized-vector differences to a spherical construction using a geodesic log-map, tangent-space covariance, and an exponential-map Jacobian. v2 also implements and evaluates an EMA target variant and introduces ImageNet-specific variance centering. These change the training procedure, beyond explanatory elaboration.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, model explanation, theoretical narrative, and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting. Experiments are reorganized around representation quality, posterior geometry, OOD detection, ablations, and synthesis. Appendix A gains implementation subsections, and a new Appendix C organizes supplementary diagnostics.

P2.justification: Figure 3 changes from one CIFAR-10 trajectory plot to three dataset panels. The anomaly-grid heatmap disappears, while posterior visualizations, ROC curves, score distributions, and diagnostic plots are added. Comparison tables are restructured, and separate loss-performance and variance tables become a combined display.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds focused discussion of variational contrastive learning, supervised contrastive learning, and SNGP. New spherical-geometry and OpenOOD references accompany the revision, while several one-class references disappear. The principal positioning relative to JEPA-style objectives, VI-SimSiam, and VSSL remains.

T1.justification: Section 4.2 replaces the extrinsic-density argument with geodesic, Schur-complement, tangent-determinant, and Jacobian derivations. Section 4.4 reformulates the variational bound in terms of conditional log-mass under a subprobability model. Appendix B also revises its claimed cosine-objective reduction to accommodate the changed geometry.

improvement.justification: Direct factorization, sampling, and anisotropy tests in Appendix C address important gaps in v1's support for its central design choices. Reproducing VI-SimSiam, documenting failed runs, and expanding implementation details substantially improve empirical scrutiny and reproducibility. These gains outweigh the lost experiments, although the revised theory needs correction: Appendix B.4 claims a constant Jacobian under isotropy, contradicting the angle-dependent expression in Eq. (25), so its exact cosine-loss reduction is unsupported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Joint Embedding Variational Bayes by the same authors. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including the substantially revised method and experiments.

after.justification: v2 reports original representation-learning, posterior-geometry, and OOD-detection results, alongside additional ablations and computational measurements in Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original representation-learning experiments, one-class CIFAR-10 anomaly-detection results, and likelihood and loss-component ablations in Section 5.

results.title: Joint Embedding Variational Bayes

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion withdraw v1's central claim that data scarcity is established as the binding constraint and that the data-to-parameter ratio determines scaling. V2 instead claims parameter scaling within one standardized setting, emphasizes test consistency and diagnostics, and explicitly limits the entropy estimate to task-specific remaining uncertainty.

C2.justification: V2 replaces the data-bottleneck and threshold interpretation with an interaction among data volume, effective epochs, and optimization budget. It corrects v1 Section 7.4.3's description of 2.3 bits as predictable information to remaining uncertainty. Residual heterogeneity now qualifies the Gaussian interpretation, and the new Broader Impact section discusses composition biases affecting the fitted floor.

D1.justification: V2 adds a dataset filename, configuration details for the supplementary experiments, the runs-directory location, and a manifest-filtering disclosure. Table 1 revises reported parameter counts, including TINY from 9,937 to 9,953 and L from 101,033,041 to 100,510,801. The repository and seed information remain; relocating reproducibility information to Appendix C is not a new code release.

E1.justification: V2 removes the 1,024-gene, 10,000-cell reconstruction setting, one of v1's two principal regimes, including its appendix coverage. It retains the 512-gene CELLxGENE task. The added 25k–200k subsets use the same gene set and preprocessing, so their sample-count variation belongs to E3.

E2.justification: Neither version experimentally compares against external methods. scVI, scGPT, Geneformer, scBERT, and scFoundation remain related-work references, while the experiments compare sizes of the same transformer family.

E3.justification: V2 centers evaluation on the existing 18-run, 60k-step standardized sweep and removes the heterogeneous additional runs and XL setting. It adds reported held-out test evaluation, an M-model data-size sweep at fixed vocabulary and training steps, and XXS/TINY direct-NLL reruns. The original 90/5/5 split and canonical optimization settings remain.

E4.justification: New Section 7.3 and Figure 2 investigate data-size sensitivity and test the homoscedasticity assumption through per-gene held-out residuals. Section 7.5.3 and Appendix A add direct-versus-derived NLL calibration for XXS/TINY. V1 discussed these limitations without these empirical checks.

E5.justification: Table 2 changes from minimum–maximum seed ranges to means and standard deviations for validation and test MSE. The retained sweep still uses seeds 7, 8, and 9; this does not establish an increase in repetitions. No confidence intervals for scaling parameters or significance tests are added.

E6.justification: V2 removes Regime B results and the 21-run Regime A fit, replaces loss ranges with standardized means, and adds test results, including alpha=0.268, c=1.462, and R²=0.859. New findings include the nearly flat data-size fit, residual heterogeneity, and NLL calibration. The canonical validation fit and Table 4 entropy estimates remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The encoder, embeddings, mask token, prediction head, 15% masking, MSE objective, and scaling-fit procedure remain unchanged. Appendix B explicitly says the direct-NLL reruns differ only in additional validation logging. Revised parameter counts do not document a new architectural component.

P1.justification: The abstract, contributions, regime descriptions, results narrative, discussion, limitations, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around the standardized sweep. The dual-regime organization is removed, Broader Impact is added, and reproducibility moves to Appendix C. Citation formatting also changes from author–year to numbered references.

P2.justification: Tables 1–3 and Figure 1 are substantially redesigned around standardized validation/test comparisons. A new Figure 2 displays the data-size sweep and residual scatter; v1 Figure 2 is retained as Figure 3 with a revised caption. Typography, headings, title presentation, and page layout also change throughout.

R1.justification: The same 24 cited works and first-systematic-study positioning remain. However, v2 Section 7.4 drops v1's specific claim that its dual-regime behavior echoes Kaplan's parameter/data-scaling contradiction, replacing it with a qualified discussion of different scaling axes and insufficient evidence for an intersection analysis.

T1.justification: Equations 1–9 retain the same mathematical content, including the scaling formulation and Gaussian entropy conversion. Homoscedasticity was already assumed in v1 Appendix A. V2 adds empirical checks and interpretive qualifications, without new proofs or substantive mathematical derivations.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves inferential reliability by withdrawing the unsupported causal conclusion from confounded regimes, correcting the entropy interpretation, and adding test confirmation and targeted diagnostics. These address central weaknesses while preserving the canonical scaling evidence. Coverage is narrower and entropy remains approximate. An unresolved discrepancy—Figure 2's 200k-cell M-model loss near 1.57 versus Table 2's 1.462 under apparently matching settings—limits the auxiliary sweep, but does not outweigh the stronger validation and more defensible conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same scaling-law study. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching v1's canonical sweep to v2's standardized sweep.

after.justification: V2 retains the original standardized parameter sweep and reports held-out test results, a data-size sweep, residual diagnostics, and direct-NLL calibration outcomes.

before.justification: V1 reports original transformer-training outcomes and fitted scaling laws for two CELLxGENE regimes, including seed-level loss ranges and entropy-floor estimates in Tables 2–4.

results.title: Scaling Laws for Masked-Reconstruction Transformers on Single-Cell Transcriptomics

C1.justification: v1's abstract claims unique reconstruction of the simplest physical law. v2 instead states reconstruction of a representable, regularization-minimizing admissible law, with recovery of the unique true law requiring an additional identifiability condition. The conclusion likewise qualifies statements about network limits, substantially narrowing the headline guarantee to match the retained theory.

C2.justification: Section 4.1.2 substantially expands discussion of regularity, measurement injectivity and applicability beyond the earlier brief remarks. New experiments motivate explanations involving architectural misspecification, enlarged search spaces and local minima. The conclusion explicitly acknowledges limited numerical performance and distinguishes the analytical contribution from a mature numerical framework.

D1.justification: v2 adds substantial reproducibility information: early-stopping patience, regularization strength, derivative estimation, per-system architectures, restart and time budgets, forward solvers, grids and initial-condition generation. Tables 1, 3 and 6 organize these details. The documented code-access link also changes from an anonymous repository to a named GitHub repository.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from two linear 1D PDE examples to seven Strogatz ODE systems, the 2D Brusselator and a 2D membrane-transport system. These introduce coupled nonlinear dynamics, Laplacian-dependent laws, and polynomial, rational, trigonometric and exponential recovery tasks.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates separate competing recovery algorithms. The new comparisons vary ParFam architecture and structural constraints as ablations; cited approaches such as SINDy and EQL do not become evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce 10–80 ODE trajectories, system-specific architectures and optimization budgets, 64×64 and 32×32 PDE grids, and distinct measurement-resolution sweeps. They also introduce Savitzky–Golay derivative estimation and coefficient thresholding at 0.015 for error evaluation. These are additional protocols, not evidence that the original linear-PDE settings changed.

E4.justification: Beyond the original domain-dependent error analysis, v2 tests underspecified, default and extended architectures, and compares unconstrained recovery with additive diffusion constraints. Figures 3–7 also examine errors around trajectories and document difficult regimes, diffusion-coefficient recovery failures and variability across optimization runs.

E5.justification: v1 provides no repeated-run counts or uncertainty bands. v2 reports medians and interquartile ranges over 10 seeds for Figure 2, 15 seeds for the ODE experiments, and repeated-seed reporting for the 2D experiments. This establishes substantially stronger uncertainty reporting, without establishing how many runs underlay v1.

E6.justification: Figure 2 contains revised median curves, although the two displayed linear-PDE reconstruction formulas remain unchanged. Table 4 adds recovered ODE formulas and errors, including Lotka–Volterra errors of 0.14 and 0.11. Figures 4–7 add substantial PDE results, including unsuccessful diffusion recovery in the hard Brusselator regime and variable rational-term recovery in membrane transport.

M1.justification: The symbolic-network architecture, objective (Pm) and alternating optimization remain. Section 5.2.3 adds a constrained ParFam variant enforcing additive diffusion and excluding cross-terms between the Laplacian and state variables, a limited procedural extension.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially revised, related work becomes a separate section, and scope, novelty and organization receive dedicated subsections. Scattered assumption remarks become a structured discussion, and extensions receive their own subsection. This materially changes the narrative organization beyond simply inserting experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 3–7 and Tables 1–6, introducing extensive multipanel results, architecture comparisons and configuration summaries. Figure 2 is redrawn with uncertainty bands and revised captions. Wider text blocks and changed typography also substantially alter the document layout.

R1.justification: Six references are added, covering transport regularity, operator learning, variational regularization and Lasso; the earlier cited works are retained. Section 1.2 sharpens the distinction from existing all-at-once frameworks and ParFam/EQL by emphasizing the nontrivial verification of symbolic networks' function-space properties.

T1.justification: The principal definitions, assumptions, reconstruction theorem, identifiability corollary and Appendix A–C proofs are retained after renumbering. However, v2 drops v1 Remark 8's assertion that the sampling operators satisfy condition (5) while failing the stronger convergence conditions discussed there, removing a limited mathematical assertion.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's narrow validation on two linear examples through nonlinear ODE and 2D PDE experiments, architecture and structure tests, and explicit uncertainty reporting. Expanded implementation details improve reproducibility, while the abstract and conclusion better distinguish reconstruction from unique identification. The experiments still expose numerical failures, but reporting those failures and their variability makes the paper's practical scope considerably better supported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same symbolic PDE recovery framework. Their text, equations, figures, tables and Appendices A–C are readable and support comparison despite substantial reorganization and expanded experiments.

after.justification: Section 5 retains the linear-PDE experiments and reports original simulations and reconstruction results for seven nonlinear ODE systems and two 2D PDE systems.

before.justification: Section 4 and Figure 2 report original numerical reconstructions of two linear PDEs from simulated incomplete, noisy measurements.

results.title: Symbolic recovery of PDEs from measurement data

C1.justification: The central taxonomy and headline findings about claim-response entailment, claim-level scoring, and UAD remain unchanged. v2 foregrounds FactScore-STEM-Geo in the abstract and introduction, but v1 already identifies it as the authors' new dataset in Section 4.1. The fifth model expands supporting evidence.

C2.justification: v2 develops the explanation of claim-QA failures through ambiguous or answer-revealing questions, interprets domain-dependent aggregation behavior, and discusses threshold portability. It also adds substantive limitations concerning intermediate granularities, reasoning budgets, Wikipedia topic-selection bias, and over-reliance on filtered UAD outputs.

D1.justification: v2 specifies a single NVIDIA T4 GPU for the retained runtime measurements, explains unavailable Llama-4 log probabilities, quantifies matched-claim comparison costs, and documents UAD implementation outputs. These are additional disclosures; the dataset-construction code and all eight prompt templates are unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the same 500 FactScore-Bio and 400 FactScore-STEM-Geo prompts. Appendix A.3 adds a cross-domain deployment scenario: thresholds calibrated on one dataset are applied to the other without target-domain calibration labels.

E2.justification: v2 adds normalized sequence probability as a white-box comparator alongside the four retained short-form black-box baselines in response-level evaluation. Tables 4 and 19–21 report this comparator for the original four LLMs; Llama-4 is excluded because its inference API did not expose log probabilities.

E3.justification: v2 adds Llama-4-Maverick-17B and substantial new evaluation protocols: 400 stratified units per grader-validation condition, manual assessment of 410 claims from 15 responses, and 50/50 calibration/test splits with F1-maximizing threshold searches. The original response-sampling budgets and main evaluation metrics are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained sample-count ablations, v2 adds alternate-grader robustness, manual decomposition validation, cross-dataset and cross-scorer threshold transfer, and aggregation sensitivity analysis (Appendix A.1–A.3 and Section 4.4). These substantially expand checks on measurement reliability and deployment behavior.

E5.justification: Table 6 newly reports chance-corrected inter-grader agreement using Cohen's kappa. Neither version reports repeated-run seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests for the main performance comparisons; the existing descriptive plus/minus reporting convention is retained.

E6.justification: The shared four-model classification/calibration entries and Bio correlations are unchanged. v2 adds Llama-4 results, STEM-Geo response correlations, and validation/transfer outcomes. Examples include Llama-4 Bio claim-response AUROC of 0.791, grader kappa of 0.63–0.84, and decomposition faithfulness of 409/410. The new STEM-Geo correlations reveal different scorer rankings from Bio.

M1.justification: Sections 3.4 and 4.4 add minimum, geometric-mean, and rank-weighted response aggregation as evaluated alternatives. The decomposition procedures, four scorer families, and uncertainty-aware decoding rule remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the original wording are retained. v2 makes local language corrections, expands discussion passages, organizes Appendices A and B into named subsections, and updates publication, contact, contribution, and employment disclosures.

P2.justification: v2 adds novelty and validation/transfer tables, converts four rotated classification/calibration tables into eight upright tables, and substantially rearranges Figures 5 and 13 into aligned five-model panels. UAD and sample-count plots gain Llama-4 panels. The workflow figures and calibration Figure 14 are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to Nikitin et al. on kernel language entropy and Bai et al. on LongBench v2. New Table 2 clarifies which existing scorer configurations reproduce, generalize, or extend prior work. Numerous other reference changes update publication metadata for already cited works.

T1.justification: Table 22 explicitly defines the claim-diversity ratio as N_m-union/N_claim; v1 only states the approximate count relationship in its computational-cost discussion. This is a limited measurement-definition addition. The formal scorer equations, centrality definitions, and UAD rule are retained, with no new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1 relies on unvalidated grading and decomposition and reports response-level correlations only for Bio. v2 adds alternate-grader and manual checks, completes the STEM-Geo response-level comparison, and tests aggregation and threshold portability. These additions materially strengthen the evaluation and clarify applicability limits. The small 15-response manual audit and remaining narrative/table ranking inconsistencies limit the conclusions, but the overall gains in evidential support and usability are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including material reorganized between versions.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds Llama-4 evaluations, grader and decomposition validation, threshold-transfer results, and aggregation comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original hallucination-detection, calibration, response-level correlation, uncertainty-aware decoding, and sample-count experiments across four LLMs and two datasets.

results.title: Fine-Grained Uncertainty Quantification for Long-Form Language Model Outputs: A Comparative Study

C1.justification: v1 presents a general-purpose unified model for arbitrary incomplete scenarios and emphasizes a novel diffusion-transformer paradigm and demonstrated clinical applicability. v3 explicitly defines unification as a shared framework with task-specific models, positions MDiT3D as a tailored DiT conditioning interface, and qualifies clinical deployment as potential. These materially narrow the central scope and novelty claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive limitations concerning fixed modality vocabularies, compression-related detail loss, and hallucinated anatomy. Appendix D explicitly states that scanner, institution, protocol, and population shifts were not evaluated. It also explains how prompts complement available latents, while Appendix C.7 links completeness-prediction errors to contrast drift, modality bias, and blurred structures.

D1.justification: v3 adds CoPeVAE parameter/FLOP and wall-clock training costs, inference latency/VRAM, and measurement conditions in Section 4.5. It reconciles cardiac training details, including the main-text batch size with the value 64 already present in v1's appendix. Most architecture specifications, preprocessing, optimization settings, sampling details, and the code-access statement remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The same brain and cardiac datasets are used. Downstream BraTS segmentation coverage expands from three real modalities plus one synthesized modality to one real modality plus three synthesized modalities (v3 Appendix C.8/Table 21), adding a more severely incomplete input scenario within the existing task.

E2.justification: The primary synthesis comparisons expand from six to nine baselines by adding DiffM4RI, APT, and ASLDM (v3 Tables 1–3). These methods also enter the retained single-synthetic-modality segmentation comparison (v3 Table 7 versus v1 Table 12). APT was cited in v1 but was not evaluated there.

E3.justification: v3 adds MAE and FVD, lesion-restricted metrics, frozen nnU-Net anatomical evaluation with Dice/HD95, and pretext-task accuracy/macro-F1. New protocols exclude specified modality combinations from both training stages and standardize inference-cost measurements. The cardiac tokenizer's training-step table changes from 200k to 100k, resolving disagreement with v1's existing 100k prose; this does not establish that training was rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's existing component, injection-position, backbone, and prompt-corruption analyses, v3 adds position-prompt replacement with mask codes, structured prompt interventions, unseen-combination robustness, lesion/anatomical fidelity, computational-cost analysis, perception accuracy, and synthesis errors grouped by prediction correctness. Figures 13–14 also introduce explicit failure analyses linking incorrect completeness predictions to degraded synthesis.

E5.justification: v1 includes ± values without an explicit multi-seed analysis. v3 Appendix C.2/Table 15 reports means and standard deviations across three independent seeds for CoPeDiT, M2DN, and ASLDM on two challenging brain settings. Figure 13 adds subgroup sample counts and dispersion. Conversely, the primary comparison tables remove the FID ± values reported in v1.

E6.justification: All 168 retained primary PSNR/SSIM/FID point estimates match, and the original segmentation results remain. v3 adds extensive baseline, metric, robustness, diagnostic, and computational results. Its new three-synthetic-modality segmentation experiment reports 87.70% average Dice for CoPeDiT, while APT slightly leads tumor-core Dice, 87.64% versus 87.49% (Table 21). These are new-setting results, not changes to v1's retained 90.23% single-synthetic-modality average. The original corruption-study SSIM/FID curves are omitted.

M1.justification: The CoPeVAE pretext tasks, prompt construction, alternating MDiT3D blocks, targeted prompt injection, and diffusion objective remain unchanged. v3 explains task-specific variants and conditioning more explicitly, but these procedures already appear in v1's methodology, architecture figures, ablations, and appendix.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method explanations, and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting. Existing segmentation and prompt-sensitivity material moves into the main text, while injection-position and backbone ablations move to Appendix C.4. The experimental narrative is reorganized, prompt-token terminology is standardized, and dedicated limitations and discussion sections are added.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column layout to a single-column journal format. The combined brain-results table is split, tables gain metric columns and comparator rows, and qualitative panels expand with error maps and additional examples. The motivation figure is redesigned, existing t-SNE and attention displays are merged, and new intervention, accuracy, failure-case, and segmentation figures are introduced.

R1.justification: Section 2 expands to broader medical image generation, reconstruction, and completion, incorporating works such as Text2CT, MAISI-v2, and DiffuX2CT alongside newer MRI methods. The introduction also explicitly repositions MDiT3D as an adaptation of DiT rather than a fundamentally new paradigm, substantially revising the novelty framing.

T1.justification: The sample partition, classification and contrastive losses, combined tokenizer loss, and diffusion objective in Equations 1–5 are mathematically unchanged. The x-prediction/x0-prediction terminology change is equivalent. Neither version supplies additional theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens support for the unchanged method through additional competitive baselines, explicit three-seed checks, held-out-combination tests, lesion-level validation, and observed failure analyses. These address gaps behind v1's broad reliability and applicability claims. Clearer definitions of unification and explicit domain-shift limitations also improve claim accuracy. Removing primary-table FID uncertainty is a reporting loss, and seed coverage remains limited, but the stronger validation and better-qualified conclusions provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CoPeDiT for brain missing-modality and cardiac missing-slice synthesis. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, multi-seed experiments, unseen-combination tests, computational measurements, and diagnostic analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original MRI synthesis comparisons, component ablations, prompt-corruption experiments, and downstream tumor-segmentation results, including supplementary material.

results.title: Exploiting Completeness Perception with Diffusion Transformer for Unified 3D MRI Synthesis

C1.justification: The central two-adapter contribution remains. v2 qualifies v1's broad claims about learned weighting superiority and wider applicability, explicitly presenting a shared design perspective with dataset-dependent benefits. It also qualifies the chosen ORDER skips as a runtime-memory choice rather than the raw-accuracy optimum, and describes LAW as competitive with the strongest KiTS19 augmentation baseline.

C2.justification: v2 substantially revises mechanism explanations and limitations. It explicitly rejects interpreting ORDER's scalar gate as a boundary-uncertainty estimator, acknowledges that SE recovers most of the segmentation gain, and explains the accuracy-versus-runtime rationale for skip selection. Removing LAW's upper clamp is now described as degrading image quality while remaining numerically stable, rather than causing collapse. Dataset-specific weaknesses and hardware-dependent profiling limits are also discussed.

D1.justification: v2 adds substantial implementation documentation: mask resizing and loss broadcasting, ORDER normalization/projections and gate construction, preprocessing and sample counts, checkpoint selection, DDIM sampling settings, and LAW's training-only overhead. New Appendix A consolidates hyperparameters, including prompt dropout, attention dimensions, weight decay, and the scheduler floor. These disclosures considerably improve reproducibility beyond v1's brief setup paragraph.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates polyp imaging and KiTS19 kidney CT. v2 adds BRISC brain MRI to LAW synthesis and downstream augmentation, and to ORDER segmentation. This substantially broadens the represented anatomy and imaging modalities.

E2.justification: The segmentation comparison removes UNeXt and adds PraNet (v1 Table 3 versus v2 Table 7). v2 Table 8 additionally evaluates matched SE and CBAM skip-attention controls on the ORDER backbone, substantially strengthening the comparator set. The main synthesis comparators—ControlNet, ArSDM, and Adaptive Distillation—remain.

E3.justification: Reported LAW training changes from approximately 500 steps with batch size 4 to 1000 Polyps or 2000 KiTS19/BRISC steps with batch size 20. ORDER training inputs change from 512×512 to 256×256. v2 adds held-out synthesis and frozen-nnUNet mask-recovery protocols, specifies cleaned Polyps splits, and changes ORDER aggregation from averaging test-image metrics to averaging Kvasir and CVC-ClinicDB subset metrics.

E4.justification: v2 adds synthetic-data dose response, an isolated maximum-weight-clamp ablation, matched SE/CBAM controls, and latency/memory profiling (Tables 5, 6, 8, and 9). The existing ORDER stage-selection analysis is revised into an internal-development-split study. v1's reported Dice-on-ratio-prior check is removed. These changes substantially expand analysis of component necessity and practical tradeoffs.

E5.justification: v1 gives point estimates without reporting seeds or repeated-run uncertainty. v2 introduces five-seed mean±standard-deviation reporting for main synthesis, augmentation, segmentation, and ORDER ablation results, specifying seeds 0–4 for ORDER. LAW's component ablation is explicitly identified as single-run. This establishes expanded statistical reporting, not a known increase from a documented v1 run count.

E6.justification: Numerous results are replaced or added. LAW's KiTS19 FID changes from 63.12 in v1 Table 1 to 50.13±0.44 in v2 Table 1. ORDER's Polyps Dice/IoU changes from 81.3/81.7 to 76.3±1.9/67.2±2.0 under the cleaned protocol. These are revised-condition results, not established same-setting gains or losses. New held-out, BRISC, mask-recovery, dose-response, and profiling results appear; the revised ORDER ablation favors mixed skips {1,2} instead of {0,1} for raw Dice.

M1.justification: LAW's stated training objective changes substantially: v1 Equation 12 includes teacher and distillation losses with weights 0.05, whereas v2 Equation 10 retains only weighted denoising and Dice regularization. This removes teacher/distillation terms from the specified procedure. The ratio-prior/delta-map mechanism and ORDER's gated bidirectional skips remain; expanded ORDER implementation descriptions alone do not establish architectural changes.

P1.justification: The abstract, contributions, results discussion, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Experiments are reorganized from shared setup and separate results/ablation sections into self-contained LAW and ORDER sections, each with datasets, implementation, baselines, results, and ablations. Method explanations expand and an implementation appendix is added.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands and restructures the displays with separate held-out synthesis, mask-recovery, dose-response, attention-control, runtime, and hyperparameter tables. It adds KiTS19/BRISC synthesis examples in Figure 7 and expands v1's ORDER qualitative figure into v2 Figure 9 with BRISC examples. Existing conceptual diagrams and LAW delta-map images are largely retained or relocated, rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: The main research lineage remains ControlNet, ArSDM, Adaptive Distillation, and MK-UNet. v2 adds Fateh et al. for BRISC and Tian et al. for foreground-aware object-centric learning, while removing references including UNeXt, BIOMEDICA, DISK, the Medical Segmentation Decathlon, and the AdEMAMix paper. Positioning becomes more qualified, without a wholesale related-work reorientation.

T1.justification: Formal revisions are localized to method definitions: v1's teacher/distillation loss definitions and total objective are replaced by v2's two-term objective, and v2 explicitly formulates the confidence gate and attention output projections. Neither version supplies theorems or proofs. The added standard Dice/IoU formulas are explanatory rather than new theory.

improvement.justification: v1's underspecified, point-estimate evaluations and inconsistent overlap entries, such as ORDER Dice 81.3 versus IoU 81.7, are substantially improved by explicit evaluation protocols, five-seed reporting, direct mask-recovery tests, matched attention controls, and Appendix A. More qualified conclusions better reflect the evidence. These changes materially improve assessability and reproducibility. Some inconsistency remains, notably Figure 4's collapse warning versus Table 6's numerically stable no-upper-clamp result.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LAW and ORDER research. Their complete text, equations, tables, and figures support comparison. v1 ends with references and has no appendix; v2 includes a readable implementation appendix.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments across Polyps, KiTS19, and BRISC, including synthesis, mask recovery, augmentation, segmentation, attention controls, and runtime profiling.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthesis, downstream augmentation, segmentation, and ablation results for LAW and ORDER in Tables 1–6.

results.title: LAW & ORDER: Adaptive Spatial Weighting for Medical Diffusion and Segmentation

C1.justification: v1 claims incompatible geometries, no common refinement and no procedure satisfying all four criteria. v3 instead claims non-nesting of componentwise classes, explicitly permits compatible guarantees and replaces 'No universal procedure' with 'No universal certificate.' The abstract also withdraws martingale necessity for general Blackwell admissibility and qualifies the coverage and approachability claims.

C2.justification: v3 distinguishes empirical calibration from self-predictive martingale coherence and explains why calibration does not imply log-loss optimality. It interprets constrained Bayes as separate criterion-specific optimization problems and explains compatibility despite non-nesting. Applications become motivations, Gaussian extensions require further verification, and covariate-shift overcoverage is explicitly interpreted outside the exchangeability guarantee.

D1.justification: v3 supplies the clipping transformation and epsilon=10^-6, identifies simulated versus theoretical table quantities, and documents initialization and split-conformal rank/tie-breaking details. These improve technical specification; they do not establish how v1's computations were implemented. No code or data-access resource is added.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same Bernoulli prediction and testing tasks and the same heteroskedastic Gaussian conformal scenarios involving Uniform and Beta covariates. The removed Gaussian location laboratory was analytical, not an additional empirical dataset or simulation.

E2.justification: The simulations retain Bayes versus plug-in MLE and likelihood-ratio e-process versus five-look z-testing. Clipping is presented as numerical handling of the MLE comparison. KT, discounted e-processes and dogmatic-prior predictors are theoretical witnesses, not new experimental baseline competitors.

E3.justification: The reported log-loss evaluation separates clipped numerical loss from theoretical unclipped risk, and the boundary diagnostic changes from an empirical frequency to an exact model probability. Sample sizes, testing thresholds, peeking schedule and conformal calibration/test sizes remain unchanged. The PDFs do not establish whether v1 already used clipping internally.

E4.justification: v3 adds an analytical failure check for fixed clipping: Table 2 states that it destroys plug-in martingale self-consistency and permits CApp feasibility only on the restricted parameter interval. Section 8.1 also quantifies boundary events below Monte Carlo resolution. The existing conformal covariate-shift analysis is retained.

E5.justification: Both versions state 10,000 Monte Carlo replications. Neither reports seeds, confidence intervals, standard errors or significance tests, and v3 establishes no increase in repeated runs or new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: The central risk table is substantially corrected: v1 Table 4 reports finite MLE risk, including 2.368 at n=5; v3 Table 3 reports clipped risk 1.286 and theoretical unclipped risk infinity at every n. These are differently specified quantities, not a same-setting performance gain. Under retained settings, e-process/peeking rejection rates change from 0.034/0.169 to 0.031/0.165, and conformal coverages change from 0.897/0.964/0.888 to 0.900/0.946/0.900.

M1.justification: The work remains a theoretical analysis of existing prediction and inference procedures. The predictive-system tuple and new separation witnesses revise the formal framework, without introducing a new predictive algorithm. The experimental Bayes predictor, likelihood-ratio construction and conformal procedure are retained.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contributions and discussion are extensively rewritten. Sections 4–6 gain substantial explanatory structure, terminology and scope remarks; proofs previously deferred to appendices appear alongside revised statements. The Gaussian laboratory and duality subsection disappear, and Applications becomes Motivations and Interpretations.

P2.justification: Several diagrams are redrawn or relabelled, especially the explicitly schematic risk plot and simplified coverage plot. The procedure-to-geometry diagram is removed, and the constrained-Bayes diagram is reorganized. The extended classification table is removed, a separation-witness table is added, and the classification and log-loss tables receive substantial structural revisions.

R1.justification: Positioning shifts from incompatible paradigms and a purported counterexample to martingale posteriors toward qualified, modular certificate transfer. v3 adds an explicit comparison with Choe and Ramdas on filtration transport and draws on Dawid, Krichevsky–Trofimov and misspecification literature. It removes the companion-paper framing and associated citations, alongside the Blackwell lecture framing.

T1.justification: v3 replaces risk-set closedness with upper-hull closedness, adds support/continuity conditions for Bayes admissibility, and replaces v1's varying-prior martingale equivalence under every true law with a single-prior implication under the prior predictive law. It revises AV dominance and restricts the martingale equivalence to point nulls. New definitions and proofs introduce rank-family coverage efficiency, the predictive-system space, active-coordinate separation witnesses and precise CApp feasibility. The Gaussian separation proposition and formal Lagrangian proposition are removed; appendix proofs are partly relocated and substantially superseded.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially improves the alignment of claims, proofs and numerical evidence. It corrects v1's inference from non-nesting to incompatibility, distinguishes the laws supporting martingale statements, supplies missing qualifications for Bayes admissibility, and resolves the finite-versus-infinite MLE risk presentation. The explicit separation witnesses strengthen the central argument. Generality is reduced, including withdrawal of the Gaussian extension, but this trades unsupported breadth for more defensible conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with readable text, equations, figures and tables. All supplied pages were inspected, including v1 Appendices A–B; their contents were matched to retained, revised or removed material in v3, which has no separate appendices.

after.justification: Section 8 retains the three original Monte Carlo studies and reports revised numerical results in Tables 3–5.

before.justification: Section 8 reports three original Monte Carlo studies of Bernoulli prediction, sequential testing and conformal coverage, with results in Tables 4–6.

results.title: Bayes with No Shame: Admissibility Geometries of Predictive Inference

C1.justification: Alongside the retained claims of separating behavior-related dynamics and scaling to large neural recordings, v2 adds prominent claims of interpretability advantages over latent-state readouts and post hoc dLDS analysis. The abstract and introduction also elevate previously unreported hindbrain asymmetry into a principal biological contribution.

C2.justification: v2 interprets comparable reconstruction with sparser behavioral mappings as support for dynamics-based readouts, develops a biological interpretation of hindbrain asymmetry, and discusses possible imaging artifacts. It explicitly limits the CLDS comparison's scope and acknowledges that robustness does not guarantee a unique identifiable decomposition. The original explicit nonstationarity interpretation of trial-type segmentation is softened.

D1.justification: v2 supplies detailed settings for the added model comparisons and TaskRNN experiments, optimization budgets, trial-type definitions, and expanded model-selection guidance. Table 3 adds runtime and memory estimates with measurement caveats. New availability statements promise zebrafish data upon request and simulation data/code upon publication; they do not establish an existing public release.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation on delayanti task-trained RNN activations, with processing, memory, and response phases and 23 input/output behavior traces (Figure 4). This substantially broadens coverage beyond the retained two-system simulations and zebrafish recording. The revised 14,000-neuron wording does not establish new zebrafish coverage: Appendix B retains the original recording and preprocessing counts.

E2.justification: The CLDS and PSID comparisons remain. v2 adds explicit zebrafish comparisons against unsupervised dLDS with post hoc behavior correlations and b-dLDS-x, including regularized and separately optimized variants (Table 3). b-dLDS-x also provides the comparator in the new TaskRNN experiment.

E3.justification: New protocols include fitting TaskRNN models on 64 of 80 trials, inference on all 80, Bayesian hyperparameter optimization, and 500-iteration final fits (Appendix B.4.2). v2 also introduces matched-size zebrafish controls, 500-iteration sensitivity sweeps, and interpretability/asymmetry metrics. The retained simulation and zebrafish parameter tables largely preserve v1's settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds ablations of the Psi penalty and step-size rescaling (Supplementary Figure 5), behavior-supervision and latent-state-readout comparisons (Table 3), TaskRNN regularization sweeps (Table 1), and model-size/regularization sensitivity studies (Supplementary Figure 11, Table 8). New asymmetry analyses examine imaging-related baselines. These directly test components and failure conditions previously receiving little experimental scrutiny.

E5.justification: v2 adds baseline-asymmetry t-tests, reporting p<0.04 and p<0.001, and descriptive standard deviations in Table 2. It also documents three-seed TaskRNN runs and provides seedwise results and averages for new zebrafish comparisons and sensitivity sweeps. The original ten-seed CLDS comparison is retained; an increase in its run count is not reported.

E6.justification: New results include TaskRNN behavior R² of 0.99 versus 0.95 for b-dLDS and b-dLDS-x, extensive variant/sensitivity results, and six of 25 operators exceeding the 17% asymmetry baseline. The single-behavior zebrafish fit is replaced: v1 Figure 4 reports R²=0.90, whereas v2 Figure 5 reports neural R²=0.91 with different learned operators. Retained appendix displays also change operator 23's Psi value from 0.59 to 0.44 and operator 24's behavior R² from 0.22 to 0.11.

M1.justification: v2 introduces the experimental b-dLDS-x variant, moving the behavioral readout and associated reconstruction objective from dynamics coefficients c to latent states x. The central b-dLDS architecture and inference procedure remain; Frobenius regularization and step-size rescaling were already present in v1.

P1.justification: The six-section main-text organization and much of the existing prose remain. v2 refines state-versus-dynamics explanations, rewrites the conclusion, reorganizes appendix subsections, and replaces acknowledgments with availability sections and an impact statement. Editorial changes are concentrated around the larger scientific additions.

P2.justification: v2 adds the TaskRNN Figure 4, Supplementary Figures 5 and 11, and six tables covering comparisons, asymmetry, settings, and sensitivity. It replaces the single-behavior zebrafish visualizations, revises Figure 3's labels, and reformats parameter tables with row separators. Original Tables 1–2 become Tables 5 and 7, while several simulation figures remain identical.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning through zebrafish laterality literature supporting its new hindbrain-asymmetry claim, Driscoll et al. (2024) for TaskRNN, and dictionary-learning identifiability work by Wu et al., Hu and Huang, and Cohen and Gillis. The original CLDS, PSID, and dLDS positioning is retained.

T1.justification: Equations 12–13 correct the differentiation variable from D to Psi, and Equation 13 places the Frobenius penalty inside the differentiated objective and adds an explicit update expansion. These are mathematical corrections beyond typesetting. Appendix A's connectivity derivation and assumptions remain unchanged, and no identifiability theorem is added.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps in v1 through comparisons within the dLDS family, the TaskRNN experiment, component ablations, and sensitivity studies (Figure 4, Table 3, Supplementary Figures 5 and 11). These substantially strengthen evidence for the central modeling choice and expose failure conditions. Detailed settings and explicit identifiability limitations improve transparency. The new asymmetry claim remains based on one fish, and resource estimates are acknowledged as rough, but these limitations do not outweigh the methodological validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Behavior-dLDS study. The complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–B are readable and support reliable matching across the revision.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds TaskRNN experiments, model comparisons, ablations, sensitivity studies, and quantitative zebrafish asymmetry analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulation experiments, comparisons with CLDS and PSID, and b-dLDS analyses of zebrafish hindbrain recordings in Section 5 and Appendix B.
