C1.justification: The central bottleneck, distance-degradation, and two-failure-mode claims remain. V2 qualifies the abstract and introduction to acknowledge that spatial information is only sometimes implicitly preserved and may lack linear encoding altogether. It extends the stated model scope and lists counterfactual sample construction as a separate contribution.

C2.justification: V2 specifies CARLA appearance biases and limits real-image support to presence and count (Section 6). Appendix C cautiously suggests that DriveFusionQA fine-tuning may weaken count information's influence on generation while preserving decodability, explicitly acknowledging unresolved causality. Section 5.2.3 removes v1's explanation linking InternVL3.5's poor transfer to insufficiently general concept directions.

D1.justification: V2 documents training-set statistics for standardization, the added models' architecture details, steering normalization, five tested steering strengths per sample, and DriveFusionQA's specific prompt. It removes v1's approximate image-resolution caps for Ovis2.5 and VST. The code-access statement and core data-generation and split details remain.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same eight CARLA categories covering presence, count, spatial relationship, and orientation, with the same distance and environment coverage. Both evaluate transfer to nuScenes Presence-Real and Count-Real. Additional models and steering measurements use retained task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds Qwen3-VL-2B and DriveFusionQA to comparisons previously comprising Ovis2.5, InternVL3.5, VST-SFT, and VST-RL. Their participation is documented in Figures 4–7 and Tables 4–5. This substantially broadens architectural comparisons and adds an autonomous-driving specialist.

E3.justification: Section 4.4 changes the reported probe formulation to training-set-standardized inputs. Section 5.3 explicitly trains new final-token-only probes to match the representation used for generation. Appendix C adds a quantitative steering protocol using 50 randomly selected samples per model/category, an unsteered baseline, explicit success and exclusion rules, and revised prompts. Existing map splits remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V1 demonstrates steering through selected examples; v2 adds systematic success-rate analysis across six models and six categories, including failures (Table 6). It also tests whether main patterns survive confidence-lower-bound estimates (Figures 8–9) and extends sparse-logit case studies to Qwen3-VL and DriveFusionQA. Existing cosine-similarity and real-data transfer analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report ten probe-training runs and their variability. V2 additionally calculates 95% Wilson confidence-interval lower bounds for every main heatmap entry and displays their chance-corrected counterparts in Appendix B. This adds systematic finite-test-sample uncertainty assessment; it does not increase the reported run count.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive results for two models and revises shared-model probe results. For example, Table 4 reports InternVL3.5 Presence-Real accuracy as 67.3% (113/168) in v1 and 81.5% (137/168) in v2. Table 5 changes Ovis2.5 Presence-2 generation accuracy from 90.1% to 91.0%. New steering results include DriveFusionQA Count-1 success of 7.9% (3/38). Revised probe procedures prevent interpreting probe-score differences as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The counterfactual construction, pooling, and linear-probing framework remains. V2 introduces final-token-only probes for cognitive-failure diagnosis (Section 5.3) and replaces steering with directly averaged probe weights by variance-rescaled, unit-normalized directions (Appendix C versus v1 Appendix B). These refine existing components.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized prose revisions, expands methodological and limitation explanations, adds a statistical-analysis subsection and appendix, and adjusts the contribution list. Most narrative and section organization is retained. Publication headers and review information are also added.

P2.justification: Figures 4–7 are reorganized into six-model displays. Table 1 adds model rows and a fine-tuning column; Tables 3–5 are revised or expanded. V2 adds two confidence-bound heatmaps and a quantitative steering table, and expands the successful-logit-analysis table with two cases. These substantially change the presentation of evidence beyond numerical updates or pagination.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for Qwen3-VL, DriveFusionQA, inference-time intervention, CARLA2Real, and Wilson intervals, while removing Kim et al. (2025). Section 2.4 more explicitly connects Fu et al. (2025b) to cognitive failure. The broader related-work organization and principal positioning remain.

T1.justification: V2 adds mathematical definitions for standardized probing and variance-rescaled, normalized steering, plus the argument that affine standardization preserves linear separability for probes with bias (Section 4.4 and Appendix C). The original pooling definitions and chance-corrected accuracy formula remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses an important validity gap: cognitive-failure probes now use the same final-token representation as generation, whereas v1 also supplied pooled visual tokens (Section 5.3, Figure 7). Quantitative steering with explicit denominators, broader model comparisons, and test-sample uncertainty analysis substantially strengthen the evidence beyond selected examples and training-run variability. Steering success remains conditional on valid descriptions, and real-image validation still covers only presence and count; v2 explains these boundaries more clearly.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same counterfactual probing study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: V2 reports original probing and transfer results, expanded model comparisons, quantitative steering outcomes, and additional statistical analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original CARLA probing experiments, activation-steering outcomes, nuScenes transfer evaluations, and analyses of generated logits.

C1.justification: The new contribution list explicitly claims first pre-additive, energy-score spatiotemporal frameworks and first stationarity analysis for this model class, and presents existing architectures as special cases. The conclusion narrows the stated theoretical contribution to closed-loop versions. The principal forecasting contributions and abstract performance claims remain stable.

C2.justification: Sections 3 and 9 newly qualify extrapolation benefits because classical engression's monotonicity assumptions fail in realistic spatiotemporal settings. Section 5.2 distinguishes idealized closed-loop theory from finite-sample forecasting without hidden-state noise. v2 also adds substantive interpretations of ablation-induced distribution collapse, model-selection tradeoffs, and recalibration as a response to overconfidence.

D1.justification: Appendix E.1 newly specifies library-default configurations for several baselines, original-paper settings for others, validation tuning of LSTM, and common input/output windows. Section 8 documents the ablation construction and MSE computation. A package-documentation link is added; the existing code repository, hardware descriptions, and proposed-model search ranges are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use Japan and China tuberculosis, USA influenza-like illness, Belgium COVID-19, Colombia dengue, and Hungary chickenpox data, alongside the same simulation setting and Guainia motivating example. The new ablations reuse existing dataset and task coverage.

E2.justification: Figure 1 adds an evaluated DeepAR median and probabilistic cloud to the Guainia comparison, which previously showed ARIMA, ARNN, LSTM, and MVEN. The twelve external baselines in the main forecasting comparisons remain unchanged; v2 additionally introduces the component controls assessed under E4.

E3.justification: Section 8 adds controlled experiments with identical hyperparameters, moving noise to the output or replacing energy-score training with MSE averaged over two sampled trajectories. The original temporal splits, forecast horizons, training budgets, and evaluation ensemble sizes remain unchanged. The added baseline configuration paragraph primarily supplies previously undocumented settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds systematic pre-additive versus post-additive noise and energy-score versus MSE ablations for all three architectures across the retained datasets and horizons. Tables 14–16, the MCB comparisons in Figure 12, and PIT plots in Figure 14 substantially extend v1's toy loss illustration and existing explainability analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions report means and standard deviations over 50 forecast-generation evaluations of a trained model, use 200 simulation trials, and employ MCB comparisons. The added ablations follow the existing reporting practices; they do not establish increased training repetitions, new seed reporting, or a new uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: The existing benchmark, coverage, and runtime values are retained after renumbering. Tables 14–16 add extensive component results: for Japan's six-month horizon, GCEN CRPS is 4.23, versus 5.90 for GCEN-Post and 6.11 for GCEN-MSE. New aggregate rankings and calibration findings accompany these results, and Figure 1 adds DeepAR and revises the displayed MVEN fit.

M1.justification: Equation (1) corrects the spatial-distance formula from cos(longitude_i)cos(longitude_j) to cos(latitude_i)cos(latitude_j), refining the specified graph and spatial-weight construction. The MVEN, GCEN, and STEN architectures and Algorithms 1–4 otherwise remain unchanged. The PDFs do not establish an implementation change or rerun.

P1.justification: Focused revisions rewrite the background and theoretical implications, expand the motivating explanation, shorten redundant STEN exposition, and add an explicit contribution list. A dedicated ablation section, broader-impact statement, and acknowledgements are introduced, while the overall methodological narrative and Appendix A–G organization remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 adopts substantially different typography and page layout, expands Figure 1 to three panels, moves the architecture diagram from v1 Figure 13 to main-text Figure 2, and adds ablation tables and plots. It removes v1's split schematic, historical-series figure, and adjacency heatmaps, and rearranges existing appendix tables and figures.

R1.justification: v2 positions engression alongside mixture density networks and normalizing flows, adding Bishop and Papamakarios citations. It also adds Jaeger for hidden-state perturbations and Hu for spatial extrapolation, while removing several introductory forecasting references. The Kipf citation's publication update refers to the same work and does not constitute a new research connection.

T1.justification: Equation (1) corrects the Haversine distance definition by replacing longitude cosine factors with latitude factors. The formal ergodicity definitions, assumptions A1–A6, theorems, corollaries, and Appendix A proofs otherwise retain their mathematical substance; expanded practical remarks mainly concern interpretation.

improvement.justification: The systematic component controls in Section 8 and Tables 14–16 address an important gap in v1: empirical support for the central noise-placement and loss-function choices relied largely on motivation and a toy illustration. Clearer limits on theoretical applicability, the distance-formula correction, and baseline configuration disclosure further strengthen the paper. These gains outweigh the loss of descriptive figures and some overstated new interpretations, particularly claims of spatial-model statistical superiority despite overlapping intervals in Figure 12.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same spatiotemporal engression work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–G are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds component ablations with numerical results in Tables 14–16 and associated ranking and calibration plots.

before.justification: v1 reports original closed-loop simulations, forecasting experiments on six epidemic datasets, and analyses of calibration, noise propagation, and spatial importance.

results.title: Deep Generative Spatiotemporal Engression for Probabilistic Forecasting of Epidemics

C1.justification: The two central contributions—temporal synthetic priors and time-aware architecture—remain. However, the abstract and conclusion replace broad state-of-the-art claims with improvements over evaluated baselines. The introduction also drops v1's categorical claim that existing PFNs are unsuitable as time-series foundation models, describing limitations in particular forecasting settings instead.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of robustness and calibration: it distinguishes tolerance of irrelevant features from degradation when informative covariates are weakened, and interprets gradual degradation as resistance to spurious signals. It also attributes SRNGN gains under fixed budgets to covariate–target relationship complexity. Existing limitations concerning quadratic attention, scarce context, and synthetic-prior coverage remain.

D1.justification: Expanded Appendix C documents evaluation windows, horizons, aggregation, preprocessing, and future-covariate selection. New Appendix D and Table 6 specify model dimensions, checkpoints, baseline implementations, optimizer, precision, quantile estimation, and checkpoint averaging. Dataset access descriptions change from GIFT-Eval/LOTSA to Monash, EPFtoolbox, and fev-bench. ApolloPFN code is identified as internal, not newly released.

E1.justification: v2 adds daily UCI Air Quality CO forecasting and hourly solar-generation forecasting with weather covariates (Table 3 and Appendix C.3). Appendix E.1 also introduces M5 scenarios with corrupted or irrelevant exogenous inputs. Existing M5, electricity-market, and univariate benchmark coverage remains.

E2.justification: AutoARIMAX and Prophet are added to the existing M5 and electricity comparisons, substantially broadening comparisons beyond foundation models. The four original foundation-model comparators remain, and the univariate comparator set is unchanged. Chronos-2 is discussed but explicitly left for future evaluation.

E3.justification: The stated training sample range changes from 34–512 in v1 to 10–512 context samples in v2. Added experiments introduce 37 air-quality windows with 14-day horizons, 51 solar windows with 24-hour horizons, controlled 50% covariate perturbations, and multi-level coverage evaluation. P1.justification: The main section sequence and most existing prose are retained. v2 makes local wording and terminology refinements, adds scope qualifications and appendix cross-references, updates publication text, and appends Sections F–I. Existing figure images are retained, but captions are extensively revised, Figure 4 changes from a two-by-two arrangement to one row, Table 2 and other displays move, and publication headers and colored links alter the presentation.

improvement.justification: The additional backbone, appearance-shift, and driving-task evaluations substantially address v1's narrow empirical coverage. E5.justification: v1 already reports means and standard deviations over three seeds in Tables 3–4. v2 retains this practice and extends mean/std reporting to additional results. No increased run count, new uncertainty-estimation procedure, confidence intervals or significance tests are reported.

C1.justification: The central contribution is redefined from addressing GNN dominance and single-granularity modeling through a multiscale hybrid to grounding reusable fragment identities in occurrence-specific atomic context. v2 explicitly positions the architecture as serving this token-grounding problem rather than generic hybrid novelty. Related-work subsections are reorganized, experimental explanations are expanded, and the appendix is substantially restructured, including relocation of the GNN-depth discussion.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates comparison methods. S4, Mamba and transformer research appear as related work, not experimentally tested baselines.

E3.justification: Neither version reports experimental splits, metrics, training budgets or testing procedures. The revised streaming-memory accounting concerns theoretical guarantees.

E4.justification: Neither contains empirical ablations, robustness tests, sensitivity studies or error analyses. V2's recommendation to study width and precision as separate ablation axes is prospective.

E5.justification: Neither reports repeated runs, seeds, confidence intervals or statistical tests. The retained error-probability threshold of 1/3 is a theoretical guarantee.

E6.justification: No empirical numerical or qualitative results are added, removed or revised. V2's new figures are explanatory schematics; changes to formal resource bounds are assessed under T1.

M1.justification: Corollary 2 changes the streaming algorithm from updating its lookup pointer immediately within a table to freezing the incoming pointer and committing the next pointer after the table ends. This is a localized algorithmic correction; the generalized SSM recurrence and two-step CoT simulator remain unchanged.

P1.justification: V2 moves lengthy proofs from Sections 4-7 into Appendices A-D and introduces main-text proof sketches and roadmaps. It also rewrites the abstract, expands the discussion and adopts the more explicit post-input/input-interleaved terminology. This substantially reorganizes the exposition.

P2.justification: V1 has no figures or tables. V2 introduces three explanatory diagrams covering forward communication, the gate-and-accumulate construction and CoT token timing, plus a boxed practitioner summary. These substantially expand the visual presentation of the central arguments.

R1.justification: The reference list is unchanged. Section 2 nevertheless refines the relationship to existing architectures: v1 describes an abstraction covering all known SSM architectures, whereas v2 presents a common upper-level lower-bound model that abstracts away architecture-specific parameterizations and constraints.

T1.justification: Theorem 4(A) replaces O(dpL + log n) memory with O(dpL + log T_n), where the newly defined T_n includes thought tokens and need not be polynomial in n. This correction propagates through Proposition 2, Corollary 4 and Appendices C-D. Corollary 2 repairs its correctness argument by freezing each table's lookup pointer. Definition 2 and Theorem 1 also make the canonical encoding explicit. These substantively revise central resource guarantees and proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 repairs important weaknesses in the online-CoT analysis: Theorem 4 counts all processed steps in its memory bound, and Corollary 2 prevents unintended repeated lookups within one function table. Its narrower claims and explicit implementation limitations also reduce overgeneralization. Together with clearer diagrams and proof sketches while retaining detailed proofs, these changes substantially improve correctness and interpretability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same theoretical study and are readable throughout. V2's Appendices A-D largely relocate proofs from v1's main text, allowing comparison of the complete arguments.

after.justification: V2 and Appendices A-D remain theoretical. Its figures illustrate constructions, and Section 8 suggests future experiments without reporting original empirical outcomes.

before.justification: V1 reports mathematical bounds, constructive simulations and algebraic proofs. Empirical findings are attributed to prior work; no original experimental or data-analysis outcomes are reported.

It participates in standard multi-vessel accuracy, qualitative, robustness, distribution and efficiency comparisons. This substantially strengthens comparison coverage beyond the retained generic neural operators and Poiseuille baseline, although it is absent from the patient-disjoint and FFR comparisons.

E3.justification: The reported multi-vessel training budget changes from 5,000 to 3,000 epochs, and warmup from 1,000 to 500 epochs. v2 adds a patient-disjoint 3,989/415/396 split with training-only normalization and inference-time perturbation protocols. Appendix A.1 substantively revises the reported meshing, outlet boundary conditions and convergence specification. These documentation changes do not establish that the CFD datasets were regenerated.

E4.justification: v2 adds anatomy-generalization testing, stratification by flow and vascular complexity, input-noise/dropout sensitivity, geometry-correlated failure analysis and failure visualizations, plus encoder/decoder cost decomposition. The original design-choice ablation, GNOT-input comparison, circumferential WSS analysis and Bland-Altman analysis are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v1 explicitly reports single runs with seed 1234 and defers multi-seed evaluation. v2 reports means and standard deviations over seeds 42, 1234 and 7890 for principal accuracy, training, validation and FFR results. Noise curves additionally average three perturbation trials. The GNOT-input ablation remains explicitly single-seed.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 replace the proposed model's single-run test means of 0.107 and 0.309 with 0.116±0.012 and 0.304±0.010 for the corresponding best configurations. Changed training and aggregation prevent interpreting these as same-setting gains or losses. New results include patient-disjoint error 0.558±0.006 and CenterlinePointNet++ mean error 0.393; its WSS error, 0.315, beats the proposed model's 0.355. FFR, training, validation and supplementary findings also change or expand.

M1.justification: The proposed model retains its Fourier-embedded centerline transformer, FiLM flow conditioning, separate anisotropic Gaussian kernels for pressure and WSS, training loss and inference procedure. Sections 3 and A.4 specify the same proposed architecture.

P1.justification: The six-section organization and most methodological prose remain. Targeted edits revise the abstract, introduction, limitations and CFD description; appendix headings and cross-references are reorganized, and publication/header text is added. Much of the expansion documents new scientific content rather than wholesale narrative rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds stratification, noise-robustness and failure-case figures, plus patient-disjoint and cost-decomposition tables. Validation columns move from the main accuracy tables into separate appendix tables. The architecture diagram, Bland-Altman plots and error-distribution plots are redrawn, and several comparisons gain CenterlinePointNet++ columns or legend entries.

R1.justification: v2 adds Corral-Acero et al. (2020), Lo et al. (2019), Nannini et al. (2024) and Suk et al. (2021) for application motivation and limitations. The existing CenterlinePointNet++ citation is repositioned as an adapted empirical comparator. The principal literature organization and claimed methodological gap remain.

T1.justification: Equations 1–10 retain the same embeddings, kernel definitions, reconstruction, loss, FFR definition and Poiseuille relation. Neither version introduces theoretical guarantees or proofs, and v2 adds no substantive formal derivation.

improvement.justification: Three-seed reporting addresses v1's acknowledged single-run limitation, while the patient-disjoint evaluation directly examines previously unchecked anatomy overlap. The domain-specific comparator, robustness tests, failure analyses and expanded implementation details substantially strengthen reliability and transparency. Important qualifications remain: CenterlinePointNet++ is absent from the patient-disjoint test, and Appendix A.12's blanket WSS-superiority interpretation conflicts with Figure 11. These shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial improvements in evaluation quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same centerline-transformer and anisotropic-RBF study. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, figures and tables, are readable and support reliable matching despite expansion and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 reports original prediction experiments, updated multi-seed results, and additional patient-disjoint, robustness and failure analyses in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original CFD-based prediction experiments on single- and multi-vessel datasets, including accuracy, FFR, ablation and computational-efficiency results.

results.title: From Centerlines to Hemodynamics: Anisotropic RBF Decoders for Coronary Arteries

C1.justification: The central phantom-specialization claim and four main findings remain. The abstract and conclusion add a bounded SVA replication claim and restrict the ≥99% LSC recovery claim to models above 70M. V2 also explicitly excludes claims about specialization at token-position or within-component feature levels.

C2.justification: V2 substantially qualifies interpretation: cross-draw variability no longer establishes that individual edges are causally irrelevant, zero-ablation collapse limits sensitivity, and SVA does not reproduce every LSC pattern. It adds limitations concerning position aggregation, residual token confounds, few-shot applicability, and the synthetic control's scope. The revised logit-lens findings also replace the slower, weaker-core interpretation with nearly matching computation and timing.

D1.justification: V2 supplies extensive SVA construction and filtering details, positive-control architecture and training hyperparameters, qualification thresholds, corruption procedures, and few-shot construction and timing information. It clarifies effective ACDC batch consumption, supplies the missing 1.4B batch size, documents mask nondeterminism, and explains head-role classification thresholds. The code/data access link is retained.

E1.justification: V2 adds subject–verb agreement, a synthetic cue-controlled retrieval versus memorization task, evaluation of the previously excluded very_low LSC population, and few-shot copying scenarios. The reverse-copy and zero-distractor variants already existed in v1 and are retained.

E2.justification: The ACDC, EAP, EAP-IG, and random-edge comparisons are retained. Additional comparisons include LSC circuits evaluated against SVA circuits on their respective tasks (Appendix J) and a length- and token-matched scrambled-prefix comparator in the new few-shot study (Appendix L).

E3.justification: New protocols include SVA two-choice scoring and subject-number corruption, independent qualification of trained positive-control models, position-resolved attribution, and paired few-shot conditions. Appendix C.4 also revises the reported LSC discovery sample counts: v1 states 256 examples per circuit, whereas v2 specifies effective single-batch counts of 256, 256, 128, 96, and 64 across model sizes. This does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds a successful pipeline positive control, independent edge-marginality analysis, position-resolved attribution checks, head-role threshold sensitivity and canonical-induction checks, and explicit mean-ablation analysis. SVA sensitivity checks examine mislabeled noun pairs and differences between ablation protocols. These address substantial questions absent from v1.

E5.justification: V2 adds draw-blocked permutation tests for SVA and positional analyses, paired McNemar tests and blocked permutations for few-shot effects, and variability across qualifying control models. The primary LSC three-draw design remains. Its transfer-test description changes from permutation testing to one-sided paired Wilcoxon testing, while the redrawn boost heatmap drops per-cell standard deviations.

E6.justification: New results include matched SVA transfer efficiencies of 0.940–0.992 (Table 14) and positive-control cross-route transfer efficiency of −0.056 ± 0.047 (Table 13). Retained analyses also change: universal-core convergence shifts move from 0.50–3.34 layers in v1 Table 59 to −0.40–0.00 in v2 Table 60. Some revised values conflict internally: v2 Tables 4 and 5 report different resample-ablation effect sizes.

M1.justification: The primary discovery procedure retains ACDC, KL-based pruning, factorized tree patching, and per-model threshold selection. The new tasks, control models, and attribution checks extend the experiments without replacing or modifying the proposed discovery pipeline.

P1.justification: Extensive paragraph and sentence rewriting spans the abstract, introduction, experimental explanations, interpretations, and appendices. V2 separates the canonical-copy mechanism discussion into its own subsection, reorganizes the positive-control material, and moves the statistical-testing summary from Appendix D to Appendix G. These changes exceed the insertion of new scientific content.

P2.justification: V2 adds the two-route task diagram and several experimental tables, consolidates duplicate displays, and moves key appendix comparisons into the main text. It redraws the transfer-boost heatmaps with a shared color scale, replaces full interchange matrices with an aggregated display, and revises logit-lens plots and captions.

R1.justification: V2 adds Mueller (2024) and connects pruning ambiguity to overdetermination in counterfactual analysis. Fisher's 1966 reference is removed alongside the changed transfer-test description. The principal related-work coverage and positioning remain substantially intact.

T1.justification: Appendix E.6 introduces the normalized edge-marginality definition ρ = r/k and its interpretation relative to the matched-size selection boundary. The principal circuit and transfer equations remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: V1 explicitly identifies the missing successful pipeline positive control as its most important limitation. V2 directly addresses this with six independently qualified models and adds a carefully bounded SVA replication, substantially strengthening validation beyond LSC. Positional checks, reproducibility corrections, and more cautious causal interpretations further improve credibility. The control remains limited to constructed models, and reporting inconsistencies persist, notably the conflicting effect sizes in Tables 4 and 5, but these do not outweigh the substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison across substantial revision and relocation.

after.justification: V2 retains original LSC results and adds SVA experiments, a learned two-route positive control, very-low-frequency evaluation, and few-shot accuracy studies.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments on 75 LSC circuits across five Pythia models, including transfer, ablation, representational, and causal-intervention results.
